en: Having paid homage to Nārāyaṇa and to Nara, the best of men. Chapter 1, transliterated by Peter Schreiner (ca. 1991), revised October 1999. Star-passages 1–22 added March 2002. :h] Having paid homage to Nārāyaṇa and to Nara, the best of men;
And likewise to the goddess Sarasvatī; thereafter, one should utter the word "Victory."
Victorious is Vyāsa, the son of Parāśara and the delighter of Satyavatī’s heart,
from whose lotus-like mouth the world drinks the nectar of speech;
whom they call the Great Sage endowed with inexhaustible power, the sixth [in line] beginning with the Grandfather (Brahmā).
The only son born from the shoulder of Nārāyaṇa, Dvaipāyana, the great treasury of the Vedas;
the primordial Person, the Sovereign, invoked by many and praised by many;
the Truth, the single-syllabled Brahman, both manifest and unmanifest, eternal.
He who is both non-existent and existent, and that which transcends both existence and non-existence; the creator of the high and the low, the ancient, supreme, and imperishable;
the auspicious one among the auspicious, Viṣṇu, the most excellent, the sinless, and the pure.
Having paid homage to Hari, Hṛṣīkeśa, the teacher of all that moves and is stationary.
In the Naimiṣa forest, the great sage Śaunaka, the virtuous head of the hermitage and master of all scriptures, questioned Sauti—
the son born to him through his own yogic power from the midst of the sacrificial fire-enclosure— who was supremely learned and most noble.
Salutations to that great seer Satyavatī who [obtained him] from Parāśara and who dispels the darkness of ignorance;
he who gives a hundred cows with horns made of gold to a brahmin learned in the Vedas and highly renowned,
and he who likewise listens to the meritorious story of the Bhārata— the fruit for both of them is exactly equal.
Whatever merit belongs here to a hundred horse-sacrifices and to four thousand sacrifices of Indra,
that merit becomes infinite from the gift of the *Harivaṃśa*, as proclaimed by the great seer Vyāsa;
and whatever fruit is seen from the Vājapeya and Rājasūya sacrifices, and another from the elephant-chariot sacrifice [is likewise attained].
Therefore, the word of Vyāsa is authoritative, as is that which was sung by the great seer Vālmīki.
That which has issued from the lips of Dvaipāyana is immeasurable, meritorious, purifying, a destroyer of sin, and auspicious.
For one who fully masters the Bhārata while it is being recited, what need is there for ablutions in the waters of Puṣkara?
The great ascetic who causes the *Harivaṃśa* to be written according to the prescribed rite immediately goes to the lotus feet of Hari, just as a greedy bee goes to a lotus;
he whom those who know the Vedānta call Brahman, and others call the Supreme Pradhāna or Puruṣa.

He who listens with faith to the *Harivaṃśa*— the cause of universal movement, the Lord, the destroyer of obstacles; Viṣṇu, the savior from saṃsāra, the unsurpassed object of meditation for yogis, and the increaser of one’s lineage— to him, the destroyer of impediments, be homage.
For every single syllable, that person shall obtain the fruit born of the gift of a Kapila cow.

The man who gives a manuscript of the *Harivaṃśa* to a learned Brāhmaṇa along with a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) shall partake in the fruit of an Aśvamedha sacrifice; this has been spoken as the very truth by the Great Sage.

May Hari, the Lord of the three worlds, whose stride possesses the power of six parts, protect you—he whose arm and hand gracefully hold a discus shining with the luster of lightning; in whose palm a conch shell shines with the radiance of the full moon; and who wears a garland of campaka, tilaka, aśoka, and blue lotus flowers;

he who, being devoid of qualities, is untouched by the three defects known as afflictions which are placed within the mind by ignorance and the rest, nor by impurities, karma, or their fruits, for he is the Supreme Teacher.

May that Vāsudeva—who is endowed with omniscience and other attributes, who is the cause for the attainment of unsurpassed bliss by ascetics, and who is beginningless—pacify the evil accumulated by you throughout all births. Victory to You, O Lotus-eyed One! Salutations to You, O Creator of the Universe!
Salutations be to You, O Hṛṣīkeśa, the Primordial Being of Great Persons!
For the pacification of all obstacles, one should meditate upon Viṣṇu, who wears white garments, is moon-colored, four-armed, and has a serene countenance; likewise,
Vāgīśā and the others, being well-disposed, [are present] at the commencement of all undertakings.
I bow to that elephant-faced one, by saluting whom one’s duties are fulfilled;
may the Man-Lion, whose chest is smeared with the sandalwood paste of Lakṣmī’s breasts,
swiftly bestow upon us intense bliss.

We purify our speech— which has become dusty from wandering through the wilderness of false rumors— by means of the Ganges that is the discourse on the deeds of Śauri, for that speech is eager for the tumultuous roar of the waves of the Yamunā's waters.
I bow to the Joy of the Yadus, who is dark as a blue lotus, who is the sprout of bliss for Lakṣmī, and who is a celestial wish-fulfilling tree for those who seek his refuge;
and to Vyāsa, the stainless son of Śakti and grandson of Vasiṣṭha.
I bow to the son of Parāśara, the father of Śuka, a treasure-house of austerity.
Salutations to Vyāsa, who is the form of Viṣṇu; salutations to Viṣṇu in the form of Vyāsa. Salutations again and again to the son of Vasiṣṭha, the treasury of Brahman.
Śaunaka said: O Sauti, you have related this very great narrative concerning all the descendants of Bharata as well as the kings.
Of the gods and the dānavas, of the gandharvas, uragas, and rākṣasas,
as well as of the daityas, siddhas, and likewise of the guhyakas.
Most wonderful deeds, heroic exploits, resolutions regarding dharma, diverse narrative connections, and a supreme, unsurpassed birth.
This ancient merit has been recounted by you in gentle words;
it delights me, being as pleasing to the mind and ear as nectar.
In that regard, you have indeed described the birth of the Kurus to Lomaharṣaṇa; however, you have not yet told me the account of the Vṛṣṇis and Andhakas—please relate that to me.
Sūta said:
Being questioned by Janamejaya, the disciple of the wise Vyāsa,
who knew the dharma, related their lineage in great detail.
I shall relate that lineage of the Vṛṣṇis to you from the very beginning.
Having heard this history of the Bharatas in its entirety,
the highly wise Janamejaya, the descendant of Bharata, spoke to Vaiśampāyana.
O Brahmin, you have narrated in detail the Mahābhārata, an account of many meanings and great extent, which has been heard by me at length.
In that regard, many heroes, bulls among men,
great chariot-warriors of the Vṛṣṇis and Andhakas, have been celebrated by their names and their deeds.
O best of the twice-born, O Lord, you have described their pure deeds both briefly and in detail in various places.
And I am not yet satiated by this narration of the ancient past;
for I consider the Vṛṣṇis and the Pāṇḍavas to constitute but a single mass.
And you, O one rich in asceticism, are skilled in genealogies and have seen them with your own eyes; tell us the lineage of those ancestors in detail.

O Lord of the Earth, I wish to know the various lineages of each individual; for you have previously related many wonderful stories concerning their diverse ancient origins, beginning from the Creator himself.
"O best of the twice-born, tell all of this in its entirety,
by the hearing of which the childlessness of men shall indeed perish.
Thus urged, O great sage, the king who was the disciple of Vyāsa [spoke].
Sūta said:
Having been duly honored and questioned, that great-souled one of mighty asceticism related that story in detail and in proper sequence.
Vaiśampāyana said:
Listen, O King, to this divine, meritorious, and sin-destroying tale,
being narrated by me— wondrous, rich in meaning, and consistent with the sacred scriptures.
O dear one, whoever should uphold this or listen to it repeatedly;
and the brahmin who should uphold it or cause it to be heard by the high-souled ones—
having ensured the preservation of his own lineage, he is glorified in the heavenly world.
That unmanifest cause is eternal, consisting of both the existent and the non-existent;
from that Pradhāna and Puruṣa, the Lord fashioned the universe.
Know him indeed, O great king, to be Brahmā of immeasurable splendor,
the creator of all beings, who is solely devoted to Nārāyaṇa.
From that Great Principle (mahat) arises the ego-sense (ahaṃkāra), and from it the elements were born; from the elements come the various manifestations of beings—such is the eternal creation.
Listen as I proclaim in detail, according to my wisdom and as I have heard it, this account that increases the fame of the ancients.
The recitation of the deeds of all those of virtuous karma, whose fame is enduring, brings merit, renown, the destruction of enemies, attainment of heaven, and the increase of longevity.
Therefore, at dawn, being alert, let me offer this entire [oblation] to you, who are alert and pure,
to that Hiraṇyagarbha, the Puruṣa, and the Lord;
to the Unborn One, the very first and most excellent Prajāpati.
Having first prostrated before that self-existent Brahmā, the Lord of the worlds, the most venerable and of immeasurable splendor,
I shall describe the unsurpassed creation of beings, beginning from the lineage of Vṛṣṇi.
The Lord Viṣṇu, the self-existent, desiring to create various beings, first created the waters alone; into them he cast his seed.
"The waters were called 'nārāḥ' by name in the beginning," so says the Śruti;
"they were his first abode (ayana), therefore he is remembered as Nārāyaṇa."
That egg, golden-hued, rested upon the waters;
there Brahmā himself was born, whom we have heard is called the Self-Existent (Svayaṃbhū).
The blessed Hiraṇyagarbha, having dwelt within that egg for a full year, divided it into two parts: heaven and earth.
The Lord made the intermediate space between those two shells;
he placed the earth floating upon the waters and established the ten directions.
Thereupon, desiring to bring about creation, Prajāpati emitted Time, Mind, Speech, Desire, Anger, and likewise Pleasure— emitting that very form of creation which he wished to produce.
The one of great splendor created seven mind-born sons: Marīci, Atri, Aṅgiras, Pulastya, Pulaha, Kratu, and Vasiṣṭha.
"These are determined in the Purāṇa to be the seven Brahmās,
who are born from Brahmā and whose very essence is Nārāyaṇa."
Then Brahmā again created Rudra, who was born from his own wrath,
as well as the seer Sanatkumāra, the first-born even of the former ones.
But these seven, O Bhārata, are born as progeny along with Rudra;
Skanda and Sanatkumāra remain having withdrawn their splendor.
Among them were seven great lineages, divine and accompanied by hosts of gods;
they were active, possessed of progeny, and adorned by great seers.
Lightning, thunderclouds, red clouds, and Indra’s bow;
Sanaka, Sanandana, and Sanātana— these seven are declared to be the sages (ṛṣis) who are firm in their vows and knowers of the truth of yoga.
In the beginning, he created aquatic creatures, and he also created Parjanya.
He fashioned the Ṛg-verses, Yajus-formulas, and Sāman-chants for the perfection of sacrifice;
the Lord generated the gods from his mouth and the ancestors from his chest;
he generated humans from his private parts and the asuras from his hips.
With those [oblations], they sacrificed to the gods for the sake of their goals; thus indeed have we heard.
From his limbs were born various beings, high and low;
having pierced the heart, the venerable Bhṛgu emerged as the determined Brahmā.
Having pierced through the right breast with the weapon born of Brahmā,
the Blessed One, the Dharma who brings happiness to all the world, took his stand.
He had three excellent sons, enchanting to all beings— Kāma, Śama, and Harṣa— who supported the worlds through their splendor.
Rati was the wife of Kāma, Prīti the wife of Śama,
and Nandā the wife of Harṣa; upon these three worlds were established as the Prajāpati Āpava created the emanation of progeny.

When the creatures being created did not increase at all, he then divided his own body into two parts; with one half he became a man, and with the other half a woman. In her, he procreated various kinds of offspring.
He stands pervading both heaven and earth with his majesty.
Viṣṇu created Virāj, and that Virāj created Puruṣa;
know that Puruṣa to be Manu, and that is indeed remembered as the Manvantara. This second interval of Manu is called the Āpava Manvantara.
That Lord Puruṣa Vairāja brought forth the creation of beings;
know that he, the powerful Lord, created Manu Prajāpati. That creation of Nārāyaṇa consisted of those beings who were not born from a womb.

A man who knows this primordial creation shall become long-lived, renowned, fortunate, and possessed of offspring; his lineage shall endure, and after death he is glorified in heaven. Having understood this first creation, he shall attain whatever destination he desires.
Chapter 2, transliterated by Peter Schreiner; version of February 13, 2002. Not yet proofread.
Vaiśampāyana said: After the creatures had been created in this manner, Āpava Prajāpati—
That man indeed obtained Śatarūpā as his wife, who was not born from a womb.
But by the greatness of Āpava, as he stood pervading the heavens,
O Great King, Śatarūpā was born through dharma alone.
Having performed most difficult austerities for ten thousand years,
she obtained as her husband a man of radiant ascetic power.
O dear one, he is indeed called Svāyambhuva Manu, the Puruṣa;
his period of authority here is said to be seventy-one yugas, known as a manvantara.
From the Puruṣa Vairāja, Śatarūpā gave birth to Vīra;
from Vīra, Kāmyā gave birth to Priyavrata and Uttānapāda.
O mighty-armed one, Kāmyā was the daughter of the patriarch Kardama; she was endowed with great ascetic power, was exalted, and was a sustainer of the world.
The sons of Kāmyā were four: Samrāṭ, Kukṣi, Virāṭ, and Prabhu.
Having approached Priyavrata as her husband, she gave birth to sons;
the patriarch Atri took Uttānapāda as his son,
and from Uttānapāda, Sūnṛtā bore four sons.
Dharma’s daughter, renowned by the name Sūnṛtā, was fair-hipped;
born from Dharma’s speech, she was the auspicious mother of Dhruva.
The Lord of Creatures, Uttānapāda, begot Dhruva, Kīrtimant, Ayasmant, and Ayaḥpati upon Sūnṛtā.
For three thousand divine years, O Bhārata,
Dhruva practiced austerities, O great king, seeking very great glory.
The Lord Prajāpati Brahmā, being pleased, granted him a station equal to his own,
and the Lord of Creatures placed him immovably in front of the Seven Sages.
Having observed his pride, his supernatural power, and his greatness,
Uśanas, the preceptor of the gods and asuras, even sang this verse:
Oh, the power of his asceticism! Oh, his sacred learning! Oh, his vow!
For having placed him at their head today, the Seven Sages stand firm.
From Śliṣṭa and Mānyā was born Śambhu;
from Śliṣṭa, Succhāyā bore five stainless sons:
Prācīnagarbha, Vṛkati, Vṛkala, and Vṛkatejas.
O King, his wife Sūnṛtā gave birth to a son named Udāradhī, who had been Indra in a previous birth. This was the offspring of Prācīnagarbha.
The noble-minded Bhadrā gave birth to a son, Divaṃjaya.
From that Divaṃjaya, Varāṅgī bore Ripuṃjaya—
the conqueror of enemies— who was a wise man, as well as Vṛkala, who possessed the splendor of a wolf.
Bṛhatī bore to Ripu a son of all-pervading splendor, Cākṣuṣa;
and Cākṣuṣa begot Manu upon Puṣkariṇī, the daughter of Viraṇa.
O best of the Bharatas, ten sons of great prowess were born to Manu, the offspring of the high-souled Prajāpati Vīraṇa, in Naḍvalā, the daughter of the Prajāpati Vairāja.
Ūru, Pūru, Śatadyumna, Tapasvin, Satyavit, Kavi,
Agniṣṭut, Atirātra, Sudyumna,
and Abhimanyu as the tenth— these were the ten of great power born of Naḍvalā.
From her thigh, the daughter of Agni gave birth to six sons of great splendor:
Aṅga, Sumanas, Svāti, Kratu, Āṅgirasa, and Śiva.
From his body, Sunīthā gave birth to a single son, Vena;
due to Vena's misconduct, a very great wrath arose.
Then, for the sake of progeny, the sages churned the right hand of Vena;
when his hand was churned, a great sage was born.
Seeing him, the sages spoke with joy: "This one of great splendor will indeed make the subjects happy and shall attain great renown."
Born equipped with bow and armor, as if burning everything with his splendor,
wearing leather arm-guards and finger-protectors,
he was filled with zeal for the protection of his subjects.
Then Pṛthu, the son of Vena and the first of the Kṣatriyas, protected this earth.
He was the first of those kings consecrated by the Rājasūya sacrifice;
and from him were born the two skillful ones, Sūta and Māgadha.
Therefore, O Great King, descendant of Bharata, this cow was milked by the gods together with the hosts of ṛṣis, who desired a means of subsistence for all creatures.
By means of serpents, Puṇyajanas, as well as by plants and mountains;
And as the earth was milked into those various vessels, she yielded milk according to each one's desire; by that [milk], they sustained their lives.
Two sons of Pṛthu, both knowers of dharma, were born as Antardhi and Pālin;
from Antardhāna, Śikhaṇḍinī gave birth to Havirdhāna.
From the Havirdhāna, Dhiṣaṇā, the daughter of Agni, gave birth to six sons:
Prācīnabarhis, Śukra, Gaya, Kṛṣṇa, Vraja, and Ajina.
O great king, the venerable Prajāpati Prācīnabarhis was great; by him, the offspring were nourished from the Havirdhāna.
O Janamejaya, the *kuśa* grasses on his earth had their tips pointing eastward;
thus they became known as the Prācīnabarhis, wandering upon the surface of the earth.
The lord,
the ruler of the earth, having performed great austerities, took Savarṇā as his wife after reaching the completion of those penances and married her, the daughter of the ocean.
Sāmudrī bore ten sons to Prācīnabarhis of her own caste;
she gave birth to those who were indeed honored by all the worlds. All of them were named Pracetas and were masters of the science of archery.
Practicing their religious duties without deviation, they performed great asceticism for ten thousand years, dwelling within the waters of the ocean.
While the Pracetasas were performing austerities upon the earth, the trees overran it as it remained unprotected; consequently, there occurred a destruction of living beings.
During the interval of Manu Cākṣuṣa, all creatures were withdrawn;
the wind was unable to blow, the sky became covered with trees,
and for ten thousand years the creatures were unable to move.
Having heard that, all the Pracetasas, endowed with ascetic power,
praised the son of Prācīnabarhis; then, their anger aroused, they released wind and fire from their mouths along with all the mountains.
Then Vāyu uprooted those trees and dried them up;
Agni, the terrible one, consumed them with fire, and thus occurred the destruction of the trees.
Then, perceiving that the trees were being exhausted and seeing only a few branches remaining,
the powerful King Soma approached them and spoke to them.
"Restrain your anger, O kings, all you descendants of Prācīnabarhis!
The earth has been stripped of its trees; let fire and wind be appeased."
And this maiden of excellent complexion is like a jewel among trees;
O father, knowing her future destiny, she was indeed held by me in my womb.
This woman, created as the one named Māriṣā among trees,
shall be your wife— highly fortunate and the increaser of the Lunar dynasty.
Or [the reading] of the Pracetasaḥ:
"By half of your splendor and by half of my own splendor,
a wise Prajāpati named Dakṣa shall be born from her."
He, being like fire himself, will further cause these creatures— who have been mostly consumed by the fire consisting of your own splendor— to flourish once more.
Then, at the word of Soma, those Pracetasas,
having withdrawn their anger from the trees, accepted Māriṣā as their wife in accordance with dharma.
Then, O Bhārata, those ten Pracetas mentally conceived an embryo in Māriṣā; and from those ten Pracetas, through a portion of Soma, the Prajāpati Dakṣa of great splendor was born of Māriṣā.
He begot sons who increased the Lunar dynasty,
as well as non-moving and moving beings— both bipeds and quadrupeds.
Having first created by means of his mind, the skillful and highly resplendent Prajāpati subsequently created women for the sake of the increase of progeny;
he gave ten to Dharma and thirteen to Kaśyapa.
The Lord gave the remaining ones, known as the constellations, to Soma, the King.
From them were born the gods, birds, cattle, nāgas, sons of Diti and the dānavas, gandharvas, apsarases, and other species as well.
From that time forward, O Indra among kings, progeny were born from sexual union;
for those who came before, it is said that creation occurred through mere intention, sight, or touch.
Janamejaya said:
"The origin of the gods, the Dānavas, the Gandharvas, the Uragas, and the Rakṣasas, as well as that of the high-souled Dakṣa, has been told previously."
O sinless one, you have stated that Dakṣa was born from the thumb of Brahmā;
likewise, his wife was born from his left thumb.
How did that great ascetic again obtain the state of being a son of the Pracetas?
O Brahmin, you ought to explain this doubt of mine here:
how did he who was the grandson of Soma come to become my father-in-law?
Vaiśampāyana said:
O Bhārata, origination and cessation are eternal among all beings;
the seers and those people who possess true knowledge are not deluded in this regard.
In age after age, O King, all these beings beginning with Dakṣa come into existence, and again they are dissolved; the wise man is not deluded by this.
O lord of men, neither seniority nor juniority existed among them from the beginning;
austerity alone was weightier, and spiritual power was the sole cause [of distinction].
For he who knows this creation of Dakṣa, together with all that is moving and unmoving,
shall be blessed with offspring, shall transcend his lifespan, and shall be glorified in the heavenly world.
He attains divine enjoyments, surrounded by women such as Rambhā and others.
Janamejaya said: *Chapter 3, transliterated by Peter Schreiner; version of March 2002. Not yet proof-read.* [h] Janamejaya said:
O Vaiśampāyana, recount in full detail the origins of the gods, the Dānavas, the Gandharvas, the Uragas, and the Rākṣasas.
Vaiśampāyana said:
"O lord of the earth, listen now to how Dakṣa, having been previously commanded by the Self-born One to 'create progeny,' brought forth all beings."
But with his mind alone, the Lord first created all beings:
the seers, the gods, along with the gandharvas, as well as the asuras and the rākṣasas.
When his offspring— including yakṣas, bhūtas, piśācas, birds, domestic animals, and wild beasts—
did not increase despite his efforts,
they were indeed cursed by the wise Lord Mahādeva.
Then, having reflected further for the sake of progeny, the Lord of Creatures (Prajāpati) [acted].
Desiring to create various offspring through the act of sexual union,
he took as his wife Asiknī, the daughter of the patriarch Vīraṇa,
who was endowed with great asceticism and possessed the power to sustain the world.
Then the energetic Prajāpati Dakṣa himself begot five thousand sons upon Vairiṇī and Asiknī.
Seeing those illustrious ones desiring to increase their progeny,
the celestial sage Nārada, who delights in pleasant conversation,
spoke these words to them for their own destruction and likewise for his own curse.
The sage Kaśyapa, the supreme lord, begot that most excellent son upon the daughter of Dakṣa out of fear of Dakṣa’s curse.
For previously that Nārada, the best of divine seers, had been born from Parameṣṭhin; now, like a father, he brought forth once more that bull among sages upon Asiknī, the daughter of Viraṇa.
By him, indeed, Dakṣa’s sons known as the Haryaśvas were all destroyed after being churned out; this was by destiny, without a doubt.
Then Dakṣa, of immeasurable prowess, having raised [his weapon] for the sake of destruction,
was entreated by the Supreme Lord (Brahmā), who placed the Brahman-sages before him.
Then Dakṣa indeed made an agreement with Parameṣṭhin:
"Nārada shall be my son through [this] daughter of yours."
Then Dakṣa gave his beloved daughter to Parameṣṭhin;
from her, the sage Nārada was born once more due to the fear of the curse.
Janamejaya said:
O best of the twice-born, how were the sons of Prajāpati destroyed by the great seer Nārada? I wish to hear this according to the truth.
Vaiśampāyana said: The sons of Dakṣa, the Haryaśvas, being of great prowess and desiring to increase their progeny, assembled together; Nārada spoke to them.
Alas, you are indeed foolish, you who do not truly know this earth!

"O sons of Pracetas, desiring indeed to create living beings,
how will you create progeny within, above, and below?"
Having encountered the fasting of Vāyu, they indeed met with defeat;
but having heard those words, they departed in all directions and have not returned even to this day, like rivers into the oceans.
Then, when the Haryaśvas had perished, the lord Dakṣa,
the son of Pracetas, again begot a thousand sons upon Vairiṇī.
O dear one, those Śabalāśvas, desiring to increase their progeny at that time,
were urged by Nārada with the very words previously mentioned.
They all said to one another, "The great seer has spoken correctly;
the path of our brothers must indeed be followed, there is no doubt about this. Having ascertained the dimensions of the earth, we shall happily create progeny."
With one-pointed minds and tranquil hearts, they have proceeded in due order along that very path toward every direction;
even today they do not return, like rivers flowing into the oceans.
When the Śabalāśvas had perished, O King, the enraged Dakṣa spoke these words to Nārada: "Go to your destruction! You shall dwell within a womb!
From that time forward, O King, the brother indeed set out in search of his brother.
O Lord, it perishes as soon as it has set out; therefore, one who possesses discernment should not perform such an act.
Having realized that those sons were lost, the lord Prajāpati Dakṣa,
out of fear of them, cursed Nārada and created only daughters;
it is heard that the lord Dakṣa created sixty daughters by Vairiṇī.
Then the lord Kaśyapa accepted them as wives,
O Kauravya, as did Soma, Dharma, and other great ṛṣis. He gave ten to Dharma and thirteen to Kaśyapa.
Twenty-seven [oblations] for Soma, and four for Ariṣṭanemi.
Two were born to Bahuputra, two likewise to Aṅgiras, and two to the learned Bhṛśāśva; hear their names from me.
Arundhatī, Vasu, Jāmī, Lambā, Bhānu, Marutvatī,
Saṃkalpā, Muhūrtā, Sādhyā, and Viśvā, O Bhārata—
these ten are the wives of Dharma; hear from me their offspring.
From Viśvā were born the Viśvedevas; Sādhyā gave birth to the Sādhyas; from Marutvatī came the Marutvats; and the Vasus are recorded as being born from Vasu.
The Bhānus, O dear one, were born of Bhānu as the Muhūrtas;
and from Lambā were born Ghoṣa and Nāgavīthī as her twin daughters.
The entire realm of the earth was born from Arundhatī;
and from Saṃkalpā was born Saṃkalpa, whose very self is the universe.

From Nāgavīthī and Jāminī, Vṛṣalambā gave birth to those who,
O King, were given as wives to Soma by Dakṣa, the son of Pracetas;
they are all known by the names of the lunar mansions and are celebrated in the science of astrology.
As for those numerous hosts of gods and deities who have light as their precursor—
the eight who are known as the Vasus— I shall describe them in detail.
Āpa, Dhruva, Soma, Dhara, Anila, Anala,
Pratyūṣa, and Prabhasa are known by name as the Vasus.
Āpasya’s sons were Vaitaṇḍya, Śrama, Śānta, and the sage Muni;
Dhruva’s son was the blessed Kāla, the destroyer of the worlds.
From Soma was born the illustrious Varcas, who is endowed with splendor;
likewise from Dhara came Draviṇa and Hutahavyavaha.
From Manoharā were born Śiśira, Prāṇa, and Ramaṇa.
Anila’s wife was Śivā, whose sons were Purojava and Avijñātagati;
these two were the sons of Anila.
The son of Agni was Kumāra, endowed with splendor, who was born in a clump of reeds (śarastamba).
His younger brothers were Śākha, Viśākha, and Naigameṣa.
Because he was the offspring of the Kṛttikās, he is known as Kārttikeya.
Skanda and Sanatkumāra were created from the energy of his foot;
they know the son of Pratyūṣa to be the Ṛṣi named Devala. Devala also had two sons who were patient and wise.
The sister of Bṛhaspati was an excellent woman who observed celibacy;
perfected in yoga, she wandered through the entire world unattached.
She was the wife of Prabhāsa, the eighth of the Vasus;
from her was born the illustrious Viśvakarman, the lord of progeny.
He is the creator of thousands of crafts, the carpenter of the thirty gods,
the maker of all ornaments, and the best among those skilled in the arts.
He who indeed fashioned all the celestial mansions of the gods,
and upon whose craftsmanship even human beings subsist— that high-souled one.

Surabhi, having been purified by her ascetic penance through the grace of Mahādeva, brought forth from Kaśyapa the eleven Rudras. (Note: This passage is inserted in various manuscripts after verse 41 or 42.)
Ajaikapād, Ahirbudhnya, Tvaṣṭṛ, and the heroic Rudra;
and the glorious son of Tvaṣṭṛ, Viśvarūpa, of great renown.
Hara, Bahurūpa, Tryambaka, Aparājita,
Vṛṣākapi, Śambhu, Kapardin, and likewise Raivata.
O lord of the people, Mṛgavyādha, Sarpa, and Kapālī—
these eleven are declared to be the Rudras, the lords of the three worlds.
Thus, the hundred Rudras of immeasurable splendor are fully enumerated.
O best of the Bharatas, learn from me of the sons of Kaśyapa, by whom the worlds, including all things moving and stationary, were pervaded; O tiger among the Bharatas,
O King, hear of those others who were devoted to truth and by whom the three worlds were sustained.
Aditi, Diti, Danu, Ariṣṭā, Surasā, Surabhi, Vinatā, Tāmrā, Krodhavaśā, Irā,
Kadrū, and Muni— O Lord of the World, hear from me about their offspring.
...and Khaṣā was the thirteenth. Indeed, these were the wives of Kaśyapa.
In the previous Manvantara, there were twelve excellent and supreme gods.
Those known as the Tuṣitas said to one another during the interval of Vaivasvata Manu:
When the immensely illustrious Akṣuṣa Manu was present,
they gathered together with one another for the welfare of all the worlds.
"Come quickly, O gods, and indeed enter into Aditi;
we shall procreate during the Manvantara, and that will be for our welfare."
Having spoken thus, all of them were born from Kaśyapa, the son of Marīci, by Aditi, the daughter of Dakṣa, during the interval of Cākṣuṣa Manu.
In a previous birth, through great austerity, they were born in the form of Pṛśni;
there indeed Viṣṇu and Śakra were born once again as Aryaman,
Dhātṛ, Tvaṣṭṛ, and likewise Pūṣan.
Vivasvat, Savitṛ, Mitra, Varuṇa,
Aṃśa, and Bhaga of great splendor— these are remembered as the twelve Ādityas.
Those who were formerly the Tuṣita gods during the interval of Cākṣuṣa are indeed remembered as the twelve Ādityas during the interval of Vaivasvata.
Now, those twenty-seven wives of Soma who were proclaimed to be of excellent vows had offspring who were radiant and possessed immeasurable splendor.
All the hosts of stars that shine in the sky are the sixteen offspring of the wives of Ariṣṭanemi. The four lightnings are recorded as the progeny of the wise Bahuputra.
The verses born of Pratyāṅgirasa are the most excellent, honored by the Brahman-sages.
The sons of the divine sage Bhṛśāśva were Devapraharaṇas;
at the end of a thousand yugas, these very ones are born once again.
O dear one, all the hosts of gods, numbering thirty-three, are born of desire;
and for them as well, O king of kings, cessation and arising are said to occur.
Just as the sun rises and sets here, O Kauravya,
so do the Yugas, O Indra among kings, as well as the dissolutions and the Manus;
in this manner, those hosts of gods come into being in age after age.
We have heard that two sons were born to Diti from Kaśyapa;
these two sons of Kaśyapa are considered the eldest of all,
O Bhārata— namely Hiraṇyakaśipu and Hiraṇyākṣa.
And Siṃhikā became the daughter who was the wife of Vipracitti.
Her sons, known as the Saiṃhikeyas, were possessed of great strength;
their host, O king of kings, is said to consist of ten thousand.

Their sons and grandsons, O mighty-armed one, were hundreds and thousands in number—indeed, they were beyond counting; hear now of Hiraṇyakaśipu.
Hiraṇyakaśipu had four sons of renowned prowess.
Anuhrāda, Hrāda, and the heroic Prahrāda.
Saṃhrāda was the fourth, and likewise Hrāda’s son was Hrada.
Saṃhrāda had two sons, Sunda and Nisunda; both of these are remembered as such.
Hrada’s sons were Āyu, Śiva, and likewise Kāla.
Among them were the venerable Saṃhrādaputra, Śibi, and Bāṣkala;
yet among them all, O illustrious one, was Prahlāda, who, self-controlled and viewing all things with equanimity,
spoke of supreme devotion toward Janārdana.
And Virocana, the son of Prahrāda, was born; from Virocana, Bali was born.
O lord of men, Bali had a hundred sons with Bāṇa as the eldest,
namely Dhṛtarāṣṭra, Sūrya, Candramas, and Indratāpana.
Kumbhanābha, Gardabhākṣa, Kukṣi, and others such as these were his sons;
among them, Bāṇa was the eldest, possessed of exceeding strength, and dear to Paśupati.
In a former age, Bāṇa, having propitiated the Lord, the husband of Umā, requested this boon:
"May there be a pleasure grove by my side."
And Indradamana was born to Bāṇa by Lohityā;
their host, O king of kings, numbered one hundred thousand.
The five sons of Hiraṇyākṣa were wise and possessed of great strength.
Jharjhara, Śakuni, Bhūtasaṃtāpana,
the valiant Mahānābha, and likewise Kālanābha.
There were one hundred sons of Danu, possessed of fierce prowess;
they were ascetics of great heroism—learn of them according to their principal names.
Dvimūrdhan and Śakuni, as well as the powerful Śaṅkuśiras, Śaṅkukarṇa, Vivāda, Gaveṣṭhin, Dundubhi,
Ayomukha, Śambara, Kapila, and Vāmana.
Marīci, Maghavan, Iḍā, Gargaśiras,
Vikṣobhaṇa, Ketu, Ketuvīrya, and Śatahrada.
Indrajit, as well as Sarvajit, Vajranābha,
the valiant Mahānābha, Kālanābha,
the mighty-armed Ekacakra, and the exceedingly powerful Tāraka.
Vaiśvānara, Puloman, Vidrāvaṇa, Mahāśiras,
Svarbhānu, Vṛṣaparvan, and the powerful Vipracitti.
Sūkṣma, Nicandra, Ūrṇanabha, Mahāhiri, Asiloman, Sukeśin, Śaṭha, Balaka, Mada,
as well as Gaganamūrdhan and the great asura Kumbhanābha.
Pramada, Maya, Kupatha, and the powerful Hayagrīva.
Vaisṛpa, Savirūpākṣa, Supatha, Harāhara, Hiraṇyakaśipu, Śatamāya, Śambara,
Śarabha, Śalabha, and the powerful Vipracitti.
All these sons of Danu were born from Kaśyapa;
they were the Dānavas, exceedingly powerful, with Vipracitti as their chief.

O lord of men, O protector of the earth, it is not possible to enumerate the offspring of these—sons and grandsons—who are infinite in number. Pulomā and Kālakā, both daughters of Vaiśvānara, were of great offspring and noble nature; they became the wives of Mārīci.
Endowed with great ascetic power, Mārīci begot sixty thousand sons, the most excellent of Dānavas, as well as another fourteen hundred who dwelt in Hiraṇyapura.
Those mighty Dānavas, the Paulomas and Kālakeyas,
who dwelt in Hiraṇyapura and were indeed incapable of being slain by the gods,
were killed by Savyasācin through the grace of the Grandfather.

Prabhā’s son was Nahuṣa, and Jayanta was the son of Śacī. Then Śarmiṣṭhā gave birth to Pūru, and Upadānavī gave birth to Duḥṣanta. After them were born other Dānavas of great heroism and extreme ferocity.
Likewise, the sons of Vipracitti were born from Siṃhikā.
Born from the union of Daityas and Dānavas, thirteen of great strength and fierce prowess became known as the Siṃhikēyas.
Vyaṅga and Śalya were powerful, as were Bala and Mahābala;
likewise Vātāpi, Namuci, Ilvala, and Khasṛma.

Among them, Rāhu was indeed the eldest, the crusher of the moon and sun;
then Śara, Potaraṇa, and the powerful Vajranābha.
Mūka and Tuhuṇḍa were the two sons born of Hradā;
and Mārīca was born of Tāḍakā as the son of Sunda.
Furthermore, the great Asura Svarbhānu, possessed of immense prowess and fighting with his mouth, was also born there.
Likewise, there was Saramāṇa and the heroic Śarakalpa.
These indeed were the most excellent Dānavas, who increased the lineage of Danu;
their sons and grandsons numbered in the hundreds and thousands.
In the lineage of the Daitya Saṃhrāda, the Nivātakavacas were born; they were those whose selves had been purified by great ascetic penance.
Those four crores were inhabitants of Maṇimatī;
they too were incapable of being slain by the gods, yet they were struck down by Arjuna—
men skilled in many illusions and masters of the science of archery.
Six sons of great being are proclaimed as the offspring of Tāmrā:
Kākī, Śyenī, Bhāsī, Sugrīvī, Śuci, and Gṛdhrikā.
Kākī gave birth to owls, Ulūkī to owls as well,
Śyenī to hawks, Bhāsī to bhāsas, and Gṛdhrikā to vultures.

Śuci is said to be the progenitor of aquatic flocks of birds; Sugrīvī, O scorcher of enemies, is the progenitor of horses, camels, and donkeys; and Tāmrāvaṃśa is likewise proclaimed [as the progenitor of these].
Vinatā had two sons, Aruṇa and Garuḍa;
Suparṇa was the best among those who fly, yet he was fierce because of his own deeds.
O dear one, there were a thousand serpents of immeasurable power belonging to Surasā—
many-headed, sky-dwelling, and high-souled.
From Kadrū were born a thousand serpents of immeasurable power, possessed of great strength,
under the dominion of Suparṇa, with many heads.
Among them, the principal ones are Śeṣa, Vāsuki, Takṣaka,
Airāvata, Mahāpadma, and both Kambala and Aśvatara.
Ailāpatra and Śaṅkha, Karkoṭaka and Dhanañjaya, Mahānīla and Mahākarṇa, Dhṛtarāṣṭra and Balāhaka;
Kuhara, Puṣpadaṃṣṭra, Durmukha, and likewise Sumukha;
Śaṅkha, Śaṅkhapāla, Kapila, and likewise Vāmana.
Nahuṣa, Śaṅkharoman, Maṇi, and others such as these—
these and many other venomous serpents with fierce poison had their sons and grandsons struck down by Garuḍa.
Know that the Krodhavaśa host consists of fourteen thousand fierce beings who devour serpents; all of them are fanged.
The land-dwelling birds and aquatic creatures are known as the offspring of the Earth.
The sons of Anāyuṣā were fifty in number and possessed great strength;
they were Surata, Guṇavṛtta, Vikṣara, and likewise Nṛpa.
Surabhi likewise gave birth to cows and buffaloes.
Irā gave birth to trees, creepers, climbing plants, and all species of grass;
Khasā, however, gave birth to the Yakṣas, Rākṣasas, and likewise the Munis and Apsarases.
Ariṣṭā gave birth to the great beings, the Gandharvas of immeasurable power;
these descendants of Kaśyapa, both stationary and moving, have thus been proclaimed.
Their sons and grandsons, by the hundreds and thousands—
this, O dear one, is recorded as the creation in the Svārociṣa Manvantara.
Now, during the great sacrifice to Varuṇa performed by Vaivasvata, while the Brahman was offering oblations in that extended rite, the creation of progeny is here described.
Formerly, in that place where the seven mind-born Brahman-sages had arisen,
the Grandfather himself appointed them to the status of his sons.
Then, O Bhārata, during the conflict between the gods and the Dānavas,
Diti, whose sons had been destroyed, propitiated Kaśyapa.
Kaśyapa, his mind pleased by her having propitiated him perfectly, invited her to choose a boon; and she then chose a boon.
He, of great ascetic power, granted her the boon she had requested: a son of immeasurable luster who would be capable of slaying Indra.
Having granted the boon, Mārīca spoke to her with composure:
"If [the child] remains in the womb for a hundred autumns, your son shall slay Indra."
"If you maintain purity, being devotedly established in this vow,
then this son shall be yours, provided that you carry him."
When she, the queen, had thus spoken, her husband of great asceticism consented;
and she, being pure, O lord of the earth, conceived a child.
Constantly bathing at the three periods of the day and devoted to the Kṛcchra and Cāndrāyaṇa penances,
Kaśyapa then, by his approach to Aditi, conceived a fetus;
he was indeed bringing forth the foremost host of the gods of immeasurable splendor.
Having accumulated an invincible splendor that was forever indestructible by the immortals,
he, firm in his vows, went forth to the mountains for the sake of ascetic penance.
And she, being fully endowed with all virtues, properly conceived that embryo.
O dear one, having learned that the embryo was intended for his own destruction, Maghavan, the granter of boons and subduer of Pāka, waited until Kāśyapa had departed; then,
seeking an opportunity against her, he prostrated at the feet of Diti.
"O Goddess of firm vows, I shall serve your feet.
When she had been addressed thus by Śakra of immeasurable splendor,
the goddess spoke these words to Śakra, the destroyer of enemies.
"O illustrious one of great splendor, with a self-restrained mind, serve him;
then you shall behold your brother born endowed with radiant energy."
Having heard those words of the goddess, Indra, devoted to serving her,
became intent on seeking an opportunity against her;
and when the hundred years were nearly complete, the infallible one saw his chance.
Without having performed the purification of her feet, Diti lay down upon her bed and fell asleep; then, having entered her womb,
the wielder of the thunderbolt (Vajrapāṇi) cut that embryo into seven pieces.
As the embryo was being split apart by the thunderbolt, it began to cry out;
"Do not cry," Śakra said to it again and again.
That embryo became divided into seven parts; Indra, enraged, further split each one into seven with his thunderbolt, O crusher of enemies.
By that sound of weeping, Diti was awakened.
Afflicted, she said to Śakra: "But why has this wretched deed been done?"
Terrified, Purandara emerged from that birth-canal and,
drawing near to the Goddess, fell prostrate at her feet.
"O Goddess, Indra is impure; you have fallen asleep with your hair resting upon your feet.
Fearing the sin of killing my own self, I have done this; you ought to forgive it."
Thus addressed, that goddess spoke these words to Śakra: "Well done, my son; you have acted rightly; no ill-deed has been committed by you."
"But I shall say something; do that, O crusher of enemies!
You are my very own son, O Lord; protect them if you so desire.
"Very well," said Indra, "it is even so, there is no doubt."
O bull among the Bharatas, those gods became known by the name Maruts.
Just as was said by Maghavan, so did the Maruts become.
"Do not weep," O Pākaśāsana— since these words were spoken by you,
let them be known by the name Maruts, if you so desire.
O Lord, O Purandara, in the battles between the gods and the asuras, your servants shall follow behind you, remaining under your command for your sake.
To the goddess who was speaking thus, Śakra spoke these words:
"The forty-nine gods are the companions of the wielder of the thunderbolt."
O Janamejaya, descendant of Bharata, when those beings had thus multiplied, Hari appointed Prajāpatis for their various classes; however, O Bhārata, those kingdoms had previously belonged to Pṛthu.
He is Hari, the Puruṣa, the Hero, Kṛṣṇa, the Victorious, the Lord of Creatures, Parjanya, the Sun, and the Manifest; this entire world belongs to him.
"O Indra among kings, become purified and then listen with a one-pointed mind; [this should never be told] to one who is impure, nor to one who is unclean, nor to one who is not a disciple."

O King, O bull of the Bharatas, I shall describe for you— provided you are grateful and well-disposed— this true account of the creation of beings, which leads to heaven, brings fame and long life, is meritorious, and is equal in authority to the Veda, for one who understands it correctly.
For one who hears or even recites this auspicious birth-story of the Maruts, there is no fear of returning [to this world] here; how then could there be fear of the next world?
Vaiśampāyana said: Having consecrated Pṛthu, the son of Vena, in the sovereignty of the overlordship,
the Grandfather then proceeded to assign the various kingdoms in due order.
He consecrated Soma in the sovereignty over the twice-born, the plants, the lunar mansions and the planets, as well as over sacrifices and ascetic penances.
He appointed Varuṇa as the sovereign over the waters, Vaiśravaṇa as the lord of kings,
and Bṛhaspati, the descendant of Aṅgiras, as the lord of the Viśvedevas.
He consecrated Kāvya, the lord of the Bhṛgus, in the kingdom;
likewise, he consecrated Viṣṇu among the Ādityas and Pāvaka among the Vasus.
Among the Prajāpatis, Dakṣa; among the Maruts, Vāsava;
and among the Daityas and Dānavas, Prahlāda of immeasurable splendor.
He consecrated Vaivasvata Yama in the sovereignty over the ancestors; likewise, he installed him as the lord of the Mothers, of religious observances, of mantras, of cows,
of Yakṣas, of Rākṣasas, and of earthly kings.

Then he appointed Vipracitti as the king of the Dānavas;
Giriśa, the wielder of the trident, as the lord of all beings and Piśācas; Himavat as the king of mountains; and the ocean as the lord of rivers.
The Lord made Citraratha the sovereign of the Gandharvas, of the Maruts, of bodiless beings, of those possessing sound and space, and of the powerful Vāyus.
Among the Nāgas he made Vāsuki his emblem, and among the serpents, Takṣaka.
And he then appointed Airāvata as the king of elephants,
Uccaiḥśravas as the king of horses, and Garuḍa as the king of birds.
Then he consecrated the tiger as the king of wild beasts, the bull among cattle, and the Plakṣa tree as the king of the lords of the forest.
He consecrated Parjanya as the sovereign lord of the oceans, the rivers, the clouds, the raining down of rain, and the Ādityas.
He consecrated Śeṣa as the king of all fanged creatures,
Takṣaka as the king of the crawling serpents,
and made Kāmadeva the lord of all the hosts of Apsarases.
Furthermore, [he knows] the seasons, the months, and likewise the days, the fortnights,
the nights, the muhūrtas, the lunar dates, and the festivals.

Having thus divided the kingdoms in due order, that Grandfather (Pitāmaha) established the Lord of the Year (Saṃvatsara) as the ruler over the measurements of time— such as the *kalā* and *kāṣṭhā*, the movement of the two solstices (*ayana*), calculation (*gaṇita*), and the conjunctions (*yoga*).
Then, O descendant of Bharata, he established the guardians of the quarters.
In the eastern direction, he consecrated Sudhanvan, the son of the Prajāpati Vairāja, as the king and guardian of that quarter.
In the southern region, he consecrated the high-souled son of the patriarch Kardama, named Śaṅkhapada, as king.
In the western direction,
he consecrated the high-souled King Ketumān, the son of Rajas, as the unshakable sovereign.
Likewise, he consecrated Hiraṇyaloman as the invincible king over Parjanya Prajāpati in the northern direction.
By them this entire earth— with its seven continents and its cities, its mountains, forests, and groves,
and its oceans and rivers— [was pervaded].
Even today, it is protected according to its respective regions in accordance with the Dharma.
And Pṛthu was consecrated with the Rājasūya by these lords of men—
by the kings— with the sovereignty of a king-king, according to the ritual prescribed in the Vedas.
Then, when the Cākṣuṣa Manvantara of immeasurable splendor had passed,
he assigned the sovereignty of the earth to Vaivasvata Manu.
O sinless king of kings, if you wish to hear it, I shall relate in detail the history of Vaivasvata Manu out of consideration for you;
for this is a great foundation established in the Purāṇas.

Janamejaya said:

Just as this earth was milked by that great-souled one.
Just as it was milked by the ancestors, by the gods, and by the seers;
and just as it was by the Daityas, the Nāgas, the Yakṣas, and the trees.

O Vaiśampāyana, proclaim how the earth was milked by the mountains, the Piśācas, the Gandharvas, the best of the twice-born, and the Rākṣasas of great power, as well as the specific vessels used by each of them.
The calves, the various kinds of milk, and everything else, in due order.
And for what reason, O dear one, was Vena’s hand churned in the past by the enraged great seers? Proclaim that reason as well.
Vaiśampāyana said:
"O Janamejaya, listen with one-pointed attention, self-restraint, and a desire to hear, as I shall relate to you the birth of Pṛthu, the son of Vena."

O King, I would not proclaim this to one who is impure, nor to one of base mind, nor to one who is not a disciple, nor to one who has not taken vows, nor to one who is ungrateful, nor to one who is harmful.
O King, listen to this secret as it truly is, proclaimed by the seers; it leads to heaven, brings fame, prolongs life, confers wealth, and is equal in authority to the Veda.
Whoever, having paid homage to the Brahmins, constantly recites this account of the origin of Pṛthu, the son of Vena, shall not grieve over what has been done or left undone.
Vaiśampāyana said:
In former times, there was a lord who protected righteousness and was equal to Atri;
born in the lineage of Atri, he was the Prajāpati named Aṅga.
He had a son named Vena, who was not particularly righteous;
he was born as a lord of creatures (prajāpati) to Sunīthā, the daughter of Mṛtyu.
Due to the fault of his maternal grandfather, Vena— the grandson of Kāla—
cast his own duty behind him and conducted himself in the worlds according to his lusts.
That king established a law devoid of righteousness;
transgressing the Vedic laws, he became devoted to unrighteousness.
While that Prajāpati existed, the people ceased their Vedic recitations and the utterance of *vaṣaṭ*;
the deities did not drink the Soma offered in sacrifices.
"One must not sacrifice, nor must one offer oblations"— this was the cruel vow of that Prajāpati when destruction was imminent.
"I am the one to be worshipped, the sacrificer, and the sacrifice itself, O best of the Kurus;
the sacrifice is to be ordained in me, and the oblation is to be offered into me."
Then all the great seers, headed by Marīci, spoke to him as he was transgressing the bounds of propriety and seizing what was improper.
"We shall enter upon initiation for many series of years;
that sacrifice will bear fruit for us, and even now it is not otherwise.
O Vena, do not commit unrighteousness; this is not the dharma approved by the virtuous."
"For you were born in the Nidhana; without a doubt, you are Prajāpati.
'And I shall protect the subjects'—this was the vow you made."
Then Vena, the evil-minded one, laughing, spoke these meaningless words regarding this matter to all those great seers who were speaking thus.

Who else is the creator of dharma, or whose word should I listen to? Who on earth is equal to me in learning, heroism, austerity, and truth? I am the source of all beings and especially of all dharmas.
Being utterly deluded, you surely do not know me in my true nature.
If I so desired, I could burn the earth or likewise inundate it with waters;
I could indeed obstruct both heaven and earth—of this there is no need for deliberation.
When the king could not be persuaded because of his pride and arrogance,
the great seers then became enraged at Vena.
Having restrained that great and powerful one as he was quivering with rage, those high-souled ones said to one another, "Let the wicked one be slain! Let him be slain!"
He who, being of base conduct, reviles Hari— the divine Lord of Sacrifice, who is without beginning or end— is not fit to be the lord of the earth.
Having spoken thus, O Blessed One, the hosts of sages struck the king— who had already been slain by their censures and other insults— with those kusha grasses purified by mantras.
O King, when he was slain, the entire world became like a realm of robbers.
Thereupon, having deliberated together, the sages, filled with indignation, churned the thigh of that monarch;
they then churned his left thigh.
While that [thigh] was indeed being churned, there was born from the king's thigh a very short man who was also exceedingly black.
Terrified, O Janamejaya, he stood with his palms joined in reverence;
seeing him thus agitated, Atri then said to him, "Sit down."
O best among speakers, he became the founder of the Niṣāda lineage;
moreover, from the impurity born of Vena, he created the fishermen.
And those others who dwell in the Vindhya mountains— the Tumuras and the Tumburas—
know them, O dear one, to be those who delight in unrighteousness and are defiled by the sins of Vena.
Then those great-souled maharṣis, exerting themselves, again churned the right hand of Vena like a fire-drill.
From that hand arose Pṛthu, blazing like fire,
shining with his own body like Agni himself in a visible flame.
Born already equipped with a bow and armor, Pṛthu himself, a man of great asceticism,
took up the primordial bow named Ājagava, which produces a great roar,
as well as divine arrows and a highly radiant coat of mail for his protection.
When he was born, O Great King, all living beings were filled with joy from every side; they flocked together, and Vena ascended to the third heaven.
O descendant of Kuru, O tiger among men, he was then saved from the hell named Put, by that high-souled and virtuous son who had been born.
Then the oceans and the rivers, bringing jewels from every quarter and waters for the purpose of consecration, all approached him.
And the blessed Grandfather, together with the gods and the descendants of Aṅgiras, [beheld] all beings, both stationary and moving, in every way.
Having assembled, they then consecrated Vainya as the lord of men,
the protector of subjects, the immensely radiant one, with the great sovereignty of kings.
Then that majestic and powerful King Pṛthu, the son of Vena, was duly consecrated in the supreme sovereignty by those learned in the Dharma.
His subjects were alienated by his father, but they were won over by him;
because of that affection, the name "Rāja" (King) arose for him.
As he advanced toward the ocean, the waters solidified;
the mountains yielded the way, and there was no obstruction to his banner.
The earth yields crops without being ploughed; foods are accomplished by mere thought;
cows grant all desires; and there is honey in every leaf-cup.
At that very time, during the auspicious sacrifice of Brahmā,
the high-minded Sūta was born from the *sūti* at the conclusion of the day of the *sautya*.
At that very same great sacrifice, the wise Māgadha was born;
both of them were summoned there by the great seers for the purpose of praising Pṛthu.
Then all the sages said: "Let this king be praised;
this deed is worthy of you both, and this lord of men is a fitting recipient."
Then the Sūta and the Māgadha said to all those ṛṣis:
"We two please both the gods and the ṛṣis by means of our own duties."
O twice-born ones, we do not know his deeds, nor his characteristics, nor his fame,
by which we might compose a hymn of praise for this radiant king.
"O sages,
let this king be praised for those qualities that the mighty universal monarch will perform as his deeds and those virtues he shall possess."
Commanded by the seers,
"Let them be praised for their future deeds," O King, Sūta and Māgadha duly offered praise for all those mighty exploits that Pṛthu, possessed of great strength, had performed later on.
This lord of men is truthful in speech, generous by nature, faithful to his word,
illustrious, victorious, patient, valiant, and a punisher of the wicked.

The king was a knower of dharma, grateful, compassionate, and pleasant of speech; he honored those worthy of honor, performed sacrifices, was devoted to the Brahmins, and was kind to the virtuous. Established in his judicial duties, he was impartial toward both enemy and friend.
From that time forth, O Janamejaya, blessings have been employed in hymns throughout the three worlds by Sūtas, Māgadhas, and bards.
At the conclusion of their praise, Pṛthu, the lord of subjects, being well-pleased, bestowed the Anūpa region upon Sūta and the Magadha region upon Māgadha.
Seeing him, the subjects and the great seers were exceedingly joyful and said,
"This lord of men will be the provider of livelihoods for you all."
At that time, when the medicinal herbs had perished and the land was without a king, the subjects, afflicted by hunger, approached that lord of the earth for refuge.
They were asked by him the reason for their coming there,
and the subjects said:
"O best of men, in a kingless land, all the medicinal herbs on the earth..."
Then, O Lord of Creatures, all the subjects, being devoured, go to their destruction.
"You have been appointed by the Creator as our provider of livelihood and protector of the people;
grant us, who are overwhelmed by hunger, the means of subsistence.
Thereupon, O Great King, the subjects rushed toward the son of Vena.
Then, at the words of the great seer, "Provide for us a means of livelihood," he did so.
Thus pursued by the subjects, yet desiring to act for their welfare,
that powerful one took up his bow and arrows and struck the earth.
Then, terrified by the fear of Vainya, the Earth fled away, having become a cow;
Pṛthu, taking up his bow, pursued her as she ran.
Having traveled through the worlds, beginning with the world of Brahmā, out of fear of Vainya,
she then beheld Vainya before her, holding his bow.
With blazing, sharpened arrows, he struck Acyuta, who was radiant with splendor,
the great-souled master of great yoga, who is invincible even to the immortals.
Finding no protection, she approached Vainya alone,
with her palms joined in reverence, she who is always worthy of worship by the three worlds.
He said to the son of Vena: "Do you not perceive the unrighteousness in the killing of a woman?
O King, how will you sustain the subjects without me?"
The worlds are established in me, O King; this universe is sustained by me. Know this, O ruler of the earth: it is for my sake that the subjects should not perish.
"You ought not to kill me, O protector of the earth, if you desire to act for the welfare of all creatures; listen to these words of mine."
All undertakings that are commenced through skillful means succeed;
therefore, I shall tell you the means—practice it if you so desire. O King, devise a means by which you may sustain your subjects.
"O King, even having slain me, you will not be able to nourish your subjects;
I shall become their food. Restrain your anger, O one of great splendor!"
O Pṛthu, by the power of my own yoga, I shall sustain these subjects.
Then the Earth, having bowed down, spoke again to that king:
"O protector of the earth, they say that women are not to be slain even among beings belonging to the animal realm; you ought not to abandon righteousness."

Having heard these various words and having reflected in many ways out of a desire for the welfare of his subjects, the high-minded and righteous king restrained his anger and spoke thus to the earth:
Pṛthu said: "He who, for the sake of one person— whether for himself or for another— should slay many living beings in this world, would incur sin in this very life."
When many prosper through the killing of one who is auspicious,
O blessed lady, there is neither a mortal sin (pātaka) nor a minor offense (upapātaka) in that killing.
When the destruction of a single evildoer brings security to many, that killing is a source of merit;
therefore, O Earth, for the sake of my subjects, I shall kill you.
If you do not carry out my word today for the benefit of the world, [it will be as stated].
Having slain you today with an arrow for turning your back on my command,
I shall manifest myself and personally sustain the subjects.
Therefore, abiding by my command, O best among the upholders of Dharma,
restore all living beings to life, for you are indeed capable of sustaining them.
And become my daughter; then I shall restrain this arrow of terrible aspect, which has been raised for the purpose of slaying you.
Vasundharā said:
"O hero, I shall accomplish all this without a doubt;
however, look for my calf so that I, being full of maternal affection, may yield milk."
"And make me level everywhere, O best among the upholders of Dharma,
so that my flowing milk may nourish everything."
Vaiśampāyana said: Then, with the tip of his bow, the son of Vena cleared away hundreds of thousands of rocks; by him, those mountains were thus leveled.
Then King Pṛthu, the son of Vena, made the earth level;
for during the previous Manvantaras, the earth had been uneven.
By their very nature, the even and uneven parts of that [earth] did not exist;
indeed, it is said that in the previous period of Cākṣuṣa Manu, such was the case.
For in the prior creation, there was no unevenness on the surface of the earth.
Then there was a division of the cities or the villages.
There were no crops, no cattle-rearing, no agriculture, and no trade routes;
there was neither truth nor falsehood, neither greed nor envy,
when that Vaivasvata interval had arrived in the present.
O Indra among kings, from Vainya onwards, there has been the origin of all this.
O sinless one, wherever the ground was level at that time,
there all the subjects chose to make their dwelling.
At that time, the food of living beings consisted of fruits and roots;
we have heard that they were beset by great hardship.
Having first conceived of the lord Svāyambhuva Manu as the calf,
O tiger among men, he then milked the earth into his own hand.
The powerful Pṛthu, son of Vena, milked all varieties of grain;
by that son of Vena, this earth was indeed milked of its crops.
By that food, O dear one, the subjects have lived perpetually even until today.
It is also heard that the earth was milked again by the seers;
Soma became their calf, and the son of Aṅgiras was the milker.
Bṛhaspati of great splendor was the vessel, and the Vedic meters were the milk, O Bhārata; the peerless austerity and the eternal Brahman were also present.
Then again, it is heard that this earth was milked by the hosts of gods, led by Purandara, who took a golden vessel.
Vatsa was Maghavan, and the all-pervading Savitṛ was the milker;
the milk was indeed that which bestows vigor, by means of which the deities subsist.
It is also heard that the Earth was milked again by the ancestors of immeasurable prowess, who took a silver vessel and drew forth their own funeral offerings (svadhā).
Yama Vaivasvata was their powerful calf;
Antaka became the milker, and Kāla, the destroyer of the worlds, was the vessel.
O best of men, it is heard that the Nāgas milked her, making Takṣaka their calf; taking a gourd vessel, they drew forth the poison as if it were milk.
Among them, O best of the Bharatas, O lord of the earth, the powerful Airāvata Dhṛtarāṣṭra was the milker for the nāgas and the serpents.
By that very [means] do those fierce ones, of massive bodies and great strength, subsist;
they have that as their food, that as their conduct, that as their vigor, and that as their refuge.
It is also heard that the Asuras, taking up an iron vessel, milked the earth once more for illusory powers that destroy enemies.
At that time, Virocana, the son of Prahlāda, was their calf;
the mighty Madhu was the officiating priest for the Daityas, and Dvimūrdhan was the milker.
By means of that very illusion, even today all these illusory asuras continue to exist with immeasurable wisdom; such, indeed, is their boundless power.
And it is heard, O King, that the Earth was milked again by the Yakṣas;
in an unbaked clay vessel, O Great King, they obtained inexhaustible power of invisibility in ancient times.
Having made Vaiśravaṇa the calf, [the milk was drawn] by the Yakṣas and Puṇyajanas;
the milker was Rajatanābha, the father of Maṇivara,
who was the son of a Yakṣa, possessed of great splendor, three-headed, and of immense ascetic power.
"But the milker, O Lord, is the giver of wealth; thus by them the earth is sustained, and by him they live here," so said the supreme seer.
Furthermore, O bull among men, the earth was milked again by the *rākṣasas* and *piśācas*,
who took up a skull containing a corpse in order to devour the subjects.
O best of the Kurus, their milker was Rajatanābha;
O descendant of Kuru, Sumālī was the calf, and the milk was indeed blood.
With that milk, the Rākṣasas, Yakṣas who are like unto the immortals,
Piśācas, and likewise the hosts of Bhūtas, sustain themselves.
Furthermore, O best of men, that [cow] was milked upon a lotus leaf by the Gandharvas together with their hosts of Apsarases,
having made Citraratha the calf, while pure fragrances were used [as the milking vessel].
And their milker, O best of the Bharatas, was Suruci,
the high-souled king of the Gandharvas, who was exceedingly powerful and resplendent like the sun.
And it is heard that the goddess Earth was milked again by the mountains,
who obtained personified medicinal herbs and various kinds of jewels.
Himavat was the calf, the great mountain Meru was the milker, and the mountain itself was the vessel;
by that [milking], the mountains were established.
It is heard that this earth, along with its trees and creepers, yields milk;
and taking a vessel made of *palāśa* wood, one observes the regrowth of what has been cut or burnt.
O Janamejaya, this earth is the milch-cow that yields all desires;
she is the nurse, the creator, the purifier, and the sustainer of wealth. She is the foundation and indeed the source of everything, both moving and unmoving.
She is the milch-cow that yields all desires and the one who causes all crops to grow.
This earth, renowned as extending to the edge of the ocean,
was once entirely drenched with the fat of Madhu and Kaiṭabha.
Therefore, this goddess is called Medinī by those who discourse on Brahman;
and because she accepted the sovereignty of King Pṛthu, the son of Vena, O Bhārata,
the goddess attained the status of his daughter and is called Pṛthivī.
The earth was divided, purified, and made prosperous by Pṛthu; it abounds in crops and mines, and is garlanded with cities and towns.
O best of kings, that son of Vena was a king of such power;
he was undoubtedly worthy of homage and worship by all the hosts of living beings.
And by the highly fortunate Brahmins who have mastered the Vedas and their auxiliary sciences,
Pṛthu alone— being the eternal provider of livelihood— is to be saluted.
And by illustrious kings who desire the status of sovereignty,
the majestic Pṛthu, son of Vena and the first king, should be honored with salutation.
Moreover, even by warriors who are valiant and desirous of victory in battle,
the first king— the primordial monarch— must be honored with salutations.
For whatever warrior goes to battle after having praised King Pṛthu, he,
being renowned, crosses through formidable conflicts in safety.
Even by wealthy Vaiśyas who follow the occupation of a Vaiśya,
Pṛthu alone— the giver of livelihoods and possessor of great fame— is to be saluted.
In the same way, Śūdras who are pure and serve the three higher castes, desiring the highest welfare, should likewise pay homage to Pṛthu alone.
These specific calves, the milkers, the milk itself, and the vessels have been described by me; what more shall I describe to you?
Whoever should constantly hear this account of Pṛthu from the beginning,
being joined by sons and grandsons, shall rejoice for a very long time on earth.
Thus, O best of the Bharatas, have the deeds of the high-souled son of Vena been told here.
"What else, O best of the Bharatas, do you ask, O lord of men?
He who always listens with devotion shall go to heaven; of this there is no doubt.
Janamejaya said:
O Vaiśampāyana, rich in asceticism, recount in detail all the Manvantaras and their prior creation.
O Brahman, I desire to hear in truth the account of the Manvantaras— how many Manus there have been and for how long a duration of time.
Vaiśampāyana said:
"It is not possible, dear one, to recount this in detail even in hundreds of years, O Kauravya; listen therefore to a summary from me of the Manvantaras."
O dear one, Svāyambhuva Manu, as well as Svārociṣa Manu,
Auttama, Tāmasa, Raivata, Cākṣuṣa,
and Vaivasvata, O descendant of Kuru, is said to be the current Manu.
Uttama and Tāmasa were the two Manus Raivata and Cakṣuṣa;
the eighth was Dakṣasāvarṇi, and Dharmasāvarṇi as well;
and the eleventh Manu will be Sāvarṇi, the son of Rudra.
And Sāvarṇi Manu, O dear one, as well as Bhautya, Raucya,
Raivata, Brahmasāvarṇi, and Sūryasāvarṇi—
likewise, the four Merusāvarṇis are recorded as Manus.
Those who were past, those who are present, and likewise those who are yet to come—
these Manus, my dear, have been recounted by me exactly as they were heard. I shall now proclaim their sages, as well as their sons and the hosts of gods.
Marīci, the venerable Atri, Aṅgiras, Pulaha, Kratu,
Pulastya, and Vasiṣṭha— these seven are the sons of Brahmā.
Likewise, O King, in the northern direction the Seven Sages are situated;
and during the Svāyambhuva interval, there were gods known as the Yāmas.
Agnīdhra, Agnibāhu, Medhā, Medhātithi, Vasu,
Jyotiṣmān, Dyutimān, Havya, Savana, and Putra.
These ten sons of great power were the offspring of Svāyambhuva Manu;
this, O King, has been declared to you as the first Manvantara.
Aurva, Vasiṣṭha’s son, Stamba, Kāśyapa, Prāṇa, Bṛhaspati, Datta, Atri, and Cyavana— these,
my dear, are the great seers of mighty vows proclaimed by Vāyu.
And during the Svārociṣa interval, the gods were known as the Tuṣitas;
[their names were] Havirdhra, Sukṛti, Jyotis, Āpas, Mūrti, and Ayasmaya.
Prathita, Nabhasya, and likewise Nabhas and Sūrya—
these, O protector of the earth, were the sons of the high-souled Svārociṣa Manu;
they have been celebrated as men of great heroism and prowess.
This second Manvantara has been described to you by me;
now I shall speak of this third one, so listen to it, O lord of men.
The seven sons of Vasiṣṭha were renowned as the Vāsiṣṭhas;
born of Urjā, they were the illustrious sons of Hiraṇyagarbha.
The sages have been mentioned here by me; now learn from me as I proclaim the ten beautiful sons of Uttama, O great king.
Iṣa, Ūrja, Tanūpa, Madhu, Mādhava,
Śuci, Śukra, Sahas, Nabhasya, and Nabha— these are the months; the Bhānus are the deities there, and this is declared to be the Manvantara.
I shall describe the fourth Manvantara to you; listen to that, O Bhārata. Kāvya, Pṛthu, Agni, Jahnu, Dhātṛ, Kapīvān, and Akapīvān were the seven Ṛṣis there, O King.
O dear one, descendant of Bharata, in the Purāṇa it is proclaimed that the sons and grandsons of Manu,
as well as the hosts of truthful gods, belonged to the interval of Tāmasa Manu.
O King, I shall now declare the sons of Tāmasa Manu:
Dyuti, Tapasya, Sutapas, Tapomūla, Tapodhana,
Taporati, Akalmāṣa, Tanvī, Dhanvī, and Paramtapa.
O great king, these ten sons of great strength were born to Tāmasa Manu;
this is the fourth interval (antara) as proclaimed by Vāyu.
Vedabāhu, Yadudhra, the sage Vedaśiras,
Hiraṇyaloman, Parjanya, Ūrdhvabāhu born of Soma,
and Satyanetra of the Atri lineage— these were the other seven ṛṣis.
The Devas and the Abhūtarajasas are likewise recorded as the primary constituents;
this is called the Manvantara of Pāriplava and Raibhya.
Now, listen as I describe these sons of his:
Dhṛtimān, Avyaya, Yukta, Tattvadarśin, and Nirutsuka.
Araṇya, Prakāśa, Nirmoha, Satyavāk, and Kṛti were the sons of Raivata Manu; this is the fifth interval (antara).
I shall now fully declare the sixth to you; listen to it, O lord of men:
Bhṛgu, Nabhas, Vivasvat, Sudhāman, and likewise Virajas.
Atināman, and Sahiṣṇu—these seven were the great ṛṣis during the interval of Cākṣuṣa Manu; O dear one, now hear of these gods.
O king of kings, the Ādyas, Prabhūtas, Ṛbhus, Pṛthukas, and those named Lekhas are known as the five classes of gods who dwell in heaven.
O great king, the sons of the seer Aṅgiras were high-souled and possessed of great luster;
they were the ten renowned sons of Nāḍvala,
beginning with Uru, O King, and this is remembered as the sixth Manvantara.
The sixth Manvantara has been declared; now learn from me the seventh.
Atri, Vasiṣṭha, the blessed Kaśyapa and the great Ṛṣi Gautama, as well as Bharadvāja and Viśvāmitra—these are the sages.
Likewise, the son of the high-souled Ṛcīka was the venerable Jamadagni; these seven are currently ṛṣis in heaven.
The Sādhyas, the Rudras, the Viśvedevas, the Vasus, and likewise the Maruts;
the Ādityas and the two Aśvins are recorded as the deities belonging to the Vaivasvata [Manvantara].
These ten sons of the high-souled Manu Vaivasvata, headed by Ikṣvāku, exist in the present interval.
O King, descendant of Bharata, they were born in all directions;
and of these great-souled maharṣis who have been glorified,
O King, there were sons and grandsons throughout all directions, O descendant of Bharata.
In all Manvantaras, seven groups of seven [sages] reside in the eastern direction for the sake of establishing dharma and for the protection of the world.
When a manvantara has passed, four groups of seven,
having performed their duties, go to heaven, to the healthy world of Brahmā.
Then others, endowed with austerity, fill that place as well,
both those of the past and those of the present, in this sequence, O Bhārata.
These seven past Manvantaras have been described to you, O Kauravya, descendant of Bharata; now learn from me all those that are yet to come.
O dear one, learn from me about those five Sāvarṇa Manus:
one of them is Vaivasvata, and four are the sons of Prajāpati Parameṣṭhin, O dear one, who have attained the status of Merusāvarṇas.
O King, these are indeed the grandsons of Dakṣa and the sons of Priyā;
endowed with great ascetic power, they possess immense energy upon the summit of Mount Meru.
The son of Prajāpati Ruci is known as the Manu named Raucya;
and the son born to Ruci by the goddess Bhūti is named Bhautya.
These seven Manus of the future are recorded in this world.
And seven great sages are likewise recorded as yet to come in heaven;
having reached the interval of Manu Sāvarṇa here on earth, hear now of them.
Rāma, Vyāsa, and likewise Ātreya—these were radiant and deeply learned;
so too was Bhāradvāja’s son, Drauṇi Aśvatthāman, of great splendor.
The son of Gotama, Gautama named Śaradvat,
Kauśika, Gālava, and Ruru Kāśyapa—
these seven high-souled ones shall be the best of sages in the future.
The qualities of the deities there were declared by the Self-Existent One to be threefold;
these sons of the high-souled Kaśyapa, the son of Marīci,
are equal to Brahmā and are remembered as the blessed Seven Sages (Saptarṣis).
Furthermore, by means of noble birth, austerity, and the exposition of mantras,
the stainless Brahmarṣis are remembered as those established in the world of Brahmā.
Those by whom the knowledge of the past, future, and present has been realized of their own accord;
those who have indeed attained perfection through austerity; those who are disciplined and contemplative;
and those who possess sovereignty in every respect through mantras, grammar, and other sciences.
Knowing these to be his wives and their names as "naiṣṭhikā," the twice-born [should know] that these seven, by virtue of their seven qualities, are remembered as the Seven Sages (Saptarṣis).
Long-lived, creators of mantras, lords, and far-sighted;
they perceive the Dharma directly through their intelligence and likewise set the lineage in motion.
In all the ages known as Kṛta and the rest,
those highly fortunate Seven Sages, who are devoted to truth and righteousness, repeatedly establish the social classes and the stages of life in every respect.
And from their lineage, those who compose the Mantras and Brāhmaṇas are born again and again when the Dharma has become lax.
Since it is remembered that the seven givers of boons, as well as others beyond them,
are [capable], therefore neither time nor age is a limiting factor for the practice of the sages.
O King, this description of the Seven Sages has been explained by me to you.
Now hear, O best of beings, of the future sons of Sāvarṇa Manu;
they are called Svayaṃtejas because they are enlightened by themselves, and Saṃbuddhas because they awaken by themselves.
Because they recite the sacred knowledge (*brahman*), they are remembered as Brahmarṣis:
Varīvān, Avarīvān, Saṃmata, Dhṛtimān,
Vasu, Cariṣṇu, Āḍhya, Dhṛṣṇu, Vājī, and Sumati.
O Bhārata, there will be ten sons of Sāvarṇi Manu.
O King, descendant of Bharata, hear now of the future Sāvarṇas who shall arise through forbearance (*kṣamā*).
By rising at dawn and reciting their names, a man’s happiness increases,
he attains great fame, and he becomes long-lived.

"These two boys of mine and this slender-waisted girl are to be entrusted to you;

Having composed herself and being told "So be it" by her,
