Restrain that one of great body out of a desire for the welfare of the worlds;
once he has been slain by you, let the worlds today become secure.
"For you alone, O Lord of the Earth, are capable of slaying him;
moreover, O sinless one, a boon was previously granted to me by Viṣṇu:
'Whoever shall slay that fierce and mighty great Asura...'"
And he, whose fame is renowned, will undoubtedly be a universal monarch;
by his own splendor, Viṣṇu will augment your splendor.
For Dhundhu of great splendor cannot be consumed by one of little splendor,
O protector of the earth, even in a hundred ages;
for his valor is exceedingly great and difficult to withstand even for the gods.
Thus addressed by the high-souled Uttaṅka, that royal sage gave his son Kuvalāśva to him for the destruction of Dhundhu.
Bṛhadaśva said:
"O Blessed One, I have laid down my weapons; however, this son of mine, O best of the twice-born, will become Dhundhumāra, of this there is no doubt."
Having assigned that son to the subduing of Dhundhu, the royal sage,
firm in his vows, went to the mountain itself for the sake of asceticism.
King Kuvalāśva, accompanied by Uttanka and a hundred of his sons,
set out for the destruction of that Dhundhu.
Then the Lord Viṣṇu, the powerful master, entered him with his splendor at the command of Uttaṅka and out of a desire for the welfare of the worlds.
As that invincible one set forth, a great sound arose in the sky:
"This illustrious son of a king shall become Dhundhumāra."
The gods scattered divine garlands all around him,
O bull of the Bharatas, and the celestial drums resounded.
Having gone there with his sons, that powerful one, the best among victors,
caused the inexhaustible ocean of sand to be dug out.
O descendant of Kuru, having then been nourished by the splendor of Nārāyaṇa,
he became possessed of great majesty and was further endowed with strength.
O King, while his sons were digging, Dhundhu, who was hidden within the sand, was then encountered by them as he covered the western direction.
As if overturning the worlds with the fire born from his mouth out of anger,
O best of the Bharatas, he violently discharged a great torrent of water, turbid with waves and streams, like the great ocean at the rising of the moon.
He had twenty-one thousand sons of immeasurable splendor;
however, three less than a hundred of his sons were consumed by the Rākṣasa.
Then that king of great splendor, the destroyer of Dhundhu, O Kauravya, encountered that immensely powerful Rākṣasa, Dhundhu.
Having drunk up that torrent of water, the lord of men,
like a yogin, extinguished the fire with water through his yogic power.
Having slain that water-demon of massive body by force,
the king, his task accomplished, showed him to Uttaṅka.
Uttanka, however, granted a boon to that high-souled king:
inexhaustible wealth and invincibility against his enemies.
May there be constant delight in the Dharma, as well as an imperishable residence in heaven;
and may those sons who were slain by the Rākṣasa attain imperishable worlds in heaven.
Of him, three sons remained; Dṛḍhāśva is called the eldest, while Daṇḍāśva and Kapilāśva were the two younger princes.
Dhundhumāri was Dṛḍhāśva, and Haryaśva was his son;
Haryaśva’s son was Nikumbha, who was always devoted to the duty of a Kṣatriya.
Saṃhatāśva, the son of Nikumbha, was skilled in battle;
O King, Akṛśāśva and Kṛśāśva were the two sons of Saṃhatāśva.
His daughter was Dṛṣadvatī, the daughter of Himavat, esteemed by the virtuous;
she is renowned throughout the three worlds, as is her son, Prasenajit.
Prasenajit obtained as his wife a devoted woman named Gaurī;
however, having been cursed by her husband, she was turned into the river Bāhudā.
Her son was the great king Yuvanāśva. To Yuvanāśva was born a son, a universal monarch (cakravartin).
"What does this boy hold? Though placed [in my lap], he cries out piteously."
"O child Māndhātṛ, do not weep," said Indra, and gave him a finger;
thus was born Māndhātṛ, the king who conquered the three worlds, the son of Yuvanāśva.
Caitrarathī, the daughter of Śaśabindu, became his wife;
she was a virtuous woman named Bindumatī, peerless on earth in beauty,
and the eldest of ten thousand brothers.
In her, King Māndhātṛ begot two sons:
Purukutsa, who was a knower of dharma, and Mucukunda, the ruler of the earth.
The son of Purukutsa was Trasadasyu, the lord of the earth;
then, born of Narmadā, his son was Saṃbhūta.
The heir of Saṃbhūta was Sudhanvan, the crusher of enemies;
the son of Sudhanvan is remembered as Viṣṇuvṛddhi.
The kings of his lineage became renowned as the Viṣṇuvṛddhas.
But these twice-born ones on the side of the Aṅgirasas were endowed with the field.
Saṃbhūta had another son, the highly illustrious Anaraṇya,
who was slain in former times by Rāvaṇa, the conqueror of the three worlds.
Trasadasyu was his son, and Haryaśva was his son;
from Haryaśva, by Dṛṣadvatī, was born a son named Sumanas.
His son was King Sudhanvan, the crusher of enemies;
and the son of Sudhanvan was the monarch named Tridhanvan.
The learned and powerful Trayyāruṇa was the son of King Tridhanvan;
he had a son, a prince of great strength named Satyavrata.
That evil-minded man created an obstacle to the marriage mantras,
for he had previously abducted the wife of another who was already married.
Out of childishness, desire, delusion, exultation, and fickleness,
he lustfully carried off the daughter of a certain city-dweller.
One day, as he was wandering through his own city, the prince, who possessed extreme valor, beheld a beautiful-eyed woman being married upon a ceremonial altar to a certain eminent Vaiśya.

The wise lord of the earth, disregarding the established boundaries of propriety, forcibly seized her who was accompanied by her husband during the seven steps and himself married her by force through the Gāndharva rite.
All the Vaiśyas, having assembled together, said this to the king:
"The maiden Vedikā has been forcibly abducted by the prince;
since the world was not protected by the king, it would surely have perished."
Neither his ancestors had ever done such a thing before, nor would anyone do it in times of distress;
yet, O King, because of that reprehensible deed committed by Kumāra,
King Trayyāruṇa abandoned him due to the stake of unrighteousness.
Filled with wrath and crying out repeatedly, "Begone!", his father Sūryāruṇa abandoned him who was thus joined with unrighteousness.
Abandoned, he said to his father again and again, "Where shall I go?
Then the father said to him, "Live among the outcaste dog-cookers;
O defiler of the family, I have no need for a son like you today."
Thus addressed, he departed from the city at his father’s word;
and the venerable seer Vasiṣṭha did not restrain him.
But that hero Satyavrata, O dear one, having been abandoned by his father, lived near the dwellings of the outcaste dog-cookers; his father, too, went to the forest.
Then, in that realm, Indra did not send rain for a long time;
because of the king’s failure to deliberate and his abandonment of the prince, Indra did not send rain.
When twelve years had passed and his progeny was destroyed,
and when the utterances of *svāhā*, *svadhā*, and even *vaṣaṭ* no longer existed,
then the destruction of Dharma occurred within the kingdom of that monarch.
O Indra among kings, twelve years passed in that manner through that very unrighteousness.
Having entrusted his wives to the care of Viśvāmitra in that region,
the great ascetic practiced intense penance on the shore of the ocean.
At that very time, Viśvāmitra’s four sons, who were learned in the Vedas, were tormented by hunger.
When the great-souled Viśvāmitra had gone far away for the sake of asceticism,
O Bhārata, they all spoke to their mother with palms joined in reverence.
"O mother, if it pleases you, let us live by selling our son;
otherwise, we shall all perish, tormented by hunger. Sell our son and live until the father's return."
"When total ruin has arisen, a man gives up half;
with the remaining half he accomplishes his purpose—such is the ancient tradition."
One should abandon an individual for the sake of the family; one should abandon a family for the sake of the village;
one should abandon a village for the sake of the country; and one should abandon everything for the sake of the self.
Therefore, O mother, sell your children and live as you please;
otherwise, we shall all go to our death along with you.
In Ayodhyā, all the high-souled and most eminent men, being contemplative,
accepted everyone who approached them for the purpose of becoming their servants.
Therefore, O Mother, sell me first and eat my elder brother;
afterwards, sell her and all the rest. Otherwise, if Indra does not send rain, his wife will bind our middle son, the legitimate one, by the neck.
For the sake of supporting the remainder, he indeed sold [himself] for a hundred cows.
But seeing that son of the great seer bound by the neck and being sold,
O Bhārata, the righteous prince caused him to be released.
The mighty-armed Satyavrata provided for his maintenance,
both for the sake of pleasing Viśvāmitra and out of compassion.
Then, out of great wrath, Vasiṣṭha mentally performed a great vow;
by that act, the great ascetic became known as Gālava because of his constricted throat.
O dear one, that great ṛṣi Kauśika was then liberated by that hero.
Vaiśampāyana said: But Satyavrata, remaining steadfast in discipline, supported Viśvāmitra’s wife out of devotion, compassion, and his promise.
Having killed deer, boars, and wild buffaloes,
he tied up that meat in the vicinity of Viśvāmitra’s hermitage.
Having undertaken a secret vow and the twelve-year initiation,
he lived there by his father's command after the king had departed for the forest.
And because of his relationship as sacrificial priest and preceptor, the sage Vasiṣṭha protected Ayodhyā, the kingdom, and likewise the inner apartments.
But Satyavrata, whether out of childishness or by the force of destiny,
constantly harbored excessive resentment toward Vasiṣṭha.
But the sage Vasiṣṭha did not restrain his beloved son, who had then been banished from the kingdom by his father, for there was indeed a specific reason.
The completion of the marriage mantras occurs at the seventh step;
therefore, Satyavrata did not take her hand at the seventh step.
Knowing that Vasiṣṭha did not protect him despite knowing the Dharma, O Bhārata,
Satyavrata then conceived anger toward Vasiṣṭha in his mind.
Out of regard for his virtue, the venerable Vasiṣṭha then performed that act;
however, Satyavrata did not perceive that secret deed of his.
Because of that dissatisfaction which the high-souled father felt,
the subduer of Pāka did not send rain for twelve years.
Therefore, by now carrying out that initiation which is so difficult to bear on this earth,
and by accomplishing that purpose,
O dear one, that atonement for the lineage has indeed been performed on this earth.
The venerable Vasiṣṭha did not restrain him when he was abandoned by his father;
for such was the thought of the sage: "I myself shall consecrate his son."
O King, that powerful Satyavrata, having undertaken that great vow of silence, maintained that initiation for twelve years; meanwhile,
meat was unavailable for the high-souled Vasiṣṭha.
That prince beheld a cow that milks all desires.
O Janamejaya, overcome by anger, delusion, fatigue, and hunger, the king, having fallen into ten states of unrighteousness, struck her.
One who is intoxicated, one who is negligent, one who is insane, one who is exhausted, one who is angry, one who is hungry,
one who is in haste, one who is afraid, one who is greedy, and one who is lustful— these ten [should not eat meat].
And they [ate] the meat themselves as well as that of Viśvāmitra’s sons.
Having heard that, Vasiṣṭha fed him and became enraged at him.
But the enraged Blessed One spoke these words to the son of the king:
Vasiṣṭha said,
"O cruel one, I could cause your iron stake to fall."
If these two pegs of yours were not made again.
"Due to the dissatisfaction of your father, the killing of your teacher's milch cow, and the consumption of meat not consecrated by sprinkling, you have committed a threefold transgression."
Seeing that he had three such spikes, the great ascetic said, "He is Triśaṅku";
thus he is remembered as Triśaṅku.
When Viśvāmitra had undertaken the maintenance of his wives,
the sage, being pleased, granted a boon to Triśaṅku; then,
being invited to choose a boon, the prince chose his preceptor as the boon.
When that twelve-year fear of drought had passed, the sage, having been thus entreated that he might go to heaven with his body,
consecrated him in the kingdom and performed the sacrifice for him.
Having consecrated him in the ancestral kingdom, the sage Kauśika, while the deities and Vasiṣṭha looked on, caused that sage to perform the sacrifice.
Then the Lord, of great ascetic power, caused him to ascend to heaven in his physical body;
he raised him to heaven with his body intact.
His wife, born of the Kekaya lineage, was named Satyarathā.
She gave birth to a son, the stainless Hariścandra.
That King Hariścandra is remembered as Traiśaṅkava;
he was renowned as a universal monarch (samrāṭ) who performed the Rājasūya sacrifice.
The son of Hariścandra was the renowned Rohita,
by whom this city of Rohitapura was built for the sake of securing his kingdom.
Having ruled the kingdom and likewise protected his subjects, that royal sage,
realizing the worthlessness of saṃsāra, gave that city to the twice-born.
Harita was the son of Rohita, and Cañcu is called Hārīta.
Vijaya and Sudeva were the two sons of Cañcu;
because he was the conqueror of all the Kṣatriyas, he was remembered as Vijaya.
Ruru’s son was Ruruka, who was skilled in the duties and purposes of kings;
from him Harita was born, likewise a righteous soul in the world.
Rohita’s son was Vṛka, and from Vṛka Bāhu was born.
Together with the Śakas, Yavanas, Kāmbojas, Pāradas, and Pahlavas,
the Haihayas and Tālajaṅghas expelled that king;
for, my dear, he was not exceedingly righteous, as he lived in a Dharma-yuga.
Sagara was born as the son of Bāhu together with the embryo;
having reached the hermitage of Aurva, he was protected by the descendant of Bhṛgu.
And having obtained the Āgneya weapon from Bhārgava, King Sagara conquered the earth after slaying the Tālajaṅghas along with the Haihayas.
O best of the Kurus, Acyuta, the knower of dharma, abolished the religious practices of the Śakas, the Pahlavas, the Kṣatriyas, and the Pāradas.
Janamejaya said:
How was that Sagara born together with poison, O infallible one?
And for what purpose [was he born] among the Kṣatriyas of great power, such as Śakra and the others?
"O one rich in asceticism, tell me all this in detail: why did the steadfast king, though enraged, cast aside the duty appropriate to his lineage?"
Vaiśampāyana said: "O dear one, O lord of the people, while Bāhu was addicted to vices, his kingdom was indeed seized by the Haihayas, the Tālajaṅghas, and the Śakas."
The Yavanas, Pāradas, Kāmbojas, Pahlavas,
Khaśas, Kāti-sarpas, Māhiṣikas, Pāradāṣṭaṅkaṇas, and Śakas—
these five tribes indeed exerted their prowess for the sake of the Haihayas.
Then, having been deprived of his kingdom, that king Bāhu went to the forest;
followed by his wife, he cast off his life-breaths in the woods while suffering in grief.
When that aged man had reached his end, his wife was about to follow him in death;
however, Aurva, knowing himself to be possessed of offspring, restrained her.
His Yādava wife, who was pregnant, followed behind him.
It is said that poison had previously been administered to her by her co-wife.
Having prepared her husband's funeral pyre in the forest, she ascended it;
but Aurva Bhārgava, O dear one, restrained her out of compassion.
And in his hermitage, she gave birth to that fetus, which had been discharged along with the poison itself,
as a mighty-armed king named Sagara.
But Aurva, having performed for that high-souled one the birth-rites and other ceremonies,
and having taught him the Vedas and the Shastras,
then bestowed upon him the Agneya weapon, O fortunate ones, which is difficult even for the immortals to withstand.
Endowed with that power of weapons and physical strength,
he swiftly slaughtered the Haihayas in battle like the enraged Rudra slaughtering animals;
and he, the best among the famous, acquired fame throughout the worlds.
Then the king resolved to utterly exterminate the Śakas, Yavanas, Kāmbojas, Pāradas, and Pahlavas as well.
Being slaughtered by the heroic and high-souled Sagara,
they sought refuge with Vasiṣṭha and prostrated themselves before that wise sage.
Then Vasiṣṭha, of great splendor, having seen them,
granted them assurance of safety and restrained Sagara by means of a solemn agreement.
Having heard his own vow and the words of his preceptor, Sagara indeed destroyed their dharma and caused them to assume different disguises.
Having shaved half of the heads of the Śakas, he released them;
he did the same for all the heads of the Yavanas and the Kambojas.
The Pāradas were made to go with disheveled hair, while the Pahlavas were made to wear beards;
by that great-souled one, they were deprived of the study of the Vedas and the utterance of the vaṣaṭ-call.
The Śakas, Yavanas, Kāmbojas, and Pāradas, O lord of the people, as well as the Kolisarpas, Māhiṣakas, Darvas, Colas, and Keralas.
All those Kṣatriyas, O dear one, have had their dharma cast aside by the high-souled Sagara, O King, according to the word of Vasiṣṭha.

The Khaśas, Śārās, Cīnas, Madras, Kiṣkindhakas,
as well as the Kauntalas, Vaṅgas, Śālvas, and Kauṅkaṇakas—
having conquered this earth, that king was a victor through righteousness.
Having been initiated for the horse sacrifice, he searched for a horse.
As he was leading it, that horse was carried away near the shore in the south-eastern ocean and made to enter the earth;
while the animal was thus released for the sacrifice, Purandara seized the horse.
Having seized him near Kapila and bound him, he returned again to the city.
The sixty thousand sons of Sumati, arrogant yet obedient to their father’s command, were intent on guarding the horse;
then the king had that region dug up by his sons.
Then, as that great ocean was being dug there, they approached that primordial Being, the divine Hari, Kṛṣṇa, the Lord of Creatures—
Viṣṇu, who at that time was sleeping there in the form of Kapila.
Searching for the horse, they dug up the earth on all sides;
in the north-eastern direction, near the Kapila fire, they beheld the horse.
"This horse-thieving thief sits here with eyes closed;
let him be killed, let this sinner be killed!"— thus shouting, sixty thousand men struck the sage with blows from their fists, whereupon the sage opened his eyes.
Likewise, [he saw] Nārāyaṇa, the creator of all beings and the one to be attained.
Having approached him, saying "This is that very thief," he cried, "Seize him! Bind this evil-minded stealer of our horse!"
Then, all those sons of Sagara, impelled by Time, raised their nooses and advanced to seize that one of great splendor;
seeing him, all the Sāgaras fled while still armed.
O Great King, as he awoke, all were consumed by the splendor arising from his eyes, yet four remained as survivors.
Barhaketu, Suketu, King Bhāradratha,
Śūra, and Pañcajana were the kings who perpetuated his lineage.
Having then commanded Aṃśumat, the infallible one, to prepare a vessel for the sake of the horse,
he remained right there, consecrated and waiting.
Having followed the path of the ancestors, he beheld the Lord Hari;
bowing his head to that God, he stood before him with humble devotion.
And the Blessed Lord Hari Nārāyaṇa granted him a boon.
"An inexhaustible lineage for Ikṣvāku and an undying fame as well"—
having granted this, O great king, that blessed Lord then gave the excellent horse to Sagara.
The Lord [granted] a son, the ocean, and likewise imperishable residence in heaven.
He also attained imperishable worlds for his sons who had been slain by his glance.
And the Ocean, taking up an offering of water, paid homage to that lord of the earth;
indeed, he obtained the state of being the ocean through that deed of his.
He obtained that horse for the horse-sacrifice from the ocean;
it is heard by us that he of great renown performed a hundred horse-sacrifices and had sixty thousand sons.
Janamejaya said:
O twice-born one, how were the heroic sons of Sagara born, those sixty thousand mighty and valiant ones? By what ordinance did they come into being?
Vaiśampāyana said:
Sagara had two wives whose sins had been burnt away by ascetic penance;
the elder was the daughter of the king of Vidarbha, renowned by the name Keśinī.
But his younger wife, who was supremely virtuous,
the daughter of Ariṣṭanemi, was peerless on earth in beauty;
listen, O lord of men, to the boon that Aurva granted to those two.
"Let one woman choose sixty thousand swift sons, and let another choose a single son to carry on the lineage; let her choose as she desires."
Thereupon, one greedy woman chose many brave sons, while another chose a single heir to the lineage; then the sage said, "So be it."
Keśinī gave birth to Asamañja as her son from Sagara;
he became the king named Pañcajana, who was possessed of great strength. It is heard in the sacred tradition that the other wife gave birth to a gourd filled with seeds.
Therein, sixty thousand embryos, each the size of a sesame seed,
came into being at the proper time and grew according to their ease.
Then, O King, they placed those embryos in jars filled with clarified butter,
and he assigned as many nurses as there were embryos for their nourishment.
Then, after ten months had passed, those princes were born in due order at the proper time, increasing the joy of Sagara.
O King, lord of the earth, sixty thousand sons were thus born to that monarch from within a gourd by means of Śukra.
When those great-souled ones had entered the splendor of Nārāyaṇa,
there was born a single son named Pañcajana who became king.
They call him Asamañja; his son was Aṃśumān.
Pañcajana’s son was the heroic one named Aṃśumān.
His son was Dilīpa, renowned as Khaṭvāṅga.
O sinless one, having come here from heaven and obtained life for but a moment,
you have by means of your intellect and truthfulness brought the three worlds into harmony.
The heir of Dilīpa was the great king Bhagīratha,
that lord who brought down Gaṅgā, the best of rivers;
he was illustrious, highly fortunate, and possessed prowess equal to Śakra.
He brought her to the ocean and ordained her as his daughter.
Therefore, she is called Bhāgīrathī Gaṅgā by those who investigate the lineages.
King Śruta was the son of Bhagīratha, as he is widely renowned;
and Nābhāga, the most righteous of men, was the son of Śruta.
Ambarīṣa, the son of Nābhāga, was the father of Sindhudvīpa;
and the powerful Ayutājit was the heir of Sindhudvīpa.
The son of Ayutājit was the highly illustrious Ṛtapaṇa,
a powerful king who was a friend of Nala and possessed knowledge of the secret of divine dice.
The son of Ṛtapaṇa was the lord of the earth Ārtapaṇi;
his son was King Sudāsa, who became a friend of Indra. The son of Sudāsa was the monarch named Saudāsa.
He was indeed known as Kalmāṣapāda, and he became [known] by the name Mitrasaha.
The highly resplendent Vasiṣṭha begot Aśmaka in the wife of Kalmāṣapāda for the sake of increasing the Ikṣvāku lineage.
From Aśmaka was born Kārūṣa, and Mūlaka was his son.
The righteous King Śataratha was also the son of Mūlaka.
From that Chataratha was born the powerful King Elabila;
the illustrious and majestic Vṛddhaśarmā was the son of Elabila.
Dala’s son was also born from him, the king Śala;
that righteous-souled one was named Ūrṇa, and he indeed became the son of Śala.
Viśvasaha was his son, whom the daughter of his father begot.
His son was named Rajas, and his son was Śṛṅkhala.
Kalmāṣapāda’s son was renowned as Sarvakarman,
and Anaraṇya was the son of Sarvakarman.
The son of Anaraṇya was Nighna, and Nighna had two sons,
Anamitra and Raghu, who were the most excellent among the best of kings.
Anamitra’s son was Stamba, and Śaṅkhaṇa was his son. Anamitra’s son was the righteous and learned Duliduha;
his son was Dilīpa, the great-grandfather of Rāma.
To Dilīpa, who possessed long arms, was born a son named Raghu.
In Ayodhyā, there was a great king named Raghu of immense strength.
From Raghu was born Aja, and likewise from Aja was born Daśaratha.
From Daśaratha was born Rāma, who delighted in righteousness and possessed great fame.
A son was born to Rāma, widely renowned as Kuśa;
Atithi was born from Kuśa, and Niṣadha was his son.
Nala was the son of Niṣadha, while Nabha was the son of Nala; Puṇḍarīka was the son of Nabha, and Kṣemadhanvan is recorded as his successor.
The son of Kṣemadhanvan was the powerful Devānīka;
the lordly son of Devānīka was named Ahīnagu.
The heir of Devānīka was indeed the powerful Ahīnagu.
The heir of Ahīnagu was the king named Sahasvān.
From Sudhanvan was born a son, King Nala;
that righteous-souled one was indeed named Uktha, who became the son of Nala.
And Vajranābha was the son of that great-souled Uktha.
Pāriyātra was of great fame, and Nala was his son.
His son was the learned Śaṅkha, who was known as Dhyuṣitāśva.
The learned King Viśvasaha was indeed the son of Dhyuṣitāśva.
Hiraṇyanābha was the son of Kauśalya and was most devoted to Brahman;
his son was Puṣpa, and his son was the learned Arthasiddhi.
Sudarśana was his son; from Sudarśana came Agnivarṇa;
Agnivarṇa’s son was Śīghra, and Maru was the son of Śīghra.
Maru, however, having applied himself to yoga, established himself on the island of Kalāpa.
That renowned Maru had a son, King Bṛhadbala;
Prasusruta was the son of Maru, and Susandhi was his offspring.
Susaṃdhi’s son was Marṣa, known by the name Sahasra;
Sahasra’s son was the king named Viśrutavat.
O bull of the Bharatas, two Nalas are celebrated in the Purāṇa.
And he who was the son of Vīrasena, the upholder of the Ikṣvāku lineage.
Those born of the Ikṣvāku lineage have been primarily celebrated here;
these kings of great splendor belong to the dynasty of Vivasvat.
By correctly reciting this creation of the Sun, Vivasvat,
the divine Lord of Śrāddha and bestower of nourishment upon all creatures,
one attains union with the Sun, Vivasvat.
He becomes free from evil, free from passion, and indeed long-lived.

transliterated by Horst Brinkhaus.
Janamejaya said:
O foremost of Brahmins, I wish to hear how Vivasvat, the Āditya, came to possess the nature of the deity of the Śrāddha, as well as the supreme rules for the Śrāddha,
the original creation of the ancestors (pitṛs), and who these ancestors are traditionally held to be.
And thus have we heard it being told by the twice-born:
"The ancestors dwelling in heaven are indeed the deities even of the gods.
Those who know the gods have said this; I desire to understand this.
Whatever groups have been described, and whatever their supreme power may be,
and how we have performed the śrāddha so that it truly gratifies the ancestors.
For by what means do the gratified ancestors indeed unite one with the highest good?
This supreme creation of the ancestors I truly wish to hear.
Vaiśampāyana said:
"Indeed, I shall relate to you the supreme creation of the ancestors,
as it was told by Mārkaṇḍeya to Bhīṣma when he questioned him."
For in the past, Dharmarāja likewise asked this very same question of him as he lay upon his bed of arrows— the very question that you now ask me.
I shall relate that to you in due order, just as it was proclaimed by Bhīṣma,
sung by Sanatkumāra in response to the inquiry of Mārkaṇḍeya.
But Bhīṣma spoke this to Dharmarāja, O Acyuta.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"O knower of dharma, how is nourishment obtained by one who desires nourishment?"
This has been told; I wish to know: by doing what does one not grieve?
Bhīṣma said:
Indeed, he who pleases the ancestors with śrāddha rites— which yield the fruits of all desires—
and who is devoted to them, self-restrained, and performs the śrāddha, rejoices both in this world and after death.
O Lord Yudhiṣṭhira, the ancestors bestow prosperity upon one who desires righteousness, one who desires offspring, and one who desires nourishment.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"The ancestors of some dwell in heaven, while those of others are in hell;
for it is said that the fruit born of action is inevitably experienced by living beings."
And those desiring rewards perform the ancestral rites (śrāddha) without doubt,
always directing them toward the father, the father’s father,
and likewise the father’s grandfather, through the three funeral cakes (piṇḍas).
How do those funeral offerings (śrāddha), once given, reach the ancestors?
And how are they capable of giving back the fruit [of the gift] while residing in hell? Who indeed are these ancestors, and who else are they; whom, then, do we worship?
Furthermore, we do not know which worlds have appeared again;
we have also heard that even the gods worship the ancestors in heaven.
O one of great splendor, I wish to hear this in detail.
May you, O one of immeasurable intellect, relate this story as to how what is given indeed serves for the deliverance of the ancestors here.
Bhīṣma said:
"In this regard, O subduer of enemies, I shall relate to you according to the truth who those ancestors of yours were, whom we ourselves worship again."
Indeed, this was sung by my father in the past when he had departed to another world.
At the time of the ancestral rite for my father, a funeral cake (piṇḍa) was prepared by me;
my father, having pierced the earth with his hand, asked for it.
With his hand filled with ornaments and bristling with armlets,
and with the surface of his fingers and palm red, he appeared just as I had seen him before.
Having decided that this was not seen as the prescribed ritual procedure,
I then offered the funeral cake upon the kusha grass itself, without further hesitation.
Then, O best of the Bharatas, my father, being well-pleased and delighted with me, spoke these sweet words, O sinless one.
Through you, my son— virtuous, knower of dharma, and wise— I have become possessed of an heir and have achieved my purpose both in this world and the next.
Just as the protector of Dharma obtains a reward,
so too, O fool of firm vows, does the non-protector incur the fruit of evil;
and this inquiry was put forth by me for the sake of testing you.
And you are able, O sinless one, to establish the order of things among all phenomena for the sake of the world.
For whatever standard a king establishes regarding the practice of dharma,
the subjects always follow that standard of conduct.
And by you, O best of the Bharatas, the eternal Vedic laws have been established as authority,
and incomparable joy has been bestowed upon me.
Therefore, being well-pleased with you, I grant you an unsurpassed boon out of affection; accept it, for it is difficult to find even in the three worlds.
Death shall have no power over you as long as you wish to live;
only after obtaining your permission will death prevail over you.
Or what further supreme boon do you desire that I may grant you?
Speak it, O best of the Bharatas, whatever dwells in your mind.
When he had spoken thus, I saluted him with palms joined in reverence and said,
"O best of beings, since you are pleased with me, I have indeed accomplished my purpose."
If, however, O one of great splendor, I deserve further favor from you,
I wish to ask a certain question that you yourself might explain.
That righteous-souled one said to me, "Speak, Bhishma, whatever you desire;
O dear one, O Bharata, I shall sever the doubt concerning that which you ask of me."
O dear one, having become curious at that time, I questioned him even as he had vanished there and departed for the world of the virtuous.
It is heard that there are Pitṛs who are gods, and even deities of the gods;
whether they are those Pitṛs or others, whom indeed shall we worship?
And how is it that the śrāddha offered by us truly delights the ancestors who have gone to another world, O dear one? What indeed is the fruit of the śrāddha?
Which worlds indeed do they worship— the worlds with their gods, men, and dānavas,
along with yakṣas, uragas, gandharvas, kinnaras, and mahoragas?
Herein lies my intense doubt and my great curiosity.
Tell that to me, O knower of dharma, for you are considered by me to be omniscient.
Having heard these words of Bhīṣma,
his father Śaṃtanu spoke:
"O Bhārata, I shall tell you in brief that which you ask of me."
O sinless one, listen with a concentrated mind to the cause of the ancestors in the Śrāddha rite, the fruit of what is given, and how the ancestors themselves originated— hear all of this.
O dear one, the sons of the Primordial God are the Pitṛs, the deities in heaven; indeed,
the worlds— including gods, humans, and Dānavas, along with Yakṣas, Rākṣasas, Gandharvas, Kiṃnaras, and Mahoragas— worship them.
"And having been nourished by the ancestral offerings (śrāddha), they indeed nourish in turn the world together with its gods and gandharvas; such is the instruction of Brahmā."
Worship those highly fortunate ones with śrāddha offerings, being diligent and faithful;
they, who bestow the fruits of all desires, will provide for your welfare.
O Bhārata, when they are propitiated by you through the recitation of their names, lineages, and other details, they will nourish us as well, even though we reside in heaven.
But Mārkaṇḍeya will tell you all the rest;
for he, O Bhārgava, is devoted to his ancestors and is one who has realized the self.
"And having appeared today at my sacrifice for the sake of showing me favor,
he said, 'Ask this illustrious one,' and then vanished."

transliterated by Horst Brinkhaus,

Version dated January 13, 2001:
Bhīṣma said:
Then, at his word, I, being composed, [approached] Mārkaṇḍeya.
I asked that very same question which my father was previously asked by me.
That righteous-souled Mārkaṇḍeya, of great asceticism, said to me:
"O Bhīṣma, O sinless one, listen with a disciplined mind; I shall speak to you according to the truth."
For by me too, through my father’s grace, O Lord, long life was indeed obtained,
as well as supreme fame in the world, solely through devotion to my father.
Thus, at the end of the eon, during a period of many thousands of years, I ascended Mount Meru and performed austerities that were exceedingly difficult to practice.
Then, on one occasion, I saw a great celestial chariot approaching from the north of the mountain, illuminating the sky with its radiance.
And there I beheld a person the size of a thumb, lying down with blazing splendor, like fire placed within fire.
Having paid homage to that Lord and bowed my head in prostration,
I worshipped him with water for the feet and the arghya offering as he sat within his celestial chariot.
And I asked that invincible one: "How may we know you, O Lord?
For it is my conviction that you are indeed a deity among the gods."
That righteous-souled one said to me, O sinless one, as if smiling:
"Your asceticism has not been well-practiced, since you do not recognize me."
In an instant, assuming another unsurpassed form, he appeared such that no man had ever been seen by me before in any place with such a beauty.
That radiant one spoke to me again with sweet words:
"O Brahmin, I shall grant you that which you desire for the sake of satisfying your curiosity.
Sanatkumāra said:
"Know me, O Lord, to be the mind-born first-born son of Brahmā,
produced through the power of asceticism, and whose nature consists of the qualities of Nārāyaṇa."
O Bhārgava, may you be blessed; I am he who was known in the Vedas of old as Sanatkumāra. What desire of yours shall I fulfill?
But those other sons of Brahmā who were younger than I are my seven invincible brothers, whose lineages remain established.
Marīci, the venerable Atri, Pulastya, Pulaha, Kratu,
Aṅgiras, and Vasiṣṭha— these seven are the sons of Brahmā.
Kratu, Vasiṣṭha, Pulaha, Pulastya, Atri, and likewise Aṅgiras.
But Marīci, likewise wise and honored by gods and gandharvas,
supported these three worlds, which are worshipped by both gods and dānavas.
But we, O great sage, though having established ourselves in our own selves according to the dharma of ascetics, nevertheless continue to follow the dharma of progeny and the pursuit of desire.
"Know me, O Kumāra, to be exactly as I have arisen;
therefore, this name 'Sanatkumāra' has been established for me."
"Through devotion to me, you have performed austerities out of a desire for my vision;
here you have seen me. What wish of yours shall I fulfill?"
When the Eternal One had spoken thus, I replied to him;
permitted by the Blessed One, O Bhārata, may he be pleased with me.

Then, O sinless Bhīṣma, I asked that eternal one about this very matter— the creation of the ancestors and the fruit of the śrāddha— and he, the Lord of the Gods, severed my doubt when questioned by me.
At the conclusion of our many years of conversation, he spoke to me with a joyful heart:
"O brahmin-sage, I take delight in you; hear everything exactly as it is."
"O Bhārgava, Brahmā created the gods with the thought, 'They shall worship me';
yet, seeking rewards, they abandoned him and worshipped their own selves."
Cursed by Brahmā, those fools became deprived of their senses and lost consciousness;
they understood nothing at all, and consequently, the world fell into confusion.
They all bowed down again and entreated the Grandfather for the sake of favoring the worlds; then the Lord spoke to them.
"Perform indeed an expiation, for you have committed an act of transgression;
inquire of your sons, and from them you shall obtain knowledge."
For the purpose of performing an act of expiation, they questioned their sons like those in distress; then those sons, with disciplined minds, explained it to them.
Those who know the Dharma, who are skillful and truly possessors of insight, always prescribe expiations for misdeeds born of speech, mind, and action.
Then those sons of the gods, who knew the true nature of expiation and had regained their composure, were told by their sons: "O dear sons, you may go."
Cursed indeed by those words of their son, the gods approached the Grandfather to have their doubt severed.
Then the god said to them: "You are indeed exponents of the Veda;
therefore, what you have been told by them is so, and not otherwise."
"You shall become gods who are the creators of their bodies,
while they, being the bestowers of knowledge, are undoubtedly your fathers."
Understand that you are their fathers and they are yours;
O dwellers of heaven, realize that you are both gods and ancestors.
Then those inhabitants of heaven, their doubts severed by Brahmā, returned once more and spoke to their sons with mutual joy.
"You are indeed our fathers, by whom we have been awakened.
O knowers of dharma, what is your desire? What boon may be granted to you?
And whatever has been spoken by you is exactly so; it cannot be otherwise."
And since you have indeed called us "little sons," therefore you shall become our fathers; of this there is no doubt.
Whoever, having satisfied the ancestors with śrāddha offerings, shall perform certain other rites,
the rākṣasas, dānavas, and nāgas shall obtain the fruit thereof.
And the ancestors, nourished by the faithful performers of ancestral rites, shall eternally cause the imperishable Soma to increase as it is being replenished by you.
Soma, nourished by those who perform the ancestral rites (śrāddha), will nourish the world—
comprising oceans, mountains, and forests, and filled with all things moving and stationary.
Those men who perform ancestral rites (śrāddha) desiring prosperity,
to them the ancestors will always grant prosperity as well as progeny.

And those who offer three rice-balls at a *śrāddha* ceremony according to name and lineage— the ancestors, together with the grandfathers, being honored by that gift of *śrāddha*, will constantly sustain them wherever they may be.
"Thus was the command formerly given by Brahmā, the Supreme Lord;
O dwellers of heaven, let those words become true today:
that we shall all be both sons and fathers to one another."
Sanatkumāra said:
These ancestors are indeed gods, and these gods are likewise ancestors;
for they are each other's ancestors—both gods and ancestors.
Chapter 13,
transliterated by Horst Brinkhaus,
proof-read by Horst Brinkhaus.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Having been addressed thus by the Blessed One, the radiant God of gods, I—
Sanatkumāra, moreover, questioned the imperishable God once again.
O Gāṅgeya, subduer of enemies, listen to me as I relate from the beginning everything in its entirety regarding that doubt concerning the Blessed One, the foremost of the immortals.
How many indeed are the classes of ancestors, and in which world do those classes abide?
O best of gods, they are the gods who increase the power of Soma.
Sanatkumāra said: O best of those who recite prayers, these seven groups of ancestors (pitṛ-gaṇas) are remembered as residing in heaven;
four of them indeed possess form, while three of them are formless.
I shall proclaim their world and its creation; listen to that, O ascetic, in detail, along with their power and greatness.
Those three supreme hosts who bear the very form of Dharma—I shall proclaim their names and their worlds; listen to that.
The worlds known as Sanātanas, where the radiant ones dwell—
those formless hosts of Pitṛs are indeed the sons of Prajāpati.
O best of the twice-born, those known as the Vairājas are the sons of Virāja;
the hosts of gods worship them with rites prescribed by the sacred ordinances.
Swift as thought, subsisting on *svadhā*, and endowed with all objects of desire,
these high-souled ones indeed abandon their yoga and,
having fallen from yoga, attain eternal worlds.
Furthermore, at the end of a thousand yugas, those who expound the Veda are born again.
Having regained that memory, those perfected ones attain again the unsurpassed Sāṃkhya-yoga and proceed to the goal of yoga, from which return is difficult to find.
These, O dear one, are the ancestors who increase the power of yogis;
they were indeed those who formerly nourished the moon by means of their yogic strength.
Therefore, O best of the twice-born, funeral offerings (śrāddha) should be given to yogins;
this indeed is the foremost and unsurpassed ritual for the drinkers of Soma.
The mental daughter of these [mountains] was named Menā,
the excellent wife of Himavat, the great mountain, from whom Maināka is said to have been born.
The son of Maināka was the illustrious great mountain named Krauñca,
a preeminent peak, white and adorned with various jewels.
The king of mountains begot three daughters upon Menā:
Aparṇā, Ekaparṇā, and the third, Ekapāṭalā.
Performing a most great penance difficult even for gods and dānavas to practice,
those three women scorched the worlds, both the stationary and the moving.

Ekaparṇā resided at a banyan tree, and Ekapāṭalā at a trumpet-flower tree; while Aparṇā, having no such shelter, performed her austerities without a dwelling for ten thousand years— a penance difficult even for gods and dānavas to practice.
Saikaparṇā subsisted on a single leaf as her food,
and Ekapāṭalā likewise took only a single *pāṭala* flower.
When a full thousand years had passed, the two of them took food twice [a day].
There, one remained without food; her mother forbade her, distressed by maternal affection, restraining her with the words, "O, do not! (umā).
Thus addressed by her mother,
that goddess of difficult conduct became renowned throughout the three worlds as the beautiful Umā.
In this very way, she shall be renowned here by that name as Yogadharmiṇī;
and this world, O Bhārgava, shall remain as the realm of these three maidens for as long as the earth endures, consumed by their ascetic power.
All those three were embodiments of austerity, endowed with the power of yoga;
they were all indeed highly fortunate, all possessed of perpetual youth,
and they were both mothers of the world and practitioners of celibacy.
And all were expounders of Brahman, and all were of perpetual chastity.
Umā was the most excellent among them, the eldest, and possessed of a beautiful complexion;
endowed with the power of great yoga, she attended upon Mahādeva.
Dattaka, the son of Uśanas and a descendant of Bhṛgu, was her son. O great Brahmin, Asita’s wife, Ekaparṇā, was given to the high-souled and wise Devala, a master of yoga.
Puṣṭi was the third among those maidens, and she, a single Pāṭalā flower,
attended upon Jaigīṣavya, the son of Śataśalāka.
Of him also, Śaṅkha and Likhita are remembered as two sons not born from a womb.
Know that Jaigīṣavya likewise possessed that same single pāṭala flower;
and these two illustrious masters of yoga have now arrived.
The worlds there are named Somapadas, where the sons of Marīci indeed dwell as Pitṛs in heaven; the gods sustain them,
and they are all known as the Agniṣvāttas, possessed of immeasurable splendor.
The Agniṣvāttas are renowned there as the Pitṛs who are celebrated;
their mind-born daughter is the river named Acchodā,
from whom that divine lake named Acchoda originated.
Her ancestors had never before been seen by her;
yet that woman of pure smiles beheld even those formless ancestors,
who were born of their own mind, though she did not recognize them as her own kin.
Afflicted by that grief, the woman of excellent complexion became ashamed;
seeing her father, she chose Vasu, who traveled through the intermediate space—
the illustrious son of Āyu, renowned by the name Vasu.
Seated upon a celestial chariot in the sky, joined by the Apsaras Adrikā,
she— having become a wanderer at will through the fickleness of her mind—
fell from her yoga after having solicited another as her father.
She saw three celestial chariots falling, having fallen from heaven;
she saw those ancestors within them, each the size of a mote of dust.
As she was falling, she saw nearby three celestial chariots;
there she beheld her own ancestors, as minute as motes of dust,
exceedingly subtle and indistinct, like fires placed within other fires.
"Save me! cried the distressed woman as she fell headlong toward them.
Addressed by them with the words "Do not fear," she remained stationed in the sky;
then, with a piteous voice, she propitiated her own ancestors.
Your ancestors said to the maiden: "Because of your transgression, your sovereignty has been lost;
O lady of pure smiles, you fall through your own fault, having lost your sovereignty."
For by those very bodies with which the deities in heaven perform actions,
it is by those same bodies that the deities here obtain the fruit of those actions.
But for a human being, good and evil [fructify] through another body; this is the established rule. Actions bear fruit immediately in the state of divinity, or after death in the human state.
Those actions which were performed in the state of divinity remain indeed present in the human state.
Therefore, O daughter, you shall obtain the fruit of your asceticism both in this world and after death.
Thus addressed by her ancestors, she sought to appease them;
having meditated, they all, out of compassion, granted her their favor.
Knowing that this was inevitable, they then said to her:
"You shall become the offspring of that great-souled King Vasu,
who will be born among men upon the earth."
Remaining a maiden, you shall again attain your own worlds, which are difficult to reach.
"Born from the womb of a fish, you shall become the daughter of a king;
you shall give birth to a Brahmin who is the heir of Parāśara.
That brahmin seer shall divide the single Veda into four parts."
And the two sons of Mahābhiṣa, who increased the fame of Śantanu,
were Vicitravīrya, the knower of dharma, and the lord Citrāṅgada.
"O highly fortunate lady, having fathered these sons— Jyeṣṭha, Vicitravīrya, and Citrāṅgada thereafter— you shall again attain the higher worlds,
despite having reached this state through your own despicable deed."
And due to your transgression against the ancestors, you shall obtain a contemptible birth.
You shall become the daughter of that very king Adrika;
in the twenty-eighth Dvāpara age, you will be born from the womb of a fish.
Thus addressed, that maidservant then became Satyavatī,
the incomparable daughter born of a fish-womb to that king, Vasu.
That Adrikā, having become a fish at the confluence of the Gaṅgā and Yamunā,
gave birth to that daughter by means of King Vīra.
Indeed, those worlds named Baibhrāja shine beautifully in the sky.
There, the ancestors named Barhiṣadas are renowned in heaven.
All those hosts of Dānavas, Yakṣas, Gandharvas, and Rākṣasas,
as well as the Nāgas, Sarpas, and Suparṇas, meditate upon him who possesses immeasurable splendor.
These high-souled sons of the progenitor Pulastya were noble-minded,
highly fortunate, endowed with splendor, and devoted to austerity.
These three groups are declared to be auspicious, bearing the very form of Dharma. Their mental daughter is renowned by the name Pīvarī;
she is likewise Yogā, Yogapatnī, and Yogamātā.
O best among the upholders of dharma, you shall become so when the Dvāpara age arrives.
Born in the lineage of Parāśara, there will be in that age a great ascetic named Śuka, a supreme among the twice-born and a master of yoga,
who will be born from Vyāsa as if from a forest-fire, blazing like smokeless fire.
Upon that daughter of his father,
Pīvarī, he will beget a daughter and four sons who will be mighty yogācāryas.
And he had four sons, practitioners of yoga who were experts in the Vedas:
Kṛṣṇa, Gaura, Prabhu, and Śambhu; and likewise a daughter, Kṛtvī, as well as a daughter, Kīrtimatī, the sixth, who was a yoginī and a mother of yoga.
She was Kṛtī, the daughter of Kīrtimān and the mother of Yoga;
she was the mother of Brahmadatta and the queen of Aṇuha.
Having produced these [sons], that righteous-souled one, the great yogin of immeasurable intellect, having heard the teachings from his father Vyāsa— the teacher of yoga who observes the great vows—
will then go to a state from which there is no returning.
Having set out upon the path from which there is no return, endowed with the rays of the sun,
he will indeed never return again, having been consumed by the sun’s beams—
that state which is free from agitation, imperishable, and the eternal Brahman.
O Sage, those formless ancestors who bear the embodiment of dharma—
therein originated the narrative concerning the lineage of the Vṛṣṇi and Andhaka clans.

These three have been described by me; now learn from me another four, O best of the twice-born, whom I shall mention, for they are remembered as being embodied. They were born of Svadhā as the sons of Kavi, the son of Agni.
O Bhārgava, the ancestors of the Prajāpati Vasiṣṭha are known as the Sukālas; they are devoted to the celestial worlds that shine with light,
where all desires are fulfilled, and the twice-born indeed honor them.
Their mind-born daughter, named Gaurī, is renowned in heaven;
she was given into your own lineage, O twice-born one, as the queen of Śuka.
Known as Ekaśṛṅgā, she increases the fame of the Sādhyas;
having encompassed the worlds filled with light, she stands established there.

But those sons of Aṅgiras who were nourished by the Sādhyas in ancient times are known as the invited ancestors (upahūta-pitaraḥ), radiant in heaven; O dear one, the hosts of Kṣatriyas, seeking rewards, propitiate them.
The mental daughter of these was the renowned Yaśodā,
who was the wife of Viśvamahaṭ, the daughter-in-law of Vṛddhaśarman,
and the mother of the high-souled royal sage Dilīpa, O dear one.
Long ago, O dear one, during that great horse-sacrifice in the age of the gods, these verses were sung by the delighted great seers at his sacrifice.
Having thus heard of the birth of Agni from the high-souled Śāṇḍilya,
those men who behold the great-souled Dilīpa performing sacrifice while being perfectly composed, and likewise the truthful one, are conquerors of heaven.
But King Dilīpa, while performing the sacrifice, was then beheld by the wise sages;
at the final purificatory bath (*avabhṛtha*) of his horse sacrifice, he ascended to heaven together with those ancestors named Susvadhās, who were the sons of the progenitor Kardama.
The high-souled Pulaha, the bull among the twice-born, was born from him.
In the worlds, there dwell birds that move through the heavens according to their desires;
it is the hosts of Vaiśyas, O dear one, who sustain them, seeking the fruits [of their labor].
O Brahmin, their mind-born daughter was renowned by the name Virajā; she was the mother of Yayāti and the queen of Nahuṣa.
"By austerity or by effort, they are seen by one's own eye.
Thus these are the Pitṛs who are gods, and the gods who are again Pitṛs; these three groups have been declared. Now learn from me the fourth.
Those who were born from their own creative power (svadhā) were indeed the Soma-drinkers, the sons of Kavi.
The Śūdras are the sons of Hiraṇyagarbha; they indeed sustain them. Those worlds named Mānasa exist for them in heaven.
Their mind-born daughter was Narmadā, the best of rivers,
who flows toward the southern region and nourishes all living beings;
she who was the wife of Purukutsa and also the mother of Trasaddasyu.
She was the mother of Trasadasyu and the wife of Purukutsa;
she was the consort of Purukutsa and Trasadasyu was their son.
O dear one, by virtue of their acceptance [of the lineage], Manu [endures] through age after age.
When the Dharma has perished, Prajāpati causes the faithful to turn back toward it.
O best of the twice-born, because he was the first progenitor of all the ancestors,
they indeed call him Śrāddhadeva according to his own dharma.
A silver vessel, or one adorned with silver,
offered by placing the word *svadhā* before it, truly gratifies the ancestors at a *śrāddha* ceremony.
Having performed the swelling of Soma and of Vahni Vaivasvata,
one should perform the northern course [of the fire] either in the fire or, in the absence of fire, in water.
To young cows of copper-colored hue or tawny ones,
whose horns have been sprinkled with water, and to beautiful daughters-in-law who have not yet borne children, but who possess calves— these pure rice-balls (piṇḍas) should be offered.
He who pleases the ancestors with devotion, the ancestors please him in turn;
the ancestors bestow nourishment, abundant progeny,
as well as heaven, health, and whatever else is desired.
Furthermore, for one desiring prosperity or desiring progeny,
the Pitṛs and the Pitāmahas bestow prosperity, progeny,
and heaven; as well as longevity, wealth, happiness, and even health.
The grandfathers would grant with pleasure whatever else is desired;
O Sage, the rite for the ancestors is superior even to the rite for the gods,
for the ancestors are traditionally held to be the first source of nourishment for the deities.
For they are quick to find faith, free from anger, the supreme nourishment for the world, and always possessed of steadfast faith; therefore, O Bhārgava, pay homage to them.
"O brahmin-sage, you are devoted to your father and truly devoted to the virtuous; of this there is no doubt.
I shall bring about your welfare today; witness it for yourself."
O sinless Mārkaṇḍeya, I grant you divine vision along with its consciousness; listen attentively to this path.
For neither the divine course of yoga nor the supreme state of the ancestors can be seen with the fleshly eye even by a perfected being such as yourself.
Having spoken thus, that Lord of the Gods, standing before me who was present there,
bestowed upon me vision along with discernment— difficult even for the gods to obtain—
and then departed to his desired destination, blazing like a second fire.
Listen to that, O best of the Kurus, which was heard by me through the grace of that god, which is difficult for humans on earth to understand.
Chapter 14,
transliterated by Horst Brinkhaus,
proofread by Horst Brinkhaus.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
O dear one, in a former age there were twice-born sons of Bharadvāja.
Having attained the dharma of yoga, they indeed fell away because of their evil conduct.
Having fallen into corruption and deviated from the practice of yoga,
they are unconscious on the far shore of the great darkness of the mind.
Meditating on that very same goal, yet deluded as if they had lost something in the water,
they all failed to attain yoga and were joined with the law of time.
Then, O bull among men, having fallen from their yoga and dwelt for a very long time among the gods, they were born as the descendants of Kauśika in Kurukṣetra.
Wandering about practicing dharma through violence for the sake of their ancestors,
they will then again attain a degraded and contemptible rebirth.
By the grace of their ancestors and by what was performed in previous births,
mindfulness will arise for them upon attaining each of those loathsome births.
They will always be practitioners of the Dharma, composed in meditation;
thereafter, they will further attain the state of a Brahmin through their own karma.
And then they shall again attain the yoga performed in their previous births;
having once more reached perfection, they will attain the eternal state.
In this way, your intellect will repeatedly be directed toward the Dharma;
and being devoted to the yoga of the Dharma, you shall attain supreme accomplishment.
For yoga is always difficult to attain at any time for those of little wisdom; even having attained it, they destroy it through vices that lead to bitterness.
They abide only in unrighteousness and constantly afflict their teacher;
they do not beg for things that should not be begged, and they protect those who have come for refuge.
They do not despise the miserable, nor do they become intoxicated by the heat of wealth.
Restraining their diet and conduct, disciplined in their own duties,
and devoted to meditation and study, they do not seek out those who have perished.
They were never devoted to sensual enjoyments, nor did they consume meat or honey;
they were never intent on desire, nor likewise were they attendants of Brahmins.
Men who are not attached to ignoble conversation, nor likewise afflicted by indolence,
nor excessively addicted to worldly affairs, nor devoted to social gatherings— they attain yoga; for indeed, yoga is difficult to find on this earth.
Those who are tranquil, who have conquered anger, and who are free from pride and egoism—
those who observe their vows become vessels for the auspicious.
Such indeed were those brahmins at that time, my dear;
for they remembered their own faults, which were caused solely by negligence,
and remained established on the path of tranquility, devoted to meditation and study.
They quickly attain supreme peace; there is no doubt in this.
Therefore, you too, O knower of dharma, become devoted to the practice of yoga.
For, O knower of dharma, there is no dharma more distinguished than the dharma of yoga.
Practice that which is the most excellent among all dharmas, O Bhārgava.
"Through the transformation of time, by eating light food, having conquered your senses,
being devoted to that, self-restrained, and faithful, you shall attain the dharma of yoga.
Having spoken thus, the Blessed Lord vanished on the spot.
It is my conviction that eighteen years constitute a single day;
and for me, who has been worshipping the Lord of Gods, those eighteen years have indeed passed as such.
Through the grace of that god, there was then no exhaustion;
O sinless one, I felt neither hunger nor thirst, nor did I perceive the passage of time.
It was only later, from my disciple, that I became aware of the time.

When that Lord had thus vanished by his word, O All-pervading One, [the king spoke].

Then, O son of the River, I indeed beheld those Brāhmaṇas, the sons of Kauśika,
whom the Lord spoke to me at Kurukṣetra.
The seventh among them, O twice-born one, became King Brahmadatta,
renowned by the name Pitṛvartin on account of his character and conduct.
Kṛtvī, the daughter of Śuka, gave birth to that king from Aṇuha,
the best of monarchs, in Kāmpilya, the most excellent of cities.
Bhīṣma said:
O King, listen as I proclaim the lineage of that illustrious Mārkaṇḍeya of great asceticism, just as he himself spoke.
Yudhiṣṭhira said: Whose son was Aṇuha, and at what time did he appear?
He was a king, the best among the upholders of dharma, whose son was the highly illustrious one.
What was the prowess of King Brahmadatta? And how did he become the seventh among them as a lord of men?

For the Lord Śuka, whose soul is absorbed in yoga and who is worshipped by the world, would not have given his daughter Kṛtvi, the illustrious one, to one of little vigor, even though he was the powerful master.
I wish to hear this in detail, O one of great splendor;
you ought to relate that life-story of Brahmadatta.
And as those twice-born ones exist within the cycles of saṃsāra,
please tell me that which was related by Mārkaṇḍeya.
Bhīṣma said:
O King, I have heard that this lord of men was a contemporary of my royal ancestor Pratīpa.
The great king Brahmadatta was a yogi, the best among royal sages;
he understood the cries of all living beings and was devoted to the welfare of all beings.
For his friend was the highly illustrious Galava, the master of yoga,
who, having perfected his training through asceticism, established the Krama system;
and Kandarikā, whose soul was devoted to yoga, became his very own minister.
In all their various births, all of them were companions;
in seven births, those of immeasurable luster became exactly seven,
just as the highly effulgent Mārkaṇḍeya of great asceticism has declared.
O King, I shall proclaim his lineage; listen to that ancient account of the high-souled Paurava Brahmadatta.
The heir of Bṛhatkṣatra was the righteous one named Suhotra;
the heir of Suhotra was indeed Hastin by name.
By him, this city of Hastināpura was formerly built.
Hastin had three heirs who were exceedingly righteous:
Ajamīḍha, Dvimīḍha, and likewise Puramīḍha.
From Ajamīḍha and Dhūminī was born King Bṛhadiṣu.
O King, the heir of Purumitra was King Bṛhadiṣu;
the son of Bṛhadiṣu was the highly illustrious Bṛhaddhanus.
The son of Bṛhadiṣu was the renowned Bṛhaddharma.
There was a king renowned as Bṛhaddharma, who was supremely righteous.
Satyajit was his son, and Viśvajit was his offspring;
the son of Viśvajit was Senajit, the lord of the earth.
Senajit had four sons who were esteemed by the world:
Rucira, Śvetakāśya, Mahimnāra, and Vatsa; and the king of Avanti was their younger brother (parivatsaka).
The heir of Rucira was the highly illustrious Pṛthuṣeṇa;
from Pṛthuṣeṇa was born Pāra, and from Pāra, Nīpa was then born.
The illustrious son of Pāra was the highly renowned Nīpa.
O dear one, O Indra among kings, Nīpa had one hundred sons of immeasurable splendor—
heroes, mighty-armed great chariot-warriors.
All those kings were indeed known as the Nīpas.
The king who continued their lineage was Samara by name, the increaser of the glory of the Nīpas; he was a warrior whose valor was celebrated in Kāmpilya.
Samaras had three sons—Pāra, Pura, and Sadaśva—who were all deeply knowledgeable in the highest dharma; among them, Pṛthu, the son of Pāra, shone preeminently.
From Pṛthu, however, was born one named Sukṛta by virtue of his well-performed deeds;
and Vibhrāja, endowed with all virtues, was his son.
The son of Vibhrāja was the king named Aṇuha;
he, the highly illustrious husband of Kṛtvī, shone as the son-in-law of Śuka.
The son of Aṇuha was the royal sage Brahmadatta, a lord;
his son was Viṣvaksena, a subduer of enemies whose soul was absorbed in yoga.
Vibhrāja, born again here through his well-performed deeds,
was known as Viṣvaksena, the son of Brahmadatta.
O King, his two eyes were gouged out by a venerable female bird that had lived with him for a very long time in the house of Brahmadatta;
thereafter, another son was born to that Brahmadatta.
Known as Viṣvaksena, he was possessed of great strength and prowess.
Daṇḍasena, the lord of the earth, became the son of Viṣvaksena.
And there was a prince named Bhallāṭa, who was slain in former times by the son of Rādhā.
The heroic and high-souled Janamejaya, son of Daṇḍasena, who increased his lineage,
became evil-minded as the son of Bhallāṭa.
He became the king of those Nīpas, a monarch who brought about their end;
it was for his sake that all the Nīpas were destroyed by Ugrāyudha.
And that Ugrāyudha, arrogant, filled with pride, delighting in insolence, and ever devoted to unrighteousness, was slain by me in battle.
Yudhiṣṭhira said: Whose son was Ugrāyudha, and in which lineage was he born?
For what purpose was he slain by you? Tell me that.
Bhīṣma said:
The heir of Ajamīḍha was the learned King Yavīnara;
Dhṛtimān was his son, and Satyadhṛti was his son.
From Satyadhṛti was born the powerful Dṛḍhanemi;
and the son of Dṛḍhanemi was the king named Sudharmā.
Sudharman had a son, Sārvabhauma,
a lord of subjects who was then known as Sārvabhauma, the sole sovereign upon the earth.
In his great lineage was born the great delight of the Pauravas;
he had a son known by the name Rukmaratha.
The son of Rukmaratha was the king named Supārśva;
the son of Supārśva was the righteous Sumati;
and from him was born the powerful king named Saṃnati, who was possessed of great humility.
The son of that Saṃnati was the very powerful Kārta,
a disciple of the high-souled Hiraṇyanābha of Kosala; by him,
those Sāma-saṃhitās were proclaimed in twenty-four ways.
Those who sing the Sāmans are known as the Prācyasāmānas, but they are called Kārtas by name.
Then that hero Kārti, the wielder of fierce weapons and the delight of the Pauravas,
became [the father of Śikhaṇḍin], by whom, through his prowess, the great king named Nīpa, the lord of the Pañcālas and grandfather of Pṛṣata, was slain.
The heir of Ugrāyudha was the highly illustrious one named Kṣemya.
From Kṣemya came Suvīra, and from Suvīra came Nṛpañjaya;
from Nṛpañjaya came Bahuratha—these are remembered as the Pauravas.
And he, O dear one, was Ugrāyudha, evil-minded and always a creator of enmity.
Possessing a blazing discus and endowed with great strength, he became the destroyer of the Nīpas.
But Ugrāyudha was evil-minded, addicted to women, and ever wicked;
he then abducted a princess, being a violator of the wives of sages. Full of arrogance, he slew the Nīpas and other kings in battle.
When my father had passed away, he made me hear of his transgression.
O Indra among kings, while I was lying on the surface of the earth surrounded by my ministers,
a messenger of Ugrāyudha approached and spoke to me.
"O Bhishma, bull among the Kurus, today bestow upon me as my wife your illustrious mother Gandhakali, that jewel among women."
Thus, your kingdom is prosperous and your forces are likewise, without a doubt;
today you stand established in your kingdom with the fourfold army.
I shall indeed bestow upon you whatever you desire, for I am a possessor of jewels on this earth.
If you desire the welfare of the kingdom, or of your own life, or of your family, abide by my teaching; for otherwise, there is no peace for you.
Lying on a bed of straw spread upon the ground, he was addressed by him with these words, which were like a flame of fire and conveyed through a messenger.
His words scorched my body,
O Acyuta; then, having understood the intention of that evil-minded one,
I gave orders to all the commanders of the army for the battle.
O Bhārata, seeing this blazing wheel of mine, which is so difficult to conquer, the enemies flee from the battlefield at the mere sight of it.
Seeing Vicitravīrya still a child and himself dependent upon me, his soul was overwhelmed with anger, and he set his mind solely on battle.
But then, O bull among men, I was restrained by my ministers skilled in counsel, by my god-like officiating priests, and by my friends.
And I was addressed with appropriate reasons for desisting from battle by those who were affectionate and learned in the scriptures, O sinless one.
The ministers said:
"O Lord, that wicked man has already set his wheel in motion, while you are in a state of impurity;
moreover, war is never the primary course of action."
Therefore, we shall first employ conciliation, as well as generosity and sowing dissension; thereafter, being purified and having saluted the deities, [we shall proceed].
Having had the benediction performed by the Brahmins, having offered oblations into the fires and caused the twice-born to recite auspicious prayers,
and being permitted by the Brahmins, you shall indeed set forth for victory.
"One who is in a state of ritual impurity must not employ weapons, nor should he enter into battle; such is the instruction of the elders."
First by means of conciliation, bribery, and so forth, or else by sowing dissension, you shall thereafter slay that Śambara with valor, just as Maghavan [Indra] did.
"Having heard that the words of the wise— and especially those of the elderly— should be listened to at the proper time, I have desisted from this, O lord of men."
Then, O best of the Kurus, at that time those experts in the scriptures employed every stratagem, and the supreme ritual was commenced.
Even when initially entreated by those who contemplate the scriptures through means such as conciliation and the rest,
that person of evil intellect cannot be persuaded.
O dear one, that wheel which had been set in motion by him who was devoted to unrighteousness was immediately turned back by his longing for another's wife.
Indeed, there is nothing in this world so detrimental to longevity as a man's pursuit of another's wife;
yet I truly do not know whether his supreme wheel has ever turned back.
That was destroyed by its own karma and was previously censured by the virtuous.
Having performed my ablutions, equipped with a water-jar and a chariot, and having emerged from the city after the Brahmins had performed the rites for my success, I set out to fight the enemy.
Then, having come together through physical strength and the power of their weapons,
the battle lasted for three days like that between the gods and the asuras, resembling a state of madness.
Burnt by the power of my weapon at the head of the battle,
that hero, O subduer of enemies, fell facing forward, having surrendered his life.
In the meantime, my dear, after the lord of the Nīpas had been slain and King Ugrāyudha had also been killed, Pṛṣata set out from Kāmpilya.
O King, having then obtained his own ancestral kingdom of Āhicchatra with my very approval, the father of Drupada, who was of great splendor, [reigned].
From that time Drupada became king, for Drona had been defeated by him;
thereafter, having swiftly conquered Drupada in battle, Arjuna surrendered Ahicchatra along with Kampilya to Drona.
Then Drona, the best among victors, having accepted both [the kingdom and the city],
gave Kāmpilya back to Drupada, as you already know.
Thus has the lineage of Drupada, of Brahmadatta, and indeed of the hero Ugrāyudha been declared to you in its entirety.
Therefore, I shall relate to you an ancient history,
sung by Sanatkumāra to Mārkaṇḍeya when he questioned him.
O Great King, descendant of Bharata, listen to that which is the certain fruit of a well-performed śrāddha dedicated to one's ancestors across seven births.
The life stories of Sāgālava and Kaṇḍarīka,
as well as those of the three yogis who were celibate students, including Brahmadatta as the third.
Chapter 16,
transliterated by Horst Brinkhaus,
proof-read by Horst Brinkhaus.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
The world is established upon the śrāddha; from the śrāddha, yoga proceeds.
"Behold, O Bhārata, I shall describe to you the supreme fruit of the śrāddha, which was obtained by Brahmadatta throughout seven lifetimes."

For it is from that very source, O sinless one, that the understanding of dharma gradually arises; indeed, even through the hardship of performing a śrāddha for the sake of dharma, as was done in the past.

"O best of men, learn from me that which was attained by the Brahmins in the past. Then, at Kurukṣetra, I beheld seven twice-born ones who were devoted to their ancestors, who were not excessively righteous [by worldly standards], and who had been pointed out by Sanatkumāra."
With that divine eye, the Lord spoke of those whom he had previously described:
Vāgduṣṭa, Krodhana, Hiṃsra, Piśuna, Kavi,
Khasṛma, and Pitṛvartin— both by their names and according to their deeds.
O dear one, descendant of Bharata, the sons of Kauśika and the disciples of Gārgya all remained observant of their vows when their father had passed away.
By the command of that preceptor, they all then milked the milch-cow, a tawny one with a calf of the same color, which had been acquired through righteous means.
O Bhārata, as they were afflicted by hunger on the road, a cruel thought arose in them out of childishness and delusion— that very thought to harm that cow.
Then the sage Kavi and Khasṛma both entreated them, saying, "Do not do this!
yet those twice-born ones could not be restrained by the two of them at that time.
But that twice-born man among them, who was devoted to his father and constantly engaged in the daily ancestral rites,
being endowed with righteousness, spoke to all his brothers out of anger:
If it must certainly be performed for the sake of the ancestors, then let us all, being properly composed, duly perform this rite with a cow.
In this way, this cow will attain merit; there is no doubt about this.
By honoring the ancestors according to dharma, no unrighteousness shall arise in this matter.
Having said "So be it," O Bhārata, they all sprinkled the cow with water and, having offered her to the ancestors, they consumed her.
Having used the cow, they all reported it to their teacher, saying, "The cow has been killed by a tiger; please accept this calf.
Out of sincerity, that twice-born man indeed accepted the calf.
But those twice-born ones, having treated that guru improperly and with false conduct,
were all joined with death in due time when their lifespans came to an end.
Indeed, O dear one, due to their cruelty, ferocity, and lack of nobility toward their preceptor,
seven brothers were then born from the hunter as his sons— men who were fierce, devoted to violence, powerful, and high-spirited.
Having worshipped the ancestors according to dharma and having then sprinkled a cow with water, memory and self-recognition arose within them in their next birth.
Seven hunters were born in Daśārṇa who were discerning in dharma;
they were all devoted to their own duty and free from greed and falsehood.
They do only so much as is necessary for the maintenance of life;
devoted to dharma, they spend the remainder of their time contemplating their own duty.
And these, O lord of men, were their names:
Nirvaira, Nirvṛta, Kṣānta, Nirmanyu, Kṛti, Vaidhasa, and Mātṛvartin; they were hunters of supreme righteousness.
While they were living thus in the forest, O dear one, though devoted to the practice of violence,
their aged mother was honored and their father was fully satisfied.
When both mother and father were joined by the law of time,
they abandoned their bows and gave up their lives in the forest.
By virtue of that auspicious karma, those deer were born with the memory of their former lives;
agitated by fear and anxiety, they dwelt on the beautiful Kālañjara mountain.
With faces upturned, perpetually terrified, with ears pricked and eyes wide,
those deer became known by the names Paṇḍita, Ghasmara, and Nādī.
Reflecting upon that very same matter arising from their recollection of past lives,
those forest-dwellers remained patient, free from the pairs of opposites, and without possessions.
All those forest-dwellers, performers of auspicious deeds who shared in the true Dharma,
having accomplished their purpose regarding Maru, gave up their lives as ascetics who subsisted on light food.
O Bhārata, O Acyuta, the footprints of those who were accomplishing the Maru rite on Mount Kālañjara are still visible there even today.
By that auspicious deed, my dear, you have become free from all inauspiciousness;
through merit, you have come to this most excellent and auspicious birth as ruddy geese.
In a beautiful place on a river island, there were seven water-dwellers who,
having abandoned the nature of their companions, became sages practicing the Dharma.
Free from longing, free from the sense of "mine," patient, beyond dualities, without possessions, detached,
and indeed composed— these are known by the name of the Śakunas.
All those birds, practicing celibacy and living according to dharma,
being devoted to austerity and abstaining from food, gave up their lives on the riverbank.
Then those brothers were born as swans wandering in Lake Mānasa;
remembering their former births, closely united, and practicing celibacy, they were exactly seven in number.
Because the teacher was treated with false conduct out of delusion while in a human womb,
they were subsequently born in animal wombs and wandered through cyclic existence.
But when the ancestral rites had been performed by those established in their own interests,
they then attained superior knowledge and birth:
Sumanas, the sage Suvāk, Śuddha, Pañcama, and Chidradarśana.
Sunetra and Svatantra are known by name as the Śakunas.
The fifth was born among the Pañcikas; there, he was born in seven lifetimes.
The sixth, however, became Kaṇḍarīka, while the seventh was Brahmadatta.
Indeed, by virtue of that asceticism performed over seven lifetimes,
through the accomplishment of yoga, and by means of their excellent eloquence, they [attained this].
Whatever Brahman was indeed heard in former births within the houses of preceptors,
that very same Brahman remains as it is, even as one moves through the cycles of worldly existence.
All those birds lived there as celibate practitioners, moving about at will,
while constantly meditating upon the dharma of yoga.
Having reached Lake Mānasa and become water-dwelling swans,
while those birds were wandering there as companions,
the king Vibhrāja, a descendant of Puru, was the lord of the Nīpas.
Radiant in body and endowed with majesty,
the illustrious one, surrounded by his inner apartments, entered that forest.
But the independent ruddy goose, seeing the king approaching endowed with splendor, longed for him, thinking: "May I become like this."
If there is any merit whatsoever, whether from austerity or even from religious observance,
for I am indeed exhausted by this fasting and fruitless penance.
I desire the status of a king, if there be merit for me.
(Chapter 17,
