Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Then two ruddy geese, his companions, said to him:
"We two shall be your ministers, desiring your pleasure and welfare."
Having said "So be it," the mind of that one whose self was yoga then became fixed;
they thus made their agreement, and he replied with well-spoken words.
Since you, being preoccupied with sensual desires, have cast aside the dharma of yoga and instead seek an inferior boon, therefore listen to my words.
"My dear son, you shall become the king in Kāmpilya, the most excellent of cities;
and these two shall be your companions and ministers."
Having cursed and addressed them, the four egg-born ones then acted against those three who,
corrupted by their transgression, desired the kingdom.
Those three birds, having been cursed, fell from their yoga and lost their senses;
then their four companions implored them.
They showed them favor, and then Sumanas spoke to them with a gracious mind,
having been moved to favor by the request of all of them.
"The curse upon you shall have an end; there is no doubt in this.
Having fallen from here and attained human birth, you shall obtain yoga."
He will know the cries of all sentient beings and will become independent;
for we have indeed obtained this paternal favor through our own actions.
Having consecrated the cow according to the Dharma, let it be prepared for the ancestors;
may our union of knowledge be the means of yoga for us all.
And having heard this single verse from the composition of words as transmitted through another person, you shall thereafter attain yoga.

transliterated by Horst Brinkhaus,
proofread by Horst Brinkhaus.

Those seven who delight in the practice of yoga and roam in the Mānasa lake are Padmagarbha,
Aravindākṣa, Kṣīragarbha, and Sulocana.
Ūrubindu, Subindu, and Haimagarbha as the seventh—
these great-souled swans were born in the lakes of Lake Mānasa.

Then the king, resplendent with his physical form, wandered through that forest surrounded by the women of the inner apartments, like Maghavan in the Nandana grove.

and out of world-weariness, reflecting upon that very same purpose, he departed for his city.

was endowed with the virtues of goodness and character, and was always devoted to the practice of yoga.

she is Yoga, the consort of Yoga, and likewise the mother of Yoga,
just as was previously told to you by me during the accounts of the progenitors.
But King Vibhrāja, having established Aṇuha on the throne,

There, abstaining from food and subsisting on air alone, that great ascetic,
having renounced all desires, performed penance on the shore of that lake.
And he formed this resolve regarding one of them:
"Having attained sonship through yoga, may I be united with him," O Bhārata.
Having formed this intention and being endowed with great ascetic power,
that one of mighty penance, Vibhrāja, shone like the sun.

In the city of Kāmpilya, those seven high-souled ones, all free from stain, were born with Brahmadatta at their head;
among them, four possessed mindfulness, while three were deluded.

Purified by knowledge, meditation, and austerity, and having mastered the Vedas and their auxiliary sciences (vedāṅgas),

at that time, he had a conversation with Pāñcāla and Kaṇḍarīka.
Devoted to the ways of village life and subject to the power of desire,
they were nevertheless experts in virtue, pleasure, and wealth due to what had been performed in their previous births.

Having spoken thus, O dear one, he, filled with wrath, cursed Yadu:
"O fool, O lord of men, your progeny shall be without sovereignty."
O bull of the Bharatas, that king spoke in this very same manner to Turvasu, Druhyu, and Anu, and he was likewise rejected by them as well.
The invincible Yayāti, filled with rage, cursed them as well,
O best of royal sages, just as I have previously related to you.
Having thus cursed all four of his sons, the descendants of Puru,
O Bhārata, the king spoke those same words to Pūru as well.
"O Pūru, if you agree, I would wander this earth in my youth, having transferred old age onto you, by means of your form."
Pūru said:
"O Indra among men, what man in this world is capable of repaying his father,
by whose grace he attains the highest state?"

The youngest son, Pūru, though he had performed no service for his father and was devoid of faith, nevertheless— having enjoyed pleasures according to his age with unimpaired senses— took upon himself the old age of his father. The majestic Pūru thus accepted the decrepitude of his sire.
Yayāti also, with his beauty, traversed the earth in the guise of Pūru.
Seeking the end of desires, O best of the Bharatas,
that lord took delight in the Caitraratha forest together with Viśvācī.
When that lord of men remained unsatiated with desires and sensual enjoyments,
and when the sovereign saw those desires increasing,
he then indeed received his own old age from Pūru.
And the Lord, being pleased, granted him a boon:
"My intention is that your lineage shall endure as long as the moon, the sun, and the planets exist;
however, the earth shall never become devoid of descendants of Puru."
In this regard, O Great King, listen to the verses sung by Yayāti,
by which one may withdraw all desires in every way, just as a tortoise draws in its limbs.
He is happy, steadfast, and blessed; he rejoices both in this world and in the next.
Desire is never appeased by the enjoyment of desired objects;
like a fire fed with clarified butter, it only increases all the more.
When a man, possessing an even vision, harbors no ill-will toward any living being, then all directions appear full of happiness to him.
Whatever rice and barley there is on earth, whatever gold, cattle, and women—
Realizing that all this is not enough for even one person, one should seek tranquility.
The horn of the Ruru deer grows as it grows;
when one does not commit any evil against any living being through action, mind, or speech, then one attains Brahman.
When one does not fear others, and when others do not fear him;
when one neither desires nor hates, then he attains Brahman.
That thirst which is difficult for the foolish to abandon, which does not age even as one ages,
and which is a disease that ends only with life— happiness belongs to him who renounces it.
The hair of an aging person decays; the teeth of an aging person decay.
But the hope for wealth and the hope for life do not decay, even as one ages.
Whatever sensual pleasure there is in the world, and whatever great divine pleasure there is—
these are not worth even a sixteenth part of the bliss that comes from the destruction of craving.
One who desires happiness should quickly abandon that craving, which is a mass of suffering.
"The eyes and ears grow old, yet craving alone remains youthful.
Having spoken thus, that royal sage entered the forest together with his wife;
and after a long time, he practiced extensive austerities.
Having performed austerities on Mount Bhṛgutuṅga, at the conclusion of his penance, the highly illustrious one,
fasting, cast off his body and attained heaven together with his wife.
In his lineage, O Great King, there were five most excellent royal sages,
by whom the entire earth was pervaded, just as by the rays of the sun.
Now hear, O royal sage, the lineage of Yadu, honored by royal seers,
in which Nārāyaṇa was born as Hari, the upholder of the Vṛṣṇi clan.

O lord of men, that man who constantly hears this righteous account of Yayāti— the life of one who was prosperous, great, virtuous, illustrious, and wise— shall become healthy, possessed of offspring, long-lived, and renowned.
He is liberated from sins and shall never be childless.
Janamejaya said: "O Brahmin, I desire to hear the lineage of Puru in its true essence."
O best of the twice-born, you ought to relate in detail and in proper sequence the lineages of Druhyu, Anu, Yadu, and Turvasu.
Vaiśampāyana said: In connection with the lineage of the Vṛṣṇis,
O great king, first hear about the lineage of the high-souled Pūru from the very beginning.
In detail and in proper sequence, [I shall tell] where you were born, O King.
"Behold, O scorcher of enemies, I shall describe to you the unsurpassed lineage of Puru, as well as those of Druhyu, Anu, Yadu, and Turvasu."
Pravīra was the son of Pūru, and Manasyu was his offspring;
the son of Manasyu was the king named Abhayada.
Likewise, Sudhanvan was the king of Abhayada;
Sudhanvan’s son was Subāhu, and Raudrāśva was his son.
And his son was Saṃpāti;
from Saṃpāti was born Raśmipātī.
Raudrāśva had ten sons by Daśārṇeyu and likewise by Kṛkaṇeyu; these were the ten Apsarases,
and Ṛceyu was the first among them.
Kakṣeyu, Sthaṇḍileyu, and likewise Saṃnateyu;
Riceyu, Jaleyu, and the mighty Sthaleyu;
Ruceyu as the sixth, and Jaleyu as the seventh;
Dharmeyu, Dṛḍheyu, and Vaneyu is recorded as the tenth.
Vananityā, Vaneyu, and the ten daughters, the women.
These ten were the sons of the Apsaras; Vaneya was known as the youngest.
They were like the senses of the Supreme Self of the universe, born of Ghṛtācī:
Bhadrā, Śūdrā, Madrā, Maladā, and likewise Malahā.
Khalā, Balā, O Indra of kings, Taladā, Surathā,
as well as Gopabalā and Ratnakūṭā— these were the ten women.
Born as a seer in the lineage of Atri, Prabhākara became their husband;
he begot upon Rudrā a glorious son, Soma.
When Sūrya was struck by Svarbhānu and was falling from the great sky,
and when the world was overwhelmed by darkness, it was he by whom light was set forth.
When the sun was told, "May it be well with you," as he was falling,
he did not fall from heaven to the earth because of the word of that brahmin-sage.
He of great asceticism was the one who established the most excellent lineages;
in sacrifices, he alone is the wealth of Atri, and by the gods his portion was set apart.
Upon those daughters,
he begot ten high-souled sons who bore the same names as their mothers and were ever devoted to rigorous asceticism.
O King, those sages who were masters of the Vedas and founders of lineages were known as the Svastyātreyas; however, they were destitute of the wealth of Atri.
The sons of Kakṣeyu, however, were only three great chariot-warriors:
Sabhānara, Cākṣuṣa, and likewise Paramekṣu.
The son of Sabhānara was the learned King Kālānala;
the son of Kālānala was indeed the knower of dharma named Sṛñjaya.
Sṛñjaya’s son was the heroic King Purañjaya;
O great king, Janamejaya was the son of Purañjaya.
O great king, Purañjaya’s son was Janamejaya;
and the son of the royal seer Janamejaya was Mahāsāla,
who was renowned among the gods and possessed established fame.
A son named Mahāmanas was born to Mahāsāla; he was righteous, a hero, and honored by the hosts of gods—that very Mahāmanas.
But Mahāmanas, O Bhārata, begot two sons:
Uśīnara, who was knower of dharma, and the mighty Titikṣu.
The five wives of Uśīnara were born from the lineages of royal sages:
Nṛgā, Kṛmī, Navā, Darvā, and the fifth was Dṛṣadvatī.
The five sons of Uśīnara, who were the perpetuators of his lineage,
were born through great asceticism as the offspring of that aged man.
From Nṛgā was born a son, Nṛga; from Kṛmi was born Kṛmi;
and from Navā was born a son, Nava; while from Darvā was born Suvrata.
From Dṛṣadvatī was born Śibi Auśīnara, O King;
from Śibi came the Śibis, my dear, and from Nṛga came the Yaudheyas.
The kingdom of Nava was Navarāṣṭra, while the city of Kṛmi was Kṛmilā; likewise, Aṃbaṣṭhā belonged to Suvrata. Now hear of the progeny of Titikṣu.
Learn from me about the sons of Śibi.
And Śibi had four sons who were indeed heroes renowned throughout the world:
Vṛṣadarbha, Suvīra, Kaikeya, and Madraka.
Their prosperous territories were those of the Kaikeyas, the Madrakas,
the Vṛṣadarbhas, and the Suvīras;
O Bhārata, Titikṣu was the king in the eastern direction.
Uṣadratha was his son, and the mighty-armed Phena was born as his son.
From Phenat was born Sutapas, and from Sutapas a son was born;
he was Bali, who, possessing a golden quiver, became a king in a human womb.
In ancient times, that great yogi became King Bali;
he begot five sons who established lineages upon the earth.
Aṅga was born first, and likewise Vaṅga, Suhma, Puṇḍra, and Kaliṅga; these are called the Bāleya Kṣatriyas. And the Bāleya Brāhmaṇas were the founders of his lineage upon the earth.
O descendant of Bharata, Bali was granted a boon by the pleased Brahmā:
the state of a great yogi, a lifespan lasting for the duration of a kalpa,
invincibility in battle, and preeminence in dharma.
You shall possess the vision of the three worlds, preeminence in procreation,
incomparable strength, and the perception of the true meaning of the principles of Dharma; indeed,
you shall establish the four castes in their fixed order.
Thus addressed by the Lord, King Bali attained supreme peace.
All those sons of his, born of Sudeṣṇā from that bull among sages, Dīrghatapas, were endowed with great luster. They were all *kṣetraja* (sons begotten on another's wife).
Bali indeed consecrated those five sinless sons.
Having accomplished his purpose, that lord, whose self was united with yoga, remained invincible to all beings; relying upon yoga and awaiting the appointed time, he wandered about,
O King, and after a long period of time, he returned to his own station.
Their five provinces were Vaṅga, Aṅga, Suhmaka, Kaliṅga, and Puṇḍraka; now hear from me about the progeny of Aṅga.
Aṅga’s son was the great lord of kings, Dadhivāhana;
and Dadhivāhana’s son was King Diviratha.
The son of Diviratha was named Dharmaratha, who was as powerful as Śakra;
his son was the learned Citraratha.
Then, while performing a sacrifice on Mount Viṣṇupada together with Śakra, that high-souled Dharmaratha drank the Soma.
Now Citraratha also had a son named Daśaratha,
who was known as Lomapāda, whose daughter was Śāntā.
To him was born the heroic son of Daśaratha, the highly illustrious one who increased his lineage, possessing a fourfold army through the power of Ṛṣyaśṛṅga.
The son of Caturaṅga was known as Pṛthulākṣa;
the son of Pṛthulākṣa was the highly illustrious king named Campa.
The city of Campa belonged to Campa, which formerly shone as Mālinī.
By the grace of Pūrṇabhadra, Haryaṅga became his son;
then Vibhāṇḍaka brought down to earth that supreme mount, an elephant who wards off enemies, by means of mantras.
Karna was the son of Haryaṅga, and Vikarṇa was his son;
Bhadraratha is recorded as the king [who followed]. Bṛhatkarman, the lord of subjects, was the son of Bhadraratha.
His son was Bṛhaddarbha, from whom Bṛhanmanas was born.
The great-minded lord of kings begot a son named Jayadratha, from whom King Dṛḍharatha was born.
O Janamejaya, Viśvajit was the son of Dṛḍharatha;
his heir was Karṇa,
who had a hundred sons who increased the lineage of the Aṅgas.
Vikarṇa’s son was Aṅgada, the enhancer of his lineage.
As for Bṛhaddarbha’s son, the king named Bṛhanmanas,
he had two wives, who were the two auspicious daughters of the King of Cedi.
Yaśodevī and Sattvī—by those two, that lineage is divided.
O king of kings, Jayadratha was born to Yaśodā;
and from Sattvī was born the renowned Vijaya, who excelled the Brahmins and Kṣatriyas.
Vijaya’s son was Dhṛti; his son was Dhṛtavrata;
and Dhṛtavrata’s son was Satyakarman, who was of great vows.
Satyakarman’s son was Sūta Adhiratha;
he indeed adopted Karṇa, and thus Karṇa became the son of a Sūta.
All this has been told to you concerning the mighty Karṇa. Vṛṣasena was the son of Karṇa, and Vṛṣa is known as his son.
Sena, who was righteous and honored by all castes, became his son.
All these kings born of the Aṅga lineage have been described by me;
they were high-souled, devoted to truth, possessed of offspring, and great chariot-warriors.
O great king, hear now the lineage of Ṛceyu, the son of Raudrāśva, which has been declared in succession— the lineage in which you yourself were born, O ruler of the earth.
Vaiśampāyana said:
The royal sage Anādhṛṣṭi is remembered as the sole sovereign;
the wife of Ṛceyu was named Jvālana, who was indeed the daughter of Takṣaka.
O King, Ṛceyu’s son was Matināra, the lord of the earth;
and Matināra had three sons who were supremely righteous.
Tansurodha, Apratiratha, and the righteous Subāhu were born;
and there was a famous and auspicious maiden named Gaurī, the mother of Māndhātṛ.
They were all purified by Vedic vows, devoted to Brahman, and speakers of truth.
All were skilled in weapons, powerful, and experts in war. Apratiratha’s son was Kaṇva, who became a king;
his son was Medhātithi, from whom the twice-born Kāṇva lineage arose.
O Janamejaya, he had a daughter named Ilā, who was a speaker of sacred knowledge and a devoted wife; Taṃsu obtained her as his wife.
The son of Taṃsu was the royal sage Dharmanetra, who was highly renowned, a proponent of the Veda, and possessed of great prowess;
his wife was Upadānavī.
Upadānavī obtained four sons from the host of gods;
thereafter, she gave birth to four gladdeners of the Puru lineage:
Duḥṣanta, Suḥṣanta, Pravīra, and Anagha.
The heir of Duḥṣanta was the heroic Bharata;
he was named Sarvadamana, possessed the strength of ten thousand elephants, and was great.
To Duḥṣanta was born a son of great fame, Bharata, by Śakuntalā; it is after his name that you are called Bhāratas.
An incorporeal voice spoke to King Duḥṣanta:
"The mother is but a skin-bag; the son belongs to the father, for he is the very one by whom he was begotten.
Cherish your son, O Duḥṣanta; do not despise Śakuntalā."
"O god among men, the son who bears the seed rescues [the father] from the abode of Yama;
you are the progenitor of this embryo—Śakuntalā has spoken the truth.
This was said when the sons of King Bharata had perished.
O dear one, it was just as you were told at that time by the wrath of the Mothers.
O King, the powerful and great sage Bharadvāja, the son of Aṅgiras and Bṛhaspati, performed great sacrifices for him.
In this very connection, they cite this account of the wise Bharadvāja and how the transmission of his dharma was indeed made over to Bharata by the Maruts,
after the birth of a son had previously been rendered fruitless for him.
Then, from Bharadvāja, a son named Vitatha was born.
Then, when Vitatha was born, Bharata ascended to heaven;
having consecrated Vitatha as king, Bharadvāja retired to the forest.
Vitatha’s heir was indeed Bhumanyu.
And these four, born from the wrath of Bhūmānya, were like the great elements:
Bṛhatkṣatra, Mahāvīrya, Nara, and the heroic Gārgya.
Nara’s son was Sāṃkṛti; his two sons were the mighty Varavīra and Rantideva, and they are known as the Kātyāyanas.
Śibi, the learned one, was also an heir of Gārgya;
from him came the Śaibyās, and thus the Gārgyas—twice-born men born of the Kṣatriya caste—are remembered.
And Mahāvīrya had a wise son named Purukṣaya. His wife Viśālā bore him three sons:
Trayyāruṇa, Puṣkariṇa, and the third, Kapi.
These three are indeed declared to be the foremost among the monkeys;
they are the Gārgyas, the Saṃkṛtis, and the Kāpyas— twice-born ones born from the Kṣatriya caste—
who, having all taken refuge in the faction of Aṅgiras, were born with great strength.
The righteous heir of Bṛhatkṣatra was named Suhotra. The heir of Suhotra was indeed Hastin;
by him this city, formerly called Gajasamāhvaya, was built.
And Hastin also had three heirs of supreme renown;
O upholder of the Kuru lineage, these were the sons born to Ajamidha.
At the conclusion of his great asceticism, virtuous sons who increased the lineage were born to the aged and righteous king through the grace of Bharadvāja.
From Ajamīḍha and Keśinī was born a son, Kaṇva;
Medhātithi was his son, and from him the Kāṇvāyanas are said to have descended. He, Vitatha, also begot five sons.
Suhotra, Sutahotṛ, Gaya, and likewise Garga.
And the son of Suhotra was the righteous Cyavana;
and from Sutahotra were two sons, the high-souled Kapila and the great being Kāśika, as well as the lord Gṛtsamati.
Likewise, O King, the sons of Gṛtsamati were Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, and Vaiśyas;
and the son of Kāśya was Kāśya, whose son was Dīrghatapas.
To Dīrghatapas was born a learned son named Dhanvantari;
and the son of Dhanvantari was renowned as Ketumān.
Now, the son of Ketumān is known as the hero Bhīmaratha.
The son of Bhīmaratha was Divodāsa, a lord of subjects;
renowned as Divodāsa, he was the destroyer of all rākṣasas.
At that very time, however, a Rākṣasa named Kṣemaka caused the city of Vārāṇasī to be laid waste.
For she was cursed by the high-souled Nikumbha, who possessed great intelligence, saying,
"O bull among men, she shall indeed remain desolate for a thousand years."
As soon as she had been cursed, Divodāsa, the lord of subjects,
established a beautiful city on the Gomati at the edge of his territory.
Formerly, the city of Vārāṇasī belonged to Bhadraśreṇya,
who was born of the Yadu lineage and devoted to asceticism;
he had one hundred sons, all of whom were excellent archers.
Having slain him, Divodāsa, the lord of subjects, established himself there.
The son of Divodāsa was the heroic King Pratardana;
Pratardana had two sons, Vatsa and Bhārgava.
And Alarka, the son of a king, became a ruler on earth possessed of humility;
that lord of the earth indeed seized the inheritance of the Haihaya.
He recovered his paternal inheritance, which had been forcibly seized by Divodāsa. In his lineage was born King Suhotra, who was supremely righteous;
he was the son of the high-souled Durdamana, the son of Bhadraśreṇya.
For that boy was indeed released by Divodāsa out of compassion.

O descendant of Bharata, there was a king named Aṣṭāratha, who was indeed the son of Bhīmaratha. O great king, desiring to bring an end to the enmity, that kṣatriya struck at the young sons of his [enemy].
Even he, while thus destroying his own sons, met his death.
Regarding Alarka, the king of Kāśī— who was devoted to Brahman and true to his promise—
this ancient verse has been sung concerning King Alarka:
For sixty thousand years and sixty hundred years.
He, endowed with beauty and youth, possessed a very great kingdom;
that upholder of the Kāśi lineage was a youth perfected in form,
and by the grace of Lopāmudrā, he attained a supreme lifespan.
At the end of his life, the mighty-armed king, having slain the Rākṣasa Kṣemaka,
resettled the beautiful city of Vārāṇasī.
The heir of Alarka was the highly illustrious one named Kṣema;
he was the king named Kṣemaka, and indeed,
he had a son.
Kṣema’s son was Ketumān, and from him Varṣaketu was born.
The heir of Varṣaketu was the lord of creatures named Vibhu;
Ānarta was the son of Vibhu, and from him Sukumāra was born.
Sukumāra’s son was Satyaketu, a great chariot-warrior; he had a son of great splendor, a most righteous king named Karandu. That monarch had two sons.
Brahmaṇya and Satyasaṃpanna were the two sons; likewise Bhārgu and Vatsa.
Vatsabhūmi was the son of Vatsa, while Bhārgabhūmi was born from Bhārgu.
But these sons of Aṅgiras were born in the lineage of Bhṛgu as Brāhmaṇas,
Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, and Śūdras, O bull of the Bharatas.
O scion of the Kuru lineage, they remain established through their deeds rooted in austerity.
Suhotra’s son was Bṛhat, and Bṛhat had three sons:
Ajamīḍha, Dvimīḍha, and the heroic Purumīḍha.
Ajamīḍha had three wives endowed with great fame:
Nīlī, Keśinī, and the beautiful Dhūminī.
From Ajamīḍha and Keśinī was born the powerful Jahnu,
who performed the great sacrificial session, the Sarvamedha, the great sacrifice.
Indeed, although Gaṅgā had rushed toward him when he was performing the sacrifice out of a desire to win him over,
she did not flood that assembly hall of his as he did not wish it.
And seeing the sacrificial enclosure inundated on all sides by her,
O best of the Bharatas, the son of Suhotra spoke to Gaṅgā in anger.
"Here, having condensed the waters of the three worlds, I drink them;
O Gaṅgā, receive immediately the fruit of this arrogance."
Then, seeing that the Gaṅgā had become yellow, the great-souled and highly fortunate maharṣis offered Jāhnavī to him as a daughter.
Jahnu married Kāverī, the daughter of Yuvanāśva,
whose body was later turned into a river by the curse of Gaṅgā.
Jahnu’s beloved son was the powerful Ajaka;
the heir of Ajaka was the lord of the earth, Balākāśva.
Kuśika became devoted to hunting; his son was a king who had grown up among the Pahlavas, those forest-dwellers.
The powerful Kuśika performed austerities, thinking, "May I obtain a son equal to Indra"; and Śakra, approaching him out of fear, begot him.
He became King Gādhi, while Maghavān himself became Kauśika;
Viśvāmitra was the son of Gādhi, as were King Viśvaratha and Ha.
O King, Viśvajit and Viśvakṛt were born [to her], as was Satyavatī;
from Ṛcīka, Jamadagni was born of Satyavatī.
The sons of Viśvāmitra are recorded as Devarāta and others;
they are renowned throughout the three worlds—listen to their names from me.
Devashrava and Kati—because of whom the Katyayanas are so named; Shalapati, Hiranyaksha, and Renu, from whom Reṇukā was born.
O King, Sāṃkṛtya, Gālava, and Maudgalya are renowned;
these are the celebrated lineages of those high-souled Kauśikas.
The Pāṇinas and the Babhruvas, as well as the Dhānañjayyas,
the Pārthivas, the Devarātas, the Sālaṅkāyanas, and the Sauśravas.
The Lohityas, the Yamadūtas, and likewise the Kārīṣayas are recorded;
the Kauśikas are renowned, O King, as are the others, the Saindhavāyanas.
Many Kauśikas are recorded who are prohibited from intermarrying with other Ṛṣi lineages.
O Great King, the connection between the Brahmarṣi Paurava and Kauśika within this lineage of the Brahman-kṣatriyas is indeed renowned.
Among the sons of Viśvāmitra, Śunaḥśepa is remembered as the eldest;
that best of sages, though born of Bhṛgu, indeed attained the status of a Kauśika.
And there were seven other sons of Viśvāmitra, namely Śabara and the rest;
and from Viśvāmitra, moreover, was born Aṣṭaka as the son of Dṛṣadvatī.
I have described to you the group of Jahnu, beginning with Lauhi, the son of Aṣṭaka;
now hear, O bull of the Bharatas, of the other lineage, that of Ājamīḍha.
From Ajamidha and Nili was born Sushanti;
from Sushanti came Purujati, and from Purujati came Bahyasva.
Bāhya had five sons who were like the immortals:
Mudgala, Sṛñjaya, and King Bṛhadiṣu.
Yavīnara was valiant, and Kṛmilāśva was the fifth;
these five were renowned as being capable of protecting the regions.
Know that there are five prosperous Pāñcālas inhabited by holy people;
they are renowned as the Pāñcālas, and they are sufficient for your protection.
The heir of Mudgala was the highly illustrious Maudgalya;
all these high-souled ones were twice-born men endowed with the status of Kshatriyas.
Indeed, these descendants of Kaṇva and Mudgala took refuge in the lineage of Aṅgiras.
Mudgala’s eldest son was a brahmin seer of great asceticism;
from him Indrasenā conceived Vadhryaśva.
The Vadhryaśva couple was born of Menakā; so says the Śruti.
And there were the royal sage Divodāsa and the illustrious Ahalyā.
Ahalyā gave birth to Śatānanda, the best of sages, the heir of Śaradvat; and he, of great renown,
had a son named Satyadhṛti, who was a master of the science of archery.
Having seen an Apsaras before him, the seed of that Satyadhṛti was discharged;
it then fell upon a clump of reeds and became a pair.
Śaṃtanu, who had gone out on a hunt, took it out of compassion;
therefore he was remembered as Kṛpa, and his daughter Gautamī was likewise called Kṛpī.
These are declared to be the Śāradvatas, and these are remembered as the Gautamas.
Henceforth I shall proclaim the lineage of Divodāsa.
The heir of Divodāsa was the royal Brahmarṣi Mitrayu.
From them came the Somas, and from them the Maitreyas are remembered;
these are the detailed branches of the Bhārgavas who were endowed with the Kṣatriya status.
Pañcavana was the son of the high-souled Sṛñjaya.
The son of Pañcavana was also the lord of the earth, Somadatta.
The heir of Somadatta was the highly illustrious Sahadeva;
and the son of Sahadeva was the king named Somaka.
When the lineage had declined, Somaka was born again from Ajamīḍha.
Somaka’s son was Jantu, who had a hundred sons who shone forth.
Among them, the youngest was the lord Pṛṣata, the father of Drupada.
Dhṛṣṭadyumna was born from Drupada, and Dhṛṣṭaketu was his son.
These high-souled Somakas are indeed remembered as the descendants of Ajamidha;
thus the sons of the great-souled Ajamidha attained the name Somaka.
Now, Ajamidha’s queen was Dhuminī, who was longing for a son.
O Lord of the Earth, your third mother was the one belonging to your ancestors.
Seeking a son, that queen, disciplined by her observance of vows,
performed austerities for a hundred years— a practice exceedingly difficult for women to endure.
Having offered oblations into the fire according to the rules, O Janamejaya, she, whose food was purified and measured, slept upon the very kusha grass used for the Agnihotra sacrifice.
Having united with that queen Dhūminī, Ajamīḍha begot Ṛkṣa,
who was smoke-colored and handsome to behold.
From Ṛkṣa was born Saṃvaraṇa, and from Saṃvaraṇa likewise came Kuru;
he, having departed from Prayāga, established Kurukṣetra.
Then, after that illustrious one had performed austerities for many years, Śakra appeared before him as the granter of boons in a place that was holy,
delightful, and frequented by those who perform meritorious deeds.
His lineage was very great, after whom you are called the Kauravas.
Kuru had four sons: Sudhanvan, Sudhanu, the mighty-armed Parīkṣit, and the excellent Arimejaya.
The heir of Sudhanvā is remembered as the wise Suhotra;
his son was Cyavana, a king skilled in both dharma and artha.
Having performed sacrifices after Cyavana had passed away, that king, a knower of dharma, offered various rites and begot a son renowned as Indra’s friend.
From Caidyoparicara was born the heroic Vasu, known as Antarikṣaga;
and from Caidyoparicara, Girikā gave birth to seven Mānavas.
The renowned Bṛhadratha, king of Magadha, was a great chariot-warrior;
as were Pratyagraha, Kuśa— whom they call Maṇivāhana—
as well as Māruta, Yadu, and the most excellent Matsyakālī.
The heir of Bṛhadratha was the renowned Kuśāgra;
the learned and heroic son of Kuśāgra was named Ṛṣabha.
His heir was the valiant King Satyahita;
his son, that righteous soul, was born as Ūrja by name.
The powerful Saṃbhava was the son of Ūrja, from whom he was born.
He was indeed born as two fragments, but he was joined together by Jarā;
because he was joined by Jarā, he is therefore known as Jarāsaṃdha.
This Jarāsandha of great strength was the conqueror of all the kṣatriyas;
Sahadeva, indeed, was the powerful son of Jarāsandha.
The illustrious and highly renowned Udāyin was the son of Sahadeva;
that Udāyin begot a most righteous son named Śrutadharmā, who, as a powerful lord, dwelt among the Magadhas.

The righteous heir of Vṛṣabha was named Puṣpavān. Janamejaya had exactly three heirs who were great chariot-warriors;
I shall now relate the lineage of Jahnu, O King, in which you yourself were born.
Jahnu, however, begot a son named Suratha, a protector of the earth,
as well as Śrutasena, Agrasena, and Bhīmasena by name.
All these were highly fortunate, valiant, and endowed with strength.
Janamejaya had two sons, Suratha and the wise Matimat.
To Suratha was born a valiant son, Vidūratha.
The heir of Vidūratha was the great chariot-warrior Ṛkṣa;
he shone as the second king, designated by that very name.
In this lineage of yours, O King, there were two Ṛkṣas and exactly two Parīkṣits;
there were three Bhīmasenas and exactly two Janamejayas.
The son of the second Ṛkṣa was Bhīmasena;
Pratīpa was the son of Bhīmasena, and Śāntanu was the son of Pratīpa.
Devāpi and Bāhlika were also his sons—these three were indeed great chariot-warriors (mahārathas).
This is the lineage of Śāntanu, O King, in which you were born;
however, the kingdom of Bāhlika, O lord of the people, is indeed the Saptabāhlya.
And the highly illustrious Somadatta was born as the son of Bāhlīka;
from Somadatta were born Bhūri, Bhūriśravas, and Śala.
The sage Devāpi became the preceptor of the gods;
he was the son of Cyavana, known as Kṛtaka, and was beloved by that high-souled one.
Śāntanu, however, became the king and the leader of the Kauravas.
I shall now relate to you, O King, concerning Śāntanu, from whom you were born.
That lord begot a son named Devavrata of the Ganges;
he was known as Bhīṣma, the grandfather of the Pāṇḍavas.
And Kālī gave birth to Vicitravīrya, O descendant of Bharata.
The beloved son of Śāntanu, righteous-souled and stainless.
And Kṛṣṇa Dvaipāyana begot Dhṛtarāṣṭra, Pāṇḍu, and Vidura in the field of Vicitravīrya.
Dhṛtarāṣṭra, however, begot one hundred sons upon Gāndhārī;
of them, Duryodhana was the eldest and the lord of them all.
Dhanañjaya was the son of Pāṇḍu, and Saubhadra was his son.
But Parīkṣit, O lord of men, was the father of Abhimanyu and your grandfather.
This is your Paurava lineage, O King, in which you were born;
now I shall proclaim the lineages of Turvasu, Druhyu, Anu, and Yadu.
The son of Turvasu was Vahni; the son of Vahni was Gobhānu;
and the son of Gobhānu was the unconquered King Triśānu.
Karaṃdhama was the son of Triśānu, and Marutta was his son;
however, another Marutta, the son of Avikṣita, has been mentioned by you as a king.
The king, a performer of sacrifices who gave abundant sacrificial fees, remained childless;
that lord of the earth had a daughter named Saṃmatā.
For she was given as a sacrificial fee to the high-souled Saṃvarta;
and she obtained Duḥṣanta Paurava as her son, who was free from all stain.
Thus, O best of kings, when Yayāti’s old age was transferred by that curse, the lineage of Turvasu entered the family of Puru.
The heir of Duḥṣanta was Śarutthāma, a lord of subjects;
from Śarutthāma came Ākrīḍa, and he had four sons.
The Pāṇḍya, the Kerala, the Kola, and the Cola king—these were their prosperous territories: Pāṇḍya, Cola, and Kerala.
O King, the son of Druhyu was the monarch Babhruṣeṇa;
his son was Aṅgārasetu, who is called the lord of the Maruts.
The powerful one was slain with great difficulty by Yauvanāśva in battle;
for the combat was truly immense, lasting for fourteen months.
The heir of Aṅgāra was the king named Gāndhāra,
after whose name indeed the great region of Gāndhāra became renowned;
moreover, the horses born in the land of Gāndhāra were the best among steeds.
Anos’s son was Dharma; Dhṛta was his son. From Dhṛta, Duduha was born, and Pracetas was his son. Sucetas was the son of Pracetas; thus have the Anus been described by me.
Listen as I describe in detail and in proper sequence the lineage of Yadu, the eldest son of supreme splendor;
by the mere hearing of which one is liberated from all sins.
Yadu had five sons who were like the children of gods:
Sahasrada, Payoda, Kroṣṭā, Nīla, and Añjika.
The three heirs of Sahasrada were supremely righteous. The king named Śatajit was the son of Sahasrada; the sons of Śatajit were renowned.
Hehaya, Haya, and likewise Veṇuhaya, O King.
Hehaya had a son known as Dharmanetra;
Dharmanetra’s son was Kānta, and from him were born the Kāntaputras.
Mahiṣmān was the son of Sāhañja, and Bhadraśreṇya was his son;
by that king, the city named Sāhañjanī was founded.
The heir of Sāhañja was the king named Māhiṣmān,
by whom the city named Māhiṣmatī was founded.
The powerful Bhadraśreṇya was the son of Mahiṣmat;
he has already been mentioned as the king who ruled Vārāṇasī.
The heir of Bhadraśreṇya was the renowned Durmada.
The wise son of Durda was known by the name Kanaka. Kanaka’s heirs were four, world-renowned:
Kṛtavīrya, Kṛtaujas, and likewise Kṛtadhanvan.
Kṛtāgni was the fourth, and likewise from Kṛtavīrya came Arjuna.
He who, with his thousand arms, became the lord of the seven continents,
alone conquered the earth on a chariot possessing the splendor of the sun.
For having performed most difficult austerities for a hundred years, Kārtavīrya propitiated Datta, who was born of Atri.
To him, Datta granted four boons of great splendor;
first, he requested the supreme boon of a thousand arms.
May there be for me the eradication by the virtuous of any unrighteousness in which I am established;
and having conquered the earth through fierce [means], may there be its pleasing only through righteousness.
Having conquered many battles and slain enemies by the thousands,
he was killed in combat while engaged in battle by one superior to him.
O Bhārata, as he fought, it is said that by the power of illusion, a thousand arms appeared before him through the yoga of the Lord of Yoga.
Thus, by means of fierce discipline, this entire earth— with its seven continents, its ports, its oceans, and its cities— has been conquered.
O Janamejaya, it is heard that by means of that ritual, seven hundred sacrifices were indeed performed by the king across the seven continents.
O mighty-armed one, all his sacrifices were accompanied by abundant sacrificial fees;
all had sacrificial posts made of gold, and all had altars made of gold.
O Great King, all of them are adorned by gods stationed in celestial chariots,
and are eternally graced by Gandharvas and Apsarases.
At whose sacrifice the wise Gandharva Nārada,
the son of Varīdāsa, sang this song, being struck with wonder by his greatness.
Surely no kings shall ever attain the state of Kārtavīrya,
whether by means of sacrifices, gifts, austerities, valor, or sacred learning.
For eighty-five thousand years, Arjuna, possessing unimpeded power, ruled the kingdom while constantly remembering Hari;
and because his memory of wealth never failed, he enjoyed inexhaustible sixfold prosperity.
Indeed, as he wanders through the seven continents, that yogi is seen by men as one bearing a sword, a shield, and a bow, and mounted upon a chariot.
There was no loss of property, nor grief, nor confusion,
among the subjects as the great king protected them through righteousness by his majestic power.
He became a universal monarch (cakravartin), a sovereign possessing all jewels;
he himself was the protector of cattle, and he himself was the guardian of the fields;
through his state of yoga, he became Arjuna, who is Parjanya by means of rain.
With his thousand arms, whose skin was hardened by the striking of bowstrings,
he indeed shone like the sun with its thousand rays in the autumn season.
For that one of great splendor, having conquered the sons of Karkoṭaka among the Nāgas in the city of Māhiṣmatī, established them in that very city.
Indeed, at the time of the rainy season, that lotus-eyed one, as if playing, caused the current of the ocean to flow upstream, breaking it apart with his arms.
Ravaged by him as he sports, the Narmadā— garlanded with wreaths of foam and possessing thousands of surging waves— approaches in fear.
As the great ocean was being agitated by his thousand arms,
the great asuras dwelling in the netherworld remained motionless, hidden out of fear.
It had its great waves pulverized, its large fish and timingalas tossed about,
its mass of foam driven by the wind, and it was unbearable due to the agitation of its whirlpools.
Then the king, with his thousand arms, set it in motion,
like Mount Mandara tossed by the gods and asuras against the Ocean of Milk.
Terrified by the agitation of Mount Mandara and fearing the production of the nectar of immortality,
they suddenly flew up in fear upon seeing that formidable and supreme king.
Those great serpents remained with their heads motionless,
like clusters of plantain trees shaken by his wind at the close of day.
Having indeed bound his bow with its strings, he forcibly bewildered the lord of Laṅkā, Rāvaṇa, along with his army using five arrows; having conquered him,
he brought him back and bound him in Māhiṣmatī.
Having heard that Rāvaṇa, the descendant of Pulastya, had been bound by Arjuna,
Pulastya then went there and saw Arjuna himself;
entreated by Pulastya, he released the Rākṣasa, the descendant of Pulastya.
The sound of the bowstring upon his thousand arms was like the roar of a cloud at the end of an eon, or like the crashing of a thunderbolt.
Oh, how great was the prowess of Bhārgava in battle,
when he severed the king’s thousand arms like a grove of golden palm trees!
Once, when he was thirsty, he was begged for water by the Fire-god;
for eighty-five thousand years, O lord of men,
that king dwelt following him as he plunged into the great ocean.
That hero gave alms to the Fire-god, who had violently transgressed his bounds like an untimely monsoon; he offered the seven continents,
along with all the cities, villages, cowherd settlements, and provinces in their entirety.
The fire blazed up, desiring to consume all of his [possessions].
By the power of that great-souled lord of men,
Kārtavīrya, he consumed both the mountains and the forests.
Terrified by that powerful [fire], that Haihaya Citrabhānu burnt down the beautiful, empty hermitage of Varuṇa’s son—
him whom Varuṇa had long ago obtained as his most excellent and radiant son.
That sage was known by the name Vasiṣṭha, and also as Āpava;
it was there that the powerful Āpava, out of anger, cursed Arjuna.
"O descendant of Hehaya, because this forest was not spared by you for me,
another shall perform that difficult task which you failed to do:
the Kuru prince Arjuna, the son of Pāṇḍu and the joy of Kuntī."
The mighty-armed and powerful son of Jamadagni named Rāma,
that ascetic Brahmin of the Bhṛgu lineage, having swiftly crushed you and severed your thousand arms by his strength, shall slay you.
O crusher of enemies, by the power of that lord of men who protected his subjects through righteousness, there was no loss of property among them.
Therefore, O Kauravya, his death shall indeed come from Rāma due to the curse of that great sage; for this was a boon chosen by him himself in the past.
Of that high-souled one’s hundred sons, five remained:
they were skilled in weapons, powerful, heroic, virtuous, and illustrious.
Śūrasena, Śūra, Dhṛṣṭokta, and Kṛṣṇa—these were the sons of Kārtavīrya, heroic and mighty chariot-warriors.
And there was a great king of Avanti named Jayadhvaja.
These were the powerful sons of Kārtavīrya, all of whom were great car-warriors.
Jayadhvaja’s son was the very powerful Tālajaṅgha;
his sons were known by the name Śata, and they were called the Tālajaṅghas.
In the lineage of those high-souled Haihayas, O Great King,
there were the Vītihotras, the Sujātas, the Bhojas, and likewise the Āvantyas.
Those known as the Tauṇḍikeras, as well as the Tālajaṅghas,
the Bharatas, and the Sujātas, are not enumerated individually due to their great number.
O King, the Yādavas beginning with Vṛṣa were performers of meritorious deeds.
Among them, Vṛṣa was the sustainer of the lineage; his son was Madhu.
Madhu had a hundred sons, but Vṛṣaṇa was the one who continued his family line.
All those born from Vṛṣaṇa are known as Vṛṣṇis, while those from Madhu are remembered as Mādhavas;
the Yādavas were first designated by Yadu, and the Haihayas likewise.
O sinless one, there were the Śūras, the Śūravīras, and likewise the Śūrasenas.
The country of that great-souled one is known as Śūrasena; for him who constantly recounts here the birth of Kārtavīrya, there shall be no loss of wealth, and he shall recover whatever has been lost.
"He shall indeed become wealthy, and his righteousness shall increase;
as was his creation when born of Yadu, so shall he be honored in heaven.
Janamejaya said:
For what reason was that forest of the high-souled Āpava burnt by Kārtavīrya through his prowess? Tell this to me who asks you.
For we have heard that this royal sage was the protector of the subjects;
how is it that, having become their protector, he destroyed that forest?
Vaiśampāyana said:
The Sun-god approached Kārtavīrya in the form of a brahmin and said, "Grant me a single satisfaction; I, the Sun, have come before you."
Arjuna said:
"O Blessed One, by what means would you be satisfied? Tell me, O Vibhāvasu; what kind of food shall I give? Having heard from you, I shall provide it."
Vibhāvasu said:
"O best of speakers, give me all that is stationary as my food;
by that I shall find satisfaction, and by that, O King, I shall find contentment."
Arjuna said:
"It is not possible for any human being, however radiant, to consume all that is stationary by his own splendor, O best of those who heat the world; I bow down to you alone."
The Sun said:
"I am pleased with you; I give you arrows that are inexhaustible and directed in every direction.
Possessed by my splendor today, you shall dry up even the immobile."
I shall reduce it to dry ashes; by that, O lord of men, I shall find satisfaction.
Then Āditya gave those arrows to Arjuna;
with them, he then consumed everything stationary in the eastern direction.
Then [he saw] hermitages, villages, cowherd settlements, and cities as well; delightful penance groves, forests, and pleasure gardens.
Thus he burned the eastern direction, and then everything in a clockwise circle;
the earth was burnt by the power of his yoga, becoming treeless and grassless.
At that very time, however, the great seer Āpava took refuge in the water and remained living within the waters for ten thousand years.
When his vow was completed, the great seer of immense splendor arose;
out of anger, he cursed the royal sage as has indeed been related by me.
These, O lord of the people, are the five lineages of the sons of Yayāti.
O Great King, those who are celebrated as the heroes of the world truly sustain the worlds, just as the five elements sustain all beings, both stationary and moving.
Having heard the *Pañcavisarga*, the king, skilled in dharma and worldly affairs,
becomes the master and lord over his five sons.
O Bhārata, by merely upholding and hearing these five groups, one shall obtain five boons that are difficult to attain in this world: long life, fame, wealth, sons, and even greater sovereignty.
A person who recites this attains preeminence and is liberated from all sins.
Now hear, O Indra among kings, of the lineage of Kroṣṭu, a lineage of supreme men,
belonging here to Yadu— the upholder of the lineage, a performer of sacrifices, and a doer of meritorious deeds.
Indeed, by hearing this lineage of Kṛṣṇa, one is liberated from all sins—
the lineage in which Viṣṇu, Hari, the lord of the Vṛṣṇi clan, was born.
Vaiśampāyana said:
Gāndhārī and Mādrī were both the wives of Kroṣṭu.
Gāndhārī gave birth to Anamitra, who was possessed of great strength.
Then Mādrī bore Yudhājit and Devamīḍhuṣa as her sons;
thus the lineage of those Vṛṣṇis, which increased the clan, became divided into three branches.
Two sons were born to Mādrī, both renowned as Vṛṣṇi and Andhaka;
likewise, two sons, Śvaphalka and Citraka, were born to Vṛṣṇi.
O great king, wherever the righteous Śvaphalka resides,
there is no fear of disease, nor even any fear of drought.
Once, O best of the Bharatas, the chastiser of Pāka did not send rain for three years within the territory of the powerful King of Kāśī.
There he caused Śvaphalka, who was highly honored, to dwell;
and during Śvaphalka’s turn, Indra, whose vehicle is green horses, sent down rain.
While she remained in her mother’s womb for many groups of years, she did not indeed give birth; and while she was still within the womb, her father spoke to her.
"Be born quickly; may it be well with you! For what purpose do you remain here?
Thus spoke the maiden staying within the womb to him, and she also spoke to the cow day after day.
"If you give her to me, then today my father shall cause me to marry her.
"So be it," said her father, and he fulfilled his desire;
Śvaphalka took the daughter of the King of Kāśī as his wife.
She gave a cow named Gāndinī to the brahmins constantly.
From that Śvaphalka was born Akrūra, a donor, a performer of sacrifices, wise, learned, fond of guests, and one who bestowed abundant sacrificial fees.
Upamadgu, Madgu, Mṛdara, Arimejaya,
Arikṣepa, Upekṣa, Śatrughna, and Arimardana.
Carmabhṛt, Yudhiṣvarman, Gṛdhramojas, and likewise Antaka;
Āvāha and Prativāha, and the beautiful woman Sundarī.
His daughter was the renowned Punarnavā, the queen of Sāmba;
she was endowed with beauty and youth, captivating the minds of all living beings.
From Akrūra, by the daughter of Kāśī, Satyaketu was born. And from Akrūra, O joy of the Kurus, by Sugātrī, the daughter of Ugrasena,
Prasena and Upadeva were born, both possessing divine splendor.
Citraka had sons, namely Pṛthu and Vipṛthu,
as well as Aśvagrīva, Aśvabāhu, Supārśvaka, and Gaveṣaṇa.
Ariṣṭanemi, Aśva, Sudharmā, Dharmabhṛt, Subāhu, and Bahubāhu; and Śraviṣṭhā and Śravaṇā were the two women.
Upon Aśmakī he begot Śūra, also known as Devamīḍhuṣa;
and upon his queen Bhojyā, ten sons were born to Śūra.
The mighty-armed Vasudeva was born first as Ānakadundubhi; at the moment of his birth, kettledrums resounded in the heavens.
A great clamor of kettledrums arose in the sky,
and a vast shower of flowers fell upon the hero’s palace.
Even throughout the entire world of men, there was no one on earth equal in beauty to that foremost of men, whose radiance was like that of the moon.
From him Devabhāga was born, and from him again Devaśravas;
then Anādhṛṣṭi, Kanavaka, Vatsavān, and Gṛñjima.
Śyāma, Śamīka, and Gaṇḍūṣa—these five were his sons—and he had five excellent wives:
Pṛthukīrti, Pṛthā, Śrutadevā, Śrutaśravā, and Rājādhidevī; these five were the mothers of heroes.
O descendant of Kuru, Śūra chose Pṛthā as his daughter; he gave her to the venerable and aged Kuntibhoja. Therefore, Pṛthā, the daughter of Kuntibhoja, became renowned as Kuntī.
O King, Agṛdhnu was born to Kuntī by Śrutadevā;
and O Bhārata, Kekaya begot five sinless sons upon Śrutadevī, with Sutardana as their eldest.
O bull of the Bharatas, the queen-consort of the king gave birth to two sons of supreme righteousness, Vinda and Anuvinda of Avanti;
and from Śrutaśravā was born the exceedingly powerful Śiśupāla, the king of Cedi.
He who was indeed slain by the high-souled Kṛṣṇa at the Rājasūya sacrifice—
that Hiraṇyakaśipu, who had formerly been the king of the Daityas—
was born as the son of Vṛddhaśarman through Pṛthukīrti.
The heroic and mighty Dantavakra, lord of Karūṣa, made Pṛthā his daughter; Kuntī’s son Pāṇḍu married her.
From her was born that king Yudhiṣṭhira, who knew the Dharma;
likewise Bhīmasena from Vāta, and Dhanañjaya from Indra—
that hero, an unrivaled chariot-warrior in the world, whose prowess was equal to Śakra’s.
From Anamitra was born Śini, the youngest son of Vṛṣṇi; from him came Satyaka, the descendant of Śini, and from him Yuyudhāna, also known as Sātyaki.
Asaṅga was the son of Yuyudhāna, and Bhūmi was his son; from Bhūmi came Yugaṃdhara—thus this lineage is concluded. Uddhava was the illustrious son of Devabhāga.
Among the wise, they say that Uddhava, the son of Devaśravas, is supreme.
O Indra among kings, Devaśravas obtained a son named Paṇḍita; Aśmakī bore him the illustrious Anādhṛṣṭi;
and Śrutadevā gave birth to Nivṛttaśatru, the slayer of enemies.
O Great King, that son of Niṣāda who was heard of by us as born from Śrutadevā—
namely Ekalavya, who was raised among the Niṣādas— is indeed the one we have heard of as the son of Śrutadevā.
The powerful Vāsudeva was indeed the son of Vasudeva;
and to Vatsāvata, who was childless, the powerful Vasudeva,
the descendant of Śūra, gave his heroic biological son Kauśika with a formal libation of water.
Śauri gave his own son, the youth of immeasurable splendor,
to Gaṇḍūṣa, who was childless; and Viṣvaksena gave his sons Cārudeṣṇa, Sucāru, Pañcāla, and Kṛtalakṣaṇa.
O bull of the Bharatas, that mighty-armed hero, the younger son of Rukmiṇī, never retreated from battle at any time.
Thousands of crows followed behind him as he went, thinking,
"Today we shall feast upon the beautiful [bodies] of those slain by Cārudeṣṇa."
Tantrija and Tantripāla were the two sons of Kanavaka; Vīra and Aśvahanu were likewise his two heroic sons, who were born of Gṛñjimā.
Śyāmaputra’s son was Sumitra, whose son was Śamīka; he, loathing the state of being a Bhoja, performed the Rājasūya sacrifice. From him was born Ajātaśatru, the destroyer of his enemies.
Now I shall proclaim the sons of Vasudeva; listen to them.
This threefold lineage of Vṛṣṇi is indeed highly branched and of great power;
however, because it is not relevant to the present subject, it is not recounted here in detail.
One who upholds this vast genealogy is not joined with misfortunes in this world.
Vaiśampāyana said: O King, the daughter of Bāhlīka named Rohiṇī was the eldest wife of Ānakadundubhi, O great monarch, and was very dear to him.
Vasudeva had fourteen excellent wives:
Pauravī, Rohiṇī by name, and another named Madirā;
likewise Vaiśākhī, Bhadrā, and Sunāmī as the fifth.
Sahadevā, Śāntidevā, Śrīdevā, Devarakṣitā,
Vṛkadevī, Upadevī, and Devakī was the seventh.
Sutanu and Vaḍavā were his two female attendants;
from them he obtained his eldest son Rāma, as well as Śāraṇa, Śaṭha,
Durdama, Damana, Śvabhra, Piṇḍāraka, and Kuśīnara.
The nine daughters of Rohiṇī were named Citrā;
O joy of the Kurus, Citrā was further renowned as Subhadrā.
And from Vasudeva, through Devakī, was born the highly illustrious Śauri; and the noble-minded one [Vasudeva] begot Kīrtimant, Suṣeṇa, Bhadrasena,
Mṛtyu, Samardana, Bhadra, Saṃkarṣaṇa, and Ahīśvara.
Among them, the eighth was Vipula, who was indeed Hari himself;
and from Rāma, his beloved son Niśaṭha was born by Revatī.
From Subhadrā, the charioteer Abhimanyu was born of Pārtha;
from Akrūra, Satyaketu was born of the daughter of the King of Kāśī.
Learn now of those heroic sons who were born to Vasudeva’s seven highly fortunate wives; bow down before them.
Both Bhoja and Vijaya were the two sons of Śāntidevā;
Devarakṣitā obtained an excellent quiver as her son;
and both Vṛkadeva and Gada were the two sons of Sunāmā.
Vṛkadevī gave birth to the high-souled Agāvaha.
Devakī bore Vijaya, Lomapāda, and Vardhamāna.
These were born of the high-souled Upadevī;
Sutanū and Narāvī were the two wives of Śūra.
Both Pauṇḍra and Kapila were sons of Vasudeva.
Kapila was born with the name Nara, and Pauṇḍra was the son of Sutanū.
Of these two, Pauṇḍra became king, while Kapila went to the forest.
From Vasudeva was born the exceedingly powerful Dvīpa Pūrvya;
he was the lord of the Niṣādas named Jarā, the master of all archers,
and the husband of the daughter of the King of Trigarta, Śiśirāyaṇa.
He exerted human effort toward his inquiry, yet that human effort did not succeed.
"You are not a man, but a eunuch, appearing like black iron; at that time, in your twelfth year, you shall appear like black iron. Thus was Gārgya falsely accused, driven by intense anger.
Taking the daughter of Ghoṣa, he proceeded to engage in sexual intercourse.
The Apsaras Gopālī, assuming the guise of a cowherd woman,
bore for Gārgya that difficult-to-sustain and infallible embryo.
Through the appointment of the trident-wielder Śiva, he was born as the immensely powerful king named Kālayavana from Gargya’s wife, who was human;
in battle, horses whose forequarters were like those of bulls bore him.
O great king, that child grew up in the inner apartments of the childless Yavana king,
and he became known as Kālayavana.
Desirous of battle, that king questioned the best of the twice-born;
the powerful Nārada then described to him the clan of the Vṛṣṇis and Andhakas.
Then, with an army consisting of an akṣauhiṇī, he marched toward Mathurā and dispatched a messenger to the residence of the Vṛṣṇis and Andhakas.
Then the Vṛṣṇis and Andhakas, placing the high-minded Kṛṣṇa at their head,
assembled and took counsel together out of fear of Jarāsaṃdha.
Having made this resolution, they all favored flight;
abandoning their homes and all their wealth, they fled with their hearts' desire,
leaving behind the beautiful city of Mathurā while honoring the wielder of the Pināka bow.
They were desirous of establishing the city of Dvāravatī at Kuśasthalī.
Thus the mighty-armed Lord Kṛṣṇa, the Prajāpati,
was born among humans as a portion of Manu for the sake of sport.
He who, pure and with senses restrained, [hears] this birth of Kṛṣṇa...
A wise person should cause [this] to be heard on the festival days; being free from debt, he shall become happy.
Vaiśampāyana said:
To Kroṣṭu was born a son named Vṛjinīvān, who was of great fame;
they call him Vārjinīvata, and he was considered the best among those who offer oblations with the Svāhā-call.
Svāhi’s son was King Ruṣadgu, the best among speakers,
who performed various great sacrifices accompanied by abundant sacrificial fees.
Desiring indeed a hundred offspring, Ruṣadgu begot that eldest son;
his son was Citraratha, who was endowed with various deeds.
The heroic Śaśabindu, the son of Caitrarathi, was a performer of sacrifices who bestowed abundant sacrificial fees; he followed the supreme conduct practiced by the royal sages.
Pṛthuśravas, of wide renown, was the king born of Śaśabindu;
and those learned in the Purāṇas declare that Antara was the son of Pārthaśravas.
Suyajña was the son of Antara;
he was the best among those who desire their own duty, performing every sacrifice with devotion.
The righteous Udyata became the best among those who have sons;
Uṣata’s son was Śineyu, the scorcher of enemies;
his son was Marutta, a royal sage and king.
Marutta obtained as his eldest son Kambalabarhiṣ;
knowing the state after death, he practiced supreme dharma out of indignation.
Desiring a hundred offspring, Śataprasūti indeed became the son of Kambalabarhiṣ; Rukmakavaca was the son of Śataprasava.
Having slain a hundred armored archers in battle with his sharpened arrows, Rukmakañcuka attained supreme glory.
And from Rukmakavaca was born Parājita, the slayer of enemy heroes;
five sons of great prowess were born to Parājita:
Rukmeṣu, Pṛthurukma, Jyāmagha, Pālita, and Hari.
The father gave Pālita and Hari to the Videhas;
Rukmeṣu became king, as did his dependent Pṛthurukma. Exiled from the kingdom by those two, Jyāmagha lived in a hermitage.
Having become tranquil while dwelling in the forest, he was enlightened by a brahmin;
then, mounting his chariot and bearing his banner, he departed for another region.
Alone, having conquered the banks of the Narmadā, the clay-rich Narmadā,
and Mount Ṛkṣavanta, he dwelt at Śuktimatī.
Caitrā, having reached maturity, became the wife of Jyāmagha;
and although that king was childless, he did not take another wife.
He achieved victory in that battle, and there he obtained a maiden;
having placed her upon his chariot, she was led away as a wife to the women's quarters.
Seeing her, the enraged Śaibyā said this to her husband:
"For what reason has this wicked co-wife been brought here?
Out of fear, that lord of men told his wife, "She is my daughter-in-law."
Having heard this, he said to him, "Whose daughter-in-law is she?
For she has not given birth to a son for you, nor do you have any other wife, O sinless one.
To which of your sons does this speech regarding the relationship of 'daughter-in-law' refer?"
Having heard that, Jyāmagha, the best of kings, spoke out, overcome with fear:
"She shall be the wife of the son who will be born to you."
Through her fierce asceticism, that fortunate Caitrā gave birth to a daughter; and having reached maturity, she bore Vidarbha as a son.
Later, Vidarbha begot upon his daughter-in-law, the princess of Kratha and Kaiśika, two wise and heroic sons who were experts in battle.
The third son was Lomapāda, who was supremely righteous.
Babhru was the son of Lomapāda, and Āhvati was his son.
From Āhvati came Kaiśika, who was learned and supremely righteous. Cidi was the son of Kaiśika, and from him the kings known as the Caidyas are said to have descended.
Bhīma was the son of Vidarbha, and Kunti was his son.
From Kunti was born a son, Dhṛṣṭa, who was powerful and bold in battle.
To Dhṛṣṭa were born three heroic sons, most righteous:
Āvanta, Daśārha, and the powerful Viṣṇuhara.
The son of Daśārha was Vyoma, who was learned and called Jīmūta;
Jīmūta’s son was Vṛkati, and his son was Bhīmaratha.
Now Bhīmaratha had a son named Navaratha;
his son was Daśaratha, and Śakuni was his son.
From him was born Karambha; Karambha’s son was King Devarāta.
Devakṣatra was the son of that great-souled one, and his son was Daivakṣatri.
Born equal to the offspring of a god, the delighter of the divine kṣatriyas was King Madhu,
the founder of the Madhu lineage, who was also sweet of speech.
From Madhu, by the daughter of Vidarbha, was born Purutvān, the best of men;
likewise, Maruvasa was his son.
Maruvasa had a son.
Then, O best of the Kurus, she was born as the mother from Bhadravatī, the princess of Vidarbha.
And Eṣvākī became his wife; from her was born [the son] who was endowed with all the qualities of a being and who increased the fame of the Sātvatas.
In that place where the Sātvatas, endowed with the six virtues and increasing their lineage, once dwelt—
having understood this account of the high-souled Jyāmagha—
one becomes joined with supreme joy and indeed becomes possessed of progeny.
Vaiśampāyana said: Kausalyā gave birth to sons endowed with goodness from Satvata— namely Bhajina, Bhajamāna, Divya, and King Devāvṛdha.
And Andhaka, the mighty-armed, and Vṛṣṇi, the joy of the Yadus—
listen here in detail to those four lineages of theirs.
Bhajamāna had two wives, Sṛñjayī, Bāhyakā, and Upabāhyakā; from them were born many sons.
Nimi, Kramaṇa, Viṣṇu, Śūra, and Purañjaya—
these were born to Bhajamāna by Bāhyakī, the daughter of Sṛñjaya.
Āyutājit, Sahasrājit, Chatājita, and Dāsaka were born from Bhajamāna by Upabāhyakī, the daughter of Sṛñjaya.
The king, a performer of sacrifices and a promoter of the gods, practiced extensive austerity,
resolved that he would have a son endowed with all virtues.
Thus uniting himself with her while touching the waters of the Parṇāśā,
the river did what was pleasing to him as he constantly performed his ritual ablutions.
Overwhelmed by anxiety, that best of rivers reached a single resolve because of the excellence of that king.
She did not find such a woman in whom a son endowed with all virtues like that of King Devāvṛdha might be born;
therefore, alas, she thought, "I myself shall become his companion in religious vows."
Then, having become a maiden and possessing a most excellent form,
she chose the king as her husband, and that lord desired her.
In her, that noble-minded one conceived a radiant embryo;
then, in the tenth month, that best of rivers gave birth to a son endowed with all virtues, Babhru, from King Devāvṛdha.
It is well known that those learned in the Purāṇas sing this in the genealogical chronicles,
extolling the virtues of the high-souled Devāvṛdha.
Just as we heard from afar, so indeed did we see him up close:
the tawny one, the best among men, equal to the gods who increase the divine power.
Sixty-six thousand and seven hundred men—
these attained immortality through Babhru Daivāvṛdha.
He was a performer of sacrifices, a lord of charity, wise, devoted to the Brahmins, and possessed of very firm weapons;
he was renowned, of great splendor, and a great chariot-warrior (*mahāratha*) among the Sātvatas.
His lineage was very great, consisting of those Bhojas who were descendants of Mārtikāvata.
From Andhaka, the daughter of Kaśya obtained four sons:
Kukura, Bhajamāna, Śami, and Kambalabarhiṣa.
The son of Kukura was Dhṛṣṇu, and the son of Dhṛṣṇu was likewise Kapotaroman; his son was Taittiri,
from whom Punarvasu was born, and from Punarvasu, Abhijit was born.
To that very Abhijit, it is said, was born a pair of children,
Āhuka and Āhukī, both renowned as the best among those who possess fame.
And in this regard, they cite these verses concerning that Āhuka:
Surrounded by a white retinue, the great Nāhuka, resembling a young colt and equipped with eighty shields, shall go forth first.
Neither one who is childless, nor one who has not given a hundred gifts, nor one who has not performed a thousand sacrifices,
nor one whose deeds are impure, nor one who has not offered sacrifice, should go toward a Bhoja king.
In the eastern direction, there was the approval of Bhoja for the Nāgas; indeed,
there were ten thousand chariots with cloud-like rumblings, equipped with quivers, undercarriages, banners, and protective fenders.
And there were also ten thousand girth-bands made of silver and gold.
In that same number of thousands, in the northern direction,
there stood the Bhoja kings, wearing small bells, until they reached their own territories.
And the Andhakas gave their sister Āhukī to the people of Avanti.
To Āhuka, however, two sons were born of Kāśyā:
Devaka and Ugrasena, both of whom were equal to the offspring of gods.
Devaka had four sons who were like the gods:
Devavān, Upadeva, Sudeva, and Devarakṣita;
he also had seven daughters, whom he gave to Vasudeva.
Devakī, Śāntidevā, Sudevā, Devarakṣitā,
Vṛkadevī, Upadevī, and Sunāmnī as the seventh.
Ugrasena had nine sons, of whom Kaṃsa was the eldest;
then Nyagrodha, Sunāman, Kaṅku, Śaṅku, Subhūmi,
Rāṣṭrapāla, Sutanu, Anādhṛṣṭi, and Puṣṭimat.
They had five sisters: Kaṃsā, Kaṃsavatī, Sutanū, Rāṣṭrapālī, and the beautiful woman Kaṅkā.
Ugrasena, born from the Kukura lineage, has been described along with his offspring.
A man who maintains this lineage of the Kukurās, who possess immeasurable splendor,
becomes possessed of offspring and attains his own extensive lineage.

Vaiśampāyana said:
Now, the son of Bhajamāna was Vidūratha, a preeminent chariot-warrior.
Rājādhideva, however, was a hero and the son of Vidūratha.
To Rājādhideva were born sons of exceeding prowess:
the mighty Datta and Atidatta, Śoṇāśva, and Śvetavāhana.
Śamī, Daṇḍaśarman, Dattaśatru, and Śatrujit were born;
and Śravaṇā and Śraviṣṭhā became sisters.
Śamīputra was the son of Pratikṣatra, and the son of Pratikṣatra was Svayaṃbhoja;
from Svayaṃbhoja, Dhṛdika was born.
He indeed had sons, all of whom were of terrible prowess;
Kṛtavarman was the eldest among them, while Śatadhanvan was the middle one.
Devānta, Narānta, Bhiṣaj, Vaitaraṇa,
Sudānta, Adhidānta, Kīnāśa, Dāma, and Dambhaka.
The learned Devānta was the son of Kambalabarhiṣ;
Kroṣṭu’s son was Anamitra, and from him indeed came Devamīḍhuṣa; likewise, the hero Asamaujas was born, and both he and [Devamīḍhuṣa] were called Asamaujas.
To Ajasraputra he gave his sons Asamaujas, Sudaṃṣṭra, Sucāru, and Kṛṣṇa; these are remembered as the Andhakas.
These and many other Andhakas have been recounted to you. Whoever constantly maintains this lineage of the Andhakas obtains a vast lineage for himself; of this there is no doubt.
Gāndhārī and Mādrī were the two wives of Kroṣṭu;
Gāndhārī gave birth to Sumitra, the delighter of his friends.
Then Mādrī bore two sons: Yudhājit and Devamīḍhuṣa;
the latter was of great strength, a conqueror of enemies, and known as Anamitra.
Nighna was the son of Anamitra, and Nighna had two sons:
Prasena and Satrājit, both of whom were conquerors of enemy armies.
While Dvārakā was being settled, Prasena obtained from the ocean a divine great jewel named Syamantaka.

Sūrya became a friend to that Satrājit, equal to his very life-breath. Once, at the end of the night, that best of chariot-warriors went by chariot to the shore of the ocean to perform ritual ablutions and to pay homage to the Sun.
As he was standing there worshipping the sun, the blessed Lord Vivasvat stood before him,
his form indistinct, surrounded by a circle of radiance.
Then the king spoke to Vivasvat, who stood before him:
"O Lord of lights, just as I always behold you in the sky as a god encircled by a halo of splendor, so do I see you standing here before me."
"What distinction is there between me and you, who have approached me with friendship?
Having heard this, the Blessed One [gave] the Syamantaka jewel.
Having unfastened it from his own neck, he placed it on the ground in a secluded spot;
then the king beheld him in embodied form,
and having seen him with joy, he conversed with him for a moment.
As Vivasvat was setting out once more, Satrajit said to him:
"O Lord, by means of which you constantly illuminate these worlds."
"Therefore, O Blessed One, you ought to give this jewel to me.
Then Bhāskara gave him the Syamantaka gem;
having fastened it on, the lord of the earth entered the city.
The people ran after him, crying out, "This is the sun that is moving!
Having caused the city to marvel, the king then went to his inner apartments.

Out of affection, King Satrājit gave that supreme and divine *syamantaka* jewel to his brother Prasenajit. Then Satrājit went to his own glorious home, where auspicious marriage rites had been performed.
Having entered the abode of the gods, he presented the jewel to the brahmins.
O Lord, day after day he shed eight bhāras of gold;
having quickly removed it from his neck, he deposited it in a secluded place.
Then Satrājit [wore] the Sun, blazing with its own form.
Having prostrated before the Great-Souled One, he stood with palms joined in reverence.
Having praised the Sun with various hymns, he gratified him;
thereupon the Blessed One, being pleased, said: "Choose the boon you desire."
Thus he spoke to the king, and the king then chose the jewel;
and having given him that jewel, he vanished right there.
And Satrājit, O great king, possessed the Syamantaka jewel.
That jewel yielded gold within the dwelling of the Vṛṣṇis and Andhakas;
the rain-cloud poured forth at the proper time, and there was no fear of disease.
Govinda desired the Syamantaka jewel from Prasena;
however, although he was capable, he did not take it by force, nor did he obtain it.
Once, while out hunting adorned with that [jewel],
Prasena met his death at the hands of a forest-dwelling lion on account of the Syamantaka.
Then the mighty king of bears, having struck down the charging lion and seized that precious jewel, entered his cave.
Then, having learned of that request for the jewel on account of Prasenajit’s murder, all the Vṛṣṇis and Andhakas became suspicious of Kṛṣṇa.
Suspected of that deed, that righteous soul, though not the doer of it,
went to the forest after making the vow, "I shall bring back the jewel."
"He is devoted to the gods and the twice-born, and he is ever-moving in search of prosperity.
Then, following the tracks of Prasena where he had been hunting,
[the king] sent reliable men to track his footprints.
To Ṛkṣavān, the best of mountains, and to Vindhya, the most excellent mountain.
Exhausted from his search, that high-minded man saw Prasena killed along with his horse, but he did not find the jewel.
Then the lion was seen not far from the body of Prasena,
killed by a bear, as indicated by the bear's footprints.
Then Mādhava followed those footprints to the cave of the bear;
in that great bear-cave, he heard a voice uttered by a woman in distress.
O King, the nurse, having taken the prince— the son of Jāmbavat—
was playing with a jewel while saying to him, "Do not cry."
The nurse said: "The lion killed Prasena; the lion was slain by Jāmbavān.
Do not weep, my dear child; for this Syamantaka belongs to you."
Having made himself known by his voice, he quickly went to the cave;
and having entered that bear’s cave directly, the Blessed One stationed the Yadus together with the wielder of the plow (Balarāma) at the entrance of the cave.
The wielder of the Śārṅga bow indeed beheld Jāmbavān staying within the cave.
Vāsudeva, however, fought with Jāmbavān inside the cave;
Govinda fought with his two arms alone for twenty-one days.
Indeed, he fought with this Blessed One, his own master,
out of anger because he was an ordinary man who did not recognize the Lord's majesty, thinking him to be a mere mortal;
it was a tumultuous duel between the two, both desiring victory.
With weapons, stones, trees, and their own arms— as if two hawks competing for meat— they entered the cave.
But when Kṛṣṇa had entered the hole, the people, led by Vasudeva,
could not see the exit of Śauri once he had gone inside.
Having waited for twelve days, they returned sorrowfully to their own city;
arriving again at Dvāravatī, they announced that Kṛṣṇa had been slain.
O King, having heard that Kṛṣṇa had not emerged from the cave, Devakī, Rukmiṇī, Ānakadundubhi, their friends, and their kinsmen all grieved; meanwhile,
Vāsudeva, having conquered the mighty Jāmbavān, [returned].
Having conquered the mighty Jāmbavanta, Vāsudeva obtained the maiden Jāmbavatī, who was highly esteemed by the king of the bears.
He took the Syamantaka jewel for the sake of his own purification,
and after conciliating the king of the bears, he then emerged from the cave.
Endowed with supreme splendor, Kṛṣṇa went to Dvārakā;
having thus recovered the jewel and purified himself, Acyuta gave it indeed to Satrājit in the assembly of all the Sātvatas.
Thus, by Kṛṣṇa, the slayer of enemies, who had been falsely accused,
his own self was purified of sin after he had won back the Syamantaka jewel.
Satrājit had ten wives, and they had one hundred sons;
among them, three were famous, the eldest being Bhaṅgakāra.
Vīra, Vātapati, and likewise Upasvāvan,
as well as three maidens, O lord of men, are renowned in the quarters.
Satyabhāmā, the best among women, observant of vows and firm in her resolve,
as well as Padmāvatī— these wives he gave to Kṛṣṇa.
From Bhaṅgakāra were born Sabhākṣa and Nāreya, the two best of men,
who were endowed with virtues and renowned for their excellence of qualities.
Then Pṛśni was born as the son of Madhu, the son of Yudhājit;
and two sons were born to Pṛśni: Śvaphalka and Citraka.
Śvaphalka took as his wife the daughter of the King of Kāśī;
she was named Gāndinī because she always gave away cows (gāḥ).
O descendant of Bharata, from her was then born the heroic Akrūra, known as Śrutavān,
who was highly fortunate, a performer of sacrifices, and a giver of abundant sacrificial fees.
Upāsaṅga, Madgura, Mṛdura, Arimardana, Girikṣipa, Upekṣa, Śatruha, and Arimejaya.
Carmabhṛt, Cārivarmā, Gṛdhra, Ojas, and Nara, as well as Āvāha, Prativāha, and the beautiful woman Sundarī.
His daughter was Vasuṃdharā, the renowned queen of Sāmba;
she was endowed with beauty and youth, captivating the hearts of all living beings.
O descendant of Kuru, from Akrūra and the fair-limbed daughter of Ugrasena were born Sudeva and Upadeva, both possessing divine splendor.
Citraka had sons, namely Pṛthu and Vipṛthu,
as well as Aśvasena, Aśvabāhu, Supārśvaka, and Gaveṣaṇa.
The sons of Ariṣṭanemi were Dharma and Dharmabhṛt, as well as Subāhu and Bahubāhu; Śraviṣṭhā and Śravaṇā were his two daughters.
