may I myself become the sun, the moon, the wind, and the fire.
The waters, the atmosphere, the constellations, and the ten directions.
I am anger and desire, Varuṇa, Vāsava, and Yama; I am Dhanada, the lord of wealth, the Yakṣa, and the sovereign of the Kiṃpuruṣas.
Vaiśampāyana said:
Having been thus addressed by the Daitya, the blessed Self-born One then spoke to that king of the Daityas with a smile, O best of kings.
"Neither by day nor by night shall death come to me.
Brahmā said:
"O dear one, these wonderful divine boons have been granted to you by me."
O dear one, you will obtain all these desires; of this there is no doubt.
Having spoken thus, the Blessed One indeed departed through the sky to the Vairāja abode of Brahmā, which is frequented by hosts of brahminical sages.
Having heard that boon granted by the one born from the waters,
the gods, led by Śakra, made a request to the Lord;
then the gods, the nāgas, the gandharvas, and likewise the sages [did so].
Upon hearing the granting of the boon, they approached the Grandfather.
The gods said:
"O Blessed One, by virtue of the boon granted to him, that asura will slay us.
Therefore, be gracious, O Blessed One; let a means for his destruction be devised."
The Blessed One is the self-existent, the original creator, and the all-pervading lord of all beings;
he is the creator of the offerings to gods and ancestors, the unmanifest, primordial nature, and the eternal.
Then, having heard those words for the welfare of the world, the Lord Prajāpati spoke these words to all the hosts of gods.
The thirty gods must certainly obtain the fruit of his asceticism;
at the conclusion of his penance, the Blessed Viṣṇu will bring about his destruction.
Having heard these words of the lotus-born one, all the gods,
filled with joy, departed for their own divine abodes.
As soon as he had obtained the boon,
the Daitya Hiraṇyakaśipu, emboldened by the granting of that boon, oppressed all living beings.
In ancient times, he indeed assailed the highly fortunate sages in their hermitages— those of rigid vows, devoted to truth and righteousness, and self-controlled.
Having defeated the gods dwelling in the three worlds and brought the triple universe under his control, the great asura, the dānava, dwells in heaven.
When the Dānava, intoxicated by the pride of his boon, dwelt upon the earth,
he made the Daityas worthy of sacrifice and rendered the deities unworthy of sacrifice.
Then the Ādityas, the Sādhyas, the Viśvedevas, and likewise the Vasus;
the Maruts, the Apsarases, the Gandharvas, and the twice-born knowers of Brahman;
the Ṛṣis, the Nāgas, the Suparṇas, and others such as these.
They approached Viṣṇu, the refuge of all, the protector, and the one of great power.

The gods, seeking refuge, went for protection to the all-pervading Lord Nārāyaṇa—the god who is the embodiment of Brahman, the sacrifice, and the eternal deity of Brahman; the sovereign of the past, present, and future; and the one honored by the worlds.
Protect us today, O Lord of Gods, from the slaughter by Hiraṇyakaśipu!
For you alone are our supreme god; for you alone are our supreme teacher;
for you alone are our supreme creator, O best of gods, even above Brahmā and the others.
O you whose eyes are like the petals of a full-blown lotus, O bringer of fear to the faction of our enemies,
for the destruction of the lineage of Diti, please become our refuge.
Viṣṇu said:
"O immortals, cast away your fear; I grant you freedom from fear.
Likewise, O gods, regain the celestial realm without delay."
Here I am; I shall slay that lord of the Dānavas, the Daitya who, arrogant because of the granting of a boon, is unslayable by the lords of the immortals, together with his host.
Having spoken thus and dismissed the lords of the thirty gods, O King, the Blessed Lord Hari went to the assembly hall of Hiraṇyakaśipu.
The Lord Hari went to the assembly hall of Hiraṇyakaśipu,
having assumed the body of a Man-Lion (Narasiṃha) with half his form as a man and half his form as a lion, touching hand to hand.
Resembling a mass of clouds, with a voice like the thundering of clouds,
possessing the radiant power of a cloud-mass, he was as swift as a cloud.
The heroic Nṛsiṃha rushed toward the son of Diti, the enemy of the gods;
springing up, he tore him open with his sharp claws and slew him in battle—
that exceedingly powerful and arrogant Daitya who possessed the prowess of a proud tiger.
With a single hand, he slew those who were protected by the arrogant hosts of Daityas.
This Nṛsiṃha has been described; furthermore, this other one is Vāmana, in which [incarnation], having assumed the form of Vāmana that destroys the Daityas, [he acts].
In ancient times, at the sacrifice of Bali, those unshakeable great asuras were shaken by the powerful Viṣṇu with his three strides.
Vipracitti, Śibi, Śaṅku, and likewise Ayaḥśaṅku;
Ayaḥśiras, Aśvaśiras, and the valiant Hayagrīva; Vegavān, Ketumān, Ugra, and the great asura Ugravyagra.
Puṣkara and Puṣkala, Sāśva and Aśvapati, Prahrāda, Aśvaśiras, Kumbha, Saṃhrāda, and Gaganapriya.
Anuhrāda, Hari, Hara, Varāha, Saṃhara, Ruja, Vepana, Mahāratha,
Bṛhatkīrti, and Mahājihva.
Śarabha, Śalabha, Kupana, Kopana, and Kratha.
Of vast renown, with a great tongue, spike-like ears, and a mighty voice;
with a long tongue, sun-like eyes, soft feet, and a gentle, loving nature.
Vāyu, Gaviṣṭha, Namuci, Śambara, Vikṣara, Mahān,
Candrahantṛ, Krodhahantṛ, and Krodhavardhana.
Kālaka, Kālakeya, Vṛtra, Krodha, Virocana,
Gariṣṭha, Variṣṭha, and both Pralamba and Naraka.
Indratāpana, Vātāpī, Ketumān, Baladarpita,
Asiloman, Puloman, Bāṣkala, Pramada, and Mada.
Khasṛma, Kālavadana, Karāla, Keśin,
Ekākṣa, Candrahā, Rāhu, Saṃhrāda, Sṛmara, and Svana.
With *śataghnīs* and discs in their hands, as well as iron clubs in their grasp,
they were equipped with stone-engines as weapons and likewise armed with slings.
With spears and mortars in their hands, and likewise bearing axes;
indeed, with nooses and mallets in their hands, as well as clubs in their grasp.
The Dānavas wielded great boulders as weapons, held spears in their hands, and possessed various other terrible arms; they were fearsome, dressed in diverse garbs, and endowed with great speed.
And those with the faces of tortoises and cocks, as well as those with the faces of hares and owls;
likewise those with the faces of donkeys and camels, and those with the faces of boars.
The Dānavas were terrifying, with faces like crocodiles, faces like jackals,
faces like mice and frogs, and likewise, they had the dreadful faces of wolves.
Some had the faces of cats and rabbits, while others had enormous mouths; those heroes had the faces of crocodiles and rams, as well as the faces of cows, goats, sheep, and buffaloes.
Some had faces like iguanas and porcupines, others had faces like cranes;
some had the faces of Garuḍas, some the faces of rhinoceroses, and others the faces of peacocks.
Some were clothed in the skins of lordly elephants, others wore garments of black antelope skin; some had their bodies covered in rags, while others were dressed in bark-cloth.
The Asuras were crested with topknots, wearing crowns and earrings;
they wore diadems, had long tufts of hair, necks as graceful as conch shells, and were full of splendor.
These Daityas bore various costumes, adorned with diverse garlands and unguents.
Seizing their own weapons, which seemed to blaze with splendor,
they all rushed from every side toward Hṛṣīkeśa as he advanced.
Then, having crushed all the Daityas with the soles of his feet and the palms of his hands,
he assumed a most terrifying form and swiftly seized the earth.
As he strode across the earth, the moon and sun were situated between his breasts; as he traversed the sky, they were said to have rested at his navel.
As Viṣṇu of immeasurable prowess was advancing, those two stood upon his knees; thus do the twice-born speak.
Having seized the entire earth and slain the foremost of the asuras,
Viṣṇu, the best among the powerful, gave the earth to Śakra.
This manifestation of the Great-Souled One known as Vāmana has been described by the twice-born who know the Vedas; it is indeed the glory of Viṣṇu.
Furthermore, there was a manifestation of the high-souled Viṣṇu, the self of all beings,
known as Dattātreya, who was endowed with supreme forbearance.
When the gods had thus perished, when the ritual procedures and sacrifices had ceased, when the fourfold social order had become confused, and when dharma had fallen into laxity;
When unrighteousness increases, truth is lost, falsehood prevails,
living beings are wasting away, and righteousness has fallen into disorder, [the world decays].
Indeed, by him the Vedas, along with their sacrifices and rituals, were truly recovered;
and by that great-souled one, the fourfold order of society was made free from confusion.
By that wise Dattātreya, the giver of boons, a boon was granted to the wise Kārtavīrya, the king of the Haihayas.
O King, these two arms of yours shall become one hundred arms for my sake; of this there is no doubt.
And you shall protect the entire earth, O Lord of the Earth;
and standing in battle, you shall be difficult for hosts of enemies to behold.

O great king, subduer of enemies, this glorious, wonderful, and auspicious manifestation of Viṣṇu has been narrated to you exactly as it was heard. Furthermore, this manifestation of the high-souled one as the son of Jamadagni [shall now be told].
There, the powerful Lord Rāma slew King Arjuna, who stood in his army, amazed and difficult to defeat in battle because of his thousand arms.
Having struck down King Arjuna from his chariot to the ground,
Rāma overpowered him at will as he cried out like a thundercloud.
And the descendant of Bhṛgu, with his flaming axe, cut off the entire thousand arms of him who was accompanied by his kinsmen.
Covered with tens of millions of kṣatriyas, the earth— adorned by Meru and Mandara—
was rendered devoid of kṣatriyas twenty-one times by him.
Having indeed rid the earth of the Kṣatriyas, Bhārgava, the great ascetic,
performed a horse sacrifice for the destruction of all his sins.
At that sacrifice of great giving, the descendant of Bhrigu,
being pleased, bestowed the earth as a sacrificial fee upon Kaśyapa, the son of Marīci.
In that great horse sacrifice, the highly illustrious and high-minded best of chariot-warriors gave away white horses of Varuṇa’s lineage, a chariot, inexhaustible gold, cows, and lordly elephants.

Even today, for the welfare of the worlds, the glorious son of Jamadagni, the delight of the Bhrigus, remains on Mahendra, the best of mountains, like a god, repeatedly performing radiant austerities again and again.
Wearing a black antelope skin as an upper garment and adorned with a crown of matted locks,
this manifestation of the high-souled Viṣṇu— the eternal and immutable Lord of the gods— is known as Jāmadagnya.
Furthermore, in the twenty-fourth yuga, there was born to Daśaratha a lotus-eyed son, preceded by Viśvāmitra.
Having divided himself into four parts, the mighty-armed Lord and Master became renowned in the world as Rāma, equal to the sun in splendor.
For the sake of pleasing the world, for the subduing of the Rākṣasas,
and for the increase of Dharma, the highly illustrious one was born there;
they call that lord of men the very body of the Lord of all beings.
And for him, the wise Viśvāmitra bestowed weapons that were difficult even for the gods to withstand, intended for the destruction of the enemies of the gods.

By that high-souled one, Mārīca and Subāhu— the two foremost among the strong— were slain and rendered hopeless by his might, for they had caused obstacles to the sacrifices of the sages of purified soul.
By him, in the past, while the sacrifice of the high-souled Janaka was underway,
the bow of Maheśvara was broken as he sported with effortless ease.
Rāma, who knew all dharmas, dwelt for fourteen years in the forest;
accompanied by Lakṣmaṇa, he was devoted to the welfare of all beings.
She who stands by his side in bodily form, renowned among people as Sītā,
is that very Lakṣmī who, due to her former association, follows after her husband.
Having performed austerities for fourteen years in the forest, that descendant of Raghu,
while dwelling in Janasthāna, carried out the mission of the gods.
Seeking the tracks of Sītā, the high-minded one slew the two Rākṣasas Virādha and Kabandha of terrifying prowess;
he also killed the two Gandharvas, those tigers among men who had been afflicted by a curse.

With arrows possessing the brilliance of fire, the sun’s rays, and lightning, with variegated shafts of refined gold, and with a potency equal to the thunderbolt and lightning of the Lord of the Gods, they were forcibly severed from their bodies.
It was by him that the mighty lord of monkeys,
Vālin, was slain in battle for the sake of Sugrīva, and Sugrīva was consecrated [as king].
For there, Rāvaṇa— the lord of the rākṣasas, invincible in battle and incapable of being slain by the hosts of gods and asuras, as well as by the yakṣas, rākṣasas, and birds— [was encountered].
He was guarded by millions of Rākṣasas, resembling a mass of black collyrium;
he was the cruel Rākṣasa lord of the Rākṣasas, the Rāvaṇa of the three worlds.
Difficult to digest, difficult to restrain, arrogant, and possessing prowess equal to a tiger,
he was hard for even the hosts of gods to look upon, being inflated with pride by the granting of a boon.
Together with his ministers, he struck down Rāvaṇa— whose body was vast, whose strength was immense, and who resembled a mass of great clouds— in battle, along with his army.

In ancient times, Rāma, that bull among men and lord of beings, swiftly slew the cruel Rāvaṇa, the descendant of Pulastya, who was of wicked resolve and had committed offenses against him, along with his brothers, sons, ministers, and army.
And the haughty Dānava named Lavaṇa, the son of Madhu—
a terrible and great Asura who had been granted boons— was slain in battle by that one skilled in combat, along with other Rākṣasas as well, in the Madhuvana forest.
Having performed these deeds, Rāma, the best among the upholders of dharma,
celebrated ten unobstructed Jārūthya horse-sacrifices.
While Rāma ruled the kingdom, no evil words were heard, the wind blew without causing distress, and there was no plundering of wealth.
There were no widows lamenting, nor did any misfortune occur;
while Rāma governed the kingdom, the entire world was subdued.
Living beings had no fear arising from water, fire, or injury;
nor did the elderly ever have to perform funeral rites for children.
The Kṣatriya attends upon the Brahmin, and the Vaiśyas follow the will of the Kṣatriya;
likewise, the Śūdras, free from egoism, serve these three castes.
Wives did not transgress against their husbands, nor did husbands transgress against their wives;
the entire world was self-restrained, and the earth was free from robbers.
Rāma alone was the lord, and Rāma was the protector.
While Rāma was ruling the kingdom, there were thousands of years [of prosperity], people had thousands of sons, and all living beings were free from disease.
While Rāma was ruling the kingdom, there was a cohabitation on earth among the gods, the sages, and human beings in every respect.
"Rāma, Rāma, Rāma"—such was the talk among the subjects while Rāma ruled the kingdom. The world became a delight for Rāma;
even those people who are knowers of the Purāṇas sing these verses here:
The true meanings are bound up in Rāma; such is the greatness of that wise one.
Dark-complexioned, youthful, with red eyes and a radiant face, he was measured in speech;
his arms reached down to his knees, his countenance was handsome, and he possessed the shoulders and great arms of a lion.
Having become the lord of Ayodhyā, Rāma ruled the kingdom for ten thousand and one thousand years.

In that kingdom, the sound of the Rig, Sama, and Yajur Vedas, as well as the twang of the great-souled king’s bowstring, never ceased; it was ever proclaimed: "Let there be giving! Let there be eating!"
Endowed with courage, perfected in virtue, and blazing with his own splendor,
Rāma, the son of Daśaratha, shone forth, surpassing both the sun and the moon.
That Raghava of great strength, having performed hundreds of meritorious sacrifices accompanied by excellent sacrificial fees, abandoned Ayodhya and ascended to heaven.
Thus this mighty-armed lord, the delight of the Ikṣvāku lineage,
having slain Rāvaṇa along with his hosts, ascended to heaven.
This is another manifestation of the high-souled Keśava,
renowned in the Māthura-kalpa, for the welfare of all the worlds.
In whom [reside] Śālva and Kaṃsa, Mainda and Dvivida,
Ariṣṭa, Vṛṣabha, Keśin, and Pūtanā, the daughter of the Daityas.
The heroic one then slew the elephant Kuvalayāpīḍa, as well as Cāṇūra and Muṣṭika— those Daityas dwelling in human bodies.
The thousand arms of Bāṇa of wondrous deeds were severed,
and Naraka was slain in battle, as was the mighty Yavana.
And by his splendor, all the jewels of the rulers of the earth were taken away,
and those kings on the surface of the earth who were of evil conduct were slain.
In the twenty-eighth Dvāpara age of the ninth cycle,
Viṣṇu formerly became Vedavyāsa, preceded by Jātūkarṇya;
by that high-souled one, the single Veda was divided into four.
The lineage of Bharata was produced by the son of Satyavatī;
these manifestations of the Great-Souled One for the sake of the welfare of the world have been recounted,
O King, as those that have passed, and those yet to come are now being told.
Furthermore, the Lord named Kalkī Viṣṇuyaśas will be born again.
...a twice-born man from the village of Sambhala,
for the sake of the welfare of all the world...
the tenth [incarnation], endowed with future perfection, preceded by Yājñavalkya.
Having caused all those who were impelled by their destined future to perish, he,
together with his followers, will reach his end between the Ganges and the Yamunā;
then, after time has passed, he will do so along with his ministers and his army.
Then, when the kings had perished, the subjects were left without a ruler.
In an instant, having been extinguished and having slain one another in battle,
with their own kin taken by each other, they were left without refuge and deeply distressed;
thus did they then fall into such misery during the period of the Kali twilight.
The subjects will go to destruction along with the Kali Yuga;
when that Kali Yuga has waned, the Kṛta Yuga will then prevail once more according to its proper order, by its very nature and not otherwise.
Leading an army crowded with elephants, horses, and chariots,
and surrounded by hundreds of thousands of Brahmins bearing uplifted weapons,
he will then leave those pure kings without a single survivor.
He [subdued] thousands of heretics, barbarian tribes, and bandits—
those who were not particularly righteous and those who were anywhere haters of Dharma;
likewise those from the North, those dwelling in the Middle Country, and those from the mountains.
Those from the east and those from the west, as well as those dwelling on the slopes and ridges of the Vindhya mountains;
likewise the southerners and the Dravidas together with the Siṃhalas;
the Gāndhāras, the Pāradas, the Pahlavas, the Yavanas, and the Śakas.

That powerful lord, whose wheel of dominion was set in motion, the mighty destroyer of bandits, [subjugated] the Tukhāras, the Barbaras, the Śvānikas, the Daradas, the Khaśas, the Lambakas, the Marundhas, and the Kirātas.
Invincible to all beings, he shall wander the earth;
for he was born as a human from the foremost and wise god.
In a previous birth, that powerful one was Viṣṇu, known by the name Pramati.
He was indeed born from a limb of the Moon during the full Kali Yuga.
Thus, these ten incarnations of Vāsudeva are remembered;
each according to its specific time, purpose, and the particular region where he acted.
Entering various wombs throughout the three worlds by means of his portions,
Kalki, arisen as the twenty-fifth principle, shall destroy all beings and men in every way for fifty years.
Having, through his cruel deeds, reduced the earth to nothing but seeds and having subdued those wicked men who were mostly unrighteous,
this Kalki, together with his army, will then have accomplished his purpose.
Having accomplished the welfare of his subjects and having himself achieved his own purpose,
he will then destroy those deluded people who have become mutually enraged;
having destroyed cities and villages, the subjects will then be difficult to restrain.
In the Kali Yuga, the sacred scriptures and the Dharma will be lost, as will the system of castes and stages of life; people will become short-statured, short-lived,
and will dwell by rivers and mountains, subsisting on leaves, roots, and fruits.
Wearing garments of bark, leaves, and skins, they have taken refuge in terrifying caves;
short-lived, deprived of news, beset by many afflictions, and deeply distressed—
these and many others are divine beings endowed with celestial qualities.
These manifestations are sung of in the Purāṇas by those who discourse on Brahman.
Where even the gods are bewildered in recounting the manifestations [of the Lord],
there exists the Purāṇa, which is perfectly consistent with the Vedic revelation.
By this mere summary,
the manifestation of the Lord, the Teacher of all worlds, who is worthy of praise, has been proclaimed.
The ancestors of that person who,
with palms joined in reverence, listens to the recitation of the manifestations of Viṣṇu of immeasurable prowess, are truly gratified.
Freed from all sins, one shall obtain wealth, sons, and cattle;
no misfortune exists for him, and he shall be possessed of sons and radiant splendor.
Having heard these yogic illusions of the Lord of Yoga, a person is liberated from all sins.
Through the grace of the Blessed One, one quickly attains supernatural power, prosperity, and vast enjoyments.
Chapter 32,
Transliterated by Atul Agarwala,
Proof-read by Horst Brinkhaus.
Vaiśampāyana said:
Listen to me regarding the universal nature of Viṣṇu and his state as Hari in the Kṛta Yuga.
He possesses the nature of Vaikuṇṭha among the gods and the nature of Kṛṣṇa among human beings.
O King, listen now to the profound course of this Lord’s actions— past, present, and future— exactly as it is.
This Lord and Master, Nārāyaṇa, who is unmanifest yet abides in manifest forms, is indeed infinite in essence, the source of all, and imperishable.
Having become Nārāyaṇa, this eternal Hari was Brahmā, Śakra, Soma, Dharma, Śukra, and Bṛhaspati.
Having attained the status of being even Aditi’s son, this delighter of the Yādavas became known as Viṣṇu, the younger brother of Indra.
For that birth of a son to the Lord by Aditi was born of his grace,
for the purpose of slaying the enemies of the gods— the Daityas, Dānavas, and Rākṣasas.
In the beginning, this Lord, whose self is Pradhāna, created Brahmā;
he, the Primordial Person, created the Prajāpatis in the first aeon.
Extending their bodies there, they produced unsurpassed lineages of Brahman;
from those great-souled ones, the eternal Brahman manifested in many ways.
This recitation of the deeds of Viṣṇu, who is himself a marvel, has been proclaimed;
now listen to me as I proclaim further that which is worthy of being proclaimed.
O dear one, when the slaughter of Vṛtra had occurred and the Kṛta Yuga was prevailing,
there arose a battle renowned throughout the three worlds known as Tārakāmaya.
There, all those terrible Dānavas, arrogant in battle,
were slaying the gods along with the Gandharvas, Yakṣas, Uragas, and Cāraṇas.
Being slaughtered in battle, turned away from the fight, and with their weapons exhausted,
they sought in their minds a protector— the Lord, the god Nārāyaṇa.
In the meantime, clouds with the luster of extinguished charcoal covered the expanse of the sky, along with the sun, moon, and hosts of planets.
Intertwined with flickering clusters of lightning, terrible and making a deafening roar,
the seven winds blew, striking one another with great force.
With the falling of blazing water and thunderbolts, and with the winds of fire possessing the speed of a diamond,
the sky, as if being consumed by terrible portents, let out a roar.
Thousands of meteors fell, and even those moving through the sky fell;
celestial chariots, turned upside down, were falling and leaping up.
At the end of the cycle of the four ages, whatever fear may arise for the worlds, during that time characterized by portents, forms appear that are formless.
Everything was rendered lusterless by darkness; nothing could be discerned, and the ten directions, enveloped by a flood of gloom, did not shine.
Kālī entered in embodied form, shrouded like a dark cloud;
the sky did not shine, overwhelmed as it were by the sun, enveloped in a terrible darkness.
Having warded off those masses of clouds accompanied by darkness with his two arms,
that Lord Hari, whose body was dark, revealed his divine form.
Resembling a dark cloud in hue, with body-hair like a cloud,
he was Kṛṣṇa by his splendor and his form, like the Black Mountain itself.
Wearing blazing yellow garments and adorned with ornaments of refined gold,
his body was like the darkness of smoke, appearing like the fire risen at the end of an eon.
He had four times twice as many thick shoulders, his hair was covered by a diadem,
his hands were joined with gold, and he was adorned with weapons.
It was as lofty as a mountain peak, endowed with the rays of the sun and moon;
it gladdened the hand of Nandaka and bore arrows that were like venomous serpents.
Variegated with power, formidable with the plow, bearing the conch, discus, and mace;
he is the Viṣṇu-mountain, rooted in forbearance, the sacred Śrīvṛkṣa tree, and the one whose horn is the Śārṅga bow.
Yoked with chariots drawn by bay horses, adorned with the banner of Suparṇa,
fashioned with wheels of the sun and moon, and having Mount Mandara as its axle-end;
Upon the hub of Mount Meru, which was joined with uninterrupted rays and difficult to behold,
there were stars like variegated flowers and it was adorned by planets and constellations.
In the sky, the gods, defeated by the Daityas, beheld the Lord standing in a celestial chariot that embodied the divine realm, granting fearlessness in the midst of terrors.
With palms joined in reverence, all those gods, led by Śakra, having placed cries of "Victory! at their head, went for refuge to the one worthy of refuge.
And they praised the Lord Nārāyaṇa, Hari, the Master of the World:
"Victory to you, O God, Master of the World! Victory to you, O God Janārdana!
Victory to you, O Lord Viṣṇu! Victory to the wielder of the conch and the mace!"
Salutations to you, O Hṛṣīkeśa; salutations, O God Janārdana!
O Primordial God, Lord of the World, Creator of the Creator of beings!
Salutations to you, O Lord Viṣṇu; salutations to the Sovereign of the origin of all beings.
Salutations to the primordial seed, salutations again and again to the Puruṣa;
let there be salutation to you, O Lord of the World, salutation again to the Great-Souled One.
Or rather, O Keśava, Lord of the World, what is the use of this prostration?
"Protect all of us gods who have been bound by the noose of the Daityas.
Having heard those words of theirs, Viṣṇu, whose own deity is his beloved,
set his mind upon the destruction of the Dānavas in a great battle.
But Viṣṇu, stationed in the sky and assuming his supreme form,
spoke these words with a solemn promise to all the deities:
"Attain peace; may it be well with you; do not fear, O hosts of Maruts!
All the Dānavas have been conquered by me; let the three worlds be received back."
Satisfied by the words of that Viṣṇu who is true to his promise,
the gods attained supreme joy, as if they had obtained the highest nectar.
Then the darkness was withdrawn, the clouds vanished,
auspicious winds blew, and the ten directions became clear.
The brilliantly radiant luminaries circumambulated the moon in a clockwise direction,
and the blazing splendors circumambulated the sun in a clockwise direction.
The planets ceased their conflict, the rivers became tranquil,
and the three paths— the celestial path and the others— shone free from dust.
The rivers flowed according to their true nature and the oceans were not agitated;
the sense faculties within the inner selves of men became auspicious.
The great seers, free from sorrow, recited the Vedas aloud;
and in the sacrifices, the purifier (Agni) received the sweet and auspicious oblation.
The worlds became characterized by the dharma of active engagement, with joyful minds;
all the worlds were filled with joy and even more so.
Filled with supreme joy upon hearing the words of Viṣṇu, the god of gods and lord of the earth, who had made a vow regarding the destruction of his enemies.
"I shall slay the arrogant Dānavas along with your bodies; the Dānavas considered those fierce words as meaning they were already slain in battle."—
Chapter 33.
Transliterated by Atul Agarwala,
proof-read by Horst Brinkhaus, version of February 24, 2000.
Vaiśampāyana said: Then, having heard that the fear arising from Viṣṇu was imminent, the Daityas and Dānavas,
who were difficult to conquer in battle, made extensive preparations for war.
But for me, there was an imperishable chariot made of gold, three *nalva*s in extent,
with four wheels, beautiful in form, and equipped with excellent great weapons.
Resounding with the tinkling of a network of small bells, adorned with a leopard skin,
and fashioned with networks of jewels and embellished with networks of gold.
It was crowded with herds of wild beasts, graced by birds,
bearing divine weapons and quivers, and resounded like the rumbling of clouds.
That excellent and noble chariot was well-seated and like a mountain;
it was filled with maces and iron clubs, resembling the ocean personified.
Adorned with golden armlets and bracelets, and with its poles topped by golden earrings,
it stood tall with banners and flags like Mount Mandara with the sun.
In one place he had the body of a lordly elephant or a cloud, possessing the brilliance of a lion's mane,
joined by a thousand bears, and roaring like a thousand clouds.
Blazing, celestial, and capable of crushing the chariots of enemies, he stood upon that sky-faring vehicle, longing for battle like the radiant sun atop Mount Meru.
Tāra, however, driving an iron chariot as wide as a krośa,
which resembled a heap of piled-up rocks and was like a mass of black collyrium, [advanced].
It had eight wheels made of black iron, with an iron pole, yoke, and shaft;
its rays vomited forth darkness, and it roared like a rain-cloud.
It was fortified with a great iron lattice complete with windows,
and filled with iron bars and hurls such as mallets.
It was adorned with spears and outstretched nooses, with suspended mallets,
and with terrifying javelins along with battle-axes.
He ascended that excellent chariot, which was yoked to a thousand donkeys and raised up for the sake of his enemies like a second Mount Mandara.
But Virocana, enraged and with mace in hand,
stood at the head of that army like a mountain with blazing peaks.
The Dānava Hayagrīva, however, drove a chariot yoked with a thousand horses—
a vehicle that crushed the armies of his enemies.
Drawing his great bow, which was many thousands of spans long,
Varāha stood at the front like a mountain with its foothills.
Dripping with sweat and shedding tears born of rage from his eyes,
his mouth quivering with bared fangs and lips, he longed for battle.
But Tvaṣṭṛ, the powerful Dānava, mounting a vehicle drawn by eighteen horses and surrounded by Dānava arrays, moved about.
The son of Vipracitti was Śveta, adorned with white earrings;
resembling a white mountain, he stood facing the battle.
But Ariṣṭa, the son of Bali, most excellent and armed with mountain rocks,
stood ready for battle, exerting himself like another upholder of the earth.
But Kiśora, out of extreme joy, like a young colt urged forward,
became like the risen sun in the midst of the Daitya army.
Lamba, resembling a hanging cloud and adorned with flowing garments,
shone as he entered the Daitya array like the sun amidst a mist.
Svarbhānu, however, fought with his mouth; his teeth, lips, and eyes served as his weapons.
Resembling a mountain, he shone at the head of the celestial army;
that planet stood with a pleasant face, laughing in the presence of the Daityas.
Some shine mounted on horses, others on the shoulders of elephants;
some are mounted on lions and tigers, and others on boars and bears.
Some were mounted on donkeys and camels, some had clouds as their vehicles; some were mounted on various birds, and some had the wind as their vehicle.
But other Daityas from Pattina— terrible and with distorted faces,
some one-legged and some two-legged— danced, longing for battle.
Roaring loudly and bursting with force, many of those bull-like Dānavas, possessing the roar of proud tigers, let out a great cry.
Those Dānavas, skilled in the practice of archery, threatened [the gods] with their fierce maces and iron clubs,
and with arms shaped like iron bars.
They sported with spears, nooses, swords, javelins, hooks, and sharp-edged axes,
as well as with *śataghnīs* and sharp-pointed mallets.
With boulders, rocks, iron bars, and excellent weapons,
as well as with discuses, the foremost of the Daityas made their army joyful.
Desiring victory in battle, the Dānavas, intoxicated by war,
stood facing the gods with that entire Dānava army, fierce with the madness of combat, like a surging mass of clouds.
That wondrous army, dense with thousands of Daityas, resembling wind, fire, water, clouds, and mountains,
surged forth for the onset of the battle-flood and appeared as if intoxicated by the desire to fight.
Chapter 34,
Transliterated by Atul Agarwala,
Proof-read by Horst Brinkhaus.
Vaiśampāyana said:
"O dear one, you have heard in detail the extent of the Daitya army in that conflict."
Now hear the detailed account of the Vaiṣṇava host of all the gods' armies.
The Ādityas, Vasus, Rudras, and the two Aśvins of great strength,
together with their armies and followers, equipped themselves for battle in due order.
Then Puruhūta, the thousand-eyed guardian of the world and leader of all the gods,
mounted the celestial elephant from the front.
And on his left side was a chariot possessing the speed of the best of birds,
with most beautiful wheels for its feet, adorned with gold and diamonds.
He was followed by thousands of throngs of gods, gandharvas, and yakṣas,
and was praised by radiant members of the assembly and by brahmin seers.
He was protected by hosts of clouds like mountains capable of moving at will, which were tossed up by the crashing of thunderbolts and adorned with lightning and rainbows.
Mounted upon that elephant, the Blessed Lord Maghavan moves about;
at the commencement of the sacrifice, the Brahmins standing at the fire-chambers sing his praises.
In heaven, followed by Śakra and resounding with the music of the gods,
hundreds of hosts of Apsarases dance before Indra.
Shining like the sun with its banner as its royal emblem,
it was yoked to a thousand horses possessing the speed of thought and the wind.
Then that excellent chariot, yoked by Mātali,
shone forth like Mount Meru entirely enveloped by the splendor of the sun.
Yama, however, raising his staff and his mallet appropriate for the occasion,
stood within the army of the hosts of gods, terrifying the Daityas with his roar.
Protected by the four oceans and by hissing serpents,
he wears bracelets of conch and pearls, bearing a body composed of water.
With a body as pure as a conch or a pearl, this lord of waters has become cool;
brandishing the nooses of Time with horses resembling moonbeams,
he performs thousands of playful movements amidst the surges of water tossed by the wind.
Clad in pale, fluttering garments, with armlets as beautiful as coral,
his excellent body darkened by jewels, and his chest adorned with the weight of necklaces;
Varuṇa, bearing his noose, stood in the midst of the host of gods;
Varuṇa, with noose in hand, took his position within the divine army,
longing for the time of battle like the ocean whose tides have been broken.
With an army of yakṣas and rākṣasas, and also with hosts of guhyakas,
Kubera— the lord and master of treasures, whose excellent body is dark as a jewel, who is borne by men, and who is joined by the two treasures Śaṅkha and Padma— [approached].
The glorious Lord of the Lords of Kings was seen with a mace in his hand.
Fighting from his celestial chariot, Dhanada, that king of kings who is borne by men, stood upon the Puṣpaka chariot; desiring battle,
he shone like Śiva himself in person, the friend of Śiva, as he looked on.
Śiva himself, clothed in linen, being Śiva in person, [upheld] the eastern wing; the thousand-eyed Indra, the king of the ancestors (Yama), the western wing;
and Varuṇa, the one whose vehicle is men (Kubera), the northern wing.
The four world-protectors, endowed with great strength, stationed themselves at the four [quarters] and guarded their respective directions for that army of the gods.
The Sun, with his chariot drawn by seven horses, traveling through the sky,
blazed with splendor and shone with radiant rays.
With its wheel of rising and setting that reaches as far as Mount Meru,
variegated with the gates to the third heaven, it shines upon the imperishable world.
Endowed with a thousand rays and blazing with splendor,
the twelve-fold Lord of Day moved in the midst of the gods.
Soma, with his white horse, shines upon his chariot like the cool-rayed moon,
flooding the world with beams filled with icy water.

He saw that lord of the twice-born, who followed the conjunction with the constellation Ṛkṣa, whose body was marked by the shadow of the hare, the cool-rayed moon that brings about the destruction of the night's darkness.
He is the impeller of the luminaries in the sky, the taster of flavors, the lord,
the protector of medicinal herbs, and the repository of immortality.
The Dānavas beheld Soma, the first portion of the world, consisting of gentle coolness and essence, standing there with snow as his weapon.
That vital breath which, divided fivefold among all beings and men,
abiding within the seven constituents, sustains and moves through the three worlds.
They call him the controller of Agni, the source of all, the Lord;
he whose origin, abiding in the seven musical notes, is extolled by sacred hymns.
That which they call the supreme being, that which they call bodiless,
that which they say moves through space, travels swiftly, and has sound as its source.
That wind, the life-force of all beings, stirred up by its own brilliance,
blew against the Daityas in a contrary direction, accompanied by clouds and causing them great distress.
The Maruts, along with the divine Gandharvas and hosts of Vidyādharas,
sported with bright swords that were like sloughed-off serpents.

And the lords of serpents, assuming the form of arrows, moved through the sky with gaping mouths against the leaders of the gods, emitting intense poison born of fury, along with yakṣas of immense splendor, pannagas, and even garuḍas.
The mountains, with their rocky peaks and trees possessing hundreds of branches,
stood ready to strike the host of Dānavas for the sake of the hosts of gods.
He who is that god Hṛṣīkeśa, Padmanābha, Trivikrama,
the one whose path is black, who resembles the end of an eon, the lord of the entire universe.

Born from the ocean, the slayer of Madhu, the consumer of oblations, honored by sacrifices, whose self consists of earth, water, space, and the elements— he is Syāma, the bringer of peace and the destroyer of enemies.
The source of the world, the seed of the world, the teacher of the world, and the noble-minded one—
the wielder of the discus and mace raised that supreme-splendored discus, the slayer of enemies, against the army of the Asuras, like the rising sun emerging from the fire.
Like the orb of the sun rising with its surrounding halo.
Grasping with his left hand the great mace that destroys all asuras— a mace dark-hued in form that brings death to his enemies— [he stood].
With his remaining arms, the illustrious Lord, whose banner bears the enemy of serpents, held various kinds of weapons, such as the Śārṅga bow and others.
He saw the bird, the self-born son of Kaśyapa, the consumer of serpents,
whose flight surpassed the wind and who agitated the sky.
It shone with the lord of serpents coiled within its mouth,
resembling the towering Mount Mandara when it was released after the churning for the nectar of immortality.
His prowess had been witnessed hundreds of times in the battles between the gods and the asuras;
he was the one upon whom Mahendra had marked his thunderbolt for the sake of the nectar of immortality.
He had a topknot and a crest, was adorned with earrings of refined gold,
wore garments of variegated feathers, and resembled a mountain rich in minerals.

With its sharp beak and fierce claws, crowded with flapping wings, it was adorned with a radiant jewel-gem fastened upon the coils of a serpent— hanging from its broad chest and possessing a luster equal to the moon.
And with his two beautiful-winged arms, he playfully covered the sky in heaven,
like the heavens at the end of an eon being covered by two clouds accompanied by Indra’s bow.
It was adorned with blue, red, and yellow banners;
its great body was a dwelling-place concealed by the appearance of a banner.
The glorious Hari, invincible in battle, mounted Aruṇa’s younger brother,
Suparṇa— the best of sky-dwellers— in his own form as Suparṇa, while gazing upon the army of the Daityas. Standing there, he was difficult for any foe to conquer in combat.
Dahana stood within the army of the gods, striking great terror into the Daityas;
the hosts of deities and the composed sages followed him and praised the wielder of the mace with hymns containing supreme mantras.
Salutations be unto you, O Hṛṣīkeśa; destroy the host of the Daityas, O All-pervading Lord! Salutations to you, the triple-formed one, whose essence is Hari, Brahmā, and Śiva!
Salutations to the form of the three Vedas; salutations to the Ṛg, Sāman, and Yajus!
Homage be to You, who are inconceivable by the yogis and the bestower of yoga;
homage to You who are empty of conceptual construction, homage to You whose form is representation-only;
and to that splendor consisting of gnosis which the wise proclaim.
We bow to that Lord of the World; O Hari, slay the hosts of Daityas!
For indeed, O God, we are not able to praise you even in hundreds of years. O God, Lord of the World, be victorious, O Puruṣottama!
Having heard these words thus spoken, Hari prepared to depart for that city which was closely embraced by Vaiśravaṇa, preceded by Vaivasvata,
surrounded by the lord of waters, and graced by the king of the gods.
Stainless with moon-like radiance, he set out for the battle, taking the path of the gods which is beneficial, blazing with the splendor of the sun,
resounding with the roar of the wind, and filled with kindled sacrificial fires.
The powerful army of Viṣṇu— the victorious, the patient, and the radiant— surrounded by splendor, was roused and mobilized for battle.
"May there be well-being for the gods," thus Angiras spoke while praising;
"May there be well-being," thus Angiras spoke while praising the gods there;
"May there be well-being for the Daityas," Ushanas spoke these words.
"May it be well with the Daityas," Uśanas also spoke these words.
(Chapter 35,
transliterated by Atul Agarwala)
Vaiśampāyana said:
Then, from those two forces, a tumultuous conflict arose between the gods and the asuras, both sides desiring victory over one another.
He who consists of all the gods and who consists of all dharmas—
by the splendor of that Viṣṇu, the lord of the gods,
the deities, along with their armies and followers, as well as the thirty [Tridaśas] intoxicated with pride, are sustained.
To strike down the Dānava army with force, they indeed advanced together;
the Dānavas, along with the deities, with various weapons raised,
encountered one another in combat like mountains colliding with mountains.
That battle, joined by gods and asuras, appeared most wonderful;
it was characterized by both righteousness and unrighteousness, as well as by pride and humility.
Then, with blazing chariots and urged mounts,
they rose up toward the sky on all sides, swords in hand.
With maces being hurled, with arrows being discharged,
with bows being drawn, and with mallets being brought down;
That battle became terrible, crowded with gods and dānavas,
generating terror for the world and resembling the destruction at the end of an eon.
With iron clubs released from their own hands and mountains hurled with great speed,
the Dānavas struck the gods led by Indra in the battle.
Being slaughtered by the powerful Dānavas who appeared victorious,
the gods, dejected in mind, fell into great distress in that great battle.
Pounded by nets of missiles and having their heads split by iron clubs,
those sons of Diti, with their chests pierced, vomited much blood from their wounds.
Bound by nets of snares and rendered motionless by arrows,
they entered into a demonic illusion and were unable to move.
The army of the gods, rendered motionless by the asuras and deprived of the effort to wield their weapons, appeared as if paralyzed, its form resembling that of lifeless beings.
Drawing back the snares of illusion and cutting those arrows with his thunderbolt,
the thousand-eyed Śakra entered the formidable army of the Daityas.
Having slain the foremost of the Daityas at the front, he then rendered that great army of Dānavas into darkness by means of a net of Tāmasa weapons.
Overcome by that terrible darkness through the splendor of Indra, they did not recognize one another, nor the gods, nor their own mounts.
But the best of gods, striving and freed from the snares of illusion,
cast down the bodies of the hosts of Daityas, which had become like darkness.
Overwhelmed and deprived of consciousness by the darkness, those hosts of Dānavas, possessing a bluish luster, fell down like mountains whose wings had been severed.
With that lord of the Daityas having become a solid mass,
the abode of the gods shone like a sea of darkness, or as if it had become total gloom.
Then Maya, burning with that darkness, created the Great Illusion (Mahāmāyā),
which produced a brilliance like that at the end of an eon and was as if created by the Aurva fire.
That illusion, conjured by Māyā, consumed all the darkness,
and the Daityas, possessing the forms of suns, immediately rose up in the battle.
Having encountered the submarine fire of Māyā and being scorched by it, the denizens of heaven sought refuge in the lunar realm, that lake of cool-rayed water.
Being consumed by the Aurva fire and deprived of their own luster,
the gods, tormented and seeking refuge, appealed to the wielder of the thunderbolt.
While the army was being tormented by illusion and consumed by the Dānavas,
Varuṇa, urged by the king of the gods, spoke these words.
O Śakra, in former times the son of a Brahmarṣi named Aurva, radiant and equal to Brahmā in his qualities, performed most severe ascetic penance.
The hosts of sages, together with the gods and divine seers, approached that imperishable world as it blazed like the sun with its ascetic fervor.
And the Dānava Hiraṇyakaśipu, the lord of the Dānavas,
once petitioned a rishi of supreme splendor in the past.
The brahmin-sages spoke these words, consistent with dharma, to him:
"O Blessed One, this lineage has its very root severed within the lineages of the seers."
You are alone and childless, and no offspring of your lineage exists; having undertaken a vow of lifelong celibacy, you pursue nothing but hardship.
Many lineages of Brahmins, whose minds are purified through meditation,
remain as single bodies, solitary and without offspring.
Since those beings upon whom the earth depends have become extinct, there is no one else who can be the cause;
for you, however, are preeminent in ascetic power and possess a splendor equal to that of Prajāpati.
Therefore, proceed for the sake of your lineage; increase yourself by means of yourself.
Bestowing your own exalted splendor, indeed assume a second body.
Thus addressed by the sages, that sage, struck in his mind,
rebuked those hosts of seers and spoke these words.
Just as this eternal dharma was ordained for the sages of old—
those who subsisted on wild roots and fruits and practiced the rites prescribed by the ṛṣis.
For a Brahmin born from the womb of Brahmā who abides in the Self,
well-practiced celibacy could even move Brahmā himself.
For those twice-born who dwell in the householder stage of life, there are three modes of livelihood;
but for us, who dwell in the forest hermitage, the forest is our mode of livelihood.
Those who subsist on water, those who subsist on air, those who use their teeth as a mortar,
those who grind with stones, and those who perform ten, five, or seven ascetic heats;
Abiding in austerity and through vows that are very difficult to perform,
they place celibacy at the forefront and seek the supreme goal.
"The status of a Brahmin is ordained for a Brahmin through the practice of celibacy (brahmacarya);
thus say the people who know celibacy in the other world."
Fortitude is established in celibacy; austerity is established in celibacy. Those Brahmins who abide by means of celibacy are established in heaven.
There is no accomplishment without yoga; there is no fame without accomplishment.
In this world, there is no root of fame, nor any austerity superior to the practice of celibacy.
For one who, having restrained the collection of the senses and the group of five elements,
practices the holy life— what austerity could be greater than this?
Wearing matted hair without spiritual discipline, performing vows without intention,
and practicing celibacy— these three modes of conduct are designated as hypocrisy.
Where are wives, where is union, and where is the reversal of states of being,
when this mental offspring was created by Brahmā through his mind?

If you possess the power of asceticism, O you of immeasurable selves, then by the change in your facial expressions and eyes, by your touch, and by your speech, as well as by your former remembrance of beautiful women and the resulting agitation of your minds— [if these signs exist, then prove your power].
Having attained birth in her, who would sow his seed in her?
According to the sacred tradition (śruti), one such as you is an evil-souled, deficient, and deluded being;
remembering this, he becomes despondent regarding the state of Brahman and, upon seeing [the woman], emits his semen.

Having created [the world], the Self causes it to dissolve; who would cast a seed into that [womb] when there is the certainty that it exists within the state of celibacy? Therefore, what living beings would take delight in it?
Firmly resolved, we practice another form of celibacy toward the pitiless and impure bodies of women— namely,
that which is desired within our hearts.
Create mental sons through the rite pertaining to Prajāpati.
The ascetic must conceive a womb created by the mind;
for ascetics, neither sexual union nor seed is said to be the means for fulfilling their vow.
That which you, who are virtuous and fearless, have spoken here for the sake of the dharma and its purpose, though it be excessive, is in my opinion like that of the wicked.
Having fashioned a mind-made body with a radiant inner self,
I shall create a son born of my own body without the union of a woman.
In this way, my self will produce a second self by means of this forest rite, as if desiring to consume all creatures.
But Uru, possessed by ascetic fervor, having placed his thigh into the fire,
churned with a single blade of darbha grass the kindling-stick for the birth of a son.
Suddenly bursting through his thigh, Agni was born as his son, wreathed in flames and devoid of fuel, desiring to consume the world.
Having split open the thigh of Urva, the fire named Aurva,
exceedingly wrathful, was born as if desiring to consume the three worlds.
As soon as he was born, he spoke to his father with a blazing voice:
"O Father, hunger oppresses me; I shall consume the world, so abandon me!"
Yawning with flames that ascended to the third heaven and burning all living beings, that fire of destruction grew to fill the ten directions.
In the meantime, Brahmā,
the Lord and Master of all worlds,
arrived while honoring the sage Urva at the place where the sage had emitted his supreme son.
He saw the thigh of Urva blazing with the fire produced from his son,
and the worlds, together with the sages, scorched by the fire of Aurva’s wrath. Then Brahmā spoke to him:
O son, let this splendor be restrained; let compassion be shown toward the worlds.
"O Brahmin, best among speakers, I shall provide the highest assistance for this child of yours;
I will grant him a dwelling and food that is like nectar.
Hear these truthful words of mine."
"And I shall provide him with food by which he will be satisfied.
Urva said:
"I am blessed, I am favored, since today the Blessed One [has come] for my child."
He indeed bestows this wisdom here for the sake of supreme grace.
When the time of dawn has arrived, at which our reunion is so longed for,
O Blessed One, with what oblations will my son be satisfied so that he may attain happiness?
Where shall his dwelling be, and what shall his food consist of?
What will you provide for this one of great majesty, who is equal to Vīrya?
Brahmā said: "O Brahmin, his dwelling shall indeed be in the Mare’s Mouth (Vaḍavāmukha) in the ocean;
water is my source, O sage, and that is my watery mouth."
There I dwelt, delighting in drinking the water with oblations;
I offer that oblation for your son and grant him his abode.
Then, at the end of the age, O observer of noble vows, he and I shall wander together here, causing the destruction of all living beings.
This fire of the time of destruction, which devours water, has been created by me as the burner of all beings, including gods, asuras, and rakshasas.
"So be it," said that fire as well; with its circle of flames withdrawn, it entered the mouth of the ocean, casting its radiance upon its father.
Then Brahmā and all those great seers, recognizing the power of Aurva’s fire, returned and each took his own way.
Having seen that wonder, Hiraṇyakaśipu,
with all his limbs bowed in prostration, honored Aurva and spoke these words.
O Blessed One, this wonderful event has occurred before the eyes of the world:
O best of sages, the Grandfather has been thoroughly gratified by your ascetic penance.
But I, O observer of great vows, should be understood as a servant to both your son and yourself, provided that I am praiseworthy for my actions.
Do not see me thus absorbed in meditation, for I am devoted solely to your service;
O best of sages, were I to fail, it would be your own defeat.
"I am your disciple, O best of ascetics; dispel my fear of the gods.
Urvashi said:
"I am blessed and I am favored, since you consider me your teacher."
O you of noble vows, by this asceticism of yours, there is no fear for you here today.
And take this illusion created by my son—
a fire made of flames yet devoid of fuel, which is difficult to touch even for fires themselves.
This [weapon], when brought under your control, will subdue the enemies of your own lineage; it will protect your own side and utterly consume your foes.
Saying "So be it," the lord of the Dānavas took her leave, bowed to that bull among sages, and departed for the third heaven, joyful and fulfilled in his purpose.
This very illusion, difficult to withstand and hard even for the gods to overcome,
was created in the past by Aurva, the son of Urva, the fire-god.
But when that Daitya has been defeated, this [earth] will undoubtedly be devoid of power;
for this curse was previously pronounced by the very same energy from which she was created.
"If she is to be repelled, then let the Blessed One act for my happiness;
O Śakra, let the moon, the source of water, be given to me as a friend. Having united with him and with the aquatic creatures, I shall remain composed."
"By your grace, I shall destroy this illusion; of this there is no doubt."
Chapter 36,
Transliterated by Atul Agarwala,
Proofread by Horst Brinkhaus.
Vaiśampāyana said:
"So be it," said Śakra, the enhancer of the thirty gods, filled with joy.
He first commanded Soma, whose weapon is the cold, to engage in battle.
Go, O Soma, and perform the service of assistance to the wielder of the noose,
for the destruction of the asuras and for the victory of the dwellers of heaven.
You possess incomparable valor and are the Lord of the lords of light;
those who know the true essence understand that the flavor of all worlds consists of you.
The waning and waxing of you are manifest in the ocean and in the orb of the sky;
you revolve day and night, joining time to the world.
O Moon, neither the gods nor those who dwell among the stars know that the mark upon your lap consists of the shadow of the world and is situated within you as a hare.
Situated above the path of the sun and above the luminaries,
you dispel the darkness with your form and illuminate the entire world.
He is the white-rayed one, the embodiment of snow, the lord of luminaries, the moon;
the maker of the year, the soul of the conjunction of time, the one to be worshipped, the essence of sacrifice, and the imperishable.
Lord of herbs, source of ritual action, lotus-born, not possessing heat,
cool-rayed, receptacle of nectar, fickle, and having white steeds as his vehicle.
You are the radiance of those with lovely forms; you are the moon for those who follow the lunar way;
you are the gentle one of all beings; and you are the king of the stars, the destroyer of darkness.
Therefore, go with this Varuṇa and his protective host;
subdue the illusory power of the Asuras by which we are being consumed in battle.
Soma said: "O King of the Gods, granter of boons, as you command me for the sake of battle,
I shall now rain down frost that will dispel the illusion of the Daityas."
Behold these hosts of Daityas in the great battle, scorched by my glance, enveloped in frost, deprived of their magic powers, and stripped of their pride.
Then, showers of snow released by Himakara, accompanied by tears,
enveloped those terrible Daityas like masses of clouds.
In that great battle, Varuṇa and the Moon, bearing nooses and white rays respectively,
struck the Dānavas with showers of snow and the hurling of nooses.
Those two lords of the waters, fighting with nooses and ice in battle,
moved through the fray with their torrents like two great oceans agitated by the waves.
That army of Dānavas was seen being overwhelmed by those two,
as if the world were enveloped by the onset of clouds at the time of universal dissolution.
Then both those gods, Śaśānka and Varuṇa, with their nooses of rising rays,
quelled that illusion created by the Daitya.
Scorched by the waters of the moon’s rays and bound by nooses in the battle,
the Daityas were unable to move, like mountains deprived of their peaks.
Struck by the cool-rayed moon, those Daityas fell, afflicted by the cold,
with all their limbs drenched in frost like fires deprived of heat.
But for those Daityas in heaven, their various celestial chariots, possessing inverted radiance, were falling down and flying up.
The illusory Dānava Maya beheld those Dānavas in the sky, their hands bound by nooses and covered by cool rays.
It was spread with networks of rock-falls, laughing aloud with its massive boulders,
its peaks towering with great trees, and its forests filled with caves.
It was teeming with lions, tigers, and elephants, resounding with the cries of herds of lordly tuskers,
filled with throngs of wild beasts, and its trees were shaken by the wind.
He created on all sides the famous illusory form of Pārvatī, fashioned by her own son Krauñca, who could travel at will through the heavens.
With stones accompanied by crashing sounds, with showers of rocks, and with falling trees,
he struck down those hosts of gods and brought back the dānavas to life.
Then the two illusions, Naiśākarī and Vāruṇī, vanished;
thereafter, he showered the hosts of gods in battle with stones as heavy as iron.
The sky became impassable, as uneven as a mass of stones and as crowded with trees and mountains as the earth itself is with its peaks.
In that battle, no one was seen by the gods who had not been struck by various stones, nor anyone who had not been pelted with rocks, nor anyone who had not been obstructed by clusters of trees.
Leaving aside the host of gods— which had its bows fallen from their grasp, was turbid with shattered weapons, and was rendered effortless— there remained only the wielder of the mace.
For that glorious Lord, the wielder of the mace and master of the world, did not tremble when he entered the battle; out of forbearance, he did not give way to anger.
Knowing the right time, resembling a dark cloud, and observing the hour for battle,
Janārdana desired to witness the conflict between the gods and the asuras.
Then, commanded by the Blessed One for the sake of quelling the expanded illusion created by Maya, Fire and Wind entered into battle; thereupon,
they grew ever more intense against one another, with the speed and flames of their fire increasing.
Urged by the words of Viṣṇu, those two drew away the illusion.
By those two, who were like agitated clouds and had increased in power during the great battle, that illusion of Pārvatī was consumed; it perished, reduced to ashes.
That fire joined with the wind, and that wind filled with fire,
burned the army of the Daityas like two forces intensified at the end of the eons.
The wind rushed there, and after it, the fire;
the wind and the fire moved through the army of the Dānavas as if playing.
As the constituent parts of the Dānavas' celestial chariots fell and flew up on all sides, they were reduced to ashes.
When the masses of wind had scattered [the clouds], when the fire had completed its task,
when the destruction by illusion was accomplished, and while the wielder of the mace was being praised.
When the Daityas were rendered effortless and the three worlds were freed from their bonds, the gods were filled with joy and cried out "Excellent! Excellent! on all sides.
When there was victory for the thousand-eyed Indra and defeat for Maya,
and when all the quarters were purified, the expansion of the Dharma proceeded.
When the path of the moon was unobstructed, when the sun stood in its own station,
when the worlds were in their natural state, and when men were bound by the ties of virtuous conduct.
Then the gods, shining resplendently together with the hosts of sages,
while death was being offered as an oblation into the fire within the unbroken bond,
and while the gods, beautifying the sacrifice, were demonstrating the path to heaven;
While all the world-protectors remain stationed in their respective directions,
and while there is the presence of the asceticism of the pure and the absence of those who perform evil deeds;
While the faction of the gods rejoiced and the faction of the Daityas despaired,
Dharma stood with three parts remaining, while Adharma possessed but a single part.
When the great gate is thrown open, while the path of the virtuous remains,
and when the social classes and the stages of life in this world abide in their own respective duties.
While the kings were resplendent, engaged in protecting their subjects,
and while hymns of praise to the gods and other such songs were being sung;
while the world was cleansed of impurity and the terrible darkness had subsided.
When that act of battle between Agni and Māruta had taken place,
the worlds became composed of them and were purified, as those two performed the deed of victory.
Having heard of the fear of the former gods and the great terror of the Maruts and Agni,
the Dānava known as Kālanemi appeared.
His crown has the form of the sun; his ornaments and armlets jingle;
he resembles Mount Mandara when it was being churned, and he is enveloped in great silver.
Exalted by a hundred weapons, with a hundred arms and a hundred faces,
the glorious one stood with a hundred heads like a mountain with a hundred peaks;
he grew in his great lair like a fire in the summer heat.
With smoke-colored hair and a tawny beard, his face was framed by fangs and pursed lips; he bore a massive body that extended throughout the interior of the three worlds.
Measuring the sky with his arms, casting down the mountains with his feet,
and stirring the rain-bearing clouds with the breath from his mouth.
With eyes red and wide-stretched, and a chest as lofty as Mount Mandara,
he approached as if desiring to incinerate all the hosts of gods in battle.
He was threatening the hosts of gods and shrouding the ten directions,
like the thirsty and arrogant Death arisen at the time of universal dissolution.
With a well-formed palm, elevated, with broad finger-joints,
adorned with hanging ornaments, and with his armor slightly shifted.
With his handsome right hand raised high,
he spoke to the Dānavas slain by the gods, saying, "Arise!"
All the gods gazed upon that Kālanemi, who was like Death itself to his enemies in battle, with eyes trembling in fear.
All beings gazed upon that Kālanemi as he strode forward,
like another Nārāyaṇa taking his three strides.
Lifting his first foot high, which caused the sky to whirl with its gusts of wind,
the asura advanced in battle, terrifying all the gods.
Embraced by Maya, the lord of the asuras, the Daitya Kālanemi shone as he advanced in battle, like Mount Mandara with Viṣṇu.
Then all the gods, led by Śakra,
were deeply distressed upon seeing Kālanemi approaching like Death itself, bringing terror with him.

Vaiśampāyana said:
That Dānava Kālanemi, desiring to please the Dānavas, spoke.
The one of great splendor grew, like a rain-cloud at the end of the summer heat.
Seeing him situated within the three worlds, those lords of the Dānavas rose up without fatigue, as if they had obtained the supreme nectar.
Free from fear and terror, led by Maya and Tāraka,
and always appearing victorious in the battle against the gods,
those Dānavas, longing for combat, shone as they entered the field of battle.
As they practiced their mantras, ran about in formation,
and watched the Dānava Kālanemi, joy arose within them.
But those who were the leaders among Māyā’s followers there, standing at the forefront of the battle,
they too all cast off fear and stood ready to fight with joy.
May Tāra, Varāha, and the heroic Hayagrīva,
as well as Śveta the son of Vipracitti, and both Khara and Lamba, protect you.
Ariṣṭa, the son of Bali, as well as Kiśora and Aṣṭra;
and Svarbhānu, the great Asura who resembled an immortal and fought with his mouth.
All these dānavas, skilled in weapons and all established in austerity, being successful, went to the supreme Kālanemi.
With heavy maces, with discuses along with battle-axes,
with pestles resembling Time itself, and with projectiles and mallets;
With stones resembling mountain peaks, with jagged crags,
with sharp-edged spears, slings, and iron clubs of the finest steel.
And likewise with heavy *ghātanī* weapons and *śataghnīs*,
with yokes and released mechanical devices, and with bolts struck from the front.
The Dānavas, invincible in battle, stood at the front of the fray with their long,
thick arms wielding spears, nooses, and mallets,
as well as serpents licking with their tongues and arrows gliding forth.
With thunderbolts and weapons to be hurled, with blazing javelins,
with unsheathed and sharp swords, and with keen, stainless spears;
With their minds fully inflamed and having taken up their supreme weapons,
they stood at the head of the battle, placing Kālanemi at their forefront.
That army of the Daityas, with its excellent blazing weapons,
shone like the sky at the onset of dark blue clouds when the stars have vanished.
The army of the gods, protected by Śakra, also rejoiced,
radiant with the heat and cold of their own splendors as well as the brilliance of the moon and the sun.
She possesses the speed of the wind, is gentle, has the hosts of stars for her banner,
wears garments tossed by the clouds, and laughs with the planets and constellations.
Protected by Yama, Indra, Varuṇa, and the wise Kubera,
with blazing fire and wind, it was entirely devoted to Nārāyaṇa.
That divine and formidable great army of the gods, resembling the surge of the ocean, shone forth,
equipped with weapons and graced by yakṣas and gandharvas.
Then that encounter between the two armies took place,
like the conjunction of heaven and earth at the end of a cosmic age.
That battle became terrible, crowded with gods and dānavas,
and was characterized by both forbearance and prowess, as well as pride and humility.
Then, from those two armies, the formidable gods and asuras marched forth in fury,
like clouds from the eastern and western oceans.
Delighted by those two forces, those gods and dānavas moved about like elephants in two mountain forests in full bloom.
Then they beat the kettledrums and blew conchs by the hundreds;
he filled the heavens, the sky, the earth, and all the quarters of space.
The sound of bowstrings striking the palms, the twanging of bows,
and the resounding blasts of kettledrums drowned out the noise of the Daitya.
Desirous of combat, they rushed at one another, striking each other down; others, eager for battle, broke the arms of their opponents with their own arms in single combat.
In the battle, the gods hurled terrible thunderbolts and iron clubs, while the Dānavas discharged swords, heavy maces, and supreme weapons of steel.
With their limbs shattered by the blows of maces and torn to pieces by arrows,
some fell down violently, while others were found lying face downward.
Then, with chariots and horses, and with swift-moving celestial vehicles,
they encountered one another in battle, highly agitated by rage.
Some, being struck down in battle, turned back, while others were hemmed in;
chariots were blocked by chariots, and foot-soldiers by foot-soldiers.
The tumultuous roar of those chariots, carried by the wind, resounded through the sky just as the thundering of clouds fills the autumnal firmament.
Then, as the chariots became entangled like clouds in the sky,
some were shattered, some were crushed by other chariots,
and some, having fallen into a dense throng, were unable to move.
In that battle, others, proud and adorned with jingling ornaments, lifted one another up with their arms and struck them down while wielding swords and shields.
Others, pierced by missiles and slain in battle, vomited blood like clouds discharging water at the onset of the rainy season.
Then the chaotic battle shone forth, interwoven with missiles and weapons, agitated by maces hurled and raised aloft, and stirred up by gods and dānavas.
That day of battle, resembling a dark storm with the great clouds of those gifts and resplendent with the weapons of the gods, shone forth as they rained showers of arrows upon one another.
In the meantime, that Dānava Kālanemi, filled with rage,
grew in size like a cloud being filled by the surging waters of the ocean.
From his body there burst forth clouds resembling the heads of serpents, crowned with flickering lightning and raining down blazing thunderbolts.
As he hissed in anger, with his furrowed brows raining sweat,
flames issued forth from his mouth like a wind-driven fire-strike.
His arms spread out across the sky, both horizontally and upwards;
black-bodied and five-faced, they seemed like licking serpents.
With various nets of missiles, bows, and even iron clubs,
he covered the divine sky as if with towering mountains.
With his garment blown by the wind, he stood at the head of the battle like the immovable Mount Meru itself, its peaks swallowed by the glow of twilight.
With mountain peaks and trees hurled by the force of his thighs,
he struck down the hosts of gods as the thunderbolt strikes great mountains.
With their heads and chests mangled and pierced by many weapons and swords,
the gods, struck down by Kālanemi in battle, were unable to move.
Some were struck down by fists, while others were torn asunder;
the yakṣas, gandharvas, and birds fell along with the great serpents.
Terrified by Kālanemi in that battle, the gods,
losing their composure, were unable to exert themselves despite their efforts, even though they strove to do so.
Having thus conquered the host of deities and brandishing his mace, that best of Dānavas spoke to Śakra, who was mounted upon Airāvata:
"Come, come, O Lord of the Gods! You have been defeated by me in battle."
"From this day forward, O slayer of Vṛtra, you are no longer the Lord of the Gods;
O Śakra, while you look on, I shall split your head with my mace."
"From this day forward, O Acyuta, I shall become the lord of the Dānavas, and the lord of the gods shall be none other than I; of this there is no doubt, for I have slain you of such fierce prowess.
As he spoke thus in battle, the slayer of Vṛtra took up his thunderbolt.
Śakra indeed struck that Dānava swiftly with his thunderbolt;
yet, upon reaching his chest, that thunderbolt shattered into many pieces.
The thunderbolt was rendered powerless by the Danava's might to slay him;
it then suddenly fell back into Shakra’s very hand. But Kalanemi, seizing his mace with great effort, rushed forward impetuously.
With great force, he struck one of Airāvata’s heads;
with its frontal globe shattered, it fell to the surface of the earth.
Then that powerful king of elephants shed copious blood;
and again, O King, at the front of the battle,
the lord of the Dānavas struck the slayer of Vṛtra with his mace by means of his might.
Suddenly abandoning the king of elephants, Śakra Purandara— his armor shattered, his bones exposed, and vomiting blood from his mouth— fled.
Having fallen to the earth, O Great King, and rested for a moment upon the ground,
Śakra suddenly abandoned the heavenly realm, O Lord of the Earth,
and having reached the world of men, assumed a human body.
By that [arrow], Śakra, the thousand-eyed one, was bound with bonds of shafts;
mounted upon Airāvata in the battle, he was unable to move at all.
Resembling a waterless cloud and possessing the splendor of a waterless ocean,
he rendered Varuna inactive and stripped of his noose in battle.
Having brought about the destruction of Agni and Māruta, that lord of the Daityas struck down the king of the gods, Soma, Varuṇa, and the two Aśvins,
as well as all the inhabitants of heaven without exception, including the Ādityas, Vasus, and Rudras.
Then Āpavasu, the slayer of enemies, exerted himself exceedingly;
like a second Guha, he slew Kālanemi in battle with a spear.
With his heart pierced by the spear, the great asura Kālanemi bled onto the ground like a mountain rich in minerals;
then, his eyes copper-red with extreme rage, he raised the spear with great force.
He struck Vasu with his own power, and he fell upon the earth;
so too did Dhanada, Kṛtānta, Varuṇa, and Śacīpati.
At that very moment, they struck him with irresistible weapons;
having warded off those missiles, he slew them one by one.
That great asura seized the staff sent by Yama.
Seeing him, all the world-protectors of great majesty were struck with wonder;
then Śatakratu, the king of the gods, roared and struck him with his thunderbolt.
Struck by the thunderbolt, the Daitya did not tremble, just like a mountain;
then Indra, standing in the path of the wind, struck that Daitya again with the thunderbolt, while Hari, having swallowed him along with his weapon, remained there in a state of yawning.
The slayer of Vṛtra entered her womb with an extremely subtle form;
at that very moment, the lord of the gods emerged, having burst through her side.
Protected by the armor consisting of Nārāyaṇa himself, Śaṅkara then took up his infallible trident to strike.
Prajāpati said this: "This powerful one has been granted a boon by me."
This great asura cannot be slain by a trident or by any other weapon;
do not employ this infallible trident against the great asura.
Thus addressed, the wielder of the trident withdrew his own weapon.
In the meantime, the gods, afflicted by the fear of Kālanemi,
praised Janārdana with hymns and spoke to the high-souled Kṛṣṇa.
Then, by the hundreds and thousands, they released their own weapons;
in that battle, Vaiśravaṇa, the lord of the world-protectors, lamenting, was deprived of his office as the Giver of Wealth by those maces capable of changing form at will.
At that very moment, the world-protectors were struck down by him in combat; Yama,
the all-seizer who wields death as his weapon,
was brought to the state of Yama by the immortal one and entered his own quarter.
But all those guardians of the world, O King, having abandoned their own stations and assumed human bodies, were disputing among themselves regarding that which pertains to man.
Having displaced those guardians of the world and seized their respective functions, he [the demon] acted thus.
Then, he divided his own body into four parts in all directions.
Having reached the celestial path of the stars shown by Svarbhānu,
he seized the splendor of the Moon and that great realm of his as well.
He caused the sun of blazing rays to waver from the gateway of heaven,
and he seized its course through the solstice as well as its daily function.
Having seen Agni at the mouth of the god, he placed him within his own mouth;
and having swiftly conquered Vāyu, he brought him under his own control.
Having brought together all the oceans and all the rivers by force, he brought them under his own control through his prowess; thus the rivers became as his very body.
Having brought under his control the waters born of heaven and those born of the earth,
he established the world well-guarded by the mountains.
That great Daitya, who consists of all the worlds and brings fear to all the worlds, shines like the Self-Existent One, the great lord of the elements.
That Dānava shone in battle, possessing the singular body of the world-protectors, embodying the moon, sun, and planets, and being a confluence of fire and wind.
Established in the supreme station, the source and the place of dissolution for all worlds,
the hosts of Daityas praised him just as the gods praise the Grandfather.
