Vaiśampāyana said:
Those five did not approach him because of their contrary conduct.
The Veda, righteousness, forbearance, truth, and prosperity have Nārāyaṇa as their refuge.
Because they did not attend upon him, that lord of the Dānavas, filled with wrath and seeking the station of Viṣṇu, went into the presence of Nārāyaṇa.
He saw him seated upon Garuḍa, bearing the conch, the discus, and the mace,
whirling his auspicious mace for the destruction of the Dānavas.
He resembled a water-laden cloud, with garments like lightning,
mounted upon his own vehicle, the bird Kāśyapa— a peacock adorned with golden plumage.
Seeing Viṣṇu standing composed in battle for the destruction of the Daityas,
the Dānava, his mind agitated, spoke to the unshakeable one.
This is that enemy of ours, of our ancestors— the Dānavas and Ṛṣis—
as well as of Madhu and Kaiṭabha, who dwelt in the ocean.
"This is that very form of ours which is said to be indeed unassailable,
by which many Dānavas have been slain by us in battles today."
This is that pitiless one in battle, shameless toward women and children,
by whom the parting of the hair was made upon the wives of the Dānavas.
He is Viṣṇu among the gods, Vaikuṇṭha among the denizens of heaven,
Ananta among the serpents in the waters, and the Self-born among those who are self-born.
"This is that very Lord of the gods who must be driven away by us;
having encountered his wrath, Hiraṇyakaśipu was slain."
Taking refuge in its shadow, the gods stationed at the mouth of the sacrifice partake of the clarified butter offered by the great seers, which has been sacrificed in three ways.
This is the cause of the destruction of all the enemies of the gods;
our lineages have entered into his wheel in battle.
It is said that he, who has indeed sacrificed his life in battles for the sake of the gods,
hurls at his enemies a discus equal in brilliance to the sun.
This is the time for the Daityas, now that I have become Time itself;
that evil-minded one shall reap the fruit of his transgressed time.
By good fortune, this Viṣṇu has now come before my very eyes;
today, crushed by my arrows, he shall bow down to me alone.
By good fortune, I shall today in battle pay my debt to my ancestors by slaying this Nārāyaṇa, who brings fear to the Dānavas.
"I shall swiftly slay Nārāyaṇa in battle with my arrows;
for though he has entered another birth, he oppresses the Dānavas in combat."
This very one, who was formerly known as Padmanābha,
became the Destroyer and slew both Madhu and Kaiṭabha in the terrible single ocean.
In ancient times, having placed the two lords of the Dānavas upon his own thighs and having split his body into two parts—
half lion and half man—
he alone slew my father, Hiraṇyakaśipu.
Aditi, the mother of the gods, conceived this auspicious embryo—
he who, having assumed the form of a dwarf at the time of Bali’s sacrifice,
seized the three worlds by taking three strides.
Furthermore, now that the battle for Tārakāmaya has arrived,
he, together with the gods, shall perish upon encountering me.
Having spoken thus and reviling Nārāyaṇa in many ways with improper words in the battle, he took great delight in the fight itself.
Though being hurled about by the lord of the asuras, the wielder of the mace did not become angry;
with a mind possessed of the power of forbearance, he spoke these words with a smile.
Enough of this pride and power, O Daitya; my strength born of wrath is steadfast.
You have been slain by the faults born of pride, you who speak having transgressed all forbearance.
In my estimation, you are base; fie upon this strength of your words!
There are no men present where women roar.
O Daitya, I see you as one who follows the path of your ancestors;
for who, having broken the bridge established by Prajāpati, could proceed in safety?
Today I shall destroy you, the one who causes obstacles for the gods;
and I shall restore the deities each to their respective places.
While the bearer of the Śrīvatsa was speaking these words in the battle,
the Dānava laughed out of anger and brandished his weapon-bearing arms.
Raising his hundred arms in the battle, he who was seizing all weapons and whose eyes were bloodshot with rage struck Viṣṇu on the chest.
And the Dānavas as well, led by Maya and Tāra,
with weapons and swords raised, all rushed toward Viṣṇu in the battle.
Though being struck by the exceedingly powerful Daityas with all their weapons raised,
Hari did not waver in battle, remaining like an unshakable mountain.
And while locked in combat with Suparṇa, the great asura Kālanemi,
exerting all his strength, raised a massive mace with his arms and,
filled with fury, hurled that blazing and terrible weapon at Garuḍa.
By that deed of the Daitya, Viṣṇu was filled with wonder;
struck by him, the bird wavered again and again,
yet Hari, his strength increased, did not fall into confusion.
By which that mace fell upon the head of that Suparṇa.
Then that bird, its body distressed, descended to the earth on foot;
thereafter, they struck Viṣṇu and the cowherd in that great battle with clods of earth, thrown stones, and thunderbolt-like weapons in the conflict.
As he was wandering and reeling, the gods offered this praise:
"Victory to you, O God of mighty arms, destroyer of Madhu and Kaiṭabha;
you who tore open the chest of Hiraṇyakaśipu with your plow-like claws!"
And Viṣṇu, praised by the immortals, rose up from the battle as of old;
but that Dānava, perceiving Viṣṇu to be slain, blew his conch shell,
while the great Asuras there sounded their mṛdaṅga drums in three ways.
And those who relied upon Tāla danced; it appeared like a great festival.
Seeing Suparṇa distressed and his own body wounded, Vaikuṇṭha, his eyes bloodshot with rage, took up his discus.
And the Lord grew with great speed, equal to Suparṇa;
and his arms grew, pervading the ten directions.
Filling the cardinal directions, the intermediate directions, the sky, and the earth,
he grew once more as if desiring to stride across the worlds with his vital energy.
The sages, together with the Gandharvas, praised Madhusūdana as he grew in the vault of heaven for the victory of the lords of the gods.
Homage be to you, O Lord of the gods of gods, wielder of the conch, discus, and mace!
O Viṣṇu, Kṛṣṇa, Hṛṣīkeśa, slay the exceedingly powerful Daitya!
Homage to you, O Virūpākṣa, the Lord of the world of Śaṃkara!
Protect us all; slay the exceedingly powerful Daitya,
who scratches the sky with his crown, makes the cloudless atmosphere turbid with his garments,
treads upon the earth with his feet, and shrouds the quarters with his arms.
It possessed a splendor equal to the rays of the sun, had a thousand spokes, was indestructible by enemies,
resembled a blazing fire, was formidable, yet beautiful to behold— the Sudarśana.
Extending as far as the golden dust, it had a navel of diamond and was terrifying;
it was drenched with the fat, bones, marrow, and blood produced by the dānavas.
Unrivaled in its strikes, with a circular edge as sharp as a razor,
it is spread with garlands and wreaths, moving at will and assuming any form at will.
Created by the Self-Existent One himself, it strikes fear into all enemies;
it is permeated by the wrath of the great seers and is ever-proud in battle.
At whose hurling, the worlds— including all things stationary and moving— and even flesh-eating beings, become bewildered and attain satisfaction in the great battle.
Raising his discus in battle against that one of incomparable deeds who was equal to the sun in splendor, the wielder of the mace blazed with fury.
Overpowering the Danava's splendor with his own splendor in battle,
Śrīdhara severed the arms of Kālanemi with his discus.
And Hari forcibly crushed with his discus that hundred of the Daitya's terrible mouths, which were emitting fire-powder and loud laughter.
With his arms severed and his headless, that Dānava did not tremble in the battle, standing as a headless trunk like a *viśākha* tree.
Spreading his great wings and equaling the speed of the wind,
Garuḍa struck Kālanemi down with his breast.
His body, turned away and branching like the Viśākha constellation, fell from the sky after wandering through the air, descending from heaven while shaking the surface of the earth.
When that Daitya had fallen, the gods, together with the hosts of ṛṣis, assembled and honored Vaikuṇṭha, crying out, "Excellent! Excellent!"
But as for the other Daityas who had displayed their prowess in battle,
they were all encompassed by his arms and were unable to move in the fray.
He seized some by their hair, throttled others by the neck,
tore open the mouth of one, and was himself grasped in the midst of others.
Consumed by maces and discuses, their vitality gone and their life-breaths departed,
they fell to the surface of the earth with all their limbs shattered from the sky.
When all those Daityas had been slain, the Supreme Person,
the wielder of the mace, having accomplished his task, remained there, having done what was pleasing to Śakra.
When that conflict, the battle of Tāraka, had come to an end,
Brahmā, the grandfather of the worlds, quickly arrived at that place.
Together with all the Brahman-sages, Gandharvas, and hosts of Apsarases,
the god of gods, while worshipping the god Hari, spoke these words.
"O Lord, a great deed has been accomplished; the thorn of the gods has been extracted.
By this slaughter of the Daityas, we too have been fully satisfied."
O Viṣṇu, this great asura Kālanemi who has been slain by you—you alone are his slayer in battle; no other whatsoever exists.
This one, defying the gods and the worlds with all their moving and unmoving beings,
and having wrought destruction upon the sages, even roars back at me.
Therefore, I am well-pleased with this fierce deed of yours,
in that this Kālanemi, who resembles Time itself, has been struck down.
Therefore come, may prosperity be yours; let us go to the highest heaven.
The Brahman-sages dwelling there, seated in their assembly, await you.
O best among speakers, O Acyuta, both I and the great sages shall honor you there according to the prescribed rites with divine words. Furthermore,
O best among the recipients of boons, what boon shall I grant to you?
Even among the gods and the Daityas, you are the granter of boons.
O Viṣṇu, in this very battle, hand over this flourishing triple world, with its thorns removed, to the high-souled Śakra.
Thus addressed by the Blessed One, Hari, the Lord,
spoke with auspicious words to all the gods, headed by Śakra.
"Listen, all you gods who have assembled here;
with your ears attentive, O deities, place Purandara at your head."
In this battle, all the Dānavas led by Kālanemi— endowed with prowess and even greater than Śakra himself— have been slain by us.
In this great tumult, only two emerged:
Vairocana, the lord of the Daityas, and Svarbhānu, the great planet.
May Śakra protect the eastern quarter favored by those who perform sacrifices, Varuṇa the western,
Yama the southern, and the Lord of Wealth the northern.
Let the moon move through its time in conjunction with the constellations as is appropriate;
let the sun, for one year, preside over the commencement of the seasons together with the solstices.
Let the portions of clarified butter proceed, honored by the members of the assembly;
let the fires be offered oblations by the Brahmins through rites prescribed in the Vedas.

May the gods be satisfied by the bali-offering and the burnt oblation, the great seers by the private recitation of the Vedas, and the ancestors by the ancestral rite (śrāddha), each attaining satisfaction according to their pleasure.
May the wind blow its course, may the fire blaze in three ways,
and may the three castes satisfy the three worlds with their own inherent qualities.
Let the sacrificial rites proceed with the twice-born officiants performing the initiatory ceremonies;
let the sacrificial fees also be distributed as prescribed for all those engaged in long-duration sacrifices.
May the sun satisfy the cattle, the moon the juices, and the wind the vital breaths within living beings,
proceeding with auspicious and gentle activities.
O Mahendra, let all the rivers, the mothers of the three worlds who carry the waters, flow toward the ocean in their proper order and due course.
"O gods, let fear of the Daityas be abandoned; attain peace.
May it be well with you; I shall go to the eternal world of Brahmā."
Whether in your own home, in the heavenly world, or especially in battle,
you must never place your trust in them, for the Dānavas are eternally base.
These strike at vulnerabilities, and their conduct is not constant;
whereas for you, who are gentle and upright in nature, your intellect is straightforward.
But I, O deities, shall bestow delusion upon you who are of wicked disposition, evil-souled, and behaving improperly;
and whenever there shall be a most difficult-to-withstand fear from the Dānavas.
"Then, having quickly approached you, I shall grant you freedom from fear.
Having spoken thus to the hosts of gods, Viṣṇu, whose prowess is truth and whose glory is great, went together with Brahmā to the world of Brahmā.
This was a marvel that occurred in the battle of Tārakāmaya,
concerning both the Dānavas and Viṣṇu, about which you are questioning me.

Janamejaya said:
[Along with] Brahmā, the god of gods, who has his origin in the waters—
O Brahman, having gone to the world of Brahmā, what did Vaikuṇṭha do?

And for what purpose was Viṣṇu led by the primordial god who originates from the waters, when the slaughter of the Daityas had already been accomplished and he had not yet received the honors due to him by the gods?
And what was his station in the world of Brahmā? What yoga did he practice? Or what discipline did that omnipresent Lord, the creator of beings, maintain?
How does this great universe, though non-existent therein,
attain abundant prosperity, honored by gods, asuras, and men?
How does he sleep at the end of the summer heat and wake at the exhaustion of the rains?
And how, while abiding in the world of Brahmā, does he bear the burden of worldly affairs?
O best of brahmins, I desire to know in full detail and according to the truth the divine life-story of that Blessed One in heaven.
Vaiśampāyana said:
Listen first to the activities of Nārāyaṇa in detail,
and how he ascended to the world of Brahmā and rejoices together with Brahmā.
Granted that his course is subtle and difficult to follow even for the gods;
nevertheless, listen as I speak that which I am able to tell you.
This god consists of the worlds, and these three worlds consist of him;
he also consists of the gods, and those gods in heaven consist of him.
Whatever indeed increases through the gods, know that all of it comes from Janārdana; and whatever proceeds from the gods, know that to come from Madhusūdana.
The Grandfather knows Viṣṇu as that world consisting of Agni and Soma, which wise people know; he knows both that Soma and that Agni-world.
Just as curd may arise from milk, and just as clarified butter may arise from curd,
so does the world arise from Janārdana when all beings are churned.
Just as the Supreme Self is established through the senses and the elements,
so too is Hari known through the Vedas, the gods, and the worlds.
Just as the attainment of the elements and the senses is ordained for embodied beings on earth,
so too is the attainment of the Lord of Life, who belongs to Viṣṇu, for the gods in heaven.
Bestowing the fruit of the Satra sacrifice upon those who perform it, the Purifier, possessed of the Supreme Self,
and indeed the upholder of the world-system, is worshipped with mantras like Mantra itself.
Many who are dependent on others do not see its further shore;
Mādhava alone knows the limit and the supreme state of the worlds.
Listen now to that ancient event which occurred in the world of Brahmā, concerning this letter *dha* which was to be sought by the gods among the deities.
Having gone to the world of Brahmā and beheld the station of the Grandfather,
Viṣṇu paid homage to all those sages through the rite prescribed for seers.
Having performed his morning rites, that one of great splendor, seeing the fire being offered oblations by the great seers at the morning pressing, paid homage to it.
He saw his own body standing there as another, being worshipped with clarified butter by the great seers in sacrifices and partaking of its sacrificial portion.
Having paid homage to the sages worthy of homage, who possessed the splendor of Brahman,
that inconceivable one wandered through the eternal world of Brahmā.
He beheld sacrificial posts raised on high, adorned with crest-pieces at their tops,
and marked by hundreds of brahmin seers at the sacrifices.
Inhaling the smoke of the clarified butter, hearing the Vedas recited by the twice-born,
and beholding his own self being worshipped through sacrifices, he moved about there.
To him spoke the sages and the gods seated in the assembly hall,
all with arms raised to offer the guest-offering (arghya), their mouths purified by the sacred grass (pavitra).
Welcome to you, O best of gods, O Padmanābha of great splendor!
Homage be to you, O Hṛṣīkeśa, slayer of Madhu and Kaiṭabha!
O Dāmodara, homage be to you, whose eyes are as broad as lotus petals!
You are the lord of all the gods, the imperishable lord of the worlds;
you are the sacrifice, you are the *vaṣaṭ* call, and everything is established in you.
May this sacrificial hospitality be accepted according to the sacred formulas.
You are the vessel for this water purified by sacrifice, the purifier of the water for the feet;
for you are the guest mentioned in the mantras, seen and ever held in high esteem.
O Viṣṇu, when you had gone forth to fight, our ritual activities ceased;
for no rite is prescribed for a sacrifice that is devoid of Viṣṇu.
"The fruit of a sacrifice accompanied by sacrificial fees would arise from you;
indeed, O Janārdana, great sacrifices with their fees have their origin in you,
if you behold yourself being worshipped here by us."
"So be it," the Blessed One replied, honoring those Brahmins;
for the Grandfather Brahmā himself rejoiced, dwelling in the world of Brahmā.

Vaiśampāyana said:
Honored by those sages, Hari, the Lord, entered.
The ancient, divine abode of Brahmā, the hermitage of Nārāyaṇa.
Having invited those assembled in the hall, he entered there joyfully,
having bowed down to the primordial god Brahmā, who is born from the lotus.
Recognizing it by its own name, the Blessed One, as he was entering that hermitage of Nārāyaṇa, cast away his weapons.
There he beheld his own abode, resembling the lord of the waters,
presided over by hosts of spirits and eternal great seers.
It was filled with the clouds of the world-destruction, crowded with the stations of the constellations,
enveloped in a mass of darkness, and unassailable by gods or asuras.
There, the domain of neither wind, nor moon, nor sun prevails;
that region is pervaded by the splendor of the body of Padmanābha.
Entering there, carrying his mass of matted hair,
he assumed a thousand heads and proceeded to lie down.
Kālī, the knower of the time of the world's end, endowed with beautiful eyes,
approached that great-souled one as Sleep in the form of Time.
The Lord of the entire world,
Nārāyaṇa, the seed of the universe,
lay upon a divine bed as cool as the waters of the ocean.
Hari, the best among those who observe vows, performed the vow described for the single ocean.
Then the gods, together with the hosts of sages, paid homage to that high-souled Viṣṇu, the Lord of the world, as he lay asleep for the sake of the universe's welfare.
As he slept, there shone forth from the center of his navel the primordial lotus-abode of Brahmā, resembling the sun.
With his hand raised in the gesture of the Brahma-thread, the Great Sage, though sleeping upon a thousand-petaled lotus— rich in color, delicate, and adorned—
causes the turning of the cycle of time for all worlds.
From his wide-open mouth, driven by the winds of his breath,
rows of living beings indeed issue forth and enter again in surging floods.
Once created, those multitudes of living beings were divided by Brahmā himself into four classes; they each followed their own destiny according to the karma prescribed by the law of necessity.
Neither Brahmā himself nor the imperishable Brahman-sages know him—
Viṣṇu, who has entered into the yoga of sleep, enveloped in darkness.
But all those brahmin seers, led by the Grandfather,
did not know where he was sleeping or where he was seated upon his throne.
Who here is awake, who sleeps? Who breathes, and who does not move? Who is possessed of enjoyment, who is radiant, and who is even darker than Kṛṣṇa?
They reflected upon that deity through divine arguments,
with words consisting of Brahmanic terms, and by means of all logical proofs and defining characteristics;
yet they were unable to discover him, whether by his actions or even by his birth.
The sages declare him to be the Ancient One among the Purāṇas— those who know his life-story through the narratives revealed by him.
And his ancient deeds are heard of even among the gods;
from the Great Purāṇa onwards, there is nothing superior to him.
Apart from the Purāṇas, no account of his life exists;
and even the Veda itself contains his life-story, born of his own power.
By him, therefore, all these Śrutis—both Vedic and worldly—are pervaded.
At the time of worldly existence, he becomes the creator of beings for all people;
Madhusūdana remains awake for the destruction of the Dānavas.
When the gods were unable to behold the infallible one while he slept, they said:
"He sleeps at the end of the summer heat, and he awakens at the conclusion of the rainy season."
For he indeed is the sacrifices, the Vedas, and all the limbs of sacrifice;
he who is declared to be the course of sacrifice is this very Puruṣottama.
When he is asleep, the sacrificial rites purified by mantras do not proceed.
For Madhusūdana remains awake, having commenced his sacrifice at the onset of autumn.
For from autumn onwards, sacrifices are indeed performed for Hari, the bearer of Śrī;
therefore,
while Viṣṇu is asleep, Indra, the lord of the clouds, causes this annual cycle of Vaiṣṇava rites to be carried out.
For this deep and deceptive illusion that dwells in the world as sleep is suddenly a terrible night of doom for kings, full of hostility.
Her body is a gateway to darkness, destroying the day as night does;
she is a terrible harvester of half the life of all living beings on earth.
No one possessed by this [power], yawning again and again,
is able to withstand its force, as if sinking into the great ocean.
For all people in the world, worldly sleep— whether born of food or born of fatigue— is not something that belongs to the night alone.
For at the end of a dream, this [consciousness] generally wanes for embodied beings on earth;
and at the time of death, it utterly destroys the vital breaths of living creatures.
Even among the gods, no one other than Nārāyaṇa could sustain her;
she is the Māyā of the All-Devourer, born from the body of Viṣṇu, and she is his friend.
This very lotus-eyed one, seen at the mouth of Nārāyaṇa,
deludes all beings and brings the worlds under her sway in a short time.
Thus, for the sake of the welfare of the worlds, she is sustained by the fire, which has blackened paths,
just as a devoted wife is supported by her husband who is worthy of service.
Covered by that sleep, the imperishable Viṣṇu then lay in that hermitage of Nārāyaṇa, deluding the world.
As that great-souled one lay there, thousands of years passed—
encompassing the Kṛta Yuga and the Tretā, the best of ages.
But at the end of the Dvāpara age, having seen the worlds in great distress,
that one of great splendor awoke while being praised by the great seers.
The sages said:
"Abandon this innate sleep, like a garland already worn;
these gods, together with Brahmā, desire to see you."
O Hṛṣīkeśa, these sages of firm vows, who know Brahman and speak in praise of Brahman, magnify you.
O Viṣṇu, creator of beings, listen to these auspicious words of the elements— earth, ether, fire, air, and water— which have become your very self.
O Lord, these seven sages, together with their circles of disciples,
are directly praising you with divine songs worthy of being sung.
Arise, O lotus-eyed one, O lotus-navelled one of great splendor!
Some cause has arisen due to the gravity of the task for the gods.
Abandon sleep for the sake of the world, O Keśava, Lord, Janārdana;
when you are asleep, the world is asleep, and when you are awake, it is awake.
"Bring about a meeting of the gods, O God of gods, Lord of the World!
Why do you sleep, O Govinda, now that the world has perished?
Behold the world, including its gods, asuras, and humans, as if it were already destroyed."
Vaiśampāyana said: Having condensed the entire universe and dispelled the mass of darkness,
Dhṛṣīkeśa arose, blazing with supreme splendor.
He beheld all the gods assembled together with Pitāmaha,
who had gathered for the sake of the world, agitated and desirous of speaking.
With eyes resting from sleep, Hari spoke to those gods in words that perceived the ultimate reality and were joined with the purpose of establishing dharma.
O gods, from where has this conflict of yours arisen? From where has this fear come upon you?
For whom is there a task, or by what means? Or what matter concerning me does not exist?
Indeed, there is no unwholesome thing in the world that arises from giving which causes men such distress; I wish to know this quickly.
Having set aside my supreme bed in the midst of these knowers of Brahman, I stand here for the sake of your welfare; what may I do for you?

Vaiśampāyana said: Having heard that which was spoken by Viṣṇu, Brahmā, the grandfather of the worlds, [acted].
He spoke these supreme words, which were beneficial for all the inhabitants of heaven.
O Viṣṇu, destroyer of the asuras, there is no fear whatsoever for those gods for whom you are the grantor of fearlessness and the helmsman in every battle.
While Śakra, the lord of gods and destroyer of the asuras, is victorious,
what fear can there be for those humans who strive in righteousness?
Men who are devoted to truth and righteousness are free from the fever of distress;
untimely death cannot even look upon them.
And the lords of men and the kings, while taking a sixth part [of the produce] from one another, do not cause mutual dissension.
Bringing auspiciousness to their subjects, they were not censured by those who paid taxes;
being free from those who did not pay, they always filled the treasury with wealth.
Protecting their own respective prosperous territories and being devoted to forbearance, they—
possessing mild punishments— rightly guarded the four social orders.
Not causing alarm among living beings and properly honored by their ministers,
they employ the six political expedients while endowed with the fourfold army.
All were devoted to the science of archery and all were firmly established in the Vedas;
they performed sacrifices at the proper times with abundant sacrificial fees.
Having studied the Vedas, they satisfy the great seers through initiations and their ancestors hundreds of times with pure ancestral offerings and lifelong celibacy.
Nothing of the three kinds existing on earth— whether Vedic, worldly, or declared in the Dharmaśāstras— is unknown to them.
Having perceived the truths regarding both the higher and the lower realms, those lords of men, whose splendor is equal to that of the great seers,
strive once more to bring about the Kṛta Yuga.
By their very power, Indra sent down auspicious rain;
the winds blew according to the seasons, and the ten directions were free from dust.
The winds became auspicious and fragrant;
the sky became stainless;
the earth was free from portents, and the planets moved in their proper courses.
And the moon, together with the constellations, moves gently through its conjunction.
The sun moved through its two solstices in a favorable manner,
and the sacrificial fire, gratified by various oblations, became fragrant with auspicious scents.
When men act thus correctly, refrain from wrongdoing, and satisfy the entire earth, whence can there be any fear of time?
The surface of the earth is oppressed by the armies of those powerful kings, whose fame blazes and who follow one another in succession.
Exhausted by this burden and oppressed by kings,
this earth has reached a state like that of a boat which, though nearing destruction, does not yet sink.
Her form was like that at the end of an eon, with her mountain-fastenings loosened;
agitated by the surging waters, she repeatedly showed signs of perspiration.
With the bodies, the splendor, and the strength of the kṣatriyas,
and with the vast kingdoms of men, the earth seems to grow weary.
And that which was spoken by Brahmā Parameṣṭhin in the abode of Brahmā—
that supreme secret, O mighty-armed one, listen to it:
in every city, the lord of men is surrounded by forces numbering ten million.
And in every kingdom, there were many villages by the hundreds of thousands.
With thousands of rulers of the earth and the forces of those mighty ones,
as well as with kingdoms enriched by tens of thousands of villages, the land was made free of any gaps.
Having made this [world] free from material desire and rendered motionless before Time, O Viṣṇu, she has reached my abode; and you are her supreme goal.
For those dwelling here, this is the land of action; it has fallen into distress.
Therefore, that which must be done so that it does not perish should be performed, for this world is eternal.
For if she were oppressed, O Madhusūdana, there would be great fault;
there would be a failure of religious rites for the worlds, and the entire universe would become corrupted.
Clearly, this earth, oppressed by the multitude of kings, is wearying;
for, having abandoned her innate forbearance, she has become unsteady despite being immovable.
We have heard this from her, and you too have heard it;
for we are deliberating with you for the purpose of removing this burden.
For all kings who increase their kingdoms stand upon the path of truth;
likewise, among men, the three castes follow the Brahmins.
Every word shall consist of truth, and likewise all social classes shall be devoted to dharma;
all brahmins shall be devoted to the Vedas, and all men shall be devoted to the brahmins.
Thus do humans conduct themselves in this world for the sake of dharma;
let the counsel proceed in such a way that there may be no destruction of dharma.
This is the path of the virtuous, and no other; and Dharma is the means for its accomplishment.
Furthermore, the killing of kings must be carried out to relieve the burden of the earth.
Therefore come, O illustrious one, for the sake of the mantra;
let us go to the summit of Mount Meru, keeping the Earth before us.
Having said this much, O Indra among kings, Brahmā, the grandfather of the worlds,
the soul of the universe, and possessed of great splendor, ceased speaking along with the Earth.

Vaiśampāyana said: "So be it," he replied; then, with a voice like the roar of clouds on a stormy day, he set forth with them—having the appearance of a dark day, like a mountain shrouded in a foul tempest.
Bearing a dark mass of matted locks that shone with pearls and gems and possessed the luster of the moon amidst the clouds, Hari appeared with a dark-complexioned body.
And upon his broad chest,
the glorious Śrīvatsa shines, marked by a line of rising bristling hair and curved at the tops of his two breasts.
Clad in yellow garments, that immutable preceptor of the worlds,
Hari, became visible like a mountain shrouded in twilight clouds.
As he proceeded on his Garuda with Brahmā following behind him,
all the gods followed him, their eyes fixed intently upon him.
Before long, they reached the Mountain of Jewels;
there they beheld the deities in their own assembly hall, which could assume any form at will.
It was situated upon the peak of Meru, closely joined with the splendor of the sun,
with pillars and bases made of gold and archways formed from masses of diamonds.
Richly adorned with various paintings created by the mind, garlanded with clusters of celestial palaces,
containing lattices of jewels within, moving at will, and embellished with gems.
It was strewn with fashioned jewels, abounding in flowers of every season,
with stairs made of gems and coral, adorned with lapis lazuli stones,
covered with nets of pearls, and beautified by hundreds of tiny bells.
Divine, possessing celestial illusion, and fashioned by Viśvakarman.
With joyful minds, all those gods entered that auspicious assembly hall according to their respective places, according to their age, and according to their instructions.
They sat down upon the celestial chariots and seats as described,
on auspicious thrones, stools, rugs, and coverlets.
Then the wind-god Prabhajana, duly exhorted by Brahmā, moved everywhere through that auspicious assembly hall, saying, "Make no noise!"
In that silent and motionless assembly of the denizens of heaven,
the Earth, speaking with compassion due to her perspiration, addressed these words.
Dharaṇī said: "O God, I am indeed to be supported by you; by you the world is supported.
You sustain all beings, and you uphold the universe."
Whatever is sustained by you through your splendor and strength,
that is subsequently sustained by me through your grace.
I uphold only that which is upheld by you; I do not uphold what is not upheld by you.
For there exists no being whatsoever that is not sustained by you.
O Lord Nārāyaṇa, you alone, out of a desire for the welfare of the world, effect the descent of the great burden in age after age.
"O best of gods, protect me who have been overcome by your very splendor and have gone to the depths of the netherworld; I have come to you alone for refuge."
Being oppressed by the Dānavas and the evil-minded Rākṣasas,
I shall eternally seek refuge in you alone, the eternal one.
My fear remains great as long as I have not mentally sought refuge in you, Kakudmin; for I perceive that in the beginning,
in the past, I was first created by this Lotus-born One.
And having previously fashioned two great asuras out of clay, he bound me.
For those two, born from the ear-cavities of this high-souled Viṣṇu while he was sleeping upon the great ocean, remained as motionless as a piece of wood or a wall.
Urged on by Brahmā, Vāyu himself entered those two;
and those two great Asuras grew, covering the heavens.
Having grasped those two, Vāyu and Prāṇa, Brahmā touched them gently;
he considered one to be very soft and knew the other to be hard.
The Lord born from the waters gave them two names:
this soft one was named Madhu, and the hard one became Kaiṭabha.
Having received their names, those two Daityas, arrogant in their strength and utterly fearless, roamed throughout the entire world— which was now a single ocean— desiring to fight.
Seeing that they had arrived, Brahmā, the grandfather of the worlds,
vanished right there into the mass of waters of the single ocean.
Upon that lotus which had arisen from the center of the navel of Padmanābha,
the four-faced Brahmā chose his secret dwelling.
Both of them, Nārāyaṇa and the Grandfather, remained within the waters of the cosmic egg;
lying in the water for many groups of years, they did not tremble.
Then, after a long time, both Madhu and Kaiṭabha arrived at that place where Brahmā was stationed.
Having seen those two terrible and great asuras, intoxicated by battle,
Viṣṇu was struck by Brahmā with a lotus stalk in the past;
then the highly effulgent Padmanābha quickly leapt up from his bed.
Then a terrible battle took place between those two and him,
at that time when the three worlds had become a single ocean and the universe had turned into water.
Then a tumultuous battle took place for thousands of years,
yet those two asuras did not experience any fatigue in that conflict.
Then, after a long time, those two Daityas, intoxicated by the pride of battle,
spoke with joyful hearts to the god Nārāyaṇa, Hari.
We are pleased by your battle; you are praiseworthy, for death in combat is glorious for you.
Slay us both before the earth is submerged by water.
And when slain, O best of gods, we two shall attain the status of your sons;
for he will be our conqueror in battle, and we two are ordained as his sons.
Seizing those two Daityas in battle with his two arms, he crushed them;
thus both Madhu and Kaiṭabha met their death.
Having both plunged into the water, their bodies attained a state of unity;
being churned by the waves of the sea, the two Daityas released their fat.
That water was pervaded by fat, and then it disappeared from between those two;
and the blessed Lord Nārāyaṇa created living beings once again.
Because she was covered with the fat (medas) of the two Daityas, she is therefore remembered as Medinī;
and by the power of Padmanābha, she was made eternal for mankind.
Furthermore, having become a boar while Mārkaṇḍeya was looking on,
I was lifted out from the midst of the waters by him with a single tusk.
Then, as you were proceeding, I was again carried away from your presence by the powerful Viṣṇu from the presence of the Daitya Bali.
Now, distressed and without a protector, I have come for refuge to this very Gadādhara, the Lord of the world and the one worthy of seeking shelter.
Agni is remembered as the preceptor of gold, Sūrya is remembered as the preceptor of cows,
Soma is the preceptor of those without a kṣatriya lineage, and Nārāyaṇa is my preceptor.
That which I alone sustain— the entire world, both stationary and moving—
is itself sustained by Gadādhara, who upholds all that is held by me.
By Rāma, the son of Jamadagni, desiring to remove the burden [of the earth],
I was deprived of my kṣatriya husbands twenty-one times out of his wrath.
Having been placed upon the sacrificial altar and satiated with the blood of kings by Bhārgava at his father’s śrāddha ceremony, I was offered to Kaśyapa.
Foul-smelling with flesh, fat, and bone, and smeared with the blood of Kṣatriyas,
she approached Kaśyapa like a young woman in her menses.
That brahmin seer also said to me: "O Earth, why are you with your face cast down?
O wife of a hero, why do you observe this vow of a hero's wife?"
I made this request to Kaśyapa, the benefactor of the world:
"O Brahmin, my husbands have been slain by the high-souled Bhārgava."
Deprived of those valiant kṣatriyas who live by the sword, I am a widow in an empty city; I do not have the strength to endure this.
Therefore, O Blessed One, let a king equal to you be given to me as a husband—
one who would protect me, this earth garlanded by the ocean, along with its villages and cities.
Having heard those words, the Lord, the Master, said, "So be it. Then he said, "Bestow me upon Manu, the lord of men."
Having reached that great and meritorious Ikṣvāku dynasty originating from Manu,
I have passed from one king to another over a vast period of time.
Thus have I been given to Manu, the wise lord of men;
and I have also been enjoyed by royal lineages equal to the families of the great seers.
Many heroic kṣatriyas, having conquered me, ascended to heaven; yet, falling under the power of time, they met their dissolution in me alone.
For my sake, conflicts among powerful Kṣatriyas who do not retreat in battle have occurred and continue to occur in this world.
This has been brought about by destiny acting through you;
for the sake of the welfare of the world, bring about the cause of the kings' destruction in battle.
If there is compassion for me, for the sake of lightening my burden,
let the one glorious wielder of the discus grant me fearlessness.
"I, tormented by this burden, have come seeking refuge;
if this burden is indeed to be laid down, let Viṣṇu himself speak to me."
Viṣṇu said:
"Do not fear, O auspicious Dharaṇī; attain peace, O composed one.
O Vasundharā, I shall establish you in your proper place."
"O deities, through his grace I shall cast off my fatigue.
Vaiśampāyana said: *Chapter 43, Transliterated and Proofread by Horst Brinkhaus, Version of October 10, 2002:* Vaiśampāyana said:
Having heard the words of the Earth, all those dwellers of heaven reflected upon the task to be accomplished for her sake and then spoke to the Grandfather.
O Blessed One, let the burden of this earth be lightened;
for you are the creator of the bodies of the worlds and indeed the Lord of the world.
Whatever must be done by Mahendra, Yama, and Varuṇa,
or whatever task is to be performed by the Lord of Wealth or by Nārāyaṇa himself;
Or whatever task must be done by the Moon, or by the Sun, or by the Wind;
or even by the Ādityas, the Vasus, or the Rudras, the creators of the worlds.
Or by the two Aśvins, the foremost of gods; or by the Sādhyas, the dwellers of the third heaven;
or by the Maruts, the best of deities; or even by Pāvaka, O Lord;
or by Bṛhaspati and Uśanas; or even by Kāla and Kali.
Or by Maheśvara, O Brahmin, or by Viśākha or Guha,
or by the Yakṣas, Rākṣasas, Gandharvas, Cāraṇas, or Mahoragas.
O Lord of the Gods, [is it] by means of mountains or the foremost of peaks, or by the oceans with their great waves,
or by the divine rivers beginning with the Gaṅgā?
Command quickly, O Lord, how the portion [of my power] is to be applied;
if you have a task concerning a king, or a task to be accomplished through the body of a king.
O Grandfather, how shall we all perform our partial incarnations—
those who dwell in the intermediate space, those upon the earth, and those who are kings?
And among the members of the assembly, the brahmins, and the lineages of kings,
we shall also create bodies not born from a womb upon the surface of the earth.
Having heard this great resolve of the gods who were united in a single purpose,
the Grandfather of the Worlds, surrounded by the deities, spoke these words.
"O best of gods, your resolve pleases me as well;
create portions of your own bodies on earth that are equal to yourselves in splendor."
O best of gods, all of you descend with your splendors,
sanctifying the goddess Earth and having obtained the glory of the three worlds.
O knower of the past, listen to what was done by me regarding this birth upon the earth within the royal lineage of Bharata.
O gods, in former times, having reached the western shore of the ocean,
I dwelt there together with my high-souled son Kaśyapa.
By means of discourses concerning past events that accord with worldly and Vedic traditions,
and by many qualities derived from ancient histories and Purāṇas.
While he was examining that Lord of Gods through various means and many characteristics,
and while they were engaged in those various conversations, the Ocean, accompanied by the Gaṅgā and joined by the winds from the clouds, quickly approached his presence.
Making his course uneven with waves and surging with speed,
he was covered by the watery garment variegated with multitudes of aquatic creatures.
His pure body was like a conch or a pearl; he was adorned with coral and jewels;
he was full, joined with the moon, and possessed a deep resonance like a thundercloud.
Disregarding me and exceeding its own appointed time,
it drenched me with its flickering outpourings of salt water.
And as the ocean resolved to overwhelm that region with its waters,
I addressed him with an agitated voice, saying, "Be at peace!"
As soon as the words "Be at peace" were spoken, the ocean became tranquil;
its mass of waves and billows subsided, and it stood there, blazing with royal splendor.
Furthermore, having formed a reasoned judgment and desiring your welfare, I have also cursed the ocean along with the Gaṅgā.
"Since you have appeared with a body like that of a king, go, O Ocean; you shall indeed become a protector of the earth, a king."
There too, maintaining your innate playfulness through your own splendor,
you shall become the lord of men and the upholder of the lineage of the Bharatas.
"Since you were told by me, 'You are Śānta,' and since you have become slender (tanutām gataḥ),
you shall be known in the world as Śantanu, possessed of a beautiful body (sutanu) through your fame."
This Gaṅgā, too, with her long-cornered eyes and beautiful in every limb—
this Gaṅgā of excellent complexion has also come for your sake; that best of rivers, truly embodied, will indeed approach you there.
Thus addressed, the enraged Ocean approached me and said,
"O Lord, O Sovereign of the Gods, for what reason have you cursed me?"
I am your obedient servant, created by you, and devoted to you;
why have you yourself cursed me, your own son, with such unworthy words?
"O Blessed One, by your grace I have grown swiftly during this festival;
if I moved, O Brahmin, what fault is there in my own self?"
O Blessed One, if you were touched by the waters scattered by the wind on this lunar festival day, what indeed could be the cause for a curse against me?
I have been agitated by these three causes: by the rising of great winds, by the swelling of rain clouds, and by the full moon joined with the lunar node.
Thus, O Brahmin, if I have offended you for reasons instigated by you, you ought to forgive me; let this curse be revoked.
Thus, since I have become weakened by the curse and am left without support,
O Lord of Gods, show compassion if you regard me as an authority.
And, O Lord, you ought to grant favor to this Gaṅgā, who has gone to the earth at your command, and who, through my fault, shares in that same fault.
"O Brahmin, show me favor; there is a cause for the curse.
Then, with gentle words, I spoke to that great ocean, who was ignorant of the reason, terrified, and driven by the wind of the curse.
"Attain peace; you need not fear, for I am well-pleased with you, O Great-minded One.
Regarding this curse upon the lord of rivers, hear the reason for its future outcome."
O Lord of Rivers, go now to the lineage of Bhārata and, by your own splendor, deposit your body within it, casting off this oceanic form.
O Great Ocean, lord of the waters, there you shall dwell as a protector of the earth, endowed with royal splendor,
while guarding the four castes.
And this Gaṅgā, the best of rivers, assuming a human form with limbs made lovely by that season, shall attend upon you.
Rejoicing with this Jāhnavī by my command,
O Ocean, you shall forget this soaking in water.
And you must perform this command of the gods with haste,
O Ocean, together with Gaṅgā, according to the rite prescribed by Prajāpati.
The Vasus have fallen from heaven and entered the netherworld;
for the sake of restoring them, you have been appointed by me.
I give those eight, born from the womb of Jahnavi, for the sake of offspring—
beings equal in quality to Vibhavasu, who increase the joy of the gods.
Having quickly procreated the Vasus and made the Kuru lineage great,
you shall cast off this body and enter once more into the ocean, O Sāgara.
Thus it was, O best of gods, that I previously spoke for your benefit,
foreseeing the future burden upon the earth that would take the form of kings.
Thus, this lineage of Śantanu has been established by me upon the earth,
wherein the Vasus, the inhabitants of heaven, were born from Gaṅgā.
Even today, the son of Gaṅgā remains on earth as the eighth Vasu;
these other seven Vasus have already attained [their celestial state], while he alone lingers behind.
From the second wife who was created, a second body of Śantanu arose;
Vicitravīrya was a radiant and powerful king.
At present, there are only two kings on earth descended from Vicitravīrya:
Pāṇḍu and Dhṛtarāṣṭra, renowned as bulls among men.
There, Pāṇḍu had two wives endowed with beauty and established in their youth—
the auspicious Kuntī and Mādrī, who were like celestial women upon the earth.
King Dhṛtarāṣṭra had one wife of equal conduct,
Gāndhārī, renowned on earth, who remained constantly established in her vows toward her husband.
"Let your portions, both the opposing side and the allied side, be divided here;
for a great conflict between the sons of those two kings will surely arise."
In the conflict over their inheritance, there will be a destruction of kings;
indeed, a great terror resembling the end of an eon shall arise.
When kings are weak and are destroying one another,
the earth— its cities and the multitudes of its provinces desolate— will fall into a state of exhaustion.
At the end of the Dvāpara Yuga, I beheld in ancient times that the kings,
together with their mounts, would go to their destruction by the sword.
There, the portion of Śaṅkara will consume with the fiery energy of his weapon those remaining men who are sleeping at night, deprived of their senses.
When he, who was like Death itself and a doer of cruel deeds, had desisted,
I declare that this third age, the Dvāpara Yuga, has come to an end.
When the portion of Maheśvara has withdrawn, then the Māheśvara Yuga will follow;
thereafter, the Tiṣya Yuga, a terrible age for mankind, shall arrive.
A person in whom unrighteousness predominates, who possesses only a meager grasp of dharma,
whose connection to truth has perished, and in whom a mass of falsehoods has increased.
All men in the world will take refuge in Maheśvara, Kumāra, and the two gods; they will no longer possess long lifespans.
Therefore, this is the supreme decision: all you gods must descend to earth as partial incarnations without delay, for the sake of bringing an end to the kings upon this earth.
Let a portion of Dharma be assigned to Kuntī and to Mādrī;
let Kali, the root of strife, be assigned to Gāndhārī.
Driven by time, these kings will belong to these two factions;
filled with passion for the sake of the earth, they will all be eager for battle.
"Let this Earth, the sustainer of the world, return to her own source;
for this world-renowned means for kings has been established as the ultimate."
Having heard the words of the Grandfather,
the Earth, together with Kāla, departed as she had come for the sake of slaying the rulers of the earth.
Brahmā exhorted the gods for the purpose of subduing the enemies of the deities,
as well as Nara, the ancient seer, and Śeṣa, the upholder of the earth.
Sanatkumāra and the Sādhyas, the gods led by Agni,
Varuṇa and Yama, as well as the Sun and Moon;
the Gandharvas and Apsarases, the Rudras, Ādityas, and the two Aśvins.
Then all the gods caused their portions to descend to the earth,
just as that descent of portions was previously described by me to you.
Those gods, born both from a womb and not from a womb upon the surface of the earth,
were slayers of Daityas and Dānavas; they were lords of men,
possessing bodies as firm as adamant and resembling clusters of kṣīrikā trees.
Some possessed the strength of ten thousand elephants, while others were endowed with the force of a rushing torrent;
capable of enduring maces, iron clubs, and spears, they had arms like iron bars;
they were strikers with mountain peaks, and all were warriors who fought with iron bars.
Born by the hundreds and thousands in the Vṛṣṇi lineage,
those gods became the Kurus and the kings among the Pañcālas.
Born from the wombs of prosperous sacrificers and Brahmins,
they were masters of all weapons, great archers, and devoted to the Vedic vows.
Endowed with all supernatural powers and virtues, performers of sacrifices, and doers of meritorious deeds—
when enraged, they could shake the mountains, split the surface of the earth,
leap into the sky, and agitate the great ocean.
Having thus instructed them, Brahmā, the lord of the past, future,
and present, merged them into Nārāyaṇa and attained peace for the worlds.
Listen further to how Viṣṇu, the Lord and master of life and wealth, descended to the surface of the earth for the sake of the welfare of all creatures.
Then, in the venerable lineage of the wise Vasudeva, born of the race of Yayāti, the Lord Nārāyaṇa was born, desiring glory.
Chapter 44, Transliterated and Proofread by Horst Brinkhaus, Version of October 24, 2002:
Vaiśampāyana said:
When Kāla had departed after having accomplished his purpose, and when the world was again in a state of disorder...
When the partial descent of the gods had taken place into the Bharata lineage,
When a portion of Dharma had descended, as well as portions of Śakra, Pavana,
the two Aśvins— the physicians of the gods— and Bhāskara.
When the eighth part of the day had already passed for the priest of the gods,
and when the sun had already reached the western quarter of the earth.
When the earth has fallen into the portion of Death, and likewise into the portion of Kali,
and when it has entered the portions of Soma, Vahni, and Varuṇa;
When the portion belonging to Śaṅkara had passed away, and when the portions belonging to the Viśvedevas, the dwellers of heaven, the Gandharvas, the Uragas, and the Yakṣas had likewise passed away;
When the portion of Mitra had descended, and likewise that of Yama,
and when the portion of Varuṇa had gone to the earth, O Janamejaya—
when these portions had thus descended from the sky to the ground—
Standing within a portion of Nārāyaṇa, Nārada was seen.
Resembling a blazing fire, with eyes like the rising sun,
he bore a massive mass of matted hair coiled toward the left.
Clad in garments white as the rays of the moon and adorned with golden ornaments,
he held a great lute tucked under his arm like a female companion.
Wearing a black antelope skin as an upper garment, with a golden sacred thread,
carrying a staff and a water-pot, he was like another Śakra in person.
With hands offered in ritual gestures (*mudrā*) and his body adorned with flowers,
he was a destroyer of secret obstacles in the world, resembling a planetary deity (*graha*).
A great seer (*maharṣi*), he delighted in debate, was learned, and was a knower of the *Gāndharvaveda*.
A Brahmin who took delight in enmity, like another Kali age personified,
was a singer of the four Vedas and the chief Udgātṛ priest among the primary officiants.
Then that great sage Nārada, the first speaker among the worlds of gods and gandharvas, an imperishable brahmin-seer who wanders through the world of Brahmā,
stood in the midst of the assembly of the gods and, being incensed, spoke to Viṣṇu.
That brahmin Nārada sang to Viṣṇu with the seven notes,
having first struck the ṣaḍja note and then the ṛṣabha following it.
Having mixed the Gāndhāra, and then the Dhaivata and Madhyama,
he then produced the Pañcama, and immediately after that the Niṣāda.
O Lord, there is the *kākalī* tone and the *vimātrā*, and from those two come the two *śrutis*;
likewise, O King, there are three by three, together with all the *layas*.
Having distinguished those hosts of *tāna* and *atāna* in their proper sequence, the Lord,
preceded by Brahmā, proclaimed the Infinite-Powered Lord of Gods through all those seven [categories], both by means of the objects to be expressed (*vācya*) and the expressers (*vācaka*).
Investigating the origin and the manifestation of the Primal Lord through these seven [means],
and having thus concluded the song, he spoke these words:
"This descent of Viṣṇu's portions which has been performed by the gods— "
All of this is causeless for the destruction of the lords of the earth.
O Lord of Ordinance, this earthly sovereignty established in you appears to me to be a purposeful undertaking joined with Nara and Nārāyaṇa.
O God, it is not fitting for you, who are wise and a seer of the true meaning of reality,
O God of gods, to undertake such an action for the sake of the earth.
For you are the eye of those who possess sight, the praiseworthy lord of the powerful,
the most excellent yogin among those possessed of yoga, and the refuge even for those who seek a refuge.
Seeing that the portions of the gods have departed, why do you, the all-pervading Lord who is foremost of all,
not apply your own portion for the sake of assisting the Earth?
Having you as their protector, these portions of the gods— composed of you and impelled by you—
shall traverse the world, passing from one task to another.
Therefore, O Viṣṇu, I have come in haste to this assembly of the gods for the purpose of urging you;
hear now the reason for this.
O Viṣṇu, hear now the destiny of those Daityas whom you slew in the Tārakāmaya battle, who have gone to the surface of the earth.
On earth there is a city arisen, known by the name of Mathurā;
it is situated on the bank of the Yamunā, prosperous and filled with tens of thousands of people.

There was once a great Dānava named Madhu, invincible in battle. He possessed a most formidable forest called Madhuvana, filled with a dense succession of massive trees, where he then resided. It was endowed with great supernatural power.
His son was a great Dānava named Lavaṇa;
Lavaṇa’s son was one of great strength and prowess,
who stood firm in his great might and terrified all living beings.
Sporting there for many series of years,
that arrogant Dānava caused the worlds, along with their hosts of gods, to tremble.
While Rāma,
the son of Daśaratha, who knew the dharma and struck fear into the rākṣasas, remained in Ayodhyā and ruled the kingdom.
That Dānava, boasting of his strength, having taken refuge in a formidable forest,
dispatched a harsh-speaking messenger to Rāma.
"O Rāma, I have come into the vicinity of your domain, and he is your enemy;
moreover, kings do not desire a neighboring ruler who is arrogant because of his power."
A king established in the royal vow, desiring the welfare of his subjects and seeking a prosperous realm,
must conquer all his enemies.
With his hair moistened by the consecration, the king, desiring to delight [his subjects], must first conquer the senses; for in their conquest lies certain victory.
For a lord of the earth who especially desires to conduct himself rightly,
there is no teacher equal to the world in the instruction of political ethics (naya).
For a king who is preeminent in strength— whether he be inferior in times of calamity, moderate in virtue, or wise— there is no fear arising from neighboring vassals.
Everyone is bound by their innate enemies, the ever-increasing senses; even a powerful lord, lacking self-control, is overcome by delusions that act as friends to his foes.
That you, out of delusion, have slain Rāvaṇa along with his army for the sake of a woman—this I do not consider appropriate; it was a great and contemptible deed on your part.
That you, while observing your vows and dwelling in the forest, struck down a lowly rakshasa— this was not seen as the conduct of the virtuous.
The virtue of the righteous, born of freedom from anger, leads one to an auspicious state of existence;
yet by you, through delusion, he has been slain and the forest-dwellers have been defiled.
That very Rāvaṇa is fortunate, who was slain in battle by you while you were observing a vow, for the sake of a woman, out of regard for worldly duties.
If that evil-minded one of unsubdued senses has been slain by you in battle,
then fight with me today in combat, if you are truly valiant.
Having heard those words spoken by the messenger who spoke the truth,
Rāghava, his body unperturbed due to his fortitude, replied with a smile:
"O messenger, what you have said out of respect for him is false;
that you cast me into blame and likewise the Vedas and the Self, which are perfectly stable."
Whether I am deluded regarding the path of the virtuous, or whether Rāvaṇa has been slain,
or whether my wife has been carried off— what cause for lamentation is there in that?
The virtuous who stand on the path of truth are not defiled by mere words;
for destiny remains ever watchful over both the good and others alike.
The task that was to be done by a messenger has been accomplished; go now, O messenger, without delay.
Those like me do not strike at base individuals who praise themselves.
"This younger brother of mine, Śatrughna, the scorcher of his enemies,
will take vengeance upon that evil-minded Daitya in battle."
Thus addressed, that messenger, having been permitted by the high-souled Raghava, the lord of men, departed together with the son of Sumitra.
Traveling with great speed, he reached that vast forest of the Dānavas;
eager for battle, the son of Sumitrā established his camp at the edge of the woods.
Then, at the messenger's word, that Daitya, overcome with rage,
left his rear guard in that forest and stood facing the battle.
Then a terrible battle took place between the son of Sumitrā and the Dānava,
as both heroes stood firm at the forefront of the fray.
They struck each other with well-sharpened arrows,
yet neither of them turned away from the battle nor experienced any fatigue.
Then, afflicted in battle by the arrows of Saumitri,
that Dānava was deprived of his spear and began to fail.
Having seized the goad granted by the gods in battle,
which draws all beings toward him, Lavaṇa roared aloud.
He seized him by the neck with a goad and dragged him;
Lavana began to force the younger brother of Raghava inside.
Then Śatrughna, the scorcher of his enemies, raised his sword with its golden hilt.
In that great battle, he severed the head of Lavaṇa with his sword.
He severed the elephant-goad as well as the great head of the Daitya;
having slain that Dānava in battle, the wise son of Sumitrā, the delighter of his friends,
destroyed that forest of the Daitya with his weapon.
Having cleared the forest, that son of Sumitrā,
the knower of supreme dharma, chose a site for a city for the prosperity of that region.
In that place where the Madhu forest stood, the city named Mathurā was formerly established by Śatrughna after he had slain that Dānava in battle.
That city was most magnificent, with its palaces, walls, and gateways;
it was prosperous, filled with a vast kingdom, and crowded with opulent mansions.
Endowed with gardens and groves, it was well-proportioned and firmly established; it possessed lofty ramparts and was girt with moats and bolts.
Her watchtowers are turrets and her armlets are excellent palaces;
her well-shuttered gates are her face, and the crossroads are her loud laughter.
Abounding with healthy and heroic men, crowded with elephants, horses, and chariots,
resembling a half-moon, and graced by the banks of the Yamunā.
Durgā possesses a market of merit and is proud of her accumulation of jewels;
her fields are full of flavor, and the god rains at the proper time.
When the partial incarnation of the gods of purified souls had taken place,
Nārada approached Nārāyaṇa and spoke these words.
O Nārada,
on the delightful bank of the Yamunā, there was a famous city named Mathurā;
that city shone forth, filled with men and women.
And because he settled there, that region thereafter became known as Śūrasena.
In that city there was a king of great heroism, a scion of the Bhoja lineage,
renowned as Ugrasena, whose prowess was equal to that of Mahāsena.
That great Daitya Kālanemi, who was slain by you, O Viṣṇu, in the battle of Tārakāmaya, has attained the state of being his son.
There was a king named Kaṃsa, large-eyed and the enhancer of the Bhoja lineage; he was renowned throughout the earth, possessing the distinct prowess of a lion.
He was a terrible source of fear to kings, suspicious to rulers of the earth,
and a bringer of dread to all living beings, having strayed from the path of the righteous.
Possessed of a cruel obsession and a cruel inner self,
and endowed with that very arrogance, he caused the hair of the subjects to stand on end.
He does not delight in the duties of a king, nor does he bring happiness to his own faction;
he does not act for the sake of his own kingdom, being fierce and always fond of taxation.
That Kaṃsa, having been born there, was defeated by you in battle;
having imprisoned his father, that king protected Mathurā.
Devouring raw flesh, he oppressed the worlds with his asura-like inner self.
That one who was known as Hayavikrānta and Hayagrīva was born as the horse named Keśin; he was his very youngest brother.
That wicked lion, skilled in neighing and unrestrained,
dwells alone in Vṛndāvana, devouring the flesh of men.
Ariṣṭa, the son of Bali, was a great Asura who could assume any form at will; taking the shape of a bull, he became the enemy of the cows.
The son of Diti named Riṣṭa, who was the most excellent among the Dānavas,
became an elephant and served as the mount for Kaṃsa.
That Daitya, who was renowned among the demons as the arrogant one named Lamba, became the mount of Kaṃsa himself; having become known as Pralamba,
he took refuge at the Bhāṇḍīra banyan tree.
The powerful bull among the Dānavas who was named Śikhara is called the Daitya Khara; that best of Asuras, Dhenuka,
is the Daitya who roams the terrible Tālavana forest, driving away the people.
Varāha and Kiśora— those two foremost among the Dānavas—
became the wrestlers Cāṇūra and Muṣṭika when they entered the arena.
O destroyer of the Dānavas, those two Dānavas, Maya and Tāra,
were residing in the city of Narakabhauma at Prāgjyotiṣa.
O Viṣṇu, these Daityas, though struck down and repelled by you,
have assumed human forms and are now harassing men on earth.
All those men who hate stories of you slay people who are absorbed in you;
by your grace alone, the destruction of those Dānavas shall indeed come to pass.
They fear you in heaven; they fear you in the ocean;
they fear you on earth—in no other way do they fear anyone else.
O Śrīdhara, even for a wicked Daitya who has been slain by you and not by another,
the earth becomes his destination after he falls from heaven.
But for one who has risen from that state and is slain upon the earth as a human being,
it is difficult to attain the way to heaven while you, O Keśava, are awake.
Therefore, come, O Viṣṇu; let us two go ourselves to the surface of the earth. For the destruction of the Dānavas, manifest yourself by means of your own self.
For your forms are unmanifest, visible and invisible even to the best of the gods;
within those forms, the gods created by you shall come into being upon the earth.
O Viṣṇu, upon your descent, Kaṃsa will perish;
and that purpose for which the earth has come [to you] shall be accomplished.
You are the master of affairs in Bhārata; you are the eye, you are the ultimate refuge.
Therefore come, O Hṛṣīkeśa, and slay those Dānavas upon the earth.
Chapter 45. Transliterated and proofread by Horst Brinkhaus; version of December 19, 2002.
Vaiśampāyana said:
Having heard the words of Nārada, Madhusūdana smiled.
The excellent Lord, the Sovereign, replied with auspicious words.
O Nārada, listen to my further words regarding that which you have spoken for the benefit of the three worlds, as it is being properly undertaken.
I have recognized that these Dānavas have been born on earth as embodied beings;
whatever body a Daitya assumes, he nourishes it as his own form.
I know Kaṃsa, born on earth as the son of Ugrasena;
and I also know Keśin, the Daitya who has the form of a horse.
I know the elephant Utpalāpīḍa, the two wrestlers Cāṇūra and Muṣṭika, and also the Daitya Ariṣṭa in the form of a bull.
Khara is known to me, as is the great asura Pralamba;
and that Pūtanā, O brahmin, the daughter of Bali, is also known to me.
And I also know, O Brahmin, the serpent Kāliya who dwells in the pool of the Yamunā, having assumed an unknown form out of fear of Vainateya.
I know that Jarāsandha stands at the head of all kings;
I also consider it well that Naraka resides in the city of Prāgjyotiṣa.
In the human world of mortals, he attained the state of a man;
and Bāṇa, in Śoṇitapura, possessed a splendor equal to that of Guha,
was arrogant with a thousand arms, and was exceedingly difficult to conquer even for the gods.
I know Śiśupāla, as well as those two, Haṃsa and Ḍimaka;
I know Pauṇḍra, Sālva, and likewise that Kālayavana.
I know Ekalavya and whoever else are of wicked conduct;
I shall slay them all—of this there is no need for deliberation.
And I know that the great burden of the Bharata lineage rests firmly upon me.
And I know all that, how those kings will stand.
I have seen the exhaustion of those human bodies on earth and their honoring in the world of Śakra, as they proceed without returning [to saṃsāra].
Having attained the human state in this earthly world, I shall enter into yoga concerning both myself and another.
And I shall also slay all those great asuras, Kaṃsa and the others,
by whatever specific means each one may find his end.
Having entered those various states of existence through yoga,
I must slay these enemies of the lords of the immortals in battle.
This relinquishing of their portions for the sake of the world which has been performed by these great-souled ones—
gods, celestial sages, and gandharvas— is also my approval.
Indeed, this decision was already made by me long ago for Nārada;
however, Brahmā, the Grandfather, does not provide a dwelling place for me.
In which country, in what manner born, or in what dress living, should I slay them in battle? Tell me that, O Grandfather.
Brahmā said:
"O Lord Nārāyaṇa, hear from me this means for accomplishing your purpose:
who on earth shall be your father and who your mother."
O mighty-armed one, in that place where you were born as the sustainer of the lineage on earth,
you shall uphold the entire great clan of the Yādavas.
Having utterly destroyed those Asuras and established your own great lineage, you shall set forth the moral boundaries for men; listen to that from me.
Long ago, O Viṣṇu, Kaśyapa seized the sacrificial cows that yield milk during the great sacrifice of the high-souled Varuṇa.
Aditi and Surabhi were both the two wives of Kaśyapa;
however, they did not accept those cows being offered by Varuṇa.
Then Varuṇa, approaching me and bowing with his head bent low, said:
"O Blessed One, my cows have been seized by my preceptor."
For my preceptor, having accomplished his purpose, did not permit me to take those cows;
he followed two wives, namely Aditi and Surabhi.
O Lord, those divine cows of mine are indeed inexhaustible and yield all desires;
protected by their own splendor, they roam throughout all the oceans.
Who, other than Kaśyapa, is capable of overpowering those cows of mine,
which yield an inexhaustible, foremost milk that is like the nectar of the gods?
Whether it be a lord, O Brahmin, or a teacher, or anyone else who has emerged from meditative absorption—
all these must indeed be restrained by you, for you are our supreme refuge.
If the power of punishment for those who act without knowing their duty did not exist in this world,
O Teacher of the World, the boundaries of the world would surely cease to exist.
Whether it be so or otherwise, let the Lord, the Master, determine what must be done;
let my cows be returned to me, and then I shall go to the ocean.

That self of yours which is the deity, and those cows which are cows—you are that imperishable one. Among the worlds set in motion by you, the cow and the Brahmin are remembered as the single essence.
Cows must first be protected; when they are protected, they in turn protect the twice-born.
By protecting cows and brahmins, the entire world becomes protected.
Thus addressed by Varuṇa, the lord of the waters, O Acyuta, I—
knowing the true cause regarding the cows— released a curse upon Kaśyapa.
In that portion by which the cows were taken away by the high-souled Kaśyapa,
he shall go to the earth in that same portion and attain the state of a cowherd.
And she who is named Surabhi and Yāditi, the source of the gods—
both of them shall indeed become his wives and go along with him.
Together with those two, Kaśyapa will take delight in the state of a cowherd on earth;
for he is a portion of that Kaśyapa, equal to Kaśyapa in splendor,
known as Vasudeva, who dwells among the cattle upon the surface of the earth.
Not far from Mathurā is a mountain named Govardhana;
there he dwelt, devoted to his cattle and paying tribute to Kaṃsa.
The two wives of that wise Vasudeva were Aditi and Surabhi, as well as Devakī and Rohiṇī.
Surabhi became the goddess Rohiṇī, and Aditi became Devakī;
O Madhusūdana, descend there for the welfare of the worlds,
while these denizens of heaven exalt you with words of victory and blessing.
Having descended yourself from your own self onto the surface of the earth,
satisfy Devakī and Rohiṇī with your two births.
There, O mighty-armed one, you shall first grow up as a mere child marked by the cowherds, just as you did previously during the three strides.
Having concealed yourself by means of your own self through your illusory power of yoga-form,
wander the earth delighting thousands of cowherd maidens.
O Viṣṇu, as you tend the cows and run through the forests,
the fortunate ones shall behold your body encircled by a forest garland.
Wearing yellow garments, with dark and curly hair,
his chest adorned with a forest garland, fanned by a peacock-feather whisk—
O Viṣṇu, lotus-petal-eyed one, when you had gone to dwell among the cowherds.
O mighty-armed one, if you are childish, the world will fall into a state of childhood.
O lotus-eyed one, your devotees, who follow the will of your heart,
shall become cowherds among the cows and shall always be your companions as you tend the cattle in the forest and roam about the cow-pens.
And as they bathe in the Yamunā, they will find delight in you.
The life of Vasudeva will have been well-lived,
O dear one, when he who was addressed by you as "Father" shall instead say "Son."
He indeed is the most fortunate in the world to whom you have become a son;
he indeed is the best among the doers of merit who may proclaim you as "son."
O God, those who pay homage to you, who bear the marks of a cowherd,
are indeed the best among the meritorious and are worthy of being saluted by all living beings;
or rather, whose sonship would they not attain, since [you were born] from Kaśyapa?
And who, O Viṣṇu, is capable of bearing you except for Aditi?
"Go indeed for victory by means of the yoga arising from within yourself;
we too, O Madhusūdana, shall go to our own abode."
Having spoken thus to the Lord of the Gods of gods, Brahmā, the grandfather of the worlds, that sovereign departed for his own abode, and the gods also returned as they had come; he,
having dismissed the gods, remained in the solitary dwelling of the third heaven.
Viṣṇu went to his own region, to the northern direction of the Ocean of Milk.
Right there on Mount Meru is a cave named Pārvatī, which is very difficult to access;
it is eternally worshipped on the sacred festival days by his three strides.
Having deposited his ancient body there, the noble-minded Lord Hari,
the Master, joined his own self to the house of Vasudeva.
