*Homage to the illustrious Horse-headed One.*
*//* Now begins the second section, the Viṣṇuparvan //*
"O abode of the virtues of Vedavyāsa, Lord of Knowledge, Master of the virtuous!
O Hari, constantly fulfill my hope by making me free from desire and devoid of affliction.
Vaiśampāyana said:
Having learned that Viṣṇu had descended to the earth along with portions of the gods,
Nārada, foretelling the destruction of Kaṃsa, went to Mathurā.
Having descended from heaven and stationed himself in the grove near Mathurā,
he indeed sent a message to Kaṃsa, the son of Ugrasena.
That messenger reported the sage’s arrival to the king:
"Nārada, having learned of the full details, stands at the gate as a doorkeeper.
Upon hearing this, Kaṃsa’s gatekeeper acted with great haste.
Having gone there quickly, O King, he spoke to Madhureshvara:
"O Indra among kings, here stands Nārada, the bringer of joy to the worlds.
Hearing of Nārada’s arrival, he of swift prowess [set out].
The lotus-eyed Asura Kaṃsa departed from his own city.
He beheld a praiseworthy guest, a celestial rishi free from all taint,
whose form blazed with splendor and whose body possessed the brilliance of the sun.
Having saluted that Ṛṣi, he performed worship according to the prescribed rites;
and having offered a seat glowing like fire, he indeed presented it to him.
That sage, a friend of Śakra, sat down upon that seat and spoke to the son of Ugrasena, who was exceedingly enraged.
"I have been honored by you, O hero, with rites performed according to the prescribed rules;
now that this has been done, let my words be heard and indeed accepted."
This being the case, O Great King, hear my words:
having ascended through the celestial worlds, beginning with that of Brahmā, I went,
my dear, to the vast Mount Meru, the friend of the sun.
Having beheld both the Sanandana forest and the Caitraratha grove,
I bathed along with the deities in rivers possessing excellent landing-stairs.
I have seen the divine, merit-bestowing river that flows through the three paths;
having seen the divine, merit-bestowing Bhāgirathī river that flows through the three paths;
the divine, merit-bestowing Bhāgirathī river has been seen, flowing through the three paths.
She alone, by the mere remembrance of her, destroys all sins for everyone;
and she who has been touched at divine bathing places in due order.
I have beheld the abode of Brahmā, frequented by hosts of brahmin-sages and resounded with the songs of gods, gandharvas, and apsarases.
Once, having taken up my lute and accompanied by the assembly of gods on the summit of Mount Meru, I went to the hall of Brahmā.
There I saw gods together with Pitāmaha, seated upon divine thrones, wearing white turbans and adorned with various jewels.
There, while I was in the state of a *mānava*, I heard from the gods this most terrible means for the destruction of you and your followers here.
In this matter, she who is your paternal aunt Devakī in Mathurā—
Kaṃsa, her eighth embryo shall be your death.
He is indeed the entire possession of the gods and the refuge of the triple heaven;
he is the supreme secret of the gods, and he shall become your death.
For these [beings], another is superior, and for those born of themselves (the self-born), there is the Self-Born;
therefore, I shall not describe that great, divine Being to you.
For that death of yours is indeed praiseworthy; remember what has occurred before, O Kaṃsa, and let an effort be made while [the child] is still in the womb, if it is possible.
"This is my affection directed toward you; for this purpose I have come. May all objects of desire be enjoyed; may it be well with you, I am departing."
"Let gifts be given in abundance;
let all desires be enjoyed!
Having spoken thus, when Nārada had departed, [Kamsa] reflected upon his words.
Then Kaṃsa laughed loudly for a long time, baring his teeth.
Standing before his servants, he spoke with a smile:
"Indeed, that Nārada is laughable among living beings; he is not wise."
I cannot be intimidated even by the gods together with Indra,
whether I am standing in battle, lying down, heedless, or even intoxicated.
"I, who stir up this earth with my two noble arms—
who in the world of men would dare to agitate me?"
From this day forward, I shall inflict a great slaughter upon all beings who follow the gods— the multitudes of men, birds, and beasts.
"Let Keśin, Pralamba, and Dhenuka be commanded,
as well as Ariṣṭa the bull, Pūtanā, and Kāliya."
Roam the entire earth at will, assuming whatever forms you desire;
and strike down all those who are detractors of our side.
The movement of embodied beings even while staying in the womb should be understood;
for Nārada has declared that we have cause for fear from those within the womb.
"May you all rejoice according to your desire, free from feverish distress;
for by relying on me as your protector, there is no fear caused by the gods."
But that brahmin Nārada, fond of sport and by nature divisive,
finds delight in creating dissension even among those who are closely united in the worlds.
Constantly scratching himself, he wanders restlessly through the worlds,
instigating the strings of enmity among kings.
Thus lamenting with mere words alone,
Kaṃsa entered his palace with a heart that was burning with anguish.

Vaiśampāyana said:
Enraged, he commanded his own well-wishing ministers:
Therefore, all of you must indeed be vigilant regarding the cutting of Devakī’s womb.
Indeed, all those embryos must be destroyed from the very beginning;
for that evil which involves doubt must be eradicated from its root.
And let Devakī, kept secret and protected by those who remain hidden,
move about freely and with confidence, while my forces apply themselves with diligent effort.
"Let my wives count the months beginning from the month of Puṣpa; once the pregnancy has reached its conclusion, we shall know what remains."

Vasudeva must be protected by those devoted to my welfare, both by night and by day, along with the women throughout the lands; he must be guarded by vigilant women and eunuchs, and no reason for his presence must be disclosed.
This human effort is accomplished by humans alone;
hear now how destiny is indeed thwarted by those such as I.
Through well-administered collections of mantras, properly applied medicines,
and diligent effort that is favorable, even destiny may be brought into accord.
Thus, having heard the matter from Nārada, Kaṃsa, being diligent in his efforts to destroy the womb of Devakī, consulted [with his ministers] out of fear.
Then Nārada, the son of Brahmā and the foremost among sages,
related everything to Viṣṇu regarding Kaṃsa’s activities;
having thus heard of Kaṃsa’s efforts known as the "Ariṣṭas," he [Viṣṇu] indeed became vigilant.
Upon hearing of King Kaṃsa’s deed, the powerful Viṣṇu, lord of the world, vanished and reflected.
"The son of the Bhoja king will kill these seven children in Devakī’s womb;
therefore, I shall place my own self into the eighth womb."
As he was reflecting in this manner, his mind went to Pātāla,
where those Dānavas known as the Ṣaḍgarbhas lay within their embryonic beds.
Possessing heroic bodies, radiant, resembling those who have consumed the nectar of immortality, and equal to the gods in battle— these indeed were the sons of Kālanemi.
In ancient times, having abandoned their grandfather Hiraṇyakaśipu,
the Daityas, wearing circles of matted hair and performing intense austerities, worshipped the Grandfather of the worlds.
For a thousand times ten thousand years, they moved through the waters and the air;
Brahmā became pleased with them and granted a boon to those six embryos.
Brahmā said:
"O tigers among the Dānavas, I am well-pleased by your ascetic penance;
tell me, what desire each of you has, and what boon shall be granted to you?"
Then all those Daityas, having a common purpose, said to Brahmā:
"If the Blessed One is pleased with us, let our most excellent boon be heard."
O Blessed One, may we be invulnerable to the gods along with the great serpents,
and even to the supreme ṛṣis who possess the power of fixed curses as their weapons.
"O Blessed One, if you grant us this boon, let there be no slaughter for us at the hands of the lords of the yakṣas and gandharvas, nor by the siddhas, cāraṇas, and mānavas."
Then Brahmā, with a deeply pleased inner self, said to them:
"All this that has been spoken by you shall come to pass."
Having granted a boon to the six embryos, the Self-Existent One departed for the third heaven;
thereupon, Hiraṇyakaśipu spoke these words in anger.
Since you have chosen a boon from the Lotus-born Brahmā instead of me, your affection has been made to depart;
therefore, I abandon you who have become my enemies.
"The word 'Ṣaḍgarbha' which was given to each of you by your father—
that very name shall cause your father to slay all of you while you are still in the womb."
There will be exactly six [sons] from Devakī’s womb; indeed, those great Asuras are the six embryos.
Therefore, Kaṃsa will kill you while you are still in the womb.

Having thus cursed the Daityas, the lord of the Daityas, overcome with rage and possessed of immeasurable prowess, cast them into the waters within Pātāla. Hari, however, having learned of that curse and Kaṃsa’s resolve, [acted accordingly].
Then Viṣṇu went from there to Pātāla, where those heroes,
the six embryos, remained restrained, lying within a chamber filled with water.
He saw the six embryos lying asleep in the water, still within their fetal state,
as if all were hidden away by sleep in the form of Time.
Then, in the form of a dream, Viṣṇu indeed entered their bodies;
having extracted the lords of their vital breaths, he delivered them to sleep.
Then Viṣṇu, whose prowess is truth, said to that Sleep:
"Go, O Sleep, released by me, to the vicinity of Devakī’s dwelling."
Having taken these lords of vital breaths, the embodied beings named Ṣaḍgarbhas—
the Ṣaḍgarbhas, the best of the Dānavas—
and also Sarvaprāṇeśvarī.
Place [the six] within the six wombs of Devakī in due order.
When these children had been born and led to the abode of Yama,
Kaṃsa’s efforts were rendered fruitless, while Devakī’s labor bore fruit.
I shall bestow upon you a grace equal to my own grace on this earth,
by which, O Goddess, you will become a goddess for the entire world.
My weapons shall likewise abide in your arms:
the Śārṅga bow, the conch, the mace, the discus, the club, and the trident;
and the seventh portion, the gentle one who was my first-born, shall be born from the womb of Devakī.
He should be transferred by you to Rohiṇī in the seventh month.
From the extraction of the embryo, that youth Saṃkarṣaṇa will become my elder brother, possessing a countenance like the cool-rayed moon.
"This seventh child in Devakī’s womb has fallen [aborted] out of fear;
when I am in my eighth pregnancy, Kaṃsa will exert his efforts."
And she who was the beloved wife of Nandagopa, the protector of Kaṃsa, named Yaśodā— the bearer of the Gopa lineage— blessings upon you.
"You shall become her ninth embryo in our lineage;
you will indeed be born on the ninth lunar day of the dark fortnight."
But I, when the conjunction of Abhijit has arrived and the first watch of the night has passed—
at midnight— I shall deliver the fetus at my ease.
When the eighth month has arrived, we two shall simultaneously undergo an exchange of wombs upon the execution of Kaṃsa's command.
"I shall go to Yaśodā, and you, O Goddess, attend upon Devakī;
through this exchange of our embryos, let Kaṃsa fall into delusion."
Then, seizing you by the foot, he will dash you against a rock;
thereafter, released from his hand through my power, you shall become auspicious.
While being cast forth, you will attain an eternal station in the sky.
Dark-complexioned like the fish-bannered god of love, with a face resembling Saṃkarṣaṇa,
she possesses long arms on this earth that are like my own.
Raising up a trident with three prongs and a sword with a golden hilt,
as well as a vessel full of honey and a perfectly pure lotus.
Wearing a dark blue linen garment with a yellow upper cloth,
she shone upon her breast with a necklace as brilliant as the rays of the moon.
Adorned with ears graced by divine earrings,
you shine with a face that has become a rival to the moon.
She was adorned with a crown featuring three wheels and with her hair bound up;
she possessed arms resembling iron bars, resonant with the hissing of coiled serpents.
Adorning the ten directions with her eight formidable arms, which were as terrifying as serpents, she shone nearby with a raised banner of peacock feathers, holding the Śārṅga bow, the discus,
and the sword.
And with a radiant armlet made from the feathers of peacocks.
Surrounded by hosts of terrible spirits and following my commands,
you shall attain the celestial realm by observing the vow of perpetual maidenhood.
There, Śakra, the hundred-eyed one, shall unite you with the deities through a divine consecration, by means of the rite prescribed by me.
There, Vāsava will seize you for the sake of his sister;
and by the lineage of Kuśika, you shall become Kauśikī.
He will grant you an eternal abode on the Vindhya, the best of mountains;
from there, you shall beautify the earth with thousands of dwellings.
Then you shall destroy the two Dānavas, Sumbha and Niśumbha, who cause distress to the mountains, along with their followers, after first taking me into your mind.
Wandering through the three worlds, you shall become one who grants boons and can assume any form at will, O highly fortunate lady, once your vow has been fulfilled upon the earth.
Followed by spirits and always fond of offerings of meat,
you shall receive worship on the ninth lunar day along with animal sacrifices.
And those humans who, knowing my power, shall bow down to you—
for them nothing whatsoever shall be difficult to obtain, whether in terms of sons or even wealth.
For men exhausted in wildernesses, or in the great ocean, or held captive by bandits, you are the supreme refuge.
You are accomplishment, fortune, fortitude, fame, modesty, knowledge, humility, and intelligence;
you are the twilight, prosperity, form, wisdom, splendor, faith, action, and the goal;
you are the twilight, night, radiance, sleep, and likewise the night of time.
But those who shall praise you with devotion by means of this hymn, O auspicious one—
I shall never abandon them, and they shall never abandon me.
Vaiśampāyana said:
I shall proclaim the Āryā-stava as it was told by the sages of old:
"I bow to the goddess Nārāyaṇī, the sovereign of the three worlds."
K₁₋₃ Ñ₂.₃ V₁ B₂.₃ Dn D₂₋₆ T₁.₂.₄ G₁.₂.₄.₅ M₄, after the repetition of verse 54;
G₃, after the repetition of 54ab: a passage given in Appendix I (No. 8).
When worshipped, you shall pacify for men terrible bondage and slaughter, the loss of sons, the depletion of wealth, as well as the fear of disease and death.
O highly fortunate one, you shall become a giver of boons, capable of assuming any form at will.
I too shall provide for my own livelihood like a cowherd among the cows;
and for the sake of my own prosperity, I shall also carry out the slaying of Kaṃsa.
Having thus instructed her, the Lord vanished;
and she, having bowed to him, departed saying, "So be it."
The person who recites this hymn or hears it repeatedly attains the accomplishment of all goals; there is no doubt about this.

Vaiśampāyana said: When the rite for the conception of the embryos had been performed, Devakī, who was like a goddess,
duly received those seven embryos as they had been described.
Kaṃsa killed those six embryos as they emerged on the surface of a stone;
she then carried the seventh embryo, which was in danger, to Rohiṇī.
At midnight, while her womb was still intact, she,
stained with menstrual blood and suddenly overcome by sleep, fell to the surface of the earth.
Having seen that embryo as if in a dream issuing from her own body,
she became distressed for a moment when she could no longer see it.
In the darkness of night, Nidrā spoke to that agitated Rohiṇī,
who was like Rohiṇī to Soma, the wife of Vasudeva.
"O auspicious lady, because he draws forth this embryo that was placed within your own womb, your son shall indeed be named Saṃkarṣaṇa."
Having obtained that son, Rohiṇī was joyful; with her face slightly cast down, she entered her dwelling like the radiant star Rohiṇī.
Through the path of that embryo, Devakī conceived an embryo for the purpose of which those seven embryos of hers had been destroyed by Kaṃsa.
The guards of that embryo,
all armed with weapons, remained vigilant and disciplined, counting the months as they protected it with great effort.
There, Hari dwelt within the womb by his own will.
On the very day that Devakī conceived the Lord of Gods as her embryo,
Yaśodā likewise conceived an embryo;
she was the sleep born from the body of Viṣṇu, acting according to his command.
But when the eighth month of pregnancy was incomplete, those two women,
Devakī and Yaśodā, gave birth at the same time.
On the very same night that the Lord Kṛṣṇa was born into the Vṛṣṇi clan,
on that same night Yaśodā,
the esteemed wife of the cowherd Nanda and daughter of the cowherd Kaṃsa, gave birth to a daughter.
For Yaśodā and Devakī were both pregnant at the same time;
on the eighth lunar day of the dark fortnight in the month of Śrāvaṇa, a great tithi,
under the asterism Rohiṇī, at midnight, and likewise at the rising of the moon.
Devakī gave birth to Viṣṇu, and Yaśodā to that girl,
when the auspicious hour of Abhijit had arrived at the midnight hour adorned with splendor.
The oceans trembled, the mountains shook,
and fires that were already extinguished blazed up while Janārdana was being born.
Auspicious winds blew and the dust became stilled;
the celestial lights shone forth as Janārdana was being born.
The lunar mansion was named Abhijit, the night was named Jayantī,
and the hour was named Vijaya, at which time Janārdana was born.
The unmanifest, eternal, subtle Lord Hari-Nārāyaṇa was born there,
the Blessed One, deluding the world with his eyes;
the unstruck kettledrums of the gods resounded in heaven.
And the Lord of the Three Heavens rained down a shower of flowers from the sky.
All the sages of rigid vows, having become invisible,
praised Janārdana, the Lord of Gods, as he was being born in the night.
Behold, this very Lord of the World, having assumed a youthful body, now remains silent in the house of Vasudeva.
Behold him with full confidence— the Lord, the Sovereign of the World himself—
dwelling in a human body as he hangs from the hand of Devakī.
He will manifest himself to slay the evil-minded Kaṃsa.
Salutations to that Viṣṇu, the sustainer of the world, who takes the form of Kṛṣṇa;
salutations again and again to him of inconceivable power, the creator of the universe. Praising Madhusūdana with words endowed with auspiciousness—
With meaningful words, the great seers, along with the gandharvas and the apsaras, thus attended upon Janārdana as he was being born.
As Hṛṣīkeśa was being born, the world became filled with joy;
and Indra, together with the thirty gods, praised Madhusūdana.
But Vasudeva, having seen that son Adhokṣaja born in the night,
marked with the Śrīvatsa and endowed with divine characteristics,
spoke then to Devakī, who was dejected, though she possessed a pure smile.
Withdraw this divine form of yours, O Hari, from all beings.
"O destroyer of the sons of Diti, let Kaṃsa not know of your descent.
Vasudeva said to him, "O Lord, withdraw this form;
O God, I am afraid of Kaṃsa, and therefore I speak thus."
"O lotus-eyed one, my eldest sons have been slain by him."
Having heard Vasudeva’s words, Acyuta withdrew his form and,
having granted him permission, said, "Take him to the house of Nandagopa as your son. Then, abiding by the counsel of Ugrasena, he gave [the child] to Yaśodā.
Thus, during that tumultuous time, the guards then fell fast asleep.
Not only were the armed guards deluded, O lord of the earth,
but that entire city of Mathurā fell asleep through the illusory power of Hari,
with the exception of Vasudeva and Devakī.
Then Vasudeva, having gone to that chamber where Devakī’s womb resided,
beheld at night the Lord of the gods, Adhokṣaja, who had been born.
With the ends of his hair dark and curled, his face like a blooming lotus,
resembling a dark blue cloud, he is lovely, possessing superhuman rays of splendor.
As before, Kṛṣṇa was lying upon a lotus leaf or a banyan leaf,
with his head toward the east and his feet placed toward the west.
There, no placenta was seen, nor were there any pains of childbirth.
Seeing her son looking on, Devakī sat down;
she was overcome with extreme amazement along with Vasudeva.
But Vasudeva, having quickly taken up the infant, [placed him on Devakī’s side].
Taking him who was lying on Devakī’s lap during the night, the Yādava,
fearing [Kamsa] and being deeply affectionate toward his son, entered the house of Yaśodā.
Then, when the gatekeepers and the citizens had been laid low and all their faculties and activities were snatched away by her,
the gates remained closed, barred, and difficult to pass.
With large door-panels, iron bolts, and chains.
When Vasudeva, whose vehicle is dark, arrived, those [clouds] dispersed of their own accord like darkness before the sun;
then the rain-god poured down rain with a low rumbling.
Śeṣa followed behind, warding off the water with his hoods.
The river Yamunā, the younger sister of Yama, rains down excessively and repeatedly;
she is foamy with the speed of her deep torrential currents and is agitated by hundreds of terrifying whirlpools.
He gave way, as the ocean does for the Lord of Śrī.
Having approached Nanda’s cow-pen and finding the cowherds there fast asleep with sleep,
Śauri placed his son upon Yaśodā’s bed.
Having taken his daughter, he returned home once more.
Without Yaśodā’s knowledge, having placed the boy there and taken that girl instead,
he laid her upon the bed of Devakī.
Then, while all the guards were fast asleep due to the illusory power (*māyā*) of Viṣṇu, Vasudeva—
overcome with fear at the exchange of those two infants,
yet having achieved his purpose— departed from the dwelling.
All the gates of the inner apartments, both inside and out, were closed as before;
then, hearing the sound of children, the gatekeepers rose up.
Having approached quickly,
they reported to Kaṃsa, the son of Ugrasena— that is, to the King of the Bhojas— who was anxiously waiting for it, the birth from Devakī’s womb; and then Ānakadundubhi [Vasudeva] spoke to him.
Then he presented that maiden of excellent complexion.
Terrified, he announced, "A daughter has been born to us!
Hearing this, the powerful Kaṃsa, hurrying with speed along with his guards, arrived at the door of Vasudeva's house.
Hurrying there to the door, he asked, "What has happened?
and thus threatened them with words, saying, "Let [it] be given quickly!"
Then all the women, headed by Devakī, raised a cry of "Alas!
and the distressed Devakī spoke to Kaṃsa with a voice faltering with tears: "A daughter, my son, has been born," she said to Kaṃsa.
"O Lord, my seven glorious sons, who were pregnant with children, have been killed by you;
this girl too has been killed. Look at her, if you so deem it right."
Upon seeing that girl, Kaṃsa was filled with joy and rejoiced;
that man of vain intellect said, "This girl is as good as dead once she is born."
Suffering within the womb, her hair drenched by the amniotic fluids,
she was placed upon the earth before Kaṃsa, though she was equal to the earth itself.
Seizing her by the foot, the man whirled her around and shook her;
even as he was lifting her up, he suddenly dashed her against a rock.
Though shaken upon the surface of the rock, she did not shatter, but flew up toward the sky.
Having cast off her fetal body, she suddenly released her hair and entered the sky; adorned with celestial garlands and unguents,
her entire body graced by necklaces and resplendent with a crown, she departed.
And she remained eternally a maiden, divine and praised by the gods.
Wearing blue and yellow garments, with breasts like the frontal globes of an elephant,
a broad hip like a chariot, a moon-like face, and four arms.
With a complexion as brilliant as lightning and eyes like the rising sun,
she possessed the sound of thundering clouds— like the twilight accompanied by rain-clouds.
Indeed, during that night when darkness had seized it and it was crowded with hosts of spirits,
she shone as she danced and laughed, appearing radiant in her inverted state.
Having ascended into the sky, the fierce goddess drank the unsurpassed beverage;
she laughed a great laugh and, filled with wrath, spoke to Kaṃsa.
O Kaṃsa, since I was killed by you for the sake of destroying you, O Kaṃsa, and was suddenly lifted up and dashed down upon a rock; [that very act shall bring about your end].
Therefore, at the time of your end, as you are being dragged away by the enemy,
I shall tear open your body with my claws and drink your warm blood.
Having spoken these terrible words, that goddess, together with her attendants, traveled through the sky to the abode of the gods by way of her own will.
That maiden grew up there in the residence of the Vṛṣṇis,
being honored and protected like a son by that goddess at the command of the gods.
Know her also as Ekānaṃśā, the goddess born from a portion of Prajāpati,
a maiden of yoga, created for the protection of Keśava.
All the Yādavas, with well-disposed minds, worship her;
by her Kṛṣṇa was protected, he who possesses a divine form like a god.
When those men on earth said, "She is Ekānaṃśā who has been born," Kaṃsa, upon her arrival, considered her to be his own death;
and in private, filled with shame, he addressed Devakī.
"O aunt, you exerted effort to destroy my embryo, but,
O Queen, my death has arisen from another cause in quite a different manner."
Driven by despair, I made an effort and struck out at my own kin;
yet I was not able to overcome destiny through human exertion.
Abandon this anxiety concerning the embryos that causes you such grief;
for I shall be the cause of their [recovery] should there be a change in time.
Time alone is the enemy of men, and time is that which brings about transformation;
indeed, it is time that leads everything, and one such as I is merely its instrument.
"O Goddess, calamities will indeed come according to their respective portions;
however, it is this that is truly painful—that a living being thinks, 'I am the doer.
Do not harbor anxiety for your son; abandon this lamentation born of grief."
Such is the nature of human birth; there is no fixed limit to time.
O Devakī, I fall at your feet with my head bowed like a son;
let your anger toward me be relinquished, for I myself recognize the wrong I have committed.
To Kaṃsa, who had spoken thus, Devakī, her face filled with tears, distressed and looking toward her husband, addressed these words like a mother: "Arise, arise, my child! she said to Kaṃsa.
Devakī said:
"The embryos that were destroyed before me by you in the form of Time—O son, you are certainly not the cause; for Kṛtānta (Death) alone is the cause here."
This act of yours, which has cut my womb, must be endured by me as you fall from head to feet, loathing your own deed.
Death is certain even in the womb; it does not turn back even in childhood.
Even a youth is subject to death, while an old man is already dead.
All this has Time as its root, for you alone are its cause.
As there is no perception of that which is unborn, so it truly does not exist;
yet even that which is born returns to the state of being unborn, wherever it is led by the Ordainer.
Therefore go, my son; let there be no cause for anger toward me on your part.
When one has already been seized by death, only the remaining factors can operate as causes.
In accordance with the method previously observed regarding the creation of beings in its true nature,
birth indeed occurs through the agency of a mother and father.
Having heard Devakī’s words, Kaṃsa entered his own residence,
greatly agitated and with a burning heart;
dejected because his purpose had been frustrated, he went along in extreme despondency.
Reflecting upon his own impending death while recollecting the words of the maiden, [he thought: (Ch.

Vaiśampāyana said:
Vasudeva, however, had already heard in Vraja that Rohiṇī had first given birth to a son whose face was more beautiful than the moon.
He quickly spoke to Nandagopa with auspicious words: "Go, you must take her along with Yaśodā back to Vraja."
And when Rohiṇī, whose eyes are like lotuses, gave birth to a son,
O Lord, Yaśodā likewise gave birth to a son at that very same time;
having gone there, [one should honor] these two boys with the rites of birth and other such ceremonies.
Having joined him, O dear one, raise him in Vraja as you please;
and protect my infant son, the offspring of Rohiṇī, in Vraja.
Therefore, O dear one, protect Vraja when it is full of negligence;
for everyone is prone to play in childhood, and in childhood superhuman beings become infatuated;
and in childhood everyone is most fierce—therefore, be intent upon effort in that regard.
"I shall be censured among those on my father's side who have sons,
for I do not see the face of even one infant son."
For even though I am wise, my discernment is being forcibly carried away;
indeed, I have this fear of Kaṃsa because of his mercilessness in the slaying of an infant.
Just as you, O Nanda Gopa, protect my own son Rauhineya,
so do likewise, dear one, for one who seeks the truth;
for indeed, many obstacles in this world terrify the young.
That son of mine is the elder, and this one of yours is the younger;
look upon both with equal affection as you please.
O Nandagopa, act in such a way that both of these boys, growing up together and being of equal age, may shine in that cowherd settlement.
And a cattle-pen must never be established in Vṛndāvana;
for there dwells that cruel, flesh-eating,
and evil-minded Keśin, and one must fear him while residing there, for he is of sinful appearance.
From reptiles, insects, and likewise from birds;
and in the cow-pens, from the cows and the calves—these two infants of yours must be protected.
"The Yamunā must not be crossed at all, for Kāliya dwells therein.
O Nanda-gopa, the night has passed; travel swiftly, for the messengers from Vraja are urging you on. These birds here, circling to the left and right, are hastening you."
Having been granted leave by the high-souled Vasudeva, he,
filled with joy, ascended the vehicle together with Yaśodā.
Having placed the prince in a palanquin carried on shoulders,
the high-minded one settled that infant upon a bed with a soft mattress and laid the child down upon his couch.
He proceeded by a secluded path, beautiful along the banks of the Yamunā, which was shaded by abundant water and fanned by cool, wafting breezes.
He beheld a pleasant region near Mount Govardhana on the banks of the Yamunā, frequented by cool breezes.
It was delightful, free from wild beasts, filled with great trees and creeping vines,
and adorned by cows submerged in grass and lowing.
The cattle grazed together in abundance, and their watering places were level;
the trees were rubbed by the horns and shoulders of the bulls.
It was followed by hawks greedy for meat seeking the bait of their cries,
and it was surrounded by jackals, deer, and lions that feed on fat and marrow.
Resounding with the roars of tigers and teeming with various birds,
it was delightful with sweet flowers and fruits, and provided with an abundant carpet of grass.
The cow-pen was auspicious with the lowing of cows, surrounded by cowherd women,
and filled on all sides with the bellowing of calves.
It was as vast as a whirlpool of carts, thick with thorny hedges,
and surrounded on its borders by great wild trees that had fallen down.
It was adorned with stakes driven into the ground for calves and with ropes,
its earth strewn with dried cow dung, and its huts and small temples covered with straw mats.
It abounded in the practice of forbearance, was filled with joyful and well-nourished people,
was crowded with many rope-tied beasts, and resounded with the gurgling sounds of water-pots.
Abounding with trickling whey, with its clay moistened by the liquid of curdled milk,
encircled by fresh butter, and adorned with the fragrance of clarified butter;
it resounded with the sounds of the cowherd girls' churning-staffs as they whirled about.
It was the playground where children with side-locks of hair frolicked;
it was crowded with boys and girls mingling with one another,
its cow-pens secured by bolts, and its center bustling with stalls for cattle.
The breeze was made fragrant by the clarified butter being cooked.
It was surrounded on all sides by young cowherd girls wearing blue and yellow garments, who had forest flowers as their ear-ornaments.

With sweet speech at the parting of their hair, with eyes made lovely by smiles and the play of their brows, and enchanting the heart, intellect, and mind with the sounds "sīt" and the movements of their eyebrows—
all those beautiful Gopa women possessed faces like the moon.
Then, at the sound of their anklets, the tinkling of their girdles,
and the noise of those who were singing, the peacocks danced;
[they were accompanied by women] holding jars upon their heads, with their garments tied and fastened.
It was filled with water-carriers along the path to the banks of the Yamunā.
Engaged in the sale of buttermilk and the purchase of curds and clarified butter,
he entered that cow-pen, which resounded with the cries of cowherds; there he was joyfully met by the elder cowherds as well as by the elder women.
He took pleasure in establishing his residence in that comfortable retreat.
Where the goddess Rohiṇī, who brings happiness to Vasudeva, was staying,
there she secretly deposited that Kṛṣṇa, who possessed the luster of the rising sun.
And Garga, of great ascetic power, commissioned by Vasudeva, performed for the two of them all the rites beginning with the birth-ceremony (jātakarman) in due order;
he gave wealth and food to the Brahmins according to tradition.
And the cowherds held a festival for the cows and for the Brahmins.

Vaiśampāyana said:
There, while performing the work of a cowherd for Nanda the cowherd at Govraja, a very long time passed for him who was [then] non-existent [in his true nature].
In secret, he performed the sacramental rites for the two among the cowherds;
having been given names, the two boys grew up happily.
The elder was named Saṃkarṣaṇa, while the younger was indeed Kṛṣṇa.
But Kṛṣṇa, Hari having entered another body, became Meghakṛṣṇa;
he grew up in the midst of the cows like a cloud over the ocean.
Now I shall relate in detail the great life-story of Bāla;
O King, listen with focused attention to that which you desire to hear.
Having applied himself to yoga there, he indeed slew the Dānavas.
A certain heroic son of Danu, desiring the death of Kṛṣṇa,
assumed the form of a cart and gained the affection of Nanda.
Once, while he was sleeping beneath the cart, his mother, longing for her son, [woke him].
Having set him down, Yaśodā went to the Yamunā river.
Then, performing the playfulness of a child, tossing his own hands and feet about,
placing his thumb in his mouth, and kicking with both feet,
the infant Kṛṣṇa laughed while rolling his eyes.
Pressing hand against hand and foot against foot,
Viṣṇu, through manifold divine sports, washed away the impurity of those whose minds were fixed on him and whose hearts were deeply attached to him.
Kṛṣṇa wept melodiously, stretching his feet upward.
There, Hari, raising his face which was smeared with collyrium, turned the cart around on one leg;
desiring the breasts of the woman lying face down, he did so and wept.
In the meantime, Yaśodā arrived, moving swiftly;
she had bathed, her limbs were smeared with the flow of milk, and she was like a cow that has recently calved.
She saw that the cart had been overturned by the wind even without it being blown;
crying out "Alas! Alas!", she quickly seized the infant.
She did not realize that the cart had been turned around by him;
thinking, "May it be well with my child," she was both filled with joy and overcome with fear.
What indeed will your father, who is extremely prone to anger, say to you when you are sleeping beneath the cart and the cart has been overturned?
"What is the use of my bathing? It was a bath in vain; and what is the use of my journey to the river? O son, since I see you uncovered while the cart has overturned."
In the meantime, Nanda the cowherd, wearing two saffron-colored garments, arrived from the forest with his cattle near the edge of the settlement.
He beheld a cart overturned, its jars and pots shattered,
its pole cast aside, its axle broken, and its wheels indeed stripped of their rims.
Terrified, he arrived in haste and suddenly with tearful eyes, repeatedly saying these words: "Is all well with my son?"
Observing his son drinking from the breast, he regained his composure and spoke again:
"By whom was my cart overturned, other than by a bull-fight?"
Terrified and speaking with a faltering voice, Yaśodā replied to him,
"I do not know by whom this cart has been overturned upon the ground."
"Noble sir, I went to the river wishing to wash my clothes;
and when I returned, I saw the cart overturned on the ground."
While the two of them were speaking thus, the boys there said:
"This carriage was knocked over by this child with his foot;
we saw it happening by chance as we were running along."
Upon hearing that, Nanda Gopa was struck with great wonder;
both thrilled and terrified, he wondered, "What is this?
Yet all the cowherds, possessing only human understanding, did not believe it.
"Marvelous! they all exclaimed, their eyes wide with wonder, and they had the cart secured by fastening its wheels in place at their respective positions.
Nanda, having placed him on his lap and gathered up the dust from the earth, performed a circumambulation of the child's head and recited this mantra:
"May Viṣṇu protect you from the east; may Rudra guard your south."
May Brahmā protect you from the west, and may Skanda guard the north;
likewise, may the Sun protect you from above, and Vāsuki from below. Furthermore, O child, may the Wind-god protect you in the remaining directions.
"May the Blessed One, the wielder of the Pināka bow whose banner bears the bull, grant well-being.
May the cows protect [us] everywhere, and may Sadāśiva protect the earth.
Having uttered this, Nanda touched Kṛṣṇa on all sides.
That very mantra is proclaimed for the protection of children.

Vaiśampāyana said:
Now, after some time, [she] appeared wearing the dress of a bird.
The nurse of Kaṃsa, the Bhoja, was well known as Pūtanā;
a bird named Pūtanā, fierce and terrifying to living beings,
arrived at midnight indeed, shaking her wings in rage.
Then the Blessed One, having firmly pressed his breast with both hands, gave it to the infant, which was fierce, possessed of terrible marks, and contained an invincible potency.
Filled with rage, he drank it along with his very life-breaths.
Crying out, "Release him! Release the child! as her every vital organ was being crushed, she opened her eyes wide and repeatedly flailed her feet and arms.
With her limbs drenched, she wept as she cast [the child] away.
By its sound, which was of exceeding depth and velocity,
the earth with its mountains, the sky with its planets, the netherworld, and the quarters of space all trembled, and the people were struck with awe.
They fell upon the earth, fearing the stroke of a thunderbolt.
Thus, with her breasts pained and deprived of life, the night-stalker spread out her hair, feet, and arms;
stretching them out in the cow-pen, she resumed her own form.
O King, he fell like Vṛtra struck by the thunderbolt.
Even as it fell, O King of kings, that body pulverized the trees within a distance of three gavūtas; that was a great marvel.
With a mouth possessing fierce fangs the size of plow-poles and a nose like a mountain cave,
with breasts like massive boulders, it was terrible, with disheveled reddish hair;
its eyes were as deep as blind wells, and it was fearsome with its ascent upon the riverbanks.
With his arms and legs bound by the bridge of the serpent’s coils, his belly submerged in the lake of the void,
and the child playing fearlessly upon her breast,
the cowherd women approached in haste and, overcome with agitation, seized him.
Yaśodā and Rohiṇī together performed a complete protection for the child on all sides by means of the "whirling of the cow-tail" and other such rites.
Having bathed the child again with cow's urine and cow-dust,
they performed a protective rite upon his twelve limbs using cow dung and [the child's] names;
then, at the time of midnight, a bird appeared.
Uttering a roar as deep as a tiger's, she lay down again and again at Śakaṭākṣa, raining forth a torrent of flowing milk.
And there, at night while the people were asleep, she gave her breast to Kṛṣṇa;
Kṛṣṇa drank from her breast and roared with all his might.
The milk of the Teacher of the World became delicious even though it was mixed with poison;
yet, beholding that bird falling, distressed by fear,
moving swiftly and restlessly at his departure, and crying out in discordant tones—
With his big toe, Kṛṣṇa caused her to be trampled by the discus; and being thus trampled by the discus, the bird fell down and died. Then that Hari let out a great roar again and again.
Terrified by that sound, the people there then woke up:
Nanda the cowherd, the other cowherds, and Yaśodā, who was greatly distressed.
They saw her fallen and unconscious, her breasts devoid of poison,
like a bird struck down on the ground and split open by a thunderbolt.
Terrified, wondering "What is this? and "Whose deed is this?", the cowherds surrounded him, placing Nanda Gopa at their head.

And they did not find any cause for it there at any time; saying, "A marvel! A marvel! they returned home. When those cowherds had gone to their houses in astonishment, as they had come, [the Lord remained there].
But Nandagopa, filled with agitation upon her arrival, questioned Yaśodā.
"What is this ritual? I do not understand; this is a great wonder to me.
O timid one, fear has come upon my son, and his timidity has been fully manifested."
But Yaśodā, terrified, said: "O women, I do not know what this is; while sleeping with this child, I have been awakened by this sound."
While Yaśodā was unaware, Nanda the cowherd, along with his kinsmen,
felt intense fear of Kaṃsa and was filled with wonder.

Vaiśampāyana said:
As time passed, those two gentle children had their names performed.
Having reached five years of age, both Kṛṣṇa and Saṃkarṣaṇa, who repeatedly graced Vraja with their beauty, became skilled in wrestling.
Those two youths, moving together from their very childhood, attained a state of oneness;
they were lovely, sharing a single counsel, and possessed the splendor of the young moon and sun.
Engaged in a single magical emanation, sharing one bed, seat, and food,
wearing a single garment, they both nourish the vow of childhood as one.
Engaged in a single task, sharing one body yet divided into two,
they followed the same conduct, possessed great heroism, and both attained the state of childhood for the sake of that one being.
The two protectors of the entire world, who were the sole authority for all people regarding both divine matters and human affairs, became cowherd boys.
Adorned by their mutually intertwined sports,
they were like the sun and moon in the sky, eclipsed by each other's rays.
Moving everywhere like the coils of two serpents,
their limbs smeared with dust, the two of them shone like two proud young elephants.
In some places their limbs were smeared with ashes, and in others they were sprinkled with cow-dung;
there they ran about like the two sons of Agni.
In some places, crawling on their knees which were rubbed raw,
they shone as they played in the calf-pens, their limbs and hair smeared with dung.
Endowed with splendor, they shone, bringing joy to their father;
and occasionally, O Brahmin, they would laugh while delighting the people.
Those two charming boys, with hair disheveling their eyes and faces like the moon, shone as delicate infants.
Having filled the cowherd station with their cries, the two boys became excessively attached to the sounds;
seeing them thus overly engrossed and wandering through the entire settlement,
Nanda the cowherd was unable to restrain those two who were exceedingly difficult to subdue.
Then Yaśodā, filled with anger, spoke to Kṛṣṇa, the lotus-eyed Lord of the universe who was moving about in the form of an infant:
"Come, my child, drink my breast-milk, which is now difficult for me to bear."
"Where have you been outside the house for all this time?"—
saying this, she took her son by the hand, cast him out from the house in anger,
and having brought him back to the base of the cart, she rebuked him again and again.
Having tied him by the belly with a rope, she bound him to a mortar, saying to him, "If you can, go! and performed her work;
while Yaśodā was thus preoccupied, he emerged from the courtyard.
Then, performing the play of a child and causing wonder in Vraja,
Kṛṣṇa went out from the courtyard, dragging the mortar along with him.
Moving through the forest with his two large, reddish-brown arms,
the child emerged from the midst of them, dragging the mortar after him.
As he was dragging it, the wooden mortar, which had been tied and positioned crosswise,
became entangled with those two Arjuna trees along with their roots, and he dragged them away together.
As those two Arjunas were being dragged by that boy with great speed, they were broken along with their roots and branches; yet he laughed in the midst of it.
In order to demonstrate his divine power to the cowherds, he relied upon his own supernatural strength,
and by the power of that boy, the rope became firm.
The cowherd girls, standing on the path along the banks of the Yamunā, saw that infant;
crying out and filled with wonder, they went into the presence of Yaśodā.
With faces full of agitation, those women said to Yaśodā: "Come, come, Yaśodā! Why do you delay in this moment of urgency?"
Those two Arjuna trees which were once the object of your truthful vow in Vraja—
those very two trees have now fallen upon your son;
those two great trees have fallen upon your son.
Bound right there with a firm rope like a calf in its mother's belly,
that young son of yours laughed between the two trees.
Laughing as if playing between two trees in a courtyard, he said:
"Rise and go, O evil-minded one! You fool who fancies yourself wise!
Bring back my son, who is alive, as if released from the jaws of death!"
Terrified, she rose up suddenly and, uttering cries of "Alas!
Alas!", went to that place where those two great trees had fallen.
Between those two trees, she saw her infant son,
bound by a cord around his belly, dragging a wooden mortar after him.
Then the entire settlement of Vraja— including the cowherds, the cowherd women, the elders, and the youths—
went out to behold that great marvel among the cowherds.
Those cowherds wandering in the forest spoke as they pleased;
filled with agitation and with minds struck by wonder, they all cried out,
"By whom have these two trees, the foremost trees of the settlement, been felled?"
Without wind, without rain, without the falling of lightning,
and without any injury caused by elephants— who has felled these two trees?
Alas! These two Arjuna trees, now rootless, do not look beautiful as they lie fallen upon the ground like two waterless clouds.
O Nanda Gopa, since these two trees, which were adorned with sound and produced auspicious sounds for you, have become thus even now, they remain gracious toward you,
for it was beneath them that your child was released unharmed, though they were stripped of their roots.
This third portentous event occurs here in the hamlet:
the fall of Pūtanā, and the overturning of the two trees and the cart.
This settlement of the cowherd village is not established in this place;
for portents are seen here that foretell misfortune.
Nandagopa, however, suddenly released Kṛṣṇa from the mortar and,
placing him on his lap, held him for a long time as if he were dead and had returned to life.
He was not satiated while gazing upon the lotus-eyed Kṛṣṇa;
then, reproaching Yaśodā, Nanda the cowherd entered [his home],
and all those cowherds likewise returned to the settlement.
And because he was bound by a rope (dāman) in the belly (udara) while in Vraja, Kṛṣṇa indeed received that very name; thus,
he is celebrated as Dāmodara by the cowherd girls in the settlement.
O best of the Bharatas, this was indeed a wondrous feat performed by the child Kṛṣṇa while he was living in the cowherd settlement at that time.

Vaiśampāyana said: Thus both Kṛṣṇa and Saṃkarṣaṇa passed their childhood.
In that very place where they had lived in Vraja, they became seven years old.
Wearing blue and yellow garments and anointed with yellow and white unguents,
both of them became cowherd boys, each bearing side-locks of hair like those of crows.
Playing leaf-instruments that were pleasant to the ear, with their beautiful faces,
singing most sweetly in the cowherd lane, and able to assume any form at will, they shone like two three-headed serpents in the forest.
With arms adorned with peacock-feather armlets,
wearing cowherd head-garlands, and their chests decorated with forest garlands, the two appeared like two young trees that had just sprung up.
Wearing lotus flowers as their head-ornaments and with cords serving as their sacred threads,
they held water-pots and baskets in their hands and played upon cowherd flutes.
Equipped with leaf-instruments, their hands hold curd and rice;
they are adorned at the waist with a network of small bells.
With pots of milk-rice suspended from yokes hanging from their shoulders,
the two calves were driving the young calves toward the various quarters with sticks.
Then, searching for honey in the thickets,
they lived on wild roots and drank honey from bees.
They gave honey-roots to the children on all sides,
while they themselves were eating and causing others to eat roots and fruits.
Let them eat the *tinduka* fruits after leaping from the trees onto the ground with their cowherds;
let them also devour the fruits by leaping from the trees upon stakes.
In some places let them laugh at one another, and in other places let them play together.
Sometimes eating curd-rice hanging from the armpits,
sometimes distracted by drinking, sometimes delighted by milk-rice,
and sometimes resting upon trees as if on level ground, they proceeded according to their pleasure.
In some places, they slept upon beds of leaves, seeking intervals of rest.
Moving at will among the calves,
the two cowherds shook the tails of the calves and tossed them about individually;
thus tending the calves, they graced the great forest.
In this way, those two cowherd boys adorned the forest,
wandering about and sporting like two restless young colts.
And in some places they sang songs that were worthy of being sung, with beautiful voices and sweet tones,
making the herds of deer prickle up their ears at the sound of the singing.
In the dense forest, making the elephants submissive through their songs,
wandering thus through the world and delighting it with their activities,
the glorious Dāmodara then spoke to Saṃkarṣaṇa.
"Noble one, it is not possible to play with cowherds in this forest."
All this has been reviled by us as food already eaten;
its grass and wood are exhausted, and its trees have been churned up by cowherds.
Those thickets, groves, and forests that were once impenetrable here are now seen today as clear as the sky, providing comfort at ease.
Even those trees that grow in cow-pens and by revolving door-bolts—
all those of imperishable luster have gone to their destruction in the fires of the cattle-pens.
The pieces of wood and grass that were nearby were dragged far away and had to be searched for upon the ground.
This forest is scanty in water, with few thickets and no shelter; it is dreadful, with trees far apart, where one must search for a place of rest among trees that are unfit for use,
and where birds stand or fly about them.

This great habitation has been devastated by the people; its trees uprooted, it is joyless, tasteless, and useless;
its cries have ceased, it is empty of birds, and like food devoid of flavor, it is utterly desolate.
With firewood and forest-grown vegetables being sold,
this cowherd settlement— its stores of grass exhausted— is acting like a city.
The cowherd settlement is the ornament of the mountains, and the forest is the ornament of the settlements.
Cows are the ornament of forests, and they are our ultimate refuge;
therefore, let us go to another forest where fresh grass and fuel abound.
Cows desire to eat grass that has not yet been grazed;
therefore, let the herds of wealthy men go to the forest where the grass is fresh.
Neither those who block doors and enclosures, nor those who own houses and fields,
are truly praised in this world as much as those who move about like wheels.
An elixir of alkaline taste produced from their very dung and urine is not fit for cattle to eat as grass, nor is it beneficial for their milk.
Let us wander together with the cows through these delightful and fresh forest groves, which are mostly dry land; let the herd be driven there quickly.
For it is heard that there is a delightful forest, with an abundance of grassy ground,
known by the name Vṛndāvana, where the trees bear sweet fruits and there is water.
The Ajhillikaṇṭaka forest, endowed with all the qualities of a woodland,
abounding in kadamba trees, and situated on the bank of the Yamunā.
It was a beautiful forest, pleasant with its cool, gentle breezes, a delightful abode for all seasons, where the cowherd women could move about with ease amidst its lovely and variegated groves.
Not far from there stands a great mountain named Govardhana;
with its long peak, it shines like Mount Mandara beside the Nandana grove.
And in its center stood a great-branched banyan tree, a yojana in height,
named Bhāṇḍīra, which shone like a dark cloud in the sky.
And down its middle flowed the Kālindī, the best of rivers, like a parting line, as if it were a lotus pond belonging to Nandana.
There, as we wander happily, we shall behold Govardhana, the lord of trees Bhāṇḍīra, and the delightful river Kālindī.
"We shall see you living happily by the auspicious river Kālindī.
Let this settlement of cowherds dwelling there abandon the worthless forest.
May prosperity be yours; let us transport them away after creating some pretext."
As the wise Vāsudeva was speaking thus,
there appeared by the hundreds those who feed upon blood, flesh, and fat.
Then, as he was reflecting, hundreds of terrifying wolves, born from the hairs of his own body, sprang forth from all sides.
Indeed, many [beasts] rushed forth for the destruction of the cow-pen;
seeing the wolves rushing out toward the cows, the calves, the men,
and the cowherd women, a great terror arose throughout the pen according to their desire.
Those wolves were bound in groups of five, and others in groups of ten; some were bound in groups of twenty or thirty, and others in groups of a hundred.
Fifty, sixty, and likewise forty [demons] emerged from his body,
marked with the Śrīvatsa sign;
they were dark like Kṛṣṇa, possessed dark faces, and increased the fear of the cowherds.
With those wolves devouring the calves, terrifying the cow-pens,
and carrying off children at night, the settlement of Vraja was being devastated.
It is not possible to go to the forest, nor to protect the cattle;
it is not possible to bring anything from the forest, nor even to cross the river.
Terrified and with agitated minds, they went and dwelt in that forest;
thus, by those fierce wolves possessing the prowess of tigers and boars,
the herd was rendered motionless in its activity and made to dwell in one place.

Vaiśampāyana said:
Having seen that unassailable plague of wolves increasing, [he...]
Then, indeed, the entire assembly of women and men held a consultation.
"We have no need to remain here; let us go to another great forest—
one that is fearless, pleasant, where the breeze is easy to traverse,
auspicious, rich in happiness, and truly brings well-being to the cattle."
Why do we delay? Let us depart this very day with our wealth of cattle, before the entire herd is led to a terrible slaughter by the wolves.
We are terrified of these wolves at night as they roar— their bodies smoke-colored and ruddy, their fangs bared, their mouths gaping wide, and their faces black.
"My son! My brother! My calf! And now my cow has been killed by wolves!"—thus they wailed in every house.
At the sound of their weeping and the lowing of the cows,
the elders of the settlement gathered together and raised the inhabitants of the cowherd village from their sleep.
Then, having understood their intention to go toward Vṛndāvana for the settlement of Vraja and for the happiness of the cows, [he acted accordingly].
Knowing that they were resolved to settle in Vṛndāvana,
Nandagopa spoke these weighty words, like Bṛhaspati himself.
If our departure must indeed take place this very day, let the proclamation be issued quickly: "Prepare yourselves without delay!"
Then, in that settlement, the common people proclaimed:
"Let the cows be driven out quickly, and let the carts be yoked!"
Let the herds of calves be driven together; let the household goods be loaded onto the carts;
and let us depart from this place for Vṛndāvana to establish our settlement.
Having heard those well-spoken words of Nandagopa,
and having heard that speech uttered by him,
the entire community of Vraja rose up, eager to depart quickly.
"Set out! Arise! Let us go! Why do you lie there? Go! Yoke the animals! As that cowherd settlement was rising up, a great clamor indeed arose among the cowherds.
As it rose up, that settlement of wagons shone forth;
it possessed the great roar of tigers and the thundering sound of the ocean.
With water-pots on their heads and jars used as crest-ornaments by the gopīs,
the procession emerged from Vraja like a row of stars descending from the sky.
With their blue, yellow, and crimson garments tied up and fluttering aloft,
the line of cowherd girls walking along the path resembles a rainbow.
And some cowherds, with the weight of their neck-ropes hanging down from their bodies as they traveled along the road, shone like trees with their branches still bearing fruit.
That cow-pen shone with the mass of moving, radiant carts,
like the ocean with its waves driven by the wind and rushing forth.
In an instant, that place where the Vraja stood became a barren wasteland,
stripped of all its material substance and strewn with flocks of crows.
Then, in due course, that cowherd settlement reached the forest of Vṛndāvana and established a vast encampment for the welfare of the cattle.
Extending as far as Śakaṭāvarta, it is situated in the shape of a half-moon;
it is one yojana in width at its center and twice that in length.
It was protected on all sides by thorny shrubs growing tall and by bristling trees whose branch-tips were driven deep into the ground and thrust upward.
And with churning-vessels being lifted up by slow turns, dragged along with their binding-ropes,
and being rinsed here and there with water from large jars.
With oxen being yoked with pegs, bound by leather thongs and snares,
held fast by tethering ropes, and with carts that had overturned;
With nooses of obligation fastened to the tops of the pillars supporting the water-jars,
and with mats and straw huts scattered about for the sake of concealment.
Branches of trees were being trimmed here and there,
cow-pens were being cleared, and mortars were being set in place.
With fires blazing as they were being sprinkled while facing the east,
and with couches provided with coverings of cowhide and accompanied by calves, which had been brought down [from the chariot].
The forest was being cleared by the gopīs on all sides, who were carrying water, sprinkling it, and pulling away the branches.
With both young and old cowherds, their hands busily occupied,
they were vigorously splitting logs and even felling trees with axes.
That station of the cowherds shone forth even more brilliantly, surrounded by forests;
it was a delightful woodland settlement, truly like nectar due to the abundant rain.
Those cows, who grant all desires, reached Vṛndāvana— a forest comparable to the Nandana grove where grass grows at all seasons.
But even before that, while wandering in the forest, Kṛṣṇa, who shows honor to cows,
beheld that grove with an auspicious mind.
Then, during the latter fortnight of that month of summer,
while the cloudless sky was as if raining nectar, the grass there grew profusely.
Neither calves, nor cows, nor other people suffer there where Madhusūdana stands for the welfare of the worlds.
Those cows, along with the cowherd settlement and the youthful Saṃkarṣaṇa, dwelt happily in that abode established by Kṛṣṇa.
Wherever Janārdana, the Lord of gods and God of gods, resides, there is no suffering for living beings; he brings all happiness.
(Chapter 54)

Vaiśampāyana said:
Having reached Vṛndāvana, both those sons of Vasudeva wandered about,
tending the herds of calves with great delight.
But the summer season arrived while the two of them were sporting happily in that forest with the cowherd boys and bathing in the Yamunā.
When that great heat had passed away, obscured by clouds of dust,
the rainy season then arrived, igniting desire in the mind;
most terrible clouds rained down, their bellies marked with rows of Indra’s bows.
The sun became invisible, and the earth showed not even a blade of grass.
With its surface swept clean by the falling wind from the clouds that drags along fresh water, the earth appears as if it has reached the prime of youth.
The flocks of *śakragopaka* insects, drenched by the rains of the new season,
shone forth like clouds from which the smoke of forest fires had vanished.
And it was the time for the dancing activity of the crested peacocks;
intoxicated with passion, they have begun their cries, producing sharp-sounding notes.
In the fresh rainy season, the youthful form of the kadamba trees, which provide sustenance for bees and delight beloved women, shines brilliantly with new clouds.
The forest was made to smile by the blossoming *kuṭaja* trees and perfumed by the *kadamba* trees;
the heat was dispelled by the clouds, and the earth was gladdened by the waters.
Scorched by the waters of the sun and heated on all sides by the fires of the gods,
the mountains seem to breathe forth with the waters released by the clouds.
The sky becomes filled with masses of great dust from the earth, stirred up by mighty winds and cast down by vast multitudes of clouds.
In some places rich with the laughter of *kadamba* flowers, in others adorned with *silindhra* blossoms,
the forest, filled with blooming *nīpa* trees, shines as if it were set ablaze.
Scented with the water of Indra and refreshed by the wind of the Maruts,
the world, having inhaled that earthly fragrance, became agitated in its mind.
With the cries of proud deer, the croaking of frogs,
and the fresh calls of peacocks, the earth became a single sound.
Whirling with great speed and swift as the onset of the rains,
the rivers carry away the trees growing on their banks and spread far and wide.
Continuous, rainless, and effortless, with their upper coverings of leaves soaked through,
they do not leave the mountain peaks, like weary birds.
As the bellies of the fresh clouds hang low and deep with water, oozing and thundering, the sun seems to sink into them.
With its rising hairs bristling from the pressure of the water,
the earth, covered in rows of young grass, shines as it searches for a path.
And the peaks of the majestic mountains, shattered as if by a thunderbolt,
fall down with their ridges completely severed by the torrents.
Like a falling rain from a cloud following the downward slope,
the rows of forest trees are filled with blood vomited from the ponds.
With their trunks raised high like faces, the wild elephants following the sound of the clouds shine like rain-bearing clouds that have descended to earth due to excessive rainfall.
Observing the onset of the rainy season and seeing the thick clouds,
the son of Rohiṇī spoke these words privately to Kṛṣṇa at that time.
Behold, O Kṛṣṇa, the dark clouds risen in the sky, adorned with the appearance of cranes and stealing the color of your limbs.
For those filled with desire, this time swiftly strikes down their hearts on all sides;
the sky resembles your body,
and like you, the moon dwells for the duration of the rainy season in an unknown abode.
Dark as a blue lotus and possessing the luster of a blue lotus petal,
the forest of Vṛndāvana shines with the hue of a blue lotus petal;
when the time of a foul day arrives, the sky indeed appears as a foul day.
Behold, O Kṛṣṇa, how the beautiful Govardhana mountain shines, with its dark clouds rising from the water and gathered together like uplifted cow-horns.
For these black antelopes, having been completely satiated with the fallen water, shine with joy in the forests like dappled deer.
O lotus-eyed one, these green and soft grasses, delighted by the water,
cover the earth with their leaves.
At the arrival of the rains, the beauty of the mountains with their trickling waters, of the forests,
and of the field boundaries rich with crops, does not diminish.
Stirred up by swift winds, causing longing in those away from home,
and possessing the powerful roar of Dāmodara, the clouds attain their full maturity.
O Hare, O Trivikrama, this middle step of yours was traversed with a bow of three colors— the rainbow of Indra— devoid of both arrow and string.
And this sky-traveler, the eye of the sky, does not shine in the month of Nabhasya; like the sun with its rays obscured by clouds, he is as if devoid of radiance despite producing cold and heat.
The union of heaven and earth was constantly maintained by dense clouds, resembling the surging waters of the ocean, with their streams of rain falling in an unbroken flow.
Showers fall upon the earth for the nīpa, arjuna, and kadamba trees;
winds blow, tumultuous with fragrances, kindling the fire of love.
With a great rain falling and massive clouds hanging low,
the sky shines like the unfathomable and boundless ocean.
With showers of arrows as pure as polished steel and lightning as its spotless armor,
the sky bore the weapon of Indra’s bow, appearing as if ready for battle.
O fair-faced one, the peaks of the mountains, forests, and trees shine forth, shrouded by dense clouds.
The sky, indeed, attains a resemblance in color to the ocean, as it is filled with clouds exhaling water like herds of elephants.
Rising from the ocean, the winds blow cold, harsh, and laden with droplets; they cause the trembling, swaying grasses to quiver.
In the nights when the moon has fallen asleep and the clouds have released their waters,
the ten directions do not shine, for the sun has sunk into the sky.
The lotus, its heart surrounded on all sides by sheaths swollen with hunger,
does not reach the solitude of those who are compassionate or beautiful;
rather, the rows of bees settle there, forming a crowded assembly.
Behold, O Kṛṣṇa, Vṛndāvana, which is now free from the defects of the summer heat and adorned by the waters of the clouds, like the Caitraratha forest.
Thus, while recounting all these events of the rainy season, the glorious and powerful elder brother of Kṛṣṇa returned indeed to Vraja.
Both Kṛṣṇa and Saṃkarṣaṇa, delighting one another,
wandered through that great forest at that time together with their kinsmen.
Chapter 55.

Vaiśampāyana said:
At one time, however, Kṛṣṇa was without his elder brother Saṃkarṣaṇa.
The handsome-faced one, capable of assuming any form at will, roamed through that excellent forest in that manner.
Wearing the side-locks of youth, glorious, dark-complexioned, with eyes like lotus petals,
his chest was marked with the Śrīvatsa, like the moon with its spot.
With his foremost foot adorned with an anklet, possessing the luster of a blooming lotus,
slightly copper-hued and delicate, he moved with a gait that was both graceful and powerful.
Wearing two fine yellow garments that bring joy to men and possess the luster of lotus filaments,
he was like a rain-cloud at twilight.
His two arms, which were well-formed and honored by the gods, were occupied with the activities of the forest and were intent upon the staff and the rope.
In his childhood, his face, with its lovely lips, shone with a fragrance like that of the white lotus and the red lotus.
With his pearl-like locks of hair, his lotus-face shone like a circle of lotuses surrounded by rows of bees.
Adorned with *arjuna* and *kadamba* trees and garlanded with *nīpa* shoots, it shone upon his head like a garland of stars in the sky.
Adorned with that garland of every kind of flower, the hero shone like the sky personified, dark as a cloud at the time of the rainy season.
He shone with a single stainless peacock feather suspended from his neck-string,
trembling gently in the mild breeze.
In some places singing, in some places playing, and in some places wandering about,
he played leaf-instruments that were pleasing to the ear here and there in the forest.
Sometimes,

having gone to the forest for the sake of delighting the cows, that youthful Lord, dark as a rain-cloud, radiant and resplendent, wandered through Gokula while playing his exceedingly sweet cowherd’s flute out of love.
And he took delight there upon the delightful and variegated forest ranges of Mount Govardhana— ranges resounding with the cries of peacocks,
which were enchanting to hear and capable of kindling passion.
Resounding on all sides with counter-echoes like the roar of clouds.
In the rivers where the paths were covered with lush grass, adorned with mushrooms, and where the *kandala* flowers served as pure white teeth, fresh water was flowing.
With the fresh fragrances of their filaments, which resembled her intoxicating sighs,
they seemed on all sides like women constantly sighing.
Fanned by fresh breezes issuing from the clusters of trees,
Kṛṣṇa found delight in those gentle forest groves.
Once, while wandering through that forest with his cattle,
he beheld a tree of immense height, the best among all trees.
It stood upon the earth, resembling a cloud, dense with its mass of leaves,
rising half the height of the sky, and filling the expanse of the air.
It was frequented by many birds with dark and variegated plumage,
dense with fruits and sprouts, and resembling a thick cloud accompanied by a rainbow.
The tree of meditative cultivation is beautifully adorned with creepers and flowers;
it spreads from its vast roots and sustains both wind and clouds.
He was performing, as it were, a lordship over the other trees of that region;
he was a performer of auspicious deeds, imperishable, and raining down [nectar] from within.
Seeing there a banyan tree named Bhāṇḍīra, which resembled a mountain, the Lord resolved to dwell there during the day.
There, O sinless one, Kṛṣṇa took his delight for a whole day with cowherd boys of his own age, as if he had returned to heaven in ancient times.
Then many cowherds delighted Kṛṣṇa, who was playing and dwelling at Bhāṇḍīra, with various forest toys.
Some cowherds, their minds full of joy, sang aloud;
other cowherds, who were fond of pleasure, sang only of Kṛṣṇa.
While they were singing, that powerful one played the flute,
the lute made of gourd, and various leaf-instruments there amidst them.
Once, while tending the cows, he whose eyes were like those of a bull went to the bank of the Yamunā, where the trees were adorned with creepers.
And he beheld that river Yamunā, whose waves were curved like sidelong glances, whose breezes were pleasant from contact with the water, and which was filled with lotuses and lilies.
It possessed excellent landing places and sweet water, abounding in pools and flowing with great speed;
its trees were bent down by the force of the currents tossed up by the wind-blown spray.
Resounding with the cries of swans and *kāraṇḍava* ducks, made musical by cranes,
and frequented by pairs of birds that move about in couples.
It was teeming with aquatic creatures, adorned with aquatic virtues,
variegated with aquatic flowers, and possessed waters that were green with aquatic plants.
With her current of flowing waters, her hips the circles of sandbanks,
her navel the deep whirlpools, and adorned with lotuses as her body hair;
She was embraced by the lake’s slender belly, bearing three wave-ridges as her folds;
she had the ruddy geese for the slopes of her breasts, and her long face reached to the banks on either side.
Her eyes were as restless as those of a fish; she was a lovely woman whose hair was like dark moss; her teeth were as white as froth; she was serene, smiling with the grace of a swan;
her eyes were like the petals of a beautiful blue lotus; her eyebrows were arched, and her gaze was like that of a water-born lotus.
Her lovely forehead extended to the edge of a lake, her hair was like moss,
her long arms were like wide-flowing streams, and her ears reached down to her broad shoulders.
She had eyes like beautiful lotuses, was adorned with earrings shaped like water-fowls,
wore garments of Kāśa grass and gold, and bore the marks of a swan.
She was adorned with ornaments born of the riverbanks, her girdle as pure as a fish,
her silken garment floating upon the water, and her anklets sounding like the cries of cranes.
Her limbs were smeared with mud and moss, and she was adorned with the markings of a tortoise;
she caused distress to the wild animals at the watering holes, her udders were sucked dry by men,
and she provided water left over from the beasts, abounding in the sites of herdsman's huts.
It was adorned with great deities worshipped by the Siddhas and with lingas made of sand;
it resounded with the great roar produced from the sage’s water-pot filled with clay;
and it was turned tawny by the saffron powder falling from the breasts of the Siddha women.

Beholding from all sides that queen of the ocean— the Yamunā, which possesses excellent bathing-ghats and destroys all the sins of those whose minds are fixed upon her— Kṛṣṇa moved about beautifully, adorning her.
While traveling along that best of rivers, he beheld an excellent lake,
one yojana in length and breadth, which was difficult even for the gods to cross.
It was deep, with unshakeable waters like the ocean;
it was deserted by water-dwelling beasts of prey, empty of aquatic creatures, and devoid of birds.
It was filled with unfathomable water like the sky filled with clouds;
it was difficult to approach due to the suffering, and its banks were infested with vast holes containing serpents.
The fire that has entered the forest of poison is enveloped by smoke.
Abandoned by the virtuous who seek [only] the three daily ablutions,
it was impossible even for birds that range through the sky to traverse from the air.
Even as grass fell into its waters, it seemed to blaze with splendor;
for a distance of more than a yojana on all sides, it was difficult to approach even from the banks.
To the north of that Vajra, at a distance of one krośa in a region free from affliction, there is a lake blazing with flames from a terrible poison-fire.
Seeing that vast lake, which was unfathomable and radiant, Kṛṣṇa reflected: "To whom does this exceedingly great lake belong?"
In this lake dwells that fierce lord of serpents named Kāliya, who resembles a mass of black collyrium and is manifest before our eyes.
He who was formerly driven by me to dwell in the ocean out of fear of Suparṇa, the king of birds and devourer of serpents.
Thus, this entire Yamunā, which flows to the ocean, has been defiled;
out of fear of that lord of serpents, this region is no longer inhabited.
This forest is of a dreadful appearance, with thickly grown grass,
containing trees with descending roots, formidable, and strewn with various creepers and trees.
The forest, guarded by the ministers of the serpent-king who dwell in the woods, was like a poisoned meal— unapproachable and appearing as if devoid of any territory;
it was constantly protected on all sides by those faithful servants.
Both banks of this lake shine with paths formed by trees soiled with moss and thick with shrubs and creepers.
Therefore, I must exercise restraint against this king of serpents,
so that the river and the ocean may once again possess auspicious waters.
"And this lake, a reservoir of cool water, must be resorted to and utilized.
Having thus addressed Saṃkarṣaṇa, Keśava spoke these words.
That sweet-spoken one addressed himself with these words of his own: [D2 after 55; K1 after the repetition of 56ab; K4, D5 after 56ab; Ds2 cont. after *675].
It is my conviction that this forest and this river are a place of refuge;
no creatures are seen here crawling upon the surface of the earth.
And once the Naga has been subdued by me, this auspicious land shall indeed be enjoyed by the Vraja people.
It is a place where one can move about happily in all seasons and a refuge that provides happiness at all sacred fords.
And for this purpose, there is this dwelling in this Vraja and this birth among the cowherds,
for the sake of punishing these evil-minded ones who stand upon the wrong path.
Having climbed this kadamba tree, I shall leap down from it with the playfulness of a child into this terrible lake and subdue Kāliya.
When this is done, my heroic strength shall become renowned in the world; by the touch of the soles of my feet, this man shall become long-lived;
and the Kadamba tree, abounding in flowers and fruit, shall be worthy of worship by those dear to me.
This very Kadamba peak, which brings happiness to all living beings,
even today shines with the splendor of Viṣṇu’s touch upon its feet.
(Chapter 56)
