Vaiśampāyana said:
Having approached the riverbank and firmly girded his loins,
the youthful Kṛṣṇa, acting with agility, climbed to the top of a kadamba tree.
Kṛṣṇa, whose eyes are like lotuses, hanging from the top of a kadamba tree and resembling a cloud, made a sound as he fell into the middle of the lake.
Dark as the petal of a blue lotus, he fell into that lake;
agitated by Kṛṣṇa as he descended, that great lake was violently churned,
like the ocean being split asunder.
Agitated by that sound, that great abode of the serpent rose up from the water, and a serpent emerged with eyes clouded by rage.
Then that lord of serpents, Kāliya, appeared enraged, with the luster of a mass of clouds and eyes with blood-red corners.
He had five faces, his breath was fire, his tongue was flickering, and his mouth was flame;
he was surrounded by five large and terrible heads.
Having filled the entire lake with his serpent-body, which possessed the brilliance of fire,
he seemed to quiver with rage and blaze with splendor.
Through his wrath, all that water became as if boiled;
and the river Yamunā, as if terrified, flowed against the current;
and from his mouth, filled with the fire of his anger, a wind issued forth.
Seeing Kṛṣṇa entered the lake and playing with the sport of a child,
flames accompanied by smoke issued forth from the mouths of the lord of serpents.
By him, as he emitted the fire of his wrath— which was like that at the end of an eon— the trees growing on the nearby bank were reduced to ashes in an instant.
His sons, wives, servants, and other great serpents—
those lords of the *pannagas* of immeasurable power— fell down, vomiting terrible fire born of poison from their mouths along with smoke.
And having been made to enter by those serpents into the coils of their bodies, Kṛṣṇa stood motionless like a mountain, his limbs rendered effortless.
Those lords of serpents bit Kṛṣṇa with their sharp fangs, which were fouled by the surging waters of venom; yet the heroic one did not die.
Though being bitten by his teeth, Keśava did not waver;
Kṛṣṇa indeed roamed for a very long time within the Kāliya lake.
In the meantime, all those cowherds became terrified.
Wailing with voices choked by tears, they went toward the cow-pen.
"Kṛṣṇa has fallen into delusion and is submerged in the pool of Kāliya;
he is being devoured by the king of serpents, so come quickly without delay!"
"Let it be announced immediately to Nanda Gopa, the cowherd:
'This son of yours is being dragged by a serpent into the great lake.'"
But Nanda Gopa, hearing those words which were like a thunderbolt falling,
went in distress with faltering steps to that excellent lake.
Accompanied by children, young women, and the elderly, that youth Saṃkarṣaṇa and the people went together to the pleasure garden of the lord of serpents.
The cowherds, headed by Nandagopa, all stood on the shore of the lake with tearful eyes, bewildered, crying out "Alas! Alas! and wondering, "What is this? Whose deed is this?"

They were ashamed, amazed, and again and again afflicted with grief; some cried out, "O Kṛṣṇa! Alas! Alas! while others exclaimed, "Shame! Still others, deeply distressed, wept, saying, "Alas, we are destroyed!"
And the women cried out to Yaśodā, "Alas, you are ruined!
You see your beloved son fallen under the power of the king of serpents,
bound by the serpent's coils and being dragged away like a deer."
Surely your heart appears to be made of the essence of stone;
for how is it that upon seeing this son, Yaśodā does not shatter?
"Alas, we behold the cowherd Nanda by the edge of the lake, distressed and standing motionless,
his gaze fixed upon the face of his son."
"Following after Yaśodā, let us all enter this lake, the abode of serpents; we shall not go on without Dāmodara."
What is day without the sun? What is night without the moon? What are cows without a bull? What is Vraja without Kṛṣṇa? Without Kṛṣṇa we shall not go, like cows deprived of their calves.
Having heard the lamentation of those women and of the inhabitants of Vraja,
as well as the wailing of Nanda Gopa and the weeping Yaśodā,
He who knows their single nature and body appeared as one body divided in two.
But Saṃkarṣaṇa, filled with rage, spoke to the imperishable Kṛṣṇa.
O Kṛṣṇa, Kṛṣṇa, O mighty-armed one, the increaser of the joy of the cowherds!
Let this king of serpents, whose weapon is poison, be quickly subdued.
"O dear one, O Lord, these kinsmen of ours, perceiving you as a mere mortal and possessing human intellects, are all lamenting piteously."
Having heard those words of Rauhiṇeya, which were uttered with full consciousness,
he shook his arms and snapped asunder that bond of coils.
Then, having stepped upon the mass of coils moistened with water with his two feet,
Kṛṣṇa bent down his head and seized it with his own hand.
He suddenly climbed onto that great middle head of his;
standing upon its summit, Kṛṣṇa, adorned with beautiful armlets, began to dance.
Kṛṣṇa performed many kinds of dance upon his head.
O King, remembering that dance of Viṣṇu, joy now arises within me,
constantly causing my hair on every limb to stand on end;
for that serpent, his head crushed by Kṛṣṇa, was utterly exhausted.
With these words, accompanied by gurgling sounds of blood, he spoke piteously.
Out of ignorance, O Kṛṣṇa, this anger was displayed by me;
I have been subdued, my venom destroyed, and I am now under your control, O fair-faced one.
Therefore, command what I, together with my wife, children, and kinsmen, should do;
or into whose power shall I go? Let my life be granted back to me.
Homage to you, who are saluted by Brahmā, Rudra, Indra, and the gods and asuras;
I have come to you for refuge—grant me my life!
Whatever offense has been committed by me, who am foolish, of unrefined intellect, and filled with pride, you ought not to remember that.
"O Lord of Gods, if you are pleased, Vainateya shall not carry me away;
therefore, O Īśvara, ordain what must be done by me. Having spoken thus, he worshipped the feet of Kṛṣṇa with his heads.
Seeing the serpent with five heads bowed down, the Blessed One, whose banner bears the enemy of serpents, replied to the lord of snakes without any anger at all.
"I shall not grant you any place here in these waters of the Yamunā;
go, O serpent, to the waters of the ocean, along with your sons and your kinsmen."
Whoever among your servants or sons should be seen here again, whether on land or in water, he shall quickly be put to death by me.
May this water be auspicious for you, and you too go to the great ocean;
for were you to remain here, there would be a great calamity that would bring about your end.
And seeing my footprints upon your head in the ocean, O serpent,
Garuda, the enemy of the pannagas, will not strike you.
Thus addressed by Kṛṣṇa,
whose banner bears the foremost of birds, that bull among serpents took hold of Kṛṣṇa’s feet with his head.
Even as the cowherds were looking on, he vanished from the lake.
When the serpent had been defeated and departed, the cowherds, filled with wonder, praised Kṛṣṇa as he stood upon the bank after emerging from the water, and they circumambulated him.
All the forest-dwellers, being well-pleased, said to Nanda the cowherd:
"Blessed are you; you are favored, for you have such a son as this."
"From this day forward, O sinless one, Kṛṣṇa— the long-eyed Lord— is the refuge and the master of the cowherds, the cows, and the settlement in times of distress."
The entire Yamunā, with its auspicious waters, has become frequented by sages;
together with all sacred fords, our cows shall always roam there in happiness.
It is clear that we cowherds did not recognize Kṛṣṇa as such a great being while he was in the forest, for he was like a hidden fire within the cow-pen.
Thus, all of them, filled with wonder and praising the imperishable Kṛṣṇa,
returned to the cowherd settlement, just as the gods return to Caitraratha.
Chapter 57,
transliterated and collated with the Viṣṇupurāṇa and Brahmāṇḍapurāṇa by Utz Podzeit,
extracted from the collation and edited by Peter Schreiner; March 4.
2002. Not yet proof-read.
Vaiśampāyana said: When the king of serpents had been subdued by Kṛṣṇa in the pool of the Yamunā,
Rāma and Keśava both went together to that very place.
Both sons of Vasudeva, proceeding together with the cattle-wealth, went to the beautiful Govardhana mountain, their hearts filled with passion.
Then those two heroes beheld a great and beautiful grove of palm trees situated on the bank of the Yamunā to the north of Govardhana.
Delighting in that beautiful palm grove, which was spread wide with palm leaves,
those two wandered about in supreme joy like two exalted young bulls.
That region was level, moist, free from clods of earth and stones,
consisting mostly of Darbha grass, vast in extent, and composed of black soil.
With those various trees of massive trunks, tall and with dark joints,
shining with branches tipped in fruit, it gleams as if with upraised elephant trunks.
There, Dāmodara, the best among speakers, uttered these words:
"Aha! This forest region has been perfumed by ripe palm fruits."
"O Noble One, let us two, moving with light steps, gather together those ripe palmyra fruits which are sweet, fragrant, dark, and full of flavor."
If their fragrance is so sweet and agreeable to the sense of smell,
it is my conviction that their taste will be like nectar.
Having heard Dāmodara’s words, the son of Rohiṇī, as if laughing,
shook those trees, causing ripe palm fruits to fall.
But that palm grove was unfit for humans to frequent and difficult to traverse; it was like a desolate wasteland created by supernatural power, resembling the abode of man-eaters.
Then, O Indra among kings, the terrible Daitya named Dhenuka, who possessed the form of a donkey, intentionally caused many stones as large as mountains and even ripe fruits to fall [upon the cows].
Surrounded by a great herd of asses, he dwells there.
That evil-minded donkey guarded that terrible palm grove, terrifying the flocks of birds and beasts of prey.
Hearing that sound of the palm trees resounding as they were made to fall,
he was provoked to anger and could not endure it, just as an elephant cannot endure the sound of clapping palms.
Chasing after the sound, enraged, with his mane and face bristling with pride,
his eyes fixed and steady, neighing skillfully, he tore up the earth with his hooves.
With his tail lashing and bristling, like Death himself with gaping jaws,
he was seen rushing forward only to find the son of Rohiṇī standing firm before him.
Seeing that imperishable one in the form of a banner beneath the palm trees,
the wicked Khara, whose weapons were his teeth, bit the son of Rohiṇī.
Turning his back, the Daitya struck the unarmed son of Rohiṇī on the chest with both of his hind feet.
With those very two feet, he seized that donkey-like Daitya by its lowered face and neck, and hurled it onto the top of a palm tree.
With his thighs, hips, and neck broken, and his back shattered, that ugly-looking donkey fell to the surface of the earth along with the palm fruits.
Seeing that donkey lifeless, stripped of its splendor, and fallen,
he cast his kinsmen and others likewise upon the king of grasses.
They all fell to the surface of the earth, both like ripe palmyra fruits and with the bodies of donkeys;
that ground, covered with fallen donkey carcasses and ripe palmyra fruits,
shone like an autumn sky obscured by indistinct clouds.
When that demon Gardabha, along with his followers, had been struck down,
that beautiful palm grove shone forth even more beautifully than before.
Free from fear, radiant, and beholding the secluded landscape,
the cows roamed happily through that most excellent palm grove.
Then all the cowherds dwelling in the forest, having been thus addressed,
were freed from sorrow and roamed happily throughout the entire grove.
Then, when the cows had dispersed at their ease, those two, possessing the prowess of lordly elephants,
sat down as was fitting upon seats made of tree leaves.
Chapter 58,
transliterated and collated with the Viṣṇupurāṇa (ViP) and Brahmāṇḍapurāṇa (BrP) by Utz Podzeit,
extracted from the collation and edited by Peter Schreiner; March 4.
2002. Not yet proof-read.
Vaiśampāyana said: Then both those sons of Vasudeva were filled with joy.
Having left that Tālavana forest, they returned once more to Bhāṇḍīra.
The two fair-faced ones wandered about, tending their flourishing herds of cattle and beholding forests where the crops had grown in abundance.
Uttering shouts and singing aloud, felling trees and calling out the names of cows with their calves, those two subduers of enemies proceeded.
With their auspicious marks, they were bound by the ropes of the yoke upon their shoulders; with forest garlands adorning their chests, they resembled two young bulls with curved horns.
Having the luster of gold and black collyrium, they were dressed in garments matching one another,
like two clouds— one white and one black— joined by a rainbow.
Both of them, wearing forest attire, were making beautiful ear-ornaments from flowers on the tips of kusha grass while walking along the forest paths.
The two attendants of Govardhana, accompanied by their own followers, roamed through the forest,
unconquered, engaged in sports well-known to the world.
Bearing that human initiation, those two, honored by the gods,
wandered through the forest with diversions suited to their species and qualities.
At the appropriate time, those two, engaged in their play, reached Bhaṇḍīra,
a banyan tree— the best among trees— abounding with excellent branches.
There, clad in armor, the two of them engaged in physical exercise using swings, martial maneuvers, and stones to be hurled with slings.
Accompanied by cowherds skilled in various modes of combat,
the two of them, joyful and possessing the prowess of lions, roamed about as they pleased.
While the two were thus enjoying themselves, the best of the asuras, Pralamba, desiring to seize them, approached them at that time, seeking to find a vulnerability in the two of them.
Assuming the guise of a cowherd and adorned with wild flowers,
he sought to entice those two heroes with jests and playthings.
Assuming a human form, that best of Dānavas, Pralamba, who was non-human, plunged fearlessly into their midst.
And they all played together with that enemy of the gods,
the cowherds regarding him as their own kinsman because of his cowherd's form.
Seeking a vulnerable point, that Pralamba,
having taken the form of a cowherd, cast a fierce glance upon Kṛṣṇa and the son of Rohiṇī.
Then, considering Kṛṣṇa of wondrous prowess to be invincible,
that best of Dānavas made an effort to slay the son of Rohiṇī.
Then, there was a children's game called "The Deer's Play";
they all played it together, leaping up two by two at once.
Kṛṣṇa, together with Śrīdāma, leaped along with the son of a cowherd;
the sinless Saṃkarṣaṇa, however, leaped together with Pralamba.
Other cowherds, however, in pairs together with other cowherds,
fled while leaping over one another, moving with swift strides.
Kṛṣṇa defeated Śrīdāman, and the son of Rohiṇī defeated Pralamba;
the other cowherds were defeated by the cowherds who sided with Kṛṣṇa.
Driving one another on with great excitement, they rushed forward suddenly,
but then returned to the boundary-marking Bhāṇḍīra tree trunk.
But the Dānava, having quickly lifted Saṃkarṣaṇa onto his shoulder,
fled swiftly with his back turned, like a rain-cloud accompanied by the moon.
Considering Kṛṣṇa to be unbearable, that bull among the Dānavas proceeded even more swiftly beyond Avarohaṇa;
he could not endure the weight of that wise son of Rohiṇī.
He grew with a truly massive body, like a cloud overtaken by the moon.
That Pralamba, the foremost of the Dānavas, revealed his own body, which resembled the Bhāṇḍīra fig tree and possessed the luster of a mountain of burnt collyrium.
With a crown of five clusters blazing with the brilliance of the sun,
the face of the Daitya shone like a cloud overshadowed by the sun.
With a massive face and a massive neck, as vast as the end of time, he was fierce; with eyes like the wheels of a cart, he pressed the earth with his feet.
Adorned with hanging garlands and ornaments, and decorated with flowing garments,
the resolute Pralamba advanced like a cloud from which water is falling.
That great asura seized the son of Rohiṇī with great speed,
just as Death seizes the entire world when it is submerged in the deluge of the ocean.
But that youth Saṃkarṣaṇa, being carried away by Pralamba,
was like the moon being swept along by a single dark cloud at the end of time.
Then the illustrious Saṃkarṣaṇa, mounted upon the shoulder of the Daitya, felt as if he were in doubt himself,
and spoke thus to Kṛṣṇa.
"O Kṛṣṇa, I was carried away by the Daitya, who possesses a splendor as lofty as a mountain,
after he had displayed a great illusion in human form."
How am I to deal with this evil-minded one?
He is Pralamba, grown great and possessing double his usual luster due to his arrogance.
Kṛṣṇa, who was fully aware of Rauhineya’s conduct and his strength, spoke to him with a smile in a gentle voice tinged with joy.
Oh, this human state is clearly being graced by you,
who have attained that secret which pervades the universe, more secret than the secret!
O Noble One, remember your own body during the dissolution of the worlds;
realize the Self by means of the self at the meeting of the oceans.
He remembered the ancient gods, Brahmā, and the primordial waters, as well as his own past conduct and his original form.
The sky is your head, water your body, the earth your patience, fire your mouth,
wind your breath— the life of the world— and Manu, the creator, is your mind.
You have a thousand mouths, a thousand limbs, a thousand feet and eyes;
you have a thousand heads, you are the soul of the universe, with a hundred tongues and a hundred bellies;
you have a navel like a thousand-petaled lotus, you bear a thousand rays, and you are the slayer of enemies.
What you have shown in the world, that the denizens of heaven behold;
for who indeed is worthy to investigate that which has never been spoken by you before?
Whatever is to be known in this world has been fully proclaimed by you;
that which is known to you alone, even the gods do not know.
The inhabitants of heaven do not behold your own body born of yourself in the sky;
rather, they worship that artificial form of yours which you have assumed.
The dwellers of the third heaven behold such a form as this;
yet no end has been seen by the gods, and for that reason you are known as Ananta (the Infinite).
For you are subtle, great, and one, difficult to approach even for those who are subtle.
Upon you alone rests the eternal earth, supported by mountain-pillars;
immovable and the source of all living beings, it sustains the entire world.
You possess the enjoyments of the four oceans; you are the knower of the divisions of the four castes;
you are the lord of the four ages for the worlds; and you are the consumer of the fruits of the four officiating priests.
Just as you are for the worlds, so am I; that is my conviction. We two are one body, manifested in two forms for the sake of the world.

"Either I, Kṛṣṇa, am eternal, or you, Śeṣa, are the ancient one; for you, Śeṣa, are the eternal and primordial god of the worlds. By means of our two bodies alone, this universe is supported in its twofold division."
I am he who you are, and you are he who I am; I am the eternal one. For we two alone have been ordained as a single body, possessed of great power.
"Why do you sit there like a fool? O God, first slay this Dānava, the enemy of the gods, with your fist which is like a thunderbolt upon his head."
Reminded by Kṛṣṇa of his ancient [exploits],
that son of Rohiṇī was then filled with strength that ranges through the three worlds.
Then the radiant one was joined by another great force;
subsequently, the mighty-armed hero struck the wicked Pralamba on the head with a well-firm fist that was like a thunderbolt.
His head entered his own body through the opening in the skull;
by that blow of the fist, the skull was split in two, and he, deprived of life,
fell to the earth upon his knees.
As he was being scattered upon the earth, his form then appeared like a cloud suspended in the sky that is being torn asunder.
From the body of him whose head was shattered, blood flowed forth like water mixed with much red chalk from the peak of a mountain.
Having slain Pralamba and withdrawn his own strength,
the powerful son of Rohiṇī indeed embraced Kṛṣṇa.
When the Daitya had been slain, Kṛṣṇa, the cowherds, and the gods dwelling in heaven praised the one of great strength with blessings of victory.
"This Daitya has been slain by a child of effortless deeds through his strength.
Thus do incorporeal voices uttered by the gods resound;
and the names of this one have been proclaimed as "Baladeva" by the gods stationed in heaven.
At that time, when the Daitya who was unassailable even by the gods had been slain, the people on earth recognized the power of Baladeva as being born of his own deeds.
Chapter 59,
transliterated and collated with the Viṣṇupurāṇa (ViP) and Brahmāṇḍapurāṇa (BrP) by Utz Podzeit,
extracted from the collation and edited by Peter Schreiner; March 4.
While Kṛṣṇa and Bala were thus engaged in their activities,
wandering through the forest, two months of the rainy season passed by.
Those two heroes returned to Vraja, and there in Vraja they heard that Śakra’s festival had arrived and that the cowherds were eager for the celebration.
Out of curiosity, Kṛṣṇa spoke these words there:
"What is this so-called festival of Śakra, because of which joy has come upon you?"
Thereupon, one cowherd who was the eldest among them spoke these words:
"Listen, dear friend, to the purpose for which this festival is intended by Śakra."
O Kṛṣṇa, Śakra is the lord of the gods and the destroyer of the enemies of the clouds; this is the eternal sacrifice of that world-protector.
Urged by him, those clouds, adorned with his weapons and obedient to his very command,
produce grain with their fresh waters.
The Lord Puruhūta Puraṃdara, the giver of water to the clouds,
being thoroughly delighted, gratifies the entire world.
By means of that, we and other human beings subsist by consuming the grain produced,
and we satisfy the deities with offerings.
When the god rains upon the worlds, the crops flourish;
and when the earth is satiated, the entire universe appears as if imbued with nectar.
These cows are full of milk and accompanied by their calves; they are at ease.
Nourished by him, these cows, along with the bulls, have flourished and are well-fed on grass.
Where neither grainless nor grassless cows are seen, nor people afflicted by hunger,
there only rain-bearing clouds are visible.
Śakra milked the celestial, milky cows of Savitṛ;
they flow with fresh, pure milk sustained by the mass of clouds.
Driven by the wind within the clouds, it produces a great roar; when impelled with speed, people understand that it is "thundering."
And as that very [cloud] is being carried along by the wind-driven rain-clouds, there arise sounds like thunderbolts and lightning that split the mountains.
Standing in the sky, roaring with sounds like thunderbolts,
he releases that water from the vault of heaven by means of the clashing of vajras,
accompanied by many clouds driven by desire, just as a lord is attended by his servants.

In some places the sky was filled with clouds resembling dark stormy days, in some places with those resting amidst hidden clouds, and in other places with dense clouds that made the firmament appear like pearls from a spray of mist.
In some places with the appearance of scattered collyrium, and in others raining down fine droplets,
the Lord of the Gods adorns the entire sky with clouds;
even so does the cloud-drinker [the sun] yield this milk-like water through the rays.
Parjanya rains upon the earth for the welfare of all worlds.
"O Kṛṣṇa, since this rainy season is destined to belong to Śakra upon the earth,
therefore during the rains all kings, filled with joy,
worship the Lord of the Gods with great festivals— both we and other men."
Having heard the words of the aged cowherd, Dāmodara— though he was well aware of Śakra’s power— spoke these words in response to Śakra’s possession [of the child].
O cowherd, we are forest-dwellers, protectors of cattle who live by our herds;
know that for us, the cows, the mountains, and the forests are our deities.

Agriculture is the livelihood of farmers; trade is for those who live by commerce; for us, the cow is the supreme livelihood—this is said to be the threefold [division]. Whatever knowledge a person is endowed with, that is their highest deity.
She alone is worthy of worship and honor, she alone is his benefactress;
that man who, while enjoying the fruit of one's labor, performs a service for another,
obtains two misfortunes— both in this world and after death.
The boundaries of the cultivated fields are well known, and it is heard that the forest marks the limit of those boundaries;
all the mountains mark the limit of the forest, and that is our certain refuge.
It is also heard that even the mountains in this forest can assume any form at will;
entering various bodies, they sport upon their own peaks.
Having become maned lions and tigers, the best among clawed beasts,
they protect their own forests while terrifying those who would cut down the trees.
And when those forest-dwellers transform themselves,
they slay those very evil-doers by means of their man-eating activity.
The brahmins are devoted to sacrifices of mantras, and the farmers to sacrifices of the furrow;
we cowherds perform sacrifices to the mountain, for it is the mountain that is to be worshipped by us in the forest.
Therefore, O Gopā, it pleases me that we perform a mountain sacrifice in the forest;
having prepared a pleasant spot, let us do so either at the foot of a tree or upon a mountain.
There, having slaughtered the sacrificial animals and having prepared the sacrificial ground, let the collection of all the cattle-herds be made; why is this being deliberated?
Then, surrounding him clockwise with their heads adorned with autumn flowers,
let all the cows go back to the forest from that best of mountains.
Indeed, this delightful autumn has arrived, gladdening with its qualities of sweet-tasting and potent grass for the cattle; it is beautiful, with its clouds gone and its reservoirs of water clear.
Pale with flowering *priyaka* trees and dark in places with groves of *bāṇa* trees,
the forest shines with hard grass and is devoid of the cries of peacocks.
Stainless and clear in the sky, the clouds— devoid of cranes and free of lightning—
revolve like elephants whose rut has subsided.
Shaken by the sharp, rainy-season wind from the clouds,
all the trees, thick with heaps of fallen leaves, attain a state of clarity.
Without Meghanāda, the forest was devoid of the cries of peacocks;
yet the rivers, flowing in various forms, carried clear water.
He was adorned with a white cloud-like uṣṇīṣa and fanned by swans as if they were yak-tail whisks.
The sky, with its spotless parasol of the full moon, appeared as if it were being consecrated.
As the clouds dissolve, all the waters— already mocked by swans and thoroughly uprooted by cranes— attain a state of thinness.
With the ruddy geese for the slopes of their breasts, the sandy banks for the circles of their hips,
and the swans for their smiles, the rivers go toward the ocean as their husband.
The water, with its blooming white lotuses, and the sky, with its canopy of stars,
seemed to smile at one another equally during the nights.
My mind delights in these forests, which resound with the cries of intoxicated cranes, where the *kalamā* rice has turned pale from ripening, and where all pleasures have been fully enjoyed.
Lotus ponds, lakes, and oblong pools with blooming blue lotuses,
as well as rice fields, rivers, and lakes, were all ablaze with splendor.
The lotuses— both the red *padmas* and other white ones—
as well as the copper-colored and white lotuses blazing with splendor,
and the blue water-lilies, all partook of the beauty of aquatic flowers.
The white-eyed gods abandoned their intoxication, the winds blew gently,
the sky became cloudless, and the ocean grew calm.
With peacock feathers, loosened by the passage of the seasons and discarded after being used for dance and song, the earth appears as if possessed of many eyes.
With her banks soiled by her own mud and overgrown with *kāśa* flowers and creepers,
the Yamunā flows along, restrained by the formations of swans and cranes.
In the fields where the rice was ripe as black grain, and in the forests,
intoxicated birds that feed on grain and those that feed on lotuses warbled.
Those young blades of grass which the clouds drenched with water at the arrival of the rainy season have indeed become hardened.
Having cast off his cloud-made garment and illuminated by the virtues of autumn,
this moon dwells joyfully in the stainless sky.
Milk-yielding cows yield twice as much; bulls are twice as vigorous when in rut;
the splendor of forests is doubled; and the earth becomes rich with the excellence of its crops.
The stars, freed from the clouds, the waters filled with lotuses,
and the minds of men indeed attain clarity.
Savitṛ, whose rays are sharp, intensely emitted into the sky— now free of clouds— the brilliance ignited by autumn, drying up all things.
Having performed the lustration ceremony for their armies,
the kings who rule the earth set forth, desiring victory and facing one another's realms.
The mind lingers upon the lovely and variegated forest ranges, which are as copper-red as the *bandhujīva* flower and covered with clinging mud.
And in the forests shine the trees that beautify the woods:
the *asanas*, the *saptaparṇas*, and the flowering *kovidāras*.
The *iṣusāhvā*, *nikumbha*, *priyaka*, and *svarṇaka* trees,
as well as sugarcane, *ikṣusasya*, *nikupya*, and especially *priyaṅgu*, along with *sṛmara*, *picuka*, and *ketakī* trees, were found everywhere.
And she wanders especially through the cow-pens,
which laugh with the rising froth of the milk-pails, as if she were the autumnal radiance incarnate.
Surely the denizens of heaven are awakening the god whose banner is a bird, who dwells in the world of the thirty-three and has been resting happily during the rainy season.
Thus, when autumn had arrived at the end of the rainy season with its excellent crops,
[the forest] was dense with many birds whose colors were like those of the blue moon and sun,
and with fruits and sprouts resembling a thick mass of Indra’s bow (the rainbow).
We worship the divine mountain, which has the branches of its meditative forms, is adorned with the finest creepers,
is bent by its vast roots, and is graced by the expanse of the wind;
and we especially honor the cows.
With earrings, with horns, and adorned with crests of peacock feathers,
and with long-hanging bells as well as autumnal flowers.
"Let cows be worshipped for the sake of Śiva; let the mountain-sacrifice proceed.
Let Śakra be worshipped by the gods; let this mountain be honored by us."
"I shall perform the sacrifice of a cow by force as well, there is no doubt;
provided that you have affection for me, or if we are indeed friends."
"Cows are indeed always to be honored by everyone; there is no doubt in this matter.
Through conciliation, however, there will be satisfaction for you and for your prosperity.
Therefore, let these words of mine be carried out without hesitation."
Chapter 60,
