2002. Not yet proof-read.
Vaiśampāyana said: Having heard the words of Dāmodara, those who live by their cattle were delighted.
They replied without hesitation to those words which were declared to be nectar.
"O child, this great intelligence of yours, which increases the joy of the cowherds, truly delights us all; for it is the wisdom that brings prosperity to men."
You are our refuge, you are our delight, you are the knower, and you are our ultimate resort;
you are the giver of fearlessness to us in times of danger, and you alone are the friend of friends.
O Kṛṣṇa, because of you, this entire settlement of Ghoṣa— secure, with its cattle-pastures delighted and its enemies pacified— dwells as if it had already attained heaven.
From his very birth, by those divine and heroic deeds so difficult to perform on earth,
and by his realization of what is to be known, our minds have been struck with wonder at his self-confidence.
In strength, supreme glory, and prowess,
you are the most excellent among mortals, just as Puraṃdara is among the gods.
By your fierce majesty, by your brilliance, and by your fullness as well,
you are the most excellent among mortals, like the sun among the gods;
by your loveliness, your fortune, your graciousness, and your smiling countenance.
And you are the most excellent among mortals, like the moon among the gods.
In dress, in physical form, in childhood, and in conduct,
you shall be equal to Śaktidhara, and no mere mortal at all.
O Lord, as for the words you have spoken regarding the mountain-sacrifice—
who is able to transgress them, any more than the shore of the great ocean?
O dear one, the splendor of Śakra has been established, and this glorious splendor of the mountain is present;
let that which was directed by you proceed today for the sake of the cowherds and the cows.
"Let foods and delicate preparations of milk be prepared;
let beautiful jars be placed at the water-stations,
and let large, wide troughs be set out for the sake of the thickened milk and the milk-rice to be licked."
Let all that which is to be chewed, eaten, and drunk be brought forward;
let vessels for meat and for boiled rice be set out;
and let the entire milk-yield of the herd be collected for three nights.
Let the animals to be eaten, such as buffaloes and others, be slaughtered;
let this sacrifice proceed, crowded with all the cowherds and attendants.
A great sound arose, generating joy, as Gokula was filled with delight;
there were the sounds of the blowing of musical instruments and the bellowing of bulls.
It increased the joy of the cowherds with the lowing of calves;
it was a lake of curd, a whirlpool of clarified butter, and abounded with streams of milk.
That sacrifice proceeded, richly provided with a mountain of meat and a visible mountain of cooked rice; it was crowded with cattle from the mountains,
filled with contented cowherds, and enchanting with the women of the cowherds.
There, hundreds of heaps of edible foods were prepared,
along with various perfumes, garlands, and diverse incenses;
and when the sacrificial arrangements had been fully completed and the cooking-vessels placed upon the fires.
On an auspicious lunar day, the cowherds, together with the twice-born, performed a sacrifice on the mountain.
At the conclusion of the sacrifice,
Kṛṣṇa, having become a mountain through his illusory power (māyā), consumed that food, as well as that excellent milk, curd, and meat.
Such indeed was the state of the cowherds there, O bull of the Bharatas;
and the foremost of the brahmins, having been gratified and satisfied with their full meals,
rose up with joyful minds after pronouncing blessings as they pleased.
Having eaten and drunk milk at will during the concluding bath, Kṛṣṇa,
saying "I am fully satisfied," laughed indeed with his divine form.
Standing upon the summit of the mountain, the lotus-eyed one laughed.
Seeing Kṛṣṇa, who resembled a mountain and was adorned with divine garlands and unguents, standing on the mountain peak, the cowherds approached him as their leader.
The Lord, the Master, was likewise covered in that very same form;
together with those cowherds, he bowed down and worshipped himself by means of his own self.
The astonished cowherds said to that god who was stationed upon the excellent mountain:
"O Blessed One, we are servants bound under your control; what shall we do, your attendants?"
Then the mountain spoke to the cowherds with a voice of radiant splendor:
"From this day forward, if you have compassion for the cows, I am to be honored with sacrifice."
"I am your first deity, the auspicious one who fulfills all desires;
and by my power, you shall enjoy tens of thousands of cows."
And I shall be a source of auspiciousness for my devotees in forest after forest;
and I shall sport with you just as I do when I am in heaven.
And to these renowned cowherds who stand here, Nandagopa and the others—
to these cowherds, being well-pleased, I bestow abundant wealth.
"May the cows, surrounded by their calves, quickly encompass me;
in this way, there will be supreme joy for me, without a doubt."
Then, for the sake of the lustration ceremony (*nīrājana*), thousands of herds of cows,
accompanied by their bulls, surrounded the excellent mountain in great numbers.
Then those cows, milked by their calves, were adorned with garlands, chaplets, and armlets;
their horns were tipped with wreaths and chaplets by the hundreds and thousands.
And the cowherds followed, driving their wealth,
their limbs smeared with decorative patterns of colored earth and wearing red, yellow, and black garments.
With arms covered by weapons and adorned with armlets variegated like peacocks,
and with hair-tying bands skillfully fashioned from peacock-feather stalks,
the cowherds shone all the more in that wondrous assembly.
Some mounted bulls, others danced with joy,
while other cowherds seized their swift-moving cows.
When that ritual of the lustration of cows had concluded,
that mountain suddenly vanished from sight in that very body.
Kṛṣṇa, too, remaining among the cowherds, entered Vraja itself,
amazed by that wonderful event which had occurred during the mountain sacrifice.
The cowherds, including both children and the elderly, praised the Slayer of Madhu;
performing dance and song together with Kṛṣṇa, they returned to Vraja.
Chapter 61.
Transliterated and collated with the Viṣṇupurāṇa (ViP) and Brahmāṇḍapurāṇa (BrP) by Utz Podzeit, extracted from the collation and edited by Peter Schreiner; March 4, 2002. Not yet proofread.
Vaiśampāyana said:
When his pride was thus humbled, Śakra, the lord of the thirty gods, filled with wrath,
then addressed the host of clouds known as Saṃvartaka.
O elephant-mothers Balāhakas, listen to my words,
if you wish to do what is pleasing to me, motivated by devotion to the king.
These cowherds, headed by Nanda Gopa, who have gone to Vṛndāvana and are devoted solely to Dāmodara, are hostile toward my festival.
Let those cows— the source of their livelihood and from whom their status as lords of cattle is traditionally known—
be afflicted by rain and wind for seven nights.
Mounted upon Airāvata, I myself shall release terrible water,
rain, and wind, possessing a brilliance equal to the thunderbolt and lightning.
And by you, by Caṇḍavarṣa, by Carat, and by Māruta,
those cows together with their herd will be slain and will lose their lives upon the earth.
Thus did the Lord, the chastiser of Pāka, issue his command to all the clouds when his decree was indeed repelled by Kṛṣṇa.
When the *maha* sacrifice was thwarted by the command of Viṣṇu, Indra, the subduer of Pāka,
then those black clouds— terrible-sounding and inspiring fear,
resembling mountains— covered the sky on all sides.
Then those clouds, producing flashes of lightning and adorned with rainbows, made the sky shrouded in darkness.
Some, like elephants, were locked in combat; others, possessing the luster of sea-monsters, moved through the sky like noble serpents or great clouds.
Bound together by one another's bodies, resembling tens of thousands of elephant herds,
they created a vast and gloomy day, shrouding the surface of the sky.

Those clouds rained down in every direction and at all times with showers of identical form— showers of human hands, elephant trunks, and bamboo poles, as well as thick elephant trunks and tree trunks.
Indeed, those with human vision perceived that sky as having become a vast ocean—
difficult to fathom, boundless, bottomless, and like a great, overcast day.
The birds did not fly about, and the various species of wild animals fled,
while clouds resembling mountains thundered everywhere in the sky.
When the sky, resembling the sun and moon while they were asleep, was covered by terrible clouds,
the body of the world became disfigured by the excessive rain.
Due to the masses of clouds, the sky became utterly lusterless— devoid of light, with the planets and stars invisible, and bereft of the rays of the moon and sun.
Repeatedly drenched by water released from the clouds,
and tossed on all sides by winds joined with the clouds,
the earth there shone as if it were entirely composed of water.
There the peacocks cried out, while the birds that had begun to sing slightly grew more vocal;
the rivers reached their full increase, and the water-fowl entered into their flight.
As if threatened by the thundering of the clouds and the roar of the rain-god Parjanya,
the grasses tremble along with the trees.
"The time of the end of the worlds has arrived, and the earth has become a single ocean"—
thus spoke the groups of cowherds, afflicted by fear.
Then, by that rain of calamitous waters, the cows were violently struck;
crying out with lowing sounds, they did not move, appearing as if paralyzed.
Their thighs and ears were motionless, and their hooves and mouths were devoid of effort.
With their bodies' hair bristling and moist, and with their waists and breasts emaciated;
Some gave up their lives, exhausted; some fell down, afflicted;
and some cows, along with their calves, collapsed, shivering from the spray.
Some mothers stand blocking their calves with their chests;
they have turned away, their thighs are exhausted, they are without food, and their bellies are emaciated.
The cows, defeated by the rain, fell down distressed and trembling;
and the young calves, their faces upturned toward Dāmodara’s face, stood there as if saying to Kṛṣṇa with piteous mouths, "Save us! in their state of affliction.
"O mighty-armed one, behold the cows, who are in extreme agony!
Seeing that slaughter of the cows and the fear born from the onset of the stormy weather, and seeing the cowherds with dejected faces, Kṛṣṇa summoned his wrath."
And seeing the cows also extremely distressed,
the glorious one, his eyes copper-red with rage,
thought: "Ah, the audacity of the Lord of the Gods, who now treats me with such disregard!"
"The slaughter of the cattle has been committed, and likewise that of the cowherds;
having reflected thus, he became agitated, perceiving the calamity to befall the cattle.
Then Priyavada, speaking kindly, addressed these words to himself by means of his own mind.
Today, having uprooted this mountain together with its forests and groves,
I shall fashion it into a place for cattle— a formidable shelter against the rain.
This mountain, which resembles an underground chamber, has been held up by me;
the cows along with their herd shall be protected, and it will come under my control.
Having thus reflected, Viṣṇu, whose prowess is truth,
spoke these words; then, lifting Govardhana Hill with a single hand,
Kṛṣṇa held it up effortlessly like a child holding a mushroom.
Desiring to display the strength of his arms, Kṛṣṇa, like another mountain himself, uprooted that nearby mountain with his two hands.
That great mountain, with its roots, branches, and trunks, shook;
the mountain, making a *ghaṇāghaṇa* sound, was as if breathing like a living being.
Held together by the clouds, that mountain was grasped by [the Lord] with his left hand.
Having attained the state of a house, he appeared there with the form and luster of a dwelling.
As that mountain was being uprooted from the earth,
the loose rocks upon its ridges shifted and fell away along with the trees.
Desiring to protect the wealth of cattle, Viṣṇu, the Lord of the cows and Hari,
as Govinda stationed in the midst of the kine, protected the cowherds along with the entire community of cowherds.
Viṣṇu,

the Lord of the lords of the worlds, assuming his primordial form, stood upon the path of the cows as a cowherd, holding the wealth of cattle and supporting the one who upholds the cows, causing amazement among the cowherds.
Govinda rendered futile the endeavor of Godhara;
with his body causing a thundering roar in the sky, he [uprooted] this Mount Govardhana,
whose peaks were crumbling and collapsing on all sides.
And with its upraised horns held aloft, that which was immovable became capable of moving through the sky.
With its flanks possessing flowing springs that had become one with the masses of clouds,
the mountain, its heaps of stones being split asunder, began to tremble.
The forms of the raining clouds, of the mountain discharging showers of stones,
of the whirling wind, and even of the flashing lightning—
overwhelmed by Viṣṇu’s splendor— were no longer visible.
People perceived the form of that Vāyu as he was roaring.
With its cloud-covered peaks and cascading waterfalls,
the mountain, filled with wild peacocks, appears as if it were blended with the clouds themselves.
"This mountain has been bathed by its wings," thus did the Vidyādharas, Uragas,
Gandharvas, and Ṛṣis utter melodious words.
Placed upon his dark palm and released from the surface of the earth,
it produced streams of gold, silver, and iron.
Some of its peaks appeared as if covered, some were partially obscured,
and others seemed to have entered into the clouds of that mountain.
As the mountain shook, the various flowers of the trees that were shaken fell scattered all over the ground.
With broad heads adorned with half-svastikas,
the lords of the double-tongued ones, enraged and moving through the air, emerged from all sides into the sky.
The flocks of birds fell into distress from both the rain and fear;
flying up again and again from the sky, they fell back down with their faces turned downward.
The enraged lions appeared like water-laden clouds;
those preeminent tigers roared as they churned about like churning-sticks.
With its uneven peaks now leveled and its level plateaus rendered exceedingly difficult to traverse, that mountain, with its body transformed, appears truly beautiful.
When he was showered upon by those clouds, his form became like that of Tripura in the sky when it had been paralyzed by Rudra.
Then, held up by Kṛṣṇa’s staff-like arm,
that massive mountain appeared like a parasol covered by a mass of dark blue clouds.
With the openings of its caves closed by clouds as if dreaming,
the mountain lay upon the pillow of Kṛṣṇa’s arm, appearing as though fast asleep in the sky.
Surrounded by peaks, that mountain appears as if it were without support, with its trees devoid of the cries of birds and its forests silent of the calls of peacocks.
With its ridges overturned, reeling, and trembling,
the forests and peaks of the mountain seemed as if they were seized by fever.
Driven by the wind and urged on by Mahendra, the clouds situated upon his head released an inexhaustible torrent of water.
Hanging from the tip of Kṛṣṇa’s arm,
that mountain with its clouds appeared like a region oppressed by a king, as if mounted upon a wheel.
That mass of clouds stood surrounding that mountain,
like a great and prosperous kingdom with its city at the forefront.
Having placed that mountain on his hand and weighed it, the protector of the cowherds, standing like Prajāpati, spoke with a smile.
O cowherds, this mountain-dwelling, which could not have been conceived even by the gods, has been constructed by me through divine means as a shelter for the cows against the wind.
"You should feel no fear regarding being struck down by my hand;
enough with the fear of wind and rain, for protection from that has already been provided for you.
Let the herds of cows enter here quickly for their own peace."
And let them dwell at their ease in windless places,
according to their herds, according to their flocks, and indeed according to their strength, in comfort.
"Let this region be divided; it has been made a place of refuge from the rains. This great land, cleared by the uprooting of mountains, has been fashioned by me.
Now, O best of cowherds, divide yourselves into groups and dwell here."
Measuring five krośas in length and one krośa in its great width,
it is capable of swallowing even the three worlds, let alone Vraja.
Then a tumultuous sound of "kila-kilā" arose from the cowherds,
accompanied by the lowing of the cows, while outside there was the roar of clouds.
Then the cows, gathered into herds by the cowherds,
entered the vast cave-like cleft of that mountain.
Kṛṣṇa also, at the base of the mountain, stood as tall as a pillar of rock;
with one hand he held the mountain as if it were a dear guest.
Then, fearing the rain, the goods of Vraja and the laden carts entered that mountain-built house.
But seeing that superhuman feat of Kṛṣṇa, the powerful wielder of the thunderbolt,
having made his promise false, restrained the clouds.
When seven nights had passed and the earth was devoid of festivities,
the slayer of Vṛtra, surrounded by clouds, departed for the supreme heaven.
When the seven nights had passed, when Tiṣya had been cast down and Śatakratu had fallen,
the sky was cloudless and stainless, and the day shone with a radiant sun.
The cows returned along that very same path, their fatigue dispelled; then the entire cowherd settlement set out once again for its own place.
The Lord Kṛṣṇa, the bestower of boons, being pleased, established that foremost of mountains in its own place as an immovable entity for the sake of Dhruva.
Chapter 62,
transliterated and collated with the Viṣṇupurāṇa and Brahmāṇḍapurāṇa by Utz Podzeit,
extracted from the collation and edited by Peter Schreiner; March 4.
2002. Not yet proof-read.
Vaiśampāyana said:
Having seen Govardhana held up and Gokula protected, [the people were amazed].
Filled with wonder, Śakra desired a vision of Kṛṣṇa.
Mounting the elephant Airāvata, who resembled a waterless cloud and was intoxicated, drenched with the flow of rut-fluid, he descended to the surface of the earth.
Purandara, the one invoked by many, beheld Kṛṣṇa, whose actions are effortless, seated indeed upon the surface of the Govardhana rock.
Seeing that child, blazing with great splendor, imperishable,
and wearing the dress of a cowherd, Purandara recognized him as Viṣṇu.
With all his eyes, Śakra gazed up at him— who was dark as a forest of palm trunks and marked with the śrīvatsa— with eyes that could never look enough.
Seeing him endowed with splendor, like an immortal in the world of mortals, ever devoted to his duties for the sake of accomplishing the work of the gods,
and seated comfortably upon the surface of a rock, Śakra became filled with shame.
As he sat there at ease, that bull among birds,
the consumer of serpents, vanished from sight and cast his shadow over him with both wings.

Abandoning his elephant, the slayer of Bala approached Keśava— who was accompanied by that shadow, who had the form of a sacrifice, who was situated in a secluded mountain region, and who was intent upon the affairs of the world— to meet Kṛṣṇa.
Having approached him, adorned with divine garlands and unguents,
the lordly king of the gods shone forth, his hand filled with the thunderbolt.
His face was constantly adorned with a crown the color of the sun that produced flashes like lightning, and with two divine earrings;
he was decorated with divine ornaments and a hanging cluster of five blossoms.
Beholding with a thousand eyes capable of assuming any form at will— eyes as beautiful as a thousand-petaled lotus that adorned his body—
he issued commands to the gods with a voice like the roar of thunderclouds.
Śakra prostrated himself and said, "May you forgive me," and he praised Hari Viṣṇu, who was adorned in the guise of a cowherd.
Homage to you, O Lord of the gods of gods, the creator of the creator of beings;
homage to you, the golden-seeded one, the bestower of the Soma.
Homage to you, the sole reality of the Vedas, the awakener who brings about the understanding of that [reality];
homage, repeated homage, to the one expressed by the syllable *praṇava* and to the one who expresses it.
Homage to you who possess all forms; homage to you, the benefactor of the world. Homage to you, the protector of diverse forms; homage to you, the sustainer of the earth.
Homage to you whose form is ancient; homage to you, O Madhusūdana!

O Keśava, Lord of the World, what need is there for this single salutation? To each and every form of the God of Gods, O Viṣṇu, who are most manifest in form, and to all those forms that grant every desire— to them I likewise offer my salutations.
O Lord of Gods, O delighter of the cowherds, O joy of the Yadus, whatever I have done out of ignorance or knowledge, or out of anger, must be forgiven by you.
O Lord, anger flares up against both the capable and the incapable;
yet you cannot be ruled by anyone, for you are indeed the ruler of all, O Lord.
All this, which is exceedingly difficult for me to obtain, belongs to Indra and is for your sake;
it is born of your grace, O Lord of the World, since you are the sovereign of the gods.
"Therefore, O Lord of the gods of gods, you must forgive me, for I am but your servant.
Having spoken thus, the husband of Śacī then uttered these words again:
He beheld Kṛṣṇa, whose eyes were like lotus petals, who was no child yet appeared in the form of a child; who resembled the *atasī* flower and was marked with the *śrīvatsa*;
and who, having performed superhuman deeds, was seated upon the surface of a stone.
"O best of masters, there is no anger in the hearts of masters toward their servants," he said,
and then he addressed him with a sweet, divine voice.
O Kṛṣṇa, Kṛṣṇa, O mighty-armed one, the increaser of the joy of your kinsmen! You have performed a deed that surpasses even destiny, out of your love for the cows.
I am thoroughly gratified that you protected the cattle while the clouds created by me were causing a whirlwind at the end of the age.
And since this best of mountains is held in the sky like a dwelling by means of self-born yoga— who indeed would not be filled with wonder at this?
O Kṛṣṇa, when my great sacrifice was forbidden, he indeed became enraged and brought down this excessive rain upon the cattle for seven nights.
This unassailable torrent of rain must be warded off by you;
while I stand here, it cannot be resisted even by the gods together with the hosts of Dānavas.
O Kṛṣṇa, it is most pleasing to me that you, having assumed a human body,
conceal your entire Vaiṣṇava splendor when provoked to anger.
I believe that the eternal task of the gods has indeed been accomplished by you,
having assumed human form, through such self-exertion.
O hero, your purpose will be accomplished; nothing at all shall be lost, since you are the leader of the gods and the one who goes before them in every undertaking.
You alone are the eternal one for all the worlds and the gods;
I see no second who could bear your burden.
For just as the most excellent bull is yoked when the burden has sunk,
so too are you, O bird-vehicled one, for the gods who have sunk down.
O Kṛṣṇa, this world-weapon residing within your body was well-revealed by Brahmā, like gold extracted from its ores.
The Blessed One, the Self-Existent One himself, is indeed unable to follow you, whether by wisdom or even by age, just as a lame man cannot follow one who moves with swift speed.
Among pillars, the Himalaya is the best; among lakes, the abode of Varuṇa;
among birds, Garuḍa is the best; and among the deities, you are the most excellent.
Below the waters is indeed the world; above that are the mountains.
Above the nāgas is the earth, and above the earth are human beings.
Beyond the world of humans, the path of birds is said to lie;
above the sky is the sun, the radiant gate to heaven.
Beyond that is the great world of the gods, dense with celestial palaces,
where I, O Kṛṣṇa, am stationed in the position of Indra among the gods.
For by you, the Lord of the World, the powerful Viṣṇu,
the world of Brahmā has been established above heaven, frequented by hosts of Brahman-sages;
and there also is the course of the Moon and of the high-souled luminaries.
Above that is the world of the cows; indeed, the Sādhyas protect it.
For that, O Kṛṣṇa, is all-pervading, great, and situated within the great ether.
Even there, your movement is ever upward, consisting of ascetic power— a state which we all do not know, even though we have questioned the Grandfather himself.
O Viṣṇu, by your grace, even the blessed Grandfather [Brahmā] has attained that state which those devoted to yoga and exponents of Brahman reach by their own will;
yet the world below belongs to evildoers, and the world of the Nāgas is indeed dreadful.
The earth is the field for those whose nature is action, for every deed.
The sky is the domain of unstable things whose behavior is like that of the wind;
heaven is the destination for those rich in tranquility and self-restraint who have performed virtuous deeds.
For those engaged in Brahmanic austerity, the world of Brahmā is the supreme goal;
indeed, Goloka belongs to the cows alone, for that state is difficult to attain.
But that world, O Kṛṣṇa, was being oppressed; it has been sustained by you, the self-realized and steadfast hero, as you struck down the affliction of the cows.
Therefore, impelled by the words of the cows and out of respect for you, O highly fortunate Brahmin, I have come here.
O Kṛṣṇa, I am the Lord of Beings, the King of Gods, Purandara; in the course of Aditi’s pregnancies, I am your ancient elder brother.
O Lord, you ought to forgive all that splendor and those radiant beings whom I have shown to you in the form of clouds.
O Kṛṣṇa, O you who possess the prowess of an elephant, having thus endured with a patient mind through your own gentle splendor, hear my words and those of the cows, O Brahmā.
The Blessed Lord Brahmā, as well as the cows who move through the sky in heaven, have spoken to you,
being gratified by your divine deeds such as their protection and so forth.
The cattle have been protected by you, and by the cattle the worlds have been protected;
for we, together with the bulls, likewise increase through our offspring.
We shall satisfy the farmers with draft oxen, the gods with pure oblations, and the goddess Śrī— who moves at will— with the purifying power of dung.
Therefore, O mighty one, you are indeed our guru and the giver of our life;
from this day forward, you shall be our king and our Indra.
Therefore, be consecrated by me with these jars of divine water, filled with gold, which I have now lowered down with my hands.
"I am indeed Indra among the gods, while you have attained the lordship of cows;
the people of the world shall praise you eternally on earth as Govinda."
O Kṛṣṇa, just as you were established above me by the cows as their lord, like Indra,
the gods in heaven shall sing of you as Upendra.
"And as for these four months of the rainy season appointed for me,
I grant you half of them, namely the latter part of the autumn."
And for half a year the banner shall always receive worship;
then the peacocks will abandon their pride born of the water [of the clouds].
Those of little vigor and pride, as well as others who roar like clouds and move about during the rainy season, shall all attain peace.
The thousand-rayed Āditya, heating the quarters with his own splendor, will traverse the region frequented by Triśaṅku and Agastya.
Then, in autumn, when the peacocks were silent and mute,
and the waters had become exceedingly pleasant, flooding and submerging the grassy grounds.
On the riverbanks filled with swans and cranes,
amidst the cries of intoxicated curlews and the lowing of rutting bulls, and while the cows were joyful and yielding much milk;
When the clouds had ceased and delivered their water to the world,
the swans were wandering in the sky, which resembled the blade of a weapon.
In ponds and rivers where lotuses had bloomed,
in lovely reservoirs with their pure waters,
and amidst rows of ripened fields where the tips of the *kalama* rice stalks bent low;
And when the rivers, flowing with water, have established their middle courses,
and the boundary of the fields is rich with crops— then even for a sage, this place is heart-stealing.
On the earth, in the kingdom of Pṛthu, during the age of Ramā, at the end of the rains;
when the paths of the Paṅktis were overgrown with grass that bore fruit,
and in lands abounding in sugarcane, while sacrifices were being performed.
Then, O Kṛṣṇa, when you have arisen from sleep, the auspicious autumn will set in for this entire world, just as it does in the celestial realm.
"O men, both you and I shall be honored upon the surface of the earth as Mahendra and Upendra upon our flagstaffs."
And those men who abide in our conduct, known as that of Mahendra and Upendra, and who shall offer salutations to them, for them there shall be no arrival of misfortune.
Having brought him from the heavenly worlds to the jeweled throne, the Lord of the Gods seated Kṛṣṇa there and consecrated him with gems, beginning with pearls;
and having performed the lustration ceremony (*nīrājana*) and adorned him with divine ornaments.
Then Śakra, the knower of yoga, taking those jars containing divine water, performed the consecration for Govinda.
Seeing him being consecrated, those cows, together with their leaders,
sprinkled the imperishable Kṛṣṇa with their udders overflowing with milk.
And clouds in the sky, with streams of water containing nectar and resembling pearls, drenched from all sides the Imperishable One who was being consecrated.
From all the lords of the forest, milk resembling the moon flowed forth;
they rained down a shower of flowers, and musical instruments resounded in the sky.
All the sages, devoted to mantras, praised him with words:
Vasiṣṭha, Vāmadeva, Jābāli, and Kāśyapa;
Viśvāmitra, Bharadvāja, Kaṇva, Atri, and the venerable lord.
And all these sages, the perfected ones, and the supreme seers,
as well as the earth itself, assumed their forms once they were released from the single ocean.
The oceans became serene, winds blew for the welfare of the world,
calamities were pacified, and kings attained a state free from enmity.
O joy of the Kurus, when Kṛṣṇa was consecrated, all these things—
even those that were cruel by nature— became free from enmity, my dear;
the sun shone as it stood in its proper course, and the moon was joined with the yoga.
The trees were variegated with coral-like blossoms and laden with fruit.
The elephants exuded rut, the deer in the forest were filled with joy,
and the mountains shone, adorned with trees whose branches were swaying in the wind.
The world was like the realm of the gods, satisfied and fully satiated with nectar;
for during Kṛṣṇa’s consecration, it was indeed sprinkled with the divine essence of heaven.
When the imperishable Govinda had been consecrated with cows, Śakra,
the king of the gods, addressed him as he wore divine white garments.
O Kṛṣṇa, this is my first command regarding the cattle that has been carried out;
now hear also the other reason for my arrival.
Quickly bring about the destruction of Kaṃsa and Keśin, that vilest of horses, as well as Ariṣṭa who is intoxicated with pride; thereafter, rule over the kingdom of kings.
Born of your father’s sister, this portion of mine exists within you;
he is to be protected by you, honored, and employed in the service of friendship.
For, favored by you, he will follow your conduct;
remaining under your control, he shall attain vast renown.
He will be the most eminent archer of the Bharata lineage and worthy of it; yet, he will find no pleasure with anyone other than you.
The Bharata lineage is dependent upon you and upon that Supreme Person;
when both of them are united, the kings shall meet their end.
And I have made this vow, O Kṛṣṇa, in the midst of the ṛṣis and the gods:
"A son named Arjuna, a sustainer of the Kurus, has been born to me by Kuntī."
He, who knows the dependence of weapons [on the wielder] and is foremost in drawing the bow—
into him all those kings who fight with arms shall indeed enter.
And the akṣauhiṇīs of heroic kings, distinguished in battle,
will be joined with death in combat according to the duty of kings.
O Lord, neither kings nor even the gods shall be able to follow his conduct with weapons, his path, or his lightness of hand with the bow, were it not for you.
"He shall be your kinsman and your ally in battles;
therefore, O Govinda, you must provide for his yoga on my behalf."
He indeed should be regarded by you just as I am, and he must always be honored;
for you alone are the constant knower of the worlds and of Arjuna.
For he must always be protected by you in great battles;
for one who is protected by you, death shall have no power.
Know me as Arjuna, O Kṛṣṇa, and know me as the Self by means of the self;
for as I am eternally your self, so too are you mine, O Arjuna.
In the past, after you had conquered these worlds from the hand of Bali with three strides,
I was made the king of the gods according to the order of seniority.
And knowing you to be composed of truth, beloved of truth, and possessing the prowess of truth,
the gods indeed approach you with truth to employ you in the destruction of their enemies.
That son of mine named Arjuna, the son of your father’s sister,
shall come here out of friendship, having previously been his companion.
O Kṛṣṇa, as you fight, whether in your own place or even at home,
the entire burden of the army must be borne by you, just as a load is carried by a bull.
O Kṛṣṇa, when Kaṃsa has been slain by you who perceive the destiny of things,
a great battle will then take place among the rulers of the earth.
Among those heroic men of superhuman deeds,
Arjuna shall be the enjoyer of victory, while you shall be united with glory.
O Kṛṣṇa, O Acyuta, you ought to explain this speech of yours to me in its entirety,
as well as [the nature of] the gods and truth, if it is dear to you and to me.
Having heard the words of Śakra, Kṛṣṇa, having attained the state of Govinda,
with a mind filled with joy, spoke this reply.
I am pleased merely by the sight of you, Śakra, Lord of Śacī;
and as for that which has been spoken by you, nothing at all shall be withheld.
I know your disposition; I know the origin of Arjuna;
I know that you were given as a paternal aunt to Pāṇḍu, the lord of the earth.
I know Yudhiṣṭhira to be a prince fashioned from Dharma;
and I know Bhīmasena to be a body born from the lineage of Vāyu.

I know well that these two auspicious sons, Nakula and Sahadeva, both born from the womb of Mādrī, were created by the Aśvins; they possess strength equal to ten thousand elephants and are the subduers of many asuras.
I also know Karna, the first-born son of the Sun,
born to his paternal aunt, who entered the status of a charioteer.
O Śakra, all the mighty Kauravas led by Duryodhana, who desire war, are known to me; as are the circumstances of Pāṇḍu’s passing, which resulted from the falling thunderbolt of a curse.
Therefore go to the third heaven, O Śakra, for the happiness of the inhabitants of the third heaven;
no enemy of Arjuna shall prevail in my presence.
And when the Bharata war has ceased, I shall restore all those Pāṇḍavas, including Arjuna, unharmed from the battle to Kuntī.
And whatever that son of yours, Śakra, shall say to me— that Arjuna—
I will do it like a servant, constrained by my affection for you.
Having heard those pleasant words spoken by the one true to his promise,
Śakra, the lord of the thirty gods, bowed his head at the lotus feet of Kṛṣṇa, the god of gods, and departed visibly for heaven.
This narrative bestows long life, is meritorious, and destroys evil; it generates joy for Parjanya and wards off drought;
it brings about all happiness and is a supreme secret of the gods.
Chapter 63,
transliterated and collated with the Viṣṇupurāṇa (ViP) and Brahmāṇḍapurāṇa (BrP) by Utz Podzeit,
extracted from the collation and edited by Peter Schreiner; March 4.
2002. Not yet proof-read.
Vaiśampāyana said:
After Śakra had departed, Kṛṣṇa was then honored by the inhabitants of Vraja.
The glorious upholder of Govardhana entered Vraja itself.
The elders and their kinsmen who lived with them rejoiced in him, saying, "We are blessed; we have been graced by the mountain being taken away by you."
The cows have crossed over the fear of the bull, and we have crossed over the great danger,
through your grace, O Govinda, equal to a god, of great splendor!
O Lord of the Cowherds, we behold superhuman deeds of yours;
by the holding up of this mountain, we know you, O Kṛṣṇa, to be the imperishable one.
Who are you among the Rudras or the Maruts, O one of great strength, or are you among the Vasus? And for what purpose is Vasudeva your father?
O Kṛṣṇa, your childhood play in the forest and your birth among us are contemptible; yet your divine activities leave our minds filled with apprehension.
For what purpose do you take delight in this contemptible dress of a cowherd among us? And though you are like a world-protector, why do you tend cattle?
Whether you are a god, a dānava, a yakṣa, or even a gandharva— you who have become our kinsman, whoever you are, homage be to you!
Homage be to Kṛṣṇa, Kṛṣṇa! Homage to the kinsman of the cowherds! Homage to the youth, the protector, the one in the guise of a cowherd, O relative!
Homage to you, the lion among children; homage to the upholder of the mountains;
homage again and again to the god, the most excellent one, and to the yakṣa.
Salutations to you, the son of Nanda and the offspring of Yaśodā!
Who are you, or what deity are you? For what purpose do you protect us? Do you dwell here by some specific task or by your own free will?
We are all your followers; we have gone to you for refuge.
Having heard the words of the cowherds, Kṛṣṇa, whose eyes resemble lotuses,
smiled and replied to all his kinsmen who had assembled there.
Just as all of you, who possess formidable prowess, regard me, so should I not be understood; I am of your own kind, a kinsman.
If, however, it must necessarily be heard, then wait for the proper time;
thereafter you shall hear it and see me in truth.
If I am a praiseworthy kinsman to you, equal in splendor to a god,
what need is there for formal recognition, if this is indeed my favor?
Thus addressed by the son of Vasudeva,
all those cowherds covered their faces and, observing a vow of silence, fled in every direction.
But Kṛṣṇa, beholding the fresh youthfulness of the moon at night and of the autumnal nights, set his mind upon amorous delight.
In the streets of Vraja, which were smeared with dried cow-dung,
that valiant youth incited fights between bulls who had become impassioned.
The heroic and powerful one fought with the cowherds who were fierce in strength;
in that forest, the lordly hero seized the cows like a crocodile.
Knowing the proper time and honoring his youth, he would gather the young cowherd girls at night and enjoy himself with them.
At night, those lovely cowherd women drank in his beautiful face with the casting glances of their eyes, as if drinking the moon that had descended to earth.
Clad in a radiant silken garment, moist with yellow orpiment,
and wearing a fine cloth, Kṛṣṇa became even more beautiful.
Adorned with armlets and a variegated forest garland,
Govinda, shining brilliantly, graced that settlement of Vraja.
"Obeisance to Dāmodara! the cowherd girls then exclaimed, having witnessed that wonderful conduct of that radiant one in the cowherd settlement.
"Homage to you, O Kṛṣṇa, O protector of the cowherds! Be gracious, O Lord!
Thus they spoke, and those excellent women pressed against his chest with their breasts turned upward, while they gazed at him with eyes rolling in delight.
Restrained by their fathers, brothers, and mothers,
those cowherd women, who were fond of pleasure, searched for Kṛṣṇa at night.
All those cowherd girls, arranged in rows and singing of the deeds of Kṛṣṇa in pairs, delighted the charming one.
Those young women were imitators of Kṛṣṇa’s pastimes; their eyes were fixed upon Kṛṣṇa, and they followed the very path of Kṛṣṇa.
In the groves, other women of Vraja wandered about, mimicking the movements of Kṛṣṇa by striking their palms with the tips of their hands like palm leaves.
Joyfully imitating his dance, song, graceful gestures, smiles, and glances,
those women of Vraja sported with him.
Singing that sweet song, perfected through their devotion, those excellent women went to Vraja and wandered happily, with Dāmodara as their sole refuge.
Devoted to Dāmodara, the women who had gone to Vraja lived happily; with their limbs smeared with dried cow-dung and dust, they followed after Kṛṣṇa,
delighting him just as joyful female elephants delight a male elephant.
Other women, their faces beaming with smiles, drink him in with eyes blossoming with emotion; insatiable, those women with eyes like those of a black antelope gaze upon Kṛṣṇa.
Beholding his face, other cowherd girls, thirsty and longing for pleasure, drink from him at night while engaged in the midst of amorous dalliance.
As he cried out "Alas! Alas!", those beautiful women, being greatly delighted, caught the words emerging from his voice as they were uttered by Dāmodara with conciliation.
The beautiful hair of those cowherd women, with its parting knotted together, became disheveled upon the tips of their breasts as they were overwhelmed with thoughts of love.
Then Dāmodara, longing for amorous sport, took hold of some of them.
In this way, the charming cowherd women delighted Kṛṣṇa;
adorned and overwhelmed with passion, they sang most sweetly.
Kṛṣṇa too, with eyes as red as honey and increasing the joy of the gopīs,
drank in their faces— Viṣṇu, causing his bee-like eyes to flutter.
Taking two other garments, Kṛṣṇa, his eyes rolling with intoxication, kissed one cowherd girl and then embraced another.
Govinda, who knows the ways of amorous play, lay with one woman;
having taken the garments of another, he drank her beautiful face as he looked upon it;
and Keśava, Govinda, scratched another with his sharp fingernails.
Then Govinda, disguised in the dress of a cowherd, seized another by the hair, lifted up her face with ease, and embraced her.
Having embraced one woman, he let go of her and released another;
while she looked on, he delighted one, and he took his pleasure with another.
Having summoned one woman, the Lord of Gods dallied with another;
then, suddenly seizing her again, he dallied with her in their very presence.

Abandoning their own husbands, those beautiful women, the gopīs, sought refuge in Hari alone, thinking, "He indeed is our eldest and most excellent. And they attained the highest state of devotion toward Kṛṣṇa, the Lord of the gods of gods.
Thus, adorned by the circles of gopīs, that Kṛṣṇa rejoiced happily during the autumnal nights when the moon was shining.
Chapter 64,
transliterated and collated with the Viṣṇupurāṇa (ViP) and Brahmāṇḍapurāṇa (BrP) by Utz Podzeit,
extracted from the collation and edited by Peter Schreiner; March 4.
2002. Not yet proofread.
Vaiśampāyana said:
Once, at the middle of the night, while Kṛṣṇa was intent upon amorous pleasure, [the following occurred].
Terrifying the cow-pens with his rutting state, he was seen unharmed.
Resembling a cloud of embers from the fire of nirvāṇa, with sharp horns and eyes like the sun, his feet had tips as sharp as razors; he was Time itself, like another personified Death.
Licking his lips repeatedly with his tongue with a grinding sound,
his tail tossed haughtily, and the muscles of his shoulders firm and taut.
With a hump as high as a mountain peak, difficult to surpass in size,
his body smeared with excrement and urine, he was a source of great terror to the cows.
He had broad hips, a thick face, firm knees, and a large belly;
his gait was like the swaying of a horn, and he was distinguished by a long skin-hanging from his neck.
He was swift among those who mount cattle, his face marked by the striking of trees;
with the tips of his horns ready for battle, he was the slayer of hostile bulls.
For there is a Daitya named Ariṣṭa, of terrible appearance,
who, in the form of a bull, runs about through the cow-pens.
Arrogantly, he went out of season, causing the destruction of the calves in the cows' wombs; and being fickle, he proceeded to mate with the young cows that had calved for the first time.
With his horns as weapons, that fierce and intoxicated bull, while attacking the cows,
found no pleasure in the cow-pens except for fighting.
Then, after some time, that bull— exceedingly powerful and intoxicated with pride— arrived before Keśava, having fallen under the power of Vaivasvata;
there, being fierce with rut, he began to violently harass the cows.
At that very time, however, an evil-minded being stationed on the path of Vaivasvata terrified the cows that were in the vicinity of Kṛṣṇa.
Like a thundering great cloud accompanied by Indra’s lightning bolt,
that mighty bull rendered the cow-pen devoid of bulls, calves, and young heifers.
As that great bull charged from afar, bellowing loudly,
Kṛṣṇa Govinda— confounding him with the sound of clapping hands and lion-like roars—
rushed toward the Daitya who was in the form of a bull.
Seeing Kṛṣṇa, that bull, its tail and eyes bristling with excitement,
bellowed in anger, desiring a fight at the sound of the clapping of hands.
Seeing the bull-demon rushing toward him with upturned horns,
Kṛṣṇa did not move from that spot, remaining as immovable as a mountain.
Fixing his gaze upon Kṛṣṇa’s flanks and baring his fangs, the bull,
longing for Kṛṣṇa’s death, suddenly sprang forward.
As that bull, resembling black collyrium, charged toward him, Kṛṣṇa— himself like a bull— received the difficult-to-restrain beast as it came head-on.
Engaged with Kṛṣṇa like a great bull with a bull,
he then discharged froth from his mouth with a loud noise.
With their limbs locked together in battle, those two, Kṛṣṇa and the bull,
shone like two clouds joined together at the onset of the rainy season.
Having destroyed his pride and strength, and having placed his foot between his horns,
he squeezed Ariṣṭa’s throat as if it were a piece of wet cloth.
Then, having again uprooted his left horn like the staff of Yama, he struck him in the face with that very same horn; being severely struck, he died.
With his horns shattered, his face broken, and his shoulders crushed, the Dānava fell,
vomiting blood like a rain-cloud discharging its torrents.
Seeing the proud bull-demon slain by Govinda, all living beings praised that deed of his, exclaiming, "Excellent! Excellent!"
And that Upendra, having slain the bull at the onset of night, shone once again with his lovely face and eyes resembling lotuses.
All those cowherds as well, filled with joy, waited upon the lotus-eyed Kṛṣṇa, just as the immortals in heaven wait upon Śakra.
Chapter 65,
transliterated and collated with the Viṣṇupurāṇa (ViP) and Brahmāṇḍapurāṇa (BrP) by Utz Podzeit,
extracted from the collation and edited by Peter Schreiner; March 4.
2002. Not yet proof-read.
Vaiśampāyana said: Having heard that Kṛṣṇa had gone to Vraja and was growing like a blazing fire...
Then Kaṃsa became agitated, suspecting that danger was imminent.
When Pūtanā had been slain, when Kāliya had been defeated,
when Dhenuka had been brought to destruction, and when Pralamba had been struck down;
When Govardhana had been upheld, when Indra’s command had been rendered fruitless,
and when the cows had likewise been protected by that most praiseworthy deed;
When Ariṣṭa, the humped bull, had been slain, while the cowherds were rejoicing,
and when destruction was visible and a great danger was at hand.
Having heard of that inconceivable deed performed by the boy through the uprooting of two trees— a feat beyond the capacity of a child— while his enemies were growing in power.
The Lord of Mathurā considered himself as one who had met with misfortune; with his senses and vital spirits deprived of consciousness, he became like one whose life-breath had departed.
Then, O lord of men, that ruler of fierce commands gathered his kinsmen together at night in Mathurā, while the city was still and silent.
And having summoned Vasudeva, who was radiant like a god, as well as Kṛṣṇa the Yādava,
Satyaka, Dāruka, and also the younger brother of Kṛṣṇa;
Bhoja, Vaitaraṇa, and the mighty Vikadru;
King Bhayesakha and Vipṛthu of great glory.
Babhru, the lord of liberality, and Kṛtavarman as well,
and Bhūritejas, the unshakable, and Bhūriśravas too.
Having addressed all these Yādavas, saying "Listen!",
the king, the son of Ugrasena and lord of Mathurā, spoke.
Sirs, you are knowers of all affairs, experts in all scriptures,
skilled in the principles of legal procedure, and promoters of the three aims of life.
They were performers of their duties, resembling the gods of the world;
they stood firm in great conduct, as unshakable as mountains.
Established in great conduct, they were as immovable as mountains;
all were free from deceitful behavior and were diligent in their duties toward their elders.
All were masters of royal counsel, and all had reached the further shore of archery.
They were lamps of glory for the worlds, desiring to proclaim the meaning of the Vedas;
they possessed innate knowledge of the stages of life (āśramas) and had reached the further shore of the sequence of the social classes (varṇas).
They were eloquent speakers, well-disciplined, leaders who possessed insight into policy,
destroyers of enemy kingdoms, and protectors of those seeking refuge.
In this way, by you— whose conduct is unimpaired, who are illustrious,
and ever-increasing in excellence— even the heavens would be graced, let alone the earth.
Your conduct is like that of the sages, your power like that of the Maruts,
your wrath like that of the Rudras, and your brilliance like that of the Aṅgirases.
The great Yadu clan, which was turning away from its duty, has been supported by you heroes of renowned fame,
just as the surface of the earth is supported by mountains.
While you were thus engaged and acting in accordance with my will,
why was my growing misfortune overlooked by you?
This one known as Kṛṣṇa, the son of the cowherd Nanda in Vraja,
like a growing rain-cloud, cuts away our very roots.
Because of me alone— who am without ministers, empty of spies, and blind—
Nandagopa has hidden that son in his house.
Like a neglected disease, like a cloud being filled with rain,
or like a thundering cloud at the end of the hot season, that evil-souled one increases in power.
I do not know his course, nor his yoga, nor his ultimate resort—
he who was born in the house of Nanda the cowherd and whose deeds are miraculous.
We do not know what being has arisen as this offspring of the gods;
he is inferred from his super-divine and non-human deeds.
In his childhood, the unassailable Pūtanā was drunk by the infant while he was still at her breast, desiring to suckle, together with her very life-breaths.
In the same way, while lying upon his bed, that boy effortlessly turned over the cart with his big toe.
Likewise, as a mere child,
he broke two exceedingly large twin *arjuna* trees that grew together with their roots and branches;
and similarly, he subdued the serpent Kāliya in the pool of the Yamunā.
The son of Nanda Gopa was led from the lake to the subterranean realm (rasātala) and made invisible in an instant; yet, having performed a yogic feat, he rose up once more.
Dhenuka was struck down from the top of a palm tree, deprived of life;
his elder brother was the exceedingly powerful and evil-minded Balabhadra,
whom even the gods were unable to gaze upon in combat when he was Pralamba.
He was struck with a single fist by a child, like an ordinary man.
Having thwarted the festival of Vāsava and rendered the rain born of Indra's wrath waterless,
he held up Mount Govardhana for the sake of Gokula.
But Ariṣṭa was slain and made powerless and hornless in Vraja;
by what being in human form could Mount Govardhana have been lifted up? I do not know the truth of this, for it is truly a marvel.
This entire rain, created by Vāsava, was most marvelous;
it was stopped for seven days—what could be more wonderful than this?
One who is not a child, assuming the state of childhood, delights in the play of children.
This is the sequence of deeds of that dweller of the cow-pens;
and the danger from Keśin is certainly imminent for both him and me.
And my death in a former life was surely this one from my previous body;
for he stands before me as if desiring battle.
Where is this inauspicious state of being a cowherd and human life, so weak against death;
and where is the play in my Vraja, performed with divine power?
"Aha! Having concealed his own form with a lowly body, this is some god who delights here like a fire situated in a cremation ground."
"O best of the Yādavas, speak with focused minds! O bulls among the Yadus, I consider this other matter also worthy of being heard.
Just as I know it, so do you know every word of it."
For it is heard that in ancient times, Viṣṇu, on account of a certain purpose for the gods,
assumed the form of a dwarf and seized this earth.
It is said that Keśava then gave it to the king of the gods;
having assumed the form of a lion,
the powerful Viṣṇu slew Hiraṇyakaśipu, the grandfather of the Dānavas.
Having slain the Dānava king in battle,
Hari assumed an inconceivable form on the summit of the White Mountain; he was the one who,
in ancient times, having struck down Tripura, drove the Daityas away by means of Bhava.
Protected by the preceptor’s son, Bhārgava, who was indeed Aṅgiras,
he entered into an Asura illusion and brought about a drought.
The infinite, eternal, thousand-faced, and imperishable God,
assuming the form of a boar, lifted the earth from the ocean.
Hari gave the earth, together with its mountains and forests, to Śakra.
Formerly, when the nectar had been produced, Viṣṇu assumed a female form and engaged in a most terrible battle between the gods and the asuras.

Furthermore, it is heard in the sacred tradition that in ancient times, during the encounter between the gods and the daityas for the sake of the nectar of immortality, Viṣṇu supported Mount Mandara upon his back as the tortoise Akūpāra.
Having formerly assumed a contemptible dwarf body,
he seized the three worlds— the abode of the gods— with three strides;
and having divided his splendor into four parts, he established them in the house of the son of Daśaratha.
He who was indeed known as Rāma then utterly destroyed Rāvaṇa.
That very Lord Viṣṇu, having become the delighter of Bhṛgu’s lineage,
slew the son of Kṛtavīrya with his sharpened battle-axe.
Having slain the preeminent kṣatriyas twenty-one times over,
he is said to have given the earth to Kāśyapa at that horse sacrifice;
thus, indeed, having resorted to various forms through deceit, he acted in this manner.
He accomplishes his own task for the sake of achieving the purpose of the gods.
Therefore, this must surely be Viṣṇu, or Śakra, or the best of the Maruts,
who has arrived with the desire to accomplish my purpose— just as Nārada told me.
O Lord, my mind has doubts regarding Vasudeva; it is because of his extraordinary intelligence that we have fallen into a state of cowardice.
For I encountered Nārada in the Khaṭvāṅga forest;
that brahmin spoke these words to me once again.
The great effort you exerted for the sake of placing Kaṃsa in the womb has been rendered fruitless by Vasudeva through his actions during the night.
Know that the girl whom you struck against a stone with a metal vessel at night is the daughter of Yaśodā, and Kṛṣṇa is the son of Vasudeva.
At night, these two fetuses were indeed exchanged for your destruction by Vasudeva, an enemy in the guise of a friend.
That maiden, however, [resided] with Yaśodā on the Vindhya, the best of mountains,
after having slain the two Dānavas, Śumbha and Niśumbha, who roamed the mountains.
Having received consecration, she is the bestower of boons and is attended by hosts of spirits;
she is worshipped by terrible bandits, for she is fond of great animal sacrifices.
It was adorned with two jars filled with liquor and meat,
and decorated with peacock ornaments and clusters of variegated plumage.
The forest resounded with the cries of proud cocks and was filled with flocks of goats and non-aggressive birds.
It resounded with the roars of lions, tigers, and boars;
it was dense with trees and thickets, and surrounded on all sides by vast forests.

On the Vindhya mountain, her abode was fashioned by his own splendor, adorned with divine censers, yak-tail fans, and mirrors, and made to resound with hundreds of the sounds of celestial musical instruments.
In that delightful place, she who constantly inspires terror in her enemies dwells with supreme joy,
honored even by the gods.
Regarding this son of Nanda Gopa who is called Kṛṣṇa,
Nārada told me that there is a very great deed which is the cause [of his name].
From Vasudeva, indeed, a second Vāsudeva shall arise;
for he will be both your natural death and your kinsman.
That very Vāsudeva, the powerful son of Vasudeva,
is my kinsman by dharma, yet in my heart he is an enemy who brings about my end.
For just as a crow, greedy for meat, perches upon someone's head with its feet and pecks at that very person's eyes with its beak.
In this very same way, this Vasudeva, along with his sons and kinsmen,
cuts at my roots while feeding off my side.
Even the murder of a fetus, the killing of a cow, or even the killing of a woman can be overcome;
however, there is no world for an ungrateful person, especially not for one who has been a kinsman.
He who, out of attachment, cherishes a cruel affection for an ungrateful person soon follows the path trodden by the fallen.
The path leading to the hells must be traversed by that person who,
though himself sinless, has a sinful heart and persists in committing evil.
He goes to a terrible hell from which return is difficult to achieve.
Whether it be I, or my own praiseworthy kinsmen, or that son who is even more praiseworthy,
[all this was done] by you through self-restraints, service to your guru, and out of a desire for the welfare of your relatives.
During a terrible conflict among elephants, the plants meet their destruction;
yet when the battle has ceased, they eat together once more in the great forest.
Likewise, when a time of division arises even among kinsmen,
he who seeks an opening for harm is slain, and his own kin undergoes a transformation [of hostility].
Indeed, you are Kali, nourished by me for the sake of destruction; though I knew this, I did so.
Go, go as you please, O Vasudeva, lowest of men!
That miserable morsel which was given by you, knowing [the truth],
would have been better for me had it been given to dogs,
since you are so intensely hostile toward this family of Vasudeva.
He is impatient, hostile by nature, always evil-minded, and deceitful.
"It is only right, O fool Vasudeva, that you have brought this lamentable ruin upon the Yadu clan; for it was in vain that you, an old man, were placed at its head by me."
One with white hair is not necessarily an elder of a hundred years;
he whose intellect is matured is indeed the eldest among men.
One does not become an elder simply because one's head is gray.
You, however, are harsh in character and not very learned in wisdom;
you are old in years alone, like an autumnal cloud.
Moreover, O Vasudeva of vain intellect, you think well of this:
"Once Kaṃsa is slain, my son shall protect Mathurā."
"Your hopes are shattered, O vainly aged one; for you have indeed deliberated falsely.
There is no one who desires to live who can stand before me."
Since you, with a healthy mind, desire to strike one who trusts you,
I shall repay that deed while your two sons look on.
Neither the killing of an elder nor the killing of a Brahmin woman has ever been committed by me before, nor shall I ever do so, especially against a kinsman.
Here you were born and raised; you were nurtured by my father, the husband of my paternal aunt, and the foremost elder of the Yadus.
He was renowned in a great and celebrated lineage of universal monarchs,
and was honored for the sake of his preceptor by the virtuous Yadus, who were devoted to righteousness.
"What shall we all do, having fallen into reproach among the virtuous,
since such is the conduct of you, the leader of the Yadu host?"
Either my death or victory will come about through the wicked policies of Vasudeva;
for the men of the Yadus, obscured by his influence, shall fall among the virtuous.
For by you, while devising a means for my slaughter in battle,
an untrustworthy deed was committed and the Yādavas were made objects of reproach.
An unappeasable enmity has arisen between me and Kṛṣṇa;
when peace comes to one of us, the Yādavas will attain peace.
Stay or go, O fool, as you please from my side.
"This scion of the Yadu lineage has risen up to slay his own kin;
O best of the Yādavas, let there be no such reproach in the world.
Otherwise, you deserve to be killed—of this there is no doubt."
"Let this patron go quickly from Vraja to bring Nanda the cowherd and the cowherds here, by my command, to pay tribute."
And Nandagopa should indeed be told: "Having taken the annual tax, come quickly to the city accompanied by all the cowherds."
Kaṃsa, together with his servants and his family priest, indeed desires to see both Kṛṣṇa and Saṃkarṣaṇa, the two sons of Vasudeva.
I have heard that these two, skilled in combat, fight with the very artifice of Time on the field; they possess firm counter-strikes and are endowed with extensive exertion.
We too have two wrestlers ready, who take pride in victory;
both of them, being skilled in combat, shall wrestle against those two.
I must certainly see those two boys who resemble immortals— the preeminent sons of my father’s sister, who dwell in Vraja yet now roam the forest.
And it should be announced in that Vraja and to those living nearby:
"The joyful King will indeed cause the festival known as Dhanurmaha to be performed."
Let the cowherds dwell there in the vicinity as they please,
so that everything may remain secure for the sake of the invited people.
For the purpose of providing milk-rice, clarified butter, curd, and the cream of curd according to desire, and for the cooking of food;
"O Akrūra, go quickly and, by my command, bring Saṃkarṣaṇa and Kṛṣṇa; for I have a great curiosity to see them."
If they come by those two means, my supreme pleasure will have been achieved;
but having seen those two of great prowess, I shall do what is beneficial.
"Even if, upon hearing these words of mine spoken thus,
they do not depart at the proper time, they both shall be punished by me."
Indeed, conciliation alone is the primary and foremost policy toward children; by sweetness alone will those two dullards quickly bring themselves back to the right path.
O Akrūra, O you of noble vows, grant me this supreme favor which is so difficult to obtain,
unless you have been instigated by Vasudeva.
"This must indeed be done in such a way that those two will come," having said this,
Kaṃsa, the lord of Madhurā, fell silent;
yet Vasudeva, who was like a Vasu, continued to be thus reviled.
He held himself as motionless as the ocean.
Though being struck by the word-arrows of the short-sighted Kamsa,
he meditated on forgiveness within his mind and did not utter a reply.
But those who saw him being hurled there repeatedly spoke softly with downcast faces, saying again and again, "Fie! Fie!"
But Akrūra, possessed of great splendor, knowing by his divine vision that they had seen water as if he were thirsty, became joyful at having been sent.
I behold the Lord of the gods of gods, who bears the conch, the discus, and the mace;
that Īśvara, the Lord of all, who is attainable through yoga by yogins.
I behold the youthful Govinda, adorned with the dress of a cowherd,
accompanied by Saṃkarṣaṇa, his eyes resembling lotus petals.
Today my birth has become fruitful, since Hari has been seen by me.

I shall behold that Lord of the World, whose limbs are variegated with peacock-ornaments, who is accompanied by the sound of a lute made from a gourd, and who rests gracefully upon the breasts of the cowherd girls.
If he looks upon me with eyes truly filled with love,
then the birth of me who beholds that Hari becomes fruitful.
Upon seeing whom all the sages desist from the power of their asceticism,
he— the best among those skilled in speech— will say something to me.
Having reflected thus in his mind, he became even swifter in his departure;
at that very moment, the lord of donors himself set out from Mathurā, full of joy, to see the lotus-eyed one.

Vaiśampāyana said:
Having seen Yadu, the bull of the Yadus, thus insulted, all those foremost of the Yadus—
Pressing his ears with their hands, they considered him to be one whose life had departed.
But Andhaka, his mind undisturbed, being the best among speakers, spoke with vigor and conciseness these unaltered words to Kaṃsa out of fortitude.
"O son, this exertion of speech of yours is, in my opinion, unworthy;
it is improper and censured by the virtuous, especially among kinsmen."
If you are not a Yādava, then listen for a moment to what is being said: O hero, the Yādavas certainly do not make you a Yādava by force.
"O son, the Vṛṣṇis are not to be praised, they whose leader you are;
for a king born of the Ikṣvāku lineage has turned back and established his own dynasty."
Whether you are a Bhoja, a Yādava, or Kaṃsa himself—whatever you may be—your head is yours by nature, my dear; you may become one with matted hair or one who is shaven.
But this Ugrasena is truly pitiable, he who is the disgrace of our lineage,
by whom you have been begotten as such a son through his base birth.
O dear one, the wise do not proclaim their own virtues;
when virtues are spoken of by another, even those consistent with the meaning of the Vedas, they become secondary.
"This Yadu lineage on earth is to be censured by all rulers,
for you, a foolish child who brings an end to your family, are their leader."
Although you are "good" because of these words spoken by you as "well said," no purpose has been accomplished by your speech, and you have merely revealed yourself.
Who would consider the disparagement of a teacher who is free from pride and honored even by the great to be auspicious? It would be like considering the killing of a brahmin to be a good deed.
O dear one, the elders are indeed to be honored and approached like the foremost sacrificial fires;
for their anger could consume even the worlds within them.
O dear one, by a wise man who is self-controlled and always uplifted in spirit,
the course of dharma must be pursued like the movement of a fish in water.
But you alone, out of pride, here burn the elders— who are like fire—
with words that strike their vital spots, like an oblation offered without mantras.
And if you reproach Vasudeva for the sake of his son, I condemn your false prattle— your wretched speech.
Even toward a son who is cruel, a father should never become cruel;
for even if a son is cruel toward his father, how could a father be cruel to his son?
Indeed, for the sake of their sons, fathers undergo even the most grievous calamities.
For sons indeed deliver their father from dire calamity.
If the child son was concealed by Vasudeva at that time,
and if you consider it an act that should not have been done, then ask your own father.
By reviling Vasudeva and censuring the Yadu lineage,
you have acquired the poison born of enmity toward the sons of the Yādavas.
If Vasudeva committed an improper act out of love for his son,
why was you, a mere infant, not destroyed by Ugrasena?
Furthermore, because a son always protects his ancestors from the hell named Put,
people who know the Dharma call a son "putra."
If a son is protected by his father, tell me now, what fault is there?
O fool, tell me why you were protected by your father!
By these words of yours, the Yādavas have been made your enemies;
for Kṛṣṇa is a Yādava by birth, as is the youth Saṃkarṣaṇa,
and you too were held in check by those two with hearts full of enmity.
Indeed, the hearts of all the Yadus here have been shaken,
now that Vasudeva has been insulted by you and Vāsudeva provoked to anger.
"O Kṛṣṇa, if we were virtuous people, we would all abandon you because of our hatred for you and because of your abuse of Vasudeva; rather,
it is we who are the wicked ones here, known in this world as the lowest of men."
"O son, if we are now able to abandon you,
there is no doubt that you will abandon us all and depart;
for these inauspicious omens portend danger for you."
We infer from various signs that the intense appearance of snakes and the dreams occurring at the end of the night portend widowhood for the city.
"This terrible planet Aṅgāraka, scraping at Svātī in the sky with its rays, has moved in a retrograde course; thus do the twice-born proclaim."
The evening twilight was pervaded by the terrible splendor of Budha;
indeed, Śukra performed an *aticāra* (transit) upon the path of Vaiśvānara.
By Ketu, the smoke-bannered one, the thirteen lunar mansions beginning with Bharaṇī are shattered; they no longer follow the Moon.
A jackal, having emerged from the cremation ground, breathes forth a rain of glowing coals.
At both twilights, the terrible one wanders around the city, crying out repeatedly.
With the sound of a thunderclap and a falling meteor, the earth fell to the surface of the ground; the world shook at an improper time, as did the peaks of the mountains.
At the morning twilight, those rays at the edge of the halo seize the sun;
and these beasts and birds cry out as they move in a contrary direction.
The sun was eclipsed by Svarbhānu, and day became night;
the quarters of the sky were pervaded by smoke and portents, struck by dry thunderbolts.
Thick clouds, accompanied by lightning and thunder, pour forth blood;
the deities have been shaken from their places and the birds abandon the trees.
Indeed, all those inauspicious omens that astrologers declare portend the destruction of the king, we truly perceive them all.
And you too, hating your own kin and turning your back on the duties of a king,
have become one whose anger arises without cause and who stands in the very presence of danger.
O evil-minded one, since you out of delusion insult Vasudeva— who is like a god, aged, and firm in his vows— how can there be any peace for your own soul?
Indeed, that affection we have for you which has been directed toward you, we truly abandon today; since you are detrimental to our own lineage, we shall no longer serve you.
Blessed indeed is that lord of donors who shall behold Kṛṣṇa, the performer of untainted deeds, whose eyes are like the petals of a white lotus, as he has gone to the forest.
He is both childlike and possessed of the conduct of the non-childlike; he is the Lord, the sovereign of all;
he is the object of meditation for yogis, ever-visible, the existent one whose nature comprises both the real and the unreal.
Salutations again and again to him who shall behold that Kṛṣṇa.
Salutations again and again to him who shall behold that God Hari— the first of the first, both with parts and without parts.
We ourselves are joyless because we have always been protected by you;
how can there be peace or delight for those whose lord you are, O unfortunate one?
For this lineage of the Yadus has had its roots severed on your account.
Kṛṣṇa, having summoned his kinsmen, will bring about a reconciliation.
That has already been forgiven by the wise Vasudeva;
his discernment is ripened by time, so speak whatever you wish.
But it pleases me, Kaṃsa, that you go to the abode of Kṛṣṇa accompanied by Vasudeva; may you find favor with him.
Ñ, V, B, Dn, Ds, T3.4 insert the colophon. While D6, S (except T3.4), G(ed. insert: [k]
"Otherwise, Kaṃsa, there is no escape for you; this is certain.
Having heard Andhaka’s words, Kaṃsa, his eyes bloodshot with rage, entered his own residence without saying anything at all out of anger.
And all those Yādavas, having heard the full account, went to their respective homes with their anxieties dispelled, proclaiming the wicked deeds of Kaṃsa.
