Vaiśampāyana said: Akrūra also, having been thus commanded and longing for a sight of Kṛṣṇa, [set out].
He departed on his preeminent chariot, which moved with a speed equal to thought.
Indeed, auspicious signs appearing on Kṛṣṇa’s own limbs portend a reunion with a kinsman who is like a father to him.
Furthermore, the king of the Māthuras, Aṅgirasena, had previously dispatched a messenger to Keśin for the purpose of having him killed on account of Upendra.
Having heard the words of the messenger, that unassailable Keśin, who causes affliction to men,
went to Vṛndāvana and began to harass the cowherds.
Devouring human flesh, enraged and possessed of wicked prowess,
that untamable horse-demon is causing a great slaughter.
Feeding on the flesh of cattle, Durdama was like an unrestrained lion who roamed at will, slaughtering cows along with their herdsmen.
That forest, covered with the bones of men, resembled a cremation ground;
for there dwelt that evil-minded Keśin, the Dānava who had taken the form of a horse.
With its hooves it tears up the earth; with its speed it shatters trees;
with its neighing it vies with the wind; and with its leaps it traverses the sky.
Exceedingly grown, intoxicated, and fierce, this forest-roaming stallion has his mane bristling; he follows the conduct of Kaṃsa.
By that deed of Saudāsa, the horse-demon who sought to slay all the cowherds, that entire forest was turned into a desolate wilderness.
Corrupted by that wicked conduct, that great forest was no longer frequented by men, nor even by herds of cattle who subsist on the forest.
The path leading to his realm has been made impassable by him, who,
having strayed from right conduct through intoxication, devours human flesh in abundance.
Once, at the break of day, driven by the law of time and enraged by the pursuit of the word "man," he went to the settlement of cowherds.
Seeing him, the cowherds and the women, together with their children,
fled while crying out, having taken refuge in Kṛṣṇa, the Lord of the World, as their protector.
At the sound of their weeping and the crying of the cowherds,
Kṛṣṇa granted them fearlessness and rushed toward Keśin.
And Keśin, with his neck outstretched and his teeth and eyes bared,
went toward Govinda, neighing loudly and impetuous with speed.
Beholding the Dānava Keśin as he charged toward him,
Govinda went forth to meet him, just as a rain-cloud approaches the moon.
But seeing Kṛṣṇa standing nearby,
the cowherds, who regarded him as a mere human, spoke to Kṛṣṇa out of a desire for his welfare.
"Kṛṣṇa, Kṛṣṇa, O mighty-armed one, increaser of the joy of your kinsmen!
You are the bestower of fearlessness upon the worlds; protect us, especially me.
Kṛṣṇa, dear one, this vilest of horses is certainly not acting with impunity against you."
"You are a child to be approached, while he is a wicked man who is difficult to overcome."
O dear one, this Dānava is Kaṃsa’s innate life-breath moving outside his body;
he is the most excellent among the lords of horses and is peerless in battle.
He is the terrifier of enemy armies, possessed of great strength among horses,
well-versed in meditation for all beings, and foremost among those who perform evil deeds.
Having heard those words of the cowherds as they spoke, Madhusūdana,
the slayer of enemies, set his mind upon fighting with Keśin.
Then, circling in mandalas to the left and to the right with both its hooves, that horse, out of rage, tore up the trees.
From his mouth, where the long mane hung down and the region of the shoulders was densely covered,
streams resembling the waves of clouds flowed forth, shedding water born of his wrath.
He showered forth foam from his mouth, enveloped in dust,
like the moon shedding mist upon the sky during the winter season.
With the spray from his neighing, mixed with foam emerging from his body, he sprinkled Govinda, whose eyes are like lotuses, on all sides.
With the dust raised by the removal of his hoof, which was pale as sweet-scented powder,
that horse made Kṛṣṇa’s hair appear reddish-brown.
Leaping and galloping with his feet, scratching the earth with his hooves,
and gnashing his teeth, Keśin rushed toward Kṛṣṇa.
But Keśin, that best of horses, having become entangled with Kṛṣṇa,
struck him on the chest with his two forefeet.
Again and again, that powerful Dānava struck Kṛṣṇa of immeasurable energy with terrible blows from his flanks using his hooves,
and indeed with his own formidable mouth, which was armed with sharp fangs.
The enraged horse bit into the armpit of Kṛṣṇa.
With his long, maned tail, Keśin, joined with Kṛṣṇa,
shone like the sun in the sky when it is joined with a cloud.
And the powerful horse, his prowess doubled by the fury of Vāsudeva, desired to strike his chest with its own chest with great speed.
As he was thus arrogant, the powerful Kṛṣṇa, of immeasurable prowess,
extended his arm and, filled with rage, thrust it into the demon's mouth.
Unable indeed to swallow or even to chew that arm,
Kṛṣṇa, laughing, playfully extended his own coiled arm straight into the mouth of the Dānava.
Vomiting frothy blood with teeth that were loosened from their sockets.
With his lips split apart and his cheeks torn asunder, his two eyes were distorted and rolled back, their sockets wide open and their lashes loosened from their bonds.
With his jaw thrust out, possessed by a spirit, his eyes smeared with flowing blood,
his ears pricked up, and his mind lost, Keśin writhed about violently.
Leaping up repeatedly and voiding urine at every step, his hair became moist with sweat; and being exhausted, his feet lost all power of movement.
But Kṛṣṇa’s arm, resting against Keśin’s mouth,
shone like a cloud curved by the rays of the half-moon at the end of the summer heat.
And Keśin, his limbs exhausted from the struggle with Kṛṣṇa,
shone like the weary moon at dawn resting upon Mount Meru.
Shaken from his mouth by Kṛṣṇa’s arms,
Keśin’s various teeth fell to the earth,
like fragments of white clouds devoid of water in autumn.
But that Keśin was utterly exhausted by Kṛṣṇa, whose actions are effortless.
Then, stretching out his own arm, he tore it off with great force.
Torn by Kṛṣṇa’s arm in battle, his face disfigured,
the Dānava Keśin then uttered a great roar in agony.
Reeling with his limbs collapsing, vomiting blood from his mouth,
his body severely mangled like a mountain with its flank severed.
With his mouth wide open, that most fierce asura fell by Kṛṣṇa’s arm like a serpent cut in two;
split apart by the span of the arm, he fell swiftly with great force.
With his body mangled by the arm [of Kṛṣṇa], Keśin’s form appeared as utterly terrifying as that of a beast slain by the wielder of the Pināka bow.
With his two halves resembling troughs filled with flesh, as if in the abode of the wielder of the Pināka bow,
Keśin— now split in two, with two legs, two backs, two tails, two ears,
two eyes, and two nostrils— lay quivering on the earth.
With its lower half severed by the vajra, his arm lay upon the earth like two mountains;
and Kṛṣṇa’s arm, mangled by Keśin’s teeth,
shone like a great palmyra tree in the forest marked by the tusks of a lordly elephant.
Having slain Keśin in battle and having divided him into parts,
Kṛṣṇa, whose eyes were like lotus petals, stood right there, smiling.
Seeing that Keśin slain, all those cowherds and cowherd women became joyful; their obstacles were destroyed and their exhaustion was gone.
And they greeted the illustrious Dāmodara with affectionate words, honoring him again and again according to his station and his age.
"Oh, father, a great deed has been done! This thorn of the world, this Daitya who roams the earth, has been slain by Kṛṣṇa while he was mounted in the form of a horse."
O dear one, by slaying this horse Keśin in battle, you have ensured that Vṛndāvana is secure and fit to be served by all men and birds, while destroying this evil.
Many of our cowherds have been slain, as well as the cows and their affectionate calves;
many other people from the countryside have also been killed by this evil-minded one.
It is said that this evildoer is now intent on bringing about the dissolution;
having rendered the world of men devoid of humans, he desires to live as he pleases.
No one who wishes to live is able to stand before him,
even among the hosts of gods, much less upon the surface of the earth.
Thus did those cowherds praise the lotus-eyed Kṛṣṇa.
Then the sage Nārada, a brahmin who travels through the air, vanished from sight and said:
"I am pleased, O Viṣṇu, Lord of Gods! Kṛṣṇa, Kṛṣṇa!"—thus he spoke repeatedly.
Homage to you, O Lord of the World, God of gods, Janārdana!
Homage to you, homage to you, O wielder of the conch, the discus, and the mace!
Salutations to you, whose form is knowledge, to Keśava, the wielder of the discus;
salutations to the primordial seed, who is beyond qualities yet the very self of all qualities.
Salutations to the thousand-headed one; I bow down to you, O Janārdana.
I prostrate before you, the Lord of the World; salutations to you who possess a divine form.
"Salutations be unto you, O Hṛṣīkeśa; protect us from all sides, O Hari!
Having thus praised the Lord of the World, he spoke these words once more:
"This difficult deed which has been performed with the intent to slay Keśin—"
This is appropriate for you alone, whether in the triple heaven or even for the Three-Eyed One.
"O father, eager for battle and with a satisfied inner soul,
I have come here from heaven to witness this combat between man and horse."
I have witnessed your deeds, such as the slaying of Pūtanā;
however, O Govinda, I am especially gratified by this particular deed of yours.
Even Mahendra, the slayer of Bala, fears this horse as it assumes a terrible form, for Keśin is evil-minded.
That he was split in two by you with your long-jointed arm—
this death has been ordained for his end by the Source of the Universe.
"Since Keśin has been slain by you, therefore listen to my command:
you shall become renowned in the world by the name Keśava."
"May it be well with you in this world; I shall depart quickly.
You are capable; do not delay in performing whatever duties remain for you."
When you are occupied with other tasks, the denizens of heaven, relying on your strength, sport as if mocking men.
The time for the ocean of battle in Bhārata is drawing near;
the wars of kings destined for the celestial realm have come within reach of their hands.
The paths leading upward for those ascending in celestial chariots have been cleared in the sky;
even in the world of Śakra, space is being partitioned for the rulers of the earth.
O Keśava, when Ugrasena’s son has been slain and you yourself are established in your position,
that great battle of the rulers of the earth will take place on all sides.
And kings will take refuge in you, whose deeds are incomparable;
during the time of dissension among rulers, you shall become a partisan.
For while you, O Lord, occupy the royal throne and bear the royal glory,
the other kings will undoubtedly abandon their own splendor due to your power.
O Kṛṣṇa, this is my message to you: "O Lord of the world, through these words you shall attain renown among the deities dwelling in heaven and throughout the entire universe."
"I have witnessed your deed, O Lord, and I have seen you. I shall meet Kaṃsa again once he has been punished; meanwhile, I shall accomplish my own purpose."
"What is the use of saying more? Protect the brahmins as you please!
I know you, O mighty-armed one, to be the deity even of the gods.
Vaiśampāyana said:
Having spoken thus, Nārada then departed into the sky.
Having heard the words of Nārada, the yogi who is celebrated among the gods,
he replied, "So be it," and once again approached the cowherds.
Having approached the cowherds, Kṛṣṇa entered Vraja itself.

Vaiśampāyana said:
Then, as the sun was setting with its rays dimmed, [the following occurred].
In the sky whose surface was reddened by twilight, the moon appeared as a pale orb.
While the birds remained in their nests and the sacrificial fires had been kindled,
all the directions were everywhere slightly shrouded in darkness.
While the inhabitants of the settlements slept and the jackals howled,
the night-stalkers rejoiced, longing for flesh and blood.
At twilight, when the sun had entered the cave of the evening as if it were made of the glow of the *śakragopa* insect, and the hand of the sky was near its setting.
When the time for placing the vessel on the fire had arrived for the householders,
the sacrificial fire was being offered oblations with the Vaikhānasa mantras used by forest-dwellers.
When the cows had returned to the pen and were being milked,
while the milch-cows repeatedly lowed with their calves tied to them;
While the cowherds, with their scattered herds, were likewise calling the cows and raising a great clamor,
the cattle wealth was being driven forward.
When the prepared dried cow-dung cakes were blazing on all sides,
the cowherds arrived with their shoulders laden with bundles of wood.
When the moon had slightly risen and was shining with faint rays,
as the day had passed and the night was but slightly entered.
When the end of the day had arrived and the onset of night had begun,
the fiery splendor of the sun having departed and the gentle luster of the moon having appeared.
At the time of the Agnihotra rite, when the moon is present in its gentle aspect,
and while the junction consisting of Agni and Soma— which pervades the entire world— is occurring;
The sky, blazing with fire in the west and glowing with light in the east,
resembled a mountain on fire, yet was still slightly crowded with clusters of stars.
Proclaiming his beauty of raiment through his birds and his reunion with his kinsmen,
the lord of donors swiftly reached Vraja by means of his chariot.
As soon as he entered, Akrūra repeatedly inquired after the presence of Keśava,
Rauhineya, and Nandagopa.
He beheld in the cow-pen the footprints of Him whose stainless foot-dust is worn upon the crowns of all the world-protectors— footprints that were wonders for the earth.
They are distinguished by the lotus, sword, goad, and other such symbols.
His agitation increased by the joy of seeing him;
with his hair standing on end from love and his eyes clouded by a stream of tears,
he leaped down from his chariot and fell prostrate before them.
"Oh, these are the dust-particles from the feet of the Lord! he exclaimed.
For embodied beings, this much is the true purpose: having abandoned hypocrisy, fear, and grief, [to act] according to the instruction of Hari through the sight and hearing of His signs;
then the Yādava was pointed out by the cowherds as "this is He," saying, "This is that."
Then that mighty one, who was like a treasury of splendor, alighted from the vehicle and entered the house of Nanda Gopa for the sake of lodging.
With a face full of joy and eyes filled with tears,
as he was entering the very gate,
he saw Kṛṣṇa standing among the calves in the cow-pen, like a bull among its calf.
Overcome with joy, that Yādava gazed intently at Viṣṇu with eyes full of emotion, his voice faltering.
Then Akrūra reflected: "Indeed, there is no one like me in this world, for I have beheld this entire Lord of the World."
Nārāyaṇa, who is more minute than the minute and greater than the great, Hari.
"Who in this world has ever seen one like me,
who would address the Lord as 'Come, Keśava, father,' as you, knower of dharma, have spoken?"
Seeing Kṛṣṇa lying on his back, and seeing him again endowed with splendor, though still in his unmanifest youth, Akrūra praised him.
This is that lotus-eyed one, possessing the prowess of a lion and a tiger;
he has the luster of a cloud filled with water and the form of a preeminent mountain.
He was well-adorned with a chest bearing the *śrīvatsa* mark, which was invincible in battles,
and with two arms skillful at destroying his enemies.
Viṣṇu, assuming a physical form that embodies the secret essence of the foremost world,
appeared wearing the dress of a cowherd, with the hair on his body standing erect in thrill.
He was adorned with a head marked by a diadem and possessing the splendor of a royal parasol,
and his ears were graced by two earrings worthy of the finest ornaments.
He was graced by a broad and expansive chest, fit for a necklace,
and by two long, rounded arms.
Clad in garments while his body is consumed by the fire of love, attended upon by thousands of women— this is that eternal Viṣṇu.
The subduer of enemies stood upon the earth with his two feet,
which served as the very foundation of the earth and were capable of traversing the three worlds.
His first hand is seen to be beautiful and like a wheel,
while his second is raised as if desiring to grasp a mace.
Having descended here for the sake of worldly existence, the foremost among the thirty gods, who bears the yoke of leadership, now shines upon the earth, having taken his first step.
This one will indeed be seen by the wise who are skilled in the future;
as a cowherd, he will cause the dwindled Yādava lineage to expand.
And by his splendor, the Yadavas shall fill their lineage by the hundreds and thousands,
like torrents filling the great ocean.
Under his teaching, this entire world shall abide eternally,
with its hostile vassals subdued, flourishing like in the Kṛtayuga.
Having occupied the earth and brought the world under his control,
he will stand above all kings, yet he himself shall not be a king.
Surely, having conquered with three strides, he has become the lord,
just as in former times Purandara became the king of the deities in Triviṣṭapa.
In that very manner, having conquered the earth previously won by him in three strides,
he will undoubtedly establish Ugrasena as king.
This [teaching] is one whose depths of enmity have been wiped away; it has been heard through many inquiries by Brahmins who discourse on Brahman, for this is indeed sung as the ancient [tradition].
For Keśava will become an object of longing for the world,
since his intellect has thus arisen to serve humanity.
But today I shall honor his dwelling according to the prescribed rite;
and in my mind, I shall worship his very nature as Viṣṇu with the appropriate mantras.
"Endowed with mantras, I shall worship you, Viṣṇu, with my mind alone;
for I know this superhuman nature of yours, as well as your manifestation among men, and those others who possess divine vision."
I shall praise the Lord, the Master of the World, Hari in the forms of Varāha and Vāmana;
I bow to the lotus-eyed one who has the form of Nara and Nārāyaṇa;
I bow to Viṣṇu as Vāmana, whose manly prowess pervaded the three worlds.
Therefore, having deliberated with Kṛṣṇa, who knows his own self, during the night,
I shall go together with him and the cowherd community, if he so intends.
Having thus observed Kṛṣṇa in his many forms through various reasons, purposes, and causes,
he entered the assembly hall of Nanda the cowherd together with Kṛṣṇa.
Chapter 69,

Vaiśampāyana said:
He, together with Keśava, entered the house of Nanda the cowherd.
Having summoned the elder cowherds, he who gives immeasurable sacrificial fees spoke to them.
And being pleased, he spoke to Kṛṣṇa, who was united with the son of Rohiṇī:
"O dear one, tomorrow we shall indeed go to the city of Mathurā for our welfare."
And all the cowherd settlements, along with their families and herds,
shall depart at Kaṃsa’s command, having paid the appropriate annual tribute.
We too shall go together, having mounted the chariot;
for that great bow-sacrifice of Kaṃsa will be a magnificent success.
You shall behold that prosperous ceremony and you shall be reunited with your own kinsmen.
Then you two shall meet your father Vasudeva, who is constantly a vessel of sorrow, wretched and exhausted by the slaughter of his sons.
Constantly oppressed by Kaṃsa of evil intellect,
the king was withered at the end of his life, exhausted by sufferings, and reduced to a state of frailty.
Trembling with fear of Kaṃsa and deprived of you both,
he burns day and night with a longing heart.
And I shall see that Devakī, who resembles a goddess, her breasts no longer pressed by her sons, sinking down with her splendor destroyed, O Govinda.
Withering away from grief for her son, intent upon the sight of you,
she is tormented by the sorrow of separation like a cow deprived of her calf.
With eyes perpetually clouded and always clad in soiled garments,
she was like the radiance of the moon seized by the mouth of Rāhu.
Constantly intent upon seeing you and longing for your arrival,
this wretched woman indeed languishes, sinking under the grief caused by your absence.
O Lord, I am unskilled in your rhapsodies, separated from you since childhood,
and ignorant of the beauty of your face, which possesses the luster of the moon.
If Devakī, O Kṛṣṇa, suffers after giving birth to you, what indeed would be the purpose of offspring for her? For childlessness itself would be better.
For women who have no sons, there is indeed prescribed a single sorrow;
but for one who has a son that bears no fruit, she suffers even more through that very offspring.
But she whose son is equal to Śakra and like you in his virtues,
and who grants fearlessness even to her enemies— she does not deserve to grieve.
Your aged mother and father have fallen into the state of servants;
for your sake, they are being reviled by the short-sighted Kaṃsa.
If Devakī is worthy of your respect, like the Earth herself who sustains all beings,
you ought to rescue her as she is submerged in the waters of grief.
And by uniting that aged Vasudeva, who is dear to you as a son and possesses great strength, with your own son, O Kṛṣṇa, you shall attain righteousness.
Just as you subdued the most wicked elephant in the pool of the Yamunā,
and just as you indeed held up the vast mountain, the supporter of the earth.
The powerful Ariṣṭa, arrogant with pride, has been struck down;
and Keśin, the evil-minded destroyer of others' lives, has been slain by you.
O Kṛṣṇa, reflect upon how, by this very effort, you may rescue these two who are suffering in their old age and thereby attain merit.
O Kṛṣṇa, all those who saw your father being reviled in the assembly shed profuse tears from their eyes, overcome with intense grief.

It is said that Kamsa was reproached by the blind man as soon as he spoke something; O Krishna, your mother Devaki, being powerless, has endured many such sufferings, including the cutting open of her womb, at the hands of Kamsa.
By one who has been born from his mother and father, the debt must indeed be repaid in its entirety and in a discreet manner, as it has been declared according to what is appropriate.
O Kṛṣṇa, by acting in this way toward your parents,
they will abandon their grief, and you will attain incomparable merit.
"Your dharma will become vast and infinite; of this there is no doubt.
But Kṛṣṇa, having understood the matter, said to him, "So be it," and the radiant Keśava did not become angry at that one of excessive generosity.
And those cowherds, having assembled with Nanda Gopa at their head and having heard Akrūra’s words, set out by Kaṃsa’s command.
The inhabitants of Vraja became ready for the journey;
and having prepared their offerings, the elder cowherds set forth.
Having brought forward the milk, ghee, and fat of the oxen, buffaloes, and those fit for leading,
according to their strength and their herds;
Having prepared that [chariot], as well as the hand-gift for Kaṃsa and the offerings,
all those leaders of the cowherds stood ready to depart.
As he remained awake conversing with Kṛṣṇa and Rāma,
the son of Rohiṇī, as the third companion, that night passed away.
Chapter 70,
transliterated and collated with the Viṣṇupurāṇa and Brahmāṇḍapurāṇa by Utz Podzeit,
extracted from the collation and edited by Peter Schreiner; March 4.
2002. Not yet proof-read.
Vaiśampāyana said:
Then, at the clear dawn, crowded with the warbling of birds, [he spoke].
When the web of rays of the moon has been withdrawn at the waning of the night.
When the sky was overspread with the glow of dawn, when the circle of luminaries had faded away, and when the surface of the earth was moistened by the showers of the morning breeze;
When the stars had waned in appearance and fallen into a sleep devoid of luster,
the nocturnal form vanished and the sun rose;
the moon, its rays stilled, became lusterless.
One [the sun] destroys the form, while the other (the moon) increases the body,
upon the grounds for exiting the cow-pen strewn with rays of light,
and amidst the gargara-vessels resounding as they are filled with the swirling of the churning-sticks.
While the young calves were being restrained with ropes and the cowherds were filling the streets of the settlement from all sides.
Right there, having placed heavy and abundant goods upon carts,
they departed in haste, traveling by means of chariots while leaving [the others] behind.
Then Kṛṣṇa, the son of Rohiṇī, and he of immeasurable sacrificial gifts—
these three, mounted upon their chariots, proceeded like the lords of the three worlds.
Then Akrūra, having reached the bank of the Yamunā, said to Kṛṣṇa:
"O dear one, protect the chariot and exert yourself with the horses."
"O dear one, having given fodder to the horses and likewise having placed the horse-trappings on the chariot,
apply yourself with great effort and wait for a moment."
For in this pool of the Yamunā, I shall propitiate the Lord of Serpents,
the sovereign of all worlds, with divine mantras dedicated to the Blessed One.
I shall bow down to the secret Lord of the Bhāgavatas, the creator of all worlds, the glorious one whose head is marked by the svastika,
the serpent-king Ananta, the thousand-headed deity clothed in blue garments.
Whatever poison may issue from the mouth of this Dharmadeva,
all of that I shall consume as if it were nectar, like an immortal.
Having seen the Svastika abode, adorned with the serpent Śrī,
an assembly of serpents will indeed gather there for the sake of peace.
"May you both remain together here,
watching over me, until I have returned from the excellent lake of the lord of serpents."
To him Kṛṣṇa, greatly rejoiced, said: "Go, O most righteous one, do not delay!
Indeed, we two are not able to remain here deprived of you."

Thus addressed by Kṛṣṇa, he who was of immeasurable generosity bowed mentally to Hari and plunged into the pool of the Yamunā; there in the netherworld (rasātala), he beheld the realm of the serpents as if it were this very world.
And just as his appearance and arrival within the lake at the bottom of the netherworld occurred,
so too was he seen in its center, with a thousand faces, a raised golden palm-tree banner,
the tip of his hand resting on a plow, and his belly leaning upon a mace.
Clad in dark blue garments, pale in complexion and with a pale face,
wearing a single earring, intoxicated, and sleeping— those lotus-eyed ones.
Seated upon a pure lotus-throne fashioned by his own body,
he sat comfortably in the svastika posture, supporting the mountain with his two excellent arms.
His crown, tipped with gold, was turned slightly to one side,
and his chest was covered by a garland of lotuses made of pure gold.
His limbs were smeared with red sandalwood paste; he had long arms and was a subduer of enemies;
he had a navel like a lotus and shone like a white cloud, his splendor blazing with light.
He beheld the Lord of serpents, the sovereign of the single ocean,
standing there as the Master being worshipped by the lords of the double-tongued ones, headed by Vāsuki.
The two nāgas Kambala and Aśvatara, both holding chowries,
fanned that lord, the god seated upon the throne of Dharma.
Vāsuki, the lord of the serpents, appeared seated upon his lap,
surrounded by other serpent ministers led by Karkoṭaka.
They bathed that king— whose hair was covered with lotuses— with divine golden jars, he who had already been bathed by the waters of the single ocean.
On his lap [he saw] one who was dark as a rain-cloud, whose chest was covered by the Śrīvatsa mark,
as beautiful as ten million Cupids,
and with a very smooth right-turning [curl of hair].
He beheld Viṣṇu, who possesses a thousand auspicious names, whose eyes have the brilliance of the sun and moon, who wears yellow garments, and who was seated comfortably.
And he saw the Lord seated with Soma, possessing a body of equal firmness,
like Saṃkarṣaṇa himself seated, though without a divine throne.
He suddenly began to address Kṛṣṇa there,
but Kṛṣṇa paralyzed his speech with his own splendor.
Having worshipped Gadādhara with Bhāgavata mantras and having praised the Lord Īśāna— the giver of boons who is affectionate toward his devotees—
he considered himself the foremost among those who have accomplished their purpose.
Having experienced that inexhaustible portion of the Bhagavān among the serpents,
he, whose sacrificial gifts were immeasurable, rose up again from the water in amazement.
He beheld Balarāma and Keśava there, seated upon their chariot,
gazing at one another with wondrous forms.
Then, out of curiosity, Akrūra again immersed himself there,
where that eternal god clad in blue garments was being worshipped.
In that very manner, Akrūra beheld Kṛṣṇa seated upon the lap of the Thousand-faced One, being worshipped according to the prescribed rites.
Furthermore, rising up suddenly and bearing that mantra in his mind,
he of immeasurable liberality proceeded in the chariot by that very same path.
To Akrūra, who had arrived and was standing there, Keśava, being delighted, said:
"What is the state of affairs in the world of the Nāgas, within the lake of Bhagavat?"
I believe you have been delayed for a long time by distractions;
yet I perceive that you have seen something wondrous, since your heart remains as steady as a mountain.
He replied to Kṛṣṇa: "Without you, what wonder will there be among the worlds, whether among moving beings or stationary things?"
O Kṛṣṇa, I have seen there a wonder that is difficult to find on earth;
even here, I see and enjoy it exactly as I did there.
I have been united here with this wondrous form of the worlds;
O Kṛṣṇa, I do not venture to behold anything more marvelous than this.
Who else in the three worlds would experience wonder except for you? Homage to you, the Self of all, the source of wonder, O Lord of the world!
Homage be to you, O Lord of the gods of gods; homage to you, the Self of all!
Homage be to you, Viṣṇu, the immeasurable Lord of the world!
"O Lord of the World, what more is there for me to do? I have now accomplished my purpose.
O Viṣṇu, why do you always leave behind some remaining task?
Therefore come, O Lord; we shall go to the city of King Kaṃsa."
Until this maker of day goes to its setting at the end of the day.
Chapter 71,
transliterated and collated with the Viṣṇupurāṇa (ViP) and Brahmāṇḍapurāṇa (BrP) by Utz Podzeit,

Vaiśampāyana said:
Having yoked that excellent chariot, all those of immeasurable splendor—
Accompanied by Kṛṣṇa and Saṃkarṣaṇa,
they reached the delightful city of Mathurā, which was protected by Kaṃsa;
they entered that preeminent city at the time when the sun was red.
Both those heroes, Kṛṣṇa and Saṃkarṣaṇa, were conducted to their own abode by the wise Akrūra, who possessed the splendor of the sun.
Then the lord of donors, being afraid, said to those two of excellent complexion:
"Father, you must abandon your desire to go to the house of Vasudeva."
For your sake, that old man is being cast out by Kaṃsa and reviled day and night with the words, "You must not stay here."
"Therefore, you two must indeed perform that which brings the highest happiness for the sake of my father;
whatever ensures he attains happiness must be done with a beneficial intent.
Deprived of you both, I shall not enter the city of Mathurā."
O Lord, you who are compassionate toward your devotees, you ought not to abandon me, your devotee.

"Come, let us go to our homes, O Adhokṣaja; make them have a protector. Purify our houses, we who are householders, with the dust of Your feet—the purity of which satisfies the ancestors, the sacrificial fires, and the gods."
The pure waters used for washing his feet purified the three worlds;
those very waters which Śarva himself took upon his head became the sons of Sagara.
"O God of gods, Lord of the world, whose hearing and chanting are meritorious,
O Nārāyaṇa, best of the Yadus, glory be to you!
Then Kṛṣṇa said to him, "We two shall go unobserved."
O hero, O righteous one, they gazed upon Mathurā and its royal highway.
"But let us go to the house of that very virtuous man, if you agree.
Thus addressed by the Blessed One, Akrūra, appearing somewhat dejected,
entered the city, reported his actions to Kaṃsa, and went home.
Vaiśampāyana said: Akrūra also, having mentally paid homage to the imperishable Viṣṇu,
went to Kaṃsa’s side with a joyful heart.
And those two gods, the lords of the world known as Bala and Keśava,
having been thus instructed, set out as heroes,
both of them eager for battle like two elephants released from their hitching posts.
And the boys followed after them on every side along the path;
seeing the washerman and dyer on the road,
they then begged those very stainless garments from him.
But that washerman said to them, "Whose clothes do you two forest-dwellers belong to,
you both fools who beg so fearlessly?"
I dye hundreds of various garments for Kaṃsa, produced in many lands, in diverse colors according to his desires.
Whose children were you two, born in the forest and raised among the deer, that upon seeing this many pieces of red clothing, passion has arisen within you?
"Aha! You have sacrificed your lives, you who have come here;
you are fools with only common knowledge, yet you dare to ask for lodging."
Kṛṣṇa became truly enraged at that washerman of little intelligence,
a fool who had met with misfortune and was discharging verbal venom.
With his palm, which was like a thunderbolt, he struck him on the head;
lifeless, the washerman fell to the earth with his head shattered.
Lamenting for him who had been slain, his wives wailed aloud;
with their hair disheveled, they went quickly to Kaṃsa’s residence.
Kṛṣṇa and Balabhadra also took garments from all sides; having first put them on, those two high-minded ones adorned themselves.
Then, having given very fine and soft garments to the children,
they all, well-dressed, shone forth by the hundreds.
But as for the many remaining garments, Kṛṣṇa then suddenly tore them apart, cut them to pieces, and crushed them.
He reduced the washerman’s dwelling to ashes;
meanwhile, those two, well-dressed, went along the street of flower-shops for the sake of garlands, like two elephants scenting fragrances.

There lived a man named Guṇaka, who made his living by selling garlands; he was pleasant-spoken, possessed of great wealth from his many flower shops, and flourished through his trade in floral offerings.
At that time, Kṛṣṇa spoke with gentle words to the fearless garland-maker, who had been sent for the sake of flowers, saying, "Give [them to me]."
Pleased by them, the garland-maker Priyadarśana gave them an abundance of garlands and said, "This is your own property."
Being pleased in his mind, Kṛṣṇa granted a boon to Guṇaka:
"O gentle one, Śrī, who has taken refuge in me, shall increase your wealth with floods of riches."
Having obtained the boon, he remained composed; though his livelihood was that of a garland-maker, he bowed his head and, falling before Kṛṣṇa, accepted that boon.
Thinking then, "These two are yakṣas," that garland-seller was seized with intense fear and could offer no reply.
Even today, his lineage remains prosperous, possessed of jewels, renowned, and ever-powerful; it was established by Keśava at that time.
By the great grace of Viṣṇu, his lineage was well protected. Then both sons of Vasudeva, while traveling along the royal highway,
again beheld a hunchbacked woman carrying a vessel of unguents.
Kṛṣṇa said to her, "O Kubjā, whose is this ointment that you are carrying?
O lotus-petal-eyed one, you ought to tell me quickly."
Becoming observant of his state, she, whose gait was as crooked as lightning, replied to the lotus-eyed Kṛṣṇa, who was as deep as a rain-cloud.
"I am going to the king's bath-house; take this ointment.
O lotus-eyed one of beautiful countenance, as soon as I saw you, I was struck with wonder.
I have been waiting; come, may prosperity be yours, for you are dear to my heart."
And from what source, O gentle one, do you come to know that I am the beloved of the great king, appointed to the task of preparing his unguents?
To that hunchbacked woman standing there, Kṛṣṇa spoke as she was laughing;
then Kṛṣṇa, as if smiling, said to Sairandhrī:
"O lady of beautiful face, this is fragrant, worthy of a king, and lovely."
"Please give us an ointment that is suitable for our bodies."
"O fair-faced one, we are indeed Mallas who have arrived as guests from our country to behold the divine bow festival and this kingdom of great prosperity."
Then she replied to Kṛṣṇa, "You are dear to me to behold. Thereupon, having bowed down, she presented the ointment, saying, "This is the most excellent ointment fit for a king; please accept it."
Then Kṛṣ� fragrant and auspicious unguent, and they both smeared their limbs with it.
Then, with his head adorned by that garland of many flowers bound upon him,
Govinda, the Lord of the Cowherds, Kṛṣṇa, shone resplendent;
and the mighty Saṃkarṣaṇa likewise shone with his many garlands.
With their limbs anointed and their bodies still wet, the two of them shone like two bulls at a sacred ford, their bodies smeared with mud, as they stood in the Yamunā.
And all the boys likewise shone, adorned with crest-ornaments;
even those who were deformed appeared beautiful through the power of the wielder of the Śārṅga bow.
Then Kṛṣṇa, with the tips of his two fingers, [touched] that hunchbacked woman.
Kṛṣṇa, who knows the rules of playful sport, slowly lifted him up.
With her pair of breasts slightly submerged, her limbs elongated, and her smile pure, she laughed loudly;
with the slope of her breasts and her straight body, she was like a climbing vine.
Out of affection as well, that woman of intoxicating beauty spoke to Kṛṣṇa:
"Where will you go, O beloved, when you are obstructed by me? Stay! Take me!"
Breaking into laughter at one another, those two imperishable ones looked at each other with playful gestures and smiled, having heard the full account concerning the hunchbacked woman.

But Kṛṣṇa, smiling, dismissed the hunchbacked woman who was afflicted by desire, saying, "Go as you please, O blessed lady; I am not the kind of man [you think]. Then, released by the hunchbacked woman, the two of them entered the royal assembly.
Both of them, having grown up in Vraja and adorned in the dress of cowherds,
entered that royal palace with their facial expressions and gestures concealed.
Those two boys, born in the forests of the Himalayas and fierce with strength like lions, went to the bow-hall without any apprehension.
Desiring to see that great bow adorned with sacrificial offerings there,
those two heroes then questioned the keeper of the armory.

"O guardian of Kaṃsa’s bows, listen to our words! O gentle one, which of those bows is that for which this great festival is being held? Show it to us, the sacrificial object of Kaṃsa, if you so desire."
He showed them that bow, which was like a pillar,
unstringable and impenetrable even by the gods together with Indra.
Then the powerful Kṛṣṇa, whose eyes were like lotus petals, took it up and lifted it with both arms, his inner soul filled with joy.
Having weighed that bow, which was worshipped by the Daityas, according to his desire,
the powerful one strung it and bent it repeatedly.
As Kṛṣṇa bent the serpent-like bow with great force, it snapped in two at the middle, its sacrificial ornament shattered.
The sound of the breaking bow filled the sky, heaven and earth, and the quarters of the horizon;
hearing it, Kaṃsa was seized with terror.
The guards, together with their followers, became enraged and, acting as assassins, surrounded him, desiring to seize him, crying out, "Seize him! Kill him!"
Then, beholding those evil-intentioned ones, Balarāma and Keśava became enraged; taking up their bows, they shattered them into fragments and struck them down.
Having slain the force sent by Kaṃsa from the hall entrance,
they then emerged and, filled with pride, roamed about while surveying the splendors of the city.
Having heard of that wondrous valor of the two, the city-dwellers regarded their splendor, boldness, and form as those of the supreme among the gods;
then Kṛṣṇa, acting with swift prowess, broke that excellent bow.
And that youth Saṃkarṣaṇa, possessing great speed, went forth.
Then, when their bows were broken by the guards, those two remained intent on their purpose;
by the sound of the breaking of the bows, which produced a roar like the wind,
the entire inner apartment trembled and all the quarters of the sky were filled.
Having emerged from the armory, they went into the presence of Gopa.
But the keeper of the armory, his mind agitated as he hurried along,
that man of the armory, terrified and moving with swift strides,
approached the king and spoke with gasping breaths.
Listen to my report concerning a marvel that has occurred in the house of the bow at this time, which was like a source of agitation for the entire world.
Two men were together, their hair disheveled and flowing like crests;
they wore blue and yellow garments and were anointed with yellow and white unguents.
Those two heroes, resembling sons of gods, entered the inner apartments unobserved, driven by the force of passion; like two young fires,
they stood in the bow-chamber, gentle yet as if suddenly descended from the sky.
Those two gentle bulls among men, intent upon the great festival,
were clearly seen by me as they arrived, adorned with beautiful garments and garlands.
Of those two, however, one— the lotus-eyed Śyāma, wearing yellow garments and garlands—
took up that jewel of a bow, which was difficult even for the gods to grasp.
Then that boy, having forcibly mounted that massive form as if it were an iron machine, bent it with ease and speed.
But as it was being drawn by that powerful-armed one, the bow,
shrieking at the grip, broke in two.
Then the earth trembled and the sun did not shine;
from the sound of the breaking of the bow, the vault of the sky seemed to whirl.
Having seen that wonder, I was struck with supreme amazement;
out of fear of those who strike fear into their enemies, I have come here to relate it.
"I do not know, O Great King, who those two of immeasurable prowess are—
one resembling Mount Kailāsa and the other possessing the luster of a mountain of collyrium—
who indeed shattered that other jewel like an elephant breaking a pillar."
Moving with the speed of the wind and accompanied by his followers, he of immeasurable prowess departed, having split that [mountain] in two; I do not know who this king might be.
Upon hearing of the breaking of the bow, Kaṃsa too, his mind agitated,
dismissed the keeper of the weapons and entered his excellent palace.
Chapter 72,

Vaiśampāyana said: Having reflected upon the breaking of the bow, that enhancer of the Bhojas—
The king became despondent, reflecting deeply and exceedingly distressed.
How did that fool, devoid of fear, disregard the one of great strength and depart while being watched by the men after breaking the bow?
For whose sake, having performed a cruel deed censured by the world,
I, being afraid, have approached these six— the sons of my father’s sister.
Fate cannot be overcome by human effort;
surely the words spoken by Nārada have now come upon me.
Having reflected thus, the king then departed from his excellent palace and went quickly to the viewing hall to inspect the seating platforms.
Having seen that the entire assembly hall was prepared by the king’s best officials,
with rows of platforms joined firmly together so as to leave no gaps;
It was adorned with gables joined to the uppermost galleries, and embellished with spacious chambers and single-pillared pavilions.
Constructed entirely of solid material, well-proportioned, and firmly established,
this excellent bed-platform is joined to a slope facing the north.
Surrounded by royal thrones, crowded with walkways,
and covered with altars, it was capable of bearing the weight of a multitude of people.
Having seen that the arena was decorated, the wise king gave the command: "Tomorrow it shall likewise be adorned with paintings, garlands, and banners."
Let the courtyards of the platforms be made fragrant, beautiful in form, provided with upper coverings, as well as the roofed walkways and the galleries.
In the arena, let inexhaustible heaps of dried cow dung be prepared,
as well as cloths for the floor-coverings, beautiful decorations, and offerings in their proper proportions.
Let large jars, capable of withstanding the weight of water, all topped with golden vessels, be firmly set in place according to their proper order.
Let offerings and decoctions be prepared in jars;
let the judges be invited, along with the guilds and their leaders.
And let an order be given to the Mallas and likewise to the spectators: "Let well-constructed platforms be prepared for the assembly."
Having thus issued these commands for the supreme ritual of the assembly, the king emerged from the grounds of the assembly and entered his own residence.
There he indeed issued a challenge to those two wrestlers,
the immeasurable Cāṇūra and likewise Muṣṭika.
Those two wrestlers, possessed of great heroism, strength, and skilled in combat,
then entered [the arena] joyfully, honoring the command of Kaṃsa.
Seeing those two world-renowned wrestlers who had approached him,
King Kaṃsa spoke these words with a specific purpose:
"You two are my famous wrestlers, worthy of the banner of heroes;
you have been honored according to custom, and are especially deserving of hospitality."
Therefore, if you remember my hospitality or my good deeds,
a great task must be performed for me by you two through your own power.
"These two who have grown up with me in Vraja,
both Saṃkarṣaṇa and Kṛṣṇa, though they are but boys, have conquered all fatigue."
These two forest-dwellers, engaged in combat upon the field of battle, must be swiftly slain at every opportunity; of this there is no doubt.
"These two children are fickle and inactive"—one must never think thus and show them contempt; rather, one must certainly apply effort toward them.
"By defeating those two cowherds in the presence of the assembly,
both for the future and for the present, my welfare will be secured."
With their hearts gladdened by the king’s affectionate words,
the two wrestlers Cāṇūra and Muṣṭika, intoxicated for battle, spoke.
If those two wretched cowherds should stand before us,
they are to be understood as already slain— miserable beings in the form of ghosts.
Or if those two forest-dwellers, overwhelmed by misfortune, should fight against us while standing before us, we shall both be filled with wrath.
Having slain those two who grew up among the cattle and became your slaves upon the earth, O King, let your fear depart; we two are the best of wrestlers in combat.
Having spoken thus, he performed a clap of his hands; likewise, those two intoxicated wrestlers let out a lion’s roar that seemed to split the very sphere of the earth.
Having thus discharged the venom of their speech, both of those preeminent wrestlers—
Permitted by the lord of men, they both returned to their own homes.

Vaiśampāyana said: Then Kaṃsa spoke to the mahāmātra, the elephant-keeper.
Let the elephant Kuvalayāpīḍa stand at the gate of the assembly.
Strong, with eyes rolling from intoxication, fickle, and wrathful toward men;
his temples swollen with the rut-fluid, fierce, and enraged at every opposing elephant.
You must incite those two forest-dwellers against Vasudeva’s two base sons, so that their lives may come to an end.
And if those two, who live off cattle, were to be killed by you, O lord of elephants, in the arena while they were in a state of fury, I would see them.
Then, seeing those two fallen, Vasudeva, along with his kinsmen and his wife,
will perish, rootless and without support.
And these foolish Yādavas, all of whom are devoted to Kṛṣṇa,
will perish with their hopes shattered upon seeing Kṛṣṇa struck down.
Having slain these two, either by means of the lordly elephant, or by wrestlers, or even by my own hand,
I shall depart from the city made free of Yādavas and wander about in happiness.
Even my father, who was the upholder of the Yādava clan, has been abandoned by me;
and all the remaining Yādavas, those followers of Kṛṣṇa, have also been abandoned by me.
Nor was I indeed begotten by Ugrasena, that man of little prowess who sought a son, as Narada has told me.
My mother, being in her courses, went with some women to see the mountain named Suyāmuna out of curiosity for the forest.
There she wandered among the delightful mountain peaks with their beautiful tree-covered slopes, as well as through the caves and along the rivers.
She heard words that brought pleasure to the ears and gave rise to desire, made sweet by the songs of kinnaras and echoed back by the surrounding mountains.
Constantly hearing the cries of peacocks and the warbling of birds, she took delight in the nature of women.
In the meantime, a wind issuing from the rows of forest trees blew— delightful, rich with the fragrance of flowers, and awakening the god of love.
And the kadamba trees, adorned with swarms of bees and shaken by the wind,
released an exceeding fragrance as they were drenched by a continuous downpour of rain.
The kesara trees, awakening with rut, rained down showers of flowers;
the nīpa trees, bearing their flower-thorns, shone like lamps.
Covered with fresh grass and adorned with cochineal insects, the earth bore a seasonal form like a woman in her youth supporting the sky.
Then the illustrious Dānava named Drumila, the lord of Saubha,
assuming the form of Ugrasena, violated my mother.
With a heart tender toward her husband, she approached him with sincere feeling;
yet afterwards, she became apprehensive upon observing his gravity.
Rising up in fear, she said to him: "Surely you are not my husband;
who are you, of such deformed appearance, by whom I have been defiled?"
"O base one, this vow of mine as a devoted wife has been defiled by you through your vile deed, having assumed the form of my husband."
"What will my enraged kinsmen say of me, a disgrace to the family? And how shall I live, despised and cast out by my husband's kin?"
Fie on you, such as you are—impatient, of base birth, with senses in revolt; fie on this violation of another's wife, which is untrustworthy and destructive to one’s life!
Provoked by anger as she persisted in her advances, that Dānava said to her:
"I am indeed named Drumila, the powerful lord of Saubha."
"Why do you cast me into blame, O fool who fancies herself wise,
for having taken a human husband who is deficient in strength and prowess?"
O modest one, women do not become corrupted by infidelity;
for the intellect of human women, especially in those times, was not such as it is now.
Indeed, it is heard that many women, despite their transgressions and infidelities,
have given birth to sons of godlike appearance and immeasurable prowess.
For you are truly pre-eminent in this world as a woman devoted to her husband;
being pure, you shake out your hair and speak whatever you desire.
And when you, O beautiful woman, asked me, "Whose [son] are you?", I said:
"A son named Kaṃsa, the destroyer of enemies, shall be born to you."
Becoming angry once more and censuring that boon of his,
the distressed goddess spoke to the Dānava of wicked speech.
Fie on your conduct, O man of evil character, you who revile all women!
There are women of base conduct, and there are indeed those devoted to their husbands.
But as for those women who are heard of as having had only one husband, headed by Arundhatī—
it was by them that all three worlds were sustained, O disgrace to your lineage!
This son of mine whom you have indeed given me is a destroyer of my livelihood;
he is not highly regarded by me, so listen also to what is being said.
"An imperishable man shall be born into my lowly husband's lineage;
he shall be your death, even though you have granted him as a son."
Thus addressed, Drumila ascended into the sky itself by means of that very same divine and unsurpassed chariot;
and on that very day, my mother departed for her city, dejected.
Having spoken thus to me, the blessed Nārada, the best of sages,
blazed with the power of his asceticism like Agni himself in person.
Playing the lute, which was resonant with the seven musical notes,
and singing the path of the dramatic styles (*lakṣyavīthī*), he went into the presence of Brahmā.
Listen to this, O great minister; understand my words.
This truth has been spoken by the wise Nārada, who knows the three periods of time.
By means of my strength, heroism, policy, and discipline; indeed, by my majesty, valor, splendor, and prowess.
"In truth and through my generosity, there is no man equal to me;
having realized all this about myself, I place faith in your words.
O elephant trainer, I am indeed the *kṣetraja* son of Ugrasena."
Abandoned by his mother and father, he was established by his own splendor.
I am hated by both [the people] and especially by my kinsmen;
therefore, having had these two— Gopa and Kilbiṣa— slain by an elephant,
and having bound my father, I remain established in the kingdom by means of superior force.
Having slain both cowherds, I shall kill these as well.
Therefore, go now, mounting an elephant equipped with a goad, a spear, and a lance;
remain firm at the gate of the assembly, O mahāmātra, and do not delay.
And seeing that they have come together, slay both cowherds. (Ch.
74, transliterated and collated with ViP and BrP by Utz Podzeit)

Vaiśampāyana said:
When that day had passed and the second had arrived,
the great arena was crowded with citizens eager to witness the battle.
Then, kings residing within the realm, leading men,
and dark-complexioned women from Mathurā gathered together in groups.
With the full breasts of Kaṃsa’s women, which were like bilva fruits,
and with their other breasts that were unscarred and resembled flower clusters,
[the scene was such that] the eyebrows were the bows, the glances were the arrows, and the nose was the twanging bowstring.
And appointed by Kaṃsa, they dragged Kṛṣṇa and struck him.
Having bound him with the stalk of a kandalī plant as if with snares of delusion,
he was defeated and cast into the deep lake of the navel known as Kāla.
Then, having bathed Kaṃsa’s nurse who had her nipples bitten by his teeth,
the cowherd was unable to seize her breasts with both hands.
Just as that child caused the breaking of the cart,
so too did he cause the breaking of our carts and the pair of breasts.
This cowherd, who slew Ariṣṭa and whose breasts are like those of a humpbacked bull, is more powerful than the two wrestlers; he will cause them to be killed.
[He shall destroy] the gates and platforms with their colorful eightfold pillars and bolts.
And they were provided with windows and crescent-shaped ornaments, adorned with excellent floors and roofs.
Facing eastward, beautifully released, adorned with garlands and wreaths,
and graced with ornaments, they shone like autumnal clouds.
With well-constructed platforms for the galleries, beautifully adorned for the purpose of battle,
the assembly ground shone like the ocean with its masses of clouds.
The platforms of the guilds and the assemblies, crowded with banners adorned with their own respective emblems and substances, shine like immovable mountains.
And not far from there, the viewing galleries for those within the inner apartments shone,
variegated with gold and filled with the flickering blaze of jewels.
Adorned with heaps of jewels and provided with footholds,
those pavilions shone like winged mountains in the sky when their curtains were drawn aside.
And there, variegated rays of light moved about, produced by the laughter of yak-tail whisks, the tinkling of ornaments, and the brilliance of various jewels.
The courtesans had separate couches adorned with beautiful coverlets and cloths; graced by the foremost of the women, they possessed a splendor equal to celestial chariots.
There, the principal seats were golden couches,
and there were scattered variegated rugs along with trees bearing clusters of flowers.
There were golden vessels for drinks and adorned drinking-grounds,
as well as cāṅgerī plants filled with fruit snacks and prepared with beverages.
And many other couches there, constructed from piles of wood, shone forth as heaps of bedding, appearing like vast collections of beds.
And other excellent mansions, with windows like fine nets, shine like female royal swans in the sky as they gaze upon the women.
Facing the east, it was beautifully constructed, possessing a splendor equal to the peaks of Mount Meru;
its pillars resembled golden leaves, and it was adorned with variegated architectural fittings.
That assembly hall of Kaṃsa shone with exceeding splendor,
adorned with garlands of flowers and marked by the signs of habitation.
In that assembly ground, crowded with people, resounding with the clamor of a multitude of men,
packed together and shimmering like a surging ocean, [he stood].

The cowherds, headed by Nanda Gopa, were summoned by King Bhoja; having presented their offerings, they entered upon a single platform. King Kuvalayāpīḍa was an elephant stationed at the entrance of the arena.
Having commanded, "Let it remain," he then proceeded to the theater.
Wearing two white garments,
with a white fly-whisk and a white crown, he shone like the moon amidst white clouds.
Seeing the incomparable form of that wise one as he sat comfortably upon his lion-throne, the citizens uttered blessings of victory.
Then the gods, along with the gandharvas, the siddhas, and the supreme rishis,
placing Purandara at their head, went forth, desiring to witness the battle.
All of them, situated in their celestial chariots and fanned with white yak-tail whisks, shone brilliantly;
and Śakra too, mounted upon Airāvata along with Mātali, was resplendent.
Then all those chief courtesans, headed by Urvaśī,
were at Śakra’s side, white chowries in their hands.
Those best of kings, headed by Dilīpa,
remained in heaven like Śakra for the duration of many yugas,
in order to behold the Blessed One, the Lord of the World, adorned as a cowherd.
But those sages who, having come from Nārada, were stationed there to witness the battle—
When the two wrestlers rose together with the two gods into the center of the arena,
the sky became densely crowded with throngs of immortals.
Then the arena was completely filled with all the people,
and the sky as well became densely crowded with hosts of gods moving through the air;
the surface of the earth and the expanse of the heavens became one and the same.
Then the Mallas, their garments fluttering, entered the arena;
and those endowed with great strength entered the three enclosures one by one.
Then, accompanied by the sound of trumpets and the noise of shouting and clapping hands,
the two sons of Vasudeva, filled with joy, arrived at the gate of the arena.
The two cowherds were clothed in garments and adorned with ornaments worthy of the gods;
with their turbans bound upward and wreaths upon their heads, they exerted themselves with weapons in their arms,
slapping each other’s arms which were like iron bars.
As those two fair-faced ones were rushing forward in haste, they were stopped;
having reached the entrance of the arena, Kṛṣṇa beheld the elephant Kuvalayāpīḍa stationed there, urged on by Ambaṣṭha.
Having girded his loins and gathered back his curling locks,
Śauri spoke to the elephant-keeper with a voice as deep as the roar of a cloud:
"O Ambaṣṭha, Ambaṣṭha, give us the way; depart without delay!
Otherwise, having slain you along with your elephant, I shall send you to the abode of Yama."
Thus rebuked, Ambaṣṭha became enraged and urged on his furious elephant, which resembled Kāla, Antaka, and Yama, against Kṛṣṇa; indeed,
that intoxicated elephant was driven forward with great force.
That wicked-natured intoxicated elephant, curling its trunk into a ring,
exerted every effort when urged on to slay Balarāma and Keśava.
Then Kṛṣṇa, being terrified by the elephant, laughed and rebuked the malice of the evil-minded Kaṃsa.
It is said that he intended to kill [him] with this chief of elephants.
"Alas! Kaṃsa is indeed evil-minded; what greater wonder than this could there be?"—thinking thus, the Blessed One looked toward Balabhadra.
Balabhadra perceived the intention of that evil-minded one:
"Indeed, this Kaṃsa hastens to go to the abode of Vaivasvata,
he who desires to assault me with this serpent."
Then, as the serpent roared nearby like a thundering cloud,
the Lord Govinda suddenly leaped up and made a sound like the clapping of palms.
Making a sound by hissing and slapping his arms before the elephant,
Śrīdhara caught its trunk against his chest.
Having positioned himself between the tusks and then again between the feet,
Kṛṣṇa tormented that elephant just as the wind afflicts a rain-cloud.
Emerging from the elephant's trunk, from the tip of its tusks,
and released from between its feet, Kṛṣṇa bewildered the elephant.
But that elephant, utterly bewildered and unable to kill Kṛṣṇa,
cried out while being crushed by his own very limbs.
He fell upon his knees on the ground and gnashed his teeth;
from his rage he shed ichor, just as a cloud pours down rain at the end of the summer heat.
But Kṛṣṇa, having played with that serpent as if with a child,
set his mind upon its destruction with a heart hostile toward Kaṃsa.
Placing his foot before him immediately after [seizing] the jar,
he then tore out a tusk with both arms and struck him with it.
Being struck by that tusk of his, which was like a thunderbolt, the elephant,
overcome with pain, voided excrement and urine and let out a great cry.
From the temples of the elephant, whose limbs were mangled by Kṛṣṇa and whose mind was distressed,
copious blood flowed forth with great force.
And Halāyudha violently pulled out his tail,
which was half-hidden on the back of the mountain, just as Vainateya pulls out a serpent.
Having slain the elephant with that very same tusk, Kṛṣṇa then struck down the formidable elephant-riders with a single blow.
Letting out a great cry of distress, that best of elephants, though still conscious, fell down along with his mahout like a mountain shattered by a thunderbolt.
Then those two bulls among men, fierce in battle, seizing the limbs of the elephant, struck down its foot-guards.
Having slain them, both of them entered the center of the arena like the two Aśvins, the Nāsatyas, descended from heaven by their own will.
The Vṛṣṇis, Andhakas, and Bhojas beheld the two [heroes] wearing forest garlands,
amidst the sound of their war-cries and shouts, and the slapping of their arms.
And with lion-roars and the clapping of their hands, they gladdened the people.
O Bhārata, seeing them and observing the affection and joy of the citizens, the foolish-minded King of the Bhojas despaired; meanwhile,
the lotus-eyed one, having slain that roaring best of elephants, [proceeded].
Together with his elder brother, he descended into the assembly that had the appearance of an ocean.
He was a thunderbolt to the Mallas, a supreme man among men, and embodied Love to women;
he was a kinsman to the cowherds, a punisher of wicked kings, and a child to his own parents;
he was death to the Lord of the Bhojas, the Virāṭ to the ignorant, and the Supreme Reality to yogis.
Known as the supreme deity of the Vṛṣṇis, Hari entered the arena;
then all the gods and sages, having paid homage to the wielder of the mace (Gadādhara),
remained stationed in their celestial chariots and fixed their gaze upon the battle.
Then the mighty-armed Kṛṣṇa, accompanied by Baladeva,
honored the people in his mind and prepared to slay Kaṃsa.
(Chapter 75)
