Vaiśampāyana said: Then,
with his elder brother placed before him, the lotus-eyed Kṛṣṇa entered with great speed, his garments fluttering in the wind.
The son of Devakī, a hero with beautiful arms, bore marks carved from elephant tusks;
he wore armlets as if in sport, and was flushed with both blood and intoxication.
Leaping like a lion and roaring like a thundercloud,
he made the earth tremble with the sound of his arms and the blows of his hands.
Beholding Kṛṣṇa with his weapon raised by the tusks of an elephant, the son of Aṅgiras,
his face deeply distressed, gazed at him with great wrath.
Even those who were on the stage beheld the lotus-eyed one with unblinking eyes and with their inner selves filled with joy;
Keśava shone with the elephant-tusk that was held in his arm.
Joined with the half-disk of the moon, like a mountain with a single peak.
As Govinda leaped, that entire ocean-like arena appeared as if it were being filled by the echoing roar of the multitude of people.
Then Kaṃsa, his eyes copper-red with rage and exceedingly wrathful,
commanded the immensely powerful Cāṇūra to fight Kṛṣṇa in battle.
Filled with rage, he commanded Andhaka, Malla, Nikṛti, and the mighty Muṣṭika— who resembled a mass of mountains— to go against Baladeva;
meanwhile, Cāṇūra had already been previously ordered by Kaṃsa.
"You must indeed fight with Kṛṣṇa with great effort."
But Cāṇūra, his eyes clouded with rage,
advanced for battle like a rain-cloud filled with water.
And he said to Govinda: "I shall remove your pride;
O cowherd, before long you shall behold Vaivasvata by my power."
Upon hearing that, Govinda spoke to him whose life was spent:
"I shall see such prowess and supreme strength in you;
before long, O wrestler, you shall see it—either through you, O lowest of men, or through me."
"If you are capable, show it; you are called base for boasting of your strength.
Having spoken thus, Govinda let out many various roars. When the assembly had been summoned and the people were hushed in silence, he spoke.
The Yādavas, gathered there together, spoke these words.
Having abandoned the use of arrows and having observed that combat through conciliation,
this wrestling match was arranged in the arena before the judges; it is free from fear,
recognized for its skill and strength, weaponless, and established as it was in ancient times.
Those who perceive the proper time should always dispel fatigue with water; it is traditionally taught that the wrestler Mallaka’s regimen was constantly performed with dried cow dung.
The manner in which they stood, their positions on the ground, how each remained according to his path,
their stability, their stations on the ground, and how those two maintained their respective courses—
all these were described by the umpires as the sequence of their combat.
Whether he be a child, or one of middle age, or an elder, or even emaciated;
whether he be strong or standing on the stage, he should indeed be known by his inner disposition.
Regarding the rules for arm-to-arm combat in battle, both in terms of strength and technique,
nothing whatsoever should be done by a wise man immediately after a thunderbolt-like blow.
This very battle between Kṛṣṇa and the Andhra wrestler is now set upon the stage;
there can be no doubt that Kṛṣṇa is a child while the Andhra is a great man.
Then a tumultuous sound of "kila-kilā" arose in the assembly;
Govinda leaped up and spoke these words.
"I am a great, blind fool, with a body like a mountain;
I take pleasure in fighting against this one who is so powerful in his arms."
No transgression of the rules of combat shall occur through my doing;
for I will not corrupt the established doctrine of those who fight with their arms.
This which consists of the nature of cow-dung, the nature of water, the dye produced [therefrom],
and the contact with the astringent— this indeed is the convention that has been devised.
Self-restraint, steadfastness, valor, physical exertion, skill in my [divine] actions, strength, and constant readiness for movement—
this is the vow at the front of battle.
Since he is now prepared to engage in a hostile battle with his arms, punishment must indeed be meted out here; thus shall I bring satisfaction to the world.
Born among the Karūṣas, he is known by the name Cāṇūra;
consider him a wrestler in body as well as in his deeds.
By him many wrestlers, intoxicated by battle, have been slain;
and out of a desire for glory in the arena, he has brought disgrace upon the path of the wrestlers.
The mastery of weapons for warriors who fight with arms in battle is their *śāstrasiddhi*;
the mastery of the arena for wrestlers, born from the striking down of rival wrestlers, is their *raṅgasiddhi*.
For one who is victorious in battle, there is eternal fame;
even for one slain by weapons in battle, the surface of heaven is ordained.
For in battle, success is achieved from both sides—whether one is slain or whether one slays;
indeed, that way of life which ends with the breath is rightly honored by the great.
But this path has emerged from strength and action; for one who has died on the stage, what is heaven? And for one who conquers, where is the pleasure?
"But those who, out of their own fault, consider the king to be a fool and say, 'We fools shall fight with our arms against those stronger than we in this crisis'—
having spoken thus, Kṛṣṇa then approached Cāṇūra."
Slapping his arms, O Indra among kings, Cāṇūra rushed toward Kṛṣṇa.
Both of them, possessing the prowess of lions like two elephants in rut,
then fought one another with these various wrestling maneuvers;
for the wrestlers were slain for the sake of glory, as such was the slaying of the wrestler-slayer.
Even as they were thus conversing, a most terrible battle took place between them both,
like that between two elephants in a forest.
With various maneuvers of attack and counter-attack, with perilous grappling with the arms, with collisions and shakings, as well as with crushing and churning.

Both of them, locked together as if they were made of stone, fought with throws and fist-blows, with roars like those of a boar, with spiked maces, with blows like falling thunderbolts, and likewise with their outstretched arms.
With the falling of sticks and nails, with the terrible stamping of feet,
with knees making the sound of stones, and with heads being violently dashed together.
That battle between the heroes became terrible, fought without weapons through the power of their arms and the strength of their vital energy, in the presence of a festive assembly.
All the people were filled with passion, rising up with shouts of acclaim;
and other people on the platforms cried out words of praise.
And the gods dwelling in heaven likewise cried out, "Excellent! Excellent!
Then Kamsa, his face perspiring and his eyes fixed upon Krishna, silenced the musical instruments with his left hand.
When those musical instruments, such as the mṛdaṅga drums and others, were indeed forbidden,
numerous divine instruments resounded spontaneously in the sky.
While Hṛṣīkeśa, whose eyes resemble lotuses, was fighting,
the sounds of musical instruments resounded on their own from all sides.
The gods, having become invisible with their celestial chariots that could assume any form at will,
moved about together with the Vidyādharas, desiring victory for Kṛṣṇa.
"Conquer Cāṇūra, the Dānava who has taken the body of a wrestler!
Thus did all the seven Ṛṣis speak, situated in the sky.
Having played with Cāṇūra for a long time, the son of Devakī drew out his strength, foreseeing the destruction of Kaṃsa.
Then the earth shook and the couches trembled violently;
even the supreme jewel fell from Kaṃsa’s crown.
Bending down with his two arms, Kṛṣṇa struck Cāṇūra, whose life was at its end,
on the head with his fist and on the chest with his knee.
His eyes, along with their sockets, flowed with tears and blood,
hanging from his chest like two golden bells suspended by their cords.
And Cāṇūra fell lifeless upon the surface of the earth in the midst of the arena at the end of his life, his eyes protruding.
With the body of that Cāṇūra of the arena, whose life had departed,
the great highway was seen to be blocked as if by a mountain.
Chapter 76, translated by Peter Schreiner; version of March 4, 2002. Not yet proofread.
Vaiśampāyana said:
When that Cāṇūra, who was arrogant in his strength, had been slain, the son of Rohiṇī...
In the arena, Kṛṣṇa seized Muṣṭika, and then he seized Tosalaka.
...and struck him violently with his fist.
He fell down, vomiting blood, and at that very moment his life departed.
Baladeva went to Andhra.
In that assembly, those two wrestlers, overcome with rage at first,
encountered Rāma and Kṛṣṇa, who were subject to the power of Time.
Becoming like a thunderclap and a mountain peak, they both leaped about in the midst of the arena.
The powerful Kṛṣṇa, having lifted Toṣala— who resembled a mountain summit—
and whirled him around a hundred times, crushed him against the surface of the earth.
As he was seized by Kṛṣṇa and oppressed by that stronger one,
blood flowed profusely from the mouth of him who was about to die.
But the mighty Saṃkarṣaṇa, that great wrestler, having fought for a very long time while displaying various circular maneuvers, [overcame] the Andhra wrestler.
With a single fist, the radiant hero struck him on the head, as if with a thunderbolt accompanied by lightning against a great mountain.
With his brain spouting forth and his eyes and face distorted, he fell there facing forward; then a great roar arose.
Having slain both Andhra and Tosala, Kṛṣṇa and Saṃkarṣaṇa,
their eyes bloodshot with rage, leaped about in the middle of the arena.
When the great wrestler Andhra and Muṣṭika had been struck down, that wrestling arena became spotless and terrifying to behold.
And those cowherds who were looking on, led by Nandagopa,
all stood there with every limb trembling with fear.
With tears born of joy flowing from her eyes and trembling,
Devakī, overwhelmed by the pressure of her milk, gazed intently at Kṛṣṇa.
With eyes clouded by tears born of the sight of Kṛṣṇa,
Vasudeva, casting off his old age, acts like a youth out of affection.
And all those chief courtesans drank in the lotus-face of Kṛṣṇa with their bee-like eyes, which moved within the blink of an eyelash.
On Kaṃsa’s face as well, a sweat born from the outpouring of his rage appeared, visible between the knitting of his eyebrows, stirred by the sight of Kṛṣṇa.
His heart, blazing within, was kindled by the fire of his mind through the smoke of his exertion for Keśava and the wind of his sighs of rage.
With his lips quivering and his brows knit together,
the body of Kaṃsa, in his rage, took on the appearance of a blood-red sun.
From his mouth, which was red with rage, drops of sweat issued forth,
like rows of trees spreading out from the rising sun.
Just as droplets of dew on trees vanish when touched by the rays of the sun,
he, filled with rage, commanded many tall men:
"Let these two cowherds, these forest-dwellers, be driven out from the throngs of the assembly."
Nor do I wish to see these two, who perceive evil and have become deformed;
not even one among my cowherds ought to remain in my kingdom.
And let the dull-witted Nandagopa, who delights in evil deeds,
be seized with iron shackles and steel bonds.
And Vasudeva, who is ill-behaved and always acts with deceit toward me—
let him be executed this very day by a punishment that does not befit an elder.
"And as for these common cowherds who are devoted to Dāmodara—
let their cows be taken away, along with whatever wealth they possess."
Thus commanding Kaṃsa, who was speaking harshly,
Kṛṣṇa, whose prowess is truth, looked upon him with eyes like molten iron.
When his father was cast down, Keśava became enraged at Nandagopa; he also felt indignation upon seeing the distress of his kinsmen and Devakī, who had lost consciousness.
Like a lion with speed, possessing a mane and having manifested his prowess,
the mighty-armed Acyuta desired to ascend [the mountain] for the sake of destroying Kaṃsa.
Kṛṣṇa leapt from the center of the arena toward the seat of Kaṃsa,
unimpeded like lightning cast by the wind from cloud to cloud.
Indeed, none of them saw him having leaped from the middle of the arena;
the city-dwellers saw only Kaṃsa standing by his side.
Kaṃsa, likewise distressed and overtaken by the law of time,
perceived the all-pervading Lord Govinda as having arrived there from the very sky.
Beholding Death thus entering his very seat,
that wise man rose up suddenly and seized his sword and shield.
As he moved swiftly with sword in hand like a hawk in the sky to the right and left,
Durviṣaha, of fierce and unbearable splendor, seized him.
Just as the son of Tārkṣya, overcome by compassion, did not wish to kill the serpent even though he had seized it by force, so too Keśava,
recognizing him as his own brother, did not then let his weapon fall.
A man who has been cherished by a woman engaged in amorous conduct becomes powerless in those very acts of passion and languishes as if gasping for breath.
Kaṃsa, however, remained upon the platforms, perspiring over all his limbs;
he was thus possessed by anxiety and filled with compassion for Keśava.
Then a voice arose from the sky, saying:
"Slay Kaṃsa, your younger brother, who is now deprived of his weapons."
Having heard this, Kaṃsa then suddenly rose up,
looking at the people and speaking these words while trembling like a mountain.
O Keśava, perform the governance of the gods' affairs,
having recognized the god as the most powerful, for human effort indeed depends upon him.
"Once, among the gods, he who brings auspiciousness to all the worlds said:
'May I attain absolute liberation (kaivalya) in heaven through the arrows from your lotus-like hand.
Then Kṛṣṇa, having extended his arm which resembled an iron club,"
Kaṃsa was indeed seized by the hair on his head in the assembly of the arena.
And his golden crown, adorned with diamonds,
fell from his head as he was seized by Kṛṣṇa’s hand.
With his hair seized by the hand, Kaṃsa became powerless;
likewise, utterly bewildered, he fell into a state of agitation.
And being seized by the hair, sighing like one whose life-force was fading,
Kaṃsa was indeed unable to look upon the face of Kṛṣṇa at that time.
With earrings displaced from his ears, with a necklace severed from his chest, with arms hanging limp, and with ornaments fallen from his limbs.
His upper garment having slipped away, Kaṃsa’s seat was suddenly shaken; whirled about and violently seized by Kṛṣṇa’s splendor, he fell.
The powerful Kṛṣṇa struck him forcefully on the head with his fist—
a fist by which Viṣṇu could have brought about a risk to his life—
and then Keśava, stepping down from the platform, dragged him across the great arena.
Having seized Kaṃsa, who had fallen into a state deserving of affliction, firmly by the hair.
Dragged by Kṛṣṇa, the highly effulgent king of the Bhojas became like a great bird tossed about by a plowman;
he drew a furrow around the arena with his body.
Having played and wrestled in the arena, Kṛṣṇa cast away the body of Kaṃsa, whose life had reached its end, not far from that spot.
His body, accustomed to comfort, now lies crushed upon the earth,
gradually made rough by dust through this contrary process.
His face, darkened and with eyes closed, shone no more without its crown; it was like a lotus that has been overturned and stripped of its petals.
Kamsa was slain without a formal battle; though pierced by arrows, he was not wounded [by them], for his life was expelled by a grip upon the throat, thus departing from the path of heroes.
Suddenly, all those nails of Keśava— dense as if they were cuts of flesh, capable of severing life— appeared upon his body.
Having slain him, the lotus-eyed one, his radiance doubled by joy and having removed all thorns, paid homage at the feet of Vasudeva.
And the joy of the Yadus, having pressed his head against his mother’s feet,
drenched Kṛṣṇa with the surging streams of her milk flowing forth from her joy.
Then Devakī performed the consecration of the imperishable Kṛṣṇa;
and Hari, having slain her son of great prowess along with his army in the assembly of the Yadus, then bowed his head to Ugrasena.
And Kṛṣṇa, blazing with his own splendor, inquired after the welfare of all those Yādavas according to their respective positions and ages.
The righteous Baladeva also swiftly crushed the powerful Sunāman, the brother of Kaṃsa, with his two arms alone.
With his arm, Baladeva struck down the one named Vasu.
Having conquered their enemies and subdued their anger, those two heroes, who had been away from Vraja for a long time,
went with joyful hearts to the house of their father.
And those gods, together with the sages, once the evil-minded Kaṃsa had been slain,
paid homage to the Lord of the World and departed for their respective abodes;
they praised the lotus-eyed, victorious, and all-pervading Kṛṣṇa.
Having slain Pūtanā, having split the cart, having struck down the two Arjunas, and having destroyed the Dānavas;
having struck and annihilated the seven [sages], having crushed the poison of Kāliya, having killed Riṣṭa and others,
having slain the intoxicated Keśin, and having uprooted the poisonous tree and Mount Govardhana;
Salutation to that Viṣṇu who slew Kaṃsa along with his lordly elephant and his wrestler.
Salutations always to the wise one who wields the plow, who took the life of Pralamba and Dhenuka, who is the enemy of Muṣṭika, and who eternally destroys Sunāman.
Having thus praised him in many ways, those gods, with delighted minds, [departed].
Chapter 77,
transliterated by John Brockington.
Vaiśampāyana said: Proofread by John Brockington, version of 7th November 2001. *The mark :h] is a typographical symbol used in the source text.*
Seeing their husband Kaṃsa slain— like a planet whose merit has been exhausted—
the wives of Kaṃsa surrounded him on all sides.
Seeing that lord of the earth lying upon his royal bed, his life departed,
his wives grieved like does at the slaughter of a deer.
Alas, we are destroyed, O mighty-armed one! Our hopes are slain and our kinsmen are lost, now that you—the hero who cherished the vows of a warrior—have been killed along with your heroic wives.
Beholding this final, ultimate state of yours,
O tiger among kings, we, along with our kinsmen, lament piteously.
We have become rootless; we have been abandoned by our noble [protectors], now that you, our mighty lord, have met your death.
Who will lead us— our limbs covered in dust, longing for the touch of love,
and writhing like creepers— to our couches?
O gentle one, this sun constantly burns your lovely face— your breathless sighs— withering it like a lotus deprived of water.
These two ears of yours are empty and do not shine without earrings;
they hang constantly against your neck, O lover of earrings.
O hero, where is that crown of yours, adorned with all kinds of jewels, which,
possessing the splendor of the sun, bestows supreme beauty upon your head?
"With this wife and retinue who adorn your inner apartments,
how shall I, now wretched, conduct myself once you have departed for the next world?"
Surely virtuous women are not deceived regarding the enjoyments dear to them;
they do not abandon their husbands, yet you, having abandoned us, are going away.
"Alas! Time is of great power, by whose transformative action you are swiftly snatched away while we look on;
equal to Death itself, you are being led away quickly from your enemies."
We are unaccustomed to suffering and have been accustomed only to happiness;
O Lord, how shall we live as widows, having resorted to wretchedness?
For women who are devoted to their character, the husband alone is the supreme refuge;
for us, you were that refuge, now severed by powerful Fate.
Overwhelmed by widowhood, our minds are tormented by grief.
Alas! All living beings must come under the power of Fate. Immersed in this inevitable weeping, where shall we go without you?
Time has passed with you, and our playing upon your lap is gone;
in an instant we have been parted, for the course of mortals is indeed impermanent.
"Alas! We are ruined, O giver of honor, for you are ruined;
though we have committed but a single misdeed, we all now bear the marks of widowhood."
We, who love pleasure, were cherished by you with the delights of heaven;
now that we are all under the sway of desire for you, where are you going, leaving us behind?
O you who resemble a god, O Lord, O giver of honor, you are indeed the protector of us who are protectorless;
it behooves you, O Lord of the World, to grant a reply to these women who are lamenting like female ospreys.
Thus, O Great King, while your kinsmen are exhausted and your wife is in distress, your departure appears terrible to us.
Surely, O beloved, the excellent women in that world must be far more beautiful;
for it is because of them, O hero, that you have departed, leaving behind these people at home.
O hero, O lord of the earth, what compassion do you have for these wives of yours as they weep with piteous cries, that you do not awaken here today?
Alas! How pitiless is the journey of men toward the afterlife, they who depart without regard, having abandoned their own wives.
It is better for a woman to have no husband at all than to have a hero as her husband;
heroes are beloved by celestial women, and they too are beloved by those heroes.
"Alas! By you, acting as the unseen God of Death, a blow has been swiftly struck at our innermost selves, you who delight in battle!"
Having slain the army of Jarāsaṃdha and conquered the yakṣas in battle;
having defeated the forces of Jarāsaṃdha and killed kings in combat;
having vanquished the hosts of gods in war and the yakṣas as well in the fray.
O Lord of the World, how is it that you have been slain by a mere human?
Having engaged in battle with Indra in a conflict of arrows, you were undefeated by the immortals in war; how then were you slain by a mortal?
Having agitated the unfathomable ocean with showers of arrows,
you conquered the wielder of the noose and seized all his jewels and possessions.
For the sake of the city's people, while Indra was raining only sparingly,
you pierced the clouds with your arrows and caused the rain to fall by force.
All the kings, bowed down by your majesty, remain at your service,
sending you precious jewels and garments worthy of the best.
How has such a terrible, life-ending danger come upon you, who are like a god and whose prowess has been witnessed by your enemies?
Now that you, our protector, have been struck down, we have become widows;
though we were once vigilant, we have been rendered heedless, cast out by the God of Death.
If it is indeed so, O Lord, that you must go, or if we have been forgotten,
then you should grant us your favor by saying simply, "I shall go."
Be gracious, O Lord; we are afraid. We go to your feet with our heads bowed. Enough of this long journey abroad; turn back, O Lord of Mathurā!
"O hero, why do you lie down thus, seated upon the grass and dust? For why does your mind not feel agitation while you are reclining upon the bare ground?"
"By whom has this unexpected blow been struck against us while we were asleep?
By whom has such a cruel act as this been committed against all these women?"
The latent tendency of weeping is not for a noble woman while she yet lives;
why do we weep when we must depart together with our husband?
In the meantime, Kaṃsa’s mother, distressed and trembling, wailed piteously: "Where is my calf? Where is my son?"
She beheld her son slain, like the moon eclipsed;
with a heart torn asunder, she exhausted herself again and again.
Gazing intently at her son and crying out, "Alas, I am destroyed!",
she fell to the ground in misery, wailing, "Alas, I am destroyed!
She lamented and wept at the piteous cries of her daughters-in-law.
Placing his dejected face upon her lap, she who longed for her son lamented piteously with a voice full of distress, crying out, "O my son!"
"O son, devoted to the vow of heroes, the increaser of the joy of your kinsmen!
Why have you, dear one, made this hasty departure?"
"And you are fast asleep in an open space; why, my son, without a bed?
Dear one, those who possess auspicious marks do not sleep upon the bare ground in such a manner."
Long ago, this verse, esteemed by the virtuous, was sung by Rāvaṇa—
the foremost in strength among the Rākṣasas in all the worlds— during an assembly of his kind.
Thus, for me, who possess such exalted vigor and am the slayer of gods,
there will arise a terrible and unavoidable fear from my own kinsmen.
In the very same way, for my wise son, who was greedy toward his kinsmen,
a great fear of his relatives arose, which brought about the end of his body.
To her husband, King Ugrasena— the aged lord who was now humbled, boatless, and bewildered as he approached his own destruction—
she spoke these words while weeping, like a cow deprived of her calf.
Come, come, O righteous-souled King! Behold your son, the lord of men, lying upon the hero’s bed like a mountain struck by a thunderbolt.
O Great King, let us perform for him rites befitting his departure,
now that he has been reborn as a preta and has gone to the abode of Yama.
"Kingdoms are to be enjoyed by heroes, yet we have been defeated;
go, therefore, and inform Kṛṣṇa for the sake of Kaṃsa’s funeral rites."
Enmities end with death; when one is at peace, there will be peace.
The funeral rites must be performed; once dead, how can he commit any offense?
Having spoken thus to her husband, the Bhoja king, she, distressed and gazing at her son’s face, tore at her hair and lamented most bitterly.
O King, what will these wives of yours do, who, though accustomed to happiness,
have found you as their husband and yet see their desires frustrated?
How shall I behold this aged father of yours, subject to the will of Kṛṣṇa, wasting away like the water of a pond?
"I am your mother, my son; why do you not speak to me?
You have set out upon a long journey, leaving behind those who are dear to you."
"Alas, O hero skilled in policy, you are being snatched away by the irreversible God of Death from me, a woman of little fortune and dull-witted!"
These [families], captivated by your generosity and honor, have been satisfied by your virtues;
their names have been taken up and their conduct made perfect by those virtues.
O leader of the clans, the families of your servants are weeping.
Arise, O tiger among men, long-armed one of great strength!
Protect all the wretched people, as well as the city and the inner apartments.
While the women of Kaṃsa were weeping and deeply distressed,
the sun, colored by the glow of twilight, went to its setting.
Chapter 78,
Transliterated by John Brockington,
Proof-read by John Brockington.
Vaiśampāyana said:
Ugrasena, however, went into the presence of Kṛṣṇa, deeply distressed.
Tormented by grief for his son, he stumbled like one who has drunk poison.
He saw Kṛṣṇa in the house, surrounded by the Yādavas,
brooding with remorse and distressed by the death of Kaṃsa.
Having heard many piteous accounts of the destruction of Kaṃsa’s enemies, he reproached himself in that assembly of the Yādavas.
Kṛṣṇa spoke everything while everyone listened:
"Alas! Out of extreme childishness and following the impulse of human anger, I have brought widowhood upon thousands of women for the sake of this Kaṃsa."
Compassion indeed arises even in a common man toward women who are thus distressed and weeping when their husband has been struck down by me.
Indeed, grief is produced merely by lamentation;
compassion arises in women because they are ignorant of the workings of destiny.
Indeed, the slaying of Kaṃsa— who is terrifying to his subjects and devoted to sinful deeds— was long ago desired by me as the best course.
For a man of little intelligence who has fallen from his conduct in this world,
death without suffering is better than a life lived in hatred.
Kaṃsa was devoted to evil and was disapproved of by the virtuous; he had fallen through the cry of "Fie!"—what compassion can there be for his life?
In heaven, the residence of those who have maintained their ascetic penance is the fruit of meritorious action;
even here on earth, one endowed with glory is held in high regard by those dwelling there.
If the worlds were established and the subjects were devoted to dharma,
and if men were engaged in dharma, the king would not become corrupted.
For those of wicked conduct toward virtuous qualities, the God of Death finds his footing;
therefore, one should perform deeds for the sake of the next world regarding those dharmas desired in this world.
The gods protect exceedingly the man who is devoted to dharma;
in this world, those who perform evil deeds find it easy to do so.
This Kaṃsa has been slain by me; let this be understood well:
the root of that perverse deed has been cut away.
If this fortunate one does not destroy that man of evil conduct, then the world will perish.
For who indeed would perform this task— binding his father by force and seizing the kingdom along with all the vassal lords— for he shall surely rule it forever?
Therefore, let all these women, afflicted by grief, be comforted;
let the citizens and the guilds throughout the city likewise be comforted in their entirety.
While Govinda was speaking thus, the highly effulgent Ugrasena, with his face cast down, entered and approached Kṛṣṇa, whose eyes were clouded with tears,
as he lamented in this manner in the assembly of the Yādavas.
Ugrasena, apprehensive due to the guilt of his son's crime, seized the Yadus.
Then, accompanied by all the Vṛṣṇis, Śini, and the others,
he spoke to the lotus-eyed Kṛṣṇa in the assembly of the Yadus with a voice faltering, distressed, and choked with tears.
O son, anger has been cast out; the enemy has been sent to the southern region;
fame acquired through one's own dharma has been proclaimed throughout the earth.
Greatness has been established among the virtuous, enemies have been made apprehensive,
the Yādava lineage has been stabilized, and friends have been made proud.
Your majesty shall be proclaimed among the neighboring lords of men;
your friends will honor you, and those seeking their own interests will take refuge with you.
The subjects will follow you; the twice-born will offer praise to you;
and the ministers, foremost in matters of peace and war, will bow down before you.
O Kṛṣṇa, accept this inexhaustible army of Kaṃsa, which is filled with elephants, horses, and chariots, and crowded with throngs of foot soldiers.
"O Kṛṣṇa, let your appointed men receive whatever wealth, grain, jewels, and garments there may be—
women, gold, clothing, and whatever other riches exist."
For when the yoga has been thus performed and the body of Kṛṣṇa is complete,
O destroyer of enemies, the earth will be firmly established for the Yadus.
O delighter of the Yadus, you are indeed the refuge and the ultimate resort of the Yadavas;
O hero, listen to these words of us who are wretched as we speak:
[regarding] this Kaṃsa of evil deeds, who has been consumed by your wrath.
Through your grace, Govinda, the funeral rites shall indeed be performed.
Having performed the funeral rites for this deceased lord of men,
I, together with my daughter-in-law and my wife, shall wander among the deer.

O Kṛṣṇa, it is said that once the rites for the deceased have been performed merely by way of funeral ceremonies and the duties toward kin have been fulfilled, I have indeed attained freedom from worldly debt.
Having placed the fire to the west of this [body] at the site of consciousness, even without the prescribed ritual,
may I attain freedom from debt to Kaṃsa by the mere offering of water.
O Kṛṣṇa, this is my request; let your affection be applied here.
May that wretched man attain a happy rebirth through this final rite.
Having heard these words of his, Kṛṣṇa was exceedingly delighted and replied to Ugrasena with these words of consolation:
"O Father, these words spoken by you are timely;
they are worthy, O tiger among kings, of both your conduct and your lineage,
that you speak thus when the matter has become impossible to overcome."
O King, Kaṃsa will receive the funeral rites even though he has already passed away.
V3, after the first occurrence of 32ab, inserts:
"Your birth was in a great family, and you have mastered the Vedas;
why, dear son, is it not understood that destiny is difficult to overcome?"
O King, the karma performed in previous births by both stationary beings and mobile beings ripens in the course of time.
They were learned and possessed of wealth, generous and pleasant to behold;
they were devoted to the Brahmins, endowed with statesmanship, and intent on showing favor to the distressed.
O dear one, O best of kings, even those protectors of the earth who are equal to the world-protectors and possess prowess like that of Mahendra are led away by Kṛtānta.
Righteous, knowing the nature of all things, and intent on protecting their subjects,
they were devoted to the duty of the Kṣatriyas, self-controlled, and met their end in due time.
Whether it be auspicious or inauspicious, the karma performed by oneself alone is seen by all embodied beings when its time has arrived.
For this illusion is hidden and difficult to discern even for the gods;
that the world is thus deluded is indeed caused by karma alone.
Struck down by Time and impelled by his past karma, Kaṃsa met his end;
for in this matter, Time alone was not the cause—both Time and Karma were the causes.
O dear one, the entire world of moving and non-moving beings, consisting of sun and moon,
passes into destruction through time and is born again by time alone;
for time is intent upon the restraint and the favoring of all creatures.
Therefore, indeed, all beings are subject to the power of time.
O lord of men, for your son who has been consumed by his own very fault, I am certainly not the cause; rather, Time is the cause there.
Or rather, I shall be the cause here; of this there is no doubt.
What can Time do, being intent on flight and itself devoid of cause?
Time, O King, is powerful, for its course is indeed difficult to discern.
Those who perceive with equanimity and know the distinction between the higher and the lower attain that goal which is the course of Time, by which everything falls within the domain of Time.
My son, let my words be carried out as I speak them.
Indeed, I have no need for sovereignty, nor am I greedy for a kingdom;
furthermore, it was not out of greed for the throne that Kaṃsa was struck down by me.
However, for the sake of the welfare of the world and for the sake of fame, your son,
who was a disgrace to this family, has been struck down along with his younger brothers.
I myself shall wander joyfully among the cattle with the cowherds, roaming through the forest like an elephant acting according to its own will.
Even though I have spoken thus to you a hundred times by way of truth, I have no need for kingship; let this which I request be done.
"May you be my honored king, the leader and lord of the Yadus;
O best of kings, be consecrated in your own kingdom for the sake of victory."
If you wish to do what is pleasing to me, or if you have no distress,
then please accept for a long time this kingdom of your own that has been bestowed by me.
Vaiśampāyana said:
Having heard these words, the king did not utter a reply;
ashamed, he stood before Kṛṣṇa with his face cast down.
Govinda, the knower of yoga, then joined that king— who stood in the assembly of the Yadus with his face cast down in shame— with the royal consecration.
With his crown bound on, the illustrious Ugrasena, lord of the earth,
together with Kṛṣṇa, performed the funeral rites for Kaṃsa.
At the command of Kṛṣṇa, all the principal Yādavas followed that king along the path to the city, like the gods following Śatakratu.
When the night had turned to dawn and the sun had long since risen,
those bulls among the Yadus performed the funeral rites for Kaṃsa.
Having placed Kaṃsa’s body upon a palanquin in due order,
they performed his funeral rites according to the rules for one who has reached the final goal.
That son of the king was led to the northern bank of the Yamunā and was cremated according to the prescribed rite by the funeral fire of the pyre.
In the same manner, the Yādavas, together with Kṛṣṇa, caused his brother Sunāman, who possessed mighty arms, to receive the funeral rites.
With those two [vessels], the great chariot-warriors of the Vṛṣṇis and Andhakas poured out water for them;
and speaking thus to the deceased, they set forth, declaring it to be inexhaustible.
And as he spoke inexhaustibly, they set out for the sake of the pretas;
likewise Hari gave ten crores of silver and gold,
as well as cows, jewels, garments, and villages esteemed as cities.
The best of kings gave [the kingdom] to the Brahmins, designating Kaṃsa as the object;
having offered water for those two [deceased kings], the Yādavas, with dejected minds,
placed Ugrasena at their head and entered the city of Mathurā.
All those related to his own lineage from every direction— afflicted by the fear of Kaṃsa— the Yadus, Vṛṣṇis, Andhakas, Madhus, Dāśārhas, Kukuras, and others.
Having honored and comforted those who had been emaciated by living in foreign lands,
the Creator of All settled them in his own homes, satisfying them with wealth.
Protected by the arms of Kṛṣṇa and Saṃkarṣaṇa, their desires fulfilled,
those perfected ones rejoiced in their own homes, freed from the fever of anxiety regarding Kṛṣṇa and Rāma.
Day after day, the glorious one gazed with joy upon the lotus-face of Mukunda,
which was eternally delighted and graced by a compassionate, smiling glance.

There, the powerful Kṛṣṇa, united with the son of Rohiṇī,
dwelt happily in that city of Mathurā, which was under the control of the Yādavas.
Then, O king of kings, having approached Nanda, the Blessed One, the son of Devakī,
and Saṃkarṣaṇa embraced him and spoke as follows.
You two have been cherished and greatly pampered by your affectionate father;
for indeed, parents' love for their own children exceeds even their love for themselves.
He is a father and she is a mother who nourish [others] like their own children.
He took charge of the children abandoned by their kinsmen, providing for them with all necessary articles, nourishment, and protection.
"Go now to Vraja, dear ones; we shall come to see our kinsmen who are pained by affection for you, after we have ensured the well-being of our friends."
Having thus consoled Nanda’s settlement, the Lord Acyuta respectfully delighted them with excellent dwellings, ornaments, and forms.
Thus addressed, Nanda, overwhelmed with affection, embraced them both;
his eyes filling with tears, he returned to Vraja with the cowherds.
But [Kṛṣṇa], his body having attained youth and blazing with royal splendor, remained there.
The hero built Mathurā, adorned with oceans of jewels.
Then, after some time had passed, Rāma and Keśava,
together and desiring to master the science of archery, both went to their preceptor Sandīpani of Kāśī, who resided in the city of Avanti.
Having announced their lineage, and being adorned by their own study and conduct,
both Rāma and Janārdana— those lotus-eyed ones who were eager to acquire knowledge, desirous of service, and free from egoism— performed their recitation according to the prescribed rules.
The King of Kāśī received them both and bestowed upon them all his knowledge in its entirety.
And let those two heroes, who possess the power of retaining what they hear, master the Veda along with its auxiliary limbs in due course, completing it in sixty-four days and nights.
May those two delights of the Yadus likewise master the Veda with its auxiliary limbs in sixty-four days,
as well as the fourfold science of archery along with the collection of weapons and their manuals,
and both writing and arithmetic.
And both of them acquired the entire science of music (gāndharvaveda), as well as the arts of painting,
and the training of elephants and horses, within twelve days.
Then those two heroes, knowers of dharma and practitioners of dharma, went together to their teacher Sāndīpani for the purpose of learning the science of archery.
Having approached and bowed down before that preeminent teacher of archery,
O King, they were honored by him as they wandered through the Avanti country.
Within fifty days and nights,

the teacher instructed them both in the entirety of the science of archery (*dhanurveda*), complete with its ten branches, its secret doctrines, and its practical applications; he taught them both in a very short time until they were firmly established in it.
Then, reflecting upon their superhuman intelligence, the preceptor considered those two who had arrived to be both the gods Candra and Divākara.
And he beheld both those high-souled ones also worshipping Mahādeva, the three-eyed one himself, who was present in person on the sacred festival days.
O descendant of Bharata, having accomplished his purpose, Kṛṣṇa spoke to his teacher Sāndīpani along with Rāma, saying, "What shall I give as the teacher's fee?"
Having understood their power, the Guru spoke joyfully:
"I desire a son named Datta, who was lost in the salt waters."
"Only one son was born to me, and he too was carried off by a timi fish;
bring him back to me from Prabhāsa during your pilgrimage to the sacred fords."
"So be it," said the radiant Kṛṣṇa, remaining in accordance with Rāma's consent;
having gone to the ocean, Hari entered beneath the waters.
Then the ocean, having joined his palms in reverence, showed him [the boy] to Kṛṣṇa. Kṛṣṇa said to him, "O sir, where is that son of Sāndīpani?"
The great Daitya Pañcajana, in the form of a whale, had swallowed that boy; thus spoke the ocean to Mādhava.
"O Bhārata, having churned these waters, he seized him," so it was said;
yet that Supreme Person (Puruṣottama), though he encountered Pañcajana, slew him,
for Acyuta did not find that boy, the son of his preceptor, at that time.
Having slain Pañcajana, Janārdana obtained the conch shell which is known among gods and men as Pāñcajanya.
Having gone to the city of Yama, Viṣṇu, his eyes bloodshot with anger, then spoke to the powerful Yama as he sat upon his throne: "Let the son of Kāśya Sāṃdīpani be given back! thus did Viṣṇu say.
Then, O Hari, he was brought by Death and spoke to Viṣṇu;
thus addressed then by Yama, Kṛṣṇa of immeasurable prowess said, "Oh, what audacity on the part of Death! and took up his bow.
Taking up a sharp arrow, he said, "Let him be given!
Recognizing that Viṣṇu was enraged, [Yama] indeed gave him the boy.
Then, having conquered the god Vaivasvata, Puruṣottama—

Then Acyuta Govinda approached that boy, the son of his preceptor; filling his conch shell, he truly struck terror into the people. Thereupon Yama approached and paid homage to that wielder of the mace.
"What is the purpose of your coming? What shall I do? he asked.
Then Kṛṣṇa said to him, "Let the preceptor’s son be given back.
Thereupon, a most terrible and great battle took place between the two;
[Kṛṣṇa] brought back the preceptor’s son, who had long been lost, from the abode of Yama.
Then, by the grace of that one of immeasurable luster, the son of Sāndīpani—
who had been dead for a long time— once again possessed a body.
Seeing that which was impossible, inconceivable, and most wonderful,
amazement arose among all living beings.
Taking the preceptor’s son, the conch Pāñcajanya, and highly precious jewels, Mādhava, the Lord of the World, returned once more.
Having brought many highly precious jewels belonging to that Rākṣasa,
the younger brother of Vāsava presented them to his preceptor.
In combat with maces and iron clubs, and in the use of all weapons, both of them soon attained preeminence among all archers in the entire world.
Then the noble-minded Kṛṣṇa gave the son of Sāndīpani— who was identical in form and age— to the gratified king, along with precious jewels.
Then, O King, Sāndīpani, having met with his long-lost son, rejoiced while honoring Rāma and Keśava.
Having mastered all weapons, those two heroes, firm in their vows, took leave of their preceptor and returned once more to Mathurā as the two sons of Vasudeva.
Then all the Yādavas, led by Ugrasena, went out to meet the two delights of the Yadu clan,
including their children, with joyful hearts.
The guilds, the subjects, the ministers, and the priests,
together with the children and the elderly, all came forth from that city.
Joyful musical instruments were sounded and people praised Janārdana;
the streets, adorned with garlands of banners, shone brilliantly on all sides.
The entire inner apartment shone with great joy and delight at Govinda’s arrival,
just like at the festival of Indra.
And joyful singers sang upon the royal roads,
singing songs that began with praises and blessings, bringing delight to the Yādavas.
The two world-renowned brothers, Govinda and Rāma, have arrived;
all of you may sport without fear with your kinsmen in your own city.

O King, when Govinda arrived in Mathurā, there was no one there— whether from those foreign lands who had fled out of fear of Kaṃsa, or anyone else— who appeared dejected, soiled, or dispirited. All shone with joy.
The birds sang auspicious songs, the cattle, horses, and elephants were overjoyed, and all the multitudes of men and women experienced happiness of mind.
Auspicious winds blew, free from dust, across the ten directions;
and all the deities in their abodes were filled with joy.
All those signs that had formerly appeared in the world during the Kṛta-yuga were seen once again when Janārdana reached the city.
Then, at an auspicious and holy time, Govinda, the crusher of enemies, entered the city of Mathurā by means of a chariot yoked with tawny horses.
As Upendra, the subduer of enemies, entered the beautiful city of Mathurā,
the hosts of Yadus followed him, just as the hosts of gods follow Śakra.
Then those two delights of the Yadu clan entered the palace of Vasudeva with joyful countenances, like the moon and the sun entering a mountain.
Endowed with supreme splendor and possessing forms like those of the lords of the gods, those two best of the Yadus,
both sons of Vasudeva, set aside their weapons and, moving about at their own will in their own home, rejoiced together.
Surrounded by the Yādavas, those two great-souled ones wandered through various gardens that were bent down with fruits and flowers.
In the vicinity of Mount Raivata, by the pure rivers abounding with lotus petals and teeming with *kāraṇḍava* ducks,
Balabhadra and Janārdana thus passed their childhood.
Thus, those two auspicious-faced emanations, having become followers of Ugrasena in Mathurā, rejoiced for some time.
Having stayed for four months, the noble-minded Nandagopa embraced Rāma and Kṛṣṇa; then,
with the approval of the Yadus and the permission of Vasudeva, he departed for his own cart.
O best of sages, this entire account of the boy's deeds has been recounted by me to you exactly as I heard it, according to its proper application, and in accordance with my knowledge.
To Kṛṣṇa, Keśava, Acyuta, Murāri, Śauri, Hari, the wielder of the Śārṅga bow,
Viṣṇu, the creator of the universe, the four-armed one, the beloved of Śrī, the upholder of Śrī,
the victorious Jiṣṇu, the enemy of the Daityas, the abode of the three-fold light, the supreme Lord of the three worlds.
I bow my head to Govinda, the Supreme Person, Nārāyaṇa, the wielder of the discus.

Vaiśampāyana said:
Now, after some time, the king, the lord of Rājagṛha—
The powerful Jarāsaṃdha heard that Kaṃsa had been slain.
From his two daughters, O bull of the Bharatas, the lord of the earth [obtained sons]; then, after not much time had passed, Asti and Prāpti became the two chief queens of Kaṃsa.
While their husband was hateful and afflicted by grief, the two went to the house of their father;
he, possessing the prowess of Indra, arrived surrounded by a great army consisting of six divisions and accompanied by a vast force.
Seeking the death of Kṛṣṇa, he followed Madhurā;
for, enraged and desiring to slay the Yadus, he was seeking to avenge Kaṃsa.
Indeed, out of fear of public scandal, wishing to protect his own reputation,
and desiring the pleasure and welfare of his daughter,
the restrainer [Yudhiṣṭhira] then set out together with an army of twenty-one akṣauhiṇīs.
O King, the daughter of the Magadha king was named Asti and Prāpti;
delighted, that Magadha king gave those two daughters to King Kaṃsa.

Therefore, O King, both those auspicious women of Jarāsaṃdha— Māgadhīs with full hips and breasts— would become widows because of that dark one, even while the hero, the leader of kings, was still alive.
King Bārhadratha gave both of those wives to Kaṃsa.
Having bound his father Āhuka, that king took delight with those two;
relying upon Jarāsaṃdha and disregarding the Yādavas,
he became the lord of Śūrasena, just as you have heard many times before.
For the sake of accomplishing the affairs of his kinsmen and for the welfare of Ugrasena, Vasudeva was ever devoted; yet Kaṃsa could not tolerate him.
When the evil-minded Kaṃsa had been slain by taking refuge in Rāma and Kṛṣṇa,
Ugrasena became king, surrounded by the Bhojas, Vṛṣṇis, and Andhakas.
Abiding by the will of Keśava,
the powerful King Jarāsaṃdha ruled Mathurā with his two beloved daughters; for their sake, he then employed various stratagems against Mathurā through those two wives of heroes.
Hearing those unpleasant words, the king, filled with grief and indignation,
made a supreme effort to rid the earth of the Yādavas.
Accompanied by twenty-three *akṣauhiṇīs*,
the king arrived at Mathurā, the capital of the Yadus, to besiege it;
having made every possible effort, he marched against the Yadus out of wrath.
For those kings who were bowed down by Jarāsaṃdha’s prowess—
his allies, kinsmen, and likewise his closely associated friends— [were all brought under his power].
All those kings who had previously departed in shame from that Mount Gomanta followed after him, surrounded by their assembled armies;
and they all followed Jarāsaṃdha in order to slay the Yadus.
Great archers of immense prowess, they were seekers of Jarāsaṃdha’s favor.
Kārūṣa and Dantavakra, the heroic King of Cedi, the lord of Kaliṅga, Pauṇḍra the best among the strong, Āhvṛti,
Kauśika, and Bhīṣmaka the ruler of men.
And Bhīṣmaka’s son was Rukmin, the foremost of archers,
who always vied with Vāsudeva and Arjuna in strength.
Veṇudāri, Śrutarvā, Krātha, and Aṃśumān as well,
along with the powerful king of Aṅga and likewise the lord of the Vaṅgas.
The king of Kausala, the king of Kashi, as well as the lord of Dasharna, the valiant lord of Suhma, and likewise the lord of Videha.
The powerful King of Madra, the lord of the Trigartas,
the valiant King of the Śālvas, and the exceedingly strong Darada;
The lord of the Yavanas, and the heroic Bhagadatta;
the king of the Sauvīras, Śaibya, and Pāṇḍya, the best among the strong;
Subala, the king of the Gāndhāras, and the exceedingly powerful Nagnajit.
The king of Kaśmīra was Gonarda, and the lord of Darada was King Nṛpa.
Duryodhana and the other mighty sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra,
as well as these and other powerful kings who were great chariot-warriors,
followed Jarāsaṃdha, hating Janārdana.
Having entered Śūrasena, which abounded in fodder and fuel, they then remained there,
surrounding Mathurā and besieging it with their forces.

Vaiśampāyana said:
Having gone to the grove on the outskirts of Mathurā, those lords of men settled there.
All the Vṛṣṇis beheld him, placing Janārdana at their head.
O King, when those Magadhan monarchs, the best of kings, had arrived, Kṛṣṇa, with a joyful heart, spoke these words to Rāma:
"The purpose of the gods is indeed hastening; of this there is no doubt."
For this King Jarāsaṃdha is indeed close at hand;
for the tops of the banners of his chariots, swift as the wind, are visible.
O Noble One, these white umbrellas, resembling the moon, stand raised aloft and shine brilliantly for men who desire victory.
Ah! These rows of spotless, white royal umbrellas, raised aloft on the king’s chariot, advance toward us like rows of swans in the sky.
Truly, at this very moment, King Jarāsaṃdha, the lord of the earth, has arrived—
the first guest of battle and the touchstone for our combat.
"Noble one, let us stay together until the lord of the earth has arrived;
once he has reached us, the commencement of battle must be undertaken, but first let our strength be deliberated."
Having spoken thus, Kṛṣṇa, composed and eager for battle,
desiring to seize Jarāsaṃdha, displayed his strength.
And beholding all those kings, the imperishable best of the Yadus,
a knower of mantras, spoke these words within his heart by means of his own self.
These rulers of the earth, established on the path of kingship,
shall meet their destruction here through actions contrary to what is seen in the scriptures.
"I believe these bulls among kings have indeed been sprinkled by Death;
for their bodies shone as if they were destined for heaven."
It is only right that this earth, exhausted by the burden, has gone to heaven,
being oppressed by the floods of troops of these preeminent kings;
for this ground is now covered without interval by the forces and kingdoms.
Indeed, in a very short time, the surface of the earth will become desolate due to the hundreds of multitudes of kings who have been struck down.
As Kṛṣṇa, the performer of wondrous deeds, was reflecting in this manner,
the Blessed One, having thus resolved upon battle,
stood together with Saṃkarṣaṇa, as immovable as a mountain.
Then Jarāsaṃdha, the lord of all kings, highly effulgent, became enraged and set out followed by a multitude of thousands of rulers of men.
With battle-chariots equipped with machines, well-maintained, yoked to long-necked, spirited horses, and possessing unimpeded movement in every direction;
With elephants resembling clouds, adorned with golden girths and great bells,
mounted by excellent mahouts, and prepared by those skilled in battle;
With horses resembling clouds, mounted by skilled riders who were leaping and watching, they seemed like foot-soldiers floating through the air.
[The army] was filled with foot-soldiers brandishing swords and shields,
leaping like serpents as they rose up, their garments fluttering, numbering in the thousands.
Thus the powerful King Jarāsaṃdha, firm in his vows, marched forth with a fourfold army that resembled trembling clouds.
With chariots having the roar of clouds, with elephants dripping with rut,
with neighing horses, and with foot-soldiers shouting their war-cries.
Making all the directions and the forests of that city resound with his roar,
the lord of men was followed by twenty akṣauhiṇīs;
that king, resembling the ocean, appeared together with his army.
That army of the lords of the earth, crowded with arrogant warriors,
resounded with the shouts of battle and the slapping of arms, appearing like a host of clouds.
With chariots swift as the wind, with elephants resembling clouds,
with horses endowed with speed, and with foot-soldiers like birds in flight.
Intermingled, it shone on all sides, crowded with rutting elephants and chariots,
just like a mass of clouds over the ocean at the end of the summer heat.
Those powerful rulers of the earth, led by Jarāsaṃdha,
all surrounded the city and prepared to encamp.
The splendor of the army of that encamped host shone indeed like the appearance of the great ocean when its white shores are full.
Then, at the end of the night, the rulers of the earth arose;
eager for battle, they gathered together to ascend the city.
All those kings, having assembled together along the Yamunā,
took up their positions and consulted one another, eager for the time of battle.
A tumultuous roar was heard from those rulers of the earth,
like the sound of oceans bursting asunder at the end of an eon.
For them, according to the king’s command, elderly attendants wearing tunics and turbans and carrying canes in their hands moved about, saying, "Do not make a sound!"
The appearance of that army, being utterly silent and still,
was like that of the great ocean when its fish and crocodiles have settled into silence.
In that silence, as still as the great ocean when at rest through yoga,
Jarāsaṃdha took up these weighty words, just as Bṛhaspati might.
Let the armies of the rulers of the earth assemble quickly;
let this city be surrounded on all sides by throngs of people.
Let stone-engines be set in place, along with slings and mallets;
let the entire ground be leveled and flooded with torrents of water;
and let bows be drawn upward, as well as spears and javelins.
Let the city be quickly breached with floods of axes and pickaxes;
and let kings skilled in the ways of war be stationed nearby.
"From this day forward, let the siege of my city be carried out by my armies,
so that I may have both these cowherds, the sons of Vasudeva— Saṃkarṣaṇa and Kṛṣṇa— slain in battle with my sharp arrows."
Even the sky was made such that it became impassable by the floods of arrows.
"Let the kings instructed by me remain in the various regions of the city;
let the city itself be quickly ascended upon those respective sites."
Madra, the lord of Kaliṅga, Cekitāna along with the Bāhlikas,
Gonarda the king of Kaśmīra, and likewise the lord of Karūṣa;
"Let Druma, Kimpuruṣa, and Dāmana of the mountains quickly ascend the western gate of the city."
Paurava, Veṇudāri, Vaidarbha, and Somaka;
Rukmin, the lord of the Bhojas, and Sūryākṣa the Mālava.
"Let the mighty lord of the Pāñcālas, the Drupadas,
and the heroic Vinda and Anuvinda of Avanti, along with Dantavaktra,
quickly take up their positions at the southern city gate."
Chāgali, Purumitra, and Virāṭa, the lord of the earth.
Kauśāmbya, Mālava, Śatadhanvan, Vidūratha,
Bhūriśravas, Trigarta, Bāṇa, and likewise Pañcanada.
Let these kings, who endure hardships and possess a dignity like that of a thunderbolt, ascend and storm the northern city gate.
Ulūka, Kaitaveya, and Vīra, the son of Aṃśumat; Ekalavya, Bṛhatkṣatra, Kṣatradharman, and Jayadratha.
And Uttamaujas, Śalya, the Kauravas, as well as the Kaikayas,
Vaidiśa, Vāmadeva, Sāketa, and Sinīpati.
Let the city gate be placed under your control;
let them rush forward with speed, driving like winds against the clouds.
I, as well as Darada and the King of Cedi, shall stand together at the southern city gate, armored and ready to defend it.
Thus, let this city, quickly surrounded on all sides by the forces,
encounter a tumultuous terror resembling the falling of thunderbolts.
Let those who possess maces strike with maces, those with iron clubs with iron clubs,
and others with various weapons tear asunder this city.
This very day, however, this city— with its uneven heights and narrow passages—
must be made entirely level with the ground by you, the lords of the earth.
Having spoken thus, Jarāsandha, whose prowess was equal to that of Śakra, drew up his fourfold army and took his stand. Then,
filled with rage, he advanced against the Yadus along with all the lords of men.
The Daśārhas, skilled strikers, returned with their troops drawn up in battle array.
Seeing those two Yādavas then arrived at the head of the army, the King of Magadha looked at them and said in anger: "O Kṛṣṇa, you lowest of men!
Out of shame, I do not wish to fight with you, a mere child."
O Rāma, since you have such faith in battle, maintain your steadfastness! Either, your body covered by my arrows, go to heaven as one slain; or else, slay me.
The Blessed One said:
"Heroes indeed do not boast; they simply demonstrate their prowess.
O King, we do not heed the words of one who is diseased and about to die."
Then that battle took place, terrible like the conflict between the gods and the asuras,
between the few and the many, with chariots and elephants entangled with one another.
Placing Ugrasena at their head, Vāsudeva and Halāyudha,
both skilled in combat, mounted their chariots and set out for battle;
seeing both sons of Vasudeva emerge from the city, [the people were amazed].
The army of the best of men was agitated, its mounts terrified and bewildered.
Stationed on their chariots and clad in armor, the two Yādavas moved about there like two enraged sea-monsters agitating the ocean.
As those two Yādavas were engaged in combat, their intelligence shone forth;
as they fought in the fray, the minds of those self-controlled men became focused on seizing ancient weapons.
Then, during that tumultuous onset of battle, there fell from the sky divine arrows— blazing, licking with flame, immense, and exceedingly firm.
Followed by flesh-eating beasts, they were large and embodied,
intensely thirsty in battle to devour the flesh of kings.
Wearing divine garlands of flowers, they struck terror into the sky-dwellers;
shining with radiance, they were armored and pervaded the ten directions.
The plow named Saṃvartaka, the club Saunanda,
the Śārṅga— the best of bows— and the mace Kaumodakī.
These four splendors are the weapons of Viṣṇu;
they descended from them, the two Yādavas, in the great battle.
First, Rāma seized his plowshare, which was like a crest-jewel;
in the battle, it coiled like a serpent and was adorned with divine garlands.
Then the glorious one, the best of the Sātvatas, took up with his left hand the Saunanda, that most excellent mace which brings joylessness to his enemies.
The heroic Viṣṇu took up that bow, which was beautiful to behold among all worlds, sounding like a rain-cloud, and renowned by the name Śārṅga.
In the other hand of that lotus-eyed one, a mace was placed by the gods according to their word; it is known by the name Kaumodakī.
Those two heroes, Rāma and Govinda, bearing their weapons and resembling the very personifications of Viṣṇu, fought back against those enemies in battle.

Those two heroes, Rāma and Govinda, bearing their weapons and grasping them firmly, were both possessed of mutual affection; known as elder and younger brothers, they displayed their prowess against their enemies like two lords.
Both sons of Vasudeva moved about like two gods;
the heroic Rāma, having raised his plow like an enraged lord of serpents,
roamed through the battle like the Destroyer of his enemies.
Dragging away the throngs of chariots of the high-souled kṣatriyas,
he made his wrath bear fruit against both elephants and horses.
Shining resplendently in battle, Rāma crushed the elephants— thrown down by his plow and struck by the hurling of his mace— just as one might grind mountains.
Being pierced by Rāma in battle, those heroic bulls among Kṣatriyas, distressed by the combat, fled to the presence of Jarāsaṃdha.
Jarāsaṃdha, established in the duty of a Kṣatriya, said to them:
"Fie upon this conduct of yours as Kṣatriyas, you who are so cowardly in battle!"
The wise declare that for one who turns away in battle, being deprived of his chariot and fleeing, it is like the unbearable sin of killing an embryo.
"Why do you turn back in fear? Fie on this conduct of the Kshatriyas! Return quickly, urged by my command;
or else remain in your chariots as spectators, standing your ground."
I shall dispatch these two cowherds to the abode of Yama in battle.
"I stand here in battle, enraged, for the victory of the Kṣatriyas.
Then all those Kṣatriyas, urged by Jarāsaṃdha,
stood ready to fight with joy, discharging nets of arrows.
They [advanced] with horses adorned with golden crests, with chariots sounding like clouds,
and with elephants resembling clouds, urged on by their mahouts.
Equipped with armor, swords, banners, weapons, and standards;
with bows strung upon them, quivers well-filled, and javelins at hand.
All those kings, mounted upon their chariots in battle, shone resplendent as they advanced, holding up white umbrellas and being fanned by beautiful yak-tail whisks.
Those chariot-warriors, the best among combatants, who were passionate for battle,
plunged in with heavy maces, slings, and mallets.
In the meantime, there Nandivardhana of the gods [blew his conch];
in that same interval, the powerful King Jarāsaṃdha blew his conch with a great sound, making all the directions resound.
Having heard that, even the God of gods blew his unsurpassed conch, Pāñcajanya,
by whose sound all the deities dwelling in heaven were terrified;
what then need be said of all the armies being struck with fear?
Mounting his excellent chariot bearing the banner of Garuḍa, Kṛṣṇa then advanced against Jarāsaṃdha and pierced him with eight arrows.
Having also struck down Viṣṇu with eight arrows, he beheld Ugrasena;
standing at the side of Hari, he said, "Listen, O King, to my words."
O Rāma, tell me now: what king were you?
For you are the foremost among the ignorant; who else on earth is like you?
But as for that funeral cake which was indeed offered by this slayer of his own son, you constantly eat it; O blind one, tell me, what is more than this?
O king, having slain your son,
this merciless Śauri has now established you alone upon the throne and is eager for battle.
Bearing the title of "King," you have come to his service;
O King, you are old only in years, but not in wisdom.
"O shameless one, attached to enjoyments, you wretched creature, lowest of kings! Depart from here, you who have grown old in vain; I cannot bear to look upon you."
Now, desiring to engage in battle, [he said]: "Stay before me for a moment;
I shall indeed slay you along with your army, and likewise Hari along with his army."
Having said this, he then took up his bow and stood before him.
Hearing that, Hari, his eyes copper-red with rage, spoke to the King of Magadha;
he then vanished from that Gomanta, the best of mountains.
Now you arrive, accompanied by all your forces;
I stand here, enraged for battle, bringing about the destruction of the Kṣatriyas.
"I am that very same child, O King, and you too are indeed that very same person.
It is not fitting, O King, to speak thus in vain to Ugrasena;
speak to me alone, O Indra among kings, for I am your enemy, O Lord."
O King, you shall see what has now been accomplished by me in this manner.
Now, what is the use of much speaking? O King, I shall cut off your head if you do not flee today, O lord of kings.
Having spoken thus, Keśava pierced the king with twenty-five arrows and struck his charioteer with five sharpened shafts;
the valiant one then slew the horses of the striving foe in the battle.
O Indra among kings, Keśava cut asunder Jarāsaṃdha’s bow,
severed his standard, and struck down his charioteer.
And he cut down his chariot while all the kṣatriyas looked on; deprived of his chariot and his bow, he stood upon the surface of the earth.
Perceiving him to be in such distress, the great car-warrior Citrasena—
Both Senānī and Kauśika pierced Kṛṣṇa with arrows.
Kauśika pierced the engaged Baladeva with three arrows,
and in that battle, Baladeva split his bow in two with a broad-headed shaft;
he then overwhelmed those enemies with swift showers of arrows.
From all sides, the heroic Citrasena, enraged, pierced him with nine arrows adorned with gold;
Kauśika struck him with five, and Jarāsaṃdha with seven.
Janārdana pierced them with three iron arrows each;
then the lord of the earth, the ruler of Magadha, taking up another bow,
struck Ugrasena with a sharpened shaft.
Then, O great king, that arrow urged the king on;
O Indra among kings, he pierced the father of Kaṃsa with seven arrows.
With seventy arrows and again with nine,
Jarāsaṃdha struck the king, the joy of the Yadus;
and while Mādhava looked on, he struck him with ten thousand arrows.
Ugrasena, bow in hand, split his bow in two.
Then the powerful Jarāsaṃdha, taking up his bow once more,
struck Ugrasena with twenty well-sharpened arrows.
While Baladeva looked on, he pierced the king of kings and,
O King, likewise severed his bow into two pieces at the handle.
Taking up a sharp arrow, O King, the powerful lord Jarāsaṃdha,
that king of kings, pierced the king in the heart.
With a straight-knotted arrow, the king cut down his horses and split his chariot in two, while also felling his standard.
And that best of kings among the Vṛṣṇis fled from the chariot.
Kauśika, Citrasena, and King Jarāsaṃdha,
O great king, each struck Janārdana with three arrows;
Jarāsaṃdha was then broken by those shafts while Vasudeva looked on.
And Baladeva [struck him] with five and five sharp arrows.
The heroic Baladeva also cut through the chariot-pole of Citrasena and,
in that battle, split his bow in two with a broad-headed arrow.
With his bow broken and deprived of his chariot, that valiant hero, seizing a mace,
rushed forward in great fury, desiring to slay the one whose weapon is the club.
As Rāma was desiring to discharge iron arrows in his quest for Citrasena’s death, the mighty Jarāsandha cut his bow;
then that lord of Magadha, out of anger, struck down his horses with a mace.
The mighty hero Jarāsaṃdha rushed toward Rāma,
and taking up his mace, Rāma charged at Jarāsaṃdha;
a battle then ensued between the two, each desiring the other's death.
But Citrasena, seeing the King of Magadha engaged with Rāma,
mounted another chariot and held Jarāsaṃdha at bay.
Then, with a great force and a division of elephants, a tumultuous encounter took place between those two in the midst of both armies; thereafter,
Jarāsaṃdha was surrounded by that vast host.
The one of great strength encountered the Bhojas, who were led by Rāma and Kṛṣṇa.
Then, a tumultuous and great roar, like that of the agitated ocean,
arose from both those armies.
O King, a great roar arose from thousands of flutes, kettledrums, clay drums, and conch shells belonging to both armies.
A tumultuous din arose on all sides from their shouting, the slapping of arms, and their war-cries;
and dust, raised by their hooves and the rims of their wheels, flew upward.
With great weapons raised and bows grasped,
the heroes stood there, roaring at one another.
Charioteers, cavalrymen, and foot soldiers by the thousands,
as well as exceedingly powerful elephants, gathered there fearlessly.
Then, O Great King, a tumultuous and fierce battle took place between those kings seeking victory and the warriors of Jarāsaṃdha along with the Vṛṣṇis, as they cast away their very lives.
Then Śini, Anādhṛṣṭi, Babhru, Vipṛthu, and Āhuka,
placing Baladeva at their head, set out armored with half of the army.
O Bhārata, O Lord, they assailed the right wing of the enemy army,
which was protected by the King of Cedi and Jarāsaṃdha.
And by the northern kings of great prowess, such as Śalya, Sālva, and others,
who had renounced their very lives, showers of arrows were discharged.
Āgāvaha, Pṛthu, Kahva, Śatadyumna, and Vidūratha,
having placed Hṛṣīkeśa at their head, went forth clad in armor with half of the army.
O king of kings, [the city] was protected by Bhīṣmaka, the high-souled Rukmin,
Devaka, and likewise the lord of Madra,
as well as by the easterners and southerners, who were endowed with concealed heroism and strength.
A great and tumultuous battle took place between them, as they had utterly renounced their lives while discharging floods of spears, double-edged swords, javelins, and arrows.
Sātyaki, Citraka, Śyāma, the heroic Yuyudhāna,
Rājādhideva, Mṛdura, and the mighty Śvaphalka.
Satrājit and Prasena, surrounded by a great force,
took their positions on the left wing of the formation against the enemies in battle.
They approached half of the array, which was protected by Mṛdura;
there a great battle took place, resembling that between the gods and the asuras, as the few fought against the many through the protection of Vāsudeva.
Thus did that battle take place among those heroes, increasing their joy,
generating terror in the timid, and swelling the kingdom of Yama,
fought together with many kings headed by Veṇudāri.
And it was protected by the westerners, fierce in their strength, and by the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra.
