Vaiśampāyana said:
Then, great battles ensued between the Vṛṣṇis and the ministers of the King of Magadha, as well as his subordinate kings.
Then a duel took place between the two armies:
between Vāsudeva and Rukmin, and between Āhuka and Bhīṣmaka;
between Vasudeva and Krātha, and between Babhru and Kauśika.
By Śambhu, [the boon was granted] to Dantavaktra, the king of Cedi, through his mace.
Vinda and Anuvinda of Avanti engaged with Yuyudhāna;
then Ekalavya, O great king, engaged with Pradyumna;
likewise, other high-souled kings fought with the heroes of the Vṛṣṇis.
For there was indeed a battle between the armies and their soldiers, O bull of the Bharatas.
For six, seven, eight, five, and one day,
O King, the warriors fought a terrible battle: elephants against elephants, horses against horses, foot-soldiers against foot-soldiers, and chariots against chariots, as well as in mixed combat.
King Jarāsaṃdha’s encounter with Rāma was as fierce and hair-raising as that between Mahendra and Vṛtra.
Having looked at Rukmiṇī, Kṛṣṇa did not strike down Rukmin.
By means of his training, Kṛṣṇa indeed warded off those arrows of his, which resembled the rays of a blazing sun and were like the venom of poisonous serpents; meanwhile,
there was a great destruction of the masses of forces belonging to the others.
O King, between the two armies there was a mire of flesh and blood.
Countless headless trunks rose up on all sides,
as did piśācas and rākṣasas craving flesh and blood;
in that clash of warriors, no distinction of number could be discerned.
The heroic charioteer Rāma advanced against Jarāsaṃdha, covering him with arrows resembling venomous serpents; and that king of Magadha likewise assailed him.
He rushed forward with speed on his swift-moving chariot;
repeatedly piercing one another with various weapons, they both roared.
With their weapons exhausted, deprived of their chariots, their horses slain, and their charioteers killed, the two [remained].
Having seized their clubs, they rushed at one another with great valor.
Making the earth tremble, those two great-souled heroes, with their mighty maces raised aloft,
appeared like two mountains complete with their peaks.
Ceasing their combat, those two bulls among men,
renowned for their skill in mace-fighting, rushed at each other in a fury.
Both those supreme teachers, renowned in the world and possessed of great strength,
rushed at one another in battle like two elephants in rut.
Then the gods, along with the gandharvas, the siddhas, and the supreme ṛṣis,
as well as thousands of apsarases from all sides, assembled there.
And the blessed Grandfather arrived to witness the battle;
adorned by gods, yakṣas, gandharvas, and great ṛṣis,
O King, it shone exceedingly, like the sky with its hosts of luminaries.
The mighty Jarāsaṃdha rushed toward Rāma,
while Baladeva moved in a clockwise circle to the right.
Skilled in the art of mace-fighting, the two of them struck each other,
making the ten directions resound like two elephants with their tusks.
The fall of Rāma’s mace was heard like the roar of a thunderbolt,
as if Jarāsaṃdha’s foot were being split apart like a mountain.
The mace hurled from the hand of Jarāsaṃdha did not shake Rāma,
the best among wielders of maces, any more than it could move the immovable Vindhya mountain.
But that lord of Magadha, through his heroism, endured the force of Rāma’s mace with great fortitude, and by means of his training, he warded it off.
Thus those two of great strength, the subduers of their enemies, moved about in that battle,
performing various and wonderful circular maneuvers.
Having exerted themselves for a long time, they stood there exhausted;
after resting for a moment, they struck one another again.
Thus those two chief warriors fought equally for a long time,
and neither of them turned away from the battle.
Then, perceiving his superiority in mace-fighting,
the valiant Rāma, filled with rage, cast aside his mace and seized an excellent club.
Seeing that terrible-looking mace raised by the enraged Baladeva in that great battle— which was indeed unfailing—
Rāmabhadra, filled with wrath, then attacked him with his own mace.
Then Jarāsaṃdha struck Balabhadra with his mace.
Then, Rāma took up the first mace, Gadāpāda the second, Magadheśvara the third, Halāyudha the fourth, and Jarāsaṃdha the fifth; but the fifth was taken by the scion of the Yadus.
And the kick of those two caused the earth to tremble.
Then the gods, along with the gandharvas, yakṣas, and supreme ṛṣis, being terrified, cried out "Svasti! for the sake of the worlds and for Brahmā.
Then the enraged son of Jarā struck him in the chest;
vomiting blood, Rāma fell into a state of exhaustion.
Having rested on the ground for a moment, the Yādava rose up again,
struck him on the head with his mace, and let out a lion’s roar.
And the hero fell to the earth, sighing like one whose life had departed;
"Jarāsandha is slain! Slain! cried the lords of the Yādavas.
Quickly regaining consciousness, the powerful Jarāsaṃdha struck Halāyudha right in the chest with his mace.
He fell into a swoon and then regained consciousness;
thereafter, that heap of blood shone like water welling up.
With all their limbs mangled by maces, O Indra among kings, they shone like two *kiṃśuka* trees set ablaze, though they were now deprived of their chariots and their bows.
Struck by maces, those two great heroes, standing alone upon the field of battle with maces in hand and desiring each other's death, shone resplendently.
O Indra among kings, these two deaths alone appear as if joined together in beauty.
Then the enraged wielder of the plow desired to strike down the son of Jarā;
he pounded his thighs with his mace in the assembly of kings.
Blood issued from his thighs, and from that marrow was produced;
then the wielder of the plow (Balarāma) raised his gaze to sever the head of Jarāsaṃdha.
Then a melodious voice arose in the intermediate space, the witness of the world.
He spoke to Baladeva, who stood with his plow-weapon raised:
"O Rāma, this man must not be slain by you; enough of this exertion, O Mādhava!"
His death has been ordained by me; therefore, desist well.
In no long time at all, the King of Magadha shall cast off his life-breaths.
But Jarāsaṃdha, having heard that, became despondent;
therefore, Halāyudha did not strike at him again.
Both of them then ceased, as did those Vṛṣṇis and those kings.
O great king, a protracted battle ensued between those very high-souled warriors as they struck one another for a long time.
O King, all of them, together with Jarāsaṃdha, were utterly defeated by Kṛṣṇa, the slayer of enemies, and departed as they had come;
for when King Jarāsaṃdha was vanquished, he fled away.
When the sun had set, they did not follow [him] then during the night.
And the highly fortunate Vṛṣṇis, who take refuge in Kṛṣṇa and Saṃkarṣaṇa—
those mighty ones who had achieved their goals— having gathered their own army,
entered the city joyfully, honored by Keśava.
Then those very weapons, having fallen from their hands, vanished right there.
King Jarāsaṃdha also returned to his own city dejected in spirit,
and the kings who were his followers likewise departed for their own kingdoms;
yet, having defeated Jarāsaṃdha, they did not consider him truly conquered.
O tiger among the Kurus, the Vṛṣṇis indeed have a king who is possessed of exceeding strength.
Indeed, what world-renowned lord of the earth could possibly defeat Jarāsaṃdha in battle, even if it were Śatakratu himself? Furthermore,
the Yādavas have already fought eighteen battles against Jarāsaṃdha.
The great chariot-warriors did not strike him, nor were they able to slay him in battle.
But Kṛṣṇa, O King, though capable in battle, did not slay the lord of Magadha, knowing that he was destined to die by another;
for he possessed twenty akṣauhiṇīs, O bull of the Bharatas.
They were those who had assembled for that purpose from King Jarāsaṃdha.
But because they were few in number, O bull of the Bharatas, the Vṛṣṇis were overwhelmed by Bārhadratha, O king of kings, together with the other monarchs.
Having exerted further effort, he set out against the Yādavas protected by Kṛṣṇa;
but after conquering Jarāsaṃdha, the lord of the earth and king of Magadha, in battle,
those lions among the Vṛṣṇis, the great chariot-warriors, lived happily.

Those who, remembering Him, obtain such supreme multitudes of qualities as vitality (*ojas*), splendor (*tejas*), strength (*bala*), wisdom (*dhī*), fortitude (*dhṛti*), majesty (*mahiman*), fortune (*śrī*), fame (*yaśas*), beauty (*rūpa*), command (*ājñā*), and heroism (*vīrya*)— He,
having commanded His devotees, does not come near anyone whose side is agitated by the minds of all people.
O mind, may you forever become a bee at the lotus-feet of that Viṣṇu.
Chapter 83,

Vaiśampāyana said:
At that very time, however, having remembered what had been done toward the cowherds,
Rāma went alone to Vraja by his own accord with the consent of Kṛṣṇa.
Having gone there, he indeed beheld vast and delightful forests and fragrant lakes that he had previously enjoyed.
Having entered that cow-pen with great speed, the Lord, the elder brother of Kṛṣṇa,
was adorned with a charming attire suited to the forest.
He addressed them all as before and according to rule; he spoke to Gopa by that same method, in accordance with propriety and according to his age.
In that very manner he spoke to them all, gladdening them just so,
while likewise delighting the gopīs with sweet conversations.
The elderly cowherds, speaking pleasant and sweet words,
addressed Rāma— the best among those who bring delight— as he returned from his journey.
Welcome to you, O mighty-armed one, the delighter of the Yadu clan!
Today we have obtained the fruit of our lives through the sight of you.
Today we are at peace, dear one, since we behold you at peace.
And we are truly delighted, O hero, that you have come here once again— you,
Rāma, who are renowned throughout the three worlds as the terrifier of enemies.
And all the Yādavas, fierce in their strength and eager for battle—
those tigers among kings, possessed of great power— stand vigilant. Indeed,
O delighter of the Yādavas, we must surely be supported by you.
Or rather, my dear, living beings take delight in their places of birth.
"O pure-faced one, we are surely worthy of honor among the thirty gods today, O dear one,
since we have been seen by you while longing for your arrival."
By good fortune, the Mallas have been slain by you and Kaṃsa has been struck down;
and Ugrasena has indeed been consecrated through the greatness of your younger brother.
And we have heard of his conflict with the Timi in the ocean,
as well as the slaying of Pañcajana and his conflict with Jarāsaṃdha.
And we have heard of the conflict on Mount Gomanta with the Kṣatriyas,
as well as the slaying of Darada and the resolve regarding Jarāsaṃdha.
And we have heard of that descent of weapons in the great battle.
The slaying of the jackal in the excellent city of Karavīra,
the consecration of his son, the consoling of the citizens,
the lamentation of his wives, and the consecration of Śakradeva.
The siege of Mathurā by the wise Jarāsaṃdha,
the battle with all the lords of men, and the entry into Mathurā of the high-souled Yādavas— these are worthy of being celebrated even by the gods.
The earth was firmly established, and all the kings were filled with apprehension.
Seeing your arrival, we are as fortunate as we were in the past; therefore, along with our kinsmen, we are both satisfied and thrilled.
Then Rāma replied to all those standing around him:
"Among all the Yādavas as well, you are my kinsmen."
Childhood was spent with us, and we took delight in the forest together;
having been raised by you, how could we undergo such a transformation?
In your homes we have eaten and the cows have been protected;
all our kinsmen have formed bonds of friendship with you.
While the wielder of the plow was thus present among the cowherds,
the cowherd women there became joyful of countenance;
having engaged in such various conversations with the cowherds, the wielder of the plow [departed].
Gazing joyfully upon Vṛndāvana, he went to the bank of the Yamunā;
then, having entered the interior of the forest, the exceedingly powerful Rāma took his delight.
In the meantime, the cowherds, who were knowledgeable of place and time, brought wine for Rāma, who was self-realized, along with other cowherds.
At that time, Rāma, possessing the luster of a pale cloud and surrounded by his kinsmen, went into the interior of the forest and drank a beverage that stirred intoxication.
Then they brought him various forest products—
fresh and delightful flowers and fruits.
Various kinds of pure foods and perfumes that reach the heart,
as well as abundant lotuses and water-lilies freshly plucked and unwilted.
With his head, its beautiful hair partially covering the crown,
he shone with a single earring hanging from one ear.
With his chest cool with sandalwood and aloe-wood paste and adorned with a forest garland, Rāma shone like Mount Mandara with Mount Kailāsa.
Clad in two garments with the luster of fresh rain-clouds,
he shone with his radiant body like the moon amidst a mass of clouds.
With his plow attached, encircling the coils of a serpent,
and likewise with his radiant club clasped in the tip of his arm.
Intoxicated, that best of the strong shone with his face reeling,
like the moon weary from its exertions during the nights of the dewy season.
Intoxicated, he said to the Yamunā, "O great river, I wish to bathe;
come here to me in personified form, O you who flow toward the ocean!"
Disregarding the words spoken by Saṃkarṣaṇa as if they were those of a madman,
she, deluded by her feminine nature, did not return to that place.
Then the powerful Rāma, impelled by intoxication, became enraged;
and the mighty one took a plough in his hand, turning it downward for the purpose of dragging.
Upon that ground of fallen petals, garlands of lotuses fell;
and from their flower-buds, they released water colored by their own pollen.
Seizing the great river Yamunā at its edge with his plowshare that had an endless tip, Rāma dragged her along like a woman who has risen up in anger.
With its stream of water agitated and its gathered waters set upon the lake,
the river turned back in fear, following the path of the plow.
With its path drawn by plows and following a swift, winding course,
it became agitated like a woman terrified by the fear of Saṃkarṣaṇa.
Her lips were like the reflection on a riverbank, marked by the signs of being crushed and struck by water, and adorned with a girdle of foam-threads that mimicked the river's edge.
Her waves were a painful affliction, her breasts were the upturned cakravāka birds, her body was deep with speed and curved, and she bore trembling fish and birds.

She, with eyes like those of a swan and glances from the corners of her eyes, had cast off her garment of kāśa-flower silk; with the ends of her hair disheveled by the wind on the bank, she moved with a gait faltering in the water.
With her outer corners of the eyes marked by the plow, agitated like the ocean-going river,
her limbs smeared with the impurity of moss, and distressed by thick bubbles,
she moves along the royal road like a crooked woman intoxicated.
She was dragged with great force along a path obstructed by the current,
led off-course until she reached the forest of Vṛndāvana.
The river Yamunā was led through the midst of Vṛndāvana,
accompanied by the birds dwelling on its banks who were crying out in lamentation.
When she had crossed the river and reached the forest of Vṛndāvana,
Yamunā assumed a female form and spoke to Rāma.
Be gracious, O Rāma; I am terrified by this contrary act.
This form of mine has become distorted, and so too has my water.
"O son of Rohiṇī, I have been placed by you in the middle of the river while I am not there!
O mighty-armed son of Rohiṇī, Nanda will mock me when I am joined with you through this plowing, for I have strayed from my own path."
Surely my co-wives, arrogant in their speed, will mock me with smiles of foam as I am cast into the ocean, my path obscured by the waters.
"Show me favor, O Hero; I entreat you, O elder brother of Kṛṣṇa!
Be forever well-disposed in mind, O best of gods.
I am dragged by the plow-weapon; let this anger be turned back."
O wielder of the plow, I approach your feet with my head bowed;
O mighty-armed one, I wish to be instructed on the path—where should I go?
Seeing Yamunā speaking thus, Balarāma,
whose weapon is the plow and who was languid from being overcome by intoxication, replied to that bride of the ocean.
O lady of lovely appearance, you whose path is ploughed by the furrow,
nourish this entire region of ours for us by providing water.
This is the message for you, O fair-browed one, daughter of the ocean;
go in peace, O illustrious lady, and depart as you please.
For as long as the worlds shall endure, so long shall my fame endure.
Vaiśampāyana said: Having been thus addressed, Yamunā acted accordingly upon Rāma’s command;
and being permitted by Rāma, she departed along her proper course.
Having witnessed the dragging of the Yamunā, all those inhabitants of Vraja then offered salutations to Rāma, exclaiming, "Excellent! Excellent!"
"Homage be to you, O Lord of the World, Balabhadra, Halāyudha!
Be gracious, O Lord of the Gods of gods, O Rāma! Thus did the cowherds cry out "Rāma, Rāma!
Having released that [weapon] of great velocity and all those inhabitants of Vraja, [he departed].
Then, having reflected with his mind and having reached a firm decision through his intellect,
the son of Rohiṇī returned quickly once more to Mathurā.
Having gone to Mathurā, Rāma beheld Madhusūdana in his palace, the imperishable essence of the earth, as he was reclining.
In that very same forest attire, he approached Janārdana,
his chest resplendent with a freshly made garland of forest flowers.
Seeing Rāma, the wielder of the plow, approaching swiftly,
Govinda rose up at once and offered him an excellent seat.
Having saluted the high-souled Balabhadra, Janārdana again offered his prostration, saying, "Welcome to you, O Halāyudha. Then,
as Rāma was seated, he inquired after his welfare in Vraja.
And Janārdana was present among all his kinsmen and among the cows as well.
Then Rāma replied to his brother, who spoke so virtuously:
"O Kṛṣṇa, all is well with those for whose welfare you desire it."
Then, in the presence of Vasudeva, there arose between Rāma and Keśava various meritorious discourses, both diverse and ancient.

Vaiśampāyana said: Now, after some time, in the assembly hall in the presence of the Yadus...
The lotus-eyed one spoke these excellent and reasoned words.
"Listen, all you Yādavas, and attend with full attention to my words:
this land of Mathurā belongs to the Yādavas and increases the prosperity of the kingdom; it is here that we were born and in Vraja that we were raised."
Now that suffering has passed and the enemies have been defeated;
the enmity provoked among the kings and the conflict with Jarāsandha have come to an end.
We possess vehicles and an infinite host of foot-soldiers,
as well as various jewels and many friends.
Moreover, this land of Mathurā is small and accessible to others;
yet our own increase is great, both in terms of military strength and through our alliances.
I perceive a great crush even here among these tens of millions of youths and these hosts of foot soldiers who dwell in this place.
Therefore, O bulls among the Yadus, I do not take pleasure in dwelling here;
you ought to forgive me as I intend to establish a city.
If these words born of my intention are agreeable to you,
may they be pleasing at this time for your welfare in the assembly of the Yadus.
Then all the Yādavas, with joyful minds, said to him: "Let that which is desired be accomplished for the welfare of these people."
Then the Vṛṣṇis deliberated upon this supreme counsel:
"He has been rendered incapable of being slain by us, and the enemy's force is exceedingly great."
A great destruction of the army has been wrought here by these lords of men;
indeed, we would not be able to destroy their forces and troops even in a hundred years. Therefore, the thought arose in them to retreat.
In the meantime, that great King Kālayavana approached Mathurā with an army of exactly the same kind.
Then, hearing that Kālayavana had arrived, they encountered that great and irresistible army of Jarāsaṃdha.
In the meantime, Keśava, the increaser of the joy of the Yadus, spoke again to the Yādavas who were true to their vows: "This very day is auspicious; let us set forth together with our followers."
At the command of Keśava, all those Yādavas set forth like the surging currents of the ocean, capable of resisting even a flood of armies.
Having gathered their wives, they, led by Vasudeva,
set out on well-equipped, rutting elephants, as well as on chariots and armored horses.
Having beaten their drums, all the Yādavas— including their wealth, kinsmen, and relatives— abandoned Mathurā and indeed departed.
With chariots adorned with golden crests, with rutting and excellent elephants,
and with horses leaping forward, urged on by whips and heels;
O bull of the Bharatas, those eminent Vṛṣṇis, gladdened and beautifying their respective army divisions, marched facing westward.
Then all the most eminent Yādavas, who adorn the battlefield, led by Vāsudeva, drew up the vanguards of their armies.
It was variegated with various creepers, filled with groves of coconut trees,
strewn with lovely forests of *nāga* trees, and adorned with clusters of *ketakī* flowers.
In some places abounding with *puṃnāga* and *tālī* trees, and elsewhere dense with groves of grapes,
the best of kings, those bulls among the Yadus, then reached the marshy region of the King of Sindhu with their well-arrayed forces.
There, in those delightful regions, all the Yādavas, together with their friends and loved ones, rejoiced like gods who had gone to heaven.
While searching for a site for a city, Kṛṣṇa, the slayer of enemy heroes,
beheld a vast region adorned by the coastal marshlands of the ocean.
It was beneficial for vehicles, consisting of sand, copper, and clay;
endowed with the auspicious marks of a city, it was as if established by the Goddess of Fortune herself.
It was the realm of the King of Rivers, fanned by ocean breezes and served by the waters of the sea, adorned with the characteristic marks of cities.
There, not far away, stands a mountain named Raivataka,
with peaks as magnificent as Mandara, shining resplendently on all sides.
There, the dwelling of Ekalavya, where Droṇa had resided for a long time,
became populated by men and filled with all kinds of jewels.
Right there, for that king, a dwelling-place was well-constructed,
named Dvāravatī, which was as vast as a checkerboard.
Keśava’s mind was set upon that city;
the Yādavas took pleasure in establishing their armies there.
On that day, when the sun was red, those foremost of the Yādavas,
abiding by the consent of Kṛṣṇa, resolved to encamp there;
and the army commanders began the layout of the military camp.
There, in that region, the powerful Keśava, the foremost of the Yadus, dwelt with the Yādavas for the purpose of establishing a city.
Then the elder brother of Gada, that best of men and foremost of the Yādavas, duly established her name and her dwellings by means of his mind.
Thus, O King, having reached the city of Dvāravatī with all their kinsmen,
they lived happily like hosts of gods in heaven.
Kṛṣṇa, the slayer of Keśin, having learned of Kālayavana and also out of fear of Jarāsaṃdha, went to the city of Dvāravatī.

Janamejaya said:
"O Blessed One, I wish to hear in detail [the history] of that Great-Souled One."
The life-story of Vāsudeva, the wise and foremost of the Yadus.
And for what purpose did Madhusūdana abandon Mathurā—
the preeminent peak of the Middle Country and the sole abode of splendor?

O best of the twice-born, the descendant of Daśārha abandoned that preeminent and most excellent city— which was like a visible peak of the earth, abundant in wealth and grain, and filled with noble and wealthy people— without resorting to war.
And what did that Kālayavana do in response to Kṛṣṇa?
And having taken refuge in Dvārakā, which was protected by the waters as its fortress, what did Janārdana do— He who is mighty-armed, a great yogi, and high-minded?
Of what prowess was Kālayavana, and by whom was that powerful one begotten,
seeing whom Janārdana retreated, finding him unbearable?
Vaiśampāyana said:
Gārgya, the preceptor of the Vṛṣṇis and Andhakas, was a man of great asceticism who,
having formerly been a celibate student, did not take a wife.
For indeed, while that Gārgya was present— celibate, imperishable, and a twice-born— one brahmin, his brother-in-law, called him "impotent" in the cow-pen;
thereupon all the Yādavas among the Yadus laughed.
"O King, for one thousand years, six hundred years measured by the king's [standard],
and twelve years more, my brother-in-law cursed Gārgya, saying, 'He is a eunuch,' because of the powder produced from iron dust."
Having been thus cursed at that time, O King, in the city of Amitaṃjaya,
he went there desiring a son and performed most severe penance.
Then, for twelve years,
he consumed the dust of ashes while propitiating Mahādeva, the inconceivable wielder of the trident.
Rudra granted him a boon: a son composed of all splendor, capable of subduing the Vṛṣṇis and the Andhakas in battle.
Then the king, the lord of the Yavanas— being childless and longing for a son— heard from the god that boon concerning the birth of a son.
Having had that best of the twice-born brought before him and having consoled him, that king,
the lord of the Yavanas, released him among the cowherds and the wives of the cowherds.
But the Apsaras Gopālī, having assumed the guise of a cowherd woman,
bore there the difficult-to-be-carried and infallible embryo of Gārgya.
By the command of the trident-bearing Śiva, he was born as the brave and mighty Kālayavana from Mānuṣī, the wife of Gārgya; and then,
as the child of that sonless king, he grew up within the inner apartments.
When he had ceased, O King, that monarch Kālayavana,
desiring battle, questioned the best of the twice-born;
and Nārada indeed informed him of the Vṛṣṇi and Andhaka clans.
Having learned that boon from Nārada, the radiant Madhusūdana observed it flourishing among the Yavanas.
When that immensely powerful king of the Yavanas had grown up,
the Mleccha kings then took refuge with him and followed him.
The Śakas, Tuṣāras, Daradas, Pāradas, Taṅgaṇas, Khaśas,
Pahlavas, and hundreds of other Mlecchas from the Himalayan regions likewise [came].
Surrounded by those fierce bandits, who wore various disguises and were like locusts, the king advanced toward his brother-in-law.
Then, with thousands and even tens of thousands of elephants, horses, donkeys, and camels,
he caused the earth to tremble with that great army.
Having completely covered the path of the sun with dust,
the king created a river out of urine and excrement along with his army.
"O lord of men, because she emerged from a heap of horse and camel dung,
the river thereafter came to be known by the name Aśvaśakṛt."
Having heard that a great army was approaching, Vāsudeva, the leader of the Vṛṣṇis and Andhakas, summoned his kinsmen and spoke as follows.
This great and terrible danger has arisen for the Vṛṣṇis and Andhakas;
moreover, our enemy is incapable of being slain because of a boon granted by the wielder of the Pināka bow.
All means such as conciliation and the rest have been prescribed for him in every way;
yet, due to pride and the power of intoxication, he desires only war.
And this much alone was told to me by Nārada regarding his dwelling here.
And this much must be said: conciliation alone is considered supreme;
for King Jarāsaṃdha never forgives us, nor do the other rulers of the earth who have been scorched by the power of the Vṛṣṇi wheel.
Furthermore, some kings who were devoted to him have become disaffected due to the slaying of Kaṃsa; having taken refuge with Jarāsaṃdha, they desire to harass us.
"Many kinsmen of the Yadus have been slain by kings;
we shall not be able to prosper in this city," said Keśava.
Thereupon, the Vṛṣṇis and Andhakas placed the high-minded Kṛṣṇa at their head.
Having assembled, they consulted one another out of fear of Jarāsaṃdha;
and having reached a decision, they all resolved upon flight.
Leaving the beautiful Mathurā while honoring the wielder of the Pināka bow,
and desiring to settle in Kuśasthalī-Dvāravatī, they resolved upon their departure and dispatched a messenger to him.
Then Kṛṣṇa cast into the jar a terrible black serpent, a venomous snake resembling a heap of crushed collyrium.
Then Govinda, having sealed that jar with his own messenger and terrifying the king for the sake of demonstration,
had that messenger show the jar to Kālayavana.
And the messenger spoke thus to the king in the assembly of kings:
"O King, Kṛṣṇa says to you: 'What use have you for these locusts?
I alone am capable and powerful enough to ward them off.'"
"And having slain you, O best of kings, along with your army and your circle of friends,
I shall certainly seize this army of yours, O King."
"Go otherwise, O King, joined by this army," having said this, he showed the jar impelled by Kṛṣṇa,
saying, "Kṛṣṇa is like a black serpent," O bull of the Bharatas.
Kālayavana, perceiving that terror instilled by the Yādavas,
filled that jar with fierce ants.
Having written a single verse, he then cast it into the middle of the jar;
that serpent, being devoured on all sides in its limbs by those many sharp ants, was then reduced to ashes.
Then the King of the Yavanas, having sealed that jar in the same manner,
sent it to Kṛṣṇa while describing its great abundance.
Then Hari, seeing the letter brought by the messengers, read it:
"One should not oppose many, for even a great multitude is difficult to conquer;
even the king of serpents, though writhing with power, will be devoured by ants."
But Vāsudeva, seeing that his own stratagem had been discovered,
quickly abandoned Mathurā and departed for Dvārakā.
O King, desiring to bring an end to hostilities, the highly illustrious Vāsudeva established himself in Dvārakā and comforted the Vṛṣṇis.
Then Madhusūdana, that tiger among men and great yogin, arrived at Mathurā on foot, using only his arms as weapons.
Seeing him, Kālayavana went forth joyfully and in a rage;
and the mighty Kṛṣṇa also emerged, having first observed the situation.
Then the lord of the Yavanas, desiring to seize Govinda, pursued him;
yet the king was unable to capture him, for he was established in yoga.
At every step, the Lord of the Yavanas was led by Hari, who showed him a distant mountain cave, as if his very self had already come within his grasp.
Kālayavana said,
"Flight is not fitting for one born in the Yadu clan.
Thus reviling him as he pursued, he did not catch him, his inauspicious fate having been struck down.
Thus, even though he was thrown, the Blessed One entered a mountain cave;
for who indeed could forcibly go against the Lord of the World? As Janārdana proceeded, he appeared as if already within reach of his hand, were it not for his beloved.
The son of Māndhātṛ was the highly illustrious King Mucukunda;
wherever that lord of kings stood, [the fire] quickly entered there.
In former times, during the war between the gods and asuras, that one of great strength had performed his duty.
Entreated by the gods with a boon, he chose sleep alone;
as he was weary, a voice indeed then manifested to him in this way.
"O gods, I shall burn with my eyes, blazing with anger, anyone who awakens me while I am asleep," he said again and again.
"So be it," Śakra said to him along with the thirty gods;
permitted by those deities, he came to the world of men.
Exhausted by fatigue, he entered a certain mountain cave and slept for as long as it took until the appearance of Kṛṣṇa.
All of that— the granting of boons to the gods and the splendor of that king— was reported by Nārada to Vāsudeva.
Followed by that enemy Mleccha, Kṛṣṇa entered the cave of Mucukunda with humility.
Having covered that king with his own yellow garment,
Keśava, the best among the wise, stood having withdrawn from the range of vision of the royal sage Mucukunda at the place of the latter's head.
Having entered, the Yavana beheld the lord of the earth;
the evil-minded one approached him as he slept, appearing like Death itself.
But regarding that king as Vāsudeva,
he struck him with his foot for his own destruction, like a moth flying into a fire.
And the royal sage Mucukunda, awakened by the touch of the foot,
was enraged both by the cutting off of his sleep and by that touch of the foot.
And remembering his boon from Śakra, he gazed at him who stood before him;
as soon as he was looked upon by the enraged one, he burst into flames on all sides.
But the fire, issuing forth from the power of his eyes, consumed Kālayavana in an instant, just as a thunderbolt consumes a dry tree.
Having accomplished his purpose, the wise Vāsudeva addressed these excellent words to that illustrious lord of men who had been long asleep:
"O King, you have been asleep for a long time; this was told to me by Nārada.
A very great service has been rendered to me; may it be well with you, I am now departing."
Then, observing Vāsudeva to be short in stature,
the king thought that the age had been transformed by the passage of great time.
Beholding him, dark as a rain cloud, clad in yellow silk garments,
with the Śrīvatsa mark upon his chest, resplendent and adorned with the shining Kaustubha gem;
Four-armed and radiant, adorned with a Vaijayantī garland,
with a lovely and serene countenance, and shimmering crocodile-shaped earrings.
Behold the Lord of the Three Worlds, whose eyes are smiling with passion,
whose youth is exquisite, and whose majestic prowess is like that of a rutting lion-king.

Overwhelmed by his splendor, the king of great intelligence questioned him; filled with apprehension, he slowly spoke to Kṛṣṇa, who was as invincible as fire in its brilliance: "O Govinda, who are you, and why have you come here?"
And what is the duration of this sleep? If you know, please tell me.
Free from doubt and devoid of fear, you have arrived in this forest and mountain cave; with feet like lotus petals, you wander upon the thorny ground.
What indeed is the splendor of those who possess splendor? Are you the Blessed One, the radiant one;
or are you the Sun, the Moon, Great Indra, or some other guardian of the world?
I consider you the bull among men, the foremost of the three gods of gods,
since you dispel the darkness of the cave like a lamp with its radiance.
"O bull among men, since we are listening without guile,
please tell us— should you so desire— of your own birth, deeds, and lineage.
Vāsudeva said:
Born of the lunar dynasty was the king named Yayāti, the son of Nahuṣa;
his eldest son was Yadu, and there were four others younger than him.
O Lord, O King, know me to be Vāsudeva, born in the lineage of Yadu and the son of Vasudeva, who has come here.
Born in the Tretā Yuga, you were known to me through Nārada;
know that this is the Kali Yuga—what else may I do for you?
"O King, my enemy Devadatta, who was favored by you, has been burnt by you—
he who could not have been slain by me in battle even in hundreds of years."
Mucukunda said:
"I know the Lord born of the Yadu lineage, the eternal, all-pervading one;
the primordial Person, the Sovereign, the Infallible Madhusūdana."
Long ago, Garga declared that in the twenty-eighth yuga,
at the beginning of the Dvāpara age, the birth of Hari will take place in the lineage of Yadu.
Salutations to that Blessed One, the Great-Souled Puruṣa,
the infinite, O mighty-armed one, to Viṣṇu, the all-powerful Lord.
Vaiśampāyana said: Thus praised then by the wise Mucukunda, the blessed Lord Acyuta Viṣṇu invited him to choose a boon.
Kṛṣṇa spoke again to the long-armed Mucukunda:
"O hero, I have come for your sake, having been awakened by Nārada.
Arise, arise! May it be well with you; conduct yourself here according to your desire."
Thus addressed by Kṛṣṇa, he emerged from the mouth of the cave,
followed by the wise Kṛṣṇa, whose purpose had been accomplished.
Then he beheld the earth covered with short men—
men of little energy, little strength, and little heroism or prowess—
and saw that his own kingdom was entirely presided over by another.

"O Kṛṣṇa, may that merit which comes from seeing you belong to me. Having thus bid farewell to Govinda, the king entered the great forest; with his mind resolved upon asceticism, he went to the Himavat.
Then, having applied himself to austerity and cast off his body,
the king ascended to heaven, which he had won through his own auspicious deeds.
The high-minded Vāsudeva, whose soul is righteous, having caused his enemy to be slain by means of a stratagem, took possession of that army.
By the high-souled Mucukunda,
having returned once more to Mathurā,
[a city] was provided with abundant chariots, elephants, horses, armor, weapons, implements, banners, and standards.
The wise one took that army, whose lord had been slain, and departed.
Then, his heart full of joy, Janārdana reported this to Ugrasena, the lord of men; and with that abundant wealth, he adorned the city of Dvāravatī.
Chapter 86,
transliterated by Kreshimir Krnic,
proofread by Kreshimir Krnic.
Salutations to you, Kṛṣṇa; salutations to you, Rāma, the delight of women;
salutations to you, Vāmana; let there be salutations to you, Kapila.
O you of manifold forms, homage to you; homage to you, the witness of karma;
O you of universal form, homage to you; homage to you, Hṛṣīkeśa.
While being thus praised by the wise Mucukunda,
he took recourse in the northern direction and performed sattvic austerity.
Vaiśampāyana said:
Then, at the clear dawn when the sun had risen,
Hṛṣīkeśa, having performed his prayers, sat down at the edge of the forest.
He wandered through that region with a desire to see difficult places;
the foremost members of the Yādava clans approached the delighter of the Yadus.

On an excellent day under the asterism Rohiṇī, having had the best of the twice-born recite benedictions, he commenced the construction of the fortress amidst the loud proclamations of "Auspicious Day."
Then Keśisūdana, whose eyes were like lotus petals and who was the best among speakers, addressed the Yādavas just as the enemy of Vṛtra addressed the gods.
"I have fashioned this ground; behold it as if it were the abode of the gods. And I have given a name to this city, by which it shall become renowned."
This city named Dvāravatī has been fashioned by me upon the earth;
it shall be a delightful city, like Amarāvatī belonging to Śakra.
I shall have those very emblems and shrines constructed for her;
and here they shall establish the abodes of Brahmā and the other gods in due order,
as well as crossroads, royal highways, and equal-sized inner apartments.
May you, free from all feverish distress, rejoice here like gods,
subduing the hosts of enemies led by Ugrasena.
Let the sites for houses be taken up, let the triple-gated squares be laid out,
let the royal highways be measured, and also the extent of the rampart.
Let the chief artisans appointed to the work of building houses be dispatched,
and let the men who serve as messengers and laborers be stationed throughout the various regions.
Thus addressed by Kṛṣṇa, those who were intent on building their homes,
being greatly delighted, carried out the acquisition of the sites according to his instructions.
Then, O Great King, on an auspicious day, those best of the Yādavas, having honored the twice-born, took up their measuring cords and performed the measurement.
And as they were performing the rites for the site-deities according to the prescribed rules,
the high-minded Govinda then spoke there to the architects.
"For our sake, let a temple be well-constructed here,
with its squares and roads properly divided, and with the tutelary deities well-installed."
Having said "So be it" to the mighty-armed one, the architects then procured the materials for the construction of the fortress according to the prescribed rules.
They constructed the gates and the sanctuaries according to rule,
and they assigned places therein for Brahmā and the others in due order.
They established four deities for the fire-altar of the Lord of the Gods and for the mortar and pestle; they likewise provided four door-guards:
Gṛhakṣetra, Indrabhallāṭa, and Puṣpadanta.
While those high-souled Yādavas were occupied with those dwellings,
Mādhava reflected upon the means for the swift settling of the city.
His divine intellect remained steady, though it was fickle and swift in action;
that city was indeed dear to the Yadus and a source of their prosperity.
There is a lord among the gods, the foremost of artisans, the son of Prajāpati;
Viśvakarman shall indeed establish the city by his own ingenuity.
Having meditated with his mind upon the reason for his arrival,
Kṛṣṇa, facing the gods, withdrew into solitude.
At that very time, the highly intelligent master craftsman Viśvakarman, the best of the gods, stood before Kṛṣṇa.
Viśvakarman said:
"O Viṣṇu, you of steadfast vows, by divine will I have quickly arrived as your servant;
command me, what shall I do for you?"
Just as the Lord of the gods, Tryambaka, is immutable, so too, O God, are you worthy of honor; there is no difference between us, O Lord.
O mighty-armed one, utter a word that makes known the three worlds;
here I am, having perceived the matter—command me, what shall I do?
Having heard the humble words of Viśvakarman, Keśava,
the best of the Yadus and enemy of Kaṃsa, replied with incomparable speech.
O Lord of the gods, you have heard the purpose of our secret; we remain here because, O best of deities, a dwelling must certainly be prepared for me in this place.
Therefore, O observer of noble vows, this earth should be settled by me for the sake of illumination,
and it should be surrounded on all sides with dwellings befitting my power.
And just as Amarāvatī is indeed the supreme city upon the earth, so too must this [city] be made by you;
for you are capable of it, O high-minded one.
"Let mortals behold my splendor, as well as that of the city and the Yadu clan, just as they behold it in heaven; let this place of mine be made so that it truly resembles the third heaven."
Thus addressed, Viśvakarman, the lord of intellect,
then spoke to Kṛṣṇa, the performer of effortless deeds and the destroyer of the enemies of the gods.
"O Lord, I shall do all this that you have commanded;
however, this city will not be sufficient for these people."
And there shall be a vast and auspicious increase for this [earth];
indeed, the four oceans shall move about within it in embodied form.
O Puruṣottama, if the ocean, the lord of waters, should wish to relinquish even a small portion here, then this city would become endowed with its own vast auspiciousness.
Thus addressed, Kṛṣṇa— the best among speakers and one who had already formed his resolve— then spoke to Sāgara, the lord of rivers.
The ocean is twelve yojanas deep;
let yourself be withdrawn into this reservoir of water if you have any respect for me.
But if you grant me space, my entire army, having occupied the full extent of the territory, will be able to withstand it.
Then, having heard the words of Kṛṣṇa, the great ocean, the lord of rivers and streams, released [the waters] through its union with the wind.
Then Viśvakarman, being pleased upon seeing that the site of the city was auspicious,
and the Ocean as well, showed great honor toward Govinda.
Then Viśvakarman said to Kṛṣṇa, the delight of the Yadus:
"O Govinda, from this day forward, let everyone board [the chariot]."
"O Lord, this preeminent city has been created by me through the mind alone;
in a very short time, it shall be adorned with rows of crowded houses."
There shall be a delightful city with excellent gates and preeminent archways,
adorned with watchtowers and turrets like armlets, resembling the very hump of the earth.
And he established a vast inner apartment for Kṛṣṇa, capable of providing every service,
within that city in a region honored by the gods.
Then, by the mental effort of Viśvakarman, that beloved city of Dvāravatī was created as a manifestation of Vaiṣṇavī.
Its gates were constructed according to the prescribed rules, beautified by an excellent rampart, and protected by a series of moats; it was adorned with watchtowers, walls, and arched gateways,
filled with groups of lovely men and women, and graced by merchants.
It was strewn with various articles for sale, like a celestial city that had descended to earth.
Adorned with gardens featuring clear waters from wells and ponds,
she was like a long-eyed woman whose limbs are covered on all sides.
Possessing prosperous crossroads and filled with the densest of excellent dwellings, abounding with thousands of millions of carriage-roads and distinguished by bright royal highways,
that city adorned the ocean like the celestial city of Indra in heaven.
On earth, it was the sole repository of all jewels; a fertile field even for the gods, causing agitation among neighboring lands;
and though the sky above was unlit, it was graced by magnificent palaces.
On earth, the multitude of Pṛthu’s kingdoms resounded with the cries of throngs of people,
while the winds were cooled by the torrents of the lord of waters.
With its lovely marshy groves,
that city of Dvārakā, charming to the people, shone forth like the starry sky.
It was enclosed by a wall the color of the sun, made of gold,
and filled with houses resonant with deep sounds and overflowing with gold.
It was adorned with palaces and gateways resembling bright white clouds,
and here and there its great highways were lined with lofty turrets.
Kṛṣṇa, the delighter of all the Yādavas, dwelt in that city which was crowded with beloved people, illuminating it like Soma illuminates the sky.
Having constructed that divine city, filled with networks of jewels, which Viśvakarman had fashioned like the city of Śakra, the god Viśvakarman,
honored by Govinda, departed for the third heaven.
Furthermore, a thought occurred to Kṛṣṇa, the knower of the self:
"If only I could satisfy these people with floods of wealth."
In his own palace at night, the powerful Upendra summoned Śaṅkha, the supreme treasure among treasures, who dwells with Vaiśravaṇa.
Having understood that the conch was summoning Keśava, Śaṅkha himself, the king of the Guhyakas,
approached the presence of the lord of Dvāravatī.
That Śaṅkha, having joined his palms in reverence and bowed low to the ground out of humility,
addressed Kṛṣṇa just as one would address Vaiśravaṇa.
"O Blessed One, what task must I perform as the guardian of the gods' wealth? O mighty-armed delighter of the Yadus, command me as to what duty is to be done."
Hṛṣīkeśa said to that excellent Guhyaka Śaṅkha:
"Fill with wealth those people in this world whose riches are meager."
I do not wish to see a man in the city who is hungry, emaciated, or even soiled, nor one who speaks the words "Give [me]," being destitute.
Receiving the command with his head bowed, he, the lord of treasures, issued orders to the treasures in every house in Dvāravatī:
"Rain down showers of wealth! And they all did exactly so.

Neither a poor man nor one of low fortune was found there in the city of Dvāravatī, belonging to the high-souled Keśava in ancient times; neither emaciated nor even soiled was anyone in every house in Dvāravatī.
Remaining right there, the Blessed One, the Supreme Person who brings joy to the Yādavas, again called out to Vāyu.
The source of life for all beings approached the elder brother of Gada,
the Lord who holds divine secrets, as he sat alone in a secluded place.
"What should I do, O Lord, who am all-pervading and swift-moving?
Instruct me, O Supreme Person;
whatever you say, O mighty-armed one..."
Just as I am a messenger of the gods, so too am I yours, O sinless one.
Then Kṛṣṇa, the Supreme Person, spoke in secret to Māruta, the life-breath of the world, who had appeared before him in embodied form.
Go, O Māruta, and having obtained the permission of the Lord of the Gods along with the immortals,
take the Sudharmā assembly hall from the gods and bring it here.
For these Yādavas are indeed righteous and valiant by the thousands;
they would surely enter that [city], but not one that might be artificial.
For that assembly hall, O Vāyu, is indeed inexhaustible, moving at will and taking any form at will;
it can support all the Yadus just as it does the Thirty-three gods.
Having accepted those words of Kṛṣṇa, whose actions are effortless,
Vāyu, whose speed is like his own, departed for the abode of the gods.
Having thus honored all the gods and communicated Kṛṣṇa’s words,
he took the Sudharmā assembly hall and returned once more to the surface of the earth.
Having given that Sudharmā assembly hall to Kṛṣṇa, the performer of effortless deeds, for the sake of his righteous purpose,
the god Vāyu vanished.
Where there is no fear, that assembly hall is devoted to dharma;
it was established by Keśava in the midst of Dvāravatī for the leaders of the Yadus,
just as Sudharmā is for the gods in the third heaven.
Thus the imperishable Hari adorned his own city with celestial, terrestrial, and aquatic objects, as if adorning a beloved woman.
That beautiful city shone, filled with networks of jewels,
crowded with various birds, and adorned with palaces;
he likewise established the boundaries, the guilds, and the constituent elements of the state.
And likewise the commanders of the army, the appointed officials, and the lords of the constituent elements of the state.
[He saw] King Ugrasena, the Purohita Kāśya,
the commander-in-chief Anādhṛṣṭi, and Vikadru, the preeminent among ministers.
There, indeed, were ten elders who were the founders of the Yādava clans:
Uddhava, Vasudeva, Kaṅka, Vipṛthu,
Śvaphalka, Citraka, Gada, and Satyaka.
The wise Baladeva likewise established Pṛthu and the other ten as internal ministers, placing them in charge of all affairs without interval.
Dāruka was indeed the charioteer of Keśava, the Atiratha among charioteers;
and Sātyaki, whose valor is truth, was the foremost warrior among warriors.
The preceptor was like another Drona in person in the science of archery;
so too were Satyaki, who was true to his promise, the slayer of enemies, and fierce in battle. Having made such arrangements in the city, that blameless Krishna—
The Creator of the World rejoiced together with the Yadus upon the surface of the earth.
Then, with the consent of Kṛṣṇa, Baladeva obtained Revatī, the daughter of Revata, who was highly esteemed for her virtuous character.

He caused to be built a heart-pleasing [temple], the ornament of the entire world, with abundant materials produced by creation that were dear to the hosts of gods, as well as those deposited in the ocean and born from the sea.
I approach that Viṣṇu in Śrī Dvārakā, the most excellent of cities.

At that very time, however, the powerful Jarāsaṃdha incited the kings with the desire to do what was pleasing to the King of Cedi.
The King of Magadha bestowed due honor upon them as was fitting and appropriate,
and he proclaimed the marriage of Śiśupāla.
The entire inner court was indeed eager for the wedding;
and on the day following that of the Caidya’s marriage, O kings,
they all became fully prepared with their respective riches in due order.
King Śiśupāla also, adorned with the attire of a bridegroom and accompanied by princes equal to himself, then became established in his vows; he,
the one adorned with gold, was there for Rukmiṇī, the daughter of Bhīṣmaka.
It is said that the marriage of King Śiśupāla will take place.
The son of Dantavaktra was Suvaktra, possessed of immeasurable splendor,
equal to the thousand-eyed Indra in battle, and skilled in the use of illusions.
Likewise, [he brought] the son of Pauṇḍraka Vāsudeva, the exceedingly powerful Sudeva,
who was endowed with heroism and the commander of a separate akṣauhiṇī.
And the son of Ekalavya, who was heroic and endowed with strength,
as well as the son of the King of Pāṇḍya and likewise the lord of Kaliṅga.
And O Bhārata, Kṛṣṇa had previously done what was disagreeable to King Veṇudārin, as well as to Aṃśumat, Krātha, and Śrutarvāṇ.
He likewise subdued the Kalinga king Nikṛttaśatru, the lord of the Gāndhāras,
the mighty-armed Paṭuśa, and the ruler of Kāśī as well.
All the Dhartarashtras of great strength who were worthy of the assembly,
Vinda and Anuvinda of Avanti, and the Bahlikas along with their followers.
All those Saṃśaptakas, as well as the Āsyandas and Yavanas, and also the son of Yavana, namely Ārṣāyaṇa, and the Śakas— these were all there.
Svabhāva, Candrahāsa, and others such as the Pārasīkas; Virāṭa and Drupada, as well as Jayadratha and Vidūratha;
Bhagadatta, Mahāsena, Śala, and the very powerful Śālva.
Bhūriśravas, Mahāsena, and the heroic Kuntibhoja.
"Sixty-one akṣauhiṇīs, accompanied by ten [counsellors],
have arrived at the residence of the Bhoja king for the sake of the svayaṃvara.
Janamejaya said:
In what land was King Rukmī born, O best among those who know the Vedas? In whose lineage did that radiant one arise, O most excellent of the twice-born?
Vaiśampāyana said: The royal seer Yādava had a son named Vidarbha,
who established the kingdom of Vidarbha on the southern slope of the Vindhya mountains.
The sons of that king, led by Kratha and Kaiśika, were of great strength;
endowed with heroism, they became kings who each established their own dynasties.
In his lineage, O King, the Vṛṣṇis were born from Bhīma;
in the lineage of Kratha, however, was Aṃśumān, while in that of Kaiśika was Bhīṣmaka.
O lord of the people, the people called that lord of the southern region Hiraṇyaloma;
he was the king who, residing in Kuṇḍina, ruled over the quarter protected by Agastya. His son was Rukmin, and his daughter was Rukmiṇī.
The mighty Rukmī obtained divine weapons from Drumas,
and likewise from Paraśurāma, the son of Jamadagni, he acquired the Brahma-weapon;
he constantly vied with Kṛṣṇa, whose deeds are ever wondrous.
O King, Rukmiṇī was peerless on earth in her beauty;
the immensely radiant Vāsudeva desired her from the mere report of her fame alone.
And Janārdana, endowed with splendor, heroism, and strength, was desired by her from the mere hearing [of his name], thinking, "May he become my husband."
But the mighty Rukmī did not give her to Kṛṣṇa out of hatred;
because of the pain caused by Kaṃsa’s death, he thought, "This man was a servant of Kaṃsa," and so he refused Kṛṣṇa, who possessed immeasurable splendor, even as he entreated him.
For the sake of Sunītha, the king Jarāsaṃdha, the ruler of the Cedis,
requested her from King Bhīṣmaka of terrible prowess.
For the Cedi king Vasu had a son named Bṛhadratha,
by whom Girivraja was built in Magadha in ancient times.
In his lineage was then born the mighty Jarāsandha;
likewise, in the lineage of Vasu, there arose Damaghoṣa, the king of Cedi.
The five sons of Damaghoṣa, who were of terrible prowess,
were born to Śrutaśravas, the sister of Vasudeva.
Śiśupāla, Daśagrīva, Raibhya, and the powerful Upadiśa—
these heroes were skilled in all weapons, heroic, and possessed of great strength.
To his kinsman of the same lineage, he gave his son Sunītha;
in his progeny were born many born of royal lineages.
O Indra among kings, in the lineage of Jarāsaṃdha was born the very powerful Damaghoṣa.
Jarāsaṃdha looked upon him as if he were his own son and protected him.
Placing the mighty Jarāsaṃdha— the enemy of the Vṛṣṇis— at their head,
the Caidya, seeking to please him, committed various offenses against the Vṛṣṇis.
When he was slain in battle, Kaṃsa became his son-in-law;
however, for the sake of Kṛṣṇa, enmity arose between Jarāsaṃdha and the Vṛṣṇis.
Then, for the sake of Sunīthā, he requested Rukmiṇī from Bhīṣmaka;
and the powerful Bhīṣmaka gave her to Śiśupāla.
Then, taking the King of Cedi with him, Jarāsaṃdha, the lord of men, went to Vidarbha accompanied by the advancing Dantavakra.
And that mighty lord of Aṅga, Vaṅga, and Kaliṅga was followed by the wise Pauṇḍraka Vāsudeva.
Desiring to honor those lords of men, Rukmī went out to meet them and,
having received them with the highest worship, led them toward the city.
For the sake of their father’s life, both Rāma and Kṛṣṇa,
along with the other Vṛṣṇis endowed with great strength, set out there on chariots.
Seeing that all of them had arrived with Vāsudeva at their head,
the lord of the Krathakaiśikas received them according to tradition and honored those worthy of honor; they then dwelt outside the city.
And Bhīṣmaka settled them all outside the city.
While that great-souled enemy Jarāsaṃdha remained alive,
all the necessary materials for their wedding were gathered from every quarter.
Then conchs and drums resounded with sound on all sides;
likewise, Brahmins arrived from various directions,
and everywhere well-adorned banners were raised up.
When the wedding was to take place on the following day, the auspicious Rukmiṇī went outside in a chariot drawn by four horses to the temple of Indra.

Surrounded by a vast multitude of hundreds of thousands of female slaves, she went forth on foot according to custom for the purpose of worshipping Ambikā; having performed the auspicious rites of adornment, she intended to honor Indrāṇī.
She was endowed with a radiant body and possessed great strength.

"May Keśava be my husband; let no other whatsoever be so," having thus resolved in her mind, she joined her palms in a handful of flowers. Then Kṛṣṇa beheld her, standing there like Lakṣmī herself in person.
Endowed with supreme beauty, she was near the temple of the deity.
Like a blazing crest of fire, like an illusion descended to the earth,
or like the profound earth itself risen from the surface of the ground.
Like a ray of the moon, she was gentle and embodied in a female form upon the earth;
like the foremost Śrī, yet without a lotus, she was the future companion of Śrī,
beheld by Kṛṣṇa with his mind alone, and difficult to be gazed upon even by the gods.
For she was dark-complexioned yet radiant, with large and beautiful elongated eyes;
her lips, eyes, and outer corners were copper-hued, and her thighs, hips, and breasts were full.
She was tall with all her limbs beautiful, slender, and with a face like the moon;
she had copper-colored, high-arched nails, lovely eyebrows, and dark, curly hair.
She was exceedingly lovely in form, with full hips and breasts.
She was adorned with teeth that were sharp, white, even, and radiant.
In this world, there is no other woman equal to her in beauty, fame, and splendor;
the goddess Rukmiṇī is truly beautiful, clothed in white silk garments.
Upon seeing that woman of auspicious appearance, Kṛṣṇa’s desire increased;
fixing his mind upon her, it was like the flame of a fire fed with sacrificial oblation.
And then Queen Rukmiṇī beheld the Lord Kṛṣṇa.
And seeing Kṛṣṇa standing there, the queen thought:
"This is that very Viṣṇu, the Lord of the World, the virtuous younger brother of Rāma, manifest in person."
His discus and conch shell shall always adorn both his arms;
may those two, the destroyers of Daityas and Dānavas, ever grace him.
The great bow Śārṅga, which strikes terror into the Daityas and Dānavas, remains forever in his hand;
it is the most renowned bow of Hari in the world.
Relying upon him, that fierce mace known as Kaumodakī, the goddess who slays Daityas and Dānavas, always rests upon his arm.
Relying upon this authorization, the sword named Nandaka slays enemies of great prowess who are unbearable even for the gods.
Viṣṇu’s vehicle shall be Garuḍa, the foremost of birds;
having conquered Śakra and the other gods, he carried away the supreme nectar of immortality.
This very Viṣṇu, the Guru himself, adorned in the guise of a cowherd,
sported at his pleasure among the heavy breasts of the cowherd women.
Hari, who had been dancing in that Yamunā lake at that time,
churned Kāliya, who was garlanded with flames of poisonous fire, within it.
This Lord of the World held up Mount Govardhana with a single arm,
as easily as a child holds a small stick.
This is that lotus-eyed one who indeed struck down the horse.
And Govinda, having slain Aṇūra and the mighty Kaṃsa in battle, danced upon the arena together with the cowherds and the Yādavas.
This is that best of the Yadavas, with eyes like the filaments of a lotus,
dark yet radiant, glorious, the successful younger brother of Indra in person.
"Young, skillful, the ancient self, lotus-eyed and radiant as a lotus—
this very Lord of the World, the Yādava, has arrived here with me today."
"I shall bear his lotus-feet; of this there is no doubt.
I shall apply myself to the service of those feet known as lotuses."
Having reflected thus, she then paid homage to Śacī.
Having deliberated with Rāma, the exceedingly powerful Keśava set his mind upon her destruction, entrusting the task to the Vṛṣṇis.
But when she had completed her service to the deity and was departing from the abode of the gods,
Kṛṣṇa suddenly seized her and led her away on his own excellent chariot.
Rāma also, having uprooted a tree, struck down the enemies as they rushed forward;
and upon learning of this, the Dāśārhas prepared themselves for battle in every way.
With chariots of various forms bearing lofty great banners,
and with horses and elephants as well, they surrounded the wielder of the plow.
Having taken Rukmiṇī with him, the heroic Kṛṣṇa departed quickly toward his city,
having entrusted that burden to Rāma and Yuyudhāna.
Also in Akrūra, Vipṛthu, Gada, Kṛtavarman,
Cakradeva, Sunakṣatra, and the mighty Sāraṇa.
When Nivṛttaśatru, Vikrānta, Bhaṅgakāra, Vidūratha, Kaṅka— the son of Ugrasena— and Śatadyumna had been slain, Keśava [acted].
In Rājādhideva, Mṛdara, Prasena, Citraka, as well as Atidānta, Bṛhaddurga, Śvaphalka, Citraka, and Pṛthu;
Having entrusted that heavy burden to the other leaders among the Vṛṣṇis and Andhakas, Madhusūdana departed for Dvāravatī.
Then all the Yādavas assembled for battle;
Dantavakra, Jarāsandha, and the heroic Śiśupāla,
fully armored and enraged, set out desiring to slay Janārdana.
Accompanied by the Aṅgas, Vaṅgas, Kaliṅgas, and Pauṇḍras, that heroic king of Cedi set forth together with his brothers, who were all great chariot-warriors.
Where is Vāsudeva, and where are those cowherds?
Whence indeed can there be a king for those born of the Yadu lineage?
And whence could there be Rāma, who is censured as being intoxicated with pride?
Where indeed is the hero Sātyaki in battle?
Speaking thus, those best of kings,
joined for battle with their armies and accompanied by the Magadhas,
struck down [the enemy] in combat with arrows and swords.
Great chariot-warriors of fierce prowess went forth.
Vaiśampāyana said: Then, O great king, in the army of the high-souled lord of Magadha,
conchs and kettledrums resounded, proclaiming the onset of battle.
And the Yādavas, O great king, blew their conchs individually.
And the sounds of kettledrums, clay drums, and cymbals arose from all sides within the assembly of the Yadu forces.
Then a battle took place between both armies;
at that time, the Vṛṣṇis were renowned for standing at the head of Jarāsaṃdha’s forces,
and the enraged great chariot-warriors among the Vṛṣṇi heroes received them in combat.
Placing Saṃkarṣaṇa at their head, they were like the Maruts surrounding Vāsava.
As the immensely powerful Jarāsaṃdha was charging with speed,
Yuyudhāna pierced him with six iron shafts in that great battle.
Akrūra, however, pierced Dantavakra with nine arrows;
the King of Kārūṣa struck him in return with ten swift-flying shafts.
Vipṛthu pierced Śiśupāla with seven arrows,
and the powerful Śiśupāla pierced him back with eight.
Gaveśana, however, pierced the King of Cedi with six arrows;
Anirdānta likewise with eight, and Bṛhaddurga with five.
The King of Cedi pierced each of them in return with five arrows,
and he slew the four horses of Vipṛthu with four shafts.
The slayer of foes severed the head of Bṛhaddurga with a broad-headed arrow and dispatched Gaveṣaṇa’s charioteer to the abode of Yama.
Having abandoned that chariot whose horses were slain,
the mighty and heroic Vipṛthu quickly mounted the chariot of Bṛhaddurga.
Vipṛthu’s charioteer, having quickly mounted Gaveṣaṇa’s chariot,
began to drive the swift horses.
Enraged, they covered Sunītha with a shower of arrows as he danced along the paths of his chariot, bows in hand and wearing feathered quivers.
Cakradeva pierced Dantavaktra in the chest with a barbed arrow; he then struck him in battle with twenty-five sharp shafts.
Pierced by those two with ten sharp arrows that struck his vital organs,
the powerful one then pierced Cakradeva with ten shafts.
And from no great distance, he pierced Vidūratha with five arrows;
Vidūratha also struck him in battle with six sharp shafts.
Dantavaktra also pierced Bhānumant Vidūratha;
the powerful one struck that mighty warrior in return with thirty arrows.
In the battle, Kṛtavarman pierced the prince with three shafts.
He struck his charioteer and cut down his lofty standard;
then Pauṇḍra, filled with rage, pierced him in return with six feathered arrows.
With a broad-headed arrow of long joints, he cut off his bow;
then Nivṛttaśatru pierced the Kalinga king with sharp arrows,
and the King of Kalinga struck him on the shoulder with a lance.
Having approached the elephant of Aṅga on his own elephant, the powerful Kaṅka pierced Aṅga’s body with a lance,
and Aṅga in turn pierced him with arrows.
Citraka, Śvaphalka, and the great car-warrior Satyaka likewise pierced the army of Kaliṅga with sharp iron arrows.
Enraged in battle, Rāma struck down the elephant of the King of Vaṅga with the discharged tree, and he also slew the King of Vaṅga himself in the encounter.
Having slain him and mounted his chariot, the valiant Saṃkarṣaṇa took up his bow and struck down many Kaiśikas with fierce iron arrows.
Having struck down the Kārūṣas, those great archers, with six arrows, that heroic and mighty car-warrior,
filled with rage, slew a hundred Māgadhas;
having slain them, the long-armed one then advanced against Jarāsaṃdha.
As he was charging, the King of Magadha pierced him with three iron shafts;
the wielder of the mace, filled with rage, struck him back with eight iron shafts and cut down his jewel-adorned banner with a broad-headed arrow.
And with his arrows alone, O great king, Halāyudha shattered that mighty bow held by him and his chariot as well, reducing them to pieces as small as sesame seeds.
With his bow broken and deprived of his chariot, that Māgadha took up a mace and struck Balabhadra, piercing him again and again.
And that Māgadha crushed his chariot with a mace.
Leaping down from that falling chariot,
Halāyudha proceeded toward the chariot of Sātyaki while all the kṣatriyas looked on.
But Sātyaki, O great king, pierced the ruler of Magadha with arrows.
O great king, Baladeva, quickly seizing his mace,
struck the King of Magadha in battle as Hari strikes a mountain with his thunderbolt;
that battle between them became terrible, like the encounter between the gods and the asuras.
The surging flood of joy from the great ocean was irresistible,
as they discharged showers of arrows and struck one another down.
Indeed, thousands of enraged elephants clashed with elephants;
chariots with chariots, and furious horsemen with horsemen as well.
Foot soldiers, with spears, shields, and swords in hand, moved about separately in the battle, severing the heads of other foot soldiers.
The great sound of falling swords and the noise of arrows striking against armor were heard like the cry of birds swooping down.
In that battle, the roar of the weapons and the twang of the bowstrings of those great-souled warriors drowned out the sound of kettledrums, conchs, clay drums, and flutes.
Janārdana struck him deeply with seventy arrows;
and the mighty one, exerting himself, cut down his standard and,
being full of valor, severed the head of his charioteer from his body.
Perceiving that Janārdana had fallen into distress,
all those southern kings, desiring to kill him, surrounded him.
The mighty-armed Aṃśumān pierced him with ten arrows;
the enraged Śrutarvā with five, and Veṇudāri with seven.
Then the valiant Govinda pierced Aṃśumat in the chest;
that lord of men, being distressed, sank down upon the seat of his chariot.
He struck Śrutarvan’s horses with four arrows;
then Veṇudāri, having cut down his standard, pierced his right arm.
In that very manner, he pierced Śrutarvā with seven arrows;
the latter, exhausted and overcome by pain, leaned against his banner and sat down.
Discharging showers of arrows, those leaders of the Krathakaiśikas then advanced toward Vāsudeva from all sides with a multitude of chariots.
In that battle, Janārdana cut their arrows with his own arrows;
enraged, he struck down many of them as they exerted themselves and strove against him.
Furthermore, the hero struck another sixty-four [enemies] with sharp arrows;
as those enraged warriors rushed forward, that army then fled.
In the meantime, the illustrious hero Balabhadra appeared.
In that great battle, he struck the hero Jarāsaṃdha with his mace.
The king fell into a swoon and collapsed upon the ground.
Sātyaki struck the king of Vaṅga with sharpened arrows,
and that army turned away even as Jarāsaṃdha was falling.
Having defeated thousands of warriors, Sātyaki and Balabhadra stood at the forefront of all and blew their conchs;
then the army fled and Jarāsaṃdha was defeated.
Hearing the sound of their conchs, Janārdana, even as he was proceeding,
[beheld] the army of the King of Magadha, which was supported by many kings, already defeated.
Having reflected thus, the powerful Vāsudeva,
the upholder of the Yadu lineage, blew his great conch shell, Pāñcajanya.
