Vaiśampāyana said:
Having heard that Rukmiṇī was being carried away by Kṛṣṇa,
the enraged Rukmin made a vow in the presence of Bhīṣmaka.
"Without slaying Govinda in battle and without bringing back Rukmiṇī, I shall not enter Kuṇḍina; this I tell you as the truth."
Mounting that chariot, which bore uplifted weapons and banners, the hero,
filled with rage and surrounded by a great force, advanced with speed.
And the kings dwelling in the southern region followed him,
as did Krātha, Aṃśumat, Śrutarvan, and the heroic Veṇudāri.
And the son of Bhīṣmaka as well, that best of chariot-warriors on his chariot,
and all the leaders of the Krathakaiśikas— all of them great car-warriors (mahārathas).
Having traveled a long distance along the Narmadā river,
they saw Govinda standing there together with his beloved, filled with rage.
Having stationed that army, Rukmi, filled with the pride of his own strength,
took up a sharp arrow and spoke thus to Janārdana:
"O heir of a cowherd, you who violate the wives of others!
Let this young woman be released, and stay for a moment longer;
if you remain before me, I shall cut off your head with my arrows."
Having spoken thus, O Lord, he fixed a sharpened arrow upon his bow and,
desiring a single combat, advanced toward Madhusūdana.
He pierced Govinda with sixty-four sharpened arrows;
Janārdana, in that battle, pierced him in return with seventy shafts.
The mighty and heroic one cut down his standard as he was striving,
and he severed the head of his charioteer from his body.
Perceiving that Janārdana had fallen into distress,
all those southern kings, desiring to kill him, surrounded him.
The mighty-armed Aṃśumān pierced him with ten excellent arrows;
the enraged Śrutarvā pierced him with five, and Veṇudāri with seven.
Then the valiant Govinda pierced Aṃśumat in the chest;
that lord of men, being distressed, sank down upon the seat of his chariot.
He struck Śrutarvan’s horses with four arrows and,
having severed Veṇudāri’s standard, pierced his right arm.
In the same manner, he pierced Śrutarvā with five arrows;
exhausted, the latter leaned against his banner and sat down, overcome by pain.
Discharging showers of arrows, those leaders of the Krathakaishikas then advanced from all sides against Vāsudeva with a multitude of chariots.
In that battle, Janārdana cut their arrows with his own arrows;
and being enraged, he struck down those shafts as they were being discharged by their striving opponents.
Furthermore, that one of great strength struck another sixty-four with sharpened arrows; he rushed toward those enraged heroes who were charging at him.
Seeing his own army in flight, Rukmī fell under the sway of anger and pierced Keśava in the chest with five sharpened arrows.
And he pierced his charioteer with three sharp arrows,
and struck his banner with a straight-knotted shaft.
And Keśava, enraged, pierced him with sixty arrows and cut the bow of Rukmin, even as he was striving.
Then, taking up another bow with the intent to slay Kṛṣṇa,
the valiant Rukmī manifested blazing celestial weapons.
The Vāyavya, the Vāruṇa, the Māhendra, and the Nairṛta;
the Paiśāca, the Rākṣasa, the Raudra, and likewise the Māheśvara.
Keśava discharged these divine weapons in battle,
but Janārdana Govinda,
the one of great strength, warded off his weapons with his own and struck them down with those very same missiles.
Furthermore, he cut that bow and the chariot pole with three arrows.
With his bow broken and deprived of his chariot, that hero took up a sword and a shield and leapt from the vehicle like the powerful Garuḍa.
As he was charging, Keśava cut his sword in battle;
then, enraged, he pierced him in the chest with three iron arrows.
Enraged, he then pierced him in the chest with five arrows;
that mighty-armed king fell, making the earth resound,
unconscious and fainted like a mountain struck by a thunderbolt.
And Keśava pierced all those kings once again with his arrows—
along with their horses, banners, chariots, charioteers, and footmen.
Seeing Rukmin fallen, the lords of men fled in all directions.
Their limbs pierced by Kṛṣṇa’s arrows, they looked at one another;
seeing her brother writhing on the ground, Rukmiṇī,
longing for her brother’s life, fell at her husband’s feet.
Having raised her up and embraced her, Keśava comforted her;
then, having granted safety to Rukmin, he departed for his own city.
The Vṛṣṇis also, having defeated Jarāsaṃdha and those other kings,
and the heroic Sātyaki having conquered the mighty Śiśupāla,
and Baladeva, the descendant of Vṛṣṇi, having likewise defeated that bull among the Magadhas;
Having conquered them as was appropriate, those heroic and best of the Yādavas,
placing Halāyudha at their head, departed for Dvārakā in high spirits.
When the lotus-eyed one had departed, Śrutarvā approached in the encounter,
placed Rukmin upon his chariot, and then went to his own city.
But Rukmin, filled with the intoxication of his own prowess, did not wish to enter the city of Kuṇḍina, having failed in his vow and not having brought back his sister.
And for the purpose of residence in Vidarbha, he constructed another great city;
it became renowned on earth by the name Bhojakaṭa.
The immensely powerful Rukmin ruled over that birthplace of the high-souled son of Bhṛgu; while he lived there,
that one of great splendor governed the southern quarter by his own energy.
And the high-minded King Bhīṣmaka dwelt in Kuṇḍina.
Jarāsaṃdha, having regained consciousness, returned to his own city together with all the kings, with his face bowed down in humility.

The dull-witted Śiśupāla, overcome with shame along with his kinsmen and watched by the citizens and countryfolk, departed from his own city, having now behaved otherwise than before. He who was once the husband of the daughter of the Bhojas now went forth.
Who indeed would now be capable of acting otherwise toward Rukmiṇī while Kṛṣṇa is alive, especially when he is accompanied by Balarāma and Sātyaki?
Thus, seeing King Sunītha proceeding toward his own city with diminished prowess, all the citizens spoke to one another as he went:
"Now that Rāma, accompanied by the Vṛṣṇi forces, has arrived at Dvārakā."
The Lord Keśava took the hand of Rukmiṇī according to the prescribed rites.
Then he took delight with that beloved wife who was filled with joy,
just as Rāma did of old with Sītā, or as Purandara did with Paulomī.
Just as King Nala was to Damayantī,
so too was that beautiful woman the eldest wife of Kṛṣṇa;
she was devoted to her husband, endowed with virtues, and possessed of beauty, character, and excellence.
Upon her he begot ten sons who were great chariot-warriors:
Cārudeṣṇa, Sudeṣṇa, and the exceedingly powerful Pradyumna.
The valiant one [also had] Suṣeṇa, Cārugupta, Cārubāhu,
Cāruvinda, Sucāru, and likewise Bhadracāru.
And Cāru, the best among the strong, as well as his daughter Cārumatī;
they were all skilled in dharma and artha, proficient in weapons, and fierce in battle.
Then the mighty-armed Madhusūdana married seven auspicious principal queens, as well as others who were endowed with virtues and born of noble lineage.
[He married] Kālindī, Mitravindā, Satyā the daughter of Nagnajit,
and Rohiṇī, the daughter of Jāmbavat, who could assume any form at will.
And also the daughter of the King of Madra, Suśīlā of auspicious eyes; Satyabhāmā, the daughter of Satrājit; and Lakṣmaṇā of lovely smiles;
and Śaibyā Sudattā, who in beauty was indeed like an Apsaras.
Hṛṣīkeśa, whose prowess is incomparable, married sixteen thousand other women; he enjoyed them all equally,
provided with the finest garments and ornaments, and was nourished by every object of desire.
From them were born his heroic sons by the thousands;
eighty thousand and sixteen more, O Bhārata,
all of whom were skilled in every weapon, powerful, and great chariot-warriors.
They were performers of sacrifices, doers of meritorious deeds, highly fortunate, and possessed of great strength.
Having thus performed the marriage with Rāma and the other Yādavas, Hari, that bull among the Yadus,
dwelt happily in that city.
"Just as Śakra [dwells] in his own city, so did the Teacher of the World.
Vaiśampāyana said:
Then, after some time had passed, the exceedingly powerful Rukmin—
The subduer of enemies caused a svayaṃvara for his daughter to be held.
There, invited by Rukmin, kings and princes of great prowess, endowed with splendor, assembled from various directions.
Pradyumna went there, surrounded by other youths;
for that maiden desired him, and he [desired] her of the beautiful eyes.
At that time, there was a daughter of Rukmin, a princess of Vidarbha named Śubhāṅgī, who was endowed with beauty and splendor and was renowned throughout the earth.
When all those high-souled kings were seated,
the princess of Vidarbha chose Pradyumna, the slayer of enemies.
For he was skilled in all weapons, possessed the powerful build of a lion, and was a youth;
he became the son of Keśava, peerless in beauty in the world.
And that princess Candrasenā, endowed with youth, beauty, and virtue, became filled with desire for him, as he was for her.
When the svayaṃvara was concluded, those kings returned to their own cities;
Pradyumna, however, taking the princess of Vidarbha with him, went to Dvārakā.
The hero Nala took his pleasure with Damayantī as he had before;
he begot upon her a son who resembled the offspring of a god,
known by the name Aniruddha, whose deeds were peerless on earth.
One who has reached the further shore of the science of archery, the Vedas, and the treatises on ethics.
O King, when Aniruddha had reached the proper age,
Rukmiṇī chose for him as a wife the granddaughter of Rukmin, who was radiant like gold and named Rukmavatī.
Then the king, having resolved to give Aniruddha— who was endowed with all virtues—
out of affection for the son of Rukmiṇī and also out of regard for Rukmiṇī herself, [prepared to bestow him].
O Janamejaya, although he was competing with Kṛṣṇa, the king cast aside that enmity and, being well-pleased, said, "I shall give it."
Keśava, together with Rukmiṇī, his sons, Saṃkarṣaṇa,
and other Vṛṣṇis, went to Vidarbha accompanied by his army.
The kinsmen of Rukmin, as well as his friends,
and those kings who were invited by Rukmin, also arrived there.
On an auspicious lunar day, O Great King, and under a highly honored constellation,
there was a supreme festival for the marriage of Aniruddha.
O Bhārata, when Aniruddha took the hand of the princess of Vidarbha,
there was a supreme festival for the people of Vidarbha and the Yādavas;
the Vṛṣṇis rejoiced there, being honored like the immortals.
Then there was Veṇudāri, the lord of the Aśmakas, who was noble-minded;
as well as Akṣa, Śrutarvā, Cāṇūra, Krātha, and Aṃśumān.
Jayatsena, the exceedingly powerful lord of the Kaliṅgas,
the illustrious King Pāṇḍya, and likewise the ruler of the Ṛṣikas.
Having consulted together, all these kings from the south, possessed of great power,
approached the lord Rukmin in private and spoke.
"You are skilled in dice, and we also desire to play;
moreover, that Rāma is fond of gambling, even though he is unskilled at dice."
"Placing you at our head, we wish to conquer him," they said;
thus addressed, the great chariot-warrior Rukmī approved of the gambling match.
Delighted, they entered that assembly hall, which possessed auspicious golden pillars, its courtyard adorned with flowers, and its floor sprinkled with sandalwood water.
Having entered there, they all— adorned with bright garlands and unguents and desirous of victory— took their seats upon golden thrones.
Challenged by gamblers skilled in dice, Baladeva, being delighted, said, "Very well; let us play together; let a stake be set."
Desiring to conquer him through guile, the southern kings brought there gems,
pearls, and gold by the thousands.
Then the gambling match began among them— a destroyer of their peace,
a terrible source of strife, and a bringer of ruin for those of evil intellect.
At the outset, Baladeva offered ten thousand gold coins as the stake in the encounter with Rukmin.
Then Rukmi defeated that great car-warrior as he was striving;
at that very moment, he further defeated Baladeva once again.
Having been repeatedly defeated by Rukmi, Keshava’s elder brother took ten million gold pieces as his stake from that high-souled man.
Then Āhvṛti, exulting at the thought "It is won!", spoke to him;
praising himself, he laughed and hurled the club-armed one.
Ignorant, weak, yet once glorious, this invincible Baladeva has been defeated by me in a game of dice despite possessing immeasurable wealth.
Upon hearing that, the King of Kaliṅga then laughed loudly;
showing his teeth in delight, he provoked Halāyudha to anger.
Having heard the words of Rukmin, which were born of his defeat,
and being rebuked with sharp words by the son of Bhīṣmaka,
the knower of dharma, though he was one who had conquered anger, summoned a fit of rage.
Having been insulted, the mighty son of Rohiṇī became enraged;
yet, restraining his mind through fortitude, he then spoke these words.
"Ten thousand crores is my stake, and the other is mine;
accept this, O lord of men, and cast the dice.
Cast the black dice and the red dice upon this dustless spot."
In this manner the son of Rohiṇī challenged Rukmin;
without saying anything further, he spoke again, "So be it."
Then the king, wearing golden ornaments, joyfully cast the dice;
when the game of four dice was concluded, that lord of men was defeated.
Then Balarāma said to Bala, "No, this is not according to dharma. Restraining his mind through fortitude, he said nothing at all;
let these kings here speak what is truthful.
Then Rukmī, smiling, said to Baladeva, "I have conquered him."
But Baladeva, having heard those deceitful words from the lord of men,
was again overcome with anger and did not utter a reply.
Then a disembodied voice spoke with a deep resonance, increasing the anger of the high-souled Baladeva:
"The illustrious Bala has spoken the truth; he has been defeated according to dharma."
It should be understood that even without uttering any words, one becomes subject to the result through action when it has been mentally approved.
Having heard these truthful and well-spoken words from the sky,
the powerful Saṃkarṣaṇa then rose up with his great golden mace; yet,
incited by that wicked king, the prince of Vidarbha disregarded him.
Impelled by Time, he spoke to Saṃkarṣaṇa while mocking him.
"You are not experts at dice, you cowherds who roam the forest;
kings play with dice and arrows, not people like you."
Thus insulted by Rukmin and mocked by the kings,
he crushed Rukmiṇī’s elder brother upon the surface of the earth.
Enraged during the dispute, Rāma, the bull among the Yadus, violently struck the reviler who spoke such cruel words with his very dice-board.
Then, drawing back in a rage, he broke the tusks of the lord of Kaliṅga as well; in his fury, he roared like a lion and,
raising his sword, terrified those kings.
In the midst of the arena, Haladhara roamed like a lion;
that best of strong men, Saṃkarṣaṇa, then uprooted the golden pillar of the assembly hall and dragged it away like a lordly elephant.
With that very [weapon], he swiftly struck the Krathakaiśikas stationed there;
terrifying the Krathakaiśikas, he emerged from the door of the assembly hall.

Seizing Rukmin by the hair, he dragged him back again and again; taking that deceitful-minded Rukmin, the bull of the Yadavas hurled him from the door of the assembly hall to the distance of an arrow's flight, having struck him down.
Having terrified all his enemies, like a lion [terrifying] small animals.
Surrounded by his own kinsmen, Rāma went to his own camp and reported everything exactly as it had happened to Kṛṣṇa.
Then Kṛṣṇa said something to the highly effulgent Rāma;
and Rukmiṇī, having heard that her beloved brother had been slain,
restrained herself and shed tears out of anger.
That elder brother of Rukmiṇī, the slayer of enemy heroes, who had previously not been slain by Vāsudeva due to his affection for Rukmiṇī,
was killed in the gambling hall by a weapon released from the hand of Rāma.
The powerful king, like the wielder of the thunderbolt, [traverses] by means of the eightfold path.
When that great minister, the king who was the son of Bhīṣmaka— equal indeed to Drumasena and Bhārgava, and trained by Drumasena and Bhārgava— had been slain.
When Kṛta, who was skilled in battle and a constant performer of sacrifices, had been struck down,
all the Vṛṣṇis and Andhakas became despondent.
Vaiśampāyana said: And the highly fortunate Rukmiṇī, lamenting with a voice of distress—
seeing her thus lamenting, Keśava comforted her.
O bull of the Bharata race, I have thus related to you everything concerning the death of Rukmin and the origin of his enmity with the Vṛṣṇis.
The Vṛṣṇis also, O great king, taking all their wealth and relying upon Rāma and Kṛṣṇa, went to the city of Dvāravatī.
Janamejaya said: O brahmin-sage, I desire to hear once more the majesty of the wise Baladeva, who is Śeṣa, the upholder of the earth.
For those people who are knowers of the ancient lore speak of that great-souled one as exceedingly powerful, an unconquered mass of splendor.
O Brahmin, I desire to hear in truth of his deeds—
those of the serpent whom they know as Ananta, the primordial deity of great splendor.
Vaiśampāyana said:
In the Purāṇas, that king of serpents is recited as the upholder of the earth;
he is Śeṣa, a treasury of splendor, glorious, unshakable, and the supreme person.
The teacher of yoga, Mahāvīrya— possessing great strength, power, and might—
is he who conquered Jarāsaṃdha in a mace-duel yet did not slay him.
And many kings, O lord of the earth,
followed the Magadha king in battle, yet they too were defeated in the fray.
Bhīma, whose strength was equal to ten thousand elephants and whose prowess was terrifying,
had been defeated more than once by Baladeva in hand-to-hand combat.
While abducting the daughter of Duryodhana in the city named after the elephant (Hastināpura), Sāmba, the son of Jāmbavatī, was captured.
Being besieged on all sides by kings and reportedly plundering by force,
Halāyudha, having heard of this, arrived there in a great rage;
Rāma came for the sake of his liberation, yet he did not find him.
Then the powerful one became enraged and performed a great and wonderful feat.
The powerful one raised his plow-weapon, which was irresistible, impenetrable, divine, and peerless,
consecrated with the Brahma-staff mantra.
Having stationed himself at the ramparts and walls of the city, that one of great strength desired to cast the Kaurava's city into the Ganges.
Perceiving that the city was in a state of agitation, King Duryodhana sent Sāmba back to that wise man along with his wife.
Then the Lord of the Kurus gave himself as a disciple to the high-souled Rāma; and he, in turn, accepted him for instruction in the art of mace-fighting.
From that time forward, O Indra among kings, this city has been agitated;
it appears as if it were turning toward the Gaṅgā, O monarch.
O King, this most wonderful deed of Rāma, performed long ago by Śauri at Bhāṇḍīra, is celebrated throughout the earth.
With a single fist, Halāyudha struck down Pralamba,
and he hurled the massive-bodied Dhenuka to the summit of a mountain.
Lifeless, the Daitya who had assumed the form of a donkey fell upon the earth;

for the great river Yamunā, the sister of Yama, whose garland of waves was driven by the swift force of her waters, having been drawn toward the city by the wielder of the plow, flowed rapidly toward it.
This majesty of Baladeva— of the infinite, immeasurable Śeṣa, the great-souled one— has been recounted to you by me.
Thus, O best of men, the many kinds of supreme and other deeds of Lāṅgalin which have not been told here today— learn them from the extensive Purāṇa.
May He whose garland of tulasī is gently swaying, who has mounted upon the son of Vinatā,
and who is dark-complexioned like a blue lotus, appear before me!
Janamejaya said:
O great sage, tell me what the mighty-armed Viṣṇu did after returning to Dvārakā once Rukmiṇī’s son had been slain.
Vaiśampāyana said:
Surrounded by them, the blessed and heroic Viṣṇu, the delighter of all the Yādavas, went to the city and gazed upon Dvārakā.
The lotus-eyed one bestowed various jewels and riches upon the Nairṛtas, granting each according to his merit.
There, the Daityas together with the Dānavas created obstacles;
the mighty-armed one slew those great Asuras who had been granted boons.
There, a Dānava named Naraka, a great enemy of the king of the gods and a terror to the hosts of deities, created an obstacle for him.
Established within the form of the Liṅga, he shone, surpassing all the deities;
at that time, he acted in opposition to both the sages and human beings.
Then Bhauma went to Tvaṣṭṛ’s daughter Kaśerū on the fourteenth day; assuming the form of an elephant, he seized her of radiant limbs.
Having violently assaulted the woman of beautiful hips, Naraka,
the lord of Prāgjyotiṣa, his grief and fear destroyed by delusion, then spoke these words.
Whatever various jewels exist among gods and humans,
and whatever wealth the entire earth and the oceans contain, he possesses it all.
From this day forward, all the Nairṛtas here, together with the Daityas and Dānavas, shall present those very things to me alone.
In this manner, Bhauma then gathered up those excellent jewels and various garments, yet he did not reflect upon that act.
The powerful Naraka carried off the daughters of the Gandharvas,
as well as those of gods and humans, and seven groups of Apsarases.
Fourteen thousand and twenty-one hundred women all wore a single braid of hair and followed the path of the virtuous.
For those [daughters], the noble-minded Bhauma caused a city of jewels to be built upon a mountain in Alakā, facing the realm of Mura.
And they— the lord of Prāgjyotiṣa, the ten sons of Mura,
and the foremost of the Nairṛtas— wait upon him while protecting him.
This very same great Asura, Varadatta, who dwells on the far shore of darkness,
has assailed Aditi for the sake of her earrings.
Indeed, those two auspicious earrings which belong to gods and humans were never before achieved by all the hosts of asuras joined together,
nor was that terrible deed ever performed in the past which the great asura then accomplished.
The goddess Earth gave birth to him whose capital was the city of Prāgjyotiṣa;
he had four frontier guards who were fierce in battle.
Hayagrīva, Niṣunda, the hero Pañcajana,
Muru, and the great asura Varadatta with his thousands of sons.
Intoxicated by pride, that asura assailed Aditi;
having blocked the path leading to the gods,
he stood there together with hideous rakshasas, terrifying those who perform righteous deeds.
For the sake of slaying him, the mighty-armed Janārdana, bearing the conch, discus, mace, and sword,
was born among the Vṛṣṇis to Devakī from Vasudeva.
Then, for that lord of men of world-renowned splendor,
the gods provided a dwelling place in Dhārakā.
For the city of Dvārakā was exceedingly beautiful, surpassing even the abode of Vāsava;
it was encircled by the great ocean and adorned by five mountains.

For that very God of gods, a hall was constructed by Viśvakarman within that city which resembles a celestial abode; it is renowned as Sudāśārhi, with golden archways and extending for ten thousand yojanas.
There, all the Vṛṣṇis and Andhakas, led by Rāma and Kṛṣṇa,
remain protecting this entire course of worldly affairs.
Everyone remained there contemplating the slaughter of Naraka;
while they were all seated there, O bull of the Bharatas,
a wind blew with a divine fragrance and a rain of flowers fell.
Then, enveloped in a mass of radiance, a tumultuous roar arose for a moment in the sky and subsequently settled upon the earth.
In the midst of that radiance, Vāsava was seen mounted upon a white elephant, surrounded by all the hosts of gods.
Afflicted by Naraka in battle and accompanied by the world-protectors,
he sought protection from the Lord of the World, the Yādava endowed with [divine] names,
as well as the slaying of the evil-minded Naraka by Viṣṇu.
When that slayer of Vṛtra had arrived, oppressed by the foremost Dānavas,
King Ugrasena, along with Rāma, Kṛṣṇa, and the hosts of Vṛṣṇis and Andhakas,
went out to meet that high-souled one, honoring him as the Lord of the Gods.
Having quickly descended from his elephant, he embraced Janārdana,
Baladeva, and King Āhuka;
then the Lord of Gods embraced Pradyumna and that son of great splendor.
And he embraced the other Vṛṣṇis according to their rank and according to their age.

Honored by Rāma and Kṛṣṇa, he entered the auspicious assembly hall. There, having prepared a seat for himself in that hall, the lord of the gods accepted the customary rites of hospitality, beginning with the offering of water (arghya), according to the prescribed rules.

O King, with offerings such as the *arghya* and with the *madhuparka*, the slayer of Vṛtra, the lord of Śacī, provided a seat equal to his own self for the younger brother of Vasava. Then the one of great splendor, Vāsava, spoke to the younger brother of Vasava.
Gently touching his auspicious face with his hand, he spoke with words of consolation.
O Madhusūdana, son of Devakī, hear my words,
O crusher of enemies, regarding the purpose for which I have approached you today.
O Hṛṣīkeśa, a Nairṛta named Naraka, arrogant due to a boon from Brahmā, is harassing us Lokapālas on all sides;
having quickly abandoned the path to heaven, we have fled in every direction.
Out of delusion, the son of Diti seized the earrings of Aditi.
"He constantly acts to the displeasure of the gods and the sages;
I am unable to conquer him, therefore I have come to you for refuge. Look for an opportunity and slay that sinful man."
But this son of Vinatā, Garuḍa— who moves at will, possesses the power of his desire, is exceedingly radiant, and travels through the sky— will carry you there.
That Asura Bhauma is a hellish being who cannot be slain by any living creatures;
having destroyed that wicked one, you should return here quickly.
Thus addressed by the king of the gods, the lotus-eyed Keśava,
the mighty-armed one, promised the destruction of Naraka.
Keśava, the slayer of Keśin, spoke this to Śakra;
it was for this purpose that the sages of rigid vows had come here.
O Śakra, O Hari, the residents of Badarī have departed after speaking to me.
And, O Lord Śatakratu, I have granted them freedom from fear;
for that reason, O God, I am prepared to slay that Dānava in battle.

For that purpose, O Lord, Garuḍa, the bull among birds, has arrived— he who can assume any form at will, who is possessed of great splendor, the son of Vinatā, and who travels through the atmosphere; he who,
together with Śakra, bears the conch, the discus, the mace, and the sword.
Indeed, that Keśava set out for the purpose of slaying Naraka;
he then departed upon Garuḍa, accompanied by Satyabhāmā.
Gradually, that powerful one, together with Vāsava, ascended through the seven celestial spheres while the lions of the Yadu clan looked on.
Śakra, mounted upon the lordly elephant, and Janārdana, seated upon Garuḍa,
shone from their distance like the sun and the moon.
Then, being praised in the intermediate space by Gandharvas and Apsarases like Śakra himself, Mādhava gradually vanished from sight.
Having settled his duties, Vāsava, the lord of the gods, returned to his own abode; Kṛṣṇa, however, went to Prāgjyotiṣa.
Then the wind, struck by the wind from his wings, blew in a contrary direction.
Then, by means of clouds making a terrifying roar, the sky-dwellers wandered about;
in an instant, he indeed reached heaven by means of his celestial vehicle.
Having seen them from afar, he proceeded to where they were stationed; there,
O Great King, he beheld at the mountain entrance the mounts of elephants, horses, and chariots belonging to the wicked-minded Naraka, as well as his guards.
Having slain those foremost hosts of Rākṣasas of great strength belonging to Naraka,
the Lord of the Gods blew the loud-sounding Pāñcajanya conch;
he then beheld six thousand nooses of Mura, which were sharp-edged as razors.
Vaiśampāyana said:
Upon Garuḍa sat the glorious Lord, bearing the conch, the discus, the mace, and the sword;
possessing the form of a dark blue cloud, he was four-armed and clad in yellow garments.

His chest was adorned with a forest garland; his breast bore the Śrīvatsa mark and resembled the moon; his head was crowned with a diadem; he possessed the brilliance of the sun like the moon accompanied by lightning;
and as he twanged his bowstring, a great sound was heard like the roar of a thunderbolt.
Having learned everything, Viṣṇu himself came here;
Mura, whose eyes were red with rage and who possessed the splendor of the Destroyer at the end of time, arrived.
Grasping a spear, the great asura rushed forward with speed and hurled that great spear,
which was adorned with diamonds and gold.
As that spear, like a blazing great meteor, was falling toward him,
Janārdana took up an arrow with a golden shaft and fixed it to his bow.
The heroic Vāsudeva split it in two with a razor-sharp arrow;
there he cut down the spear, which was blazing like a mass of lightning.
Then Muru, his eyes red with rage, seized his great mace,
which thundered like the roar of Indra’s thunderbolt hurled by Indra himself.
The best of gods discharged a crescent-headed arrow drawn back to his ear;
it cut that gold-adorned mace in mid-air,
and then, with a broad-headed shaft, he severed the head of the Dānava in battle.
In that battle, Keśava slew the entire host of Piśācas belonging to the evil-minded Mura— both a hundred thousand and ten million strong.
Having severed all those bonds, he joined together with Mura;
O King, that Dānava Mura beheld the joy of the Yadus and let out a lion’s roar, then struck him with his mace.
The great asura struck Garuḍa on the head and battered Keśava with spears, javelins, double-edged swords,
and lances; thereupon the enraged Hṛṣīkeśa severed his head with a razor-sharp arrow.
Then Hari blew his conch shell at that chief of the Dānavas.
All the Dānavas and even the mountains were shaken by that sound;
having severed all those bonds and slain Mura along with his kin,
he leaped over the masses of rocks and crushed Nisunda.
...the Blessed One, the son of Devakī,
beheld the army of the Dānavas,
as well as Hayagrīva, the son of Diti, and other warriors of diverse combat skills.
The exceedingly powerful one blocked that path with his own army.
Niśunda, the best among the powerful, quickly mounted his chariot and seized a divine, gold-backed, and unassailable bow.
Niśunda pierced Madhusūdana with ten arrows,
and Keśava also pierced him with seventy sharp shafts;
however, Mādhava cut those arrows down in the sky before they could reach him.
All those soldiers surrounded Kṛṣṇa on all sides;
the best of gods was covered by a great net of arrows.
Seeing all those Dānavas, Madhusūdana Janārdana became filled with wrath; then, with the divine Pārjanya weapon,
he checked that army with a great rain of arrows.
With five arrows for each of them, and with one for each of those many [others],
he struck them all in their vital spots by the power of the Pārjanya weapon;
shattered and terrified by fear, those Dānavas fled from the battle.
Seeing his own army in flight, he emerged once more into the battle;
discharging showers of arrows, he covered Keśava.
Neither the sun shone in the battle, nor did the sky or the ten directions appear;
Nisunda covered the one whose banner is Garuda with his arrows.
The Supreme Person, Hari, took up the divine weapon named Sāvitra;
with that arrow, he cut those arrows down in the battle.
Having cut through his arrows with his own arrows, the mighty Kṛṣṇa then severed his parasol with a single shaft, the chariot pole with three arrows,
and those four horses with four more arrows.
With five arrows he cut down the charioteer, and with one he severed the banner; then,
O best of gods, Kṛṣṇa once more used a single, extremely sharp and whetted broad-headed arrow (bhalla) to strike off the head of Nisunda.
That great Daitya died and fell upon the surface of the earth as Nisunda,
mace in hand, rushed forward upon the field of battle.
Then Keśava pierced him with arrows released from the Śārṅga bow;
but Nisunda, O great king, struck Hari with his mace.
Then Satyabhāmā, enraged, struck that lord of the Dānavas with a mace released from her arm, even as Keśava looked on.
Then Hṛṣīkeśa, being pleased, looked toward Satyabhāmā;
pierced by that mace and vomiting much blood, he became bewildered, but having regained consciousness, Nisunda then rushed at him.
Then Hṛṣīkeśa, filled with rage, struck him with feathered arrows—
he who alone, equal to a thousand, had crushed all the gods.
Seeing Niśunda fallen, the powerful Dānava Hayagrīva seized a massive rock and lifted it up.
Having suddenly brandished a boulder that shone like a mountain,
he who was endowed with yoga and was the best among those skilled in weapons took up the divine Pārjanya weapon.
With his divine weapon and fiery energy, Viṣṇu split the rock into seven pieces;
having shattered that great stone, he caused it to fall upon the earth.
Thereupon, the enraged Hayagrīva fixed a razor-headed arrow to his bow.
Then the enraged Hayagrīva, taking up another bow,
struck Keśava with various weapons in that battle;
but Keśava, having severed that bow as well, caused it to fall.
O bull of the Bharatas, just as the battle between the gods and the asuras occurred,
so did that terrible conflict unfold, strewn with various weapons.
Then, mounted upon Garuḍa, the mighty-armed one struck down the great asuras with various colored, great arrows released from the Śārṅga bow.
Torn apart by great plows and struck down by arrows and swords,
the Dānavas perished there upon encountering Janārdana.
Some Dānavas, scorched by the fire of the discus, fell from the sky; others, having come into close proximity, perished with their faces disfigured and their lives departed.
Some were struck by the wings of Garuḍa with their heads crushed;
some were felled to the surface of the earth by blows from his bow; and other birds were slain by the strikes of his palms and the flapping of his wings.
Afflicted by Kṛṣṇa’s arrows, all those Asuras with deformed limbs discharged showers of shafts like rain-bearing clouds.
Smeared with blood, they appeared like flowering *kiṃśuka* trees;
broken in their weapons, those versatile warriors fled in great terror.
And again, the Dānava, his eyes red with rage,
climbed a tree ten fathoms high by the force of the wind;
having uprooted the tree and seized it with speed, he rushed forward.
Possessing a form as solid as a cloud, he hurled a massive tree with great skill;
as it was tossed by the wind-force of the tree's momentum, a tremendous roar was heard.
Then Janārdana, acting with haste, cut that [bow], which was decorated with various colorful patterns, into many pieces with a thousand arrows.
And again, with a single arrow, he pierced Hayagrīva in the center of his chest between the breasts; that shaft, blazing with light,
entered with great force, pierced through the heart, and emerged.
He of boundless splendor, invincible, and the delighter of all the Yādavas, slew that most terrible great Asura Hayagrīva.
In the middle of the Lohitagaṅgā, the Blessed One, the son of Devakī,
the Supreme Person, [subdued] Virūpākṣa, the evil one, in Alakā.
Having slain eight hundred thousand Dānavas, that tiger among men, the scorcher of foes, rushed toward Prāgjyotiṣa; there,
Puruṣottama struck them down within the middle of the outer wall.
Janamejaya said:
"O Blessed One, I desire to hear this story in detail."
O one rich in asceticism, tell me how Kṛṣṇa slew Naraka and that terrible great asura Pañcajana of Naraka.
Then he reached the city named Prāgjyotiṣa, which was as if blazing with splendor; there a great battle took place.
Then the one of great strength blew his conch, Pāñcajanya;
its immense sound was heard like the roar of the clouds at the end of an aeon.
A sound, both terrifying and profound, was heard throughout the three worlds;
hearing it, Naraka’s eyes became bloodshot with rage.
A chariot joined with eight iron wheels, resembling three nalvas in size.
It was richly adorned with various jewels and gold, and its expanse featured an extensive surrounding terrace.
It was resplendent with a great golden vajra-banner,
enriched with banners on golden staffs, and possessed a pole made of lapis lazuli gems.
Yoked with a thousand horses, that chariot, which crushes the chariots of enemies,
was covered with iron lattices and adorned with variegated patterns.
The hero, standing in the midst of his chariot like the sun at twilight,
stood upon that vehicle adorned with gold and strewn with various weapons.
His breastplate was like a vajra and the color of the moon;
it was fastened with pearls possessing a brilliance equal to fire.
His crown upon his head shone like the sun and the sacrificial fire.
Likewise, his two ears were blazing with earrings.
Smoke-colored, massive-bodied, red-eyed, and with distorted faces,
all those Daityas, Dānavas, and Rākṣasas were clad in various types of armor.
Some bore swords and shields, some were equipped with quivers; some held spears in their hands, and others likewise held tridents.
Causing the earth to tremble with throngs of elephants, horses, and chariots,
the heroes, well-armored and skilled in striking, marched forth from the city.
Naraka, resembling Time itself, was surrounded by hosts of Daityas.
He heard thousands of kettledrums, conchs, mṛdaṅgas, and paṇavas being played, sounding like the roar of thunderclouds.
Having gone where Kṛṣṇa was, all those hideous-faced ones surrounded Garuḍa and, having gathered together, fought him;
the soldiers covered him with a great shower of arrows.
Releasing spears, tridents, maces, barbed missiles, lances, and many arrows by the thousands,
they covered the sky.
Then Kṛṣṇa, appearing like a dark rain-cloud, took up his Śārṅga bow and,
having drawn that great bow whose sound was like the roar of a thundercloud, [prepared for battle].
Janārdana discharged showers of arrows at the Dānavas;
by that shower of arrows, the army fled from the great battle.
That battle with the Rākṣasa of terrible form became a horrific one.
And all those [warriors], their battle arrays shattered and tormented by Kṛṣṇa’s arrows,
were seen with some having their arms severed, others their necks and heads cut off,
some split in two by his discus, and others with their chests pierced by arrows.
Some elephant, horse, and chariot riders were split in two by his power;
some were pierced by the Kaumodakī mace, and others were torn asunder by the discus.
Thus was that entire army of elephants, horses, and chariots utterly crushed.
There, his battle with Naraka was exceedingly terrible;
listen as I describe it to you in brief.
The radiant Naraka, who terrified the hosts of gods, fought Madhusūdana— the Supreme Person— as if he were fighting Madhu.
With eyes and face red with rage, the heroic Naraka, resembling Death itself,
seized a bow as lofty as Indra’s rainbow.
Likewise, Keśava took up an arrow resembling the rays of the sun and,
with a divine weapon, filled that chariot in the battle.
The powerful Naraka released the supreme weapon, Mahāpāta.
Seeing the thunderbolt approaching with a flash of light, the illustrious Keśava,
the Supreme Person, cut down that weapon with his discus.
Jarāsandha struck his charioteer with a single arrow,
and with ten arrows he destroyed the chariot along with its banner and horses.
And Madhusūdana cut through his armor with an arrow;
thereupon, his body was freed from its mail like the sloughed skin of a serpent.
His horses slain, his chariot destroyed, and his armor shattered, the heroic Dānava seized a firm spear of pure radiance, forged with loads of iron,
which he whirled and suddenly hurled, blazing like Indra’s thunderbolt.
Then, beholding that gold-adorned spear as it came flying toward him,
Kṛṣṇa of wondrous deeds cut it in two with a razor-edged arrow;
thereafter, that battle became terrible between him and the Rākṣasa of fearsome form.
Madhusūdana fought with Naraka for a moment in that great slaughter caused by the falling of weapons;
then, with his fiercely blazing discus, he split Naraka in two.
His body, split asunder by the discus,
fell upon the earth like a mountain peak divided in two by a saw.
Having encountered Kṛṣṇa, the Lord of Gods, he went to his destruction like the sun at sunset.

Having slain Naraka Bhauma— whose limbs were severed and tossed by the discus as he lay fallen on the battlefield like a mountain of red chalk split apart by a thunderbolt— Viṣṇu, the joy of the Yādavas, [departed].
Having slain Tripura, he rejoiced like the Destroyer of Tripura in ancient times;
but the Earth, beholding her fallen son and taking his two earrings,
approached Govinda and spoke these words:
He was given by you alone, O Govinda, and by you alone he has been struck down.
Play as you wish, like a child with his toys. These two earrings are yours, O Lord; protect these subjects of his.
May the sages and the gods move about free from obstacles and free from fever;
may the subjects move about happily through your protection, O Lord.
By your command, O Lord, may the brahmins be free from obstacles.
Having spoken thus, she gave him those world-renowned earrings;
then the goddess vanished from her husband's side.
Vaiśampāyana said:
Having slain Naraka, the son of the Earth, Viṣṇu— whose prowess is equal to that of Vāsava and who is the younger brother of Vāsava—
beheld the abode of Naraka.
Then, having reached the treasury house of Naraka, Janārdana beheld inexhaustible wealth and various kinds of jewels.
He gave collections of gems, pearls, and corals, as well as heaps of beryl,
great mounds of silver, and likewise heaps of diamonds.
There were couches made of Jāmbūnada gold and Śātakumbha gold,
possessing the luster of blazing fire and the radiance of cool rays;
likewise, there were highly precious beds and lion-thrones.
And he beheld a great, radiant, golden-colored parasol, possessing a luster like that of the cool-rayed moon, appearing as if it were raining down from a cloud.
We have heard that hundreds of thousands of streams of pure gold were formerly brought from Varuṇa by Naraka.
Indeed, such a vast accumulation of wealth belonging to Naraka as was seen in his house had never before been seen or even heard of by King Kubera, nor by Śakra, nor by Yama.
Then, when Hayaśiras had slain Bhauma, Nisunda, and the Dānava Hayagrīva, they brought those jewels and the women of the inner apartments.
Those Dānavas who remained after the slaughter were the guardians of the accumulated treasury;
they brought to Keśava those highly precious things which Janārdana deserved.
The Dānavas said:
"Here are these various precious gems and riches, as well as elephants of fearsome form with goads fashioned from coral."
Wearing golden neck-chains as their great girth-bands, adorned with javelins and lances, and draped in various colorful rugs along with beautiful banners;
And there were twenty thousand female elephants, twice as many again,
along with eight hundred thousand excellent horses born in the [proper] regions.
O Janārdana, we shall deliver as many cows as you desire to the abode of the Vṛṣṇis and Andhakas.
There were also fine woolen beds and seats,
as well as birds of pleasing appearance that warbled according to their desires.
Sandalwood, agalloch wood, and likewise kālīyaka—
whatever wealth you have acquired through righteous means throughout the three worlds,
we shall deliver all of that to the abode of the Vṛṣṇis and Andhakas.
The jewels of the gods and Gandharvas, and whatever wealth belongs to the Pannagas—
all these are present here in the abode of Naraka.
Thus informed by those Dānavas,
Janārdana Hṛṣīkeśa accepted all of that, examined it,
and had everything brought from the Dānavas to the city of Dvārakā.
Then Mādhava, having himself raised up that Varuṇa-parasol which was raining down a shower of gold, ascended it as it flew through the air.
Then Garuḍa, the best of flyers, appearing like a personified cloud,
approached that foremost of mountains from all sides— the Maṇiparvata.
There, auspicious breezes blew and pure radiances arose from the gold-colored jewels, outshining even the sun.
There Madhusūdana beheld gates of lapis lazuli color,
along with archways, banners, and couches.
The mountain of jewels shone with the luster of clouds streaked by lightning,
adorned with palaces and celestial chariots variegated with gold.
There Madhusūdana beheld those beloved daughters of the foremost Gandharvas and Asuras, who possessed the luster of excellent gold.
He saw those women of broad hips, confined within a mountain cave,
brought there by Naraka and guarded on all sides.
Dwelling in a region equal to Triviṣṭapa, they lived like goddesses— happy and free from desire— even while standing before the unconquered one.
Women wearing single braids, all dressed in saffron robes and with their senses fully restrained, surrounded the mighty-armed one.
Desiring a vision of Kṛṣṇa, all the women, their bodies emaciated by vows and fasts, gathered together and joined their palms in reverence before the lion of the Yadus.
Knowing that Naraka, the great asura Mura, Hayagrīva, and Niśunda had been slain, they surrounded Kṛṣṇa.
And all those elderly Dānavas who were their guardians, being advanced in age, bowed down before the joy of the Yadus with their palms joined in reverence.
Then, upon beholding that bull-eyed one, a thought arose in all those supreme women to have him as their husband.
Beholding his moon-like face, those of restrained senses were greatly delighted and spoke these words to the mighty-armed one:
Truly, in former times, Vāyu spoke these words to us here,
as did the divine seer Nārada, who knows the cries of all living beings.
The god Viṣṇu, Nārāyaṇa, who bears the conch, discus, mace, and sword,
shall slay the earthly Naraka and indeed become his husband.
"How wonderful it is that we behold Supriya, the subduer of enemies, after so long!
Indeed, by the sight of this high-souled one, we have today achieved our purpose."
Then Mādhava, the younger brother of Vāsava, consoled all those lotus-eyed women with his gaze and his speech.
Having consoled and addressed them as was fitting, Keśava,
the slayer of Madhu, conveyed them away in vehicles accompanied by his servants.
A very great clamor arose there from thousands of *kiṃkara* demons, swift as the wind, who were carrying the palanquin.
On that preeminent mountain, there was a peak most highly honored,
resembling the stainless sun and moon, and adorned with gateways of jewels and gold.
It was filled with flocks of birds, elephants, wild beasts, and serpents; it was frequented by troops of monkeys and possessed stone surfaces that were excellent for reclining.
It was inhabited by nyankus, boars, and ruru deer; it possessed great plateaus with precipices and was adorned with various trees upon its peaks.
It was most wonderful and inconceivable, stirred by herds of deer,
and made resonant by flocks of jīvañjīvaka birds and peacocks.
Then Viṣṇu, of exceeding strength, uprooted that radiant [tree] with his two arms and placed it upon Garuḍa, the best of birds.
And Garuḍa, the best of birds, effortlessly bore Janārdana along with his wife from the peak of Mount Maṇi.
With the flapping of his powerful wings, that king of birds, resembling the peak of a great mountain, produced a thunderous roar in all directions.
Shattering the mountain peaks and uprooting trees, he gathered together great clouds and sported with some of them.
Having transcended the domain of the two gods, the Moon and the Sun,
the bird, possessing the speed of the wind and remaining under the control of Janārdana, went forth.
Having reached Mount Meru, which is frequented by gods and gandharvas,
Madhusūdana beheld all the abodes of the gods.
O lord of men, that scorcher of foes surpassed the radiant splendors of all the Maruts, the Sādhyas, and the Aśvins.
Having reached the worlds of the merit-makers and attained the realm of the gods, Janārdana, the subduer of enemies, entered the abode of Śakra.
Having descended from Tārkṣya, he beheld the lord of the gods;
and Śatakratu, the king of the deities, joyfully greeted him.
Having presented the two divine earrings, Janārdana, the best of men and the infallible one, together with his wife, then paid homage to that foremost of the gods.
He was honored by the king of the gods and worshipped with jewels;
and Satyabhāmā was likewise greeted with due courtesy by Paulomī.
O Great King, those two queens, world-renowned, embrace one another.
Paulomī spoke thus to Satyabhāmā, the beloved of Hari:
"O Goddess, I am pleased by the sight of you; what more may I do for you?
By good fortune, the evil-minded Naraka has been slain by you."
Having been addressed thus, the goddess then said to her, "It is done.
Then Vāsava and Vāsudeva, together, went to the holy abode of Aditi, the mother of the gods, which was possessed of great splendor.
There, the two high-souled ones beheld the highly fortunate Aditi, endowed with ascetic power, being worshipped on all sides by Apsarases.
Then, having given those two earrings, the husband of Śacī paid homage to her,
placing Janārdana at his head, and related that very matter to her.
Having bestowed [the boon],
Purandara, the delighter of the Ādityas and husband of Śacī, paid homage to his own mother.
Aditi, having affectionately embraced those two sons and congratulated them, [was filled with joy].
Then he addressed them both with appropriate benedictions.
Filled with supreme affection, Paulomī and Satyabhāmā both took hold of the auspicious feet of the goddess who was worthy of the highest honor.
The illustrious mother of the gods also greeted them with affection and spoke these words to Janārdana exactly as was appropriate.
"You shall be unassailable by all beings and invulnerable,
just as this King of the Gods is unconquered and honored by the world."

And this woman of noble form, who is ever pleasing to behold, renowned throughout all the worlds, possessing divine fragrance and enchanting to the mind— she shall be yours; you shall become the sovereign of the gods with her as your foremost companion.
Satyabhāmā, the most excellent of women, fortunate and possessed of perpetual youth,
shall not grow old as long as you, O Kṛṣṇa, remain a mortal man.
Thus honored by the mother of the gods, the mighty Kṛṣṇa,
permitted by the king of the gods, was further worshipped with precious jewels.
Having mounted Vainateya together with Satyabhāmā,
he wandered through the pleasure-gardens of the gods while being honored by the celestial sages.
The mighty-armed one beheld, in the pleasure garden of Vāsava,
the divine and honored Pārijāta, that great celestial tree.
It bears divine flowers perpetually and possesses unsurpassed, meritorious fragrance;
having reached it, every person remembers their former birth.
Though it was being guarded by the gods, Viṣṇu, of immeasurable prowess,
forcibly uprooted that great tree and carried it away.
Then Hari beheld Satyabhāmā and a divine Apsaras behind her; and Satyabhāmā, being gazed upon by that celestial woman,
proceeded toward Dvāravatī by a path fanned by the wind.
Having heard of that deed of Kṛṣṇa at that time, the mighty-armed king of the gods indeed gave his approval and said, "The deed has been well done."
Being honored by the gods and praised by hosts of great seers,
Kṛṣṇa, the subduer of enemies, set out from the world of the gods for Dvārakā.
Having set out, that mighty-armed one traversed a long distance as if it were short;
then, honored by the king of the gods, the mighty-armed one beheld the city of Dvāravatī, the city of the Yādavas.
Having slain Naraka, the son of the Earth, having given the excellent earrings,
and having taken that Pārijāta tree,
the Blessed One, the younger brother of Vāsava, paid homage to the Mother of the Gods after performing such a great deed.
By means of his skillful stratagem, the glorious Viṣṇu, whose vehicle is Garuḍa, [reached] Dvārakā.
Chapter 93,
Transliterated by Julie Bélanger,
Proofread by André Couture.
Version of May 25, 2002:
Vaiśampāyana said: Then Kṛṣṇa, seated upon Garuḍa, beheld the city of Dvārakā.
Resembling the abode of the gods, it resounded on all sides.
For when the son of Devakī had gone on the journey to Mount Maṇi,
as well as to the pleasure-houses,
the chief gardens and groves, and the terraces and courtyards.
When Kṛṣṇa had arrived,
the king of the gods summoned Viśvakarman and spoke these words.
"O best among artisans, if you wish to do what is pleasing to me,
you shall create another enchanting form for the sake of Kṛṣṇa's delight."
O best of the gods, make Dvārakā, crowded with gardens and groves and resembling heaven, just like my own city.
Whatever you perceive in the three worlds that is worthy of being a jewel,
let the city of Dvāravatī be quickly endowed with it by you.
For Kṛṣṇa, ever intent upon all the tasks of the gods,
plunges into battles of terrible form, he who is possessed of great strength.
Then, having gone to that city at the word of Indra, Viśvakarman adorned it on all sides so that it was like Amarāvatī, the city of Indra.
The Lord of the Daśārhas, whose vehicle is a bird, beheld her adorned with divine ornaments fashioned by Viśvakarman according to his designs.
Having beheld that city of Dvārakā, the Lord Nārāyaṇa Hari,
joyful and endowed with all prosperity, began to enter it.
That descendant of Daśārha beheld delightful groves of trees, enchanting to the sight,
and saw Dvārakā, adorned by Viśvakarman.
The city was surrounded by moats resembling the Ganges and the Indus, filled with clusters of lotuses and waters frequented by swans.
With its golden rampart, brilliant as the sun,
set upon the summit of the mountain peak, it resembled the sky with its abode of clouds.
Surrounded by groves resembling Nandana and comparable to Caitraratha,
Dvārakā shone beautifully, like the sky encircled by clouds.
The Raivataka mountain shines, its lovely peaks, caves, and courtyards resplendent; in the eastern direction it stands majestic, with gateways of jewels and gold.
In the south, the Latāveṣṭa shines forth in five colors;
likewise, in the west, there is the Akṣaya, which resembles the banner of Indra.
O bull among kings, the mountain Veṇumān— delightful with its variegated forests,
frequented by lions, white as Mount Mandara, and resembling a king of mountains— greatly adorns the northern quarter.
And the great forest of Pāñcajanya, possessing the colors of a variegated woolen blanket,
as well as the Sarvartuka forest, shine forth toward Mount Raivataka.
The great abode of Meruprabha is entwined on all sides by creepers;
the Bhārgava forest and the great Puṣpaka forest also shine forth.
It was adorned with *akṣaka*, *bījaka*, and *mandāra* trees,
as well as groves of *śatāvarta* and thickets of *karavīra*.
The Caitraratha grove shines forth, as does the great Nandana forest; likewise, the Ramaṇa and Bhāvana forests, along with Veṇumān, are radiant on all sides.
O Bhārata, in the eastern direction, the delightful Puṣkariṇī pond shines with lotuses having leaves of beryl, as does the river Mandākinī.
There, the mountain peaks were adorned by many gods and gandharvas, who desired to please Keśava and were directed by Viśvakarman.
The great river of meritorious waters entered Dvāravatī through fifty great mouths, nourishing it on all sides.
Immeasurable and of great height, endowed with unfathomable moats,
perfected with excellent ramparts, and coated with white plaster as bright as nectar.
He beheld the city of Dvārakā adorned with sharp *śataghnī* engines, networks of mechanical devices, and great iron wheels.
In the city were eight thousand chariots adorned with small bells,
with their banners raised aloft, just like those in the city of the gods.
He beheld the city of Dvārakā, eight yojanas in width and twelve in length, with its surrounding suburbs twice that size, standing firm and immovable.
It has eight great enclosures and sixteen great crossroads,
surrounded by a single path, and was built by Uśanas himself;
therein even women could fight, let alone the great chariot-warriors of the Vṛṣṇis.

In that most excellent of cities belonging to the illustrious Daśārhas, there were indeed seven principal roads, the best of all thoroughfares, which had been directly constructed by Viśvakarman himself in various ways.
Then the son of Devakī rejoiced upon seeing the mansions,
which were adorned with golden staircases inlaid with jewels and were a source of delight for men.
With palaces and excellent courtyards resounding with terrifying and great noises,
the banners were raised high and fluttered to and fro.
With their golden peaks shining like the summits of Mount Meru,
and with pale white ridges covered in gold,
they were like variegated mountains possessing beautiful slopes, caves, and peaks.
And the pinnacles of palaces and delightful houses were covered with rains of flowers, possessing the luster of a uniform five-colored hue.
With a roar like that of the rain-cloud, they were like mountains of various forms.
Constructed by Viśvakarman, they resembled the blazing of a forest fire;
they were as radiant as the moon and sun combined, as if scraping the very sky.
With those illustrious Daśārhas,
who were like the ocean-born Vāsudeva, Indra, and Parjanya, the city shone, adorned by houses that resembled clouds.
Dvārakā appeared beautiful, like the sky shrouded by clouds;
it was the very residence of the Blessed One, fashioned by Viśvakarman himself.
The immeasurable camp of Vāsudeva was seen to be four yojanas long and just as wide, filled with vast treasures.
The illustrious Tvaṣṭṛ, impelled by Vāsava, constructed it for the world with mountains endowed with the finest palaces.
And there was a palace, golden-hued and enchanting to all beings,
lofty like the great golden peak of Mount Meru;
it was the preeminent dwelling for Rukmiṇī, constructed by Viśvakarman.
Furthermore, when Satyabhāmā dwelt in that white palace with its staircases of variegated jewels, people knew it as "Bhogavatī";
it was adorned with banners having the brilliance of the stainless sun.
That palace, which had a clearly visible courtyard and great banners in the four directions,
and which was adorned by Jāmbavatī, surpassed all those other palaces in splendor, just as the sun outshines everything else.
Resembling the color of the rising sun, it stood between the two of them;
fashioned by Viśvakarman, it was divine and like a peak of Mount Kailāsa.
Resplendent like Jāmbūnada gold, resembling a blazing fire,
and standing like the ocean, he is renowned as Meru.
O best of the Bharatas, the daughter of the King of Gāndhāra,
the noble Gāndhārī, was bestowed upon him by Keśava.
Known as Padmakūṭa, it is lotus-colored and possesses great radiance;
it is the vast peak of Subhīmā, her dwelling, most highly honored.
O best of the Kurus, the palace named Sūryaprabha, endowed with all desirable qualities, was assigned for Lakṣmaṇā by the wielder of the Śārṅga bow.
The palace has the luster of the finest lapis lazuli gem and a green radiance;
O Bhārata, all beings know it indeed as the Supreme.
Among those dwellings was the residence of Mitravindā, the queen of Vāsudeva— a place honored by hosts of celestial sages and serving as an ornament to those houses.
But that preeminent palace constructed here by Viśvakarman,
though exceedingly serene, stood there like a mountain.
That dwelling of Sudattā, the queen of Vāsudeva, was praised by all the gods; it was renowned as Ketumān.
Therein was indeed a preeminent palace which Tvaṣṭṛ himself fashioned;
it was a thousand yojanas in length and breadth, composed entirely of all kinds of jewels, and auspicious.
There, the illustrious and radiant one named Viraja shone forth,
where the assembly hall of the high-souled Keśava was located.

In that palace of Vāsudeva, all the golden-staffed banners with their streamers were well-arranged along the paths, courtyards, and gateways; and networks of jewels were set in various places throughout it.
Having brought the great Vaijayanta mountain from Haṃsakūṭa,
the lion of the Yadus [brought] its peak toward the Indradyumna lake—
a peak sixty tālas in height and half a yojana in length.
That world-renowned Kinnara-Mahānāga was also brought there by him of immeasurable splendor, while all beings looked on.
Even that supreme peak of Meru, which traverses the path of the sun,
is divine, made of Jāmbūnada gold, and renowned throughout the three worlds;
it too was uprooted and brought by Viśvakarman for the sake of Kṛṣṇa.
Tvaṣṭṛ brought that tree, which was exceedingly radiant, fierce, and adorned with all kinds of medicinal herbs,
for the sake of his purpose at the word of Indra;
however, the Pārijāta tree itself was brought there by Keśava himself.
As that tree was being led away, a battle took place there involving Kṛṣṇa of wondrous deeds; the gods protected that supreme tree,
which was adorned with hundreds of white lotuses and golden celestial chariots.
For the sake of Vāsudeva, great trees were planted in the sacred precincts;
there were lotus-pools and lakes filled with water teeming with lotuses, containing fragrant gems and blue lilies, and strewn with rafts of jewels and gold.
Great trees beautify their supreme banks:
sāla trees, tāla trees, kadamba trees, and rohiṇa trees with hundreds of branches.
And those trees from the Himalayas as well as those growing on Mount Meru were brought and fashioned by Viśvakarman for the sake of the lion of the Yadus.
In those forest glades, there were trees resembling red, yellow, and crimson in hue, as well as those with white blossoms, all of which were endowed with fruit throughout every season.
In that excellent city, there were rivers and lakes with clear waters, filled with agitated currents and possessing sands of yellow sugar.
There were other rivers as well, filled with water thick with flowers and crowded with various trees and creepers, with sands of golden gravel.
...adorned with blue lotuses;
rivers radiant with clusters of lotuses;
and [forests] with flocks of intoxicated peacocks and ever-intoxicated cuckoos.
In that city, there were many trees endowed with supreme excellence.
Right there in that city, herds of elephants as well as cattle and buffaloes were kept, and it was also made the dwelling place for boars, deer, and birds.
In that beautiful city, the golden rampart was clearly constructed by Viśvakarman, rising to a height of one hundred cubits.
By him, those great mountains, rivers, and lakes,
as well as the forests and groves, were encompassed by the earthly [enclosure].
And palaces, adorned and renowned throughout the world,
[issued] from that very abode of the lion of the Yadus, which is famous among the people.
Therefore, a residence even more magnificent than that was constructed by Viśvakarman for Rāma, that lion among the Yadus; it is exceedingly beautiful and enchanting.

Thus did the bull-eyed Kṛṣṇa gaze upon Dvārakā;
he beheld his own home, adorned with hundreds of palaces.
It was supported by tens of thousands of white jeweled pillars,
adorned here and there with archways resembling blazing fires made of jewels, coral, and silver, and with variegated golden pedestals shining everywhere.
There was a very great palace there for Kṛṣṇa’s use;
supported by crystal pillars, it was spacious and entirely made of gold.
Endowed with waters crowded with lotuses, red fragrant lilies, and blue water-lilies;
variegated with the luster of jewels and gold, they were adorned with staircases made of precious gems.
And the ponds, filled with blossoming lotuses, became exceedingly beautiful, frequented by flocks of intoxicated peacocks and ever-intoxicated cuckoos.
The mountain, fashioned by Viśvakarman, served as the rampart for that palace;
it was clearly one hundred cubits in height and was encircled by a multitude of moats.
That house of the lion of the Vṛṣṇis was constructed by Viśvakarman;
it resembled the palace of Mahendra and measured half a yojana on all sides.
Then Śauri, standing upon the head of Garuḍa,
joyfully blew that white conch shell, which caused the hair of his enemies to stand on end.
By the sound of that conch, the ocean was violently agitated, and the entire sky resounded; that was truly marvelous at that time.
Upon hearing the roar of the Pāñcajanya conch and seeing Garuḍa, the Kukuras and Andhakas were freed from their grief.
Seeing him standing upon Garuḍa, holding the conch, discus, and mace,
and possessing a splendor equal to the sun, the inhabitants of the earth rejoiced.
Then there arose the sounding of musical instruments and the great roar of kettledrums, along with the lion-like shouts of all the city-dwellers.
Then all the Daśārhas and all the Kukuras and Andhakas,
being filled with joy, gathered together upon beholding Madhusūdana.
Placing Vasudeva at the head, King Ugrasena went to the residence of Vāsudeva amidst the sounds of kettledrums and conch shells.
Anandinī attended to her own quarters, as did Devakī,
Rohiṇī, and the women of Āhuka, each according to their assigned place.
Then Kṛṣṇa, the Lord’s attendant, returned to his own abode on Suparṇa and wandered according to his purpose.
Having descended at the door of the house, Kṛṣṇa, the delight of the Yadus and bull among the Yādavas,
honored the Yādavas according to their rank.
Worshipped by Rāma, Akrūra, Gada, Pradyumna, and others,
Śauri entered his home taking the mountain of jewels with him.
And Pradyumna, the son of Rukmiṇī, caused that great tree, the Pārijāta, beloved of Śakra, to enter his home.
They beheld one another’s superhuman bodily forms upon the earth;
then, by the power of the Pārijāta tree, the people rejoiced.
Being praised by those joyful lords of the Yādavas,
the glorious Govinda entered the palace constructed by Viśvakarman.
Then, within the inner apartments, the immeasurable Acyuta, accompanied by the Vṛṣṇis, established that peak as a mountain of jewels.
And that conqueror of enemies, having honored that divine and most excellent tree, the Pārijāta—
which was itself already honored— placed it in a desired location with composure.
Then Keśava, the slayer of enemy heroes, having given leave to his kinsmen,
honored those women who had been confined by Naraka.
With garments, ornaments, enjoyments, female slaves, and stores of wealth;
with necklaces resembling the rays of the moon, and jewels of great luster.
Those women had previously been honored by Vasudeva with various ornaments, as well as with various divine perfumes.
Together with Vedakī, Rohiṇī, Revatī, and Āhuka.
At that time, Satyabhāmā was the most excellent of women by virtue of her good fortune,
while Rukmiṇī, the daughter of Bhīṣmaka, became the mistress of the household.
The supervisor of all affairs and the most beloved of Keśava,
Kṛṣṇa, assigned to them palaces, the tops of mansions, and abundant household furnishings according to their respective merit.
Satyabhāmā, Viṣṇu’s beloved, always remained by his side in the assembly.

"All the sages are pleased, and the best of the Yadus have been protected.

A man wearing polished earrings, acting as a cākrīka, made this proclamation.
"O King, let the sages practice their various austerities without hindrance;
the wicked Naraka has been slain along with his followers and his army.

Then, his eyes filled with tears and his heart overcome with joy,
the younger brother of Vāsava paid homage to his father along with Rāma.
Then, having approached the remaining ones and honored them as was fitting,
Adhokṣaja took the names of all the Daśārhas.
Then Upendra and the others entered all those foremost seats, which were divine and composed of every kind of jewel.
Then, by the command of Kṛṣṇa, the men brought that inexhaustible wealth which had been collected by the servants into the assembly hall.
Then Janārdana, intending to honor them all, caused the best of the Yadus, the descendants of Daśārha, to pay their respects with the sound of kettledrums.
By the command of Kṛṣṇa, those most worthy of the Daśārhas entered that beautiful residence of the Daśārhas, which was provided with seats and featured gateways of jewels and coral.
Then, O bull of the Bharata race, that assembly hall— surrounded on all sides by the Yadus, those lions among men, and endowed with every excellence and purpose—
shone forth even more brilliantly, like a bright mountain cave filled with lions.
Accompanied by Rāma and preceded by the Vṛṣṇis, Govinda took his place upon a great golden throne, having placed Ugrasena at the forefront.
Having addressed those heroes, the best of the Yadus, who were seated there according to their pleasure and seniority, Madhusūdana spoke to them.
