Vāsudeva said:
"By means of the ascetic power and meditative absorptions of you all, whose fame is meritorious..."
And because of his evil intent, that sinful-souled Bhauma was slain in hell.
The great and well-guarded inner apartment of the maidens has been liberated from its bonds;
having uprooted Mount Maṇi, this very peak has been brought here.
"This vast flood of wealth has been brought by me through my servants;
you are its masters," he said to them, and then he fell silent.
Having heard those words of Vāsudeva, the Bhojas, Vṛṣṇis,
and Andhakas rejoiced with their hair standing on end, honoring Janārdana.
Then those heroes among men, with palms joined in reverence, said to him:
"O mighty-armed son of Devakī, this is not surprising in you."
Having performed deeds difficult to accomplish, which are exceedingly hard even for the gods,
you yourself should cherish your own kin with enjoyments and jewels acquired by your own effort.
Then the wives of all the Daśārhas and of Āhuka, filled with joy, went to the assembly hall out of a desire to see Vāsudeva.
The seven goddesses, with Devakī as the seventh, and the fair-faced Rohiṇī,
beheld Kṛṣṇa seated there, as well as the mighty-armed Rāma.
Having first passed by Rohiṇī and having saluted her,
the two gods, Rāma and Keśava, paid their respects to Devakī.
With those two bull-eyed sons, she shone all the more,
like Aditi, the mother of the gods, with Mitra and Varuṇa.
Then those two foremost of men arrived at her daughter,
whom men indeed call Ekānaṃśā, who is capable of assuming any form at will.
Likewise, by means of the *kṣaṇa* and *muhūrta* [yogas], she gave birth to the Lord;
for his sake, the Supreme Person (Viṣṇu) slew Kaṃsa along with his hosts.
That maiden grew up there in the residence of the Vṛṣṇis,
being honored and protected like a son by the command of Vāsudeva.
Men call that one who was born Ekānaṃśā;
she whom men on earth call Ekānaṃśā when she was born is an invincible yoga-maiden, created for the protection of Keśava.
All the Yādavas honored her with joyful minds,
for by her Kṛṣṇa had been protected like a god with his divine form.
And having approached her there, Mādhava took hold of his beloved friend with the tip of his right hand, as a companion would a dear friend.
In the same way, the exceedingly powerful Sāma embraced his destined daughter,
smelled her head, and took her by the hand with his left hand.
They beheld their beloved sister in the midst of Rāma and Kṛṣṇa,
her hands occupied with golden lotuses, like the goddess Śrī herself whose abode is the lotus.
Then, having scattered unbroken grains, a great rain of flowers, various auspicious blossoms,
and parched grain over her, those women departed as they had come.
Then all those Yādavas, honoring Janārdana,
sat down near him with joy, praising the wonderful deed he had performed.
Being honored, the mighty-armed one of great fame, who increased the joy of the citizens, sported with them as if with the gods.
While all the Yādavas were seated together, Nārada came to the assembly hall to see Janārdana at the command of the Lord of the Thirty-three.
Then, having been honored by those heroic bulls of the Yadu clan, that worshipful one touched Govinda with his hand and sat upon the great throne.
Then the mighty-armed King Āhuka said to the sage:
"O Sage, please recite some portion of a most excellent Purāṇa."
"So be it," said Hari; O King, Nārada then placed the manuscript of the Harivaṃśa upon the auspicious seat and began to read it aloud.
Having quickly risen from his seat and assumed a posture of silence,
Nārada sat comfortably and recited that story in silence.
Then, sitting at ease, he spoke to those Vṛṣṇis who were seated.
"O bulls among men, know that I have come at the command of Śakra."
Listen, O tigers among kings, to the prowess of this Kṛṣṇa—
those deeds which Keśava has performed from his childhood onwards.
The evil-minded Kaṃsa, son of Ugrasena, having oppressed all his kinsmen and having bound his father Āhuka, seized the kingdom.
Relying upon his father-in-law Jarāsaṃdha, that evil-minded defiler of his lineage held all the Bhojas, Vṛṣṇis, and Andhakas in contempt.
Desiring to perform a duty for his kinsmen, the powerful Vasudeva protected his own son for the sake of Ugrasena's safety.
Reared in the house of Nanda Gopa and in the cow-pens,
that righteous-souled Madhusūdana, dwelling in the groves on the outskirts of Mathurā with the cowherds, performed most wonderful deeds.
A great marvel is being heard directly from the Śūrasenas,
how by this one lying down, moving within the interior of a cart—
The fierce Rākṣasī named Pūtanā, who was of terrible body and great strength, wearing the disguise of a bird, has been slain;
that cruel woman offered her poison-smeared breast to the Great-Souled One.
Those forest-dwellers beheld that most terrible Rākṣasī,
the daughter of Bali, who was fearsome and had a deformed face,
lying slain; they said, "He has been born again," and for this reason he is called Adhokṣaja.
And this was most wonderful: that the infant Puruṣottama, while playing, overturned the cart with his big toe.
While eating curd and drinking milk, Govinda, along with his elder brother,
bound by a rope to a mortar for having misbehaved with the young boys,
crushed two trees that were growing there as a result of their truthful conduct.
From him was born the son of Vasudeva, renowned as Dāmodara.
Then he broke two famous *arjuna* trees, and thus he became known as Dāmodara;
furthermore, the great serpent Kāliya, who was difficult to overcome and possessed of great strength,
was defeated by Vāsudeva while he was playing in the pool of the Yamunā.
And in the presence of Akrūra, while being worshipped by the Nāgas in the abode of the serpents, the Lord then assumed a divine form.
Seeing the cows afflicted by cold winds, the wise and high-souled Kṛṣṇa,
the infant Vāsudeva, desiring to protect the cattle, held up Mount Govardhana for seven nights.
Likewise, the exceedingly wicked, extremely powerful, and massive-bodied Ariṣṭaka,
the slayer of men known as Gopati, was slain on earth by Vāsudeva.
That great-bodied Dānava Dhenuka, possessed of immense strength and evil intent, was slain by Vāsudeva for the protection of the cows.
He caused the wolves to scatter with cries, in order to capture Sunāman, the slayer of enemies, who had approached at the head of his entire army.
Furthermore, having united with the son of Rohiṇī as he wandered in the forest,
even while wearing the very dress of a cowherd, he brought fear upon Kaṃsa.
Likewise, having gone to the forest, Śauri, the Supreme Person, slew the horse of the Bhoja king, whose strength lay in his fangs as weapons, by seizing its reins.
And the long-armed and massive-bodied Dānava, the minister of Kaṃsa, was struck down by the wise son of Rohiṇī with a single fist.
For these two high-souled sons of Vasudeva, resembling the sons of the gods, grew up consecrated by Brahmagārgya.
Moreover, from their very birth, these two were recognized for what they truly were by the supreme seer Gārgya and were provided with the appropriate sacraments.
But when these two best of men stand at the threshold of youth,
like two powerful lion cubs, intoxicated like those from the Himalayas.
Then those two heroes of great strength, possessing a splendor equal to the sons of gods, remained wandering in the cow-pen, stealing away the hearts of the gopīs.
Neither in speed, nor in combat, nor in various games were the cowherds of Nanda Gopa able even to look upon these two.
Hearing that these two, broad-chested and mighty-armed, had risen up like the trunks of *śāla* trees,
Kaṃsa became distressed and sat together with his ministers.
When Kaṃsa was unable to seize Balarāma and Keśava,
he then, out of anger, imprisoned Vasudeva along with his kinsmen.
Then, bound tightly like a thief by Ugrasena,
Ānakadundubhi lived for a long time in great hardship.
But Kaṃsa, having imprisoned his father, ruled over the Śūrasenas,
relying upon Jarāsaṃdha as well as Āhṛti and Bhīṣmaka.
Then, after some time had passed, King Kaṃsa organized a great festival in Mathurā dedicated to the wielder of the Pināka bow (Śiva).
There, O lord of the people, wrestlers arrived from various lands,
as well as dancers and singers skilled in the arts of dance and song.
Then the highly energetic Kaṃsa had that magnificent arena constructed by skilled artisans who were thoroughly proficient in their craft.
There, thousands of couches were seen crowded with people from the city and the countryside, like the sky filled with stars.
Then Kaṃsa, the King Bhoja, ascended the magnificent royal dais graced with splendor, like a virtuous man ascending a celestial chariot.
At the entrance to the arena, the powerful Kaṃsa stationed an intoxicated elephant, equipped with abundant weapons and guarded by brave warriors.
For when that great king heard that Rāma and Kṛṣṇa— those tigers among men— had arrived together like the sun and the moon, he was filled with joy.
From that time forward, the lord of men was constantly occupied with providing protection;
he could not sleep peacefully at night, as he brooded over Rāma and Kṛṣṇa.
Having heard of that unsurpassed assembly, both heroes, Rāma and Kṛṣṇa,
entered it like two tigers entering a herd of cattle.
Then, as those two bulls among men were being held back by the guards at the entrance,
the two subduers of enemies slew Kuvalayāpīḍa along with his rider;
having trampled him, those invincible heroes entered the arena.
Having crushed Cāṇūra and Andhra with Keśava and Bala,
that evil-minded son of Ugrasena was struck down along with his younger brothers.
What deed was performed by Keśava, the lion of the Yadus, which is so difficult even for the gods to endure— that what man other than Keśava would be capable of performing such an act?
For that which was not attained previously by Prahlāda, Bali, and Śambara—
this very state of mind has been achieved here by Śauri for you.
By this [bow], having attacked the Daitya Mura as well as Pañcajana,
and having traversed the masses of mountains, Nisunda was slain along with his host.
Naraka, the son of the Earth, has been slain, the two auspicious earrings have been recovered,
and Keśava has attained great glory among the gods in heaven.
Free from sorrow, fear, and affliction, and relying on the strength of Kṛṣṇa’s arms,
let the Yādavas, devoid of envy, perform many sacrifices.
A very great task for the gods has been accomplished by the wise Kṛṣṇa;
I shall report this to you quickly—may prosperity be yours.
"O best of the Yadus, whatever you desire, I shall do without weariness;
I am yours, and you are mine, for I abide within you."
Thus addressing Kṛṣṇa, the subduer of Pāka said:
"The best of the gods has sent me; we, likewise, are pleased and satisfied."
Wherever modesty and prosperity abide, there is humility; wherever there is prosperity, there is humility; likewise, humility, modesty, and prosperity always reside in the Great-Souled Kṛṣṇa.
All haters of Brahman have been slain; O Brāhmaṇas, perform sacrifices always!
Pay homage to Hari; always bow down to Mādhava.
Worship him constantly with sacrifices—he who is honored by the worlds.
May forest-dwellers always be present for you as causes for knowledge.

this wise man married Gāndhārī, his beautiful and beloved queen.

The highly illustrious tiger among men, the crusher of enemies, slew Jambha, Airāvata, Virūpa,

Likewise, having conquered the lord of serpents, the highly powerful Kāliya, in the water,
the lotus-eyed one sent him away to the ocean.
Likewise, having conquered Yama Vaivasvata, Hari, that tiger among men, restored the dead son of Sāndīpani to life.

O King, Janārdana, having slain Naraka, the son of the Earth— who always hated the gods and the brahmins— and having recovered the jeweled earrings from the Daityas, Dānavas, and Rākṣasas;

And great glory was attained by Keśava among the gods in heaven. Thus, the highly illustrious Kṛṣṇa— the all-pervading Lord of all the worlds— is the one who bestows both fear and fearlessness upon the gods, Daityas, and Suras.
Having established the dharmas among mortals, having sacrificed with rites accompanied by abundant sacrificial fees,
and having performed immeasurable service for the sake of the gods, he will attain his own station.
The highly illustrious Kṛṣṇa, having brought the beautiful Bhogavatī, beloved of the sages,
under his own control, shall cause Dvārakā to enter the ocean.
Studded with many jewels and marked by hundreds of shrines and sacrificial posts,
Dvārakā, together with its groves, shall enter the abode of Varuṇa.
The ocean will submerge that [city], which resembles the abode of the sun, released by Vāsudeva at the command of the wielder of the Śārṅga bow.
Among gods, asuras, and humans, there has never been, nor will there ever be,
anyone other than Madhusūdana who could dwell within this [city].
Thus, having performed the ritual for the Daśārhas according to the prescribed rule,
Viṣṇu Nārāyaṇa himself shall become Soma and Sūrya.
Immeasurable and beyond injunction, going wherever he wishes and self-controlled,
he always rejoices with the elements as a child does with toys.

This mighty-armed Madhusūdana cannot be measured; for in this regard, the standard of measurement is severed, as he is the Lord of the gods of gods, who does not become an object of measurement within the scope of all things that can be measured.
For there exists nothing higher nor anything lower than this one who possesses universal form.
In this way, he alone is worthy of praise hundreds and even hundreds of thousands of times;
for the end of his deeds has never before been seen by anyone.
Thus did the lotus-eyed one, accompanied by Saṃkarṣaṇa, perform these deeds as a child and likewise in his middle age.
Thus spoke Vyāsa in former times, the great yogi of vast intellect who perceives all things directly through the eye of his long-cultivated asceticism.
Having thus praised Govinda at the command of Mahendra,
the sage Nārada, honored by all the Yadus, departed for the third heaven.
Then Govinda, the lotus-eyed Madhusūdana, distributed that wealth among the Andhakas and Vṛṣṇis according to their merit and in accordance with the prescribed rites.
Having bowed their heads with deep devotion to the Lord of the World,
and having obtained wealth, those high-souled Yādavas performed sacrifices according to the rules with abundant sacrificial fees, and then dwelt in the city of Dvārakā.
Chapter 98,
Transliterated by Julie Bélanger,
Proofread by André Couture.
Version dated June 26, 2002:
Janamejaya said:
"Among the many thousands of women, eight wives have been proclaimed."
May the Blessed One tell me of the offspring of those eight.
Vaiśampāyana said: Eight principal queens are traditionally remembered as having borne sons; all of them gave birth to heroic offspring. Hear from me about their children.
Rukmiṇī, Satyabhāmā, and Queen Nagnajitī,
as well as Sudattā, Śaibyā, and the sweetly smiling Lakṣmaṇā.
Mitravindā, Kālindī, Jāmbavatī, Pauravī,
Subhīmā, and Mādrī— now hear of these sons of Rukmiṇī.
Pradyumna was the first son born in the sacrifice, the destroyer of Śambara;
the second was Cārudeṣṇa, a lion among the Vṛṣṇis and a great chariot-warrior.
Cārubhadra, Bhadracāru, Sudaṃṣṭra, and Druma;
Suṣeṇa, Cārugupta, Cāruvinda, and Cārumān;
Cārubāhu was the youngest, and the daughter was likewise Cārumatī.
To Satyabhāmā were born Bhānu, Bhīmaratha, Kṣupa,
Rohita, Dīptimat, Tāmrajākṣa, and Jalāntaka;
and from him whose banner bears Garuḍa, four sisters were born to them.
Bhānu, Bhīmarikā, Tāmrapakṣā, and Jalandhamā were born;
and from Jāmbavatī was born a son, Sāmba, who graced the assembly,
as well as Mitrabāhu, Mitradhāman, and likewise Mitrasena.
Mitravān, Mitravinda, and also the woman Mitravatī.
Listen to the offspring of Nagnajitī: Mitravāha and Sunītha;
[and her sons were] Bhadrakāra, Bhadravinda, and likewise the daughter Bhadravatī.
To Sudattā, the daughter of Śibi, was born Saṃgrāmajit,
as well as Satyajit, Senajit, and likewise the heroic Sapatnajit.
Subhīmā’s sons were Mādrya, Vṛkāśva, Vṛkanirvṛti, and the prince Vṛkadīpti; now hear of the offspring of Lakṣmaṇā.
Gātravan, Gātragupta, and the heroic Gātravinda were born;
these Gātravants were born together with their sister's younger brother.
A son named Aśruta was born to Kālindī; he was the most excellent among those of learning.
Madhusūdana gave Aśruta to Śrutasenā.
Having given her away, Hṛṣīkeśa joyfully said to his wife:
"May this son be the heir to both of you for eternal years."
They say that from Bṛhatī, the wife of Gada, was born a son named Śaibya; and from her were born Aṅgada, Kumuda, Śveta, and likewise a daughter named Śvetā.
Agāvaha, Sumitra, Śuci, Citraratha, and Citrasena were his sons;
and his two daughters were Citrā and Citravatī.
From Vanuṣṭamba were born two sons, Stamba and Stambavana;
also Nivāsana, Vanastamba, and a daughter named Stambavatī.
Upāsaṅga, however, had two sons, Vajra and Sukṣipra.
From Kauśikī and Sutasomā, two sons of Yudhiṣṭhira were born to Yudhiṣṭhira: Kāpālī and Garuḍa, both of whom were skilled in diverse modes of combat.
Understand that there were thousands of sons such as these;
indeed, ten thousand are declared to be the sons of Vāsudeva.
Likewise, there were eighty thousand heroes skilled in battle;
this is the lineage of Janārdana as it has been proclaimed.
As for the son of Pradyumna by the princess of Vidarbha, O best of kings—
Aniruddha was born as a warrior in battle; he had a deer for his emblem.
Under the asterism Revatī, two brothers, Niśaṭha and Ulmuka, both resembling gods and being the best among men, were born to Baladeva.
Sutanu and Narācī were the two wives of Śauri;
Pauṇḍra and Kapila were the two sons of Vāsudeva born of them.
Kapila was born of Narā, and Pauṇḍra was the son of Sutanu;
of these two, Pauṇḍra became king while Kapila went to the forest.

Established in meditative absorption, that high-minded king, showing compassion toward all beings and possessing a mind of equanimity, attained union with Viṣṇu. From Vasudeva, that powerful hero was born as Turya.
The lord of all archers among the Niṣādas was named Jarā.
From Kāśyā, Sāmba obtained a swift son named Supārśva.
Aniruddha’s auspicious wife was Rukmavatī, the princess of Vidarbha; from her was born Vajra. Now hear of the son of Vajra.
The thunderbolt of Sānu was Aniruddha’s; however, the thunderbolt originated with Ādi in the beginning.
From Vajra was born Prativāha, and his son was Sucāru;
from Anamitra, the youngest son of the joy of the Vṛṣṇis, Śini was born.
From Śini was born Satyavāk and the great chariot-warrior Satyaka;
from Satyaka was born the heroic Yuyudhāna.
Asaṅga was the son of Yuyudhāna;
his son was Bhūmi, and from Bhūmi came Yugaṃdhara—thus the lineage comes to an end.
Chapter 99. Transliterated by Julie Bélanger, proofread by André Couture, version of June 29.
Janamejaya said:
"This one who was previously described by you as the 'Slayer of Śambara'—"
Tell me how that Pradyumna slew Śambara.
Vaiśampāyana said:
To Rukmiṇī, Vāsudeva, who was firm in his vows and desirous of the goddess Lakṣmī,
was born Pradyumna, the destroyer of Śambara, who appeared like the god of love himself.
When seven nights had passed, at midnight, Kālaśambara carried off from the maternity chamber the infant son of Kṛṣṇa, he who is celebrated in the Purāṇas as Sanatkumāra.
And this was known to Kṛṣṇa, who follows the ways of divine illusion;
therefore, that Dānava, intoxicated by battle, was not restrained.
His life span being encompassed by death, that great asura carried him away by means of his illusory power; lifting him up with both arms, he went to his own city.
He had a wife who was childless, endowed with beauty and virtue,
named Māyāvatī, who in her auspicious appearance was like Māyā herself.
Driven by fate, the Dānava gave that son of Vāsudeva to his queen— who was seeking a protector— just as one would give one's own son.
But Māyāvatī, seeing him, her hair standing on end with joy,
filled with great delight, gazed at him again and again.
Then, as she was looking at him, memory suddenly arose within her: "This is that very lover of mine. Having remembered this, she reflected further.
This is that lord and husband for whose sake I am indeed submerged day and night in a lake of anxiety and grief, finding no pleasure anywhere.
In another birth, I saw this Anaṅga, who had previously been made bodiless by the Lord of Gods, the wielder of the trident, when he was provoked to anger.
Knowing this through my nature as a mother, how shall I give him my breast?
For though I have become a wife to my husband, shall I now say, "He is my son"?
Having reflected thus in her mind, she entrusted him to a nurse and caused him to grow up quickly through the application of elixirs.
Hearing her from the presence of his nurse, that son of Rukmiṇī,
through ignorance, believed Māyāvatī to be his own mother; she then raised that lotus-eyed son of Kṛṣṇa.
And she gave him all her illusory powers, being herself deluded by desire for the Dānava.
When Pradyumna reached his youth, he was like the very embodiment of desire;
he knew the hearts of women and had mastered the application of all weapons.
That passionate Māyāvatī desired her lover;
gazing at him with gestures, she enticed him with a smile.
But as the goddess of lovely smiles was thus falling into [despair], he spoke to her:
"Why do you behave in such a contrary manner, abandoning your maternal nature?"
"Alas! You are of a wicked nature, with a mind made fickle by womanhood, you who, having cast aside the state of being my son, behave toward me out of lust."
"O gentle one, am I not your son? What is this transgression of proper conduct?
Therefore, O Queen, I desire that you explain this; what kind of ritual is this?"
Truly, the nature of women is as fickle as a flash of lightning;
they cling to men just as clouds settle upon the mountain peaks.
O gentle one, whether I am your son or not your own child, O auspicious lady, I wish to know what you have said; what is it that you intend to do?
Thus addressed, that timid woman, her senses distressed by desire,
spoke these words to her beloved, the son of Keśava, in that secluded place.
"O gentle one, you are not my son, nor is Śambara your father.
You are handsome and valiant; by birth, you are a joy of the Vṛṣṇis. You are the son of Vāsudeva and Rukmiṇī, the increaser of their delight."
On the seventh day, as soon as you were born,
O child, you were carried away from the midst of the maternity chamber while still lying on your back as an infant.
O hero, you were carried away by my husband Śambara, who exerts great strength and prowess; having overpowered the great house of your father Vāsudeva,
who is like Indra himself, you were indeed abducted by him.
And that compassionate mother of yours, grieving for you as a child, is exhausted beyond measure,
O hero, like a cow deprived of her calf.
For he, whose banner bears the Garuda, is indeed greater than even Śakra and is your father;
he does not recognize you here, as you were carried away while still a child.
"O beloved, you are a Vṛṣṇi prince; you are certainly not the son of Śambara.
O hero, Dānavas do not indeed give birth to sons such as these."
Therefore I desire you, for you were not begotten by me;
beholding your beauty, O gentle one, I sink down, weak at heart.
O beloved Vārṣṇeya, you ought to keep in mind that which I have resolved and that which dwells within my heart.
O gentle one, I have told you this true state of affairs regarding me:
that you are not my son, nor are you the son of Śambara.
And you are Kāmadeva, O hero; know me indeed to be Rati, O Lord.
Formerly, by the curse of Śaṅkara, you were rendered bodiless.
Having assumed a form through that time-born illusion, I entered the abode of the Daitya;
thus I dwelt for a long time in the house of this Daitya.
Having heard all of this spoken by Māyāvatī, [he understood] everything in its entirety.
The son of Cakrāyudha, filled with rage, challenged Śambara to combat.
The knower of all illusions, valiant and imperishable in battle,
Kālaśambara was slain in combat through illusion on the eighth day.
Having slain that foremost of asuras in the city of Ṛkṣavanta and having taken the goddess Māyāvatī, he returned to his father’s city.
Having ascended into the air and moving swiftly by means of his illusory power,
he arrived at the beautiful city protected by the splendor of his father.
That infant fell from the sky into the inner apartments of Keśava, together with that Māyāvatī; he was as handsome as the god of love himself.
When that had been cast therein, the queens of Keśava were then filled with wonder, joy, and fear.
Then, beholding him— who resembled the God of Love— united with his beloved,
they gazed with joyful faces, drinking in the nectar of his sight with their eyes.
Seeing him with his face cast down in shame, faltering at every step,
the women of Kṛṣṇa’s household became joyful, their hearts filled with affectionate intent.
But Rukmiṇī, seeing him, afflicted with grief and longing for her son,
spoke these words through tears while surrounded by hundreds of co-wives.
Such was the dream I saw when the night had passed into its youth: the enemy of Kaṃsa brought me and gave me a sprout with food.
Having placed upon his lap a beautiful string of pearls resembling the rays of the moon,
Keśava fastened it around my neck.
A dark-complexioned woman with beautiful hair, adorned with white garments and holding a lotus in her hand, entered my house while gazing [at me].
Furthermore, she took me and bathed me with delightful water.
Then, having taken a garland made of lotuses in her hand and having smelled my head, she gave that wreath to me.
Thus recounting her dream with a joyful heart, the queen Rukmiṇī,
surrounded by her circle of female companions, gazed repeatedly at that youth;
immediately thereafter, she spoke these words there.
Truly blessed is this son of hers— long-lived, lovely to behold,
and standing in the first bloom of youth, resembling the very embodiment of desire.
"O son, who is that woman adorned with fortune whose son lives because of you?
And for what purpose, O one dark as a rain cloud, have you come here together with your wife?"
At this age, it is quite evident that my little son Pradyumna would have been [alive],
had he not been carried off by powerful Death.
"Clearly this is the prince of the Vṛṣṇis; my conjecture was not false. You have been recognized by me through your marks as Janārdana, even without the discus."
The face, the hair, and even the hairline of my father-in-law, the wielder of the plow, are just like those of Nārāyaṇa; he is equal to him in head, chest, and arms.
Who are you, standing here illuminating the entire Vṛṣṇi clan with your form?
Oh, you are surely another divine body of this Janārdana!
In the meantime, having heard Nārada’s words regarding the slaying of Śambara, Kṛṣṇa suddenly entered.
With a joyful heart, Janārdana beheld his eldest son, who was perfected by the marks of love, as well as his daughter-in-law Māyāvatī.
He suddenly said to Queen Rukmiṇī, who was like a goddess:
"O Queen, this lordly son of yours, bearing his bow, has arrived."
Having slain Śambara, who was skilled in illusory warfare,
he destroyed all those illusions by which he had oppressed the gods.
Moreover, this virtuous and noble wife of your son is known as Māyāvatī; she lived in the house of Śambara,
so let there be no distress in you because she was his wife.
Long ago,
when Manmatha had met his destruction and attained the state of being bodiless by the fire from the eye of the three-eyed, trident-bearing Śiva in a former age,
this auspicious girl was indeed Rati, the wife of Kāma, who desired her husband.
The auspicious goddess repeatedly deludes that Daitya by means of her illusory form.
And that beautiful woman did not remain under his control during his youth;
having assumed a form consisting of her own illusory power, she entered into Śambara.
"This wife of my son is your daughter-in-law, O beautiful woman;
she will provide spiritual assistance to him who is beloved by the world."
"Lead her into the palace, for she is my daughter-in-law and worthy of honor;
embrace your son who has returned after being lost for a long time."
Vaiśampāyana said:
Having heard those words then uttered by Kṛṣṇa,
Queen Rukmiṇī attained incomparable joy and spoke these words.
"Aha! I am most blessed indeed through this reunion with my heroic son.
Today my desire has borne fruit; today my heart's wish is fulfilled—to behold my long-lost son together with his beloved."
Come, my son, enter the palace together with your wife.
Then, having saluted the feet of Govinda and his mother,
Pradyumna paid homage to the exceedingly powerful Balarāma.
Raising him up, embracing him, and smelling the crown of his head,
the heroic Keśava, slayer of enemy heroes, [honored] Pradyumna, the best among the strong.
And having raised up her daughter-in-law, Queen Rukmiṇī, who was adorned with golden ornaments,
embraced and clasped her with affection, her voice faltering with emotion.
Just as Aditi brought Indra together with his wife Śacī to her own abode,
so then did Rukmiṇī cause her son, who had arrived, to enter.
Thus addressed by Kṛṣṇa, Rukmiṇī, the best among women, [acted accordingly].
Having embraced her son with affection and smelled the head of her daughter-in-law,
the beautiful woman caused him to enter the house along with his wife.
Chapter 100, transliterated by Julie Bélanger, proof-read by André Couture, version of July 7.
Vaiśampāyana said:
At the very same time that Pradyumna was abducted by Śambara, who intended to kill him,
Sāmba was born of Jāmbavatī.
From his childhood, he was appointed to positions of honor by Rāma,
and after Rāma, he was likewise honored by all the Vṛṣṇis.
He became the beloved eldest son of Rāma alone;
as soon as he was born, O Kṛṣṇa, that city was filled with auspiciousness, and having struck down his enemies and vassals, he entered it like an immortal entering the garden of Indra.
Having seen the splendor of the Yādavas, Indra despised his own splendor;
and out of fear of Janārdana, the kings found no peace.
Then, after some time, all the kings assembled at the sacrifice of Duryodhana in the city named Vāraṇasāhvaya.
Having heard that Mādhavī Lakṣmī, Janārdana together with his sons,
and the city of Dvārāvatī itself were established within the ocean;
Having established alliances through those messengers, all the kings on earth came to Kṛṣṇa’s palace to behold the splendor of Hṛṣīkeśa.
All those headed by Duryodhana, who were obedient to the will of Dhṛtarāṣṭra,
as well as the kings headed by the Pāṇḍavas, beginning with Dhṛṣṭadyumna.
The lords of Pāṇḍya, Cola, and Kaliṅga, the Bāhlīkas, Draviḍas, and Śakas—
these eighteen kings, leading their akṣauhiṇī divisions,
arrived at the city of the Yādavas, which was protected by the arms of Govinda.
Then those lords of the earth, having surrounded Mount Raivataka,
entered their respective territories, each extending for many yojanas.
Commanded by messengers, the Lord, preceded by Balabhadra and accompanied by his army and followers, placed Sātyaki at the head.
Taking up his Śārṅga bow and reflecting, "What might happen?",
the illustrious Hṛṣīkeśa, whose eyes are like lotuses, then went forth from the foremost of the Yādavas into the presence of the lords of men.
In the midst of those lords of men, that slayer of Madhu,
the best of the Yadus, shone like the moon in the sky during the autumn.
Having conducted himself there according to rank and age,
Kṛṣṇa sat down upon a golden throne.
Then the kings, the lords of men, sat down in their respective places upon various colorful thrones and seats.
Then that assembly of the lords of the Yādavas shone like the gathering of gods and asuras in the abode of Brahmā.
The Blessed One spoke this to the Kṣatriyas who had come to see him:
"O kings, all of this has been declared to you."
"O best of kings, whatever is ours is always equal to yours;
O most excellent of monarchs, please accept whatever divine wealth you desire."
"So be it," they said to the Lord of the World in the assembly of the Yādavas; and there,
in that gathering, various conversations proceeded among those Yādavas and kings while Keśava listened.
Upon seeing the Lord of the Gods of gods, the Kṣatriyas were then filled with joy.
In that interval, a wind blew, raised by the roar of clouds;
there was a tumultuous storm, accompanied by lightning and thunder.
Then, having pierced through that mass of storm clouds, Nārada appeared,
his mass of matted locks coiled about him and one arm resting upon his lute.
Singing a *sāman* to Hari while He resided in the assembly of the Yadus,
the illustrious sage Nārada— the friend of Śakra— fell into the midst of the kings who possessed the splendor of fire; he was like a crest of flame.
When that bull among sages, Nārada, had fallen to the ground,
that foul day with its towering great clouds was withdrawn.
Having plunged into the midst of the lords of men, which was like the ocean,
the imperishable sage spoke to the best of the Yadus as he sat upon his throne.
It is truly a marvel that you alone among the gods are the Supreme Person;
O mighty-armed one, you are blessed, for there is no one else like you in the world.
Thus addressed, the Lord smiled and replied to the sage:
"I am indeed both wonderful and blessed, along with these sacrificial gifts."
Thus addressed, the best of sages spoke in the midst of the kings:
"O Kṛṣṇa, my words have been sufficient; I shall go back as I came."
Seeing him set out, the kings, unaware of the secret counsel spoken by Nārada, addressed the lord.
When Nārada had replied, "O Mādhava, you are blessed; this is indeed wonderful," and added, "along with sacrificial fees," [Nārada continued]:
Why is this? We do not recognize this great, divine mantra-word.
If it may be heard, O Kṛṣṇa, I wish to hear it according to its true meaning.
Then Kṛṣṇa said to all those bulls among kings:
"This twice-born Nārada must be listened to; he will narrate it to you."
"Speak the true meaning, O Nārada; let the rulers of the earth hear that which was spoken by you and that which has been replied by me."
Seated comfortably upon a bright golden throne and well-adorned,
he began to speak of the source of those words.
Listen, O best of kings, all of you who have assembled here,
to how I have reached the further shore of this great question.
Once, at the end of the night when the sun was becoming visible, I was wandering alone on the bank of the Gaṅgā, having performed my three daily ablutions and attended to my guests.
I saw a being with a body composed of two skull-halves, resembling a mass of stone,
extending for a *krośa* in circumference and as wide all around.
A tortoise with four legs clinging together, wet and mired in moss,
shaped like my lute, and resembling a layer of elephant hide.
Having touched him with my hand, I said to that water-dweller:
"O tortoise, you possess a wondrous body; in my opinion, you are blessed."
Since you, thus enclosed by these two impenetrable skull-halves, move through the water without fear, reflecting upon nothing at all;
That water-dwelling tortoise spoke to me himself in human fashion:
"O sage, what is so wonderful about me? And how am I blessed, O Lord?"
Blessed is this river Gaṅgā; what wonder could be greater than this, that here tens of thousands of beings move about in the water just as I do?
Thus, filled with curiosity, I approached the river Gaṅgā and said:
"O best of rivers, you are blessed, for you constantly display wonders."
You, who are thus adorned by great-bodied beasts of prey,
proceed toward the ocean as a river, protecting the dwellings of the ascetics.
Thus addressed, Gaṅgā then appeared in bodily form and replied to Nārada,
the celestial Gandharva and beloved twice-born friend of Śakra.
"O best of the twice-born, I am neither blessed nor graced by wonders;
yet your words, directed toward me, obstruct you as you are firmly established in truth."
O twice-born one, the ocean is a source of wonder to the world and truly blessed,
for into it flow hundreds of rivers as vast as I am.
Having heard the words of the triple-pathed river, I approached the ocean:
"O great ocean, you are indeed a marvel to the worlds and blessed;
for you are truly the source of all waters and the lord of the liquid realm."
It is fitting that these world-sustaining rivers, who carry the waters and are honored by the worlds, approach you as your wives.
Thus addressed, the ocean, impelled by the wind, rose up, having pierced through the depths of its own mass of water, and then spoke these words to me.
"Do not say so, O celestial Gandharva; I am no marvel, O best of the twice-born.
Blessed is this earth, O sage, upon which I stand.
Apart from the earth itself, what greater marvel could there be in the world?"
Thus, at Sāgara’s word, I stood upon the surface of the earth and,
filled with curiosity, spoke to the one who knows the course of the world.
O auspicious Earth, you are indeed blessed, for you are the source of embodied beings;
you are a marvel among all creatures, endowed as you are with great forbearance.
By you indeed was the earth, the supporter of the worlds and the source of mankind, sustained;
from you was patience born, as well as the movement through the sky of those who travel by means of their deeds.
Then, abashed by those words of praise spoken by me,
she abandoned her natural composure and addressed me in reply.
O Deva-gandharva, do not speak thus, you who delight in the clamor of battle!
I am neither blessed nor marvelous; this fortitude of mine belongs to another.
These blessed mountains, O best of the twice-born, support me;
in them wonders are seen, for they are the embankments of the world.
Thus, at the word of the Earth, I approached the mountains;
these blessed mountain ranges appear most wonderful and full of many marvels.
Because of gold, the foremost of jewels, and especially because of the mineral ores,
all you jewel-mines exist eternally upon the earth.
But having heard these words of mine, the mountains— the best among those that stand firm and adorned with forests— spoke words full of consolation to me.
"O Brahman-sage, we are neither fortunate nor do we possess wonders.
Our lord is the trident-bearing Giriśa, whose banner is the bull;
there is nothing on earth more wonderful or more fortunate than he."
Having abandoned that Mahādeva, you ought not to praise us here.
Having heard these words of theirs, I came to Kailāsa;
and having seen that Lord of Pārvatī, I then spoke these words.
O God of gods, Mahādeva, Blue-throated One, Bull-bannered One!
You alone are a marvel; you are blessed, O Lord of the world.
There is no deity whatsoever in the universe superior to you.
O God, O Destroyer of Tripura, you alone are the support of this entire world that is seen, including all things mobile and immobile.
Then the three-eyed god Virūpākṣa said to me:
"I am neither blessed nor am I a marvel; you ought not to speak to me in this way. O best of the twice-born, the Creator of the world is to be known as superior even to me."
Brahmā, the Lord of Creatures, is blessed and he is a marvel even among the gods.
Therefore, having approached my grandfather, the source of all and the imperishable,
I perceive that his statement was indeed sufficient as an explanation.
Thus, having approached the self-existent God, the four-faced source of the world, through traditional succession, I bowed with my face bent low in salutation.
Therefore, for the sake of concluding my speech, I cause the Self-born One to hear:

How was that Bāṇa, who was worshipped by the Daityas possessing hundreds of powers of illusion and by the immortals and others,
defeated in battle by Vāsudeva? And how was he, being enraged and seeking single combat, released alive?
Vaiśampāyana said: Listen attentively, O King, to how the great conflict with Bāṇa occurred in the world of men involving Kṛṣṇa of immeasurable splendor.
There, Vāsudeva, having conquered that son of Bali— who was accompanied by Rudra and Skanda and who boasted of his prowess in battle— released him alive.
And just as a boon was granted to him by the high-souled Śaṅkara— namely,
his eternal presence and his imperishable status as a leader of the Gaṇas.
Just as that battle of Bāṇa took place, and how he was released alive,
and how that asura attained the status of being the son of the God of gods.
And hear all of that in its entirety for which this great battle was fought.
Having seen the body of the high-souled prince as he played,
the son of Bali, possessed of great heroism, was struck with supreme wonder.
The thought arose in him to perform most severe austerity for the sake of propitiating Rudra, so that he might become his son.
Then that best of asuras emaciated himself through asceticism,
and the god, together with Umā, attained supreme satisfaction.
Nīlakaṇṭha, having attained supreme delight, spoke to the Asura:
"Choose a boon—blessings be upon you—whatever dwells in your mind."
Then Bāṇa spoke these words to the eternal God of gods:
"O Three-eyed One, I desire to be granted by you the status of being the son of the Goddess."
And Śaṅkara, having said "So be it," spoke thus to Rudrāṇī:
"Let this younger son of Kārttikeya be accepted."
In that city of Rudhira, where Mahāsena was born from fire, there shall be his city; of this there is no doubt.
That supreme city shall be known by the name Śoṇitapura;
protected by me, it will be glorious, and no one at all shall be able to overcome it.
Then, dwelling in the city named Śoṇitapura,
Bāṇa ruled his divine kingdom, agitating all the gods.
Then Bāṇa, possessing a thousand arms and intoxicated with the pride of his prowess,
disregarded the hosts of gods and constantly longed for battle.
Being pleased, Kumāra gave him a banner possessing the brilliance of fire,
and he also gave Bāṇa a peacock as his vehicle, blazing with splendor.
Neither the gods, nor the gandharvas, nor the yakṣas,
nor the pannagas could stand before him in battle, due to the splendor of that god of gods.
Protected by Tryambaka, that great asura, arrogant with pride,
again sought a battle and approached the wielder of the trident;
having propitiated Śaṅkara, the Lord of the World, who has the bull as his vehicle.
He holds a trident, his limbs are smeared with ashes, and he is ever devoted to dwelling in the mountains.
He constantly praised the god Īśāna— the matted-haired one, the shaven-headed one, the three-eyed one, the refuge of the Mountain’s Daughter, the most excellent, the granter of boons, and Śiva.

O Bāṇa, salutations to you whose limbs are smeared with ashes; salutations again and again to you who bear the trident. Salutations to the one of diverse forms, and to the one who delights in the cremation grounds.
Salutations again and again to Hara, to Śaṅkara who has the form of Hari;
salutations to you, O Virūpākṣa, who are clothed in a tiger skin.
Homage to the god with the protruding snout, to the naked one, and to the formidable one;
homage to you, the bestower of knowledge, the yogi of restrained mind.
Salutation to the primordial seed, to the bull, to him who has the form of a bull;
salutation to the terrible one, to the most terrible, and salutation to you, the most terrible of the terrible.
Salutations to the one dear to the terrible, to the terrible one, to Rudra, and to the bull; to the one with bull-like shoulders, to the unerring, and to the wielder of the mace and the sword.
Salutations to you who are shaven-headed and deformed, and to Vāmadeva;
salutations to the destroyer of Dakṣa’s sacrifice and to the one who took away Bhaga’s eyes.
Homage to the destroyer of Smara, the father of Guha; salutations again and again!
Homage to you, homage to you, who are clothed in a leopard skin!
Homage, homage to you, O Paśupati, the self of all, the creator of all beings!
O Lord of the World, may my heart’s desire be fulfilled through your grace.
Thus praised, the Lord of the World— the trident-bearer whose banner is the bull—
[said], "Grant me a thousand arms and invincibility even against the gods.
Then, having approached Rudra, prostrated himself, and offered salutations, [he made his request].
The son of Bali addressed these words to the bull-bannered god.
"Many times the gods, along with the Sādhyas and the hosts of Maruts, were utterly defeated by me and my army through the arrogance of my pride in strength— yet all because of your protection."
Having come to this region, they lived happily in the city;
terrified of defeat and despairing of my victory,
they ascended to the surface of heaven and dwell there at their ease.
Thus, hopeless of victory in battle, I do not desire life today;
for it is in vain that I bear these arms of mine without fighting them.
Therefore, tell me: will there perhaps be the arrival of battle?
O Lord, I have no pleasure without battle; be gracious to me.
Then, smiling, the Blessed One whose banner is the bull said:
"O Bāṇa, there shall be a battle for you; listen to how that will be, O Dānava."
O dear one, when the breaking of this banner occurs while it is stationed in its proper place, then the battle shall take place.
Having been addressed in this way, Bāṇa, laughing with great joy and with a serene countenance, fell at his feet and said:
By good fortune, the bearing of my thousand arms has not been in vain;
by good fortune, I shall again be the conqueror of the Thousand-Eyed One in combat.
With eyes filled with tears born of joy, the crusher of enemies prostrated himself upon the ground, worshipping the god with five hundred añjali-gestures.
Maheśvara said:
"Arise, arise, O hero! You shall obtain a battle in the field that is worthy of your arms, of yourself, and of your own lineage—an incomparable combat."
Having been addressed thus by the high-souled Tryambaka,
Bāṇa then rose up quickly with joy and bowed to the one who has the bull as his emblem.
The arrow released by Śitikaṇṭha, the conqueror of enemy cities,
went to his own abode, where the great banner-house stood.
Seated there, he spoke these words to Kumbhāṇḍa with a smile:
"I shall announce something pleasing that accords with your mind."
"O Kumbhāṇḍa, listen to my words as to why I have arrived here.
When he had spoken thus, [Kumbhāṇḍa], laughing, said to Bāṇa, who was peerless in battle:
"O King, what is this that you wish to say so pleasing to me?"
O best of beings, his eyes were wide open with wonder, as if from great joy.
I wish to hear from you what boon you have obtained through the grace of the God of gods and the high-souled Skanda;
O great asura, tell me what desired object you have attained.
Through the grace of Śitikaṇṭha and by the protection of Skanda,
has the sovereignty over the three worlds been ordained for you by the wielder of the trident?
Will Indra, out of fear of you, descend to the netherworld?
Will the sons of Diti be liberated from their terror of Viṣṇu?
Will the asuras, terrified by the fear of him who dwells in the ocean and holds the Śārṅga bow and mace in hand, not flee in all directions out of dread of Viṣṇu as he stands in the supreme battle?
Having abandoned their residence in the netherworld, will the great asuras, by relying on your strength, come to delight in the abodes of the gods?
O King, your father Bali has been bound, overcome by the power of Viṣṇu;
having emerged from the flood of waters, will he regain his kingdom?
Wearing divine garlands and garments, and adorned with celestial wreaths and unguents—
O dear one, shall we behold your father, the son of Virocana?
O Lord, having conquered all the inhabitants of heaven, shall we by these same means restore these worlds that were previously seized?
With its smooth and deep resonance, preceded by the sound of conchs,
will we indeed conquer the god Nārāyaṇa, the victor in battle?
I hope, my dear son, that the bull-bannered god is well-disposed toward you with favor,
since this trembling of your heart occurs along with falling drops of tears.
I trust that, through the gratification of the Lord and by the counsel of Kārttikeya,
you have attained the status of king over us all.
Thus urged by the words of Kumbhāṇḍa, Bāṇa, that bull among men and best of speakers, spoke these unhesitating words.
While T1.2 G M insert:
"Then, although the minister was possessed of statesmanship, that misconduct [prevailed]. O Kumbhāṇḍa, for a long time now I have not encountered battle."
Then, with joy, I questioned the powerful Śitikaṇṭha.
Then I prostrated myself with my head before the wise God of gods.
"O Lord, a very great desire for battle has arisen within me;
shall I indeed obtain a fight that will bring satisfaction to my mind?"
O King, having been informed by me, the bull-bannered god spoke to me;
then, O Lord of Gods, Hara, the slayer of enemies,
smiling for a very long time, spoke these pleasant words today.
"You shall encounter a truly great battle, O Bāṇa, one that is peerless and vast;
when it occurs, O Asura, there shall be the breaking of your peacock-banner."
Then you shall obtain a most great battle, O son of Diti;
thereafter, being exceedingly delighted, I bowed my head to the Blessed Lord whose emblem is the bull, the God, and approached your presence.
Thus addressed, Kumbhāṇḍa then spoke to the king:
"Alas, O King, it is not auspicious that you speak such words!"
Even as they were thus conversing with one another,
their raised banner fell down with force, struck by Śakra’s thunderbolt.
Seeing that excellent banner fallen in such a manner, the asura attained incomparable joy and considered the battle to have arrived.
Then the earth trembled, struck as if by Indra’s thunderbolt;
the cat, hidden beneath the ground, hissed and roared.
Vāsava, who is the god even of the gods, also rained blood from all sides upon the city of Śoṇitapura from close at hand.
A great meteor, having pierced the sun, fell upon the surface of the earth;
and the sun, impelled by its own destiny, afflicted the constellation Bharaṇī.
From the sacred trees of the caityas, hundreds of thousands of terrible streams of blood suddenly flowed forth, and fierce meteors fell in great abundance.
O lord of the people, Rāhu swallowed the sun out of season, and at that time which portended the destruction of the world, a great atmospheric thunder occurred.
Taking his stand in the southern direction, the comet remained fixed there;
and most dreadful winds blew incessantly and without interruption.
White at its edges, red, with a black neck and the brilliance of lightning,
that three-colored iron bar of the sun then veiled the glow of twilight.
The terrifying Mars moved in a crooked course through the Kṛttikās,
as if threatening Bāṇa’s birth star from every side.
And the shrine with its many branches,
which had been worshipped by all the daughters of the high-souled Dānavas, fell to the surface of the earth.
Thus, observing various forms and signs,
Bāṇa, intoxicated by the pride of his strength, could not arrive at a certain conclusion.
But the wise Kumbhāṇḍa, who perceives the truth,
became distraught there as Bāṇa’s minister, recounting his many misdeeds.
For portents are seen here that announce what is not auspicious;
they will undoubtedly lead to the destruction of your kingdom.
O King, we, as well as our other ministers, servants, and those who follow you,
will all before long go to destruction because of your wicked policy.
Just as the fall of the tree that is Śakra’s banner occurs through its own pride,
so too was the fall of the roaring Bāṇa brought about by his delusion in desiring battle.

Having attained victory over the three worlds through the grace of the God of gods, Bāṇa—desiring battle—roared aloud; yet, due to his arrogance, his destruction was seen approaching. With a joyful mind, he drank the most excellent liquor.
Possessed of supreme valor, he was together with the women of the Daityas and Dānavas.
Then Kumbhāṇḍa, overcome with anxiety, approached the royal palace;
and by means of those various omens he beheld, he reflected upon the true significance of the matter.
The king is negligent, evil-minded, and intoxicated by victory; this great asura desires only battle and, due to his arrogance, does not perceive his own faults.
And this fear of a great portent shall not prove false;
otherwise, even now, every appearance of a portent would be false.
But here dwells the three-eyed Lord and the heroic Kārttikeya;
therefore, even if a fault has arisen among us, will it perhaps meet with defeat?
This great destruction arising from the emergence of faults will come to pass;
it is my firm conviction that there shall be no end to these faults.
This will certainly be a fault, there is no doubt;
for due to the wickedness of this king, the Dānavas have indeed become his source of trouble.
He who is the creator of the hosts of gods and demons and the lord of the worlds—
that Bhava and Kārttikeya have indeed made their dwelling in our city.
Guha was always dearer to Bhava than his own life, and Bāṇa, being even more distinguished than him, was likewise constantly beloved by Bhava.
Out of arrogance and pride, however, that greedy one requested a boon from Bhava for the sake of battle, saying,
"He shall not exist in any way whatsoever."
If the gods, headed by Viṣṇu and led by Indra,
were to obtain freedom from fear, it would mean that they have been delivered from the hand of Bhava;
for who here could possibly engage in battle with these two, Kumāra and Bhava?
He was capable of granting [their request] when they had come together, desiring Bāṇa's assistance.
"The word of the gods shall not prove false in any way;
there will be a great war that brings about the destruction of all the Daityas.
Thus did Kumbhāṇḍa, the seer of truth, become absorbed in thought.
That great asura formed a resolution directed toward his own welfare.
For those who oppose in battle the gods who perform meritorious deeds go to their destruction, just as Bali was bound.
Chapter 107,
Transliterated by Julie Bélanger,
Proofread by André Couture.
Version of August 2nd:
Vaiśampāyana said: Once, Bhava became engaged in playful recreation.
That lord was with the goddess on the delightful and glorious bank of the river.
There, hundreds of apsarases sported on all sides,
as did the lords of the gandharvas in that delightful grove containing the trees of every season.
With the flowers of the pārijāta and the blossoms of the saṃtānaka,
the sky and the entire riverbank were made as if overflowing with fragrance.
Then, as thousands of flutes, lutes, drums,
and cymbals were being played, he heard the singing of the apsarases.
And hosts of Apsarases praised the God of gods, who possessed a beautiful form, wore garlands, and was clad in red garments, with the compositions of Sūtas and Māgadhas.
The enchanting women delighted Hara, the bestower of boons, who was accompanied by Umā. Then the excellent Apsaras Vikralekhā, with her beauty,
sought to propitiate Bhava, and the goddess laughed at that time.
The divine attendants of Bhava, of various forms and great prowess, laughed as the Apsaras and goddesses gladdened the Lord.
For by the command of the Goddess, they all indeed sport here and there.
Then those attendants, highly learned in that secret doctrine,
assuming forms marked by the appearance of Mahādeva,
danced as lords of beings, accompanied by various dramatic gestures.
Then, because of the goddess’s beauty, her grace, and her countenance,
the goddess let out a laugh, as did those very apsarases at that time.
Then a cry of "kili-kila" arose on all sides,
and Bhava, with a joyful mind, experienced incomparable delight.
There, Bāṇa’s daughter, a beautiful maiden named Uṣā,
saw the god sporting with his consort as they had gone to the river.
Then, desiring to please the Goddess, Uṣā formed a body of various forms— shining Mahādeva with the splendor of the twelve Ādityas—
and made a mental resolve in the presence of Pārvatī.
Blessed indeed are those who, united with their husbands, thus enjoy themselves in this way.
Then, having understood through her mind that resolve which Uṣā had spoken, the daughter of the Mountain,
the goddess, spoke these words slowly to Uṣā, gladdening her.
O Uṣā, you too shall soon sport with your husband in this very way,
just as the god Śaṅkara, the destroyer of enemies, sports with me.
When these words had been spoken by the goddess, Uṣā, her eyes clouded with anxiety, formed a thought in her heart: "When shall I rejoice together with my husband?"
Then Haimavatī, smiling, spoke these words:
"O Uṣā, listen, O auspicious one, to what will happen when you enter into union."
On the twelfth day of the month of Vaiśākha, at the end of the day, he who shall violate you while you are staying in your palace during a dream will become your husband.
Thus addressed, the daughter of the Daitya, surrounded by a multitude of maidens,
departed with joy, sporting as she pleased.
Then, laughing with her friends and her eyes wide with joy, she and they,
full of vigor, struck one another with the clapping of their hands.
Kinnarīs, yakṣa maidens, daughters of the lords of the nāgas and daityas,
and daughters of the hosts of apsaras became friends of Uṣā.
And there they said to her, "O fair-faced one, your husband shall be found in no time at all, as ordained by the word of the Goddess."
For the word of the goddess shall never be false;
she has envisioned a husband endowed with beauty and noble birth.
Uṣā, having duly honored those words of her companions and contemplating the fulfillment of her heart's desire granted by the goddess, remained there; then,
having enjoyed that pleasure-garden together with Umā, she stayed on.

The blessed Lord, the destroyer of Tripura, went to his own city; the God of gods, the Lord of the world, Hara, then ceased [his dance]. When the day had passed, all those wonderful women went forth once more.

They all went to their own abodes, and the Goddess herself vanished from sight; some entered the city on horses, others on vehicles, elephants, or chariots, while some, remaining in the sky, entered joyfully.
Then, in the month of Vaiśākha, on the twelfth day of the bright fortnight, that beautiful woman was lying on the palace roof, surrounded by her circle of female companions.
Just as described, the man, urged by the words of the goddess, assailed Uṣā while she was writhing and weeping in her sleep.
Violated by him in a dream and having assumed a female form,
she rose up suddenly in the night, weeping and smeared with blood.
Seeing her thus weeping and filled with fear, her friend Citralekhā spoke these very wonderful and affectionate words.
"O Uṣā, do not fear; why are you weeping and grieving so?
You are the daughter of Bali's son and are renowned; why are you filled with fear?"
No fear exists for you in this world, O fair-browed one, especially not from your father Devāntaka, who is a source of terror to others in battle, O lovely-thighed one.
Arise, arise; may it be well with you. Do not despair, O auspicious one.
In dwellings such as these, O lovely-faced one, there is no cause for fear.
More than once, the lord of the gods, the husband of Śacī, accompanied by the deities,
was crushed in battle by your father before he could even reach the city;
this father of yours was a source of terror to the host of gods in combat.
O beautiful lady, that Airāvata was crushed by his mace;
the glorious son of Bali, the great and powerful chief of the Asuras, along with the gods and the wielder of the thunderbolt, became hopeless of life.
Thus addressed by her friend, the illustrious and blameless daughter of Bāṇa reported the form she had seen in her dream;
Uṣā said:
Thus defiled, how can that virtuous woman venture to live?
What indeed shall I say to my father, the subduer of enemies and foe of the gods?
Thus, as one who brings such ruin to this lineage of great majesty, I consider death to be better; life is no longer good for me today.
Or perhaps some desired man has been found by me;
for as if I were awake, this state has been brought upon me—
by whom have I, while awake during the night, been led to this condition?
How indeed could a maiden treated thus wish to live—
she who brings reproach upon her family, a coal of ruin to her kin, and left without refuge?
How could a woman standing before these virtuous ladies desire to live?
Thus, with her eyes filled with tears and surrounded by her circle of friends,
the lotus-eyed Uṣā lamented for a long time.
Seeing Uṣā weeping in her state of helplessness, all her friends gathered together, their eyes overflowing with tears and their minds distraught, spoke to her.
O Goddess, O fair-browed one, whether good or evil is performed with a wicked mind, it does not belong to you; is your mind not indeed wicked?

"O Goddess, O beautiful lady, if you have been enjoyed through forceful union, O auspicious one, there is no violation of the vow due to that occurrence in a dream. O Goddess, there is no transgression whatsoever on your part through such deviation."
"O beautiful one, no fault incurred in a dream exists in the world of mortals;
thus, O Goddess, the brahmin-sages who know the dharma truly declare.
[This applies] especially to those [acts] performed through mind, speech, and deed."
But she who is corrupted by these three is declared on earth to be a wicked woman.
O timid one, your mind is never corrupted;
how then can you, who are indeed free from fault, be constrained as a celibate student?
If that virtuous, pure-minded, and wise woman was brought to this state while she was asleep,
then dharma is not violated at all.
"She whose mind was previously corrupt and who has been brought to such a state by her own actions—her they call 'unfaithful' (asatī); but you, O beautiful lady, are truly faithful (satī)."
Born of noble lineage, endowed with beauty, and steadfast in the practice of celibacy—you have been brought to this state; for time is indeed difficult to overcome.
When she had spoken thus, weeping with eyes covered by tears,
the daughter of Kumbhāṇḍa addressed these supreme words to her.

Abandon your grief, O large-eyed one; you are sinless, O fair-faced lady. Listen to this speech which I have remembered exactly as it was spoken by the goddess to you, O Uṣā, when you were then meditating upon your husband.
O beautiful woman, remember those words of the God of gods in our presence.
On the twelfth day of the bright fortnight in the month of Vaiśākha, he who shall, at night, lead a woman lying on a palace roof and weeping back to her female state—
"He shall indeed become your husband, a hero who destroys his enemies"—
thus did the goddess, being delighted, speak that which was in your mind.
The word spoken by Pārvatī is certainly not false;
why then do you weep so excessively, O moon-faced one? What is this reality [behind your tears]?
Having been addressed with these words, and then remembering the speech of the goddess,
that fair-eyed daughter of Bāṇa became free from grief.
Having remembered the words of the goddess, she then replied to her friend;
Uṣā said:
"O beautiful lady, I remember the words of the goddess when Bhava was engaged in play."
Everything exactly as described has been obtained by me in its entirety upon the palace roof.
"If this man is indeed my husband as designated by the wife of the Lord of the World, how is he to be recognized? Let the necessary action be taken in that regard."
When these words had been spoken, the daughter of Kumbhāṇḍa,
who was skilled in the true nature of meaning, spoke again in accordance with what was right.
For no one truly knows his lineage, O Queen, nor his fame, nor even his prowess; why then are you so distressed?
O sinless one, how can that thief of pleasure— who was neither seen nor heard of before, yet was seen by you in a dream— be identified by us, O timid lady?
O friend with dark-cornered eyes, O intoxicated one, it was by him that you were forcibly entered into the inner apartments and enjoyed while weeping, through his prowess.
For this is no ordinary man who has entered our city by force—
renowned throughout the world— alone, as a destroyer of his enemies.
The Ādityas, Vasus, Rudras, and the two Aśvins of great majesty—
though they possess terrifying prowess— were not able to enter Śoṇitapura.
While Bāṇa was ruling the city after having conquered Śakra, the lord of Śacī,
this very slayer of enemies— hundredfold more distinguished than him—
has entered Śoṇitapura, having stepped upon Bāṇa’s head.
O Goddess, what man in this world who desires life would, while that great Asura rules this city, enter it with a mind set on living,
disregarding Bāṇa or even his assault?
O fair-eyed one, what purpose would there be in life or in enjoyments for her who has no such husband as this, skilled in battle?
"Blessed are you, O Mattakāśinī, favored by fortune, for such a husband as this has been obtained by you through the grace of the goddess Pārvatī."
But hear now this most important task to be done by you as told by me:
you must learn who his son is, what his name is, and what his lineage is.
When these words had been spoken, Uṣā there, deluded by passion,
pierced by his arrows, with wandering eyes and distressed,
fell into a final state, utterly infatuated by the pleasure of sleep.
He said to the daughter of Kumbhāṇḍa, "How shall we know, my friend?"
"Consider this yourself, friend; no answer occurs to me. The world is bewildered regarding its own affairs, just as I am bewildered about how I might regain my life."
Having heard Uṣā’s words, Rāmā, the daughter of Kubhāṇḍa, spoke these words again to her weeping friend.
"O large-eyed one, you are skilled in every way in matters of peace and war;
O friend, let the Apsaras Citralekhā be informed at once."
The entire three worlds are always known by her in their entirety, without exception.
Having been addressed thus, Uṣā was immediately filled with wonder by her joy;
she summoned her dear friend, the Apsaras Citralekhā,
and with palms joined in reverence, spoke these words in a piteous voice.
Having heard those words spoken by Uṣā,
she consoled her illustrious friend, the daughter of Bāṇa;
then, overcome with anxiety, she spoke these difficult words.
Out of affection, that female friend [addressed] her friend, the Apsaras Citralekhā.
Listen to my supreme words, O beautiful lady, which I shall speak to you:
if you do not bring back my beloved husband to me today, [the consequences will follow].
O lotus-eyed one, I shall renounce my dear life for the sake of that beloved one with eyes like lotus petals and the gait of an elephant in rut.
Vikralekhā, smiling softly, spoke these words to Uṣā:
"O beautiful one of noble vows, this matter cannot be understood by us."
"O friend, that thief was not recognized by me through his lineage, nor his caste, nor his conduct, nor his appearance, nor even by his location; however,
O friend, this task can indeed be accomplished by me through the use of my intelligence."
Listen to my words so that you may obtain that desire.
She gently gladdens the dawn,
according to what is possible for us among the gods, dānavas, yakṣas, gandharvas, uragas, and rākṣasas.
Those who are distinguished by their power, their appearance, and their noble lineage.
"O friend, I shall paint all of them according to their importance—
those who are preeminent in the world of men and renowned throughout the world."
"In seven nights, O timid one, I shall show them to you;
then, having recognized your husband upon the cloth, you will recover him."
"If I do not show him, my friend, then I shall enter the fire. Thus addressed by Citralekhā, who desired to accomplish her purpose,
Uṣā said to her dear friend Citralekhā, "Let it be done so."

Then, because of his skillful hands, having said, "Just as they were described on all sides," he completed them within seven nights and brought those principal figures, beautifully rendered upon a painted cloth, before him.
Then Citralekhā, having spread out her own handiwork—
a magnificent and brilliantly colored great painting adorned with the color yellow—
showed it to Uṣā and especially to her friends.
These are the foremost among the gods, as well as those born of the lineage of the Dānavas;
what [of them] is there among humans, serpents, Yakṣas, and Rākṣasas in their entirety?

Behold all these— the Gandharvas, Asuras, Daityas, and others who are known as enjoyers of worldly pleasures; and all men, including those who are the most distinguished among humanity— all of them depicted by me exactly as they are.
"O friend, recognize him as your husband— of such a form and with such qualities as you desired— who was seen by you in the dream."
Then, having gradually beheld all those hosts of gods, dānavas, gandharvas, and vidyādharas,
that woman of intoxicating beauty passed beyond all the Yadus and beheld the joy of the Yadus.
Then, having seen Balabhadra, Pradyumna, and Sātyaki,
he beheld that lion of the Yadus, his own grandson Aniruddha— the son of the high-souled Viṣṇu—
held captive in battle like the five-arrowed god of love.
Then, seeing the hero Yadu depicted on the cloth in the form of a painting,
and seeing Aniruddha there as well, her eyes blossomed with wonder,
and she said to Citralekhā: "O friend, this is indeed that thief!"
"O auspicious lady, from where has this thief come, whose form I now recognize, by whom I was previously defiled while staying in my palace during a dream?"
"O Citralekhā, O beautiful one, tell me truly of him:
what are his name, virtues, character, and lineage, O lovely lady?"
"After that, I shall determine the course of this undertaking.
Citralekhā said:
"This is the grandson of the wise Kṛṣṇa, the lord of the three worlds."
The god of gods, the lord of the world, the manifest wielder of the discus and mace,
the slayer of the Dānavas in battle, Viṣṇu, the victorious one, the master of the universe.

This [is the power] of that God of gods, the wielder of the conch, discus, and mace, who, as the Lord of the world, made the three worlds with all things moving and unmoving rest within his own single lotus-foot by means of his valor.
O beautiful lady, O large-eyed one, your husband is the renowned grandson of Kṛṣṇa, the son of Pradyumna, who possesses formidable prowess and is famous throughout all the worlds.
For there is no one equal to him in prowess throughout the three worlds;
having uprooted mountains, he would shatter them with those very same mountains.
Blessed are you, and favored by fortune, since this bull among the Yadus, a virtuous man worthy of you,
has been ordained as your husband by the consort of the Three-Eyed One.
Uṣā said:
"O large-eyed one, if you are indeed fit to be the wife here of this husband of mine, who is like an immortal, O large-eyed one, O lovely-faced one, then become such."
For another path is impossible; therefore, become my path by being pathless.
You are a sky-faring yoginī, able to assume any form at will; skilled in means and arts, bring my beloved to me quickly!
"O timid one, devise a plan, for happiness with my beloved is beyond calculation;
O beautiful one, return successful by whatever means possible."
That friend who stands by one in times of calamity is praised as a true friend by the wise.
O lady of beautiful hips, I am tormented by desire; become the sustainer of my life.
If you do not bring me [to him] quickly today, O auspicious one, I shall give up my life.
Having heard Uṣā’s words, Citralekhā spoke these words:
"O auspicious one of pure smiles, you ought to hear my words."
Just as the city of Bāṇa is protected on all sides, O Goddess,
so too, O timid one, is Dvārakā especially unassailable.
That city was covered with iron plates and its gates were well-guarded;
likewise, it was protected by the Vṛṣṇi youths as well as by the inhabitants of Dvārakā stationed at the gates.
At its edge, it was fashioned by Viśvakarman to be joined with water;
by the command of Padmanābha, it is guarded by fierce men.
With its stone walls and moats, it is accessible only by difficult paths;
it is constructed with seven enclosures of mountains adorned with precious minerals.
It is not possible for those who are unacquainted with it to enter the city of Dvārakā.
"O Queen, do not urge me toward this rash deed;
therefore, desist from this thought of an object as elusive as a dream.
Protect yourself, protect me, and especially protect your father."
Uṣā said:
"O friend, it is possible to enter the face of Aniruddha, which resembles the full moon,
by means of the power of your yoga."
What is the use of my many lamentations? Listen, friend, to the reason:
if I do not see him, I shall go to the abode of Yama.

"O beautiful lady, success in one's undertakings comes upon reaching a messenger; therefore, go on my behalf as a messenger, if you wish me to live. If you recognize my friendship with you and understand what I have spoken out of love."
Bring my beloved to me quickly; otherwise, I shall abandon my dear life-breaths.
For those afflicted by desire do not perceive the danger to their lives, nor the destruction of their lineage, nor indeed the corruption of the family.
"Effort should be applied to tasks"—this is the teaching of the scriptures.
"And you, O large-eyed one, are capable of entering Dvārakā;
you have been praised by me, O timid one—grant me a pleasing sight.
Citralekhā said:
"O timid one, here I go, having entered the city of Dvārakā.
In every way, I have been honored by you with words like nectar, and I have been incited to this effort by your dear and beloved speeches."
Today I shall bring back your husband, the upholder of the Vṛṣṇi clan.
Having entered the city of Dvārakā with the mighty-armed Aniruddha,
I spoke those truthful words— inauspicious and terrifying to the Dānavas,
yet likewise concerning the origin and lineage of the Yādavas.
Having spoken thus, Citralekhā, who was as swift as thought, quickly vanished from sight.
Accompanied by her friends, Ūṣā remained there reflecting;
then, in the third muhūrta, she vanished from Bāṇa’s city,
desiring to do what was pleasing to her friends and honoring those whose wealth is asceticism.
In an instant, they reached Dvārakā, which was protected by Kṛṣṇa.
He beheld Dvārakā, adorned with palaces shaped like the peaks of Mount Kailāsa, standing there like a star in the sky.

Vaiśampāyana said: Then, in the midst of Dvāravatī, [he saw the city] adorned with ramparts.
Then, in the midst of Dvāravatī, she saw the auspicious palace of Kāma, and near it, the palace of Aniruddha.
It had pillars with golden railings and archways of gold and lapis lazuli;
it was draped with garlands of flowers and adorned with full water-jars.

He beheld the palace where the son of Pradyumna dwelt in happiness— a residence with peacock-necked pillars, its neck-like towers gathered together, strewn with jewels and corals, and resounding with the music of divine gandharvas.
Then, having suddenly entered that great palace of his,
the excellent Apsaras Citralekhā beheld Aniruddha there;
she saw him in the midst of women like the risen lord of the stars.
Being attended here and there by women during his playful pastimes,
drinking honeyed wine (*mādhvīka*), endowed with supreme splendor,
and seated upon an excellent throne, he was just like Ailavila himself.
The music was played with rhythmic precision and songs were sung sweetly; yet his mind was not there, for he thought only of that very object.
Women endowed with every virtue were dancing here and there,
yet Citralekhā did not find satisfaction for his mind;
he took no delight in sensual enjoyments, nor did he partake of wine.
"Clearly, that dream of his was revolving in his heart"—
thus, having reached this certainty through her intellect right there, she became free from fear;
and she saw him, resembling the banner of Śakra, in the midst of the most excellent women.
While beloved songs were being sung and dances performed on all sides, the high-minded Citralekhā, her body possessed by anxiety, thought:
"How is this task to be accomplished? How may it go well for me?"
Having reflected, the illustrious and fair-eyed Citralekhā vanished and concealed her with a magical spell.
Having then placed the son of Pradyumna, who was intoxicated with the pride of battle, in the midst of a group of women within the palace and made himself invisible, she took him up and flew away.
Having traversed that path frequented by perfected beings and celestial musicians,
she, swift as thought, suddenly entered Śoṇitapura.
Having brought Aniruddha there by means of her illusory power, she who could assume any form at will, the illustrious woman, went to where Uṣā was.
And Uṣā showed him, adorned with variegated ornaments.
Wearing variegated garments, a hero whose form was equal to that of Kandarpa—
she then arrived at Bāṇa’s city during the third muhūrta and showed Uṣā [the picture], saying, "Look at him, if he might be the one."
Having been addressed thus, the maiden Uṣā, daughter of Bāṇa,
standing then on her palace roof in the presence of her friends, was filled with wonder upon seeing him;
she then had him ushered into her own home.
Once he had been ushered in and had not yet departed, she— delighted,
accompanied by her friends, bashful, and possessing a pure smile;
skilled in worldly affairs and seeing her beloved with eyes wide open in joy— was filled with great gladness.
Standing on the palace roof, she honored that Yādava with the guest-offering;
having embraced Citralekhā, she consoled her with pleasant words.
Then the longing woman, overcome by fear, spoke hurriedly to Citralekhā.
"O friend, skilled in affairs, how indeed should this secret matter be handled? If it remains secret, all will be well; if it is revealed, there will be the destruction of life."
