Citralekhā spoke these words: "Listen, my friend, to my resolve."
For destiny, O friend, destroys the human effort that has been performed.
"The favor of the Goddess will not be favorable to you;
however, because this secret was kept with vigilance, no man shall know of it."
Having been addressed in this way by her friend, she, with her mind firmly resolved, spoke these words to Aniruddha: "It is even so."
By good fortune, that fortunate man, the thief who appeared in our dream, is seen;
for his sake we have been distressed by our longing for a beloved so difficult to attain.
O mighty-armed one, is all well with you?
For the hearts of women are tender; it is for this reason that I ask you.
Having heard those smooth and meaningful words of Uṣā,
that tiger among the Yadus also spoke these words, even more beautiful in their syllables.
Wiping away the tears from her eyes, which were overflowing with joy,
he laughed with a smile and spoke these heart-captivating words.
It is well with me everywhere, O lady of excellent limbs, O you who speak with moderation;
by your grace, O Goddess, I announce this pleasant news to you.
"O lady of auspicious appearance, this region has never been seen by me before;
yet last night in a dream, I beheld for a moment a great inner apartment of maidens."
"In this very way, O timid one, I have come here through your favor;
and the word of Rudra’s wife shall certainly not prove false."

"O lady of noble nature, having perceived the Goddess's pleasure and for the sake of your own welfare, I have arrived this very day; be gracious, for I have come to you for refuge. [Colophon: *Bāṇayuddha*] [Continuation: "O lady of noble nature, having perceived the Goddess's pleasure and for the sake of your own welfare, I have arrived this very day; be gracious, for I have come to you for refuge."
Having spoken thus, the highly illustrious Aniruddha took his pleasure with her.
Having said this, she, being well-adorned, quickly joined with her beloved in a secret place and remained there as if trembling with fear.
Then, according to the law of marriage, they united by the Gāndharva rite;
and they took delight in one another, like a pair of cakravāka birds during the day.
The beautiful woman rejoiced with her husband Aniruddha;
united with her beloved and adorned with divine garlands and ointments,
that lovely lady remained concealed in a secluded part of this house.
Having come together, she chose him as her mate, just as a female elephant chooses a bull elephant.
The virtuous daughter of Bāṇa, that goddess, embraced Yadu in due order and kissed his face; she also kissed his eyes.
Embracing him again and again as she desired, she, infatuated by passion,
found no satiety in embracing that best of the Yadus.
Then, endowed with that dark magic (tāmasī vidyā), the son of Pradyumna,
having seen those wonderful women in the house, reflected upon it at that very moment.
"What is this great rite of mine? I do not know its cause. Is this a dream seen by me, or is it a delusion?"
I am awake; this is not a dream, nor is it a great delusion of mine. Who is this fair-browed one standing before me, like a well-flowered creeper?
Her rows of eyes were like startled deer; she spoke with the graceful movements of her creeper-like eyebrows;
she possessed full breasts, thighs, and hips; and her feet, hands, and lips were copper-red.
Abounding with dark, curly hair, speaking with a sweet smile,
she has entered the path of my vision like an autumnal crescent moon;
I do not know what this is, nor by whom it has been brought about here.
Upon seeing Uṣā, who was intoxicated with passion, his desire increased;
and she, in turn, stood before him, ready to drink visibly.
Then, having understood her intentions through gestures and having heard the truth of the matter,
he gratified that beautiful woman Manorama according to his desire.
And she too, having approached him, her eyes agitated by joy and fear,
took her pleasure with him according to her desire, her skin becoming rough with the rising of thrills.
With playful and charming conversation, the woman attended upon him,
like a female elephant in a mountain cave attending her mate,
the mighty-armed Aniruddha, who had fallen under the power of sleep.
Then, while asleep, Niruddha was instantly led by Citralekhā from his own city to the city of Bāṇa, where he was united with Uṣā.
Having thus seen this wondrous union with Uṣā in a dream, she was further bewildered by her own words.
Then, having seen Citralekhā, that Yādava said:
"I have been brought quickly from the city of Dvārakā by Citralekhā."
"Having reached the city of Bāṇa, I met Uṣā in secret;
such was the wonderful dream seen by me, never before witnessed."
"What manner of fate has come upon me? Who are you, and who is this beautiful woman?
What city is this, and whose house is it? You ought to tell me."
Seeing him speaking thus, Citralekhā spoke these words:
"Is it well with you everywhere, O hero, joy of the Yadus?
At that time, Aniruddha was sporting with her, yet he remained unrecognized."
The amorous Yadu, having firmly embraced her face, drank from it;
and so, embracing one another, they drank from each other's mouths.
Then he drank the honey-wine she offered and made her drink what remained;
thus, in the midst of the assembly of people, their passion increased.
Then the virtuous Citralekhā adorned him with ornaments,
with garments, with various jewels, and with many fragrant garlands.
The hero of the Yadus shone like the moon with Rohiṇī;
then that couple took delight for a long time upon the path of the palace.
Thereupon, the joy of the Yadus delighted her as much as she desired.
There,
having come together in private with her who was adorned with ornaments, he drank from her face; and that virtuous woman, embracing him, drank from his face in due order.

And at that very moment, when he— the bull among the Yadus— had arrived, wearing divine garlands and garments and anointed with celestial unguents, the goddess, the friend of Bāṇa’s daughter, kissed him on the eyes.
United with Uṣā, he was discovered by Bāṇa’s guards.
Just as Nala sported with Damayantī, so did he enjoy himself at will, delighting that auspicious Uṣā.
Vaiśampāyana said: Then, O King, in that state of affairs, chamberlains with canes in their hands and wearing tunics stood on all sides around the elderly women.
Then, having learned that Aniruddha was staying in the maidens' quarters together with Uṣā,
the daughter of Bāṇa, enjoying himself as he pleased;
Then the guards, having gone there suddenly, were terrified in the presence of Bāṇa.
Then those guards, fierce with their blazing weapons and ever vigilant,
became afraid and reported the actions of Aniruddha.
"O Great King, this is someone who has united with Uṣā and remains in the maidens' quarters; O King, who is he and from where does he come?"
"He has arrived suddenly, O King; we do not know his destination, O Lord."
Having heard this and beholding that army, Bāṇa was filled with rage;
then those scouts reported to Bāṇa the entire transgression regarding the maiden exactly as it had been witnessed.
Then the army of *kiṃkaras* was commanded by Bāṇa, the heroic son of Bali, the slayer of enemies, who performs terrible deeds.
"Go all together; let this evil-minded man be slain, by whom our family conduct has been defiled through his corrupted soul."
For when Uṣā was violated, our great lineage was indeed violated;
since he did not receive her from us, he violated her by taking her himself.
Oh, what energy! Oh, what fortitude! Oh, what audacity belongs to this evil-minded one, this most foolish wretch who has entered our city and our very abode!
Having spoken thus, he again urged those kiṃkaras vehemently.
Then, having received his command, those mighty warriors, well-armored and with various weapons raised in their hands, set forth; assuming various forms, they went to where Aniruddha was.
The Dānavas, filled with rage, were desirous of slaying the son of Pradyumna.
Seeing that army, the illustrious daughter of Bāṇa, her eyes veiled with tears and terrified by the slaughter of Pradyumna’s son, wept.
Then, seeing that fawn-eyed Uṣā weeping and trembling, crying out "Alas, alas! My beloved!", Aniruddha addressed her.
May you be fearless, O Śroṇī; do not fear while I stand here.
The time for your joy has arrived; there is no cause for fear for you.
O illustrious lady, if this entire host of Bāṇa’s servants were to come here, I would have no anxiety; O timid one, behold my prowess today!
Hearing the roar of that approaching army,
the illustrious son of Pradyumna suddenly rose up, asking, "What is this?"
Then he saw his army standing all around, surrounding that great house, with various weapons raised.
Then, enraged and biting his lip, he quickly approached that encircled army, relying upon his own strength.
Then, having heard that the Bāṇeyas had been repelled from battle,
Citralekhā remembered Nārada, who has the vision of a god.
Then, in the mere twinkling of an eye, that bull among sages reached the city named Śoṇita, the capital of Citralekhā, as soon as he was thought of.
Standing there in the sky, he then said to Aniruddha:
"Have no fear; may it be well with you, O hero; I have arrived, your desired one."
Then, seeing Nārada and saluting him, that mighty one became joyful and cheerful in mind, and advanced for the sake of battle, crying out:
"Let him be slain! Let him be slain! Seize him! Seize him!"
"Kill him! Kill him quickly! the Dānavas cried out at that time.
Then, hearing the roar of all of them shouting, the hero suddenly rose up like an elephant tormented by a goad.
Although he had been repeatedly restrained by her there, that one who was fierce in battle,
being terrified himself by her fear, fled toward the asuras;
and seeing him rushing forward with his great arms and bitten lip, [the asuras were struck with awe].
And as he was descending from the palace, those afflicted by fear fled in all directions.
Then, roaring like a lion,
O King, by that roar he indeed seized the incomparable iron bar standing at the gate of the inner apartments.
Skilled in various weapons, he hurled them for their destruction.
They all struck down those engaged in the field of battle with showers of arrows, maces, lances, swords, spears, and tridents.
Though being struck from all sides with iron arrows and clubs by the enraged Dānavas, who were experts in weaponry, the son of Pradyumna—
the soul of all beings— was not shaken, roaring like a cloud at the end of the hot season.
Brandishing his terrible iron club, he stood in their midst like the sun moving through the sky in the center of clouds on all sides.
Carrying a wooden staff and an antelope skin, Nārada, his heart filled with joy, exclaimed "Excellent! Excellent! and spoke thus to Aniruddha;
meanwhile, those [demons] were being struck by that fierce iron club of immeasurable power.
They all fled in fear, like a cloud driven by the wind.
Having put the Dānavas to flight with his iron club, the hero Aniruddha, of swift prowess,
shone forth as he roared joyfully with a lion’s roar,
like a thundering rain-cloud at the end of the summer heat resounding loudly in the sky.
"Stay! he cried out to the Dānavas, who were intoxicated with the frenzy of battle;
and Prādyumni, the destroyer of all enemies, struck them down.
Being slaughtered in battle by that high-souled one, they all fled from the field,
turning their backs on the fight and fleeing wherever Bāṇa was.
Then the Daityas, standing near Bāṇa, panting and drenched in blood, found no refuge, their eyes overwhelmed by fear.
"Do not fear, do not fear!"— thus urged by the king, they cast off their terror and stood together, saying, "Fight, O bulls among the Dānavas!"
Bāṇa spoke again to them, whose eyes were trembling with fear:
"Why do you abandon this world-renowned glory from afar and fall into such dejection, like senseless eunuchs?"
Who is this, terrified of whom you all flee so many times,
even though you are renowned for your noble lineage and are all experts in various modes of warfare?
"Indeed, you have no need to assist me in battle today," he said; "go away, perish! Vanish from my presence!"
Then the powerful one, terrifying them in many ways with fierce words,
again commanded all those heroes by the tens of thousands for battle.
At night, a vast army, abounding with hosts of fierce demons and equipped with various raised weapons, was commanded for his suppression.
There, the atmosphere became filled with multitudes of arrows that were like clouds containing lightning, appearing as if they possessed blazing eyes.
Some, standing upon the ground, roared on all sides like elephants;
then others thundered in the sky like clouds at the end of the summer heat.
Then that great battle broke out once more, and everywhere the cries of "Stay! Stay! were heard on all sides.
The heroic Aniruddha advanced against them in battle;
it was a marvel that he, being alone,
engaged in combat with those Dānavas of great prowess in the fray.
And the mighty one seized their very iron clubs and javelins as well,
and with those very weapons he struck them down in the great battle.
Having seized them, he struck them with weapons in the battle;
then, grasping a terrible iron club (parigha) once more at the front of the fray,
he slew the hosts of mighty Daityas in the encounter.
Alone in battle, that grandson of the wielder of the Śārṅga bow slew eight thousand swift kiṃkaras;
he let out various roars, making both heaven and earth tremble.
Having cast aside his sword and shield, he took them up again at the head of the battle;
with those weapons, that sole destroyer of enemies moved through various paths.
Moving in thirty-two varieties— whirling, leaping upward, tossing aside, bounding forward, scattering about, and leaping across— he was seen as he roamed.
There, at the forefront of the battle, they beheld him as one who had become ten thousand;
sporting in many ways in the fray, he was like Death himself with his mouth wide open.
Then, scorched by him and drenched in streams of blood,
they were broken once more and fled to where Bāṇa stood on the battlefield.
Carried on all sides by floods of elephants, horses, and chariots,
they fled in every direction with their vigor destroyed, uttering a terrible cry of distress.
Thus did fear seize those Dānavas in that great battle;
then, each one oppressed by the fear of the others,
they vomited blood and turned away from the fight out of despondency.
Never before in battle had the singers experienced such fear as that which arose among those fighting with Aniruddha in the encounter.
As they fought with Aniruddha, a terrible battle unfolded; such fear as they had experienced in the encounter with the gods did not arise for them then.
Some, vomiting blood, fell upon the surface of the earth.
The Dānavas, resembling mountain peaks, held maces, spears, and swords in their hands.
Some had their brains churned out, others had the insides of their throats split open;
abandoning their arrows in battle, those Dānavas, utterly overwhelmed by fear, then fled into the vast expanse of the sky, having been utterly defeated.
Seeing that great army then shattered and rendered helpless,
Bāṇa blazed up with rage like a kindled fire at a sacrifice.
Moving through the atmosphere and praising him from all sides,
Nārada danced with joy at the battle of Aniruddha.
In the meantime, the heroic Bāṇa, extremely enraged,
mounted the chariot driven by Kumbhāṇḍa and went to where Aniruddha was, raising his terrible sword.
Raising up spears, swords, maces, pikes,
and battle-axes with his thousand arms, he shone like a hundred banners of Śakra.
With his mighty arms bound with leathern finger-guards and equipped with various weapons, that long-armed and preeminent Dānava shone resplendent.
Then the mighty Dānava, roaring a lion’s roar in his wrath, with his great bow drawn and discharging arrows by the hundreds,
rushed with speed toward where the son of Pradyumna stood.
With eyes bloodshot with anger, he said, "Stay! Stay!"
Having heard those words of Bāṇa as he spoke in battle, the unconquered son of Pradyumna looked up and then laughed.
And Uṣā, seeing her father, her eyes overwhelmed with fear,
hid herself within the palace and gazed intently at her husband.
Stupefied as to what should be done and utterly bewildered, the excellent Apsaras Citralekhā became despondent and thought, "I am dead.
[She beheld the chariot] resounding with the tinkling of hundreds of small bells and adorned with red banners and flags.
His body was covered with bear-skin, and his great chariot measured ten *nalvas* in size.
Having mounted his chariot, the hero, possessing a thousand arms, shone resplendent;
for that great-souled one, a thousand horses were yoked to his chariot,
just as they had been for Hiraṇyakaśipu in the ancient war between the gods and the asuras.
The bull among the Yadus beheld that Dānava as he was rushing toward him;
he then rejoiced greatly in the battle and was filled with splendor.
Then he beheld one approaching, bearing a sword and shield— a hero, self-composed and eager for battle, like the Man-lion (Narasimha) of old intent on slaying the primordial Daitya.
O King, seeing him thus marked by the nail-marks of his beloved,
wearing sword and shield, and on foot, Bāṇa experienced incomparable joy, desiring the slaughter of Pradyumna’s son.
Thinking that the Yādava was invincible— being both without armor and with sword in hand— as he stood facing him for battle, [he approached].
In that battle, the mighty Bāṇa, appearing victorious, spoke these words in a rage: "Seize him! Slay him!"
Hearing those words as Bāṇa spoke them in the battle, the son of Pradyumna,
laughing in his wrath, glared at him.
Then Uṣā, trembling with fear and weeping there, the beautiful woman,
was consoled by Aniruddha, who smiled and comforted her as she stood there.
Then Bāṇa, enraged and desiring to slay Aniruddha, discharged volleys of small arrows from all sides in the battle.
But Aniruddha, desiring his defeat,
severed [the bow] and rained down nets of arrows made of small shafts from all sides;
Bāṇa, meanwhile, desired his death in battle and aimed them at Aniruddha’s head.
Having warded off those thousands of arrows with his shield,
he stood facing him like the sun at its rising.
Having overcome the arrow in battle, that delight of the Yadus stood firm,
like a lion seeing a single elephant before him in the forest.
Then, with a flood of thousands of swift arrows, sharp and keen, which pierce the vital organs,
he struck the unconquered son of Pradyumna.
Then, standing his ground, he pierced the son of Pradyumna with sharpened arrows.
Struck by those arrows, O King, the wielder of sword and shield then struck him with sharp shafts as he was charging forward.
Deeply pierced by those straight-jointed arrows, the mighty-armed one blazed with rage, desiring to perform a difficult feat.
With his limbs drenched in streams of blood and struck by showers of arrows, he was overwhelmed;
yet, filled with great rage, he advanced toward Bāṇa’s chariot.
Though pierced deeply by swords, clubs, spears, sharp-edged missiles, and lances,
as well as by floods of arrows, the son of Pradyumna did not tremble.
Suddenly leaping up in anger,
he severed the chariot-pole of Bāṇa and slew his horses with his sword at the front of the chariot.
Furthermore, Bāṇa,
who was skilled in the ways of battle, rendered him invisible with a rain of arrows, as well as with javelins and spears.
Realizing "He is slain," the hosts of the Nairṛtas roared;
then, suddenly leaping down, he stationed himself at the side of the chariot.
Then Bāṇa, enraged in battle, seized a spear of terrible form that inspired fear, blazing and radiant, and adorned with a garland of bells.
Resembling a blazing sun, like the staff of Yama, auspicious,
warding off [enemies], invincible, adorned with gold,
heavy with a thousand loads, and fashioned by Viśvakarman at that time— [he took up] that mace.
He hurled it with detachment, like a great flaming meteor.
Seeing that spear approaching, which was then capable of ending his life,
he hurled back at it that very same spear which strikes fear into all enemies;
then that Supreme Person, having leaped forward, seized the spear.
Then the exceedingly powerful one pierced Bāṇa with his own spear alone;
having pierced through his body, it entered the surface of the earth.
Vaiśampāyana said:
Then the powerful son of Bali fell into a swoon;
his limbs drenched in blood, he was severely afflicted by his own [exhaustion].
Deeply pierced and pained, he leaned against his flagpole;
then Kumbhāṇḍa spoke these words to him who was overcome by fainting:
"O Lord of the Dānavas, why do you thus neglect an enemy who is so intent?"
For this hero, having attained his mark, is seen today to be unshakable;
fight by resorting to illusion, for he could not be slain otherwise.
Protect yourself and me from negligence; why do you disregard this?
Let him be slain this very day, lest he destroy us all.
Having slain hundreds of others and having carried off Uṣā, he will depart;
thus urged by the words of Kumbhāṇḍa, the lord of the Dānavas,
the best among speakers, spoke these harsh words in great anger.
"I shall ordain his death in battle, taking his life;
indeed, I will seize him just as Garuḍa seizes a serpent."
Having spoken thus, together with his chariot, horses, banner, and charioteer,
he vanished right there like a city of the Gandharvas.
Having perceived that Bāṇa had vanished, the unconquered son of Pradyumna,
endowed with prowess, gazed toward the ten directions.
Then, resorting to the knowledge of darkness (tāmasī vidyā), the powerful son of Bali, enraged and concealed by his mastery of illusion, released sharp arrows.
Bound on all sides by arrows that had become serpents,
the son of Pradyumna’s body was coiled in many ways by heaps of snakes.
His body was coiled in many ways by heaps of arrows;
with all his limbs thus enveloped and bound in battle, the son of Pradyumna remained motionless and composed, like Mount Maināka.
Enveloped by serpent coils whose faces were licked by flames,
the son of Pradyumna stood fearlessly in battle, resembling a mountain.
Though he remained motionless, even while completely encircled on all sides by arrows consisting of coiled serpents, that self of all beings felt no pain.
Then, enraged,
Bāṇa, relying upon his banner, threatened him with fierce words and spoke these words in indignation.
"Kumbhāṇḍa, let this defiler of the family be slain quickly—
he by whom my conduct in the world has been corrupted through his corrupt soul."
When these words had been spoken, Kumbhāṇḍa spoke this speech:
"O King, I shall say something; listen to me if you so desire."
Let it be known: whose is he, from where has he come here, or by whom was this one, whose prowess is equal to Śakra’s, brought here?
O King, I have seen him many times in battle during this great conflict;
he appears as if playing amidst the combats like the son of a god.
Endowed with noble lineage, virtuous conduct, austerity, and heroism— all these combined—
he shall be invincible in every battle; he shall be superior to you in prowess,
powerful, possessed of great courage, and learned in all the scriptures.
O best of Daityas, he does not deserve the fault of being killed;
once you have understood this, you shall either slay him or even offer him worship.
This maiden has been united with you by the Gāndharva rite of marriage; she is indeed neither to be given away nor to be accepted [by another]. Therefore, deliberate upon her execution.
For in killing her there is great sin, whereas in protecting her there is very great merit.
For this preeminent among men deserves honor in every respect.
With his body coiled on all sides, he is not distressed by these serpents;
endowed with noble lineage, pride, heroism, and strength,
behold, O King, this Supreme Person, possessed of fame and valor.
This powerful one does not count us all, even though he has met his death.
Ds D1-5.6 (second time) T2 G2-5 insert after 94 (Dn D6 [all first time] after 77ab):
"If he were not bound here by the power of illusion..."
One would fight all the hosts of asuras in battle; of this there is no doubt.
In all battles, he shall be a knower of the path and superior in valor to you;
with limbs drenched in floods of blood and entwined by the coils of serpents,
he will knit his brows into a three-pronged frown and pay no heed to us standing here.
O King, although he has been brought to this state, that certain heroic youth, relying on the strength of his own arms, does not think of you.
In battle, he who stands with two arms against one of a thousand arms—
if this is pleasing to you, O King, he should be known as one endowed with heroism and strength.
"And this maiden, having united with him, must not be given to anyone else."
If this one is indeed the most beloved in the lineage of that great-souled one,
then this hero, the best of asuras, shall surely receive worship.
Having said, "Let her be guarded," and having replied,
"So be it," Bāṇa, who was indeed intent on killing him, said,
"Very well," and bound Uṣā with firm fetters and tightly secured nooses.
Then Bāṇa commanded many servant-guards:
"Let this evil-minded one be guarded, and let that lowest of women also be guarded!"
Having thus instructed them all, the powerful Bāṇa, filled with the intoxication of pride,
went to his own abode together with Kumbhāṇḍa;
for he had heard Kumbhāṇḍa’s words within the inner apartments, which were crowded with serpents.
When these words had been spoken by the high-souled Kumbhāṇḍa,
Bāṇa, the destroyer of enemies, said to Kumbhāṇḍa, "So be it."
Then, having appointed guardians for the wise Aniruddha and having caused Aniruddha to fight,
Bāṇa entered his own palace.
Having seen the mighty Aniruddha bound by means of his illusory power, the great Asura, the son of Bali, departed for his own abode; meanwhile,
Nārada, the best of sages, proceeded toward Dvāravatī.
Then, indeed, by way of the path of the sky, the Sage went to Dvāravatī.
When the foremost of sages had departed, Aniruddha reflected:
"Without a doubt, this cruel Dānava has perished upon encountering battle."
Having gone there, Nārada will explain this matter exactly as it is, in its true essence, to the wielder of the conch, the discus, and the mace.
Seeing Pradyumna’s son enveloped by the nāgas, Uṣā wept in distress;
her eyes reddened with tears, she spoke again to him as he was crying.
"Why do you weep, O timid one? Do not fear, O fair-eyed lady;
behold, O woman of beautiful hips, Madhusūdana has arrived for my sake."
Upon hearing the sound of his conch and the roar of Bala’s arms,
the Dānavas shall meet their destruction, as shall the fetuses within the wombs of the Asura women.
Vaiśampāyana said:
Having been addressed thus by Niruddha, Uṣā felt confident;
yet that slender-waisted woman grieved for her cruel father.
He reported that the son of Pradyumna had been bound to the one whose banner bears Garuḍa.
Chapter 109,
transliterated by Julie Bélanger.
Proofread by Horst Brinkhaus;
version dated February 4, 2003.
Vaiśampāyana said: Then,
in the house of Aniruddha, all the women wept together like groups of Kinnarīs, not seeing their beloved lord.
Alas, what a tragedy! While Kṛṣṇa, our protector, remains in this world, why do we weep like those who are helpless, terrified and bewildered by fear?
Relying upon the shadow of his arms, the gods in heaven— headed by Indra, together with the Ādityas and the hosts of Maruts— dwell there as deities.
This great fear has arisen in the world for that giver of fear,
since his grandson Aniruddha— that hero— has not been carried off by anyone.
Ah! Surely there is no fear in this world for that evil-minded one who ignites the unbearable wrath of Vāsudeva.
He who moves within the fangs of Death with his mouth wide open,
like a highly enraged lion slaying the finest of elephants,
desiring to drink blood and biting with its fangs upraised.
Out of delusion, that enemy advanced against Vāsudeva in battle.
Having committed such an offense against the bull among the Yadus,
how could he escape with his life, even if he were Indra himself?
He who committed the offense is not to be pitied, but we, now deprived of him,
have been brought under the power of Fate through separation from our lord.
Thus, weeping and speaking again and again,
those excellent women shed the inauspicious tears born from their eyes.
Their eyes, filled with tears,
shone like lotuses drenched by water at the arrival of the rainy season.
Their beautiful eyes, with curved lashes and radiant pupils, shone as if drenched in blood.
As they stood upon the terraces of the palace, a great cry suddenly arose from those weeping by the thousands, like that of female ospreys in the sky.
Hearing that terrible and unprecedented roar, a great fear arose,
and those bulls among men suddenly sprang up from their houses through the windows.
Why is this very great sound heard from Aniruddha’s house? From where has fear come upon us, who are protected by Kṛṣṇa?
Thus they spoke to one another, their voices faltering and choked with affection,
like lions who had emerged from their caves after being provoked.
Then the armor-drum of Kṛṣṇa was struck in the assembly hall;
by its sound, they all came and stood within the hall.
"What is this? the Yādavas asked one another, and they all informed each other according to the facts.
Then those Yādavas, intoxicated by battle, stood there sighing, their eyes filled with tears and bloodshot with rage.
When everyone had become silent, Vipṛthu spoke these words—
he who was skilled in policy, a speaker of what is beneficial, and a bringer of joy to the Yādavas—
addressing Kṛṣṇa, the best among strikers, who was sighing again and again.
O Indra among men, why are you thus possessed by anxiety here?
All the Yādavas depend upon the strength and life-force of your arms; they rely on you, O Kṛṣṇa, and are supported by you in every way.
In the same way, Śakra, the slayer of Bala, having entrusted both victory and defeat to you, sleeps happily and free from anxiety; why then are you filled with such anxiety?
All those kinsmen of yours have entered the unshakeable ocean of grief;
O mighty-armed one, you alone must rescue them as they are sinking.
Why are you thus possessed by anxiety and say nothing at all?
O Lord Mādhava, you ought not to indulge in such vain worry.
Thus addressed, Kṛṣṇa, sighing deeply for a long time,
spoke these words again— he who was skilled in speech, like Bṛhaspati himself.
Vipṛthu, overcome with anxiety, was reflecting upon this matter;
and as I too reflected upon this matter, I could find no way forward.
Thus, even when addressed by you, I did not offer any reply at all.
Today, in the midst of the Dāśārha host, I speak these meaningful words;
listen, all you Yādavas, for I am indeed filled with anxiety.
Now that the hero Aniruddha has been carried off, all the kings on earth consider us and all our kinsmen to be as if powerless.
In the past, our king Āhuka was indeed carried off by Śālva;
we then recovered him after engaging in a most terrible battle.
Moreover, Pradyumna was indeed carried off by Śambara while we were still in our childhood;
having slain him in battle, that son of Rukmiṇī has now returned.
But this is a very great hardship: where has the son of Pradyumna been exiled?
O bulls among men, I do not recall such a transgression as this.
"Who has forcibly rendered my eye— so full of foul discharge— blind, by whom my foot, covered in ashes, was placed upon my head?
Or what dull-witted person would take from my crown the true jewel?"
Who indeed stands before him, disregarding his invincible strength?
Or who, O Lord, does not remember the bow of Śini’s son? I shall take away the life of that man, along with his followers, in battle.
When Kṛṣṇa had spoken thus, Sātyaki addressed these words to him:
"O Kṛṣṇa, let spies be dispatched in search of Aniruddha."
Search this earth, including its mountains and forest regions;
for it is most likely right here that he has been held by someone.
Once he is found, I shall take whatever measures are appropriate to be taken immediately.
Then Kṛṣṇa, having smiled, spoke these words to Āhuka:
"O King, let spies be dispatched, both internal and external."
Vaiśampāyana said:
Having heard the words of Keśava, Āhuka quickly spoke;
he then dispatched spies for the search of Aniruddha.
Then the messengers were commanded by the illustrious king:
"Search both the interior and the exterior on all sides."
The horses and chariots were commanded by the high-souled king:
"Search for Mount Veṇumant, Mount Latāveṣṭa, as well as Mount Raivataka and Mount Ṛkṣavan, traveling swiftly on your horses."
Each individual park there must be searched thoroughly on all sides;
one must also proceed without attachment throughout the parks in every direction.
Mounting thousands of horses and numerous chariots,
all of you must go quickly and search for the joy of the Yadus.
The commander-in-chief Anādhṛṣṭi spoke these words to Kṛṣṇa, the performer of effortless deeds and the infallible one, like one who is utterly terrified:
Listen to my words, O Kṛṣṇa, if they please you, O Lord;
for a long time now, my mind has been inclined to speak to you.
Asiloma and Puloma were slain, as were Nisunda and Naraka; Saubha and Śālva were killed, as were Mainda and Dvivida;
and the great Hayagrīva was destroyed by you along with his followers.
Kaṃsa was slain by Kṛṣṇa, and Naraka was cast down;
many other soldiers there, numbering in the hundreds of thousands,
perished when such a most terrible conflict took place for the sake of the gods.
O Govinda, you have performed all these deeds in their entirety in battle after battle; moreover, you have no one to attack you from the rear.
O Kṛṣṇa, this deed was performed by you in battle along with its consequences—
that difficult task which was accomplished in the seizing of the Pārijāta tree.
In that place, O Kṛṣṇa, Śakra himself, who is skilled in battle, was defeated by you with the strength of your arms while mounted upon the head of Airāvata.
Therefore, you must engage in enmity with him; of this there is no doubt. Furthermore, you must maintain a great persistence toward him.
There, the abduction of Aniruddha was carried out by Maghavan himself;
for no one else would have had the power to exact such revenge.
When these words had been spoken, the wise Kṛṣṇa, hissing like a serpent,
addressed the mighty Anādhṛṣṭi with these words.
"O General, my dear, do not speak thus! The gods are not performers of trivial deeds;
they are neither ungrateful, nor impotent, nor arrogant, nor foolish."
I have exerted great effort for the sake of the gods in the destruction of the Dānavas;
and for their pleasure, I slay the arrogant great Asuras in battle.
I am devoted to that, my mind is fixed on that, I am a devotee of that, and I delight in what is dear to that;
for knowing me to be such as this, how could they commit sin?
They are noble, truthful, and always follow their devotees;
no evil is to be found among them, yet you, O fool, speak thus.
Perhaps Aniruddha has been abducted here by a harlot;
such an act is not ordained even among the gods, including Indra himself.
Vaiśampāyana said:
While Kṛṣṇa, the performer of wondrous deeds, was reflecting thus, [he thought]:
"O best of the Yadus, this wicked thing must not be spoken by one such as you."
Having heard Kṛṣṇa’s words, Akrūra, who was skilled in meaningful speech, then spoke these words in a sweet and gentle voice.
Whatever is the task of the lord Śakra is certainly our own;
and whatever is our task is also the task of the husband of Śacī.
We are to be protected by the gods, and we too must protect the deities;
for the sake of the gods, we have indeed descended into human form.
"Viṣṇu, the slayer of Madhu, the hero, the eternal God of gods"—
thus urged by the words of Akrūra,
Kṛṣṇa, the Supreme Person, spoke again in a voice that was both affectionate and profound.
This son of Pradyumna was not carried off by gods, nor by Gandharvas, nor by Yakṣas, nor by Rākṣasas; he was carried off by a woman, a harlot.
The women of the Daityas and Dānavas are skilled in illusion and unchaste;
there is no doubt that he has been carried off by them, for there is no danger from any other source.
When these words had been spoken by the high-souled Kṛṣṇa to the charioteers, bards, and panegyrists,
he then understood in their true essence what had occurred within the circle of the Yadus.
Then a great roar arose as they praised Kṛṣṇa; that sweet sound,
gladdening everyone,
was heard in the residence of Mādhava.
All those spies, having approached the gate of the assembly hall from every direction,
spoke these words in soft, faltering voices:
O King, gardens, rocks, mountains, caves, rivers, and lakes—
each one was searched by the hundreds, yet he was not to be seen.
O King, other spies approached Kṛṣṇa and then said to him:
"All our regions have been searched, yet the son of Pradyumna is not to be seen;
since they too are peaceful in mind, how could they possibly lead us away?"
O delighter of the Yadus, whatever other arrangement must be made for the search for Aniruddha, command us quickly regarding that.
Then, all of them, dejected in mind and with eyes clouded by tears, spoke to one another: "What should be done next?"
Some had their lips bitten by their teeth, some had eyes clouded with tears,
and some brave men, knitting their brows, brooded in thought.
As they were thinking thus and speaking at great length,
a very great agitation arose as to where Aniruddha had gone; filled with indignation,
the Yādavas looked at one another.
With distracted minds, they should somehow pass that night.
"Aniruddha has been carried off!"—thus they cried again and again, O subduer of enemies.
And as they were speaking thus, the night turned into dawn;
then, with the sounding of trumpets and the great blasts of conch shells, [the morning broke].
The awakening of the mighty-armed Kṛṣṇa was performed in his abode.
Kṛṣṇa, the lord of the gods of gods, likewise remained as if bewildered regarding what ought to be done.
"What must I do? From where has this fear come?
Thinking thus, "By all means, applying effort, I shall strive for the subsequent task," he resolved.
I shall go to the end of the quarters, to the ocean, the abode of Varuṇa;
I will indeed go this very day to where that grandson of mine resides.
"In which direction shall I go first? By whom can everything be heard?
If someone were to understand this, then it would be a virtuous deed.
Then, when the dawn had become clear and the sun had appeared, [he set out].
Nārada entered the assembly alone, as if smiling.
Having seen all the Yādavas assembled together with Kṛṣṇa,
he then honored Mādhava with shouts of victory;
and Ugrasena and the others likewise honored that sage.
Then, rising up with a troubled mind, the powerful Lord Kṛṣṇa, who is invincible in assembly,
offered the honey-mixture and a cow to Nārada.
Seated upright according to the rule upon a bright seat covered with a costly rug, he spoke these meaningful words.
Why are you all thus possessed by anxiety, shrouded in darkness and devoid of resolve;
with your energy destroyed, you are all indeed like eunuchs, deprived of your senses?
On the previous day, O hero, the Yādavas witnessed a great marvel when these words had been spoken by the high-souled Nārada;
then Vāsudeva spoke these words: "O Blessed One, let this be heard."
"O Brahmin of firm vows, Aniruddha has been carried off by someone during the night;
because of him, all of us have our minds possessed by anxiety."
O sage, if this account has been heard by you, or even seen, as well.
"O Blessed One, let it be told well; this is dear to me, O sinless one.
When these words had been spoken by the high-souled Keśava, Nārada laughed and said: "Listen, O Madhusūdana!"
A truly great battle, frequented by great beings,
took place in that great conflict between the solitary Aniruddha and Bāṇa.
The daughter of that Bāṇa of incomparable prowess was named Uṣā;
for her sake, the Apsaras Citralekhā indeed quickly carried him away.
Between both Pradyumni and Bāṇa there occurred a great and most terrible battle in that conflict,
like that between Bali and Vāsava.
We too witnessed that most great and wonderful battle:
how the mighty Aniruddha, who never retreats in combat, was bound by Bāṇa through the use of illusion and his snakes out of fear.
"O Viṣṇu, O Garuḍa-bannered one, I have witnessed such a battle by Pradyumna, who likewise slew hosts of Dānavas by the hundreds and by the millions;
yet his death was ordained by Bāṇa."
His minister named Kumbhāṇḍa restrained him;
for that prince Aniruddha was unable to prevail in combat,
Bāṇa resorted to illusion and bound him with serpents.
"Arise quickly, sir, for the sake of glory and victory!
O dear one, this is no time for those who desire triumph to protect their lives."
"When his life-breaths have departed only slightly, the hero remains standing, having summoned his fortitude"—
when these words were spoken, the powerful and heroic Vāsudeva gave orders for the provisions necessary for the journey.
Then the proclamation of "Auspicious Day," uttered by the Brahmins, was heard;
and as he was being strewn with sandalwood powder and parched grain on all sides,
that mighty-armed Janārdana went forth.
The Lord of the World desired to go in order to slay the great asura Bāṇa.
Nārada said:
"O Kṛṣṇa, you ought to summon Vainateya to mind."
For indeed, O mighty-armed one, it is not possible for anyone else to travel along that path.

And listen to that path which must be traversed, O Janārdana; it is eleven thousand yojanas long and exceedingly difficult to conquer. From here, it leads to Śoṇitapura, where the son of Pradyumna currently resides.
"O Govinda, summon Vainateya, who is swift as thought, of great heroism, and full of majesty; for he will lead you there. In a single moment, he will show Bāṇa to you."
Having heard those words of his, Hari meditated upon Garuḍa;
he, approaching Kṛṣṇa’s side, stood there filled with joy.
He has black hair, wears bracelets, is victorious, and is black in complexion;
he has four tusks, four arms, and is a knower of the four Vedas and the six auxiliary sciences.
He bears the Śrīvatsa mark, has lotus-like eyes, hair that grows upward, and soft skin;
his fingers are even, as are his nails, and the spaces between his fingers and nails are reddish.
With a smooth and deep resonance, rounded arms, and mighty limbs;
with arms reaching to his knees, a lion-like face, and a body as firm as a lion’s, that youth shines forth,
radiant like a thousand suns.
He who shines as the Lord, the self of all beings, the Lord who brings all beings into existence—
him, the Prajāpati, being pleased, bestowed with the eightfold sovereignty.
The eternal one among the Prajāpatis, the Sādhyas, and the thirty gods,
was being praised with all manner of hymns by sūtas, māgadhas,
and bards, as well as by highly fortunate ṛṣis who had mastered the Vedas and their auxiliary sciences.

Then, having issued orders for the arrangements in Dvārakā and having entrusted Satyaki with the task, saying, "Let Dvārakā be protected," the mighty-armed and powerful Vāsudeva set his mind upon departing.
The god [Viṣṇu] was mounted upon Garuḍa, and behind him was Halāyudha;
following even behind Bala was Pradyumna, the crusher of enemies.
Then the voices of the sūtas, māgadhas, and bards were heard:
"Victory to Bāṇa, O mighty-armed one, and to those who are his followers in battle!
For no one is able to stand before him in the great fray."
In your favor, prosperity is certain, and in your prowess, victory;
you shall conquer in battle the enemy, the lord of the Daityas, along with his army.
Standing in the midst of the sky, Keśava proceeded toward the battle, listening from all sides to the words of the hosts of Siddhas and Cāraṇas and of the great ṛṣis.

proof-read by Peter Bisschop. This is the version of April 5, 2004.
Vaiśampāyana said: Then, with the sounds of trumpets and the great blasts of conch shells, and by all the bards, chroniclers, and panegyrists by the thousands, [the assembly was awakened].
Victory, victory, O Lord of the World! Victory, O wielder of the discus and the mace!
Victory, O abode of the three worlds! Victory, O you who consist of the entire universe!
Victory to you, seated upon the lotus arisen from your navel, O Four-faced One!
Victory to you, who illumine the three worlds with the rays of the Kaustubha jewel!
Victory to you, O abode of glory, whose two lotus-feet rest upon a lotus;
victory to you, the Lord of all, the threefold light; victory to you, the Grandfather of the worlds!
Victory, O Lord of Sacrifice, O God! Victory, O Hari, Teacher of the Universe!
Victory, O You whose lotus-hands shine with the discus, mace, conch, and lotus!
Victory to you, whose thousand-fold circle of arms raises weapons such as the Śārṅga bow;
victory to you, who have consumed the entire host of Asuras with the fire of your discus!
Victory to you, O lotus-foot that awakens the mind-lotus of the yogis!
Victory to you, O Hari, who holds the three worlds within your own single foot!
Victory to you, the cause of all causes, the source of maintenance, dissolution, and creation!
Victory, O Viṣṇu, Hṛṣīkeśa! Victory over the great asura Bāṇa!
Thus was he indeed praised by men with uplifted faces and blessings of victory.
Hari assumed a form resembling that of Soma, Arka, and Śakra.
The form of him as he was about to spring upward shone exceedingly, O blessed one,
like that of Vainateya when he is strengthened by the splendor of Hari.

"Remembering again and again that form of Hari, Govinda, who bears the conch, the discus, and the mace, we do not yet attain satiety, even though we contemplate him constantly. Then Kṛṣṇa appeared with eight arms, resembling the very form of a mountain."
The lotus-eyed one shone forth, desiring the destruction of Bāṇa.
The sword, discus, mace, and arrows are situated on his right side;
likewise, the shield, the Śārṅga bow, and the conch are on his left.
Indeed, a thousand heads were ordained for him by the wielder of the Śārṅga bow,
and at that time Saṃkarṣaṇa bore a thousand bodies as well.
With his white weapon, invincible like the peaked Mount Kailāsa,
Rāma sat upon Garuḍa like the rising moon.
The body of the high-souled Sanatkumāra appeared,
like that of the mighty-armed Pradyumna when he was about to display his prowess in battle.
Shaking many mountains with the forceful flapping of his wings,
that powerful one proceeded along the path, obstructing the wind.
Then Garuḍa, having attained a speed even greater than that of the wind,
descended upon the auspicious path frequented by hosts of Siddhas and Cāraṇas.
Then Rāma spoke these words to Kṛṣṇa, who is incomparable in battle:
"O Kṛṣṣṇa, why are we deprived of our own splendors, as if something unprecedented has occurred?"
"We have all become golden in hue; of this there is no doubt. Tell us the truth of this: have we come to the side of Mount Meru?"
The Blessed One said:
"O subduer of enemies, I believe Bāṇa’s city is nearby;
this fire stands blazing here, restrained for the sake of its protection."
O Halāyudha, we were struck by the radiance of the Āhavanīya fire; by that, this disfigurement of our complexions has arisen.
Rāma said:
"If they are standing nearby, or if they have lost their luster,
then by your own intelligence, determine what is beneficial to do next in this situation."
The Blessed One said:
"O Vainateya, perform that which is our immediate task;
once you have carried out the preliminary arrangement, I shall perform what follows."
Having heard these words of the high-souled Keśava,
and having heard what Vāsudeva had spoken, the mighty Garuḍa, who can assume any form at will, created a thousand faces.
Then the powerful son of Vinatā quickly approached the Gaṅgā.
Having plunged into the celestial Gaṅgā and drunk a great deal of water,
the powerful son of Vinatā, the wise Vainateya, rose up above and rained down; by that means, he extinguished the fire.
Taking up much water with his two wings, he rained it down;
having taken that water, he sprinkled it upon the fire,
and thus the Āhavanīya fire attained peace.
Seeing that the Āhavanīya fire had been extinguished by the celestial Gaṅgā,
Suparṇa was struck with great wonder and spoke these words.
"Oh, what power indeed belongs to Agni, who at the end of the eon would burn [the world]!
Yet the wise Kṛṣṇa has rendered even that very [power] disfigured by its color.
It is my conviction that these three are sufficient for the three worlds."
Kṛṣṇa, Saṃkarṣaṇa, and the exceedingly powerful Pradyumna.
Then, once the fire was extinguished, that king of birds set forth,
making a terrible and great sound by the flapping of the strength of his own wings.
Seeing them there, the fires who are the attendants of Rudra—
having been previously appointed by the wielder of the trident for the protection of the city—
became exceedingly enraged and spoke while setting the ten directions ablaze.
"Indeed, these beings of various forms, inspiring fear, are mounted upon Garuḍas;
for what purpose have they arrived here, and who are these three persons?"
Those fires of Girivraja did not reach a definitive conclusion;
they continued the battle with those three Yādavas.
As they were engaged in battle, a very great clamor arose.
And having heard that great roar like the shouting of lions,
the wise Aṅgiras then dispatched his own man, saying:
"Go without delay to where that battle is taking place."
Then, commanded by Bāṇa, a man swift as thought,
having seen all that, was told, "Come here," and then, bowing low, he departed in haste.
Having said "So be it," he watched that battle as it unfolded—
the great conflict in which the fires were engaged with Vāsudeva.
All those Jātavedas— Kalmāṣa, Khasṛma,
Dahana, Śoṣaṇa, and the mighty Tapana—
are the five renowned fires in the domain of the Svadhākāra.
Then other highly fortunate beings, stationed with their own divisions,
were seen as blazing fires in that great battle:
Paṭara, Pataga, Svarṇa, Agādha, and Bhrāja.
Those five fires also, which have the utterance of "svāhā" as their basis, fought.
Furthermore, the two portions of the *jyotiṣṭoma* oblation, which are the substrates for the *vaṣaṭ*-call,
were again the two fires; those two great-souled and highly effulgent ones contended with each other,
and between them shone the powerful great seer Aṅgiras.
Having seen the descendant of Aṅgiras standing upon a fiery chariot, brandishing a radiant trident,
Kṛṣṇa, the Supreme Person, spoke these words as if smiling again and again.
"Stay, O fires! I have ordained this fear for you;
burnt by the power of my weapon, you shall go forth with your quarters shattered."
Then Aṅgiras rushed forward with his blazing trident,
as if seizing the life-breaths of Kṛṣṇa out of wrath in that great battle.
In that battle, with supreme arrows resembling the God of Death, he cut down his blazing trident with sharp crescent-headed shafts.
Then, with the blazing Sthūṇākarṇa weapon, which was equal to the God of Death, the highly illustrious one pierced him in the chest and let out a roar.
Then, with his limbs drenched in a flood of blood, Agni, as if reeling,
suddenly fell to the surface of the earth with his body paralyzed.
Then all the remaining fires, the four sons of Brahmā,
quickly summoned [the others] from the vicinity of Bāṇa’s city.

Then Kṛṣṇa plunged into that place where the city of Bāṇa was located. [After the additional colophon, K₁.₂ Ñ₂.₃ V B Ds D₄.₆ insert; K₃.₄ D₂.₃.₅ T₄ G₅ insert after verse 33: There he saw the city of Bāṇa, which was adorned with various kinds of trees and filled with many mansions and palaces. It was crowded with elephants, horses, and chariots, and resounded with the noise of various musical instruments. It was inhabited by hundreds of thousands of people and protected by a great army. It was guarded by many heroes who were skilled in weapons and possessed of great strength. It was surrounded on all sides by a moat filled with water and by a wall made of gold. It was like the city of the gods, frequented by Siddhas and Cāraṇas. Having seen that city, which was like the city of the gods, Kṛṣṇa spoke these words to his charioteer: "O charioteer, behold this city of Bāṇa, which is like the city of the gods. Bring me quickly to the gate of that city. Hearing Kṛṣṇa’s words, the charioteer brought him to the gate of the city. Then Kṛṣṇa, having approached the gate of Bāṇa’s city, stood there with his bow drawn. Seeing Kṛṣṇa standing at the gate with his bow drawn, the guards of the city, being terrified, fled in all directions. Some entered the city, while others went to the king. Having informed King Bāṇa of everything, they returned to the gate of the city. Then Bāṇa, hearing that Kṛṣṇa had arrived at the gate of his city, mounted a chariot and set out from the city. He was accompanied by his ministers and surrounded by a great army. Having reached the gate of the city, Bāṇa saw Kṛṣṇa standing there with his bow drawn. Seeing Kṛṣṇa, Bāṇa spoke these words: "Who are you, O hero, standing here at my city-gate with your bow drawn? Tell me truly, for I wish to know who you are. Hearing Bāṇa’s words, Kṛṣṇa replied: "I am Kṛṣṇa, the son of Vasudeva, come here to fight with you. Hearing Kṛṣṇa’s words, Bāṇa laughed and said: "O Kṛṣṇa, go back to Dvārakā; I have no quarrel with you. Kṛṣṇa, however, did not turn back, but challenged Bāṇa to battle. Then Bāṇa, enraged, discharged arrows at Kṛṣṇa. Kṛṣṇa, too, cut down those arrows with his own arrows. A great battle then took place between Bāṇa and Kṛṣṇa, like the battle between Vṛtra and Indra. With arrows, maces, swords, and clubs, they struck each other. They fought with various weapons, displaying their skill in combat. Then Kṛṣṇa, having severed Bāṇa’s bow and arrows, struck him with a mace. Struck by the mace, Bāṇa fell to the ground, unconscious. Seeing Bāṇa fallen, his ministers surrounded him and carried him away. Then Kṛṣṇa, having defeated Bāṇa, entered the city and was honored by the citizens. Having stayed there for some time, he departed for Dvārakā. Thus ends the [section] concerning the defeat of Bāṇa.

Vaiśampāyana said: Then, having seen Bāṇapura from afar, Nārada spoke.
Behold this very city of Śoṇitapura, O mighty-armed Kṛṣṇa!
Here the immensely radiant Rudra dwelt together with Rudrāṇī,
and Guha also resided there constantly for the sake of Bāṇa’s protection and for the purpose of ensuring security.
Having heard Nārada’s words, Kṛṣṇa then spoke as follows:
"O great sage, let that which concerns the welfare of this matter be heard."
If Rudra should indeed descend for the protection of Bāṇa,
we too shall certainly fight with him there according to our power.
While Kṛṣṇa and Nārada were thus disputing there,
they were brought by Garuḍa with such speed that it took but a moment;
then the lotus-eyed one, having brought the conch shell, placed it in his mouth.
In that battle, Kṛṣṇa blew [his conch], filling the quarters with its roar;
he blew it with the force of the wind, like a cloud pouring forth the moon.
Then, having blown that conch shell and instilled fear,
the heroic Viṣṇu, having conquered Agni, the guardian of Bāṇa’s city,
entered the city of Bāṇa, whose deeds were wonderful.
Vaiśampāyana said:
Then, having reached the city of Bāṇa, Janārdana blew his conch;
thereafter, Balabhadra indeed blew an unsurpassed conch.
And Pradyumna, filled with rage, blew his unsurpassed conch;
Garuḍa, by the wind from his wings, shook Bāṇa’s army.
And, O Great King, a tumultuous sound like the roar of the four oceans arose toward Bāṇapura;
then, with the blare of conchs and the great sounds of kettledrums, it resounded.
The divisions of arrows suddenly equipped themselves for battle on all sides.
Then that great army of Kiṃkaras,
with its many millions of blazing weapons, advanced toward him in battle.
That [mass] was incalculable, gathered into one, resembling a great dense cloud,
appearing like a heap of blue collyrium, immeasurable, and likewise inexhaustible.
With their weapons blazing, those Daityas, Dānavas, and Rākṣasas,
led by the chiefs of the Pramatha hosts, fought while joined with Kṛṣṇa.
Then, from all sides, those fierce yakṣas, rākṣasas, and kiṃnaras— with flaming mouths like blazing fires—
rushed forward and drank the blood of even the four [protectors] in that battle.
Then the mighty-armed Rāma spoke these words to Keśava;
and having encountered that army, the exceedingly powerful Balabhadra there uttered speech that destroys the strength of the enemy.
O Kṛṣṇa, Kṛṣṇa, O mighty-armed one, inflict great fear upon them!
Thus urged by the wise Balabhadra, Kṛṣṇa,
the Supreme Person and best among those skilled in weapons, took up the fiery weapon (āgneya-astra), which possessed a radiance equal to Yama, the Ender.
Having shaken off the hosts of flesh-eating asuras by the power of his weapons,
he proceeded with haste toward where that army was seen.
Armed with spears, sharp-edged pikes, javelins, double-edged swords, the Pināka bow, and iron clubs,
that army, consisting mostly of the Pramatha hosts, took its stand upon the earth.
With Vetālas and Piśācas, resembling mountains and clouds, of various forms and terrifying, devouring flesh,
all the warriors stood there together with their mounts in great numbers.
Like clouds driven by the wind, or like mountains scattered about.
There, it shone with numerous divisions consisting of many archers,
as well as with clubs, swords, spears, maces, and iron bludgeons.
That innumerable army rushed forward and shone brilliantly on all sides.
Then Saṃkarṣaṇa spoke to the god Madhusūdana;
having mounted Vainateya and seen them, Rāma said to Kṛṣṇa:
O Kṛṣṇa, Kṛṣṇa, O mighty-armed one, O Supreme Person, I desire to fight in battle with these [heroes] together, against this army that is now seen.
To Rāma, who was speaking thus, Kṛṣṇa addressed these words:
"This very same thought has arisen in me as well," he said to him;
"for this desired wish had already occurred to me long ago."
I wish to encounter these men together, who are fierce in battle.
As I fight facing the east, let Suparṇa indeed be before me;
let Pradyumna be on my left side, and you likewise on my right.
"Furthermore, we must protect one another in this terrible great battle.
Speaking thus to one another, they mounted the best of birds.
Then the wielder of the plow engaged in a great battle with the plow;
Rāma slew thousands and tens of thousands of the sons of Diti in the fray with maces,
clubs, and plows that resembled mountain peaks.
As the son of Rohiṇī fought, his form then became terrible,
like that of Time itself at the end of an eon, desiring to consume all beings.
Having dragged him with the tip of his plow, he crushed him with his mace;
exceedingly powerful and skilled in the ways of war, he moved through the battle.
Pradyumna, that tiger among men, warded off those thousands of fighting Dānavas from all sides with volleys of arrows.
Resembling a mass of glossy collyrium and bearing the conch, the discus, and the mace,
Janārdana blew his conch shell many times and fought.
In that battle, the majestic son of Vinatā struck down his enemies with blows from his wings and mangled them with the tips of his beak and his talons.
Led by the wise son of Vinatā into the presence of Vaivasvata,
that army of Daityas, being struck by those of terrible prowess and assailed by a rain of arrows, was then shattered in the battle.
Having utterly defeated Kaiṃkara’s army, Hari, who is honored by the worlds,
blew his great conch Pāñcajanya, which strikes fear into the Daityas; as the ranks were being shattered, he advanced, desiring to protect them.
In the meantime, O King, Nārada departed from the battlefield for Kailāsa, which resembles Mount Meru; having been seen by Rudra and honored, he was asked:
"O divine sage, tell me why you have arrived here."
Then, O lord of the earth, the celestial sage Nārada laughed and said to Rudra:
"O Lord, Bāṇa is indeed being slain by Kṛṣṇa, the wielder of the plow."
His entire army was indeed broken and did not stand its ground.
"Why do you remain unconcerned today, when your master is reportedly suffering?
Render him assistance, for you are dependent upon your devotion to him."
Having heard the words of Nārada, O King, Hara’s lips quivered; he let out a sigh as if some internal heat had been expelled.
To Hara, who was asking, "What shall I do?", the Lord of Beings replied:
"Go quickly to Bāṇapura and slay Kṛṣṇa and Halāyudha."
Saying "So be it," he vanished, and he too went to where Hari, the wielder of the plow, was;
Rudra then said to the Pramathas, "O best of beings, be ready!"
"Go with your weapons ready; [let] Matsyārddha and Mayūrondaravāhana go as well.
Go there, O Lord Nārada, and console Bāṇa."
"O best of Daityas, behold me come here for your sake;
I shall have those two foremost of the Yadus slain, now that they have arrived here, you dull-witted one."
Saying "So be it," Nārada then returned to Bāṇa and informed him;
thereafter, like a sky-farer on Garuḍa, he went once more to the side of Kṛṣṇa.
Rudra, however, caused the supreme preparations for the expedition to be made.

Jvara, having arrived at the battle, beheld the wielder of the plow (Balarāma) slaying the Dānavas and Daityas in the fray; he then approached to strike him— Jvara, who was three-legged, three-headed, and difficult to conquer in combat.
Terrible, with ashes as his weapon, he was like Yama, the Ender of Time;
his roar was equal to the crashing sound of a thousand clouds.
Enraged, he addressed Halāyudha with these reproachful words:
"Why do you fight me, O evil-minded one, while I am so powerful and renowned?
Why are you thus intoxicated by your own strength; do you not see me in this battle?"
Stay, stay! You shall not escape from me alive at the head of the battle.
Having spoken thus, laughing, he rushed at Halāyudha,
striking with terrible fists resembling the fire at the end of an eon and instilling fear.
As that son of Rohiṇī moved through thousands of circles in battle, his speed was such that no stationary position could be seen.
With his left arm, he threw ashes onto Balāka’s chest;
that ash, when thrown by Jvara of incomparable power,
fell with great speed upon his mountain-like body as its intended target.
That ash from his chest reached the peak of Mount Meru;
falling there in a blazing mass, it shattered that mountain summit.
The elder brother of Kṛṣṇa blazed up with rage,
sighing and yawning repeatedly, his body overcome by sleep.
Then, wandering about while repeatedly making his eyes restless,
with his hair standing on end and his eyes languid, he sighed like one whose mind was distracted.
Then Haladhara, intoxicated and deprived of his senses, said to Kṛṣṇa:
"O Kṛṣṇa, Kṛṣṇa, O mighty-armed granter of fearlessness! I am ablaze;
I am burning on all sides, my dear brother. How may there be peace for me?"
When these words had been spoken,
Halāyudha was embraced by Kṛṣṇa, the best among strikers, who laughed and spoke these words to him with his immeasurable power.
Having said, "Do not be afraid," Kṛṣṇa, out of supreme affection, then released him from that burning.
Having suddenly released Bala from the fever in that battle so that he might be pacified by ashes,
Madhusūdana Vāsudeva, becoming extremely enraged, then spoke to the Fever.
Then, in that battle, Balabhadra attained peace from Hṛṣīkeśa.
Having reached the space between them, Keśava stood ready for battle;
suddenly brandishing his arm, he spoke thus to Jvara:
"Come, come, O Jvara! Fight! Display whatever power you have in this great conflict!"
Show that [skill] to me in battle, O you who are expert in combat!
"And may you show us all that manly prowess of yours. Then, O King, Jvara— the foremost of all miseries— being thus addressed, became enraged at Hari and [seized] him with his two right arms.
And that great weapon cast forth those ashes, which were filled with flames.
When his body was pierced by the ashes, Janārdana, the god of gods,
the all-pervading Lord, then blazed up for a moment;
but Kṛṣṇa, the best among strikers, then again brought the fire to a state of calm.
Then, with those three arms shaped like serpents,
he struck Kṛṣṇa at the neck with one and on the chest with a fist.
Then Hṛṣīkeśa, filled with rage, struck him with his fist on the chest,
and that soul of all beings was likewise struck again and again on the head.
Then Jvara, brandishing his arms which were covered with veins,
struck the chest with both of them and bit the best of the Yadus.
Then the Lord of the World, unable to endure it, struck him on the face.
That tumultuous clash between those two lions among men—
the fever and the high-souled Kṛṣṇa— was great indeed.
It was like the sound of thunderbolts falling upon mountains.
Then, while the gods looked on, a most terrible battle took place with eight and three arms;
there was a truly dreadful combat involving the life-force of Kṛṣṇa’s fever-like arms.
"There must not be struck in this manner; it must be struck thus"—such was the voice that arose there.
For a moment, a battle took place between those two great-souled ones.
Then Viṣṇu desired to slay Jvara, who causes terror to the worlds;
thereupon, in the encounter, he seized Jvara— who was adorned with various golden ornaments— with his arm-bracelet,
as the Lord of the Universe, assuming a physical form, brought that indestructible sky-walker under his power in the great battle.
Chapter 111, transliterated from the critical edition (P. L. Vaidya, Poona 1969) by Arlo Griffiths (Leiden/Groningen);
proof-read by Arlo Griffiths. This is the version of April 5, 2004.
Vaiśampāyana said:
Perceiving that Jvara was dead, Kṛṣṇa, the destroyer of enemies, then hurled him onto the surface of the earth with the strength of his arms.
As soon as he was released from his arms, he entered the body of Kṛṣṇa, who possesses incomparable splendor, without casting off his own physical form.
Having entered his heart, it oppressed the best of the Yadus;
for Kṛṣṇa, possessed at that time by that fever of incomparable power, moved about on the ground as if repeatedly stumbling.
Then Kṛṣṇa yawns and stumbles greatly once more;
his body is covered in horripilation, and he is overcome by sleep.
Maintaining his composure, Kṛṣṇa, the conqueror of enemy cities and great yogi, underwent transformations while yawning again and again;
the Supreme Person, perceiving himself to be afflicted by a fever, [acted accordingly].
He then created another fever, one that destroys the previously created fever.
That Vaiṣṇava fever, having seized that other fever by its power,
delivered it to Kṛṣṇa; Hari, in turn, took back that terrible,
most fierce Vaiṣṇava fever which causes terror to all living beings.
Then the radiant one, powerful and of terrible prowess, created [him]. [Ś1 cont. after 1335*:
But Jvara, having been dispatched by Kṛṣṇa, seized that Jvara by force.
The delighted one presented it to Kṛṣṇa, and then Hari took it.
Then the exceedingly enraged and powerful Vāsudeva, full of heroism, caused that fever to issue forth from his own body by means of his own fever.
Brandishing him, he prepared to cut him into a hundred pieces upon the ground;
then the Fever proclaimed there, "O, you ought to protect me!
Then the Fever of Maheśvara and the Fever of Viṣṇu both fought each other.
Afflicted by force with the Vaiṣṇava [fever], the Māheśvara [fever] cried out;
having seized the previous fever by means of its own splendor,
that exceedingly powerful Vaiṣṇava [fever] let out a tremendous roar.
He has four arms and four faces, with all his weapons raised.
The battle between those two, mighty-armed and afflicted by fever, was tumultuous.
Then the gods, together with the gandharvas, stationed in heaven and eager for battle,
as well as all beings on every side, beheld that great conflict.
Then, in the fray, the follower of Maheśvara struck the follower of Viṣṇu.
Struck by him with his arm, it roared most loudly.
O King, he went toward the Vaiṣṇava and Raudra weapons, which were armed with ashes in battle;
then the powerful one seized them with both arms and struck [the enemy].
Striking with his other two arms, the Vaiṣṇava fever let out a tremendous roar while all the worlds looked on.
Then, O King, the fierce Fever struck him with his fist;
in that battle, he bit Keśava repeatedly with his teeth.
O King, those two foremost of fever-demons fought with great maces using only their arms, and they struck one another with their fists.
And those two world-renowned fevers let out a great roar;
then, O King, the fever belonging to Viṣṇu seized the one known as Raudra.
He struggled there in many ways; then [the other] struck him with his fist, and having struck him again with his arm, he crushed him over and over.
With his heart crushed, that most excellent fever of Śūlin quickly let out many kinds of cries and rolled about upon the ground.
Having seized the fierce one by force and dragged him back again and again,
he joyfully presented him to Kṛṣṇa and said, "What shall I do with this further?"
"O Lord of the gods, I shall slay you, or else I shall devour you!
Having said this, he let out a tremendous roar at the forefront of the battle.
Then Hṛṣīkeśa Keśava, having risen, desired to destroy the fever of Maheśvara in battle, thinking, "May the world be free from fever.
As that fever was being whirled about by him of immeasurable splendor, [the world was filled with light].
Then a bodiless voice, coming from the sky, spoke to him.
"O Kṛṣṇa, Kṛṣṇa, O mighty-armed one, increaser of the joy of the Yadus!
Do not slay this Jvara; he must indeed be protected by you, O sinless one.
When these words had been spoken, Hari himself released him.
The supreme teacher of the world—past, present, and future.
Thus addressed, Jvara then spoke these words to Hṛṣīkeśa;
that Jvara sought refuge at the feet of Kṛṣṇa, bowing his head.
Listen to my request, O Govinda, O delighter of the Yadus;
O God, O mighty-armed one, fulfill that desire of mine which I have in mind.
To him, Jvara spoke again, standing with palms joined in reverence and bowing his head to the god who was like Viṣṇu himself manifest before him.
O Jvara, obeisance to Kṛṣṇa, to Hari, to Viṣṇu, the all-powerful,
the primordial god, the divine, the ancient, the wielder of the mace.
Salutations to the one with a thousand heads and a thousand feet;
O thousand-eyed one, eternal salutations to you, the granter of fearlessness to the worlds!
Salutations to the Udgītha, O God, and salutations to the Lord of Sacrifice.
Homage to you, the eternal wielder of the discus; homage to you, who hold the sword in your hand.
Salutations to you, the infinite and the multiform, O Madhusūdana;
salutations to you, O Lord of the gods of gods, O divine Kapardin!
Salutations to you, the slayer of Rākṣasas; salutations to him who has the form of Rāghava;
salutations to the divine one, the knower of knowledge and the object of knowledge; salutations to the primordial Viṣṇu.
Homage to you, O Narasiṃha, who sported with the king of the Daityas;
homage to you, O Varāha, who lifted up the earth with your tusks.
O Trivikrama, salutations to you, the destroyer of Bali’s sacrifice;
salutations to the divine Vāsudeva, the destroyer of Kaṃsa.
Salutation to the God who is the self of all, the creator of all; salutation, salutation!
Be gracious, O Lord of the gods, O bestower of fearlessness upon those who are afraid!
I bow to the Lord of the gods of gods, the most excellent one who bestows fearlessness; O Viṣṇu, Lord of all lords, I bow to you, the wielder of the mace, the imperishable one.

"Salutations to you, O Lord of the gods of gods; I am terrified, O Destroyer of Existence! Having thus praised the Lord of the World, Jvara, as if dancing, then fell at the feet of Viṣṇu, sighing like one utterly afraid.
"Be gracious, O Viṣṇu, Lord of Gods; I am oppressed, O Janārdana.
To him Jvara spoke again: "I alone am the fever on earth;
I alone am the fever, dear one—let there be no other fever in the world."
"O ornament of the assembly, by your grace, may there be no other fever [of distress]."
The god said:
"So be it; may it be well with you, O Jvara, just as you desire.
A boon must be granted to those who seek one, and you have come to me for refuge."
The Blessed One said: "Let there be only one fever in the world; may you be as you wish. After the reference, T1.2 G1.3.4 M G(ed. insert: [k]
Then Keśava Hṛṣīkeśa, being pleased by this hymn,
became joyful and spoke to Raudrajvara:
"At the time of the end for human beings, may my [fever] serve as their means of enjoyment."
May this fever which was created by me be dissolved back into me alone.
Vaiśampāyana said:
When these words had been spoken regarding Jvara,
Kṛṣṇa, the most illustrious among those who strike, spoke these words once again.
Listen, O Jvara, to my instruction on how you shall move about in the world,
being distributed among all classes of beings, both stationary and moving.
If you desire what is dear to me, divide yourself threefold:
worship the four-footed creatures with one part, and the stationary beings with the second.
And as for that third portion of yours which will be reborn among humans,
O Jvara, having divided your body into three parts, become a bird.
That which belongs to the third [type] will certainly be fourfold for you:
the single-interval, the fourth-part, the *khoraka*, and the quartan.
Now, dwell among human beings by dividing yourself;
indeed, having divided yourself, dwell among the remaining species as well—listen to me.
Among trees, he exists in the form of insects, as well as the *saṃkocapatraka* and the famous *pāṇḍupattra*; and among fruits, he is indeed disease itself.
One should know that it becomes the dark-green moss upon the waters and the sprouting crests of peacocks;
having become frost among the lotus ponds, it also becomes saline soil upon the earth.
By my grace, you shall become a white bull among the mountains;
having become one afflicted by epilepsy among cattle, you shall also become a sterile bull.
In this way, you will exist upon the surface of the earth in various forms.
Through seeing you and even through touching you, you shall bring about the death of living beings;
except for gods and humans, no one else shall be able to withstand you.
Vaiśampāyana said: Having heard Kṛṣṇa’s words, Jvara became joyful in heart;
bowing with palms joined in reverence, he spoke these words.
"O Mādhava, I am blessed by your sovereignty over all births;
and furthermore, O bull among men, I wish to carry out your word. Therefore, command me, O Govinda, O mighty-armed one: what shall I do?"
The god said:
"So be it; may it be well with you, O Jvara, according to what you desire.
I am [the one] who crushes the race of the Asuras."
He who was created by Hara, the destroyer of Tripura,
has been utterly conquered by you on the field of battle;
you are my lord today, and I am your servant.
Vaiśampāyana said: Having heard the words of Jvara, Vāsudeva spoke these words:
"Listen now to the agreement that I shall declare to you with certainty."
"You two shall become fevers during times of affliction as well as at death;
likewise, during affliction you shall be my lord, and at death, he shall be mine."
"Let this fever of mine dissolve right here!
The Fever replied, "I am blessed; I am graced, since you have done what is pleasing to me."
"Command me, O wielder of the discus; what dear service may I perform for you?"
A person who praises me with this hymn joined with devotion,
while properly contemplating the wonderful battle between us, the two gods of fever,
shall not suffer any affliction born of fever upon this earth.
The Blessed One said:

"O Great Battle, that man who, having bowed to me with a single-minded heart, shall recite this account of the prowess of both you and me— whose weapons consist solely of the strength of our arms— shall indeed be freed from his fever."
May Jvara, the lord of all diseases— three-footed, having ash as his weapon, three-headed, and red-eyed— being pleased with me, grant me happiness.
May Aniruddha— those ancient seers who possess a beginning and an end,
who are subtle and vast, and who are the instructors—
destroy all my fevers.
[They are] Pradyumna, Saṃkarṣaṇa, and Vāsudeva.
Thus addressed by the high-souled Kṛṣṇa, Jvara spoke to that tiger among the Yadus: "So shall it be."
Having received the boon from Kṛṣṇa, Jvara was delighted;
he then spoke to Govinda Keśava, saying "So be it," and having bowed his head to Kṛṣṇa, he withdrew from the battle.
To Vāsudeva, the Great Soul, the bestower of fearlessness upon his devotees. — Chapter 112, transliterated from the Critical Edition (P. L. Vaidya, Poona 1969).
