Vaiśampāyana said:
Then all of them together, like three fires,
mounted Vainateya and stood ready for battle in the fray.
Then all those mighty and exceedingly powerful warriors, mounted upon the son of Vinatā, roared in battle and afflicted all the enemy ranks with showers of arrows.
Afflicted by the falling of discuses and plows and by showers of arrows,
the great army of the high-souled Dānavas grew enraged.
Like a fire that has grown in a thicket fanned by dry fuel,
the fire of Kṛṣṇa’s arrows, once arisen, attains full growth.
Scorching thousands of Dānavas at the forefront of that battle,
he shone resplendent like the blazing fire at the end of an eon.
There, eighty thousand nāgas were slain,
and a hundred thousand hosts of chariots were destroyed by Keśava’s arrows.
A hundred thousand horses and ten thousand foot soldiers were likewise utterly destroyed; that vast army,
though raising various weapons, became intent on flight as it was being torn asunder.
Having approached the army and restraining it, Bāṇa spoke these words:
Having met with such humiliation, why are you so overwhelmed by fear that you flee from this great battle, you who were born of the lineage of the Daityas?
Casting aside armor, swords, maces, and spears, and discarding again and again their scimitars, shields, and battle-axes, why do you proceed as if moving through the sky?
One should not go away while honoring one's own caste, one's dwelling, and even association with Hara; for here I am, firmly established.
Hearing those words thus uttered, and indeed regarding them as inconceivable,
all those Dānavas, oppressed by fear, fled away.
Then, that remnant of the Pramatha host, led by their commander and consisting of those who had survived the rout,
again set its mind upon battle.
The powerful Kumbhāṇḍa, the minister and friend of Bāṇa,
beholding the army broken, spoke these words:
Here stands Bāṇa in battle, as do Śaṅkara and Guha;
for what reason have you abandoned the fight, bewildered by fear?
"Abandoning your lives, fight, all you foremost of Dānavas!
Though they were thus being praised by the high-souled Kumbhāṇḍa, those Daityas did not even stand their ground; they fled in every direction.
Hearing these words of the kumbhāṇḍas, they were overwhelmed by fear;
terrified by the dread of the wheel-fire, they all fled in the ten directions.
Then, seeing his army broken by Kṛṣṇa of immeasurable splendor, Sthāṇu,
with blood-red eyes, turned toward the battle.
In order to protect Bāṇa,
the god [Śiva] and Kumāra likewise mounted a radiant chariot, indeed a chariot resembling fire;
thus says Vaiśampāyana.
Then the powerful Śiva Hara, manifest in person, became enraged; equipped with a sword,
an axe, a trident, quivers, armor, arrows, and a bow,
he mounted his chariot accompanied by Nandīśvara.
With his lips bitten together, Rudra runs toward wherever Hari is.
Following him were vetālas and piśācas wearing garlands of moons,
drinking copious amounts of blood— fearsome beings with sunken bellies.
Then there was a loud-voiced chariot yoked with lions, which seemed to drink up the very sky.
The chariot shines like the moon on the night of the full moon when released from the clouds.
Then, amidst thousands of hosts of terrifying forms of various kinds,
uttering diverse roars, that chariot of the god moved fearlessly.
Some there had the faces of lions and likewise the faces of tigers;
others there with the faces of serpents, horses, and camels trembled, being greatly oppressed;
and some there of great strength had serpents as their sacred threads.
And those with the faces of donkeys, camels, and elephants, as well as those with the necks of horses, stood there.
Some had the faces of goats and cats, while others had the faces of rams;
some wore bark garments, others wore crests, and still others had matted hair with their locks standing upright.
Broken, they fell amidst the sounds of conchs and drums;
some there had gentle faces and were adorned with divine weapons.
Wearing wreaths made of various flowers, bearing diverse weapons and missiles, they were both dwarfish and misshapen, clad in the skins of lions and tigers;
with great fangs dripping with blood, they were fond of offerings of human flesh.
Then, surrounding the god who crushes great enemies,
they stood playfully, facing forward toward the battle.
Then, seeing the divine chariot of Rudra of unwearied deeds,
Kṛṣṇa mounted Garuḍa and went forth to meet Rudra in battle; and Hara, the foremost of gods, advanced against him as he approached seated upon Vainateya, discharging his weapons.
"Stay! Stay! he cried out, enraged and arrogant with egoism.
The Blessed Lord Govinda also remained there as if smiling and said, "I stand here for your battle; do as you wish.
Enraged, he pierced Hari with a hundred iron arrows.
Afflicted by those arrows from Hara, the slayer of enemies,
Hari became enraged and seized the supreme Pārjanya weapon.
Then the earth, oppressed by Viṣṇu and Rudra, trembled.
There, the nāgas, being tormented, writhed with their faces turned upward;
the mountains there were set in motion and drenched by torrents of water.
There, some peaks on all sides gave way,
as did the cardinal directions, the intermediate directions, the earth, and even the sky.
At the conjunction of Sthāṇu and Kṛṣṇa, things appear as if ablaze,
and thunderbolts fall upon the surface of the earth from all sides.
And auspicious beings of fearsome appearance roared out inauspicious sounds;
Vāsava thundered terribly, and he also rained down blood.
A meteor stood covering the faces of Bāṇa’s army;
the wind did not blow, and the celestial bodies fell into agitation.
The medicinal herbs lost their luster, and the sky-dwellers did not move about.
In the meantime, Brahmā, surrounded by all the hosts of gods,
learned that Rudra was rising up to destroy Tripura and approached him.
Then the Gandharvas and Apsarases, as well as the Yakṣas, Vidyādharas,
and hosts of Siddhas and Cāraṇas, remained stationed in the sky, watching.
Then that Pārjanya weapon, discharged by Viṣṇu against Rudra,
went blazing forth toward where Rudra stood upon his chariot;
thereafter, hundreds of thousands of straight-knotted arrows [issued from it].
They fled in all directions from wherever the body of Hara was.
Then Rudra, the best among those skilled in weapons, being enraged, released the great and fierce Agneya weapon; it was like a marvel.
Then, their bodies shattered on all sides,
even those four were no longer visible, being covered by arrows and consumed by fire.
Then all living beings were terrified and the gods were overwhelmed by fear;
then all the foremost asuras let out lion-roars,
perceiving that Hari had been slain when he vanished within the fire.
Then, having withstood that weapon in battle, Hṛṣīkeśa, the best among those skilled in weapons, became enraged; the powerful Vāsudeva then warded off the mass of fire and seized the Vāruṇa weapon.
When the Vāruṇa weapon was raised by the wise Vāsudeva and discharged by Vāsudeva— this Vāruṇa weapon of exceeding brilliance— the Āgneya weapon was extinguished by the power of the Vāruṇa weapon.
When that weapon had been repelled by Vāsudeva in the encounter,
Bhava released four other weapons— the Paiśāca, the Rākṣasa, the Raudra, and the Āṅgirasa— which resembled the fires at the end of an eon.
Vāsudeva, having seen those weapons indeed discharged by the Brahmin,
then released the Vāyavya, Sāvitra, Vāsava, and Mohana weapons for the sake of neutralizing the Varuṇa weapon.
Having warded off those four weapons with four of his own, Keśava took up the Vaiṣṇava weapon, which resembled the gaping mouth of Death.
But when the Vaiṣṇava weapon was released, all the foremost Asuras,
as well as the hosts of Bhūtas and Yakṣas and the entire army of Bāṇa,
fled in every direction, their eyes bewildered by fear.
Vaiśampāyana said:
When the army, which was mostly composed of the Pramatha hosts, had been shattered, the great asura Bāṇa then emerged, hastening toward the battle.

He was surrounded by the lords of the Daityas, who were possessed of great strength, heroic great chariot-warriors with terrible and fearsome weapons, just as the wielder of the thunderbolt is surrounded by the best of the gods.
With recitations of mantras and likewise with medicinal herbs,
the high-souled ones performed a rite for his well-being;
there he [received] garments and auspicious cows.
Likewise, fruits, flowers, and gold coins.
The son of Bali quickly bestowed wealth upon the most excellent brahmins, like the Lord of Wealth himself;
he possessed a chariot with a thousand suns and many small bells.
Variegated with gold from the most excellent Jambū river.
And that great chariot, possessing a thousand moons and ten thousand stars, shone like a fire;
mounted upon it was he who had been seized by the Dānavas.
He holds a great banner, he wields a bow, and he carries arrows.
Intending to uproot the bulls among the Yadus,
he assumes an exceedingly fierce form;
impetuous and crowded with a multitude of heroic chariots, he advances.
The ocean of Daityas set out toward them.
Like an ocean agitated by waves arising from the great sea for the destruction of the world,
[the beings] appeared with terrifying forms that inspired dread.
Those forces shine before him.
O King, those great chariot-warriors with their uplifted bows were like forests together with mountains,
having emerged from their dwelling in the waters of the ocean.
And he was desirous of witnessing that most wonderful battle.
When the world was enveloped in darkness and the Three-Eyed One blazed forth,
neither Nandin, nor the chariot, nor Rudra could be seen.
Then, while the gods looked on, the trident-wielder Bhūtātman, his body twice as radiant through both fury and power, seized the weapon named Nārāyaṇa with the intent to slay Nārāyaṇa.
And Rudra, born from the self of Brahmā, released that weapon according to his power;
once released by him, the weapon went toward [the enemy] nearby.
Then Keśava, laughing, playfully seized that weapon of Śaṅkara; Viṣṇu took it and cast both the weapon and the two quivers aside.
Enraged in the form of Rudra, he was Rudra himself, possessing the form of universal destruction.
Then, taking up his trident which tears asunder all enemies and causes terror to the gods, dānavas, gandharvas, yakṣas, pannagas, and rākṣasas, Śaṅkara discharged it, aiming at Kṛṣṇa.
And Hari, seeing that spear, warded it off with his own power.
Then Trilocana, enraged like Yama the Destroyer at the end of time,
seized with his own power the Pāśupata weapon— which is renowned in the world for its inherent might and equal to himself— in order to slay Keśava by force.
Then, having understood that, Viṣṇu took up that very weapon.
For when those two weapons had been pacified by being restrained by the other two,
the Four-faced One then took up the arrow that brings about the end of Tripura.
"The splendor arising from Agni, Māruta, Soma, and Viṣṇu—
by means of this, I shall slay him in battle along with his kinsmen and his sons."
Thinking thus, Virūpākṣa, the destroyer of Dakṣa’s sacrifice,
the three-eyed one, fixed an arrow upon his bow, desiring to shoot it;
he was perceived by the high-souled Vāsudeva, who knows the thoughts of others.
Thinking, "The Lord of Beings has indeed resolved to kill me with this arrow," Kṛṣṇa then began a countermeasure;
that Supreme Person took up a weapon named Jṛmbhaṇa.
Then, by means of that weapon purified by mantras, the swift-acting and mighty Keśava, Kṛṣṇa, caused Hara to yawn.
Then Keśava, the one of great strength, took up the weapon named Vijṛmbhaṇa; with that weapon he caused Hara to yawn. Together with his arrow and his bow, Hara was quickly made to yawn by it.
The Blessed One, the conqueror of asuras and rākṣasas, lost consciousness.
Having seen himself expanded, complete with arrow and bow, [he repeats them] in their proper place. :k] :

Then Bāṇa, intoxicated by his own strength, repeatedly urged Śarva,
saying, "Create another creation," in order to increase his arrogance.
Then, creating another power for the sake of increasing his pride,
the Soul of Beings let out a roar with a smooth and deep sound;
at that time, the mighty Kṛṣṇa blew his conch shell.
And while that Hari was yawning, Keśava blew his conch shell,
twanged his Śārṅga bow, and let out a lion’s roar.
Overcome by helplessness through the power of the yawning,
by the roar of the Pāñcajanya conch, and by the twanging of the Śārṅga bow,
all living beings were terrified upon seeing the God thus expanded.
The Dānavas likewise fled toward the cardinal and intermediate directions,
and Bāṇa also, O King, being utterly terrified, took heart.
Then, O King, as the wielder of the trident looked on, the army raised a cry of "Alas!
and the foremost of the Dānavas stood with their faces turned away, bewildered as to what should be done, thinking, "What shall we do? Where shall we go?"
Then Rudra, suddenly stupefied by the Jṛmbhaṇa weapon,
his mind bewildered as to what ought and ought not to be done, did not know what to do.
Meditate, O dear one, with your mind upon Viṣṇu— the Father, who is attainable through devotion, who transcends the senses, who is higher than the highest, the Lord of the lords of all worlds,
the Sovereign Nārāyaṇa, Kṛṣṇa, the Infinite, the Supreme Person.
"If Dharma were superior, it would be right for me to withdraw.

Janamejaya said:
When the god and the high-souled Kṛṣṇa had departed from there,
how did the hair-raising battle with the enemies resume?
At that time, Guha stood upon a chariot whose horses were controlled by Kumbhāṇḍa.
And he rushed toward Kṛṣṇa, as well as Balarāma and Pradyumna.
Then Guha, the foremost of Kumāras, roaring and incensed by indignation and rage, pierced them in battle with hundreds of fierce arrows;
Guha struck them in the encounter with hundreds of thousands of shafts.
In that battle, Guha struck Vāsudeva with a thousand arrows, Bala with a hundred,
and Pradyumna with a thousand shafts;
their bodies covered by the flood of arrows, those three appeared like the three fires.
Then, with their limbs drenched in streams of blood, they fought back against Guha.
Then those three, skilled in the ways of battle and blazing with radiant energy, pierced one another with three unsurpassed weapons: the Vāyavya, the Āgneya, and the Pārjanya.
Having warded off those weapons with three very powerful weapons,
that son of Agni pierced them with arrows— namely the Śaila, Vāruṇa, and Sāvitra weapons—
as he held his blazing bow and discharged a flood of flaming shafts.
By means of the illusions of their weapons, they swallowed the showers of arrows belonging to that great-souled one.
When that flood of arrows had been dispersed, Guha, inflamed by supreme rage and as if blazing with splendor,
became furious and [discharged] the weapon named Brahmashiras, which was as formidable as Time itself and difficult to withstand.
Then, in that battle, Guha seized him with his lips firmly bitten together.
Then he employed the Brahmaśiras weapon, which possessed a radiance equal to the thousand-rayed sun,
fierce, supremely difficult to withstand, and capable of destroying the worlds.
While all beings were fleeing in every direction, burning on all sides,
and while all the great elements were scattering hither and thither,
the Lord [appeared] when the world was despondent and utterly bewildered by the splendor of the weapon.
The heroic Keśava, the slayer of Keśin, seized his discus.
In the world, the discus of the great-souled Apraticakra is renowned for its power to ward off and destroy all the forces of other weapons.
By that Brahmashiras weapon, he rendered it lusterless with his power,
just as the great orb of the sun is obscured by clouds at the end of the summer heat.
Then, when that Brahmāśiras weapon had lost its luster and its great power was destroyed, he seized a golden spear.
With eyes bloodshot with rage,
Guha blazed in battle like a fierce fire fed with oblations.
The divine Śatrughnī, blazing and unfailing, beloved yet terrible, bringing fear to all the worlds—
like a great meteor, radiant, with a splendor equal to the fire at the end of an eon.
Enraged, Guha hurled a spear adorned with a garland of bells.
And he also let out a powerful roar that struck fear into his enemies.
Then, hurled by that high-souled one who is devoted to Brahman, that great spear—
yawning as it were in the sky with its mouth blazing forth— rushed forward,
desiring the slaughter of Kṛṣṇa.
Then all the Vidyādharas, Gandharvas, and Ṛṣis,
as well as those led by Indra and preceded by all the immortals, became deeply despondent upon seeing the blazing spear; they cried out, "Kṛṣṇa is burnt!"
But as that great spear approached him in the great battle,
he rebuked it with a mere "hum" sound and cast it down to the ground.
When the great spear had been hurled, all the gods, together with Indra, uttered a lion’s roar from every side, crying, "Excellent! Excellent!"
Then, while the gods were roaring, the powerful Vāsudeva again seized that discus which brings about the end of all beings.
Enraged, Balarāma seized the pestle and the plow;
then Bhīma became like the god Guha, and [the enemy] was forgotten regarding what ought to be done.
While the discus was being whirled by Kṛṣṇa of immeasurable splendor, [the enemy was struck down].
Then, having divided her own body for the sake of protecting the prince,
Kauṭavī stood before him;
at the word of the god, the naked Kauṭavī took her stand there.
The highly fortunate one named Lambā is likewise the eighth portion of the Goddess;
she is Citrā, possessing a golden spear, and stands naked in the intermediate space.
Then, seeing the queen between him and the prince, the mighty-armed Madhusūdana turned his face away and spoke these words:
"She is naked, hideous, smoke-colored, terrifying, and has a sunken belly."
Stretching out his arms, as if suddenly swallowing the vast sky, he cried out, "Begone! Begone! Fie, fie upon you!"
Why do you thus create an obstacle for one who is resolved upon his own death?
Vaiśampāyana said:
O Lord, as soon as she heard his words,
Kautavī did not even adjust her garment, out of concern for protecting the prince.
The Blessed One said:
"Having quickly led Guha away, depart from the field of battle;
for in this way there will be well-being today, and you shall be released by me in combat."
And seeing her standing at the head of the battle, the divine Lord Hari,
the younger brother of Vāsava, then withdrew his discus.
When these words had been spoken by the wise God of gods,
the Goddess withdrew Guha and came into the presence of Hara.
While this period of great danger was thus unfolding,
Bāṇa arrived at that place where the prince had been protected by the goddess.
Seeing Guha withdrawn from the battle after being released by Kṛṣṇa, Bāṇa thought there: "I myself will fight Mādhava. Therefore, O Vaktrākṣī, go to where Skanda approaches.
"This alone shall be his supreme [attainment], of this there is no doubt.
Vaiśampāyana said:
"There, the hosts of Bhūtakṣaya and the entire army of Bāṇa [were destroyed]."
They all fled in every direction, their eyes bewildered by fear.
When the army, abounding in hosts of violent spirits, had been shattered, the great asura Bāṇa then rushed forth from there, hastening toward the battle.
With those lords of the Daityas, who were great chariot-warriors, possessed of terrible and fearsome weapons,
endowed with great strength and great heroism, like the best of the gods led by the wielder of the thunderbolt.
The domestic priests, proclaiming the slaughter of the enemy,
as well as others who were advanced in learning, character, and age,
[performed their rites] with prayers, mantras, and medicinal herbs.
They performed a rite for the well-being of the Great-Souled One;
and he, being enraged, cursed her: "Whatever great fruit has been obtained by one who, endowed with devotion, offers salutations to me for twelve years, [that fruit shall be his]."
Then, by the mere sight of him, let that great fruit of yours perish;
henceforth, remain always naked, or stay as you please.
Having spoken thus, the infallible God of gods, leaving Guha behind,
then quickly turned back and stood with his army and his son;
from that time forward, O King of kings, he became one clothed in the directions (naked).
Guha withdrew from the battle, while Keśava, whose banner bears the emblem of Garuḍa, advanced for the sake of combat, accompanied by Rāma and Pradyumna upon Garuḍa.
Vaiśampāyana said:
When Jvara had been conquered and both Hari and Guha were present,
there then arose the sounding of trumpets and the great roar of kettledrums.
Amidst the lion-roars of the Daityas, Bāṇa rushed toward Kṛṣṇa.
He held spears and maces, various kinds of bows,
most terrible iron clubs, and many discuses;
he bore a thousand arrows of immeasurable power.
Seeing Bāṇa come forth and standing firm for battle,
Kṛṣṇa mounted Garuḍa and went toward Bāṇa.
Then, seeing that bull among the Yadus approaching him in the fray, [Bāṇa prepared for combat].
Then, having gone a short distance and seeing his own army, Keśava beheld Kṛṣṇa of incomparable splendor mounted upon Vainateya.
Then Nāṇa, seeing the swift Vāsudeva standing before him, spoke these words in anger. Bāṇa said:
Stay! Stay! You shall not escape from me alive today;
you shall neither see Dvārakā nor the friends who dwell in Dvārakā.
"O Mādhava, today you shall see the golden-topped trees;
for today, having been overcome in battle by me who possess a thousand arms, you— though yourself eight-armed— will perish in the fray, impelled by Time."
O you whose banner is Garuḍa, how will you, possessing eight arms, encounter me in battle today with only a thousand arms?
For today, having been defeated by me in battle along with your kinsmen,
you shall remember Dvārakā when you have been struck down in Śoṇitapura.
Behold today my thousand arms, equipped with various weapons and adorned with various armlets, multiplied ten millionfold!
"I am neither Guha, nor Hara, nor Jvara, nor even the fires;
know me to be Bāṇa, the son of Bali, peerless in battle.
As he roared these words, his torrents of speech issued forth like rivers from the ocean.
Endowed with the essence of valor, these most terrible [arrows] issue forth like spray from intoxicated elephants, or like waves tossed up by the wind.
And his two eyes became agitated with rage,
like two great suns risen in the sky as if wishing to consume the world.
Overcome by death, Kṛṣṇa drank [the poison] and rushed toward Bāṇa.
At his agitation and trembling, his two eyes became red,
like two great suns risen simultaneously desiring to incinerate the world.
The Blessed One said:
O Bāṇa, why do you roar? Heroes standing in the midst of battle do not roar. Come, come! Fight in the fray; what is the use of your false boasting?
O son of Diti, if battles were won by words alone, you yourself would always be victorious; yet you speak much that is nonsensical.
"Come, come, O Bāṇa! Either conquer me or be conquered upon the surface of the earth;
after a long time, you shall lie fallen, dejected, with your face cast downward, O Asura!"
"Or else, let him be torn apart on all sides by crows, vultures,
and ravens! Having spoken these words, Kṛṣṇa pierced [his enemy] in battle with unerring, swift arrows of blazing splendor that strike at the vital organs.
Pierced by Kṛṣ�ṇa with arrows that strike the vital organs,
Bāṇa then, smiling, overwhelmed Kṛṣṇa with showers of shafts that seemed to blaze as they struck in that most dreadful battle.
Then, with arrows, swords, maces, clubs, and lances—
and then with clubs, swords, maces, lances, and spears—
the two, prepared for battle and reviling one another, moved about the field with vigor.
And with maces and sharp-edged spears, he covered Keśava.
With eight arms he fought with a thousand arms;
then, as if in play, he caused the two-armed one to fight him in battle. Then, in that conflict, [he prepared] to slay [him], just as [Viṣṇu had slain] Hiraṇyakaśipu.
The wielder of the conch, discus, and mace fought with Aṣṭabāhu against Sahasrabāhu, having encountered Bāṇa.

Beholding the agility of Kṛṣṇa, the powerful Bāṇa, son of Bali, filled with rage,
then released a weapon in the battle;

Unimpeded in battle and the destroyer of all enemies,

At that time, the wind did not stir and the clouds did not move,
even as the weapon was released by Bāṇa and Keśava was being consumed by its flames.
Then the Blessed Madhusūdana seized a most powerful weapon called Pārjanya in that battle, which resembled Yama, the Ender.
Then, as the world became free from darkness, that fire was extinguished;
all the Dānavas then became utterly frustrated in their purpose,
for the Dānava weapon was neutralized once the Parjanya weapon had been consecrated with mantras.
Then all the hosts of gods roared and rejoiced.
O great king, when his weapons were exhausted, the Daitya, overwhelmed with rage,
once again covered Keśava, who was seated upon Garuḍa,
with maces, spears, pikes, clubs, and slings.
Keśava, the slayer of enemies, again warded off that entire shower of arrows which had been raised with such force.
While that great battle between Keśava and Bāṇa was underway,
With arrows resembling thunderbolts released from his Śārṅga bow, he reduced that chariot— along with its horses, banner, and pennants— to pieces as small as sesame seeds.
The immensely radiant Keśava severed from his body the armor and the crown of great splendor,
as well as the bow and the arrow from his hand.
And smiling as it were, he pierced him in the chest with an iron shaft.
Struck in his vital organs during the battle, he, being of little strength, lost consciousness.
Seeing Bāṇa thus unconscious and tormented by the blow,
Nārada, the bull among sages, stood upon the pinnacle of his excellent palace.
Then, rising up and intent on slapping his armpits and scratching his nails, he exclaimed, "By good fortune! By good fortune! and spoke thus.
Oh, my birth has borne fruit and my life is well-lived,
since I have beheld this wondrous display of Dāmodara’s prowess!
Victory over Bāṇa, O mighty-armed one, O son of a Daitya, worshipped by the gods!
Make fruitful that purpose for which you have descended [to earth].
Having thus praised the god, Nārada then moved about the battlefield, illuminating the sky with sharp arrows that flew hither and thither.
There, the two banners rushed at one another and fought;
and a battle took place between the two mounts of the god and the daitya—
the fighting Garuḍa and the peacock.
With blows from their wings and beaks, as well as with the tips of their claws,
both the peacock and the garuḍa struck one another in rage.
Then Vainateya, enraged, seized the peacock of blazing splendor by the head and struck him with his beak.
And with his right wing, the one of great strength struck him,
having repeatedly delivered many terrible blows with his feet and sides.
Having dragged him forward with force and then pulled him back, the one of great strength cast him down unconscious, like a mountain from the sky.
When that peacock had been struck down by the bird Garuḍa,
the powerful Bāṇa, greatly agitated and reflecting upon his own purpose, suddenly fell from there with great speed.
"Overpowered by excessive pride, I did not heed the words of my friends;
while the gods and daityas looked on, I have fallen into this supreme calamity.
Perceiving Bāṇa to be thus dejected in mind and utterly distressed in battle, [he spoke].
The Lord Rudra, distressed, reflected upon the protection of Bāṇa.
Then Mahādeva spoke to Nandin with a deep voice:
"O Nandikeśvara, drive the chariot to where Bāṇa is."
"O sinless one, quickly harness Bāṇa to this divine, radiant chariot drawn by lions; it is sufficient for battle. For my mind will not remain steady while in the presence of the Pramatha hosts."
"By which you are able to prevail, my dear, protect Bāṇa; let us go."
Having said, "So be it," Nandin, the best of chariot-warriors,
went by chariot to where Bāṇa was and spoke these words slowly to him.
"O Daitya, mount this chariot quickly; come, O one of great strength!
With me as your charioteer, O hero, come and fight without delay.
Thus addressed by Nandin, Bāṇa, the crusher of enemy forces, [mounted].
"Therefore, fight Kṛṣṇa, the destroyer of the Dānavas, in battle!
Having said "So be it," he mounted that chariot of Mahādeva.
Having said "So be it," that Dānava mounted the chariot of existence.
As Bāṇa had ascended that chariot fashioned by Brahmā,
his form shone exceedingly, like that of the sun in the sky.
Just as in the past when he desired to burn down Tripura,
that best of weapon-knowers, having mounted the chariot of Bhava of immeasurable splendor, then manifested the Raudra weapon.
The exceedingly powerful Bāṇa, filled with rage, [discharged] the blazing arrow named Brahmaśiras.
When the Brahmaśiras weapon blazed forth, the world fell into agitation;
for it had been created by the Lotus-born One for the purpose of protecting the worlds.
Having destroyed that weapon with his discus, the powerful Kṛṣṇa spoke to Bāṇa,
who was renowned for his fame in the world and peerless in battle.
Where are those arrows of yours now, O Bāṇa? Why do you not boast?
Here I stand in battle; fight and be a man!
Formerly there was one named Kārtavīryārjuna, who possessed great strength;
he had a thousand arms, but in battle he was rendered two-armed by Rāma.
...who formerly possessed a thousand arms and was endowed with great strength, [was slain] by Rāma;
likewise, this pride of yours, born from the prowess of your arms, [shall likewise perish].
Your discus subdues his pride at the forefront of the battle.
"Until I have destroyed your arms that produce such pride,
and until I have quelled your arrogance today with my own arm—
stand now! You shall not escape from me today on the front line of battle."
Then, beholding that rare and most terrible battle,
which was like the conflict between the gods and the asuras, Nārada danced out of joy.
All the hosts were utterly defeated by the high-souled Pradyumna;
their arguments cast aside, they returned once more to the God of gods, saying, "Fight!
Then, like a thundering cloud at the end of the hot season, he [Pradyumna] hurled his thousand-spoked discus.
That tiger among men seized it for the purpose of subduing Bāṇa’s arms.
The splendor of the luminous Pataṅga, as well as that of the Moon,
whatever radiance belongs to the luminaries, the brilliance of the thunderbolt and lightning,
and the energy belonging to Prajāpati— all that was concentrated within his wheel.

The splendor of the three sacrificial fires, the power of the fire of the religious student, and the ascetic heat and knowledge of the seers— all that was gathered together and established within him.
The splendor and the vital breath of chaste women, that which exists in beasts and birds,
and that which resides in those who bear the discus— all that has been concentrated within the discus.
Whatever splendor belonged to the Nāgas, Rākṣasas, and Yakṣas, as well as to the Gandharvas and Apsarases,
and whatever splendor resided in the entire triple world— all that was established within the discus;
and likewise the splendor of Śambhu, Yama, and Varuṇa.
Endowed with that radiant splendor and blazing intensely,
he stood before Bāṇa and absorbed his energy with his own body.
Having perceived that the wheel of immeasurable and irresistible splendor raised by Kṛṣṇa in battle, Śiva spoke to Rudrāṇī.
"This invincible discus, which cannot be defeated in the three worlds, is being wielded by Kṛṣṇa;
O Goddess, protect Bāṇa as long as he has not been released by the discus."
Then, having heard the words of the Three-eyed One, the Goddess spoke to Lambā:
"Go, O Lambā, go quickly for the protection of Bāṇa."
Then, having composed herself through yoga, the daughter of Himavat became invisible;
she approached and revealed her form to Kṛṣṇa alone.
Seeing the Blessed One on the field of battle with his hand raised holding a discus, she appeared before him.
In the presence of Vāsudeva stood Koṭavī, clad in the directions as her garment.
Then, seeing that the goddess had returned and was united with Rudra,
standing there as a second Lambā, Kṛṣṇa,
having entered into invisibility, spoke these words after she had again cast off her two garments.
Then, for the sake of Bāṇa’s protection,
she stood upon Vijaya in the battle once more, her eyes copper-red with indignation and remaining unclothed.
Intent on protecting Bāṇa, she spoke these words:
"I shall kill Bāṇa, there is no doubt.
Thus addressed by Bāṇa, she [replied].
Desiring to protect Bāṇa,
the goddess spoke with sweet words:
"I know you, O Supreme Person, to be the creator of all beings."
To the highly fortunate Mahādeva, the infinite, the blue-hued, the imperishable,
the lotus-navelled Hṛṣīkeśa, the primordial source of the worlds;
O God of gods, Lord of the universe, Viṣṇu, Conqueror, Master of the world!
O Lord, you ought not to slay Bāṇa, who is indeed peerless in battle.
Grant indeed safety to Bāṇa, and likewise the status of being the mother of a living son.
For this boon was granted by me and is now being further protected;
O Mādhava, you ought not to make my exertion in vain.
When these words had been spoken, Kṛṣṇa, the conqueror of enemy cities, spoke these words in anger: "Listen, O passionate lady, to the truth."
Bāṇa roars, relying on his pride and his thousand arms;
their severing must be accomplished by you today, of this there is no doubt.
"And by means of Bāṇa, who has two arms, you shall become the mother of his living son;
having abandoned your asuric pride, he will not take refuge with me."
When these words had been spoken by Kṛṣṇa of unwearied deeds,
the goddess replied, "May this Bāṇa become a god among gods."
Then, having addressed that mother of Kārttikeya, Keśava said to her, "Fie, fie! O wicked woman, perish! Thereupon, the mighty-armed Kṛṣṇa, the best among strikers, became enraged.
Whirling his supreme discus, he spoke to Bāṇa in the battle.
Then the slayer of Kaṃsa’s enemies spoke these words to Bāṇa:
“Fight, fight in battle! Koṭavī stands before you; fie on your manliness, O Bāṇa, like that of those who are powerless in war!”
Having spoken thus, the mighty Kṛṣṇa, the supreme knower of weapons, then discharged that discus with closed eyes toward Bāṇa.
At whose hurling, the worlds— including all things stationary and moving—
and the flesh-eating beings, attain satisfaction in the great battle.
Raising his discus in battle, the wielder of the mace, blazing with anger, confronted him whose deeds were incomparable and who was equal to the sun in splendor.
Sapping the splendor of the Dānava with his own splendor in battle,
Śrīdhara, endowed with supreme vigor, severed his arms with his discus as it whirled rapidly upon the field of combat like a circle of fire.
But the discus of Viṣṇu, hurled by Vāsudeva at the head of Bāṇa’s battle along the path of Bāṇa’s chariot, was not seen due to its extreme velocity, appearing like a second sun.
That discus repeatedly severed Bāṇa’s thousand arms one after another at the forefront of the battle.
Having made that two-armed Bāṇa resemble a tree with its branches lopped off,
the Sudarśana discus reached Kṛṣṇa’s hand once again.
Vaiśampāyana said:
When the Daitya had been brought to his end and his wheel destroyed,
he lay there with blood streaming from his body, drenched in a flood of gore.
The great asura, with his arms severed, took on the appearance of a mountain.
Like a tree with its branches cut off, like a bird with its wings clipped.
Having cut off Bāṇa’s thousand arms and his Sudarśana discus,
he went to the side of the God of gods, the slayer of enemies.
Cakra, covered in fat, spoke to the best of speakers:
"Command me, O Lord of the World, to cut off the head of this evil-minded one."
Then Hṛṣīkeśa Kṛṣṇa took up that Sudarśana,
which emitted various roars like a cloud intoxicated with blood.
At that great roar, Keśava, the slayer of enemies,
Kṛṣṇa, suddenly brandished his discus and began to sever the head;
he, Acyuta, was desirous of hurling the discus once more for the sake of destroying Bāṇa.
Desiring to hurl the discus once more for the sake of destroying the Nāgas, Acyuta approached Mahādeva, who was accompanied by Kumāra, and spoke to him.
"O Lord Hara, accompanied by Umā and possessed by Jvara,
O Kṛṣṇa, Kṛṣṇa, Mahādeva, I know you as Puruṣottama;
for you do not desire his death, since you wish what is beneficial for Pārvatī."
Kṛṣṇa said: Hiraṇyakaśipu had four sons, world-renowned:
Hrāda, Prahrāda, Saṃhrāda, and Anuhrāda as the fourth.
A boon was granted to Prahlāda, who among them sought a boon:
"O Daitya, may your lineage be forever invulnerable to me."
Thus was it previously promised to her who had committed no offense:
[to behold] the eternal God of gods, the slayer of Madhu and Kaiṭabha.

O God, you are the primordial deity, the unborn Viṣṇu, the ancient sovereign of the gods; you are the refuge of the worlds, for this universe has been produced from you. You are invincible by the three worlds, including the gods, asuras, and humans.
Brahmā was born from your grace, and likewise I am born from your wrath;
I bow to you, Hari, the Lord of the world and the Sovereign of all beings.
I bow to you, O Viṣṇu, who are beyond qualities, the primordial and all-encompassing in battle;
I bow to you, O Lord Hari, the partless Puruṣottama.
O Janārdana, embodiment of the three Vedas and soul of the Purāṇas, I bow to you;
O Viṣṇu, you are forever invincible. I entreat you, the eternal and immutable one:
therefore, withdraw this divine discus that has been raised.
Irresistible, unassailable, and terrifying to enemies in battle.
Those men who take refuge in you, O God, are not easily perceived [as ordinary];
Janārdana is their eternal protector when they are submerged in great fear.
And those who shall recite this hymn composed by me with devotion,
they shall become free from all fear and devoid of ailment.
"You are the protector of all the worlds, and especially my own lord, O Master.
May Bāṇa be forgiven for my sake, O God, O Supreme Person.
Protection from fear has been granted to this Bāṇa by me, O Slayer of Keśin."
Therefore, my word would not be false; for this reason, I ask your forgiveness.
"For he does not wish to kill him; if he desires the welfare of Pārvatī, it must be forgiven by you again for what has been done, O you who are compassionate toward your devotees.
The Blessed One said:
"O Lord, while they still live, this arrow remains and this discus has been withdrawn;
for you, O Lord, are to be honored by both gods and asuras in every respect."
"Otherwise, I would have cut down this evil-minded Bāṇa.
Since he is always to be honored by you, O God, let Bāṇaka live.
Homage be to you; I shall depart, O Maheśvara, for that which was my purpose has been accomplished."
Therefore, it cannot be done; you ought to grant me permission.
Having spoken thus to Mahādeva, Kṛṣṇa quickly departed on Garuḍa to that place where the son of Pradyumna lay covered with arrows.
When Kṛṣṇa had departed, Nanda then spoke these auspicious words to Bāṇa:
"Go, Bāṇa, even with your wound before the God of gods."
Having heard those words of Nandin, Bāṇa departed with great speed. Then, seeing Bāṇa with his arm severed, the powerful Nandin carried him away on his very chariot and went to where the god was.
Then Nandi again spoke these further words to Bāṇa:
"Bāṇa, Bāṇa, dance! Prosperity shall be yours."
"O great Daitya Kṛttabāṇa, you shall then attain prosperity;
this god Mahādeva is well-disposed toward you with favor,
urged by the words of Nandin, as your limbs are drenched in floods of blood."
Then Bāṇa, desiring to live, indeed stood before Śaṅkara.
Having heard these words of Nandi, that Dānava, whose body was smeared with blood,
set out for the sake of his life and stood before Śaṃkara;
when fear arose, that senseless Dānava began to dance.
Victory, O God, Lord of the World! Victory, O unconquerable, O Hara, O imperishable one!
Victory, O you who are ever fond of devotion! Victory, O you who are worshipped by the hosts of beings!
Victory to you whose limbs are smeared with ashes! Victory to you, the foremost among those who know nakedness!
O Lord of Umā, Lord of the Universe, victory to you, the unconquerable and imperishable Master!
Lamenting in this manner for the sake of his own welfare,
Bāṇa then fell into a wretched state, his eyes clouded with fear.

Then Bāṇa began to dance, and the incomparable discus in battle reduced Bāṇa to having only two arms, restoring him to his natural state. Seeing him dancing again and again, agitated by fear, [the discus]—
Urged by the words of Nandin, Bhava, the Great God who bestows grace upon his devotees, being overcome by compassion, spoke these words:
"O King, he danced many times so that Bhava might be pleased."
Then, O King, Maheśvara became pleased with this Bāṇa’s effortless feat and said,
"Choose a boon, Bāṇa, whatever dwells in your mind."
I am well-disposed toward you with a gracious countenance; this time for granting boons has arrived.
"O Bāṇa, whatever boon you desire that has long been cherished by your mind,
I shall grant it to you, even if it be difficult for the gods themselves to obtain.
Having heard Rudra’s words, Bāṇa was filled with joy in his heart.
Keeping his boons in mind,
Bāṇa began to speak: "O Lord, may I be forever free from old age and immortal."
O God, if you so deem it right, let this be my first boon.
Maheśvara said: "O Bāṇa, you are equal to the gods; death does not exist for you.
Choose another boon today; you are always worthy of my favor."
Bāṇa said:
"O Bhava, just as I am smeared with blood, deeply distressed, and tormented by wounds,
may there be the birth of a son for those devotees who dance in this manner."
Maheśvara said: "For those devotees of mine who dance— being abstemious, endowed with forbearance, and devoted to truth and uprightness— for them it shall be thus."
Then,
O Bāṇa, choose a third boon that is desired by your heart.
"I shall provide that for you, my son; may you be successful here.
Bāṇa said:
"Indeed, the terrible and intense pain arising from the shattering of the discus is mine."
By this third boon, may my existence come to peace.
Maheśvara said: "So be it; may it be well with you. No pain shall arise, and your body shall remain uninjured and in a state of health."
"O best of gods, the terrible pain born from the shattering of the wheel shall not remain in your limbs, and you shall become strong.
O Asura, I grant you this fourth boon; choose what you desire."
I am not turned away from you, my dear; indeed, I am well-disposed toward you with favor.
Bāṇa said:
"O Lord, O Īśvara, may I be the first of the lineage of the Pramatha hosts; known as Mahākāla, may I attain renown."
Vaiśampāyana said:
"The god of great splendor said to Bāṇa, 'It shall be so:
through my protection, you shall possess a divine form, with limbs uninjured and free from disease.'"
"O Bāṇa, by my grace, may you be free from fear from every quarter.
Maheśvara said:
"I grant you yet another boon, O you of renowned strength and prowess."
"It shall surely be so; whatever boon you desire here, choose it, for it shall be yours—may prosperity be yours, O great asura, whatever you wish."
Bāṇa said:
"O best of gods, O Bhava, let there not be even the slightest deformity born of my body;
even though I have only two arms, let my form not be misshapen."
Hara said:
"O great Asura, all this shall be yours exactly as you desire;
for you are my devotee, and there is nothing that should not be granted to my devotees."
Then Mahādeva spoke to Bāṇa, who was standing nearby:
"O Bāṇa, it shall be exactly as you have declared."
"Abandon this foolish mindset, Bāṇa; do not fall under the sway of delusion.
Having said this much, the three-eyed Lord, surrounded by his hosts, vanished right there while all beings were looking on.

proof-read by Arlo Griffiths. This is the version of April 5, 2004.
Vaiśampāyana said:

Having thus obtained many boons, Bāṇa became filled with joy;
having attained the state of Mahākāla, he departed together with Rudra.
