After the reference, insert: Vāsudeva also questioned Nārada in many ways:
"Where is the venerable Aniruddha, bound by the fetters of the serpents?"
I wish to hear this in its true essence, for my mind is moistened with affection.
Now that the hero Aniruddha has been carried away, the city of Dvārakā is agitated;
I shall quickly liberate him for whose sake we have come here.
Today we truly wish to see him whose enemies have been destroyed;
O Blessed One of noble vows, that region is indeed known to you.
Thus addressed by Kṛṣṇa, Nārada replied:
"O Mādhava, that prince is bound by the Nāgas within the inner apartments."
In the meantime, Citralekhā quickly arrived;
[she said to] the high-souled Bāṇa, the lord of the Daityas of supreme courage:
"O Lord, enter this inner apartment as you please."
Then, for the sake of liberating Aniruddha, they all entered:
Balarāma, Suparṇa, Kṛṣṇa, Pradyumna, and Nārada;
Vāsudeva also suddenly entered the inner apartments of his enemy.
Great serpents in the form of arrows stood encircling his body.
All those arrows suddenly emerged from the body of that serpent and rushed toward the earth, returning to their natural state as arrows.
Having been seen and touched by the high-souled Kṛṣṇa,
Aniruddha became established in joy and, with palms joined in reverence, spoke these words.
O God of gods, you are always victorious in battle;
who indeed is capable of standing before you, even Śatakratu himself?
The Blessed One said, "Mount Garuḍa quickly; let us go to the city of Dvārakā.
Thus addressed, he mounted [Garuḍa] together with the daughter of the Dānava.
Then, permitted by their gurus, they set forth.
Accompanied by Citralekhā, who was his constant beloved,
those bulls among men then set out upon the long journey,
with the wielder of the discus (Kṛṣṇa) taking Aniruddha with him.
He brought Bāṇa’s wheel-weapon to naught;
having severed Bāṇa’s circle of arms,
the wielder of the discus then took Aniruddha by the hand.
When the great Bāṇa had been struck down before them by the uplifted discus, his limbs shattered and his arms mangled,
they all mounted Garuḍa after having conquered the great asura Bāṇa.
Then those high-souled ones, situated in the vault of the sky and facing the western quarter,
beheld thousands of cows of various colors roaming in the forests on the shore, bestowing divine milk.
Then, having understood that form from hearing the words of the Kumbhāṇḍa,
Kṛṣṇa— the best among strikers and truly skilled in discerning the meaning—
having observed the flight of Bāṇa’s arrows, then fixed his mind upon them.
The imperishable God, the source of all worlds, was seated upon Garuḍa.
The Blessed Lord said: O Garuḍa, go to that place where Bāṇa’s herd of cows is;
by drinking whose milk one indeed attains immortality.
Satyabhāmā said to me, "Bring me the cows of Bāṇa,
the milk of which, it is said, great asuras cannot digest even after drinking."
"Indeed, living beings who are free from old age cast off aging;
bring them to me—blessings be upon you—if your task is not thereby frustrated.
But if there should be an obstruction to your business, do not set your mind on them at all."
Thus spoke Satyā to me, and those [cows] are known to me;
these cows that are seen here, upon seeing me, all enter together toward the abode of Varuṇa. Let the necessary action be undertaken in this matter.
Having said "So be it," Garuḍa suddenly plunged into the ocean, the abode of Varuṇa, nearby, by means of the wind from his wings.
Seeing Garuḍa arrive at the abode of Varuṇa with such speed,
all the hosts of Varuṇa became bewildered and fled;
then the exceedingly formidable army of Varuṇa advanced against him.
In the presence of Vāsudeva, [he stood] with various weapons raised.
Then that battle became terrible between the followers of Varuṇa and the enemy of the serpents (Garuḍa).
But then, in the presence of the wise Vāsudeva, as those thousands of Varuṇa’s followers were attacking in the fray, [he struck them down].
Their bodies illuminated the entire ocean, the abode of Varuṇa.
With his discus, the Blessed Lord Śauri wrought a great slaughter;
the invincible army was shattered by the high-souled Keśava.
Broken, they go suddenly back to that very abode of Varuṇa.
Sixty thousand chariots and sixty hundred chariots,
equipped by Varuṇa and bearing blazing weapons, were deployed in the battle.
Those [demons] fought against Kṛṣṇa, Pradyumna, and Balarāma;
Hari suddenly struck down all of them in battle.
That army was being consumed on all sides by the floods of Kṛṣṇa’s arrows.
Having taken refuge with Varuṇa, he found no place at all to stay.
That army was being struck on all sides from every direction by powerful heroes— Baladeva, Janārdana, Pradyumna, Aniruddha, and Garuḍa— with various kinds of sharp volleys of arrows.
Then, seeing his army broken by Kṛṣṇa of unwearied deeds,
Varuṇa became enraged and went forth to where Keśava was,
accompanied by sages, gods, gandharvas, and likewise by hosts of apsarases.
Being praised in many ways, Varuṇa stood there surrounding him.
With a beautiful, white umbrella being held over him that dripped water, he stood there having raised his excellent bow.
The Lord of Waters, enraged and accompanied by the strength of his sons and grandsons,
stood with his great bow drawn as if challenging them to battle.
Blowing his conch shell, Varuṇa rushed forward;
like Hara attacking Hari in his wrath, he covered him with a net of arrows.
Then, having blown his conch shell Pāñcajanya, the mighty Janārdana filled all directions with a tumultuous rain of arrows.
Then, afflicted in battle by the many showers of arrows,
Varuṇa, as if smiling, fought back against Kṛṣṇa.
Then, standing in the midst of the battle, Vāsudeva consecrated the terrible Vaiṣṇava weapon with mantras and, stationed directly in front of him, spoke these words.
This most terrible Vaiṣṇava weapon, the crusher of enemies, has been raised by me for your destruction; stand firm now!
Then the god Varuṇa, that one of great strength, having neutralized that raised Vaiṣṇava weapon with his own Vāruṇa weapon, let out a roar.
For the waters flowing forth from the mouth of Varuṇa are spread out as his weapon;
O conqueror in assembly, they serve to neutralize the Vaiṣṇava weapon.
The waters there, belonging to Varuṇa, indeed blazed up whenever they were thrown;
then the Lord of the World, taking up his discus which was wreathed in garlands of flames and desiring to release it, appeared before Varuṇa.

Then all the Varuna weapons were set ablaze by the splendor of the discus; as all the Varuna weapons were thus consumed and the Vaiṣṇava weapon blazed forth with great power, the quarters of the sky, struck with fear, fled away.
Seeing them blazing, Varuṇa spoke these words:
"Remember that former nature of yours, which is unmanifest yet characterized by manifestation; destroy darkness, O illustrious one, for why are you deluded by passion?"
O great-minded Lord of Yoga, you have always remained established in sattva;
now completely abandon the defects based on the five elements as well as the ego-sense.
Of this Vaiṣṇava form of yours, I am indeed the eldest;
as your elder, I am worthy of your respect—why do you wish to burn me?
For fire does not prevail against fire; abandon your anger, O best of warriors!
They shall have no power over you, for you are the sovereign of the world.
For previously, that nature (prakṛti) which was created by you— consisting of transformations,
possessing attributes, and serving as the seed-state dependent upon prior attributes— [remains].
Since this world was created by you from the very beginning according to its own nature— consisting of both the fiery and the lunar elements— how can you think [otherwise] regarding me?
O you of great splendor, you alone are invincible, eternal, constant, self-existent, the creator of all beings, inexhaustible, and indeed immutable.
Protect me, protect me; I am worthy of being protected by you, O Sinless One; homage be to you!
You are the original creator of the world, and by you alone has it been multiplied.
"Why do you play, O Mahādeva, like a child with toys?
For I am not one who hates by nature, nor am I one who corrupts by nature."
O Supreme Person, you act according to the rule to bring about the cessation of the transformations of that primordial nature which abides within those very transformations.
O sinless one, you are the transformation of all transformations within the abode of transformation;
you always cause those dull-witted people who do not know the Dharma to undergo change.
For this nature is always joined with the defects; whether corrupted by tamas or by rajas, from that delusion proceeds.
O Knower of the high and the low, the Omniscient One who abides in the ordinance of sovereignty,
why do you delude us all like Prajāpati himself?
Thus addressed by Varuṇa, Kṛṣṇa, the refuge of the world,
who understands the inner state of beings, the all-knowing hero, became truly delighted in mind.
Having been spoken to in this way, Kṛṣṇa, smiling, spoke these words:
"O God of terrible prowess, bestow cows upon me for the sake of peace."
Thus addressed by Kṛṣṇa, Varuṇa, who is skilled in speech, spoke these words once more: "Listen to me further, O Madhusūdana.
Varuṇa said:
"O Lord, an agreement was previously made by me with Bāṇa;
having made such an agreement, how could I act otherwise so as to render it fruitless?"
O Lord, you alone are the breaker of everyone's compact;
thus, O Father, one's conduct is corrupted and is not praised by the virtuous.
The Lord, the partaker of dharma, always avoids him;
the sinful breaker of agreements does not attain the worlds.
Be gracious, O Madhusūdana, and let there be no violation of dharma for me.
You ought not, O Mādhava, to bind me with the breaking of my vow.
As long as I live, O bull-eyed one, I shall certainly not give away the cows.
"Kill me and take the cows; this is the agreement I have made."
And this rule has been fully explained to me by you, O Madhusūdana;
it is indeed the truth, O mighty-armed Lord of the Gods, and not false.
"If I am indeed worthy of your favor, O Madhusūdana, protect me;
or else, O mighty-armed one, if you are intent upon the cattle, take them away after killing me. I honor you as a knower of dharma, for you are dearer to me than my own life."
Since you speak the truth, you are therefore permeated by my own nature.
Thus informed by him, Kṛṣṇa, the conqueror of enemy cities,
related the entire account of Bāṇa’s conduct in the presence of Pārvatī.
Having placed the Asura Bāṇa at the forefront, Hari accepted the wealth of cattle given by Varuṇa and departed for Dvāravatī;
the glorious Kṛṣṇa, whose vehicle is Garuḍa, arrived at Dvārakā.
He dwelt together with the Vṛṣṇis, being praised by them as they gathered around him.
"O Janamejaya, O King, this domain of Bāṇa has been described to you as you asked; what more do you wish to hear?
Having been addressed thus by Varuṇa, the highly illustrious one released the cows."
Thus addressed, the highly illustrious Mādhava, having released Bāṇa’s cows and considering the inviolable nature of his pledge, withdrew his speech regarding the cattle;
then, smiling, he paid honor to the god Varuṇa.
Then, laughing, the god who is skilled in matters of meaning spoke these words; honoring Varuṇa, he released Bāṇa’s cows:
"Therefore you are released, provided that such an agreement was made with Bāṇa."
By means of extensive and sweet words that express the meaning of reality.
"O Lord Varuṇa, how could I commit a sin against you?
Go, you are released; may you be true to your promise to us.
For your sake, I have released the arrows and the cattle—of this there is no doubt."
Then, with the sounding of trumpets and the great roar of kettledrums,
Varuṇa, taking up the water of honor (*argha*), worshipped Keśava.
Then Keśava, the joy of the Yadus, having taken half of that [water] from Varuṇa,
the god worshipped Bala and remained healthy and composed.
"Having granted immunity to Varuṇa, the powerful Vāsudeva said,
'For your sake, the cows have been released from the wicked-souled Bāṇa.
Having spoken thus to Varuṇa, the god commanded, 'Release the cows of Bāṇa.'"
And he proceeded to Dvārakā, surrounded by Śakra and the other immortals.
The Lord, accompanied by the husband of Śacī, set out for Dvārakā;
there, O conqueror in assembly, were the gods along with the Maruts and Sādhyas,
as well as Gandharvas, Apsarases, and Kinnaras who travel through the atmosphere.
The sages headed by Nārada, Vasiṣṭha and others whose wealth is asceticism,
follow the Lord of the Universe, the imperishable source of all beings.
The Ādityas, Vasus, Rudras, and the two Aśvins of great strength,
as well as the hosts of Vidyādharas and others who are Siddhas and Cāraṇas,
follow him as he approaches with glory and victory.
And the highly fortunate Nārada, having seen the victory over Bāṇa and Varuṇa having had his kindness done for him, set out toward Dvārakā, well-pleased.
Seeing from afar that city of Dvārakā, garlanded with gates, those [gopas] who resembled the peaks of Mount Kailāsa and wore blue necks,
the wielder of the discus and mace produced the roar of the Pāñcajanya conch.
The god gave a signal to the inhabitants of the city of Dvārakā;
by him, the great conch was blown, filling heaven and earth with the sound of the Pāñcajanya, which resounded like the noise of a divine procession.
Having heard this, all of Dvāravatī attained incomparable joy.
Having adorned the entire city of Dvāravatī with full jars and heaps of parched grain arranged in great abundance,
he made its streets well-aligned, most beautiful, and embellished with jewels.
The brahmins, as well as the members of the clans and guilds,
took up the respectful offering (argha) and honored Mādhava— who was seated upon Vainateya and resembled a mass of black collyrium— with various shouts of victory.
The non-giving demons paid homage to Kṛṣṇa, who was endowed with supreme splendor.
The three castes in their proper order worshiped Mahābala;
likewise did the guilds led by the merchants worship Ananta, the slayer of Keśin,
while he was surrounded on all sides by sages, gods, gandharvas, and celestial minstrels.
Being thus praised, Govinda stood above Dvārakā.
Beholding that wonder, the best of the Daśārha hosts attained incomparable joy upon seeing the mighty-armed Kṛṣṇa,
the Supreme Person, returning after having conquered Bāṇa and Mahādeva.
Then, when the highly fortunate Kṛṣṇa, the great chariot-warrior of the Sātvatas, arrived, the words of the inhabitants of Dvārakā went forth in many ways.
Having traveled a long distance, Suparṇa returned swiftly and said:
"We are blessed and we are favored,
for Janārdana, the Lord of the World, with his long arms, is our protector, guardian, and defender."
Having mounted Vainateya and conquered Bāṇa, who was exceedingly difficult to defeat,
this lotus-eyed one has arrived as if gladdening the hearts of all.
While the residents of Dvārakā were still speaking thus,
those great car-warriors, the gods, entered the house of Vāsudeva.
Then Vāsudeva, Bala, Pradyumna, and Aniruddha descended from the *suparṇa* and entered their homes; meanwhile,
those celestial chariots of theirs continued to move through the sky.
They are seen remaining exactly as they were, in all their various forms on every side.
Those thousands of radiant celestial chariots are seen, adorned with lions, bulls, deer, elephants, horses, cranes, and peacocks.
Then Kṛṣṇa spoke these words to all those thousands of youths,
beginning with Pradyumna, in a gentle and sweet voice:
"These are the Rudras, as well as the Ādityas, the Vasus, and the two Aśvins."
The Sādhyas, the gods, and others likewise paid homage to them in due order.
Worship together Śakra, the thousand-eyed one, the highly fortunate, the terrifier of the Dānavas, who is accompanied by his hosts and has the elephant as his vehicle.
The highly fortunate Seven Sages have come here for my sake;
you noble-souled rishis should also pay them homage as is fitting.

"These are indeed the holders of the discus; speaking thus in every way, the oceans and the lakes have come here for the sake of my pleasure. You must also salute the cardinal and intermediate directions in due order."
And the Nāgas, headed by Vāsuki and possessed of great strength,
as well as the cows— for the sake of my pleasure— should indeed pay homage in due order.
The luminaries together with the constellations, along with the yakṣas, rākṣasas, and kiṃnaras, have indeed come for my sake; pay homage to them in due order.
Having heard the words of Vāsudeva, the princes stood bowed in reverence,
each according to his rank before all those high-souled deities.
Seeing all the inhabitants of heaven, the citizens were filled with wonder;
they then quickly returned, taking up materials for worship, exclaiming,
"Oh, what a great marvel this is, through the protection of Vāsudeva!"
For indeed, such words are uttered here: "That which is obtained by us in this world."
Then the citizens, honoring all those gods of heaven, scattered sandalwood powder and showers of flowers from every side.
Restraining their speech and intellect, all the inhabitants of Dvārakā worship the denizens of heaven with parched grain, prostrations, incense, and likewise with words.
Āhuka, Vasudeva, Sāmba the joy of the Yadus,
Sātyaki, Ulmuka, and the mighty Vipṛthu.

And [he sent] the highly fortunate Akrūra, as well as Niṣadha. *K V1 B2 Dn Ds D1.3-5 insert after 63ab; V2 B1 T2 G4.5 insert after 63:* "O best of the twice-born, go quickly to the city of Ayodhyā. There you will see the son of Daśaratha, who is endowed with great splendor. Having bowed at his feet, you must speak these words on my behalf: 'O King, O protector of the earth, I am your servant and dependent; therefore, please grant me your protection.'"
Then, O illustrious one, Śakra spoke these further words there in the assembly of the Yadus, in the presence of the slayer of Keśin as he was offering praise.
And then he spoke these words to Andhaka and Śubhākṣa.
Vāsava has joined all the Sātvatas with glory and prowess in battle; he is this very delighter of the Yadus.
Possessing exceeding splendor, he gladdens [the people] like the gods in heaven;
even as Mahādeva and Guha look on,
he has returned to Dvārakā after defeating Bāṇa in battle.
Having brought about the unsurpassed destruction of the thousand arms of the thousand-armed one and having established him in the state of having two arms, Hari returned to his own city.
That purpose for which the birth of the high-souled Kṛṣṇa among humans occurred has now been entirely accomplished; we have been made free from grief.
Drinking honey-sweet wine, we shall rejoice, filled with delight;
time will pass incessantly for us as we remain attached to sense objects alone.
By taking refuge in the arms of this great-souled one, we shall all,
like immortals, dwell happily, having entirely cast off our grief.
Having spoken thus, having embraced the lotus-eyed Kṛṣṇa,
and having thus praised Keśava, the destroyer of the Dānavas, the thousand-eyed Indra,
that illustrious one surrounded by all the hosts of gods, took his leave of him.
Then, having again embraced Kṛṣṇa, who is honored by the worlds,
and having spoken thus to all the Yādavas and worshipped Kṛṣṇa, Vāsava [departed].
And the high-souled sages [honored] the one of great luster with blessings for victory.
The yakṣas, rākṣasas, and kiṃnaras departed again just as they had come.
When Purandara had departed for heaven, the immensely powerful and highly fortunate Padmanābha inquired after the eternal welfare of them all.
Then, uttering shouts of joy by the thousands,
they went to see the Kaumudī festival; that sinless Kṛṣṇa, having reached Dvārakā with his beloved, took delight surrounded by the hosts of Yadus.
Endowed with supreme glory, he bestows all various objects of desire;
thus, O Lord of the Earth,
this Viṣṇu, the foremost of the Yadu clan, has indeed descended upon the earth, renowned as Vāsudeva.
And for these reasons, O illustrious one, the Lord was born among the Vṛṣṇis in the family of Vasudeva through Devakī, concerning which you question me.
When Nārada’s question had ceased, I told you in brief;
all those details that were previously mentioned to you, O Janamejaya, have now been told at length.
Regarding the Māthura-kalpa of Viṣṇu, concerning which you have great doubt,
I have fully explained the path of Vāsudeva.
There is no other wonder whatsoever; Kṛṣṇa is the abode of wonders. Among all things that are like wonders, there is no wonder that is not Vaiṣṇava.
He alone is the blessed among the wealthy, the creator of prosperity, and the source of fortune;
even among the gods and the Daityas, there is none more blessed than Acyuta.
The Ādityas, Vasus, Rudras, the two Aśvins, and likewise the Maruts;
the sky, the earth, the quarters, as well as water and light.
All this is Viṣṇu alone, the sustainer of the world, and none other;
he is the creator, the ordainer, the destroyer, and time itself;
he is truth, righteousness, austerity, and the eternal Brahman.
Ananta is indeed remembered as the foremost among the Nāgas, and Śaṅkara is remembered as the foremost among the Rudras.
The entire world, both moving and unmoving, originates from Nārāyaṇa;
from this Janārdana, the whole universe is produced.
The entire world is that Lord of Gods; pay homage to him, O Bhārata!

This eternal one is always to be worshipped by all the gods; this Lord of the Gods of gods is worthy of worship even by those who worship Indra. He is the one to be sacrificed to, the Lord of the Gods of gods—bow down to him, O Bhārata!
The original creator and the enjoyer, the source of all beings and existence itself—
bow down again and again, O Lord of Men, to the Lord of the World!
Always pay homage to Viṣṇu, the descendant of Yadu, the creator of all beings;
we always bow down to Hari, the Lord of the World, and to Devakī.
Meditate constantly on the Lord of the World and be supremely diligent;
Viṣṇu will always provide for your welfare, of this there is no doubt.
"Salutations! Fix your mind upon that; meditate upon that Supreme.
O best of kings, you must always worship Viṣṇu with your mind. Pay homage again and again to the Lord of the World, O Master of the Universe!"
Always meditate upon Vāsudeva, Keśava, the slayer of Keśin.
"Meditate with effort upon Nārāyaṇa, the most excellent one, who is more subtle than the subtle;
for when meditated upon, he will undoubtedly destroy all sins.
Thus have been told to you the battle with Bāṇa and the majesty of Keśava.
Upon merely hearing it, you shall obtain incomparable stability for your lineage.
And those who shall uphold this unsurpassed account of the battle with arrows and the majesty of Keśava— unrighteousness shall not take hold of them.
O King, their dharma shall be such; there is no need for deliberation on this matter.
O dear Janamejaya, since you have asked, I have now fully described to you this Vaiṣṇava conduct once this sacrifice has concluded.
O King, whoever should indeed retain this entire *Āścaryaparvan* in its entirety,
being liberated from all sins, he goes to the world of Viṣṇu;
and whoever, rising at dawn every day, should recite it with a well-composed mind.
For him, nothing whatsoever is difficult to obtain in this world or in the next.
The Brāhmaṇa shall become a knower of all the Vedas; the Kṣatriya shall be victorious;
the Vaiśya shall be enriched with wealth; and the Śūdra shall attain a good rebirth.
He shall encounter no inauspiciousness whatsoever and shall obtain a long life.
The lord of the earth who hears this meritorious Harivaṃśa shall obtain long life, health, sovereignty, and incomparable prosperity;
one without a son shall obtain a son, and even one without wealth shall attain riches.
One attains the pacification of all misfortunes and a continuous stream of auspiciousness.
A human being shall obtain supreme devotion to Vāsudeva, incomparable enjoyments on earth, unimpeded majesty, and fame.

One who hears this *Harivaṃśa* shall become a sovereign of a realm; until the moon and stars [endure], he shall obtain all remaining prosperity on earth. He who constantly hears this from a preeminent twice-born devotee of Viṣṇu [shall likewise attain these fruits].
May he always be victorious in his conquests of the quarters, endowed with a fourfold army.
In the Vedas, the Rāmāyaṇa, the Harivaṃśa, and the Mahābhārata— indeed,
in the beginning, the middle, and likewise at the end, Hari is sung everywhere.
Therefore, Hari—the bearer of the conch, discus, and mace; the primordial creator, the sustainer of the earth, and the Lord of the universe—should always be meditated upon together with Śrī.
Those men who shall proclaim this meritorious and ancient history of his lineage shall suffer no defeat.
O Indra among kings, recite repeatedly the *Harivaṃśa*, which possesses great supernatural power.
"May your mind be steady; may Janārdana be gracious.
Sūta said:
Thus spoke King Pārikṣita to the words uttered by Vaiśampāyana.
O best of the twice-born, having become pure through hearing this Harivaṃśa, [one attains liberation].
Thus, O Śaunaka, both in brief and likewise in detail—
in brief as well as in detail— all those lineages have been declared there by all those whose wealth is austerity. What more shall I tell you?
Then the sages, headed by Śaunaka, became joyful and satisfied;
bowing with devotion, those lords of sages paid homage to the Lord of Gods,
and they prostrated before Hari, Viṣṇu, Mādhava, the Primordial God.
To him whose pure intellect was perfected through the Vedas and Shastras,
who wore a garment of skin, who was praised by the lords of gods and sages, the supreme poet,
dark-complexioned and possessing a mass of matted locks tawny as gold—
I bow my head to Vyāsa, the tilaka of the twice-born.
I bow to the sage Vyāsa, who resembles a gentle rain-cloud, who is free from all taint,
the abode of the Vedas, and the dwelling place of Sarasvatī.
I pay homage to the goddess Sarasvatī, the mother of the three worlds,
by whose grace my tongue does not fail to move smoothly.
Śaunaka said:
O Lomaharṣaṇa, who are recorded as the sons of Janamejaya?
Tell me the story of the remainder of the Harivaṃśa, which destroys all sins. Upon whom is the lineage of the high-souled Pāṇḍavas established?
"I wish to hear this; my curiosity is great.
As you tell it all, I shall understand it clearly from you.
Sūta said:
To Pārikṣita, by Kāśyā, two sons were born:
King Candrāpīḍa and Sūryāpīḍa, who was a knower of liberation.
Candrāpīḍa had a hundred sons who were preeminent archers; they were renowned on earth as the Kṣatriya clan known as the Janamejayas.
Among them, the eldest was the king Satyakarṇa, mighty-armed, a performer of sacrifices with abundant sacrificial fees, who ruled in the city named Vāraṇasāhvaya.
The heir of Satyakarṇa was the powerful Śvetakarṇa;
being childless, that righteous-souled man entered the forest of asceticism.
From him, while he was dwelling in the forest,
Mālinī— the daughter of Sucāru and sister of Māli— who possessed beautiful eyebrows, conceived a child.
But Śvetakarṇa, the lord of subjects, followed that infallible great departure even before the birth of his son.
Seeing that he had departed, Mālinī followed after him;
on the way, that woman of beautiful brows gave birth in the forest to a lotus-eyed son.
And having seen him there, she followed the king right then and there,
like the highly fortunate Draupadī followed her husbands in former times, being devoted to her husband.
That delicate prince wept in the mountain bower;
out of compassion for that high-souled one, clouds appeared.
And the two sons of Śraviṣṭhā, those two brahmins who were descendants of Paiṭhīnasi, seeing him, were moved by compassion; they took him and washed him in water.
When his two flanks were rubbed by Khela, blood flowed from them; both those flanks became dark like goats and remained perfectly even.

As they approached his side and drank from his breasts, they likewise ascended him; thus he became Ajapārśva (Goat-Sided). When they had indeed ascended the sides of that one who was dark as a goat, they became known as Ajaśyāma (Dark-as-a-Goat).
And because that boy remained right there by the side of the goat,
they therefore gave him the name Ajapārśva.
He, however, was reared by both [parents] in the Vemaka workshop.
Vemaka’s wife married him for the sake of obtaining a son;
and they both married that wife of Sevaka for his sake.
That son was born of Vemaka’s wife, and those two were pure Brahmins.
Their sons and grandsons lived simultaneously with equal lifespans;
this is that Paurava lineage established among the Pāṇḍavas.
And on this subject, this verse was sung long ago by the wise Yayāti, the son of Nahuṣa, when he was pleased at the transfer of his old age.
The earth might even become devoid of the moon, the sun, and the planets— of this there is no doubt—
but the earth shall never be without the lineage of Puru.
Then, when they had all sat down together with the members of the assembly, Śaunaka said:
"Śaunaka spoke:
This *Harivaṃśa* has been told to you, along with all its sections (*parvan*) in their entirety."
Just as they were previously stated, so too [were they] by the wise disciple of Vyāsa.
That which is being told, like nectar and endowed with ancient history,
delights us like ambrosia and destroys all sins.

"O wise one, this narrative, being so pleasant to hear, truly gladdens our minds. But after hearing this unsurpassed account, O Sauti, what did King Janamejaya do next, following the conclusion of the snake sacrifice?"
"O observer of noble vows, tell me what Pārikṣita undertook.
Sūta said:
"But King Janamejaya, having heard that unsurpassed narrative..."
I shall relate that which he undertook immediately after the snake-sacrifice.
When that sacrificial session was completed, King Pārikṣita then began to prepare the materials for performing a horse sacrifice.
Having summoned the officiating priests, the family priest, and the teachers, he spoke this:
"I shall perform the horse sacrifice; let the horse be released."
Then, having understood his intention, the high-souled Kṛṣṇa Dvaipāyana, who knows all that is high and low, suddenly arrived to see the son of Parikṣit, whose spirit was undaunted.
But King Pārikṣita, seeing that the sage had arrived,
offered him water for his hands and feet and a seat, and honored him according to the scriptures.
And those two sat down on either side of him, O Śaunaka;
then, once they had sat down together with the members of the assembly, O Śaunaka, they engaged in various and wonderful conversations concerning the Vedic collections.
Then, at the conclusion of the conversation, the king urged that sage,
the grandfather of the Pāṇḍavas and his own great-grandfather.
The narrative of the Mahābhārata, with its many meanings and great extent,
passed for me like a mere moment because it was so pleasant to hear.
O Brahmin, this discourse on the expansion of the Vibhūtis, which brings glory to all,
has been set forth by you like milk poured into a conch shell.
Just as there can be no satisfaction even with nectar or with the pleasures of heaven,
so too do I find no satiety in hearing this narrative of the Bhārata.
Having obtained the permission of the Omniscient One, I ask you, O Blessed One:
in my view, the Rājasūya sacrifice was the cause of the destruction of the Kurus.
Just as the destruction of the unbearable Kshatriyas was a calamity,
so too do I consider this Rajasuya sacrifice to have been prepared for the purpose of war.
For it is heard that the Rājasūya sacrifice was previously performed with Soma;
at its conclusion, there occurred a very great battle known as the Tārakāmaya.
At the conclusion of that great sacrifice, Varuṇa also brought about a battle between the gods and the asuras, which brought about the destruction of all beings.
The royal sage Hariścandra performed this sacrifice;
even there, a battle occurred between Āḍīvaka and Bakasura, which brought about the destruction of the Kṣatriyas.
Immediately after that, the noble Pāṇḍava also undertook the Mahābhārata-saṃhāra, which was as difficult to cross as a sacrificial fire.
For the root of that war which brought about the destruction of the world was indeed the great Rājasūya sacrifice; why was it not prevented?
For in the Rājasūya sacrifice, which is indestructible and possesses components difficult to assail,
if a sacrificial component is wrongly performed, the destruction of the subjects is certain.
And you, moreover, are the grandfather of all our ancestors;
you are the knower of the past and the future, our protector, and our original founder.
How, O Blessed One, have those wise ones, who were our guides, fallen from the right path?
For these men, having lost their protectors and possessing poor leadership, commit transgressions.
Vyāsa said:
"O child, your grandfathers have now been overtaken by time;
they did not ask me about the future, nor do I speak unless I am asked."
And I see that the announcement of what is to come is powerless;
for I shall not be able to avoid that destiny which is determined by time.
But since you have asked me this, O guest, I shall tell you what is destined to happen;
nevertheless, powerful Time will prevail even after you have heard it, and you will not act upon it.
Neither through agitation nor through exertion will you indeed stand upon human prowess;
for the lines inscribed by Time are as impossible to overstep as the shore of the ocean.
The horse sacrifice is renowned as the most excellent rite for Kṣatriyas;
with that intention, Vāsava will attack your sacrifice.
If that [misfortune], O King, can somehow be averted by human effort against destiny, then do not perform that sacrifice.
It is not Śakra’s fault, nor that of your assembly of preceptors, nor yours as the sacrificer; here, Time is the supreme lord.
This establishment of his is indeed subject to the power of Time;
understand that the three worlds, with all things moving and unmoving, are led by it.
Just as the king who performs the sacrifice shall go to heaven at the end of the age,
so too shall the twice-born who sell the fruits of sacrifices [attain that same state].
Janamejaya said:
"O Blessed One, what will be the cause for the cessation of the horse sacrifice? Having heard it, I shall avoid it, if it is possible."
Vyāsa said:
"O Lord, the cause there will be the wrath of Brahmā;
strive to avert it—may prosperity be yours."
O scorcher of foes, this horse sacrifice (vājimedha) has been performed by you alone;
as long as the earth shall endure, other kṣatriyas will not perform it.
Janamejaya said: "If it is true that I was the cause for the cessation of the horse sacrifice through the fiery power of the brahmins' curse, then a sharp fear arises within me."
For how can a virtuous person like me, joined with infamy,
venture to go to the higher worlds, like a bird with a snare in its talons?
For just as this destruction of the sacrifice was foreseen here in the future,
if there is indeed a renewal of the sacrifice, then comfort me.
Vyāsa said:
"The sacrifice that was taken from the gods shall now reside among the Brāhmaṇas;
this sacrifice has been ordained here by both the gods and the Brāhmaṇas."
Energy brought forth by energy remains established within energy itself.
A certain twice-born man of the Kaśyapa lineage, Audbhida by name, will become a commander of armies;
he shall restore the Aśvamedha sacrifice once again in the Kali age.
In that age, O Indra among kings, one born of his lineage will also perform the Rājasūya sacrifice,
just as Death seizes the White Planet.
According to the strength of human agents, the fruit shall be bestowed;
the gate to the end of the eon, though closed by the sages, shall remain open for them to traverse.
From that time forward, the life-forces of men will abandon their ancient forms;
even among those possessing a livelihood, the traditional way of life will cease to exist in the world.
Then, the Dharma— subtle, of great consequence, difficult to traverse, rooted in generosity, and weakened by the four stages of life— will begin to waver.
For at that time, O Janamejaya, men will attain perfection through slight austerity; blessed indeed, they will practice dharma at the end of the age.
Janamejaya said: Whether that time is near or far away, since we do not know it,
I long for the end of the age following the destruction of the Dvāpara Yuga.
Indeed, through this thirst for the Dharma, we have reached that very time;
and by means of little effort, we have attained our own true Dharma and happiness.
The end of the age, which causes terror among living beings, has arrived.
Therefore, O knower of dharma, since the terrifying end of the age has arrived and dharma has perished, you ought to describe it by means of its signs.
Sūta said:
Having been thus questioned, he reflected upon the destiny of the future in its true essence;
indeed, reflecting upon the course of the future through yoga alone, he spoke.
Then the Blessed One spoke of the portents that appear at the end of the eon.
Vyāsa said: At the end of the age, kings will arise who do not protect their subjects but seize their share of the tribute, being solely intent on protecting themselves.
At the end of the age, there will be kings who are not Kṣatriyas, Brahmins who live like Śūdras, and Śūdras who adopt the conduct of Brahmins.
At the end of the Yuga, O Janamejaya, Śūdras will practice the Dharma;
and at the end of the Yuga, O bull of the Bharatas, those who live by the sword and those learned in the Vedas will eat sacrificial offerings from the same row, O Janamejaya.

At the end of the age, O Janamejaya, men will be skilled in crafts but devoted to falsehood, fond of wine and meat, and dull-witted; they will destroy the supreme Dharma and will have their wives as their only friends.
At the end of the age, clouds will hold little water, the earth will yield scant crops,
thieves will abide by the conduct of kings,
and servants will have hands that do not receive their wages.
In the Kali age, wealth will be praised while the conduct of the virtuous is held in disrepute; women too will practice agriculture,
and at the end of the age, there will be no reproach for one who has fallen.
In the Kali age, ascetics will be perpetually restless;
mortals will have lost their sense of discernment, with disheveled hair and no topknots;
and at that time, men will reach maturity before they are even sixteen years old.
At the end of the age, the countryside will have its thorns in lawsuits, crossroads will have their thorns in jackals, and women will have their thorns in their hair.
"Alms-food" is declared to be food; "the stake" is said to be trade.
"The crossroads" refers to a Brāhmaṇa, O King, and "Śiva" is cited as the Veda. "Hair" is known as the vulva; of this there is no doubt.
At the end of the age, all will claim to be exponents of the Veda, all will be followers of the Vājasaneya school, and even Śūdras will address others as "Bho."
At the end of the age, the twice-born will become sellers of asceticism, sacrifice, and the Vedas, and even the seasons will become inverted.
With white teeth and unblemished eyes, shaven-headed and clad in saffron robes, Śūdras will practice the Dharma, subsisting on the teachings of the Śākya Buddha.
One should know that when the age has reached its end, there will be an abundance of wild beasts, a total depletion of cattle, and the cessation of delicious foods.
At the end of the age, those of the lowest caste will dwell among the middle class, and those of the middle class will become outcasts;
all people will follow the downward slope as the yuga comes to its close.
Likewise, two-year-old calves will be used for breaking in, and those who plow will work in mere puddles;
furthermore, the rain-god Parjanya will send down rain in a variegated manner when the age has declined.
All will be born into families of thieves and will steal from one another; having acquired even a little, they will become wealthy, yet upon losing whatever they have, they will fall into misfortune.
When the age has passed away, those men will not practice the Dharma.
In the Kali age, the earth will abound in saline soil, the roads will lie between cities, and all people will indeed become mere merchants.
At that time, sons who are driven by greed, falsehood, and hostility will seek to seize the ancestral offerings, even as they are being presented.
Sons who speak falsehoods out of greed always seek to seize the wealth given by their fathers;
likewise, when delicacy, beauty, and even jewels have fallen into decay, they strive to take them for themselves.
At the end of the age, women will be adorned only by their hair.
For a householder who is devoid of a dwelling and is afraid,
when the end of the age has arrived, there will be no pleasure equal to that of a wife.
Abounding in the unvirtuous and the ignoble, covered in false appearances, with few men and many women— these are the characteristics of the end of the age.
The world will abound with beggars who will give to one another;
likewise, they will accept gifts from those of other castes without discrimination.
And the people, oppressed by punishment from kings, thieves, and others, will fall into ruin.
When the Yuga has passed, the ripening of crops will be fruitless, the young will possess the character of the old, and people will find no happiness in their endeavors.
During the rains, winds will blow like base men raining down gravel; and at the end of the Yuga, the next world will become uncertain.

Those of evil conduct who were intent on reviling the Veda considered themselves superior; wrath indeed overcame the twice-born. And the Kṣatriyas, adopting the conduct of Vaiśyas, lived off wealth and grain.
At the onset of the Yuga, the twice-born will first come into being.
In this degenerate age, when the Yuga has declined, agreements and oaths will no longer be observed, debts will go unpaid, and there will be a falling away from discipline.
At the end of the age, the joy of men will be fruitless while their anger will bear fruit;
even goats will be slaughtered for the sake of their milk.

Wisdom not ordained by the scriptures will become exactly like this; for men who do not know the scriptures, such will naturally occur. Those who pride themselves on being learned will treat such policy as invalid.
At the end of the age, there will be those who do not proclaim what has been taught in the scriptures.
Without serving the elders, no one knows everything;
indeed, when the end of the age has arrived, there is no one who is not called a fool.
When the end of the Yuga has arrived, the twice-born will engage in improper occupations and cease to perform their duties, while kings will consist mostly of thieves.
At the end of the Yuga, O Janamejaya, those who are like sacrificial pits, bull-like, deceitful, drunkards, and yet claim to be expounders of the Veda, will perform the horse sacrifice.
When the end of the age has arrived, Brahmins afflicted by thirst for wealth will officiate at sacrifices for those unworthy of sacrificing, as well as consume what is forbidden to eat.
They will pursue their goals for the sake of enjoyment, and no one at all will study;
likewise, women will wear single conch-shell ornaments and be clothed in garments made of gavedhuka grass.
The constellations will be diminished, the directions will be inverted,
and there will be the glow of twilight and the burning of the quarters in the future age.
Sons will employ their fathers in menial tasks, and daughters-in-law will employ their mothers-in-law;
likewise, disciples will threaten their teachers with word-arrows,
and men, becoming heedless, will direct them into the very faces of their elders.
At that time, men will engage in sexual intercourse with women of improper species.
Men who maintain the sacred fire will eat without first offering the ritual portions;
and men will eat for themselves without having given alms or the sacrificial offering.
Women will go elsewhere, deceiving their sleeping husbands;
and men, while their wives are fast asleep, will go to the wives of others.
When the age has declined, no person will be free from disease or pain; everyone will be envious, and no one will repay what they have received.
Janamejaya said:
When the world has thus been thrown into confusion, by whom will men be protected?
What will be their conduct, what will be their food, and what will be their pastimes?
What will be their duties, what will they strive for, what will be their stature, and what will be their lifespan? And having reached what limit will they attain the Kṛta Yuga?
Vyāsa said:
Thereafter, when dharma has declined, the people will be devoid of virtue;
having encountered the ruin of their character, they will suffer a decrease in lifespan.
From the loss of vitality comes the exhaustion of strength; from the exhaustion of strength comes discoloration of the complexion;
from discoloration comes the affliction of disease; and from the affliction of disease comes despondency.
Through disenchantment comes self-awakening; through awakening, the nature of the Dharma.
Having thus reached the highest pinnacle, they shall attain the Kṛta Yuga.
By way of brief description, some are of virtuous character, some have attained a state of neutrality,
while others are of a reflective nature, curious about the discourse on causes.

Those who consider themselves wise have determined that perception and inference are the means of valid cognition; yet they will ask, "What will a means of valid cognition accomplish? and deny its validity. Others, however, will treat even what is declared in the Vedas as invalid.
At that time, there will be other women whose faces resemble the female organ;
and there will be certain foolish men, dull-witted yet imagining themselves to be wise, who are devoted to nihilism and destroyers of the Dharma.
At that time, they will be people who rely solely on faith for the present moment, devoid of knowledge of the scriptures,
hypocritical, and devoted to the habit of mere debate.
Then, when the Dharma has declined, people who honor their elders will practice only virtuous deeds, endowed with generosity and truthfulness.
For then the world will become a consumer of all things, unrestrained, devoid of virtue, and shameless; that is the characteristic of the age of degeneration (kaṣāya).
When people of lower castes seek to obtain the eternal livelihood of the Brahmins for the sake of their own subsistence, that is a sign of the degenerate age (kaṣāya).
In this time of affliction by the defilements, when knowledge and wisdom are destroyed,
those who remain unadorned will attain perfection in a short time.
A great war, a great clamor, a great rain, and a great terror will occur when the age has declined; that is the characteristic of the degenerate era (kaṣāya).
Rākṣasas in the form of brahmins and kings who pierce the ears [of others] will roam the earth,
and the duties of the social classes will have perished.
They will enjoy the earth when the end of the age has arrived.
Devoid of Vedic study and the utterance of *vaṣaṭ*, these conceited sages are flesh-eaters in the guise of Brahmins, devouring all things while their vows are in vain.
Fools, intent on their own interests, greedy, base, with base retinues,
and engaged in worldly transactions, they have fallen away from the eternal dharma.
They were stealers of others' treasures, violators of others' wives,
slaves to their desires, evil-minded, deceitful, and fond of reckless violence.
While those of similar character prevail everywhere,
there will arise sages of manifold forms who do not exist [in truth].
Those eminent persons who appeared in the Kṛtayuga, taking refuge in the Pradhāna,
all of them humans shall worship through the means of storytelling.
There will be thieves of grain as well as stealers of clothing; there will be those who seize food and drink, and indeed those who carry off household goods.
Thieves will be the stealers of thieves, and the slayer shall belong to the stealer;
and when the destruction of thieves has been accomplished, there will be security.
In a world devoid of essence, agitated, inactive, and standing empty,
men, oppressed by the burden of taxes, will take refuge in the forest.

When the end of the age has arrived, sons will command their fathers in every way regarding their duties; likewise, daughters-in-law will treat their mothers-in-law so. And from all sides, disciples will threaten their teachers with arrows of speech.
When the sacrificial rites have ceased, the *rakṣasas*, beasts of prey,
and crores of mice and serpents will assail human beings.
O best of men, at the end of the age, there will be security, abundance, health, and harmony with one's kinsmen through the teaching.
Acting as their own protectors and their own thieves, sustained by the accumulated burdens of the age,
they will prevail in various circles, each separately in their respective regions.
Deprived of their own countries and rendered destitute along with their kinsmen,
all men at that time will become mere waiters for their end.
Then, taking their children upon their shoulders, men afflicted by the fear of hunger will flee in terror and take refuge with Kauśikī.
Afflicted by famine and disease,
men will wander through Aṅga, Vaṅga, Kaliṅga, Kāśmīra, and Mekala; they will take refuge in the mountain valleys and forest retreats of the Ṛṣikas.
The entire side of the Himalayas, the shore of the salt ocean,
and the wildernesses will be inhabited by men together with hosts of barbarians.
The earth will be neither empty nor non-empty;
there will arise rulers who are both protectors and non-protectors.
Humans will subsist on deer, fish, birds, beasts of prey, and all kinds of insects;
indeed, they will live upon deer, fish, birds, insects, beasts of prey, and monkeys, as well as honey, vegetables, fruits, and roots.
Having fashioned for themselves rags, various leaves, bark garments, and skins, they will dwell just like the sages.
They will strive with wooden stakes to mark the shapes of seeds in low-lying places; they will also diligently tend to goats, sheep, donkeys, and camels.
Those who dwell on the banks will block the currents of the rivers for the sake of water,
while they trade with one another through the commerce of cooked food.
Those whose body hairs grow irregularly, who are covered with internal impurities,
who have many offspring yet lack progeny, who are cruel, and who are devoid of auspicious marks [are so described].
Thus will humans be at that time, driven by their own end;
then the people will follow a dharma that is inferior, even more inferior.
And there the maximum lifespan of mortals will be thirty years;
they will be weak, exhausted by sensual objects, and overwhelmed by passion.
Then, for them, there will be a decay of the sense faculties due to diseases;
and because of the obstruction caused by the exhaustion of their lifespan, violence will cease.
When the world has been thus overwhelmed and oppressed during this time of destruction,
those who possess knowledge will find their efforts rendered fruitless by that oppression;
yet they will become desirous of hearing the truth and take delight in the sight of the virtuous.
And they will also resort to truth out of apprehension regarding their legal dealings.
And due to the failure to obtain their desires, those who possess the nature of Dharma will come into being; and, afflicted by the destruction of their own side, they will practice restraint.
In this way, those men who are intent on service, generosity, truthfulness, and the protection of living beings shall attain the Dharma that proceeds upon four feet.
For those who take pride in their qualities regarding the Dharma,
once they have discerned what is truly sweet, it will be the Dharma alone that will taste sweet.
Just as decline arrives in due order, so too does prosperity come in its proper sequence.
O Lord of the Earth, when the decline of the Kali age occurs,
then, once Dharma has been fully embraced, the Kṛta age shall be attained once again.
In the Kṛta age, conduct is virtuous; in the degenerate age (kaṣāya), decline is said to occur.
Yet time is truly one and the same, like the moon when its luster has faded.
For Soma is obscured by darkness in the Kali age,
and likewise he is deprived of his fullness of ascetic merit in the Kali age.
The wise know that the meaning of the Veda consists of the Dharma which has explanatory passages (*arthavāda*) as its core;
yet it is maintained like an unrefined inheritance that remains unexamined and unknown.
Sacrifice, charity, austerity, and celibacy are well-honored;
the accomplishment of action arises from qualities, and qualities arise from action performed with truthfulness.
But a blessing, conforming to place and time, is uttered by the seers for each person according to the requirements of each age at the appropriate moment.
In this [work], there is the exposition of dharma, artha, and kāma, as well as of the Vedas;
likewise, there are auspicious and meritorious blessings, and [the determination of] lifespan in each successive age.
O Great King, at that time there will be men of great longevity,
just as the revolutions of the ages have proceeded for a long time by the very nature of destiny.
The world of living beings does not remain still for even a moment, revolving through decline and rise.
Sūta said:
As the sage was thus consoling King Janamejaya with words concerning the past and the future, the assembly heard his speech.
Like the taste of nectar and like the radiance of the moon,
that essence consisting of speech satisfied the ear of the great seer.
That entire narrative, which was connected with virtue, wealth, and pleasure, compassionate, heroic, and exhilarating, and full of delight, was heard by the assembly.
Some shed tears upon hearing it, while others reflected thus on that history revealed by the seer Pārāśarya.
O bull among the twice-born, having spoken concerning the past and the future,
and having received permission from the members of the assembly and performed a circumambulation,
the blessed rishi departed, saying, "We shall see you again."
Then all the disciplined ones, whose wealth is asceticism, followed that best of sages as he departed— the foremost among those who speak in this world.
When the Blessed Vyāsa had departed, the Brahmins along with the great seers,
the officiating priests, and the kings each returned the way they had come.
Having inflicted that terrible vengeance upon the serpents,
the king cast off his rage and departed, like a snake that has discharged its venom.
Having saved Takṣaka, whose head was ablaze with the sacrificial fire,
the great sage Āstīka returned to his hermitage.
The king also entered Hastināpura surrounded by the people,
and being delighted, he then ruled over his joyful subjects.
Then, after some time had passed, King Janamejaya was duly initiated for a horse sacrifice, in which abundant sacrificial fees were distributed.
Then, having approached the horse that had been consecrated there, his queen Vapuṣṭamā, the daughter of Kaśya,
entered it according to the prescribed ritual.
Then Vāsava desired her, whose every limb was faultless;
having entered the horse that had been prepared for sacrifice, he united with her.
When that transformation had been produced and he had understood it in its true nature, he said to the Adhvaryu priest: "This horse of yours has not been properly prepared; it will perish."
The Adhvaryu priest, endowed with knowledge, related that deed of Indra to the royal sage; he then cursed Purandara.
Janamejaya said:
"If there is for me the fruit of sacrifice or the merit of austerity from protecting my subjects, then by all that fruit I say: let this be heard!"
"From this day forward, O Śaunaka, the Kṣatriyas shall no longer perform the horse sacrifice for the sake of the Lord of the Gods, who has not conquered his senses and is unstable."
And King Janamejaya, filled with rage, said to the officiating priests:
"This weakness is yours, that this sacrifice has been thus insulted."
"You must not dwell in my realm; perish, perish along with your kinsmen!"—having been addressed thus, the brahmins, filled with indignation, abandoned that king.
Out of indignation, King Janamejaya, who was supremely knowledgeable in dharma, then commanded the women gathered in the wife’s chamber:
"Expel this unchaste Vapuṣṭamā from my house!"
By her, my foot was placed upon my head, covered with the dust of ashes.
"My heroism has been shattered by her, my fame and honor defiled;
I do not wish even to look upon her, who is like a withered garland."
That man who, in this world, attends upon a beloved wife who has been ravished by another, does not eat with relish nor does he sleep peacefully in seclusion.

Just as dogs do not consume sacrificial offerings that have been licked by them, so too did Viśvāvasu, the king of the Gandharvas, speak these words to King Pārikṣita, who was speaking loudly and in anger: "O King, those who know the dharma do not eat food that has been touched by a dog, nor do they consume the sacrificial offering (havis) that has been licked by a dog. In the same way, O best of kings, you must not consume this food while you remain in such a state."
Vāsava cannot endure you, who have performed three hundred sacrifices;
nor does this wife of yours incur any fault, for she was created as the most beautiful of forms.
The goddess named Rambhā, the daughter of the King of Kāśī, is considered to be this very woman;
O King, let this best of women, who is like a jewel, be experienced by you.
Having found a flaw in your sacrifice, an obstacle was created for you by Indra;
for you are a performer of sacrifices, O best of the Kurus, equal to Vāsava in prosperity.
O King, Śakra fears being surpassed by the fruits of your sacrifices;
therefore, O Lord, the sacrifice was turned back by Indra for you.
"This is an illusion employed here by Vāsava, who desires to create an obstacle for the sacrifice; having found an opening, he caused the horse to be slaughtered.
As for that most beautiful woman Rambhā, whom you think was enjoyed by Indra—[it was an illusion]."
Then those preceptors, who had performed three hundred sacrifices,

were cursed; and you, O Indra-like one, along with the brahmins who had performed three hundred sacrifices, were deprived here of the fruit [of your merit] because of you, who are so difficult to overcome.
For Vāsava always fears you, as he does even the Brāhmaṇas;
yet by means of his illusory power (māyā), Śakra alone has indeed overcome both.
This very Purandara, possessed of great majesty and desirous of victory,
how could he transgress against the wife of his grandson— a path never trodden by others?
For just as there is supreme wisdom, supreme righteousness, and supreme self-restraint,
and just as there is supreme sovereignty and fame in the one who has Hari as his vehicle,
so too, O invincible one, do these belong to you, the performer of three hundred sacrifices.
Do not go to Vasava, nor to your guru, nor to yourself, nor to your most beautiful body;
for time is altogether impossible to overcome.
Having entered the horse by means of his sovereign power and being impelled by the Lord of the Gods,
one who desires happiness must act in accordance with the will of the God.
For this jewel among women is difficult to overcome and contrary, like the current of a river against its flow; enjoy her, who is free from sin, with your fever of anxiety dispelled.
Indeed, even women who are sinless might curse when being abandoned;
however, O King, women who are faultless—especially divine women—are never at fault.
The radiance of the sun, the crest of fire, the sacrificial altar, the officiating priest, and likewise the oblation—even when touched, they are not defiled; so too are women.
Women who possess virtuous conduct should always be accepted, cherished, honored, and saluted by the wise; they are to be revered just like women of noble birth.
Sūta said:
Thus exhorted by Viśvāvasu, he attained a state of grace toward Vapuṣṭamā;
though his mind was still falsely suspicious, he performed there that supreme peace which is cherished by the righteous.
Having completely turned back his weary mind and desiring for himself the glory of Janamejaya,
he— possessing a righteous intellect and a joyful heart— ruled over his realm while delighting that most beautiful woman, Vapuṣṭamā.
He does not cease from honoring Brahmins, nor does he turn away from the practice of sacrifice;
he does not fall away from protecting his realm, nor does he reproach Vapuṣṭamā.
"That which was ordained by fate is impossible to make otherwise, as the Sage of inconceivable asceticism declared of old;
and yet, that is not impossible to make otherwise.
Having reflected thus upon those words, the self-possessed king then became free from his resentment.
Thus the king, whose valor was undaunted, reflected upon that and became at peace.
By reciting this great poem of the high-souled seer, a man shall become most worthy of honor among men;
having attained an excellent and rare lifespan, he shall obtain the singular fruit of omniscience.
By reciting this account of Śatakratu’s liberation from defilement, a person is freed from all taints;
likewise, they enjoy various desires and, having fulfilled their desires, rejoices for a long time.
For just as fruit arises from a tree through the production of flowers, and from that fruit trees are born again,
so too these words produced by the great seer cause that very seer to flourish when they are set in motion.
One who is childless obtains sons of great luster; one who has fallen from his state regains his own position;
he does not suffer from disease nor long imprisonment, and endowed with virtues, he attains meritorious action.
Having approached the Sage and heard his auspicious words, a virtuous maiden obtains a husband;
moreover, she gives birth to sons endowed with excellent qualities and possessed of the prowess to crush the ranks of their enemies.
One who follows the kṣatriya way of life conquers the earth and obtains incomparable wealth and victory over enemies;
a vaiśya shall obtain abundant wealth; and one of the śūdra caste shall attain a happy rebirth through hearing [this].
Having studied this ancient life-story of the great-souled ones, one attains a resolute intellect;
casting off all sufferings and freed from attachment, he, with passion departed, may wander the earth.

Thus has this narrative been recounted to you; remembering it within the circles of the twice-born, and remembering again with the steadfastness that has arisen, may you wander the world in happiness.

Thus has this life-story of the great-souled ones, composed by the sages and consisting of deeds of wondrous power, been told both in brief and in detail. What more do you desire? What shall I tell you?
